Egyptian mission discovers rare rock-cut tombs dating to late New Kingdom in Nile Delta
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:58:37 CST
21:58:37 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- An Egyptian archaeological mission has uncovered a number of rock-cut tombs dating to the late New Kingdom (1550-1069 BC) at the Tell el-Yahudiya archaeological site in Qalyubia province, north of Cairo, the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said Saturday.
The tombs feature different architectural designs, shedding light on burial practices in the eastern Nile Delta, the ministry said in a statement.
The tombs fall into two main architectural types, the statement read.
The first consists of tombs with an entrance reached by a staircase leading to a hall containing burial niches, while the second features a rectangular shaft leading to two burial chambers, it said.
Such rock-cut tomb designs are rare in the Delta, where the region's clay-rich soil makes this type of burial uncommon, it added.
Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities, said the discovery provides valuable evidence for understanding burial practices and their development in the eastern Delta across different historical periods. ■

CAIRO, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The ongoing Chengdu Panda Week activities in Cairo have opened new opportunities for mutual visits, cultural exchange, and deeper tourism cooperation between China and Egypt, an Egyptian official has said.
"Egypt is stepping up efforts to tap the Chinese tourism market by participating in professional tourism exhibitions in China, organizing promotional activities, and maintaining direct contacts with Chinese tourism companies and travel agencies," said Mohamed Shoman, an adviser to the Minister of State for Media for Public Communication and Training.
China-Egypt tourism cooperation is expanding beyond tourist exchanges to areas including tourism services, infrastructure development, investment, and the management of resorts and hotels, Shoman added.
The four-day events, running Thursday through Sunday at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization (NMEC), feature a Chengdu promotion, showcasing the southwestern Chinese city renowned for its giant pandas, and an exhibition on the ancient Shu civilization, a Bronze Age culture from today's Sichuan Province.
More than 100 representatives from the Chinese Embassy in Egypt, Egypt's Ministry of Information, the NMEC, the Grand Egyptian Museum and Cairo University, among other institutions, took part in an event, themed "Dialogue of Solar Civilizations -- Chengdu Panda Week Activities."
At a Chengdu cultural tourism promotion titled "Chengdu: More Than Giant Pandas," Zhu Xiaozhong, minister-counselor of the Chinese Embassy in Egypt, said, "The embassy is ready to continue serving as a bridge between the two countries and promote people-to-people exchanges, tourism and mutual understanding." ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: Transport upgrades bringing China's mountain riches to the world
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:58:26 CST
21:58:26 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 18, 2026 shows Taozibao tea mountain, one of the main tea production areas in Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Lu Jinbo)
WUHAN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- When Yin E enrolled in college in Enshi in 2010, she was among the first cohort of students in the school's newly established department of tourism.
"It used to be very hard for people to come in or out of Enshi," she said. "We had world-class scenery, but poor roads cut it off."
Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture in central China's Hubei Province sits deep in the Wuling Mountains. The region averages about 1,000 meters in elevation, with peaks rising above 3,000 meters and steep cliffs at nearly every turn.
"Back then, it took three days by car just to reach Wuhan, the provincial capital," Yin said. The two cities are about 460 kilometers apart.
That situation began to change around 2010, when Enshi inaugurated its first railway and expressway, both of which were considered among the most technically challenging projects in China or the world.
"That's when the tourists really started coming," said Fan Houtao, general manager of a tourism company in Hubei.
Enshi Grand Canyon, one of the region's best-known attractions, opened to visitors in 2008 and received more than 100,000 visitors that year. By 2025, annual visitor numbers had climbed to 2 million, with more than 80 percent coming from outside the province.
The canyon has been designated a national 5A-rated tourist attraction, the highest in China, and included in the UNESCO Global Geoparks network.
"A growing share of our visitors now come from Southeast Asia, the Republic of Korea and Mongolia," Fan said. In 2025, the prefecture launched regular foreign-language training for tour guides and scenic-area staff to meet rising demand.
The region's well-preserved traditions, architecture and cuisine of the Tujia and Miao ethnic groups have become part of the draw as word has spread.
Tea tells a similar story. "Growing tea is one of the basic ways farmers here have always made a living," said Liu Qiangsheng of the Enshi Tea Industry Association. The high-altitude environment produces quality tea, but getting it out of the mountains used to be costly and difficult.
Improved transport has enabled tea producers in Enshi to scale up, with total industry output value tripling over the past decade to 30 billion yuan (about 4.44 billion U.S. dollars).
Tea is now Enshi's leading agricultural product, reaching every corner of China and more than 20 countries and regions abroad, including Morocco, Australia and Russia.
Enshi now has four railway lines and nine expressways in operation. The journey to Wuhan can now be completed in about four hours.
"Our tea now reaches markets by both sea and rail. Some is shipped from Ningbo in Zhejiang Province, while some travels to Europe on the China Railway Express," Liu said. "Some of our best-known varieties have even been served at state diplomatic events."
Other goods once locked away in the mountains, including selenium-rich vegetables, potatoes, and herbal medicines, are also finding their way to markets across China and overseas.
For Enshi, once one of the poorest areas in China, better transportation has opened up new markets and helped local people increase their incomes.
"Enshi underwent tremendous changes during the fight against poverty," said Xia Xifan, governor of the prefecture. "Every village with 20 or more households was connected by road with investment coming from both the central and local governments."
Enshi is a small piece of a much bigger story: China's sustained and massive push to expand its infrastructure.
China's high-speed rail network has surpassed 50,000 kilometers, accounting for over 70 percent of the world's total and more than the rest of the world combined. Its expressway network, at nearly 200,000 kilometers, is likewise the largest on earth -- a web of roads and rail stitching together the country's wealthier regions with its more remote ones.
Before entering college, Yin had never left Enshi. Her home village lies deep in the mountains, where her parents grew potatoes and corn. They used to carry their produce for two hours to reach the township market, and Yin herself also spent two hours walking to school.
"Life in Enshi has changed so much," she said. "I've been able to travel around the country, and now I've even been selected to showcase Enshi's culture and tourism to people around the world."
"Improving transportation is a project that speaks directly to people's hearts," Xia said. "Everything the government does comes back to one goal -- giving people a better life, and achieving common prosperity."
As China maps out its transport development for 2026-2030, the country aims to raise the completion rate of its integrated transport network from 91 percent to 95 percent by 2030. It also plans to basically complete a more connected high-speed rail network featuring eight vertical and eight horizontal main routes and a national expressway system.
The country will build or upgrade 500,000 kilometers of rural roads and strengthen railway and regional airport infrastructure in rural and less-developed areas.
In Enshi, the transformation is continuing.
Enshi Airport was upgraded to an international airport in 2025. Passenger traffic has exceeded expectations, prompting plans to relocate and rebuild the airport. Construction of the first high-speed railway linking Enshi began in late 2024.
From 2026 to 2030, Enshi plans to invest 268.8 billion yuan in transport infrastructure.
"These efforts will help Enshi achieve its goal of basically realizing modernization by 2035," Xia said. ■

Nepal continues power exports despite flood damage to hydropower projects
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:58:26 CST
21:58:26 KST

KATHMANDU, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Nepal earned more than 5.09 billion Nepali rupees (33.11 million U.S. dollars) from electricity exports to India and Bangladesh from mid-August to mid-September, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA).
The country exported a total of 565.6 million units of electricity during the month through bilateral agreements and India's electricity exchange market despite the Aug. 26 flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers damaging a dozen hydropower projects, the state-owned power utility said on Saturday.
However, electricity exports to Bangladesh have currently been suspended following damage to structures at the Chilime and Trishuli hydropower plants caused by the flood.
"Despite the floods affecting exports to Bangladesh and partially affecting exports to India, Nepal's export earnings in the month remained higher than in the same month last year," Achyut Babu Ghimire, a director at the NEA, told Xinhua.
The NEA said it has requested the Indian side to provide the necessary approval to resume electricity exports to Bangladesh from other hydropower projects.
In recent years, Nepal's electricity exports have grown rapidly as the country has been generating more power than domestic demand, particularly during the summer months.
According to the NEA, Nepal earned a total of 29.32 billion Nepali rupees (190.70 million dollars) from electricity exports to India and Bangladesh in fiscal year 2025-26, representing a 68 percent increase from the previous fiscal year. ■

Egypt welcomes more Chinese investment, broader trade cooperation: minister

21:58:16 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Egypt views China as an important and distinctive strategic partner and welcomes more Chinese companies to invest in the country, Egyptian Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh said recently.
Egypt also looks forward to expanding trade and economic cooperation with China and bringing more Egyptian products to the Chinese market, Saleh said.
He made the remarks during a reception hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Cairo on Thursday evening to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China.
Speaking on behalf of the Egyptian government, Saleh noted that this year also marks the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Egypt and China.
"Over the past 70 years, Egypt and China have consistently maintained a solid friendship, mutual trust, and mutual respect, working together to promote development and prosperity for their peoples," the Egyptian minister said.
Saleh said Chinese companies operating in Egypt have made significant progress in recent years, with their products exported to markets around the world.
He said Chinese companies have also played an important role in Egypt's major national projects over the years, creating jobs, facilitating technology transfer and promoting industrial localization.
Egypt attaches great importance to cooperation with China in high value-added sectors, including automobiles and auto components, energy storage batteries, solar panels, and seawater desalination, Saleh said, adding the country also welcomes more Chinese investment in household appliances, electronics, textiles, and petrochemicals.
He welcomed China's zero-tariff policy for 53 African countries that have diplomatic ties with China, saying Egypt is working to bring more of its products to the Chinese market, tap into the market's enormous potential, and expand and diversify its exports.
Saleh said the Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade is ready to work with the Chinese side to address difficulties facing Chinese companies investing in Egypt, further improve the investment environment to attract more Chinese companies, and encourage existing Chinese investors to expand their operations.
For his part, Chinese Ambassador to Egypt Liao Liqiang said that, over the seven decades since the establishment of diplomatic ties between China and Egypt, the two countries have been closely linked by their shared pursuit of independence and stability.
Looking ahead, he said, the endeavor to build a China-Egypt community with a shared future will bring the two countries even closer, and they will work together to make greater contributions to safeguarding world peace and promoting common development. ■

Feature: Harvest artistic experience unveiled for Mid-Autumn Festival in Malaysia bridges cultures
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
20:58:15 CST
21:58:15 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Long before the Mid-Autumn Festival became synonymous with mooncakes, lanterns and family reunions, the season was rooted in the autumn harvest, a time when farming communities gathered to celebrate a good harvest after months of hard work, while preparing for winter ahead.
Bringing this ancient heritage into the present, an immersive artistic experience has been unveiled at Kwai Chai Hong, a restored historical laneway in Kuala Lumpur's Chinatown, known for its captivating murals depicting the life of the capital city's long-standing Chinese community.
At the heart of the Kwai Chai Hong installation are paddy stalks harvested from Malaysian rice fields. While the exhibition celebrates Chinese cultural heritage, its core message reflects Malaysia's broader multicultural fabric.
"Every grain of rice begins as a seed, nurtured by fertile land, favorable weather and dedicated hands before making its way to the table. This enduring relationship between effort and abundance resonates deeply across Malaysia's diverse cultural landscape," the laneway's founders said in a statement.
This harmony is reflected in local folklore: while the Chinese proverb "lì lì jiē xīn kǔ" reminds us that "every grain of rice comes from hard work," the Malay phrase "kalau tak habis makan, nanti nasi menangis" (finish your rice or the rice will cry) uses empathy to discourage waste and respect for labor. Together, these cultural pillars foster a foundational sense of gratitude, resourcefulness and lifelong respect for labor from a young age, it said.
Kwai Chai Hong co-founder Zeen Chang said every harvest begins with hope and ends with gratitude. "From a tiny seed, every stage carries a story of care, dedication and hope. For us, Mid-Autumn is an opportunity to bring these values into the present and remind ourselves to appreciate not only the abundance we enjoy, but also the people, traditions and communities behind it," she said.
Meanwhile, the nearby Petaling Street hosted cultural performances, dazzling lantern displays and fireworks. Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Tiong King Sing, who attended the festivities, said the festival reflected Malaysia's multicultural identity and the importance of embracing diverse traditions.
"I am delighted to see people from different races and religions celebrating together today. We should appreciate our diverse cultures with open hearts and share them with one another," he said.
Beyond these areas, decorations marking the Mid-Autumn Festival have sprung up across Kuala Lumpur, with lanterns featuring dragons, rabbits and other traditional designs decorating shopping malls, popular tourist areas and even people's homes, while mooncakes, traditional pastries dedicated to the festival, are found for sale around every corner, with a huge variety available.
Halal mooncakes epitomize the degree to which the festival has become a part of the Malaysian culture as a whole, according to Kat W. Wong, executive director and chief strategist at the Center for Advanced Studies and Research.
"In Malaysia, the Mid-Autumn Festival is celebrated by the Chinese community with the tradition of family gathering, a sense of gratitude and prayers for future prosperity, with a little touch of modernity. Although many have done away with moon-gazing, the young and old continue to gather with family and friends as a symbol of togetherness and appreciation," she told Xinhua.
"Over the decades, the Mid-Autumn Festival in Malaysia has also evolved into a significant celebration beyond the Chinese community. Mooncakes and gatherings are now enjoyed with the participation of friends from Malay and other communities," she added. ■

Who is behind the stadiums hosting Ed Sheeran but rejecting Macklemore?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:57:57 UTC
21:57:57 KST

Earlier this week, the US rapper Macklemore was removed from the remaining dates of Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after several venues objected to his participation following his public statements of support for Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Macklemore has been an outspoken critic of Israeli genocide in Gaza, using his concerts and public appearances to express solidarity with Palestinians and calling for a “free Palestine” during performances.
Sheeran is still scheduled to perform at the stadiums that objected to Macklemore, drawing renewed scrutiny to the people and organisations behind some of the biggest sporting venues in the United States, and, in several cases, to their documented financial and political ties to Israel.
The venues reportedly objecting to the rapper include Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina, AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, and Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida.
The episode became particularly significant after New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft confirmed that he had intervened over Macklemore’s participation.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Kraft spoke directly with Sheeran and other NFL owners, including Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper, Atlanta Falcons owner Arthur Blank and Philadelphia Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie, who also opposed keeping Macklemore on the tour.
The intervention raises a broader question as Sheeran prepares to continue performing at the venues: who controls these stadiums, and what are their documented ties to Israel?
Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium
The most direct connection is Robert Kraft, whose Kraft Group owns and operates Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform next week.
Kraft, also has a longstanding relationship with Israel, having donated millions of dollars to Israeli causes.
In 2016, he donated $6 million towards the construction of the Kraft Family Sports Campus in Jerusalem. The facility was developed as a multi-purpose sports complex and named after Kraft and his family.
The Kraft Group says the family has donated millions of dollars to develop American Football Israel and highlights the Jerusalem sports campus among its Israel-related “philanthropy”.
Kraft also drew attention earlier this year after his name surfaced in connection with the Epstein files.
In 2019, after he was charged with soliciting prostitution, Kraft added a lawyer who had previously represented Jeffrey Epstein to his legal team. The charges against Kraft were dropped the following year.
Kraft’s intervention against Macklemore has also sparked a backlash, as the decision quickly escalated into a broader dispute, with artists and supporters accusing the billionaire of using his influence to silence a pro-Palestinian voice.
Macklemore responded by challenging Kraft directly.
After saying he had been removed from the tour for supporting Palestinians, he pledged $1 million of his tour earnings to organisations supporting Palestinians and invited Kraft to match the donation.
Kraft subsequently sought to reframe the dispute as one about antisemitism rather than opposition to Palestinian advocacy. He then said he would commit $2 million to “aid in the region”, though it’s unclear where the money would go.
Arthur Blank and Mercedes-Benz Stadium
Another stop on Sheeran's tour is Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta.
Mercedes-Benz Stadium is owned by the Georgia World Congress Center Authority, a state agency. The authority says the stadium is one of its assets and that it manages it.
The Atlanta Falcons, however, are owned by pro-Israel billionaire Arthur Blank, whose organisation is closely involved in the stadium and its operations.
Blank also has documented ties to Israel. In October 2023, the Arthur M Blank Family Foundation announced $750,000 in grants to Barzilai Medical Center, Soroka Medical Center and United Hatzalah in Israel.
The foundation had previously given at least $75,000 to the Jewish Agency for Israel’s North American Council, according to reports.
In an essay published by the Jewish National Fund, one of his sons describes being inspired by his father’s commitment to supporting Israel, saying "Zionism in my family has always been steadfast."
Blank was also among the NFL owners who opposed Macklemore remaining on Sheeran’s tour.
David Tepper and Bank of America Stadium
Sheeran is also scheduled to perform at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, which is managed by Tepper Sports & Entertainment, the organisation owned by Carolina Panthers billionaire David Tepper.
Tepper has a documented history of donations connected to Israel. In 2006, he gave $1 million to the United Jewish Communities of MetroWest New Jersey for its Israel Emergency Campaign.
In October 2023, the David and Nicole Tepper Foundation also directed millions of dollars of aid to Israel.
Tepper was among the owners who opposed Macklemore’s continued participation in the tour, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Jeffrey Lurie and Lincoln Financial Field
Sheeran is due to perform at Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field, the first venue after Macklemore's removal.
The Philadelphia Eagles, owned by Jeffrey Lurie, play at the stadium under a public ownership-and-leasing structure.
The publicly available evidence reviewed by TRT World does not establish comparable documented grants by Lurie to Israeli institutions.
Lurie nevertheless appears in the current controversy, reportedly joining Kraft, Blank and Tepper in opposing Macklemore's continued presence on the tour.
Lucas Oil Stadium and the Colts
Lucas Oil Stadium is a public facility rather than a privately owned NFL stadium. Indianapolis and Marion County operate it through a public stadium structure, while the Indianapolis Colts are tenants.
The Irsay family controls the Colts. Following the death of longtime owner Jim Irsay, his daughters Carlie Irsay Gordon, Casey Foyt, and Kalen Jackson assumed ownership responsibilities.
Unlike Kraft, Blank, and Tepper, the current Colts ownership group has no comparably documented record of Israel-specific donations in the public sources reviewed.
AT&T Stadium and the Dallas Cowboys
The City of Arlington owns the stadium, while the Dallas Cowboys hold a lease to operate there. The city approved an agreement in April 2026 extending the Cowboys’ lease through 2055.
Jerry Jones and his family own the Cowboys.
The material reviewed for this story includes no comparable publicly documented Israel donation by Jones.
Raymond James Stadium and the Glazers
Sheeran's North American tour is scheduled to conclude at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa in November.
Raymond James Stadium in Tampa is publicly controlled as well.
The Tampa Sports Authority, an independent public agency created under Florida law, manages the stadium. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers, owned by the Glazer family, are its NFL tenants.

Smoke, flames seen near Riyadh airport, ‘major’ flight disruptions reported
A plume of smoke and flames rose near Riyadh's main international airport on Saturday and residents reported hearing loud booms hours after Saudi authorities issued the first alert for the country's capital since the latest escalation with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. An Aramco fuel tank near the airport was reportedly on fire, according to a journalist in Riyadh.
A large plume of smoke was visible near Riyadh's main airport on Saturday after booms were heard and Saudi Arabia sent alerts overnight warning of potential danger around the capital, amid an escalation in attacks by Yemen's Houthi group.
Two residents of the Saudi capital said they saw black smoke and flames emanating from the area near the Riyadh King Khalid International Airport, while other people in the city reported hearing explosions.
"In the direction of the airport we saw black smoke and fire," one of the residents told AFP.
An Aramco fuel tank the airport was on fire Saturday, according to an AFP journalist. Firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt out fuel tank with the Saudi oil giant Aramco logo appearing on the structure.
Meanwhile aircraft tracking website FlightRadar24 reported major issues at the airport, including cancellations and delays.
The Riyadh King Khalid International Airport was listed under the site's maximum disruption index of 5.0, meaning the airport was seeing "major problems with long delays and several cancelled flights".
The disruption follows an overnight air raid alert issued by Saudi authorities.
Hours after the early morning alert, residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.
The alert in Riyadh was the first for the Saudi capital since the latest escalation with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Yemen's Houthis have staged a lightning offensive this month, seizing swathes of territory in one of the world's poorest countries, leaving the internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, scrambling to respond.
Saudi Arabia itself, one of the region's powerhouses, has conducted scores of air strikes on Houthi-held areas but failed to stop the advance. It has also sought help from its ally the US, that has not materialised.
Watch moreHas Trump Left MBS hanging over Yemen?
'Terrifying'
A Riyadh resident on Saturday described the attack as "terrifying".
"I was extremely anxious – especially because, unlike previous times, the 'all-clear' signal didn't come right away," the central Riyadh resident said.
"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said another Riyadh resident, 27, living in the city's north. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the threat mentioned in the warnings sent overnight to residents of several regions and has not identified where it originated from.
The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a "cowardly terrorist attack" on Islam's holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year, both Sunnis and Shias.
The Iran-backed Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a "worn-out lie".
Watch moreSaudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca, warns of 'red line'
The group has reported scores of retaliatory strikes carried out daily by Riyadh since their offensive this month to take over the country's entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.
Riyadh was targeted with waves of attacks during an earlier period of the war, including a drone strike on the US embassy in the capital's diplomatic quarter in March.
While the US, according to news platform Axios, last week refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis, Washington on Thursday approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom to help Riyadh "deter current and future threats", the US State Department said.
Reduced Saudi exports
The United Nations said on Friday that the renewed fighting had displaced more than 112,000 people while nearly 3,000 others had fled across the sea to Djibouti.
War in Yemen broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sanaa and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015.
The fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July, when the Houthis defied Riyadh's control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.
Their recent takeover of the coastline has sparked global concern, with international maritime trade already impacted by Iran's imposition of a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz since the Middle East war erupted in late February.
The Houthis insist there is no threat to shipping in the sea lane – except for ships from Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter.
The attack targeting Riyadh came as the Houthis improve their defences in newly conquered territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, with members of the group telling AFP they have been installing radar and digging tunnels.

What’s behind reports that the Israeli army is low on troops, equipment?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:51:43 UTC
21:51:43 KST

What’s behind reports that the Israeli army is low on troops, equipment?
Israel’s Channel 12 and Maariv newspaper claim the military is facing ‘severe shortages’ and lost a planned purchase of 12 Apache attack helicopters from the US.
In recent days, Israeli media reports have claimed the military is running low on certain equipment and troops.
On Tuesday, Israel’s Channel 12 said the army had lost a planned purchase of 12 Apache attack helicopters from United States manufacturer Boeing.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Serbia opens factory to assemble Israeli-made drones
- list 2 of 4‘Outrageous lies’: How Israeli voters are shrugging off Western sanctions
- list 3 of 4Two injured by Israeli shelling as troops advance in southern Lebanon
- list 4 of 4UK court clears woman of voicing support for Hamas in university speech
The newspaper Maariv then reported on Friday that, on top of “severe” shortages, the Israeli military is preparing to suspend soldiers’ leave.
But is one of the world’s most heavily financed armed forces, which has received billions of US dollars from the US in recent years, really struggling with shortages?
What has Israeli media reported?
Israeli newspaper Maariv reported: “The Israeli army does not have enough tanks and armoured personnel carriers,” adding that three years of war had worn down vehicles while hundreds have been damaged.
“For political reasons, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich can cut funding to the Israeli army and busy himself with complaints, while the opposition is preoccupied with internal struggles like reckless children,” the newspaper wrote.
Channel 12 reported that the planned purchase of a dozen Apache attack helicopters from Boeing failed to take place because of a shortfall in the army’s procurement budget.
The report came a day after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu failed during a routine meeting to persuade opposition leader Yair Lapid to cooperate on increasing the military procurement budget.
Channel 12 said the army was already warning that unless the requested funding increase arrives soon, efforts to return tanks and armoured personnel carriers damaged during the war to service capability would cease, while some ammunition production lines would also be affected.
Are these reports reliable?
Israel’s military is unlikely to be suffering from any real shortages, defence analyst Hamze Attar told Al Jazeera, adding that reports like this are part of a longstanding strategy to “over-exaggerate shortages to speed up replacements”.
According to Attar, the Israeli military operates with a policy of such extreme surplus that while other nations might consider a stockpile “combat ready”, Israel would view the same level as “critically low” as it aims to continue wars on multiple fronts without being restrained by external political pressure.
He said “leaked reports” often play favourably to Israel’s military by creating a sense of urgency in Washington and Europe to speed up weapons transfers.
He added that there is a perception in Israel of an increasing “change of hearts and minds” in the US when it comes to its support, and Israel is therefore looking to accelerate deals before any potential future policy shifts.
He used the example of recent reports that US President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing to sell 60,000 highly destructive, 2,000lb (907kg) bombs to Israel in a multibillion-dollar package.
What weapon stockpiles and troop numbers does Israel have?
Israel doesn’t publish munitions inventories, so estimates about its weapons stockpiles come from a mix of leaks, think-tank estimates, and official denials.
Troop numbers are better documented.
According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ Military Balance in 2023, Israel had 169,500 active military personnel in the army, navy and paramilitary.
A further 465,000 were serving in the reserves, while 8,000 served in the paramilitary.
Military service is mandatory from age 18 for most Jewish, Druze and Circassian Israelis, while most Palestinian Arab citizens aren’t drafted.
Men currently serve 32 months under a temporary law passed in July 2026 that reverts to 30 months in 2029, while women serve 24 months, with some roles requiring longer.
The military Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has repeatedly urged the Israeli government to extend mandatory military service for men to 36 months.
The push to enlist Ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) men does suggest Israel has been looking to boost the number of reservists amid almost three years of war.
Ultra-Orthodox men enrolled in full-time religious study had been exempt from military service since the state of Israel was created in 1948.
Israel’s High Court of Justice ruled this illegal in 1998, and repeatedly struck down a series of temporary measures intended to defer Haredi recruitment.
In 2024, the High Court again intervened, ordering the government to finally break the deadlock and begin actively conscripting ultra-Orthodox men.
In response, the military issued tens of thousands of draft notices to Haredi Jews, but compliance has remained minimal.
According to a testimony presented to the Knesset in July 2025, only 1,200 ultra-Orthodox recruits responded to the roughly 24,000 summons issued.
Does Israel need more weapons for its wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran?
Over the past three years, the Israeli military has waged wars across the region, including on the besieged Gaza Strip, where it began launching strikes in October 2023 in response to the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, and continues in different forms.
Israel is also fighting wars in Lebanon and Iran, alongside continuing military attacks in the occupied West Bank and Syria.
Attar said Israel appears to have enough stockpiles to maintain the current status quo in these conflicts.
However, given its history of military expansionism and recent rhetoric towards countries such as Turkiye, it is likely that Israel is “preparing for its next round of war with new enemies”, he said, adding that this will require more weapons.

Police had struggled to maintain order as people fought to secure a spot at the new site on Friday after weeks of living on the beaches and streets.
More than 2,000 migrants in Ceuta had to return to the beaches after there was not enough space to accommodate them at a new facility located in the autonomous city's port.
Thousands of migrants had been moved from the territory's Trampolín and Benítez beaches on Friday morning, escorted by officers from Spain's Civil Guard and National Police towards the new temporary reception centre, which is designed to accommodate 1,700 people.
However, there were over 4,000 people coming from the beaches, meaning many had to return after the new camp filled up. According to government sources, around 3,000 migrants remain on the city’s streets in total.
Police had struggled to maintain order on Friday as people fought to secure a spot at the new site after weeks of living on the beaches and streets, with officers firing warning shots into the air in an attempt to contain the crowd. No serious incidents were recorded, however, according to local authorities.
The migrants' return meant a clean-up operation that had been planned for the beaches once they were cleared also had to be put on hold.
As a result, Trampolín still looks much as it had in recent days, with makeshift tents and shacks strewn across the sand.
The Ceuta migrant crisis began in late July when more than 70,000 people crossed into the Spanish exclave from Morocco.
Kissy Chandiramani, a member of Ceuta's autonomous government, has described the port transfer as chaotic and said that neither the city government nor port authorities had been given advance warning.
Chandiramani also called for procedures to return the migrants to be speeded up, warning that otherwise, Ceuta risked becoming "the great CETI of North Africa," in reference to the Temporary Immigrant Reception Centres.
She noted that around one hundred migrant cases were being processed each day and that, with more resources, the process could be completed in 15 days.
If the current pace continues, she warned, the situation "is going to drag on forever."

INTERVIEW - ‘What was possible in New York can be possible in Berlin’: German Left candidate looks to Mamdani model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:47:54 UTC
21:47:54 KST

- Eralp points to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 win as a blueprint, campaigning on lower rents, cheaper transit and a more affordable Berlin
- She condemns Berlin’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian protests, stressing that criticizing Netanyahu’s war crimes in Gaza is not antisemitism
Germany’s capital Berlin -- also a city-state -- is preparing for one of its most closely watched state elections.
Elif Eralp, a human rights advocate of Turkish origin, has surprised many observers and is now leading in the polls. She has embraced New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s vision of democratic socialism as her campaign blueprint.
If her Left Party finishes first on Sunday and forms a coalition, the 45-year-old would become the city-state’s first governing mayor with a migration background and the first from the socialist party.
“I think we have a real chance to make history in Berlin,” Eralp told Anadolu. “To finally put the interests of Berliners first -- without dividing people by origin or social background.”
The Left Party leads with 23% in the latest survey by public broadcaster ZDF, two points ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). The anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) stands at 17%.
If Eralp wins and manages to forge a Left Party-led coalition, it would signal a significant political shift in one of the world’s most cosmopolitan cities.
Eralp’s campaign echoes Mamdani’s New York win
A member of Berlin’s state parliament since 2021, Eralp has built her campaign around soaring rents, costly public transport and persistent problems with waste collection on Berlin’s streets.
She said Mamdani’s 2025 victory offered a model for left-wing parties worldwide, including Germany’s left, and that both campaigns share a focus on making a big city affordable.
“He focused on social demands and that's what we also do. And he brought different communities together, that was a big success, and that's what we also try to do,” she said. “I hope what in Manhattan, in New York was possible will be possible here in Berlin as well.”
Eralp’s campaign centers on three main pledges -- curbing rent hikes, cutting bus and train fares, and tackling what she calls chaos in the city’s waste collection -- issues she says affect Berliners overall regardless of social or ethnic background.
“We want to make Berlin affordable again and the biggest problem is the housing problem because the rents are much too high,” she said. “So we want to lower the rents and we want to have cheaper buses and trains and also we want to solve the garbage problem in our streets.”
‘Berlin vote would send a strong message to the AfD’
The election comes just two weeks after the right-wing AfD’s strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6.
Eralp said a Left Party victory in Berlin would send a “powerful signal” against the far right and show mainstream parties that campaigns focused on people’s real problems --and backed by a strong program -- can succeed.
“A lot of people are very frustrated with the mainstream politics. They think that the politicians, they just make for themselves politics and that's why we should go and listen,” she said.
Eralp said her team is going door to door, including in AfD strongholds. Many voters, she said, fear economic decline and slipping down the social ladder. Some have embraced the far right’s anti-immigration rhetoric, blaming refugees and immigrants for the city’s problems.
“The root cause lies in neoliberal policies, austerity measures, and cutbacks that fail to support the poorest and those struggling in our city and country,” she said.
Eralp accused Merz’s CDU of echoing the AfD’s anti-immigration line, ultimately strengthening the far right rather than weakening it.
“They are making policies against refugees, against migrant people and I think they made just the AfD stronger instead of fighting against them,” she said. “We need a social policy, we need affordable Berlin, affordable cities that would be a big step against the rise of the far-right.”
Reaching out to Berlin’s Palestinian community
Eralp also criticized the outgoing Governing Mayor Kai Wegner’s CDU-led government for failing to ease the city’s social and economic problems, and for cracking down on pro-Palestinian protests, including the cancellation of events in recent years and disproportionate police force against peaceful demonstrators.
“The mayor of Berlin never listened to the issues of the Palestinian people here in Berlin, which is a big mistake. He should see all the people, the Palestinians, the Jewish people, the Muslim people, everybody who lives here,” she said.
“We saw a lot of violence and repression against the people. And I want that this stops. I think the freedom of speech and the freedom of manifestation is very important in all fields and that’s what we want to change when I’m in the government.”
Eralp rejected accusations of antisemitism against her party, saying she and her colleagues have backed initiatives to combat antisemitism and support Israel’s right to exist, just as they support Palestine’s right to exist. Condemning war crimes by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in Gaza is not antisemitism, she stressed.
“The far-right government of Israel is accused by doing war crimes and genocide in front of the international court,” she said, pointing to International Criminal Court cases involving Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity.
“And I think that it’s time to take responsibility for all these crimes and that the international politicians will support that this happens.”

The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games kicked off in Japan on Saturday with an opening ceremony.
Japan is hosting the Games for the third time, following Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994, according to Kyodo News.
The event features 43 sports, 71 disciplines and 469 medal events. More than 17,000 athletes from 45 countries and regions are competing.
Japan has also put forward its largest-ever contingent of 932 athletes, aiming to surpass its record of 78 gold medals set at the 1966 Asian Games in Bangkok.
Qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics is at stake in sports including hockey, surfing and squash.
Non-Olympic sports such as sepak takraw, described as kick volleyball, and kabaddi, an elevated version of contact tag, are also featured, along with esports.
Events are being held in Nagoya and other cities in Aichi Prefecture, as well as in neighboring Shizuoka and Gifu prefectures, Tokyo and Osaka.
The Games will run for 16 days through Oct. 4 under the slogan "Imagine One Asia."
The event is held on a four-year cycle.
In a related incident at the event, the organizing committee of the Games apologized for mistakenly playing the North Korean national anthem before a South Korean men's hockey match a day earlier, Kyodo News reported Saturday.

According to intelligence files, the head of the military contract selection center in Khanty-Mansiysk, identified as Lieutenant Pervushin, submitted a formal request to the Russian border service in July 2026 seeking expedited legal status for a group of Yemeni citizens.
Following their formal entry and residency legalization, Russian defense authorities prepared standard military service contracts for their enlistment.
The intelligence service reported that the identified cohort includes individuals born in 2006 and 2007.
Administrative pipeline
The recruitment mechanism relies on presidential decrees issued by Russian Vladimir Putin that established simplified and expedited pathways for foreign nationals to obtain temporary residence permits and fast-track Russian citizenship in exchange for military service.
The SZRU noted that the administrative scheme functions by first granting foreign recruits legal status inside the Russian Federation under simplified migration rules, after which regional military recruitment centers execute contractual enlistment procedures.

Regional security analysts noted that economic hardship in Yemen has facilitated recruitment efforts by foreign networks. The European Union has called on the United States to reconsider visa restrictions on Palestinian officials ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is due to address delegates by video.
The EU said on Saturday that it regretted the continuation of restrictions for a second year.
“In light of its existing headquarters agreements with the UN and its obligations as host state, we urge the United States for this decision to be reconsidered,” Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the EU’s diplomatic service, said.
The appeal comes before the 81st UN General Assembly high-level week, which starts on 20 September. EU leaders and foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas are due to attend meetings in New York.
The UN General Assembly voted 152-3 on 17 September to allow Mahmoud Abbas to address the session remotely after Washington denied him entry.
The United States has maintained restrictions affecting Palestinian Authority travel documents. US State Department guidance says visa issuance for people applying with Palestinian Authority-issued or endorsed travel documents has been suspended across immigrant and non-immigrant categories, subject to limited exceptions.
Washington has also imposed measures targeting Palestinian Authority and Palestine Liberation Organization officials. According to the State Department statement cited in the supplied reports, the US accuses the Palestinian leadership of failing to carry out reforms and pursuing actions that Washington says undermine prospects for peace.
The US also objects to Palestinian efforts to seek international recognition outside direct negotiations with Israel and to cases brought before international courts.
The restrictions do not have an equivalent for Israeli officials. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant issued in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity connected to the war in Gaza.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has expressed concern about the restrictions, saying they affect the ability of Palestine to participate in UN work.
Abbas is expected to use his recorded address to discuss Palestinian statehood, the two-state solution and conditions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The EU maintains support for a negotiated two-state solution based on international law and relevant UN Security Council resolutions, with Israel and Palestine living alongside each other within recognised borders.

France’s debt climbs to highest since 1995: Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

France’s debt climbs to highest since 1995: Ministry
PARIS – France’s debt mountain is growing and will in 2026 be at its highest level since 1995 because of a soaring deficit, the country’s finance ministry said on Sept 19.
A ministry source told reporters the public debt will reach 119.3 per cent of gross domestic product in 2026 and 121.7 per cent in 2027 – double the 60-per cent-of-GDP reference limit EU member countries are required to aim for.
Those debt figures will set records since the state statistics agency INSEE started recording debt levels under the current methodology in late 1995.
The source said the rise in France’s debt was “automatic” as “a consequence of a deficit that remains high”.
Under EU rules, the public deficit – the annual shortfall of revenue to spending – is meant to be no more than 3 per cent of GDP.
But in 2025, it came in at 5.1 per cent of GDP, and the government forecasts it will hit 5.4 per cent in 2026.
France, which has been under special EU monitoring for the past two years because of those high figures, expects its deficit to drop to 5 per cent in 2027 – when it holds elections to choose its next president and government.
The government has submitted its draft 2027 budget measures to an independent fiscal watchdog, the High Council of Public Finances, to evaluate their viability in macroeconomic terms.
Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu said on Sept 17 as he outlined the draft budget that the government planned to make adjustments and cuts worth €54 billion (S$79 billion) in the 2027 budget.
But with elections on the horizon, he left it to Parliament to decide some of the more sensitive measures, such as a government proposal to reduce tax breaks for pensioners.
The French economy has been slowing since the third quarter of 2025, hit by weak consumer spending and, more recently, the surge in energy prices from the US-Israeli war against Iran. AFP

UN condemns 'shocking pattern' of sexual violence by Russian troops in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:33:01 UTC
21:33:01 KST

Russia was added in May to the UN Secretary-General's list of countries credibly suspected of committing sexual violence in conflict — codified into international law decades ago as war crimes and crimes against humanity.
More than 1,000 cases of sexual violence recorded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 involve victims as young as 4 and as old as 82 in a "shocking pattern of torture, intimidation and coercion," according to the report published on Friday by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights.
"I am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine," said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk.
Both crimes were committed by Russian troops, who account for 89% of perpetrators in the 1,004 cases included in the report.
While the majority of documented victims are men, particularly those held in places of detention, women and children have been most severely affected in occupied Ukrainian territory.
Crimes against Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained medical workers include gang rape, genital mutilation and other acts of sexual humiliation.
The most common single method recorded was the use of a Soviet-era military field telephone known as a "tapik" to administer electric shocks to the genitals: 155 cases, or 27% of the total, involved this form of abuse at least once, the report says.
Individual survivor testimonies documented in the report include Ukrainian prisoners of war sexually assaulted with objects such as batons, cell door keys or shovel handles.
A woman in Zaporizhzhia was raped several times a week for a month by a Russian soldier who promised better treatment for her detained husband. A woman in Kherson was assaulted nightly and repeatedly threatened with gang rape.
In the Kyiv region, two Russian soldiers broke into a family home in 2022, shot and killed a woman's husband, then gang-raped her, threatening to shoot her in front of her four-year-old son if she resisted.
"Sexual violence is a grave feature of the full-scale armed attack against Ukraine. It must stop immediately, irrespective of the perpetrators," Türk said.
"Given the high prevalence of cases attributed to its forces, however, the Russian Federation in particular must take concrete and discernible steps to protect civilians and prisoners of war from all forms of torture, including sexual violence."
The 20-page report covers the period from 24 February 2022 to the end of July 2026 and draws on confidential interviews with hundreds of victims, along with court documents and official records.
Of the 11% of cases attributed to Ukrainian forces, nearly half involved threats of sexual violence against Russian prisoners of war and prisoners of war from third countries. The remainder included forced nudity, electric shocks and beatings to the genitals, sexually degrading treatment and two cases each of sexual assault and attempted rape.
Conventions disregarded, withdrawn from
Russia was added to the UN Secretary-General's list of parties credibly suspected of committing sexual violence in conflict in May of this year — a list that includes Sudan, Somalia and Haiti as repeat offenders. The Kremlin rejected the findings as politically motivated.
The UN Human Rights Council's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has separately documented widespread use of torture by Russian authorities against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war in occupied territory and inside Russia.
Russia formally withdrew from the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture in September 2025 following its expulsion from the Council of Europe, ending visits by European monitors to Russian detention facilities.
Russia remains a formal party to the UN Convention Against Torture and prohibits torture under its constitution and criminal code.
The Ukrainian foreign ministry welcomed the report, saying it had "once again demonstrated the scale of systematic human rights violations committed by the Russian Federation."
Rape and sexual violence were codified as war crimes and crimes against humanity under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, which entered into force in 2002.
The use of systematic rape as a weapon of war was first formally prosecuted as a crime against humanity and an act of genocide by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s.

“What we see is that air defense, drone defense, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems,” Rinkēvičs said. “And let’s be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole of Europe and NATO has it.”

European commercial rocket reaches orbit from Norway
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:30:47 BST
21:30:47 KST

German company Isar Aerospace has successfully placed satellites into orbit from Norway’s Andøya Spaceport, opening a new commercial route to space from the European continent, according to NATO Allied Air Command.
The mission, named “Onward and Upward”, was the second flight of Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum launch vehicle and lifted off from the company’s launch complex at Andøya at 10:12pm CEST on 5 September. NATO said the rocket crossed the Kármán line, completed main engine cut-off and stage separation, ignited its second stage and subsequently deployed its payloads after reaching orbit.
According to Allied Air Command, the flight made Isar Aerospace the first European commercial space company to successfully deliver satellites into orbit. The mission itself was a civilian commercial launch rather than a NATO operation, but the Alliance has highlighted it as an example of the wider commercial space infrastructure on which NATO members increasingly depend. NATO does not intend to develop its own independent constellation or launch capability. Instead, it relies on space capabilities, data and services supplied by member states and the civilian and commercial sector.
That makes access to multiple launch providers and launch sites important to resilience, particularly if military communications, navigation, surveillance or other space-enabled services need to be replenished or expanded.
Norwegian Lieutenant Colonel Jørgen Tovsrud, who serves with NATO’s Space Theater Component at Ramstein, was also a director of launch operations for the mission at Andøya.
Tovsrud said: “This launch is significant because NATO’s resilience in space is closely connected to the strength of the wider space ecosystem.”
He added: “A healthy civilian and commercial sector drives innovation, expands access and strengthens the services on which modern societies and military operations increasingly depend.”
NATO formally recognised space as an operational domain in 2019 and now treats access to space-based communications, navigation, tracking, detection and situational awareness as an important part of its wider military posture. The Alliance’s Space Theater Component at Ramstein works to integrate those capabilities into NATO operations rather than operate national or commercial systems itself.
US Colonel Jonathan L. Whitaker, Chief of Staff of NATO’s Space Theater Component and Director of the NATO Space Operations Center, said the success of national programmes remained central to the Alliance’s own use of space.
He said: “Norway has been a great partner with the NATO Space Theatre Component. We are glad to call several Norwegian space officers and NCOs our teammates here at Ramstein.”
Whitaker added: “Jørgen brings a deep skillset and leadership to the NATO Space Operations Centre, and we could not be prouder to lend him back to his Nation to ensure that this launch at Andoya was a success. The success of NATO Space depends on the success of National space programs.”

With United Russia’s Election Victory All But Certain, Some Russians Are Still Pushing Back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:23:14 UTC
21:23:14 KST

Across Russia, the outcome of this weekend’s State Duma elections seems like a foregone conclusion: a sweep for the ruling United Russia party and its allies. Even so, in St. Petersburg, one woman plans to head to her local polling station as an election observer from the liberal Yabloko party.
“What’s the motivation? A sense of responsibility, I guess — the feeling that this is one part of changing Russia that’s actually within my power,” the woman told The Moscow Times on condition of anonymity due to the risk of political reprisal.
“I can’t overthrow anyone, but I can show up and observe,” she said.
In what experts say is Russia’s most restricted parliamentary elections to date, voters have few options to make a difference at the ballot box. Instead, many are finding other ways to push back against United Russia and show their distrust in the process, from subtle acts of protest to organized voting strategies and poll watching.
The Kremlin has sidelined nearly all real opponents, making it almost impossible to vote for candidates who truly challenge the status quo. With United Russia facing some of its lowest approval ratings since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, President Vladimir Putin is framing the election as a referendum on the war effort, now in its fifth year.
For authorities, showing strong public backing is critical. A crackdown on anti-war candidates ahead of the vote peaked in August when Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko, the only party campaigning on a pro-peace platform, from the party-list ballot.
Voters will elect 225 State Duma representatives through party lists and another 225 in single-member districts, where a few Yabloko candidates are still allowed to run. United Russia, which controls 70% of Duma seats, is expected to keep its usual supermajority, with remaining seats going to Kremlin-approved parties that support the war.
The protest efforts that have emerged mostly focus on calling out the lack of real choices and showing that people do not support the war. They are far fewer and smaller than in previous election cycles and are unlikely to yield anything more than symbolic wins for regime critics. For many taking part, though, that is reason enough.
In the northern Vologda region, United Russia candidate Natalia Moskvitina has become a target of one such campaign. Earlier this summer, feminist activists petitioned authorities to remove Moskvitina, the head of an anti-abortion group, from the party list, arguing her platform threatens women’s rights.
When that effort failed, activists shifted their tactics, calling on voters to support any party other than United Russia. The goal is to drive down the party’s vote total enough so Moskvitina loses her spot on the regional representative list.
“I don’t think the campaign will lead to her losing the election,” said Daria Serenko, co-founder of the Feminist Anti-War Resistance group leading the initiative against Moskvitina. “But that doesn’t mean she should get there easily, smoothly and unnoticed.”
Serenko said the summer campaign gave Moskvitina “national negative notoriety,” and she believes authorities will take note of the pushback. Even if she wins a seat, Serenko hopes the public backlash will hamper her legislative agenda.
Elsewhere, activists are organizing a symbolic demonstration to draw attention to opposition surrounding the biggest issue in the elections: the war.
Organizers of an initiative called “Noon for Peaceful Russia” are asking voters to show up at polling stations simultaneously — at 12:00 p.m. on Sept. 20, the final day of elections. The goal is to generate striking photos of long lines wrapping around polling stations across Russia and at embassies abroad, giving Russians a way to engage in a low-risk yet visible form of protest.
Organizers say they want to disrupt the tightly controlled optics of the elections and show that Russians are united — not behind Putin, but behind an end to the war in Ukraine.
“It’s important not only to see that you are not alone,” said Katerina Kiltau, chairwoman of the political council for Peaceful Russia, the exiled party leading the event. “A simultaneous turnout will also show the world that there are Russians who want a peaceful and democratic future.”
Exiled opposition figures Yulia Navalnaya and Maxim Katz are also calling on Russians to vote for any party other than United Russia. It remains a controversial strategy, as every other option on the ballot, though nominally in opposition, largely backs the Kremlin’s and United Russia’s core policies.
Debate has flared over whether to cast a protest vote or boycott the election entirely. In a rare rebuke aimed at the exiled opposition, Yabloko Chairman Nikolai Rybakov criticized the strategy of voting for systematic opposition parties like the Communist Party or the right-wing Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR) given their support of the war against Ukraine and political repression inside Russia.
“We understand that this is a choice between bad and very bad,” Kiltau said. “But that is how protest voting works in an environment where elections are not free. The more people who go to the polls and vote for alternative parties and candidates rather than the ruling party, the harder it will be to distort the actual picture of the vote.”
Yet another initiative, called “Vote Abroad,” is taking a different tack by organizing volunteers to conduct exit polls overseas. Irina Vesikko, a coordinator for the group, told The Moscow Times they will work across roughly 40 international cities to survey voters and document potential fraud.
“We’re not encouraging anyone, we’re not calling on anyone to vote or to do anything specific,” Vesikko said. “We’re simply recording the fact that [voting] will happen, and that’s it. A statement of fact. Who will verify [the results] otherwise?”
Still, many anti-war Russians are skeptical that any form of activism will make a difference, and some see no point in taking part at all.
“It doesn’t decide anything and has no impact,” Anastasia, a woman living in St. Petersburg, said of her decision not to vote in the elections. However, she said that she stands in solidarity with those who do engage in some form of protest voting.
Ivan, a Russian living in Europe, said he is disillusioned with both pro-Kremlin and anti-war voices and believes getting involved in politics at this point is a waste of time.
“I can’t influence the government in Russia through my vote, so I'll spend my time on something else,” he added. “I don’t consider this apathy, but rather a realistic assessment of the situation.”
Mack Tubridy contributed reporting.

International Youth Festival 2026 in Russia ends with 50 Iranian youth participants
The festival highlights Russia’s focus on youth potential for development and international cooperation
YEKATERINBURG, Russia — The International Youth Festival 2026 concluded in Yekaterinburg on September 17, bringing together around 10,000 young people from 191 countries, including approximately 50 young participants from Iran.
Held from September 11 to 17, the festival combined cultural, educational, scientific and diplomatic programs. More than 113,000 young people from around the world reportedly applied to participate, with 5,000 Russian and 5,000 international participants ultimately selected.
 
 
 Beyond cultural activities, the festival provided a platform for young leaders, government officials and youth representatives to develop international contacts and discuss cooperation in education, science, entrepreneurship, culture and youth policy.
 
 
 A major theme of the festival was the role of young people in innovation, national development and international cooperation. Russia also used the event to showcase its capabilities in different fields, particularly projects, technologies and initiatives in which its younger generation has played an important role.
 
 
 Iran was represented by a delegation of around 50 young participants. Alireza Rahimi, Deputy Minister of Sports and Youth Affairs of Iran, also attended the festival with an official delegation and held bilateral meetings with counterparts from several countries. The meetings focused on expanding cooperation in youth affairs and developing joint initiatives.
 
 
 The experience may also offer an important lesson for countries facing sanctions and external restrictions, including Iran. The capabilities demonstrated by Russia in different fields, particularly those developed with the participation of young people, show how the potential of a country's younger generation can help reduce the impact of external restrictions, foster innovation and create new channels for international cooperation and development.
 
 
 For Iran, greater investment in young researchers, entrepreneurs, innovators, cultural figures and international youth networks could similarly help transform its considerable human potential into new opportunities for cooperation, innovation and economic development despite external constraints.

Europe falls behind in drone warfare technology, vulnerable to Russian missile attacks — Latvian President
Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs issued the warning in an interview with The Guardian, as reported by Ukrinform.
The Latvian president said that drone warfare in Ukraine is developing at "lightning speed," while current efforts and preparations for aerial warfare could become outdated as early as the middle of next year.
"What we see is that air defence, drone defence, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems. And let's be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole of Europe and Nato has it," Rinkēvičs said.

Ukraine and its European allies are currently facing delays in the delivery of critical missiles for Patriot systems and other air-defense capabilities.
The United States has considered transferring production of Patriot systems to Ukraine and European countries, but no agreement has yet been concluded.
Rinkēvičs said that the matter depended on the US government and the company itself, adding that negotiations were still ongoing and that there were certain technical difficulties related to licensing.
According to Rinkēvičs, acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, and recent incidents involving drones and missiles indicated that Russia was testing Europe's resolve to continue supporting Ukraine. He said that he did not consider a conventional military invasion likely, but stressed that Europe needed to remain very vigilant about other possible scenarios.
He also suggested that, in the coming months following the local elections, Russia could intensify its mobilization and then use the winter period to put pressure on the Ukrainian front and take every possible measure to discourage countries supporting Ukraine from providing further assistance.
