Surviving the summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

The summer of 2026 was one to remember — though for many people, it was for all the worst reasons. June and July were Western Europe’s hottest months on record, and more people than usual died during the heat wave. Many of the deaths were in countries such as France and Germany, where major heat waves are historically rare and the populations are underprepared.
In the United States, the Lower 48 states had their hottest July on record, beating out a Dust Bowl record from 1936. Almost half of the states experienced drought. Some reservoirs on the Colorado River, the water source for 40 million people in the West, hit record lows.
The scariest thing is that this may become the new normal. In this issue, we investigate what’s driving the scorching weather and how people might adapt to survive.
The residents of Kearny, Ariz., are the vanguards. The town’s supply of water from the dwindling Gila River, a tributary of the Colorado, was cut by 87 percent this year. Residents have embraced strict water use restrictions, and that will get them through, staff writer Nikk Ogasa reports. But there are no guarantees for next year. The latest research suggests that the megadrought that has persisted for decades across the Southwest might not relent anytime soon.
Scientists are working on ways to help people adapt to extreme heat. Human bodies learn and adjust with repeated exposure to heat, freelance journalist Katarina Zimmer reports. But older people and those with chronic conditions are more vulnerable to heatstroke and related illnesses. Physiologists are now working with older volunteers to see if their bodies can be heat-proofed in advance with simple techniques like sitting in a hot bath.
And if those threats aren’t enough to give you the heebie-jeebies, humankind could also be facing peril from space. In July, the Federal Communications Commission gave the Los Angeles–based company Reflect Orbital permission to launch and orbit a giant mirror, the first of many thousands the company plans to launch to reflect sunlight to Earth. Goals include generating solar power and “enhancing urban life.” This may sound worthy, but scientists say the mirrors could interfere with space research and harm people and other terrestrial life-forms. Our senior astronomy writer Lisa Grossman explains what’s at stake and why current laws are ill-equipped to address such risks.

Lopez: We don't need AI to threaten the future of humanity. We've got Trump's climate policies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

We don’t need AI to threaten the future of humanity. We’ve got Trump’s climate policies
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Trump has gutted environmental protections and scientific research, and dismantled clean energy initiatives.
- Activists of all ages are organizing events to promote sustainability, biodiversity and other environmental causes.
You need a boost, right?
We’re living under a dark cloud, with a steady downpour of graft, thuggery and baloney.
There’s the raffling of presidential pardons and the attacks on reporters for doing their jobs, the clownish trade war with Canada, the bungled disaster in Iran, the petty obsessions with the ballroom and the Kennedy Center, the hogwash about a stolen election, the attacks on immigrants and the shameless presidential profiteering while working people suffer the cost of Trump’s countless broken promises.
I could go on, and I will. But rest assured, I have not forgotten about the boost I promised.
For all the affronts, nothing strikes me as more sinister than the Trump administration’s ambitious assault on the planet. Despite nearly daily headlines about the global calamity of overheated oceans, melting glaciers, stark weather transformations and species extinction, Trump keeps shoveling more coal onto a fire that will rage long after he’s dead and gone.
He’s gutted environmental protections and scientific research and dismantled clean energy initiatives. Now his administration is rolling back limits on power plant emissions, attempting to open the California coast to more oil drilling and sabotaging the state’s ambitious goals on emission controls and electric vehicle conversion.
We don’t need AI to threaten the future of humanity. We’ve got Trump.
It’s tempting to duck under the covers and wait for the nightmare to end, but the good news is that a lot of people are standing up rather than rolling over, rebelling against the ignorance and callous disregard that threatens our most precious and fragile shared inheritance.
In August, hundreds showed up to defend California’s authority to govern its own coast at a Santa Monica hearing of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Agency, and 18,000 more people filed comments online.
Letters to the Editor: The Coastal Commission has done the right things. Trump should back off
‘It is not the job of the people of California to compensate for Trump’s financial losses,’ writes an L.A. Times reader.
The rollback of environmental safeguards is, for many, a call to arms.
“Yes, I am discouraged. … But I am not despairing,” said Bill McKibben, an author and environmental activist who is organizing a worldwide event called Sun Day for next year to promote clean energy. “We’re reacting to multiple crises, and we’re led by a pack of fools, so why would anybody not stand up?”
McKibben launched a national movement five years ago called Third Act, and tens of thousands of people 60 and older have signed on to advocate for climate action, voting rights and civic participation. Third Act now operates in about 30 states, with a robust chapter in Southern California.
Former Times reporter Zan Dubin has worked as both a volunteer and a paid communications consultant for Third Act, and I asked her what someone could expect to do if they became a member of Third Act/SoCal.
“We do it all,” Dubin said, from promoting climate-friendly candidates to running phone banks and testifying at public meetings. She said Third Act co-sponsors protests at Dodger Stadium, and she and others planned to meet at Vin Scully Avenue and Stadium Way for Sunday’s game against the San Francisco Giants. They want the Dodgers to stop doing business with Big Oil and bench their sponsorship deal with Phillips 66.
She also called out Disneyland for its exhaust-spewing Autopia attraction, along with former Times climate columnist Sammy Roth, and Disneyland responded by announcing in 2024 that it was switching to electric cars beginning in 2027.
Dubin, co-founder of National Drive Electric Week, said 170 volunteer-led events were being held nationwide over the next month to promote EVs, and she was leading one Friday in Irvine.
“Action is absolutely the antidote to despair,” Dubin said. “I find that despite the onslaught of these horrifying headlines … taking action invigorates me.”
Claremont resident Margaret Davis knows that feeling. She emailed me in 2023, prior to participating in a Third Act event, and said many retirees have time on their hands, which puts them in a powerful position.
“The climate crisis is the greatest existential threat humans have ever faced, hence we live in a time when we can make the greatest change for the better,” Davis wrote at the time.
When I called her a few days ago, Davis told me she’s now a member of Senior Stewards Acting for the Environment. She lives at Pilgrim Place — a senior community with a focus on justice, peace and environment — where residents meet regularly to study, discuss and advocate for sustainability, biodiversity and environmental causes.
As legislative session closed, Newsom pushed environmental break for donor.
“When I was in college in 1970, we had the antiwar movement and that was the first year of Earth Day,” Davis said. “At the time, I thought Earth Day was just a distraction from what was going on in the world.”
Later, she said, “I came to realize it was the biggest issue of all time.”
Like Davis, I went to college in the ‘70s, and there’s no denying that our aggressively consumptive generation played a key role in manufacturing a crisis for our children and grandchildren. We’ve got matches in our hands and smoke on the horizon, and if we’re honest with ourselves, we’d see atonement not as a hobby, but as a duty.
As for the next generation, climate activist Sim Bilal, 24, said he too shares the sense that this is both a wickedly frightening time and a moment of opportunity.
“In the last month, we’ve gotten more young people involved,” said Bilal, executive director of Youth Climate Stewards 4 Local Action. “We usually have to reach out to them, but so many people have been wanting to get involved, and they’re so eager, and that’s been affirming for me. The policies are depressing, but the fact that people are reenergized and want to fight back is really exciting.”
Bilal said faith in politics, government and corporations is not high among his peers, but he’s trying to grow a network of young people to cultivate and support future leaders.
“A mentor told me there are two kinds of power — organized people, and organized money,” said Bilal, whose activism began when his grandmother died and he began wondering if her cancer, and global warming, were connected to the oil drilling in his South L.A. neighborhood. “We don’t have the money, but a lot of the work we do is political and civic education, demystifying power, and making people understand they have agency.”
You needed a boost, right?
There you go.
Whatever your age, do not despair.
Get off the chair.
steve.lopez@latimes.com

The chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Steven Kolb, has resigned after he was filmed physically restraining two animal rights activists during an altercation at New York fashion week.
“After 20 years leading the CFDA, I have made the difficult decision to step down as CEO and president,” Kolb said in a statement. “I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organisation to begin a new chapter.”
Kolb had been placed on leave on Tuesday pending a review of an incident during a COS show at New York fashion week on Sunday.
In a video, Kolb could be seen trying to restrain two People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) protesters who attempted to disrupt the show in a demonstration against the use of wool by the H&M group, which owns COS.
Kolb pushed a protester, identified as Mason Melito, and covered his mouth. Kolb also wrestled a second protester to the ground, using his arms and a leg to restrain her and putting his hand over her mouth.
Speaking to the Guardian after the incident, Melito described the situation as scary and said Kolb’s behaviour had been “completely uncalled for”.
The CFDA is a non-profit organisation that supports and promotes US designers and brands. It also organises the official New York fashion week schedule.
A statement issued by the CFDA board, which includes designers such as Ralph Lauren, Thom Browne, Tory Burch and Michael Kors, said: “Steven Kolb has been a dedicated leader and tireless champion of American fashion throughout his more than two decades at the CFDA, including 15 years as CEO.
“We respect Steven’s decision to step down and are grateful for his many years of leadership and service to the CFDA and our industry. He leaves the organisation well positioned, with a clear mission and dedicated team, to carry out the important work ahead as we look to the future of American fashion.”
The group is yet to name a successor.
A Peta USA spokesperson said in a statement: “This unfortunate incident, which has cost Mr Kolb his job, would never have taken place if Daniel Ervér, CEO of H&M, had, as Peta requested so many times, taken action to avoid extreme violence to animals exploited for clothing.
“We will still be meeting with Mr Kolb, and hopefully others in the industry will meet and take meaningful steps to stop this epidemic of cruelty to animals for nothing more than a look.”
Peta staged another protest on Thursday night during London fashion week when three protesters stormed the catwalk during an H&M show. Each one held a sign stating “H&M: Wool is bloody cruel. Drop it.” After stepping down from the catwalk, they were escorted out of the venue by security.

In Monaco, banks have begun closing the accounts of wealthy Russians
Kyiv • UNN
Monaco's regulator has tightened bank checks due to FATF requirements. Banks are closing the accounts of clients who have not confirmed the source of their funds.
Monaco has tightened checks on banks and asset management companies, bringing the accounts of wealthy clients with Russian connections under close regulatory scrutiny. About one-third of the problematic client files identified during the checks are linked to Russia, The Moscow Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
The checks are being conducted by the principality’s financial regulator, AMSF, amid Monaco’s efforts to exit the FATF “grey list,” to which the country was added in 2024 due to shortcomings in combating money laundering.
The regulator inspected UBS Monaco, Banque Havilland, Julius Baer, Guardian Management, and International Corporate Structuring. The violations identified included insufficient checks into the source of clients’ wealth, their possible criminal, sanctions-related, and political ties, as well as suspicious financial transactions.
Banks began closing accounts
Among the clients identified through the data published by the regulator was Saodat Narziyeva, the sister of Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov. UBS Monaco closed her account in March 2025 after the regulator established that the bank did not have sufficient documentation on the source of the funds gifted to her by her brother.
Julius Baer ended its relationship with Viktor Fedotov, the former head of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium. The regulator established that the bank reported its suspicions regarding the client only a year after the relevant grounds had emerged.
AMSF also raised claims regarding services provided to Leonid Novitsky, the brother of Russia’s former agriculture minister Yelena Skrynnik, and Alexey Fedorichev, the owner of Fedcominvest. The latter was suspected of corruption and money laundering in Ukraine, and in 2024, assets linked to him worth €41 million were seized in Italy at Ukraine’s request.
The checks also affected other wealthy clients with Russian connections whose identities have not been disclosed. In some cases, the regulator recommended that banks close accounts because it was impossible to verify the source of the capital or explain the economic rationale for the transactions.

Attacks on nuclear sites becoming normalized: Mikhail Ulyanov

Speaking at the IAEA General Conference, Mikhail Ulyanov said Russia had warned that if IAEA member states and the agency's leadership do not find the resolve to condemn attacks on nuclear facilities "anywhere, at any time," such attacks would become a new norm. "It appears this is exactly what is happening," he said.
According to Russia's Novosti news agency, Ulyanov added that Moscow wants the agency to respond to attacks on nuclear facilities, particularly those under IAEA safeguards.
Separately, Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry's European Cooperation Department, told a press briefing that Western countries' "playing" with nuclear weapons is a particular concern and portends a troubling outlook.
For decades, he said, the Baltic Sea had been a stable and peaceful region. But once NATO decided to deploy there — or rather, once its member states decided they needed to strengthen their defenses in the Baltic — the region ceased to be the stable, peaceful area it once was.
Maslennikov said the efforts of Russia's "Western neighbors" to play with nuclear weapons are a particular source of concern in this context. He pointed to Finland's recent decision to join France's nuclear deterrence initiative as a development that has added to the situation, following Helsinki's move this past summer to lift restrictions on nuclear weapons imports.
Noting that Moscow is the only Arctic Council member that does not belong to NATO, Maslennikov said such an "erosive" trend in non-proliferation policy, and deliberate actions to weaken it further, can only be described as "utterly reckless and highly dangerous." He added that the EU, through successive rounds of sanctions that are illegal under international law, is creating further obstacles to the development of the Russian Arctic and to international cooperation in the north.

The US has warned allied nations to anticipate delays of up to five years for deliveries of key weapons systems as Washington works to replenish domestic munitions stockpiles depleted by the war against Iran, Bloomberg reported.
According to government officials, multiple European nations anticipate significant postponements in receiving contracted air defense assets and precision-strike missile systems.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Germany requested accelerated deliveries of Raytheon-manufactured Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles and land-based Typhon mobile launchers, but defense officials indicated that contractor production lines are unlikely to fulfill the orders within the next five years due to acute US inventory shortfalls.
Officials added that several Eastern European countries reliant on American defense hardware began experiencing delivery delays shortly after the US initiated military combat operations against Iran in February 2026.
Delays have also extended to Asian partners; in April, Washington notified Japanese defense officials that scheduled deliveries of Tomahawk missile systems would be deferred by two years.
Media assessments indicate that US forces have expended more than half of their operational inventory of advanced Patriot missile variants, one-third of their Tomahawk cruise missile stocks, and nearly half of their THAAD interceptors during operations in the Middle East.
Pentagon officials acknowledged that high expenditure rates in the opening months of the conflict created strategic reserve deficits and exposed structural manufacturing constraints across the domestic defense-industrial base.
AfD Leaders Plan Talks With Putin Envoy on Russian Gas
European procurement delays
The Pentagon’s prioritization of domestic stockpile reconstitution has complicated Ukrainian and European efforts to reinforce Ukrainian airspace protection ahead of anticipated winter Russian bombardments.
Despite broader supply constraints, the US continues to facilitate deliveries of arms procured for Ukraine by European allies through EU and NATO financing frameworks.
European leaders plan to approach US President Donald Trump during next week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York to lobby for additional Patriot interceptor allocations for Ukraine.
In addition, EU officials are seeking to negotiate production licensing agreements that would permit European manufacturers to produce Patriot missiles domestically to supply Kyiv’s defense requirements.
US operations in the Middle East consumed more than 1,500 Patriot interceptors, leaving total US inventory at fewer than 1,700 units. The inventory drawdown has constrained the availability of long-range precision assets, including Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM).
Production bottlenecks
In response to the supply strain, the US Department of Defense has directed US defense contractors to accelerate serial production lines. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed that the department is working to compress procurement schedules to meet expanding operational requirements.
US Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg reportedly issued a formal directive to prime defense contractors demanding actionable acceleration plans within 21 days, stating that multi-year development timelines are unacceptable given prevailing geopolitical conditions.
The strategic redirection of munitions has also affected the US force posture in the Indo-Pacific. To sustain Middle East operations, the Pentagon redeployed hundreds of interceptors, advanced naval destroyers, a carrier strike group, and Tomahawk inventories from the US Indo-Pacific Command, drawing down regional assets previously stationed in South Korea and Japan.

According to the UN assessment, long-range weapons served as the primary cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 47 percent of all deaths and injuries in August, with 194 killed and 1,077 wounded. The majority of these casualties occurred in urban centers far removed from active frontlines, with the highest tolls recorded in Kyiv, Kherson, Kryvyi Rih, and Zaporizhzhia.
Concurrently, short-range tactical drones, particularly first-person view (FPV) loitering munitions, accounted for 30 percent of total civilian casualties nationwide in August, remaining the leading cause of death and injury in frontline communities such as Kherson.

The world in which we live, more than ever before, requires a fundamental change, of course, because in this world, war, intervention, sanctions, and the use of force, rather than being exceptions, have become standard instruments of policy. Now the fundamental question is, how have we arrived at this point? How has a system established to prevent war, support peace, protect human dignity, and ensure the administration of justice become so powerless today in the face of aggression, the slaughter of civilians, and the blatant violation of international law?
The answer must be sought in a bitter reality. Decades of foreign intervention, military pressure, and endless wars in the Middle East have proven an undeniable truth. Military intervention does not create security, and the exertion of pressure and coercion does not lead to peace. Instead, war has been normalized as a primary instrument of international relations and has led to the perpetuation of patterns of perpetual confrontation and conflict.
The tragedy of Gaza and the ongoing crimes committed by the Israeli regime are among the clearest and most horrific manifestations of this failed pattern. What is taking place in Gaza is not merely a humanitarian tragedy. It is a test of the conscience and collective responsibility of the international community. The slaughter of civilians, forced displacement, collective punishment, and the destruction of vital infrastructure, having gone without effective accountability, have extended to Lebanon as well. Unfortunately, a dangerous pattern has now taken shape, a pattern in which military force is no longer used as a last resort, but has turned into a permanent mechanism for redesigning the political and security landscape of the region.
Under such circumstances, aggression becomes normalized, escalation becomes institutionalized, and destruction turns from a consequence of war into an instrument for advancing political goals. This trend did not stop at the borders of Gaza and Lebanon. The military aggression of the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran is also understandable within this very framework, a war that was illegal, unjust, aggressive and unprovoked. If these are not met with an effective response from the international community, they will gradually erase the prohibited boundaries of international law. Such policies will yield no result other than the tragedy of the killing of 168 innocent students in Minab. The victims of such crimes are not merely numbers among the statistics of war casualties. Behind each of these lost lives, there was a family, a future, and the life. This is the very point where we must ask ourselves, how far? When do we say enough is enough?
Ladies and gentlemen;
If international law is disregarded whenever the interests of major powers dictate, one can no longer speak of the rule of law. If human rights are an inherent right for some nations and a conditional privilege for others, they can no longer be called universal. If international institutions, including the United Nations, cannot stand up against aggression and hold accountable the violators of international law, it is only natural that the credibility and legitimacy of these institutions will be damaged. Yet the solution is not the abandonment of multilateralism. On the contrary, today's world needs genuine, effective, and just multilateralism more than ever before.
A global turnaround requires the political will and courage to alter the course of the current trajectory, from militarism toward sustainable development, from interventionism toward respect for national sovereignty, from collective punishment toward the protection of civilians, from selective accountability toward universal justice, and from endless wars toward the lasting peace.
What the world needs is a new paradigm; a paradigm in which development is regarded as part of security; the sovereignty of countries is respected; international law is applied equally and without discrimination to all; and no political, strategic or geopolitical interest is given priority over human lives.
In the Middle East, sustainable security cannot be dictated from outside the region. Regional security must belong to the region itself. The countries of the region must be able to discuss their security, stability, development and common future and find their own solutions without the intervention of foreign powers.
For the Islamic Republic of Iran, this is not merely a theoretical view. This approach is the result of a historical experience and a lesson for which the Iranian nation has paid a heavy price. We believe sustainable security is achieved through dialogue, confidence-building, cooperation and mutual respect among the countries of the region, not through the military presence of foreign powers and the imposition of their will.
Today the international community stands before a historic and civilizational choice. We can continue down this very path, the path of militarism, intervention, confrontation, and endless wars. Or we can have the will and courage to change course. We can place development back at the center of attention. We can prioritize human dignity over power calculations. We can remove justice from monopoly and selectivity. and we can once again restore real meaning and credibility to international law. This is the very fundamental turnaround that today's world needs, and its time is neither tomorrow nor in an uncertain future. Its time is now.
Thank you for your attention.

Leidos joins Anduril in U.S. Air Force design deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:44:59 UTC
20:44:59 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Leidos an $85 million ceiling contract for aircraft design software, a day after making a similar award to Anduril Industries.
- Both companies won under the same eight-offer competition, suggesting the Air Force structured the VOLARE program as a multi-award contract.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Leidos an $85 million ceiling contract for digital design tools meant to help engineer future aircraft, the second company in as many days to win a spot under the same research program that Anduril Industries joined a day earlier.
The Air Force Research Laboratory made the award to Leidos, a Reston, Virginia-based technology and engineering contractor, under the VOLARE program, formally known as Digital System-Level Mission-Driven Integrated Design Methods for Aerospace Systems. Like the earlier Anduril award, this is an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, meaning the $85 million is a ceiling rather than guaranteed funding, with the Air Force issuing individual task orders as work is needed.
Work will take place in Dayton, Ohio, and the contract runs through Sept. 18, 2036, a 10-year window that closely mirrors Anduril’s own VOLARE deal, which was awarded one day earlier and runs through Sept. 17, 2036.
Both awards stem from the same competition, in which eight companies submitted offers. The near-identical contract numbers, Anduril’s FA2391-26-D-B013 and Leidos’s FA2391-26-D-B015, along with matching $85 million ceilings and the shared eight-offer count, indicate the Air Force Research Laboratory structured VOLARE as a multi-award IDIQ, selecting more than one contractor to compete for task orders rather than picking a single winner. As with Anduril’s contract, no funds are obligated on the base agreement itself. The first task order under this award, worth $75,000 in fiscal 2026 research funds, has been issued to get the work started.
VOLARE covers two related goals: building software that can model an aircraft’s overall vehicle systems, and developing methods for designing thermal management systems, the cooling architecture that keeps an aircraft’s engines, electronics and sensors from overheating. Modern military aircraft pack growing amounts of high-power radar, computing and directed-energy equipment into the same airframe, making heat management as much a design challenge as the weapons or sensors themselves.
Leidos is a large federal technology and engineering contractor with a long history supporting defense, intelligence and civilian government agencies, though the company has not previously been publicly tied to this specific style of digital-engineering work for aircraft design in the way Anduril has through its recent missile-development prize win.

Germany cuts fuel tax as Middle East conflicts send prices soaring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:39:22 UTC
20:39:22 KST

Germany will lower tax on petrol and diesel by 17 cents per liter in a relief package worth €2.5 billion, the German government announced Friday.
"Those who rely on their cars every day are reaching their financial limits. ... The relief package of €2.5 billion is no small sum in times of strained budgets," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said. The tax discount is to be implemented next month.
The measure, brokered between Germany's federal and state governments, is part of the package promised by Merz as fuel prices continue to climb in response to the war in Iran and the escalating conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
Two weeks ago, a key oil benchmark reached $100 a barrel for the first time since July following the latest escalations in the Middle East, sending pump prices soaring all over Europe.
The Merz government also plans to introduce a temporary fuel price cap on petrol and diesel modeled on similar policies in Luxembourg and Belgium. The price cap would take into account price moves on the oil markets, transportation and distribution costs, and retailers’ profit margins. Berlin aims to introduce the measure by Jan. 1, 2027.
Germany, through the voice of its Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, is among the EU member countries calling for a bloc-wide windfall tax on oil companies that have reaped billions of euros in excess profits since the start of the war. The topic is high on the agenda at an informal meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday and Saturday.
Ahead of the meeting on Friday, Klingbeil has called on the European Commission to present a proposal by the end of October.
“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil, from Germany's Social Democratic Party, told reporters. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”
But Merz's conservatives have pushed back on the proposal. Germany's Economic Affairs and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche said a windfall tax would only make sense in case of abusive price increases, she told Handelsblatt.
“The fact that eleven refineries are producing in Germany makes us less dependent on foreign countries; that must not be put at risk,” Reiche said.

UN reports 1,004 verified cases of sexual violence in Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:39:00 UTC
20:39:00 KST

Russian forces committed widespread sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war in Ukraine, including gang rape and electric shocks to the genitals, while Ukrainian authorities were also responsible for a smaller number of violations, the U.N. human rights office said Friday.
The report documented 1,004 verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence between Feb. 24, 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and July 31, 2026. The U.N. said the cases included rape, attempted rape, sexual assault, genital mutilation, forced nudity, beatings and electric shocks to the genitals.
Of the verified cases, 89% were attributed to Russian authorities, including members of the armed forces, prison service and security agencies. The remaining 11% were attributed to Ukrainian authorities, including members of the armed forces, prison service and security service.
The U.N. said the findings were based on confidential interviews with hundreds of victims and survivors, as well as court documents, official records and other evidence. It stressed that the figures do not represent a comprehensive account of sexual violence in the conflict, which remains significantly underreported.
Russia's permanent diplomatic mission in Geneva declined to comment on the report.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said it welcomed the report, saying it demonstrated the scale of human rights violations perpetrated by Russia while also highlighting measures taken by Ukrainian authorities to prevent sexual violence and provide compensation to victims.
The statement did not directly address the report's findings of abuses allegedly committed by Ukrainian forces.
The report said Russia's refusal to grant the U.N. Human Rights Office access to occupied Ukrainian territory, prisoners of war and civilian detainees meant the figures likely underestimate the true scale of the violations.
In occupied areas of Ukraine and within Russia, Russian authorities carried out sexual violence against Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained civilians at various stages of captivity, including during capture, transfer, interrogation and detention, the report said.
The violations included gang rape, rape, genital mutilation and electric shocks to men's genitals using a Soviet-era field telephone known as a "tapik." The findings were based on interviews with victims of sexual violence committed by both sides.
Most victims in detention were men, particularly prisoners of war and detainees, although women and children were also affected, mainly in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
"Sexual violence in conflict is often misunderstood to be mainly affecting women and girls, whereas in the Ukraine war context, the majority of survivors are men," Danielle Bell, head of the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said.
"And men and women require different solutions and approaches to their recovery," she said.
The report concluded that Russia had failed to take steps to prevent, investigate or prosecute sexual violence committed by its personnel and had not engaged with requests for information from the U.N. Human Rights Office.
In Ukrainian government-controlled territory, nearly half of the violations attributed to Ukrainian authorities against Russian and third-country prisoners of war and detainees involved threats of sexual violence and beatings to the genitals.
The U.N. Human Rights Office said it did not document any cases of rape of Russian prisoners of war by Ukrainian forces.
The office said Russian and third-country prisoners of war reported sexual violence at 10 official detention facilities and 55 unofficial or transit locations.
The Ukrainian government had taken some steps to prevent such violations and cooperated with requests from the U.N. Human Rights Office, although efforts to ensure accountability remained limited, the report said.
"I am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine," U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said.

U.S. Army buys Ukrainian Raybird unmanned aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:38:14 UTC
20:38:14 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Skyeton Inc., the American subsidiary of Ukrainian drone maker Skyeton, a $10.6 million contract for Raybird unmanned aircraft.
- Raybird has logged more than 350,000 combat flight hours in Ukraine and can fly nearly 28 hours and 2,500 km on a single mission.
The U.S. Army has awarded a $10.6 million contract for Raybird unmanned aircraft hardware and services to Skyeton Inc., the American arm of Skyeton, a Ukrainian company that has spent the past several years proving the drone in combat over Ukraine.
Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, issued the firm-fixed-price contract after soliciting bids online and receiving just one, from Skyeton. The contract doesn’t specify a delivery location or exact funding upfront; both will be determined as individual orders are placed against it, with an estimated completion date of Dec. 15, 2026.
Raybird is a small, fixed-wing surveillance drone built for long missions rather than speed or firepower. It can stay airborne for close to 28 hours at a stretch, fly more than 2,500 km (1,550 miles) without landing, and operate at altitudes up to 5,500 meters (18,000 feet), carrying a sensor payload of 5 to 10 kilograms (11 to 22 pounds). The airframe is rated to work in temperatures ranging from minus 35°C to 55°C (minus 31°F to 131°F), a range meant to cover everything from Arctic cold to desert heat.
Skyeton was founded in Ukraine in 2006, originally building light sport aircraft before shifting toward unmanned systems. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Raybird has flown more than 350,000 combat hours for Ukrainian forces, mostly on long-range reconnaissance missions, and the company has marketed that record as evidence of low attrition rates and resilience against electronic jamming.
The Army contract adds the United States to a growing list of countries showing interest in the platform. Skyeton has formed a joint venture with British firm Prevail Partners, called Skyeton Prevail Solutions, to manufacture Raybird for NATO markets and to compete for a contract to replace the British Army’s aging Watchkeeper drone. The company has also partnered with French sensor maker Harmattan AI to integrate AI-driven payloads onto the aircraft, and sells Raybird in Poland through a local distributor. In the past year, Skyeton has added satellite communications to the system to remove range limits on its data link, and it has been testing a hydrogen fuel cell version of the aircraft in combat conditions in Ukraine since December 2025.
This appears to be among the first confirmed contracts putting Raybird directly into U.S. Army hands, following its adoption by Ukraine’s own military and growing interest from the UK and Poland. The Army has not said how many Raybird systems the $10.6 million will buy, which unit will operate them, or where the aircraft will ultimately be delivered.

French channel apologizes after depicting nuclear strike on Tel Aviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:33:32 UTC
20:33:32 KST

French television channel RMC Découverte publicly apologized and removed a documentary about the future of French weaponry from all its platforms after it emerged that a 3D simulation used to illustrate a future nuclear strike actually depicted Tel Aviv as the target.
The documentary, “Nouveau Rafale, drones et canons: la révolution dans l'armement français” — “New Rafale, Drones and Cannons: The Revolution in French Weaponry” — aired Sept. 1 and examined the next generation of French weapons systems, including the Rafale F5 fighter jet and the future ASN4G hypersonic nuclear missile, which is designed to be launched from the aircraft.
The missile, which reports say could be 10 to 20 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb and have a range of more than 1,000 kilometers, does not yet exist operationally. According to the Brussels Signal website, France’s defense procurement agency, the DGA, commissioned its development in early June with the aim of introducing it into service around 2035.
To illustrate the weapon’s capabilities, the documentary used a 3D simulation showing a fighter jet launching a missile toward a coastal city, followed by a nuclear mushroom cloud rising above it.
According to Libération, French researcher Héloïse Fayet, who specializes in nuclear issues at the French Institute of International Relations, identified the city in the simulation as Tel Aviv rather than a fictional location and alerted the channel.
An independent Jewish-owned production company involved in making the documentary had taken the explosion footage from a video game, apparently without realizing the location depicted.
On Sept. 18, RMC Découverte posted a statement on X, rather than on its official website, saying it was “immediately removing the documentary from all its platforms” and “suspending any further broadcast.”
The channel explicitly acknowledged that the simulation “uses an image of Tel Aviv” in Israel rather than a fictional city and offered its “sincere apologies” to viewers.
According to the broadcaster, the clip “came from a professional image database, which incorrectly identified and cataloged it.”
The channel added that it would consider “any appropriate legal action against those responsible for the error” and said a corrected version of the documentary, without the disputed segment, would be released later.
The apology came about 17 days after the original broadcast, which was watched by about 241,000 viewers, according to figures published in France.
Israel’s ambassador to France, Joshua “Yosh” Zarka, brought wider attention to the incident when he shared the clip on X, describing it as “an animated demonstration of a French nuclear strike on Tel Aviv.” He also noted that the explosion shown was significantly less powerful than the yield attributed to the ASN4G missile.
Zarka said, however, that he did not believe there had been malicious intent behind the use of Tel Aviv in the simulation.
The film’s director, Alex Gary, said he was “deeply shocked” by the incident. He said the description accompanying the clip in the image database did not indicate at any point that it depicted a real city or a location in Israel and that, had he known, he would not have included the simulation.
By then, however, the footage had already circulated and was amplified by figures hostile to Israel.

U.S. Navy secures long-term support for EMALS catapult system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:33:11 UTC
20:33:11 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Kato Engineering a $49.3 million sustainment contract for the EMALS Energy Storage Subsystem aboard Ford-class carriers.
- The contract covers repairs, technical support and parts sourcing through September 2031 for a system that has struggled with reliability since its debut.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Kato Engineering a $49.3 million contract to keep maintaining the power system behind the electromagnetic catapults on its Ford-class aircraft carriers, covering engineering support, repairs and spare-parts sourcing through 2031.
The contract covers the Energy Storage Subsystem of the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System, or EMALS, the technology that replaced traditional steam catapults on the Navy’s newest carriers. Kato Engineering, based in North Mankato, Minnesota, will handle most of the work at its home plant, with smaller shares performed in Portsmouth, Virginia, and Lakehurst, New Jersey. The contract structure is an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity agreement, meaning the Navy will issue individual task orders as needs arise rather than pay the full amount upfront, and no money has been obligated yet. Naval Air Systems Command awarded the deal without competition, since Kato built the original hardware and remains the only source with the technical knowledge to sustain it.
EMALS uses a linear induction motor and stored electrical energy instead of steam pressure to fling aircraft off a carrier’s deck. The Energy Storage Subsystem is the part that makes that possible: a motor generator, a control tower and a power supply that together store energy and then release up to 60 megajoules, or 60 megawatts at peak, in the roughly two to three seconds it takes to launch a jet. That burst of power is comparable to what it would take to run thousands of homes for an instant. Each Ford-class carrier needs 12 of these units, since its four catapults share several energy storage and power conversion systems rather than each having its own dedicated set.
Kato has built these motor generators since the system’s earliest testing, completing the first full-size unit for factory acceptance testing back in 2008. EMALS first went to sea aboard USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78), and it took years of software tuning and hardware fixes to work through reliability problems that dogged the system early on. In 2022, the Pentagon’s testing office found EMALS was falling well short of its reliability target, managing only around 600 launch cycles between failures against a goal of more than 4,000. The Navy and General Atomics, EMALS’s original developer, have continued refining the system since then, and reliability figures have improved as more carriers and more flight hours accumulate.
This new contract focuses specifically on keeping the fielded system running rather than fixing design flaws, covering ongoing maintenance, technical support, and the tricky problem of sourcing parts for components that may fall out of production over the system’s service life. That work matters more as the Ford class grows: USS Gerald R. Ford is already in service, USS John F. Kennedy (CVN 79) is in the fitting-out stage, and USS Enterprise (CVN 80) and USS Doris Miller (CVN 81) are both under construction, putting the Navy on track to operate four EMALS-equipped carriers by the early 2030s.

Three questions to ask to find out if its really love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:31:09 UTC
20:31:09 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at the Buddhist philosophy of laziness with Tulku Lobsang Rinpoche. Paid members can find the full version here.
On Monday, I spoke with a reincarnated Lama.
That’s a sentence to invite an eyebrow raise and a bit of old-fashioned self-analysis. For one, it’s made me appreciate how lucky I am to do what I do. To speak with a Tibetan Buddhist master on Monday and a cognitive scientist on Friday is a rare and wonderful thing. But it’s also made me aware of just how little I know about philosophical schools outside my niche.
I’ve spent decades studying mostly the Greek to Roman to European to American philosophical tradition. Everything else is kind of an embarrassing darkness. It’s like having a house and living only in one room. This room has all the lights on, pictures on the walls, and all the fluffy pillows you’d like. But all the other rooms are hidden behind locked doors.
Well, this week I unlocked a door. I interviewed Buddhist master Tulku Lobsang Rinpoche with the intention of exploring the other rooms in the house, and it was a joy. I don’t know if it’s Rinpoche’s ability to teach so well or something structural to Buddhism itself, but everything is presented in neat, numbered packages: “Three roads to enlightenment,” “Three kinds of laziness,” or “Four kinds of liars.”
Buddhism is a content creator’s dream. Hook the audience, pull them along, and give them an actionable mnemonic to wear on their belts. And here I have selected one of the best. Today, we look at “the three elements of love.”
Go well,
Jonny
The loving cure-all
There’s a particularly saccharine quote I’m rather fond of: “If you love someone, set them free. If they come back, they’re yours; if they don’t, they never were.”
It might look good plastered all over Facebook, but it’s also got philosophical pedigree. It’s there in Plato, Aristotle, and Seneca, all the way up to Simone Weil, Erich Fromm, and Iris Murdoch. Of course, these names are all firmly inside my wheelhouse. They live as books on the shelf in that well-lit room of my house. It turns out that Buddhism has a similar but subtly different angle to offer.
Rinpoche argues that there is a difference between attachment and love. Attachment is when we cling to another person. We get possessive of them. We get jealous. We don’t give them space. But for Rinpoche, love is something else entirely. And he told me that the love of another involves three things.
First, there is kindness. Rinpoche frames all of these elements of love as “antidotes” to something that wears us down. Love is a force that cures the “three poisons” of Buddhism that often cause us to suffer. And kindness is seen as the antidote to anger. Because we get angry when we feel people are out to get us.
Imagine you’re in the shop and someone barges into you. You turn around, angrily thinking someone has wronged you. You’re ready to be furious at an aggressive lout. But then you see an embarrassed 7-year-old pushing a shopping cart. Your anger dissipates.
Anger is often about perceived offense, and kindness is what sees people not as obstacles or as enemies, but as allies. Kindness softens the way we look at others’ intentions. It assumes it was a mistake rather than malice, and asks what someone might be struggling with before grumpily assuming they are out to get us.
Second, there is compassion. Compassion is the antidote to attachment, because attachment is what holds people too tightly. Attachment is what keeps the bird in the cage.
Compassion, though, gives somebody space. It allows them to make mistakes, to be imperfect, and to try something new. In a lot of relationships, we become attached to a certain version of a person. It might be the person we first met at the start of a relationship or an idealized, disconnected image we hold of them in our heads. But compassion gives someone the room to change into somebody different from what we might have expected of them. Love allows the other to move forward on their own terms and not according to some rat’s maze we’ve constructed for them.
Third, there is bodhicitta. Rinpoche describes bodhicitta as the antidote to ignorance, and it’s a great way to understand the idea. Because it is ignorant to try to understand the world from only your point of view. It is ignorant to assume the limits of your mind are the limits of the world. As Francis Bacon put it, when you spend your life living in a cave, it’s poor philosophy to assume that is all there is. The limits of your cave are not the limits of the universe. My reading philosophy in one room is not the same as learning all philosophy.
Bodhicitta accepts this and seeks to see things not only from another point of view but, in love, from another person’s point of view. It tries to see the world with their eyes, to understand their needs, and to experience things from their position. For example, I will often get irritated at my wife for leaving things too late. It takes 30 minutes to get to a 2 p.m. meeting, so why is she still getting changed at 1:40 p.m.?! Bodhicitta is what puts me in her shoes — or, more precisely, into her bare feet as she frantically looks about for her shoes that our eldest has hidden under the kitchen sink.
And so, the question of love actually comes down to three different questions:
Do I see them in the best possible light?
Do I give them enough space?
And do I see the world from their position?
Because love is not about desperately clinging to somebody or seeking your own happiness in somebody else. It’s when you find your own joy in the joy of another. It’s when you make a home into the room that they live in.
IN A QUOTE
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

Hungary's "punishment" for Ukraine: how Magyar aims to humiliate Kyiv and block its EU future
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:30:00 EEST
20:30:00 KST

Hungary's "punishment" for Ukraine: how Magyar aims to humiliate Kyiv and block its EU future
On 18 September, Ukraine hosted the inaugural Carpathian Initiative summit, which brought together leaders or senior officials from all the countries linked by the Carpathian mountain range: Ukraine, Poland, Slovakia, Romania, Serbia, Czechia and Austria. Only one country was missing – Hungary. To meet with presidents and prime ministers, Hungary sent... a deputy ambassador.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar did not simply ignore the event.
It appears that while preparations were still underway, Budapest attempted to humiliate Kyiv and provoke a reaction, while Ukrainian officials tried to defuse the conflict.
Unfortunately, these events reflect Hungary's new policy.
A demonstrative contempt for Ukraine is at its centre.
The main tool of this policy remains the artificial crisis in relations that was created under former prime minister Viktor Orbán. While Magyar's government publicly declares its intention to restore good-neighbourly relations with Ukraine, it is actually cementing the problems that have built up over time.
Magyar's government policy is also punishing the Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia, firstly by blocking their path towards EU membership, and secondly by creating obstacles to the passing of laws the minority needs.
The lack of political dialogue with Hungary means Kyiv has no realistic scenarios for resolving this crisis. The only hope is that European and US partners will be able to convince Magyar to change his policy.
Instead of thanks, a diplomatic slap in the face
Two weeks ago, experts, politicians and diplomats working on Ukrainian-Hungarian relations had an excellent reason to be optimistic.
The Ukrainian parliament became the first parliament in the world to officially condemn the repression of Hungarians during the Soviet era. This crime, known in Hungary as "málenkij robot" (from the Russian for "little work"), was committed after the end of World War II. Hundreds of thousands of Hungarians, most of them civilians, were deported to the Soviet Union for forced labour. Tens of thousands never returned home, dying in camps, on the way, or in other circumstances.
Residents of Zakarpattia were also affected by these actions, so condemning the Soviet repression was an entirely logical step for the Ukrainian parliament.
The timing of the decision regarding "málenkij robot" was no accident. Ruslan Stefanchuk, speaker of the Ukrainian parliament, was preparing to visit Budapest and wanted to create a diplomatic bargaining chip that could help thaw relations with Ukraine's neighbour.
But no one could have imagined what Hungary's response would be.
The speaker of the Hungarian parliament, Ágnes Forsthoffer, refused to meet with her Ukrainian counterpart while he was in the country. And so did every other Hungarian official. A few days later, Stefanchuk happened to be in Budapest again on his way home from a G7 meeting, and once again, no one was available to meet him.
Despite these actions by his counterparts, the Ukrainian speaker decided not to escalate the conflict. In a comment to European Pravda, his office emphasised that they were continuing to work on arranging a meeting. However, they also pointed out that Forsthoffer herself had invited her Ukrainian counterpart, only to later refuse to meet with him.
Stefanchuk’s spokesperson Vadym Kolodiichuk told European Pravda: "The Ukrainian and Hungarian teams are actively working on arranging the first meeting between the Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada and the Speaker of the National Assembly of Hungary, Ágnes Forsthoffer. We are grateful to the Hungarian side for their official invitation to visit Budapest. At the same time, we are ready to welcome Ágnes Forsthoffer in Kyiv or any other Ukrainian city, subject to mutual agreement."
Members of parliament who spoke with European Pravda off the record tended to be harsher in their assessments, describing the situation as a "slap in the face" from Budapest.
But what happened next is even more striking.
How Magyar is avoiding reaching agreements with Ukraine
A popular explanation in Budapest is that the two leaders, Zelenskyy and Magyar, should meet first.
European Pravda sources had also expressed hopes that the Hungarian prime minister would attend the Carpathian Initiative summit. The thinking was that this was why Forsthoffer, who has no authority over foreign policy, had been unwilling to meet.
These explanations are contrary to the rules of diplomacy. On the contrary, if a leaders’ meeting is to be successful, it needs to be prepared for in advance. The fundamental agreements are worked out first, and the leaders then meet to settle politically sensitive details. Given that decisions by the Verkhovna Rada will be required to resolve the crisis in relations with Hungary, a meeting between the parliamentary speakers would have been appropriate.
That said, Magyar does often act contrary to established rules and conventional logic.
But the main problem is that he isn’t just avoiding meetings with Ukraine.
The Carpathian Initiative summit provided a vivid example.
European Pravda is aware that negotiations with Budapest over Magyar’s attendance at the summit had been going on for quite some time. Several sources claim that only two days before the summit began, the Hungarian prime minister’s office had still not said whether he would be travelling to Ukraine. Then an upcoming trip to the Hungarian city of Pécs was announced on Magyar’s Facebook page that would have been impossible to fit in if he had been visiting Ukraine as scheduled.
All previous attempts to arrange a meeting also failed.
Since the beginning of the summer, Magyar has rejected numerous proposals from Kyiv for a meeting – in Budapest, Brussels, Lviv and elsewhere. Twice, Zelenskyy has caught up with Magyar in person at multilateral international events – the EU and NATO summits. Magyar promised to agree to a full-fledged meeting, but then nothing came of it.
This rather undermines Budapest’s official explanation that the speaker, Ágnes Forsthoffer, was reluctant to meet because she wanted to give priority to Magyar.
It looks more like Budapest is avoiding any political dialogue with Ukraine.
It also looks as if they are trying to humiliate the Ukrainian government.
Forsthoffer is generally not very active in foreign policy, and up until this week she had not held a single meeting with speakers of other countries’ parliaments in Budapest. So technically it could have been argued that that was the reason for her reluctance to meet with Stefanchuk, despite Ukraine’s gesture ahead of his visit.
But two days before the Carpathian summit, a signal came from Budapest: no, this had been a targeted refusal specifically aimed at Ukraine. To prove the point, the speaker of Moldova’s parliament, Igor Grosu, was invited to Budapest to meet with Forsthoffer.
Moldova is not a priority partner for Hungary. Inviting Grosu was apparently intended as a signal or even a slap in the face for Ukraine.
Hungary is the only EU member state that is advocating for Moldova and Ukraine to be decoupled as they progress towards EU membership. It has proposed several times that the EU open the next negotiating clusters for Moldova while freezing the process for Ukraine.
European Pravda sources say that Kyiv got the message.
A veto without conditions
The biggest problem is that Hungary is blocking EU membership for Ukraine without clearly stating what Kyiv needs to do for the veto to be lifted.
The blockade is just there, and no one knows how to bring it to an end.
That is precisely why meetings between senior officials – whether parliamentary speakers or heads of government – are necessary: so that the two sides can understand each other’s positions and find a way out of the crisis. Hungary is doing everything it can to prevent such a dialogue from taking place.
Moreover, even in the EU negotiations, Hungary avoids being specific about what it demands of Ukraine. All we hear is that Ukraine has to "show progress" in implementing agreements on minority rights. Yet we are currently on track for reviewing legislative changes according to a schedule that was agreed on with the Hungarians. For example, in September we submitted a draft on implementing the agreements in the field of education to the European Commission and the Hungarian side.
In other words, Ukraine is fulfilling its commitments, whereas Hungary, which promised back in June to unblock all the clusters, is breaking that promise.
The veto remains in place, just as it was under Orbán, with no explanations and no dialogue whatsoever.
That’s the most shocking part.
Last spring Hungary got rid of Viktor Orbán, who had been moving further into Russia’s orbit (while his foreign minister, Péter Szijjártó, was openly carrying out the Kremlin’s wishes and leaking information from closed EU meetings to Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov).
Magyar, who replaced him, emphasises his opposition to Russia...
But when it comes to Ukraine, his actions often differ little from those of his predecessor.
The shadow of Orbán over the new government
What is Péter Magyar’s true objective? That question remains unanswered. The explanations offered by Hungarian politicians and diplomats do not seem convincing.
In Budapest they claim that Magyar is constrained by public opinion, which is largely negative towards Ukraine. It’s true that after years of Orbán’s propaganda machine, anti-Ukraine prejudices have become entrenched among many Hungarians, and it will take years to overcome them.
But that doesn’t explain the logic behind these actions. Is Magyar really planning to wait five, seven or even 10 years before the next negotiating clusters are opened? Or is this just a convenient excuse?
What’s more, Hungary has already enabled two clusters to be opened for Ukraine (Cluster 1 in June and Cluster 6 in July) without any political or reputational losses ensuing for the government – in fact Magyar’s approval ratings went up. Nor has this been a particularly noticeable topic in Hungary’s domestic political debates or a source of criticism within the country.
Ukraine has its own version of events, which was recently outlined by Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry. "Even after losing power, Orbán’s team continues to undermine the normalisation of relations between Hungary and Ukraine," he said.
Indeed, the Hungarian leadership may have changed, but Orbán’s people are still influential.
Hungary’s ambassador to the EU is still Bálint Ódor, who was appointed by openly pro-Russian minister Péter Szijjártó. So it’s not surprising that Hungary’s representation in Brussels should continue Orbán’s longstanding policy with respect to Ukraine: block, block and block. There have been no changes at the Hungarian embassy in Kyiv. Nor has the Hungarian Foreign Ministry replaced the diplomats responsible for Ukraine.
Despite this, Péter Magyar personally bears political responsibility for the course that has been set.
It was he who chose a policy that, in effect, aims to "punish" Hungarians in Ukraine.
You don’t need to be a Hungarian expert on Ukrainian affairs to understand that ostentatious slaps in the face and gestures of contempt towards the Ukrainian parliament is not going to help secure the adoption of the minority rights legislation that Ukraine is planning to approve as part of its pre-accession agreements.
And ultimately, how does it benefit the Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia if Péter Magyar continues to block Ukraine’s path towards EU membership?
How to resolve the crisis in relations
There is only one avenue of influence over Magyar that could realistically produce results: pressure from Western partners.
After Orbán, who was pretty much seen as "absolute evil", Péter Magyar was initially viewed positively in the EU. But as time has passed, more and more questions have been raised about him. His dismissive policy towards Ukraine, his seemingly arbitrary blocking of Ukraine’s EU aspirations and his deliberate gestures of disrespect should all change how Western partners view the Hungarian government.
There is hope that this will be understood in Berlin and Warsaw – the two European capitals that matter most to Magyar – as well as in the EU institutions in Brussels, and in Washington.
The United States remains highly influential with the Hungarian leadership, particularly following the passing of the Lindsey Graham bill, which will penalise buyers of Russian energy – one of which is Hungary. It is no coincidence that one of Magyar’s close advisers, National Assembly member Márton Hajdu, rushed to Washington this week.
At the same time, Péter Magyar’s policy on Ukraine is damaging to Donald Trump’s peace initiatives.
All proposals for ending the war include EU membership for Ukraine as one of the key elements of the postwar order and security guarantees. Yet Magyar is doing all he can to make this impossible.
The reasons for his actions remain unclear. Is the Hungarian prime minister simply making mistakes because of his inexperience? Is he, contrary to logic, genuinely afraid of how voters will react? Is the influence of Orbán’s "deep state" the decisive factor? Or is there some other explanation? It’s impossible to say.
What is clear is that Magyar’s policy on Ukraine is harmful to Ukraine, Hungarians, Europe and the United States alike.
This needs to end at some point. But without help from Western partners, it will be difficult to find a way out of the deadlock.
Ukraine also needs to be careful not to make mistakes of its own along the way.
Kyiv’s initial reaction to Hungary’s deliberate insults may be a desire to respond in kind – to block progress on minority rights legislation, for example.
But that would amount to Ukraine shooting itself in the foot.
Magyar’s current policy notwithstanding, Ukraine will still have to fulfil its commitments on minority rights as it moves towards EU membership – otherwise, Romania and Bulgaria could join Hungary in raising objections. Kyiv’s strategy, therefore, should be to implement the agreements in such a way as to leave Hungary without legitimate grounds for its objections once other Western capitals begin to apply pressure.
If this path is chosen, rebuilding trust will become possible, step by step. For example, negotiating the gradual opening of additional clusters alongside progress on the relevant legislation.
But given the deep crisis of trust, this process needs to be coordinated. Contact and meetings are necessary, including at the highest level.
The problem is that one side is opposed to finding a way out of the crisis. That side is Péter Magyar’s government.
Sergiy Sydorenko
Editor, European Pravda

Lockheed gets $76.6M for next-gen of Trident II nuclear missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:29:32 UTC
20:29:32 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed Martin a $76.6 million contract modification for continued design work on the next-generation Trident II D5LE2 nuclear missile.
- The program aims to keep the submarine-launched missile in service through roughly 2084, arming the future Columbia-class and Dreadnought-class submarines.
The U.S. Navy has added $76.6 million to a Lockheed Martin contract for continued design work on the next generation of the Trident II D5 nuclear missile, part of a long-term effort meant to keep the submarine-launched weapon in service into the 2080s.
The modification adds to an existing contract with Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office that manages the country’s submarine-launched nuclear deterrent, and covers advanced design and development work under the Trident II D5 Life Extension 2 program, known as D5LE2. Lockheed Martin’s Titusville, Florida division will lead the effort, though the work itself is spread across more than a dozen locations, with Denver, Colorado handling 51 percent, followed by smaller shares in Elkton, Maryland; Montville, New Jersey; Greeneville, Tennessee; and Cape Canaveral, Florida, among others. The Navy is obligating the full $76.6 million now from fiscal 2026 weapons procurement funds, with work scheduled to run through Sept. 30, 2030. The award was not competitively bid, a legal option the Navy can use for specialized defense work, and only one company submitted a proposal after the opportunity was posted publicly.
Trident II D5 missiles form the sea-based leg of the U.S. nuclear triad, the three-part system of submarines, land-based missiles and bomber aircraft that has underpinned American nuclear deterrence for decades. The missile first entered service in 1990 and went through its first major refresh, called D5LE, in 2017. This second life extension effort is meant to keep the weapon effective for decades beyond that, with the Navy targeting continued service through roughly 2084, nearly a century after the missile’s original design.
The current Trident II D5 weighs about 130,000 pounds (59,000 kilograms), can fly roughly 4,000 nautical miles (7,400 km), and reaches speeds reported to exceed Mach 20. It currently arms the Navy’s Ohio-class submarines and Britain’s Royal Navy Vanguard-class boats, both of which are approaching retirement. The D5LE2 version being developed now is intended to carry over onto the submarines replacing them, the Navy’s incoming Columbia-class and the Royal Navy’s future Dreadnought-class, making this a joint U.S.-U.K. modernization effort rather than a purely American one.
The program has moved forward in stages. The Navy first awarded Lockheed a $383 million contract in January 2025 to begin D5LE2 design and development, followed by an $850 million contract modification announced in April 2026 to continue that work. Lockheed is separately building a roughly 225,000-square-foot (20,900-square-meter) production facility in Titusville expected to open in 2027, while the Navy is constructing its own 130,000-square-foot Engineering Test Facility at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, one of 28 facility projects the Naval Ordnance Test Unit plans to complete between 2024 and 2032 to support the missile’s development and testing.
Even as the newer version moves through design work, the current fleet of missiles remains active. The Navy conducted four unarmed Trident II D5LE test flights from an Ohio-class submarine off the coast of Florida in September 2025, a demonstration officials said confirmed the continued readiness of the sea-based deterrent while the next generation is still years from completion.
