Samsung Galaxy Watch9 Review: I Don’t Need Another Health Score
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:08:00 UTC
19:08:00 KST

This past summer, Samsung launched the Galaxy Watch9 alongside the Galaxy Watch Ultra2, its more rugged, shock-resistant smartwatch for outdoor adventures.
The Watch9 is the everyday option, and it’s a solid smartwatch and fitness tracker with a plethora of health features. It’s available in a 40-mm size in cream and graphite, and a 44-mm size in graphite and silver, starting at $80. Compared with last year’s Galaxy Watch8, it’s a modest update, though. There’s a faster processor, a slightly larger battery capacity, and an expanded suite of wellness metrics.
After two weeks of testing the 40-mm model, I wouldn’t necessarily upgrade to the Watch9 from the Watch8. But if you have an older Galaxy Watch or you’re invested in Samsung’s ecosystem and are looking for a smartwatch, the Watch9 is the best choice.
A Familiar (Squircle) Face
The Galaxy Watch’s main hardware update is its new processor. It now utilizes Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform, which Samsung claims enhances CPU and GPU performance along with efficiency. In testing, the watch responded smoothly when scrolling menus, launching apps, and dismissing notifications.
Wear OS 7 also adds more customizable widgets and live updates from compatible apps. One of the more exciting new additions is raise-to-talk for Gemini. Lift your wrist toward your mouth, and you can start talking to Google’s AI assistant. The Google Pixel Watch has had this feature for two generations now, so I’m happy to see Samsung finally catch up.
Samsung has also slightly increased the battery capacity. The 40-mm model has a 390-mAh battery (up from 325 mAh), while the 44-mm models get a 445-mAh cell (up from 435 mAh). Unfortunately, that doesn’t translate to an improvement in battery life, which is probably because it’s being used to power the watch’s expanded suite of health features (more on that later). Samsung still estimates up to 30 hours of battery life, but I averaged closer to 25 hours with Always-On Display enabled. That’s enough to get through a full day and night, but not enough to make charging something you can forget about. A full recharge also took me about 100 minutes on average, which is significantly longer than the 45 minutes it takes the Pixel Watch 5 to reach a full charge.

Man targeted in village shooting arrested over cocaine shipment

Man targeted in village shooting arrested over cocaine shipment
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The man whose farmhouse was besieged by dozens of gunmen in a suspected drugs feud has been arrested in Germany, Dutch media report.
German police said a 28-year-old man was detained in a car park in Soest, 150km beyond the Dutch border in North Rhine-Westphalia, on suspicion of trying to smuggle nearly four tonnes of cocaine through the French port of Dunkirk.
NOS quoted sources saying the suspect was Jan G., who is believed to have been the target of a group of heavily armed men who killed a security guard and injured two police officers in a shoot-out in Overasselt, Gelderland, three weeks ago.
Police traced G. in the wake of the shooting, as well as another man who was arrested in Dordrecht a week ago in connection with the drugs shipment.
French customs officers said the cocaine, with an estimated value of €225 mln, was concealed among plastic waste in a container from Ghana.
The Telegraaf reported that the shipment belonged to Jos Leijdekkers, known as “Bolle Jos”, the Dutch drugs baron at the top of Europol’s list of most wanted fugitives. The cross-border police force has issued a €200,000 reward for information leading to his capture.
G.’s house was closed on the orders of local mayor Joerie Minses, who also ordered the man to stay out of the village for three months in an attempt to restore order.
Some 33 men of varying nationalities, including Dutch, French, Algerian and Belgian, were arrested in the wake of the shooting on September 1. Six were from the Amsterdam area. Some were caught while hiding in fields or trying to flee the area by car or train.
Judges ordered all but one of the suspects to be detained in custody for the next three months while investigations continue.

Germany cuts energy tax to lower soaring petrol prices

Germany cuts energy tax to lower petrol prices as Merz faces state key elections
Germany will cut taxes on gasoline and diesel by about 17 cents a litre from October, the government said Friday. The move comes ahead of state elections in the capital Berlin and the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania where Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats are expected to be soundly defeated.
The German government has agreed to tax reductions that will cut gasoline prices by €0.17 ($0.1952) a litre in response to soaring fuel prices, people with knowledge of the matter said on Friday.
The move includes a €0.14 cut in the energy tax and an additional €0.03 cut from the sales tax, the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said.
The decision came after Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised this week to offer relief to consumers hit by soaring gasoline prices. It followed extended negotiations between the federal government and state governments over how to finance the cuts.
As the Iran war has helped push benchmark oil prices over $100 a barrel, gasoline prices have become a pressing political issue for Merz, whose approval ratings have plunged to record lows. Earlier this week, the nationwide daily average price for a litre of E10 gasoline hit a record €2.286 ($10 per gallon).
On Sunday, the capital Berlin and the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a sparsely populated and heavily rural region where many people rely on their cars for transport, both go to the polls in elections expected to see Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) heavily punished.

The results will be particularly closely watched after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party came near to winning an absolute majority in a separate election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the incumbent state premier Manuela Schwesig has accused Merz's government of standing by while fuel prices surge, and called for a fuel price cap based on the Luxembourg model of a nationwide maximum.
Earlier this year, the government offered some relief to motorists by reducing the energy tax from May through June, effectively lowering petrol and diesel prices by around 17 cents per litre and there were widespread calls for the cuts to be extended.
The Bild newspaper reported that Berlin is also working on a gasoline price cap that would be contingent on the oil price, with plans subject to talks with the heads of Germany's regional states.

Ukraine Backs Foreign Recruitment Center for National Guard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:03:00 UTC
19:03:00 KST

The Ukrainian government has approved the establishment of a dedicated Recruitment Center for Foreigners and Stateless Persons within the National Guard of Ukraine, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on Friday, Sept. 18.
Speaking on the initiative, Koretskyi stated that the specialized center is designed to centralize and oversee the recruitment pipeline for foreign volunteers seeking contract military service.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The institution will coordinate all administrative and operational phases of accession, managing candidate interviews, background checks, credential verification, and subsequent military training programs.
Koretskyi emphasized that the intake process must be streamlined and accelerated to ensure that vetted volunteers can rapidly reinforce frontline combat units facing persistent Russian pressure.
“Recruiting foreign volunteers to the Defense Forces is one of the state’s priorities. The task is to scale up this work and attract more people to the Ukrainian army who are ready to defend our state together with Ukrainians,” Koretskyi said.
Military contract service
The establishment of the center reflects ongoing efforts by Ukrainian authorities to institutionalize and scale foreign participation within statutory security structures.
While thousands of international volunteers have served across various branches of the Defense Forces since the start of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion – primarily within the International Legion – the new structure within the National Guard aims to formalize intake standards, improve operational vetting, and eliminate administrative delays.
Putin Accuses Ukraine of Sabotaging Peace Negotiations
Under the new operational mandate, the National Guard will work to guide candidates through legal documentation, medical evaluations, and specialized combat instruction before deploying them to operational brigades.
Government officials noted that standardizing the recruitment pipeline will also enhance integration and coordination between foreign personnel and regular Ukrainian units, providing clear contractual guarantees, competitive pay, and medical coverage equivalent to domestic service members.
AWOL simplified return deadline
The push to expand foreign recruitment coincides with broader domestic force replenishment and personnel retention programs across the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
Alongside external recruitment drives, the Ukrainian military is preparing to conclude its temporary simplified return program for service members who left their units without official leave, which is scheduled to close on Sept. 20, according to the General Staff of the AFU.
Military authorities reported that voluntary returns accelerated significantly in late summer, with the number of soldiers returning to active duty in August 2026 exceeding new unauthorized departures.
Under that framework, service members who departed their posts on or before June 12, 2026, are permitted to voluntarily resume active duty with significant procedural flexibility, including the option to choose their preferred military branch, duty station, and operational role while retaining standard pay, allowances, and social protections without facing punitive administrative penalties.
The General Staff highlighted that the simplified return mechanism does not extend to unauthorized departures occurring after the June 12 cutoff date.
Personnel who left their units after that deadline remain subject to standard statutory prosecution under Ukrainian criminal law, underscoring Kyiv’s calibrated balance between enforcing military discipline and recovering trained manpower for frontline operations.

In China, an increasing number of digital face-licensing platforms are connecting ordinary individuals with content creators, enabling them to authorise the use of their likenesses in AI-generated short dramas, advertisements, and games.
Since April, private “face-selling” transactions that once circulated within film and television industry chat groups have progressively transitioned to public platforms.

Among the leading platforms, Shenzhen-based Yuanxiang Xinsheng, launched in May, allows users to create “digital actor profiles” following registration and identity verification.

Navy yet to settle on guns for support ships
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:00:49 BST
19:00:49 KST

Consideration of the most appropriate gun solution for the Fleet Solid Support ships is ongoing, according to a written answer published on Thursday.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what the Royal Navy’s most likely future gun solution is.
Mr Pollard said: “Consideration of the most appropriate gun solution for the Fleet Solid Support ships is ongoing.”
The question followed an answer given on 7 September, in which the minister confirmed that the automatic small calibre gun requirement had been removed from the manufacture contract with Navantia UK at a cost of £1.704 million recorded as a constructive loss, on the basis that it no longer matched the service’s likely future gun solution.
In that earlier reply he described a gun rationalisation programme introduced since the manufacture contract was placed, aimed at reducing the number of gun variants across the fleet and bringing commonality, which he said would provide longer term value for money. He also said at the time that changing the requirement then avoided incurring greater losses later, which would have been associated with fitting and then replacing an incompatible system, and that the ships would be designed to accept a range of future gun systems.
The three Fleet Solid Support ships are being built by Navantia UK to carry ammunition, stores and provisions to the carrier strike group and the wider fleet. Construction is spread across the company’s British facilities, with Harland and Wolff in Belfast having begun work and the Methil yard in Fife having delivered the Seahorse pontoon that will move ship blocks between Appledore and Belfast.
Harland and Wolff completed the installation of eleven new cranes this week, bought for £1.5 million from Walter Watson Ltd of County Down as part of a £98.5 million modernisation of the Belfast yard.

China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:45 UTC
19:00:45 KST

When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China.
“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.
Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.
“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.
The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.
In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.
AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.
As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.
Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.
Amodei’s worst China fears
Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.
Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.
“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.
Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.
“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.
Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.)
But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.
Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.
“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.
Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.
Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.
“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”
Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.
“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”
Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.
“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”
Silicon Valley’s China hawks
Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.
Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.
Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.
“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.
The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.
Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.
“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.
Nuclear considered an option
Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.
“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay.
Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.
Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.
Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.
“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”
The view from China
While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.
As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.
“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.
China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.
“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”
A race to the bottom
While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.
“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.
Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.
“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

Domestic datacentres: how computer power can help heat your home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:44 UTC
19:00:44 KST

‘When Giles Gibson turns on the hot tap in his home, the water that comes out of it is not heated by gas but by the tiny datacentre strapped to the tank.
Attached to the hot water cylinder in his London home is a compact computer server that generates heat and then transfers it as it operates.
Gibson gets the benefit of hot water when he needs it at a reduced cost, while the heat that is generated by the server is not lost into the air, a big environmental problem with large datacentres around the world.
“As soon as I read about it, I thought: ‘This is obvious – why wouldn’t you do this?’”he says. “It just makes sense to take a computer out of a datacentre and to strap it next to your water tank and get free heat.”
Gibson estimates that the hot water bills for his four-bedroom house in south-east London have fallen by between £10 and £15 a month since he had the system installed last year.
“So over a year, it adds up, and it’s just another little extra that helps,” Gibson says. “Having one of these units is a no-brainer.”
Saving waste heat
With domestic energy bills set to rise again next month, and growing disquiet about the impact of large-scale datacentres on the environment, there are lots of projects looking at how to harness the heat being thrown out by computers.
Gibson’s system, supplied by the Surrey-based company heata, is one of a number of innovative ideas on the market that aim to tackle the problem of waste heat on a domestic scale.
Heata operates a sustainable cloud computing business that sends processing jobs from its clients to the servers in people’s homes. The devices have the combined power of about eight laptops.
“What the home gives us is effectively somewhere to put a server that has a power connection, and a fibre connection, and a place for heat to go,” says Charlie Beharrell, commercial director of heata.
He says the company aims to provide about 80% of the heat needed for a home’s hot water. “The water in their hot water cylinder will effectively be heated by our server, and they might have to use the gas boiler for the peakier moments in the day, like when they have a bath,” Beharrell says.
“The idea is that the primary heating system is working a lot less hard to heat the water than it would normally have to do if our system wasn’t in place.”
How it works
It can only work in homes with vented, unpressurised water cylinders, typically recognisable by the blue insulation around the outside.
A container with the server in is attached to the front of the cylinder after engineers cut a hole in the insulation.
It is glued to the boiler with a thermal paste so the unit can conduct heat to the cylinder with no plumbing involved. There is no cost for the installation.
“It takes a couple of hours and we retrofit it to the domestic water system,” Beharrell says.
Heata pays for the electricity that is used to keep the server running, while the homeowner pays for the fibre broadband connection that is necessary.
Beharrell says that millions of homes are fitted with vented water cylinders, while the units can also work with heat pumps.
However, the system is not suitable for homes with combi boilers. A version for unvented cylinders is in development.
Heata’s units are now in 100 homes and there are 3,000 people on the waiting list for installation.
Anyone interested in having one can sign up on the company’s website, heata.co.
The company says hundreds more are expected to be installed next year.
Easy as Raspberry Pi?
In a separate project in Essex, two households are testing a concept where almost 500 matchbox-sized computers are stored together to form a mini datacentre, and the heat generated from them is converted into energy.
The freezer-sized HeatHub units are made by the Wales-based company thermify and, like heata’s, also recycle the energy created when computers process tasks.
They work differently from the heata system and the makers say they could one day replace domestic boilers.
The heat created by the rows of Raspberry Pi computers warms a mineral oil that surrounds them.
“The computers get the mineral oil hot,” says thermify’s chief executive, Travis Theune. “We send that through a heat exchanger. The heat exchanger heats up the water that’s going through a radiator, and the radiator delivers heat to the room. It’s the same basic concept as an induction heater.”
The existing units have 480 computers in them, which carry out tasks for companies that buy time to process the work they want done.
Theune says that the company plans to make a range of units to cater for different-sized homes. For example, a three- to four-bedroom house will have a unit which is about the size of a washing machine, while a flat could have one the size of a microwave.
He says that the thermify systems will cost homeowners £90 a month, based on an average-sized home. A bigger house, that requires more energy, will cost more, and a flat less, he says.
The planned cost includes installation, leasing the unit, repairs, and will have a minimum 10-year contract.
The company claims that the device will lead to a 14% reduction in bill costs compared with homes with a gas boiler, and 34% for those households with a heat pump, over a 15-year period.
The savings come from not having to pay for the installation of a boiler or the heat pump.

Musical compatibility often outshines personality matching in romantic couples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:26 UTC
19:00:26 KST

Sharing a favorite band with a romantic partner might mean more than just having an easy time picking out a concert to attend. A recent study published in Social Psychological and Personality Science suggests that romantic couples share much more similar musical tastes than they do personality traits or personal values. The research indicates that a shared love for specific artists is modestly associated with better relationship quality.
In psychological research, musical preferences refer to the specific genres, styles, and artists that a person habitually enjoys listening to. These preferences are more than just entertainment habits; they act as a reflection of an individual’s psychological makeup, emotional regulation strategies, and personal identity. People routinely use music as a social signal to communicate who they are to others.
Past research indicates that individuals use musical taste to size up potential partners and form initial bonds. For instance, a 2006 study found that music is the most common topic of conversation when young adults get to know each other, functioning as a shortcut to judge someone’s personality. Another study demonstrated that discovering a shared taste in music promotes attraction by signaling similar underlying values.
At the same time, relationship scientists have mapped out how couples match across various psychological traits. A 2023 meta-analysis showed that romantic partners tend to be similar across dozens of behavioral and physical traits. Yet sharing those traits might not actually guarantee happiness. In fact, a 2025 study covered by PsyPost found that actual similarity in personality or personal interests has surprisingly weak and inconsistent links to relationship satisfaction.
Bridging these two areas of research, Julia Vigl and Marcel Zentner of the Music, Emotion, Assessment, and Personality Lab at the University of Innsbruck designed a new project. The researchers wanted to test whether real couples actually share musical tastes to a greater degree than they share personality traits or values. They also sought to determine whether a musical match genuinely predicts how happy a couple is in their relationship.
“We know quite a lot about similarity between romantic partners in personality, values, and other personal characteristics, but much less about similarity in aesthetic preferences,” Zentner, a professor for personality psychology and psychological assessment, told PsyPost. “Music seemed particularly interesting because it is such an important part of how people express themselves and connect with others.”
“Several years ago, I conducted a side-project that suggested an association between similarity in music preferences and relationship satisfaction,” he added. “Julia and I then decided to take up this question again in a more rigorous way.”
To investigate this, the researchers conducted three separate studies involving a total of 309 couples, primarily from Germany and Austria, who independently completed several questionnaires. They rated their preferences for different musical genres and listed their specific favorite and least favorite artists. The researchers used online social tags to categorize these artists, allowing them to measure stylistic overlap even if the partners listed different bands. The participants also filled out standard assessments of their personality traits, personal values, and relationship satisfaction.
To figure out if the couples were more similar than random chance would dictate, the scientists compared the real couples to pseudo-couples. These pseudo-couples were created by randomly pairing up participants from the dataset into artificial relationships. By comparing the real partners to these shuffled pairs, the researchers could measure exactly how much of a couple’s similarity was due to their specific romantic bond rather than just broader cultural trends.
In the first study, which included 99 relatively young couples, the data showed a strong pattern. The real couples were far more alike in their music preferences than the random pairings. This musical overlap was much larger than their similarity in personality traits or personal values. Matching on personality and values had no reliable link to relationship quality, but sharing favorite artists was associated with a modest increase in relationship tenderness.
The second study included 99 couples with a wider age range and longer relationship durations. The researchers used slightly different questionnaires to measure personality and values, but the core findings remained the same. Couples consistently demonstrated higher similarity in their musical preferences than in their personalities. In this older group, the researchers again found a small positive association between sharing favorite artists and feelings of tenderness, though general relationship satisfaction did not show an overall boost.
In the third study, the researchers tested 111 couples and added measures for specific components of love, such as intimacy, passion, and commitment. They also asked the participants about their musical backgrounds, like whether they played an instrument or how much time they spent listening to music. Even when factoring in whether both partners were musicians, the couples still showed an unusually high similarity in their musical tastes. In this group, sharing least favorite artists was linked to a slight increase in feelings of love and relationship satisfaction.
To make sense of the slight variations across the three studies, the researchers pooled the data from all 309 couples into a combined analysis. This broad look confirmed that romantic partners are highly similar in their musical tastes, far exceeding their similarities in personality or values. “Romantic partners tend to have significantly more similar music preferences than would be expected by chance,” Zentner noted. “We were surprised by how consistently the effect emerged across our studies, and by the fact that similarity in music preferences was substantially greater than similarity in personality and values.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The association between shared music and relationship happiness is fairly small, meaning that having identical playlists does not guarantee a perfect romance. “The difference between couples and randomly paired individuals was fairly substantial for music preferences,” Zentner said. “The association between music similarity and relationship quality, however, was smaller, so shared musical taste is not what makes or breaks relationships but it seems to help a little.”
The couples who volunteered for the research also tended to be highly satisfied in their relationships. This is a common hurdle in psychological research, as happy couples are more likely to volunteer for relationship studies together. The findings might not fully reflect the dynamics of couples who are experiencing conflict or considering a breakup. “Our studies were correlational, so they cannot tell us whether shared musical preferences contribute to relationship quality, whether partners become more similar over time, or whether similar people are simply more likely to choose one another,” Zentner pointed out.
He also emphasized that the results shouldn’t discourage people whose partners have different favorite bands. “Nor do the findings imply that couples with different musical tastes are incompatible.”
Future studies could look at couples over longer periods of time to see how musical tastes might shift. It is still an open question whether people seek out partners with similar musical preferences from the beginning, or if their tastes slowly merge as they spend years attending concerts together. “We would like to understand how similarity in musical preferences between romantic partners emerges in the first place,” Zentner explained. “Do people generally prefer potential partners who share their music tastes, and are couples already similar at the beginning of a relationship, or do their preferences become more similar over time?”
To unravel these dynamics, the researchers are planning follow-up investigations. “Finally, we will again explore whether sharing music preferences is associated with relationship satisfaction,” Zentner said. “To address these questions, Julia is conducting an online dating experiment and launching an 18-month longitudinal study of early couples this month.”
The study, “Harmonies of Taste: Shared Music Preferences and Compatibility in Romantic Relationships,” was authored by Julia Vigl, Felix Lene Ihrig, Miriam Greif, and Marcel Zentner.

What 1,000 Women Workers Can Teach Us About Surviving Extreme Heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

On Sept. 2, 2026, the United Nations Environment Program report, Limiting Overshoot, declared that the world has fallen short of keeping global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, and that urgent action is needed to course-correct. That same week, NPR reported that extreme heat killed nearly five times as many people in the United States as official records indicated.
These findings followed two consecutively brutal summers. Death counts from heatwaves across Europe dominated news cycles this year as the continent’s aging infrastructure struggled to cool down. “Heat domes” trapped heat across the United States.
But merely counting deaths from heat risks missing its impact on human life. Each heat dome in the U.S. affected over 100 million people. Among them were construction workers, outdoor workers, delivery workers in unairconditioned cabs, farm workers, the unhoused, the poor who could not afford air conditioning, those on medications on whom the impact of heat was amplified, those with mental health disorders, and those with little or no access to healthcare.
According to the International Labor Organization, billions of workers around the world are exposed to extreme heat every year. While the vast majority of them do not die, many suffer deeply from the arduous ignominy of a life exposed to heat, day and night, year after year.
While counting deaths from heat is an imperfect science, the quantification of heat’s impact on mental health, physical well-being, wages, food security, habitat, and infrastructure is even more complex. One thousand women working in India’s informal labor economy have set out to quantify this burden—to understand what impact the heat and humidity in their lived environments at home and at work have on their health, wages, and well-being.
Partnering with our team at Harvard, the Self Employed Women’s Association in India has recruited women from trades including street vendors, waste recyclers, home-based artisans, and farmers to participate in the Community Heat Adaptation and Treatment Strategies (CommHATS) study. For 13 months, each woman is equipped with a wrist wearable, microsensors measuring heat and humidity at home and workplaces, labs measuring critical biomarkers, and surveys documenting home and work layouts, wellbeing, and wages. Considered together, this data constructs one of the world’s largest such databases of the impact of heat on human health.
Building on prior work that has shown that long exposure to heat impacts multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys, the CommHATS project seeks to address unanswered questions in our attempts to adapt to extreme heat: How do we know if cool roofs work? What should our metric of success be? If the temperature drops a bit, but I still cannot sleep restfully, is the intervention valid? What should the threshold for a new heat insurance product be: the temperature at the airport where the weather station is, or the temperature in my home, which is actually how hot I feel? In India, where over half of women of reproductive age are anemic, how does heat further stress their hearts?
Through community meetings and WhatsApp groups, research findings are regularly shared with all participants, who routinely ask how the data will help improve their lives. Early findings, which we will share at New York Climate Week, reveal devastating wage losses on hot days, shortened sleep spans, and high cardiac stress. This kind of relentless, unforgiving heat forces a different kind of reckoning that goes beyond OSHA regulations and market solutions.
In places like India, where around 90% of workers are informally employed, there is no employer to hold accountable. The poor have no choice but to adapt. They change working hours at the cost of childcare. They reallocate savings to protect health and wages. They buy water jugs to carry potable water, and awnings to create shade, and ice chests to cool their produce. The woefully underfunded global financial instruments for heat adaptation have no existing structural mechanism to actually reach the most vulnerable, and so those most at risk bear the price themselves.
The CommHATS project is implemented daily by grassroots workers, a testament to its ease of use. They check on the sensors and the wearables, and most importantly, the participating workers. The participants are invested in the questions, the tools, and the analysis. The tool is thus built for scale and can help communities anywhere in the world understand what their environmental exposure is at an actionable scale that is relevant to decision-making. It helps measure exposure as well as the efficacy of interventions.
In our study, we find that the cost of our collective inaction is already being borne by those whose lives are already stressed. The human spirit is resilient, and perhaps life goes on. But in this warming world, life is compromised and diminished. Millions may still live through extreme heat and not yet enter the death counts, but they cannot thrive.

Mathematicians Hate AI. They Can’t Quit It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster believes OpenAI used his work to rush ahead and beat him to solving a legendary math problem with a $1 million bounty.
But that’s not been enough for him to stop using the company’s models—and he’s not the only mathematician that feels that way.
“Even if you don't agree with any of this, you're kind of stuck. With AI being so useful, it's hard to completely prevent oneself from using it,” Buckmaster tells WIRED. “These companies have a monopoly, and there is not much choice,” he adds.
In the week and half since the New York University professor accused OpenAI of copying his approach, Buckmaster has been using the company’s coding agent Codex to tidy up his research papers. When he has time to do math (which he says is rare, since the fallout thrust him into the spotlight), the tool has been helping him understand the logical steps OpenAI’s agents might have taken to get from his earlier workings to the final proof.
Buckmaster had used Codex as well as Anthropic’s competing Claude to work on what’s known as the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, alongside Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. OpenAI deployed tens of thousands of agents to reach the solution, but only after it learned the equation was close to being solved, Buckmaster says.
When Buckmaster went public with his claims, it ignited a firestorm about artificial intelligence and whether it would make human mathematicians obsolete. It also led OpenAI to do an investigation and amend its announcement about solving Navier-Stokes to say it “confirmed that Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the two months preceding this announcement and paper on September 8, 2026, could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training.” The company pointed WIRED to its announcement in an email.
Showing that AI was pushing the boundaries of mathematics was “more important than the result,” Buckmaster says. But churning out solutions to long-standing math problems without fully crediting the human work undergirding them—especially ahead of major IPOs—is irresponsible and “childish,” he says.
Other mathematicians have raised similar concerns. Only a handful of people on the planet understand the techniques in geometric group theory that German mathematician Andreas Thom has dedicated the last two decades to developing. So when OpenAI said in August that its Astra model had used them to prove a long-standing problem he had been working on, “I was amazed,” says Thom. “And of course I was wondering, how did they learn about it?”
So he says he asked OpenAI researchers Mark Sellke and Sébastien Bubeck. In an August email, he pointed out that the firm’s assertion that “no progress” had been made on the problem in the last decade overlooked a 2019 paper of his, as well as other mathematicians’ work. The company amended its press release. He and a colleague had been using ChatGPT to assist their work on the problem in the months running up to the result, but when he asked if their interactions had been fed into training data, Thom says Sellke replied: “That did not happen.”
“I set it aside,” Thom recalls. “I'm not so much interested in these political things; I want to work on mathematics.”
While Thom has seen OpenAI’s statement that Buckmaster’s prompts couldn't have influenced the system, he says he doesn’t trust this and concedes he will probably never know whether his work actually fed the result.
“AI really kills this entire idea that you could trace back who contributed what,” he says. “That is probably over.”
It’s a big change from how science is typically done, with academics subjecting their findings to peer review and building on each others’ work with credit. Beyond upending attribution, the fact that humans still don’t fully understand each step OpenAI’s agents took to arrive at the Navier-Stokes result also poses existential questions for mathematicians, who see their field slipping from their understanding.
"If I want to make a contribution to mathematics, how do I do that as just a human nowadays when these trillion-dollar companies are in on the game?" says Cornell mathematician Alex Townsend, the coauthor of a forthcoming book on the field’s evolution.
Since August, Townsend has seen many of his colleagues start to ask what they need to know about the technology and how they can set up subscriptions to access higher-powered models.
"I feel both excited and nervous simultaneously," Townsend says. "Excited because I can achieve things that I couldn't achieve without it, and nervous because I'm questioning: 'OK, what's my purpose here?'"
Thom accepts that his area of study is changing, and has continued to use ChatGPT—with updated privacy settings to stop his work being used to train the data—to speed up writing papers because it is “extremely efficient.” (OpenAI’s offerings through universities and at the enterprise level default to not training models on users’ data.)
“If a human had actively done that, then I would be very, very angry,” he says of someone using his work without attribution. But if information was pulled into the model through a back door, by an algorithm which nobody fully understands, “I could probably live with that,” he says.
Some mathematicians are less forgiving. Twenty-five Fields medalists wrote in an open letter that AI companies and mathematicians are “severely misaligned.” More than 4,000 people have signed the Leiden Declaration, which has a series of recommendations for how mathematicians, funders, and politicians can ensure that AI doesn’t swallow the field.
Buckmaster fears the possibility of using AI to “clean up some of your grammar, and suddenly your years of work [could be] gobbled up in user data and sold to another mathematician or grad student. That's what I think most of the mathematicians tend to be worrying about, and I think it's a real issue.”
With no oversight on the horizon and AI further engraining itself in the field, some mathematicians want to find a way to at least tap the brakes. That includes more than 2,000 people with ties to Caltech who called on organizers of an AI math hackathon at the school to suspend the event. The hackathon was sponsored by Anthropic and OpenAI, though the latter has since dropped out. But any attempts to slow things down may be for naught, especially in the long term.
“I don't think this is really sustainable because of the efficiency gain” that AI offers, says Thom. Any mathematicians—especially early-career researchers—risk being “isolated” if they don’t use AI to accelerate their work, he adds. He and Buckmaster both believe the community needs to start thinking about what the technology means for younger mathematicians and how to smooth the transition.
The next generation of mathematicians is already looking for guidance: Students have also been asking about what their future could look like now that AI is becoming so capable at solving math problems, Townsend says.
Buckmaster is calling for a detente in AI-driven mathematics while mathematicians and AI laboratories set some ground rules on how to release results, including getting their references right. He himself is going to clean up the papers he published prematurely last week to beat OpenAI’s announcement, one of which he described as “AI slop.”
”I have a responsibility to clean up the papers that I did post that weren't completed, and I think I have a responsibility to explain to mathematicians what we did,” he says.
He’s also open to discussing this with OpenAI. “I don't want to just engage in fights” he says. As for whether he would ever actually work on a problem with the company, “we have to be careful with that,” he says with a wry smile.

Agricultural Museum renamed MUHK, opens new permanent exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Agricultural Museum renamed MUHK, opens new permanent exhibition
Starting Friday, the Estonian Agricultural Museum in Ülenurme, Tartu County, will operate under a new name: Maaelu uudishimukeskus (Rural Curiosity Center), or MUHK. The new name reflects the museum's expanding scope.
Alongside the history of Estonian rural life and agriculture, the museum will now place greater emphasis on the present and the future, exploring connections between the past, today's questions, and tomorrow's possibilities.
For decades, the Agricultural Museum has collected, preserved, and showcased Estonia's rural and agricultural heritage. That mission will not disappear with the old name. MUHK will retain its history, collections, artifacts, machinery, stories, and skills — but the way rural life is presented will change.
According to Kadri Valner, head of the SA Eesti Maaelumuuseumid (Estonian Rural Life Museums Foundation), the museum has long moved beyond focusing solely on the past.
"The museum doesn't just talk about history — it also looks to the future. Our new exhibition covers everyday rural topics, food security, and even the future of our dinner table. As the Rural Curiosity Center, we will bring contemporary and forward‑looking perspectives alongside the museum's traditional historical approach," Valner said.
The name change is one of the most visible milestones in a broader transformation, and the new approach will gradually shape all of the center's activities.
On Friday, MUHK will open a new permanent exhibition of more than 600 square meters titled "Why Do I Need Soil?! From Seed to Harvest, From Harrow to Robot." The exhibition also blends history, the present, and the future, moving from the world of soil through agriculture and food production to satellites, robots, artificial intelligence, and the future of food.
The name and structure of the Estonian Rural Life Museums Foundation will not change. The foundation will continue to operate three sites: MUHK (Rural Curiosity Center) in Ülenurme, the C. R. Jakobson Farm Museum in Kurgja, and the Tori Horse Breeding Farm in Tori.

Editor: Mirjam Mäekivi, Argo Ideon

California is losing its oaks. One man is planting 10,000, including in tree-scarce Altadena
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Ten thousand times, Jim Crouch has picked up an acorn. Ten thousand times, he’s planted that acorn. And 10,000 is about the number of oak seedlings he’s entrusted to the hands of people who pledged to care for the tree that has become his mission and obsession.
It began after he retired. For years, he’d been a classroom science teacher in suburban San Diego County, and now, with that chapter behind him, the trees have become his life. He hopes to meaningfully contribute to the regrowth of burned Altadena.
California has Thousand Oaks, Sherman Oaks, Oak Park, Fair Oaks, even Oakland. That’s just in English. Consider Encino, Encinitas and Paso Robles. They paint a picture of a California covered in oaks. But many regions have lost their oak canopy. Some trees succumbed to insects after being weakened by drought. Some were cut for developments, some were cut down illegally. Some oaks have been cut after fire.
Crouch witnessed this loss. He felt it. He took to collecting acorns — the seeds of oak trees. He planted them in deep pots. For the first eight years, he was a one-man operation working out of his backyard He began handing off the seedlings to others. Then many seedlings, to many others.
He began opening small nurseries, staffed by volunteers. He named his organization Re-Oak California after a group in the Bay Area with the same name. His motivation “started with climate, but then I learned you can’t do anything better for nature than protect the best keystone species.”
Oaks support a wide range of organisms, anchoring entire ecosystems, and also serve the vital task of storing carbon on a warming planet.
In a kind of treasure hunt, Crouch gathers all the acorns on private lands. He uses a hunting app to identify who owns which patch of remote land, then mails the property owner a letter asking for permission to gather.
A growing cadre of volunteers increasingly helps with the next step, the actual harvest, scooping acorns off the ground and into bags and buckets. That’s in part because Crouch is 75, and a bicycle accident has him using a cane. “My constant companion,” he says.
Recently, one volunteer leveled up Crouch’s game by making him a mapping app that includes not only the property ownership information but also tree locations from the app iNaturalist, layered together with research from Victoria Sork, a UCLA professor and dean of life sciences, who has studied oak trees for more than 30 years. 
 Sork’s lab, along with the Nature Conservancy, is sequencing oak DNA to identify which trees are best built to survive a hotter, drier California. The goal is to put those findings to work on the ground by planting acorns from trauma-affected trees that still survive. In other words, the toughest oaks could help produce the next generation. 
 It’s a strategy Sork hopes can make California’s forests more resilient to climate change — something she’s hoping Crouch can help her with. For Crouch, it’s a partnership he’s still a little starstruck about. He compares getting a call from Sork to being asked for shooting tips from NBA star  Stephen Curry. 
 Sork sees the value in the partnership too. 
“My best role is to generate knowledge and then partner with the people who are trying to get things going,” she says. Crouch, she adds, is one of the keys to getting her research “out from the ivory tower to the practitioners.”
On a recent Tuesday, Crouch steered his 2011 Nissan Frontier from his home in Escondido up to La Cañada High School off the 210 Freeway. This is where Re-Oak is opening its first nursery in the Los Angeles area, intended to serve hard-hit Altadena. It will be the group’s sixth, on Oak Grove Drive.
“It’s a bit of a challenge because I can’t be there every day, you know?” Crouch says. But “Altadena needs more trees, [and] we’ll give them whatever they need.” The new La Cañada nursery is going up in the high school’s garden: a crescent-shaped plot between the track and field and tennis courts, carpeted with mulch and sectioned off with native plants, annuals and edibles. It was started three years ago by English teacher Daryl Bilandzija, a former student of Crouch’s who saw that handing over the plot to his old teacher would mean learning for his students. “If we could get them to put a couple of acorns in the ground wherever they go, it could start to have an effect on the local environment,” Bilandzija said. “And before you know it, you’ve re-oaked a neighborhood.”
Some Altadena trees survived the 2025 fire there, yet those that remain are more vulnerable because of the overall loss of what arborists call “friction” that helped them weather storms as a group. More trees are vital to the overall health of the remaining population in Altadena. This nursery joins several other tree efforts in the community.
Altadena Green estimates that west Altadena lost roughly 70% of its tree canopy in the Eaton fire, and the losses haven’t stopped, with developers and homeowners continuing to clear what’s left.
A mother-daughter team called the Los Angeles Humane Society had given away more than 1,000 coast live oaks in Altadena and Santa Monica by the end of last year. The Los Angeles County Fire Department Forestry Division also has been offering free oaks, in addition to other native plants, at its two nurseries in San Dimas and Malibu for years. 
In addition to the La Cañada High School nursery, Crouch is establishing a smaller one in Santa Clarita. It will be staffed by 20-year-old Anderson Khalil, who found Crouch the way most young volunteers do now: social media. 
“I just saw him on Facebook giving away free oak trees, and here we are,” Khalil said. 
He had been searching for a tangible way to help the environment and allay his anxieties about the planet’s future when he came across Crouch’s posts. 
“I can’t speak so much for the rest of my generation because I have a few close friends and they’re all pretty aware,” he explained, “but we have to care more about the environment if we want to keep living the way we are living.” 
Re-Oak California has an eighth nursery planned for Irvine, its first outpost in Orange County. 
The oaks they give away are about 6 inches tall with six leaves, plus a whole foot of roots. Oaks are considered neither fast nor slow growing. A homeowner planting one today might wait more than a decade to sit in its shade. 
But it’s a wait advocates say is well worth it, one that will prove that a community, Altadena or elsewhere, can rebuild its canopy if it’s willing to invest now.
His reliance on the cane has slowed him down, so Crouch has shifted roles, from field hand to recruiter, operating mainly as the guy behind the keyboard, lining up volunteers to plant, scout, harvest and build the next nursery. He is working, with a volunteer’s help, to formalize Re-Oak California as a nonprofit.
The costs of the pots, racks and soil are nominal individually but add up fast at the scale he now operates. For 10 years he’s covered the gap himself, supplemented by donations and buoyed by a 2025 segment on CBS 8 San Diego that brought in $12,000. Re-Oak California needs donated acorns, volunteer planters and propagators, and money — especially if Crouch is to reach his dream goal of planting 20,000 trees a year.
“I’ve never been so ambitious,” he says, “and I’ve never done a project with as much love in it and as little ego.”
He’s betting that as more people understand what’s at stake, they will keep showing up — even if they are planting trees for a future he’ll never see.

Australia pulled out of West Bank sanctions at last minute, EU diplomats reveal - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
09:57:59 UTC
18:57:59 KST

European diplomats from 12 countries revealed that Australia withdrew from joining the UK-led decision to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank late in the proceedings, according to a report from the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).
The UK’s trade embargo was followed by a collective statement from 12 Western-aligned governments who said they would also commit to, or consider the possibility of, establishing sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
EU officials lobbied Australia as it tried to expand its coalition of countries to increase pressure on Israeli settlements that they view to be illegal under international law.
Australia was reportedly open to taking more aggressive action against settlements, but ultimately decided not to join the action late in the discussions, sources told the ABC.
In the end, Canada was the only non-European country to join the statement.
Australia has placed diplomatic pressure on Israel before
Over the last year, Australia has collaborated with other Western countries to add pressure on Israel over its war in Gaza and its settlements in the West Bank. In September, 2025, Australia recognized the State of Palestine at the United Nations General Assembly along with Canada and Portugal.
The ABC said it spoke with eight diplomatic sources familiar with the matter in Sydney, Canberra, Jerusalem, and Tel Aviv, who said the coalition of countries hoped Australia would join the decision to impose sanctions on Israeli West Bank settlements and were disappointed when it did not. The ABC’s sources wished to remain anonymous.
Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Australia and its partners were “working closely together towards the same objective, even if we are not all taking exactly the same measures at the same time.”
“We are concerned blanket import bans present practical challenges, including how to ensure they do not inadvertently harm Palestinian businesses, workers and livelihoods. The UK government has acknowledged these challenges as they work on their legislation over the next year,” the statement read.
“In the meantime, Australia is pursuing further targeted measures, in coordination with international partners, to deter illegal settlements and settler violence.”
EU officials 'surprised' by Australia's decision
Two EU officials who spoke with the ABC said they were “surprised” Australia did not sign the statement in the end. However, a different official involved in the negotiations said that while Australia had signaled it was open to signing on, Canberra never finalized a decision to join the coalition.
The ABC also reported that some of the diplomatic sources it spoke with attributed Australia’s decision not to join the statement to domestic politics.
Sources speculated that criticism from Australian Jewish groups following the Bondi Beach terror attacks and increased antisemitism may have played a part in Australia’s decision not to level sanctions on Israeli settlements.
Another source told the ABC that the UK’s characterization of Israel’s policy in the West Bank took officials by surprise.
British Secretary of State, Edward Miliband, told parliament that settler violence against Palestinians constituted “ethnic cleansing” and that Israel’s government was turning a “blind eye” to it.
One EU source claimed that Miliband’s language departed from the agreed-upon final joint statement.
Last week the Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia was “pursuing further targeted measures in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence.”
In June of this year, Australia, the UK, Canada, France and Norway all announced sanctions against Israeli firms connected to financing and “enabling” settler violence in the West Bank.
Australia said it was “ready to take more action if the Government of Israel does not take urgent steps to address the situation on the ground.”

Inside the Houthi advance: How Iran's allies are helping tighten Tehran's grip on the Red Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
09:57:44 UTC
18:57:44 KST

In recent days, the Houthis have seized control of the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands in the southern Red Sea, continuing their lightning advance that has brought the organization to effectively control the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Earlier this month, their forces captured the strategic port city of Mocha, expelling forces linked to the Saudi-linked Presidential Leadership Council (PLC). They also overran Perim Island, located directly inside the strait, and the Zuqar islands further north.
The Iran-supported Shi’ite militiamen are now located at the narrowest point of the coastline, just 20 km. from the African coast. This affords them, and by extension the Iran-led regional alliance of which they are a part, effective control over maritime traffic making its way through the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea.
In statements made as they advanced, the Houthis made it clear that they intend to target Saudi shipping on the strait, rather than institute a general naval blockade.
The Houthi advance was accompanied by an Iraqi Shi’ite militia drone attack on the Saudi East-West pipeline on September 10. The pipeline had served as a means for Riyadh to transport oil to the Red Sea, thereby avoiding the Strait of Hormuz, which is subject to Iranian attacks. It is expected to be out of service for three to five weeks.
Iran’s allies coordinate pressure across the Red Sea corridor
The coordinated action between the Iraqi Shi’ite militias and the Houthis is clearly intended to extend the Iran-led alliance’s ability to impose rules on maritime traffic from Hormuz to the Red Sea. The focus on Saudi Arabia (which initiated the current round of fighting with its attack on Sana’a airport in July) avoids inviting US retaliation, which a more general effort to blockade Bab el-Mandeb might trigger.
The events of the last days demonstrate the Iran-led regional bloc’s continued ability to act in coordination for shared objectives. While Israel has pummeled and drastically weakened (though not destroyed) Iran’s clients in the Levant, further south in the Gulf area, Tehran and its allies remain very much in business.
Nuances and details are important here. The Houthis, like Hamas and unlike Lebanese or Iraqi Hezbollah, are not a direct franchise or proxy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. Like Hamas, the Houthis are an authentic and deep-rooted local movement, with their own agenda and preferences.
It is notable, for example, that the Houthis preferred to avoid direct engagement in the current round of fighting prior to the Saudi attacks, and are now directing their efforts specifically against Riyadh. This confirms the considerable extent to which the organization is not simply a puppet of the Iranians, acting militarily in response to orders from Tehran.
At the same time, this operational independence should not be exaggerated. While the Houthis do not simply take orders from the Iranians, much of their impressive military capacity derives directly from their relationship with Tehran.
Indeed, close examination of the evidence indicates that the military activities of the Houthis are enabled by the direct presence of Iranian and other allied personnel on Yemeni soil, and the close involvement of Iranian and allied Iraqi and Lebanese personnel who are instructing and managing the Houthis. Notably, China and Russia support these efforts on the basis of their shared geopolitical interests.
Documents reveal Iranian, Iraqi and Lebanese support for Houthis
Documents recently obtained by The Jerusalem Post from Yemeni sources provide details regarding this reality. The documents list the names and identifying information of Iranian, Iraqi, and Lebanese experts in Yemen who are providing expert advice and supervision to the Houthis regarding drones, missiles, and intelligence/security operations.
The documents name, for example, the Iranian citizen Haji Murtaza Mokhles and the Iraqi Abu Mukhtar Bari Mashour, who are giving expert advice in the field of intelligence and security operations. They are working closely with Abu Jihad Muhammad Alawi al-Tiri, a senior Houthi official from the village of Bayt Baws, located 8 km. south of Sana’a. He is described as a senior official of the “Houthi Security and Intelligence Service,” serving as “administrator of the Military Intelligence Center and supervisor of the Presidential Information Center.”
Similarly, in the field of drones, the documents reference the Iranian citizen Hasan bin Hasan Danbous, and the Iraqi Hasan Iyad al-Ameri, both senior experts in this field, as working with the senior Houthi commander Hassan Sharafi in development in this area.
Regarding missiles, the Iraqi Muhammad Sayed al-Hakim and the Iranian citizen Karar Mumammad al-Musawi are named as working with Abu Bashar Saleh al-Saree, who is named as managing the central information department of the missile forces.
These examples are part of a much longer list. Identifying details, location, and sometimes the telephone numbers of the officials are in the documents.
Iran, Russia and China links emerge in Houthi supply chains
The documents also include details regarding the smuggling methods that enable the Houthis to bring vital components and equipment into Yemen, and the roles played by Iran, Russia, and China. They name a number of businessmen residing in the Houthi-controlled part of Yemen, who are responsible for the import of spare parts for drones from China to Houthi-controlled Yemen. Among them are Safwan al-Dabai, Yasser al-Dabai, and Rami al-Hajj al-Alimi, along with several others. Yemeni, and in one case Chinese phone numbers, are included, along with the men’s names.
According to these documents, following a meeting held under Iranian auspices in Muscat, Oman, in March 2024, several Chinese shipping companies have been paying the Houthis in hard currency so their ships can pass through the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea undisturbed. The list of companies includes two major Chinese concerns: COSCO Shipping and Sea Legend Shipping.
In two further passages, the documents reference a communications system south of Saada city, and connected to centers in the mountains of Hajjah, Amran, Sana’a, and the mountains overlooking the west coast.
“This network was created by experts from Iran and uses Iranian-made encryption devices, in addition to the use of Russian communication and encryption devices, especially in the Morse messaging system…
“US airstrikes were able to destroy many communication networks and jamming devices, and the Houthi militias are currently trying to replace them with Chinese devices, even if temporarily, so that Iran can then smuggle devices to Yemen and restart the jihadi communications department with all its capacity.”
It is also noted that “most of the electrical and optical infrared sensors used by the Houthi militias are Iranian-made systems that were smuggled from the Iranian ports of Bandar Abbas and Shahbar to the port of Saleef, Hodeidah, and the coasts of Al-Mahra governorate (the process is still ongoing), where the components of the missiles, and the devices, are also smuggled in the form of parts that are reassembled when they arrive in Yemen. As for the thermal cameras – the Houthis use Chinese thermal cameras, imported through official means.”
 
This evidence showcases an integrated de facto alliance in which the Houthis, in the service of shared goals but not under the direction of any other element, are provided with advanced capacities and assistance, enabling them to better pursue their aims. This structure, in addition to the undoubted religious-ideological zeal of the Shi’ite Islamist fighters, is what underlies the successes of recent days. 
Divisions weaken the anti-Houthi coalition
It is instructive to compare these arrangements with the contrasting divisions on the anti-Houthi side. There, the Saudis acted militarily against the United Arab Emirates-supported, highly capable South Yemeni element earlier this year, removing them from the field. They then concluded a pact with Turkey and Pakistan, which seems to have brought some ineffectual Turkey-supported Sunni jihadi fighters to Yemen, and little else.
The United States, meanwhile, has been looking for a way to avoid escalation, and for now seems to be staying uninvolved. Its position is based on the grounds that the Houthis are only targeting a US ally, and not the general shipping traffic that traverses the strait.
The developments witnessed this week highlight both the deep structures of cooperation and assistance from which the Houthis benefit, and the relative disarray of their opponents. Reversing these advances will mean addressing both of these elements.

Debt to 'Autostrada' amounts to UAH 15 bln; company hopes to resume financing for key projects
