Inside the secret race to become NATO’s next top general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:56:24 UTC
17:56:24 KST

BRUSSELS — NATO’s most senior commanders elect a new leader on Saturday in a consequential vote that will help shape how the alliance prepares for a potential Russian incursion and navigates persisting transatlantic tensions.
The alliance’s 32 chiefs of defense staff will elect a new chair of NATO’s most senior military body, the military committee, in Copenhagen in a hush-hush ballot — and choose between two candidates: Germany’s Gen. Carsten Breuer and Canada’s Gen. Jennie Carignan.
“NATO is in a very decisive moment and in a demanding spot — there’s a large conventional war raging in Europe and NATO is transforming itself again into a more robust, more European NATO,” said Janne Kuusela, Permanent Secretary at the Finnish defense ministry. “That of course means … we need the best possible individuals to fill these positions.”
Advertisement
Although little-known, NATO’s military committee is the alliance’s most senior military authority, with the chair expected to give honest military advice to allies — helping assess the feasibility, financing and capabilities of operations. They oversee dozens of working groups of NATO military staff, and broker consensus on formulating military advice.
The position is a “highly complex role,” said Eleonora Russell, the spokesperson of former chair Adm. Rob Bauer, because it requires simultaneously gaining the trust of both the military and the political leadership across the alliance — and not taking sides.
Such a role is particularly challenging today given enduring transatlantic tensions, she said, and important as sensitive talks on NATO’s next four-year war planning cycle will kick off in October. “The trick is you have to be … an extremely good listener,” Russell said, “but then you have to also have a very strong backbone.”
Germany’s Breuer, who Berlin announced as a candidate in February, is seen as the front-runner, according to one NATO diplomat and two European national security officials, who were granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive matter.
Berlin is now Europe’s leading defense spender, the officials said, and the U.S. has previously nudged Germany toward leadership roles in the alliance as it seeks to reduce its military engagement on the continent. Strained bilateral ties between Ottawa and Washington might also make Carignan’s case more difficult, the officials said.
That support was on display in Washington on Jul. 23, when Breuer briefed Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby on Germany’s new military strategy. Colby later called the strategy “historic” and “highly laudable” and said Germany was positioning itself as “a key leader of Europe’s conventional defense” in a post on X.
Advertisement
“Both candidates are exceptional military leaders,” said another military official, who nonetheless wondered whether it was more important today to have a European in charge given the alliance’s push for the continent to take charge of its own defense, dubbed NATO 3.0.
Breuer’s pitch for the job has included its leadership role on NATO 3.0, the officials said, as well as the four-star general’s strong existing relationships with his counterparts since he took over as Germany’s chief of defense in 2023.
Carignan, Ottawa’s top general since 2024, has focused her campaign on reinvigorating the role of the military committee, the officials said, and signaling enduring transatlantic unity inside NATO. That comes as the alliance has repeatedly been rocked by feuds with U.S. President Donald Trump since he retook office last year.
Germany’s defense ministry didn’t respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Canada’s defense ministry said Carignan’s “candidacy reflects Canada's enduring commitment to NATO and to strengthening collective defence and transatlantic security.”
Out of sight, out of mind
Yet the campaign is enigmatic and behind closed doors — all the way down to the blind vote.
That’s because “the whole point of this is for this to be a military group of professionals who trust each other,” Russell said, since “on the military level you need to have boundless loyalty, and if you know exactly who voted for you and who didn't, then you lose that.”
Advertisement
To ensure that loyalty, the vote count will stop once a majority — or 17 votes — is reached, leaving the real result unknown, one NATO official said. Adding to the mystery, some chiefs of defense are under strict instructions by their ministries to vote for one candidate, the official said, while others can make up their own minds.
Behind the scenes, the candidates have lobbied their counterparts through letters, face-to-face pitches with NATO ambassadors, at security summits and with phone calls to ministries, said the three officials.
Since Berlin nominated Breuer, he has been a frequent visitor to NATO capitals. His recent stops have included Albania, North Macedonia, the U.S., Slovenia, Latvia and Estonia — all in the past two months. Breuer has used trips and meetings with fellow military leaders to make the case for Germany’s candidacy, said a person familiar with the effort.
The next military committee chair is expected to take over from Italy’s Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone next July, the same NATO official said.

US court restricts Trump policy on third-country deportations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:55:00 UTC
17:55:00 KST

US court blocks Trump policy on third-country deportations
September 19, 2026
A US federal appeals court has largely upheld a ruling blocking the Trump administration from rapidly deporting migrants to third countries without giving them a meaningful chance to raise safety concerns.
The three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in Boston said Friday that migrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture there.
What did the court say about the DHS policy?
The case challenges a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy allowing migrants with final deportation orders to be sent to countries other than their own, provided authorities have diplomatic assurances they will not face persecution or torture.
The court said the policy could deny protections to migrants sent to unfamiliar countries without notice.
The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court.
DHS General Counsel James Percival said on X that the policy remains in force because Friday's ruling has not yet taken effect.
"If you claim fear in your home country, DHS has the right to send you elsewhere," Percival wrote.
The order comes as two men deported by the US to Equatorial Guinea were arbitrarily detained, with police covering their heads with bags, beating them and holding them at gunpoint in a hotel turned into a detention center, the AP reported.
More than 25,000 deported to third countries
Since US President Donald Trump returned to office, his administration has sent more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.
Some of the third countries immigrants are being deported to are:
- South Sudan
- Eswatini
- Uganda
- Equatorial Guinea
- Liberia
- Central African Republic
The third-country deals have drawn criticism from human rights groups, as several participating nations have notoriously repressive governments and poor human rights records.

Trump Signs Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:53:59 UTC
17:53:59 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, the White House said in a statement, paving the way for increased economic pressure on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.
The measures target Russia's energy and defense industries, as well as its "shadow fleet" of tankers that evade existing sanctions, in order to deprive Moscow of funds used to pay for its war with Ukraine.
The legislation faced opposition from Democrats because it also authorizes Trump to impose stiff tariffs of up to 100% on China, India and other countries to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas, as well as to extend sanctions on Iran.
Critics argue that Trump already has the authority he needs to impose sanctions on Russia, but has chosen not to do so.
The bill, now called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," to honor the South Carolina Republican who died in July, passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday and the Senate last month.
Graham, a longtime Russia hawk, was a staunch backer of the legislation.
The Kremlin said earlier this week that further U.S. sanctions against Russia would make it harder to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
"We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this bill. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine," spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,

US reaches permanent Greenland security deal with Denmark: Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:49:00 UTC
17:49:00 KST

President Donald Trump said Friday that the United States, Denmark and Greenland have reached an agreement that would expand the U.S. military presence on the Arctic island and prevent American adversaries such as Russia and China from establishing bases or making sensitive investments there.
Trump said the agreement gives Washington permanent control over Greenland's security needs and has no expiration date, describing it as an “Infinite Life” agreement. He said the United States would soon begin building up a larger military presence on the strategically important island.
“I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
He added that no U.S. adversary would be allowed to establish a base, deploy a military presence or make sensitive investments in Greenland without Washington's written approval.
The announcement came after Reuters reported Friday that Washington and Copenhagen were nearing an agreement to strengthen the U.S. military presence in Greenland.
The arrangement appears to fall short of Trump's earlier calls for the United States to acquire the territory, a proposal that has repeatedly strained relations with NATO ally Denmark.
The exact terms of the agreement remained unclear Friday night.
A senior State Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the deal, said the agreement would prevent non-NATO countries from establishing military bases in Greenland and would restrict sensitive investments. The official said Washington would retain permanent access, basing and overflight rights, including if Greenland eventually becomes independent from Denmark.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the agreement “permanently and completely” addresses Washington's national security concerns over Greenland.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” Rubio said.
The Danish prime minister's office said the agreement would strengthen security in the North Atlantic and Arctic while preserving Denmark's sovereignty.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the arrangement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark as well as Greenland's right to self-determination.
“I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States,” Frederiksen said, adding that it was also good for NATO and Europe.
Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the agreement recognized the territory's interests and its place in international cooperation while strengthening its security.
The uncertainty surrounding the agreement is particularly significant in Greenland, whose population of about 57,000 has long sought greater autonomy and independence from Denmark. Greenlanders have also strongly resisted Trump's repeated suggestions that the United States should take control of the island.
Trump's push for control of Greenland intensified after he returned to the White House in January 2025. He has argued that the territory is vital to U.S. national security and has repeatedly cited concerns over growing Russian and Chinese activity in the Arctic.
The dispute alarmed Denmark and created tensions within NATO, particularly after Trump declined to rule out using force to obtain control of Greenland.
The new agreement could mark a shift toward a security arrangement rather than territorial acquisition.
The United States already enjoys extensive military rights in Greenland under a 1951 defense agreement with Denmark, which was updated in 2004. The pact gives Washington broad rights to deploy forces and establish military facilities, subject to notification and other provisions.
The U.S. currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwest Greenland, a strategically important installation used for missile warning, space surveillance and other military missions.
Several reports have said Washington is seeking to establish as many as three additional military facilities in southern Greenland, although Trump and Danish officials did not confirm Friday whether the new agreement would result in additional bases.
Imran Bayoumi, a former Pentagon official now with the Atlantic Council, said it would represent a significant development if Washington gained the ability to establish bases without approval from Greenland or Denmark.
He also said many of the U.S. security objectives appeared achievable through diplomacy without placing additional strain on relations between Washington and its NATO allies.
The deal is expected to be formally signed on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York next week.
It remained unclear whether the agreement is connected to a separate understanding Trump said he reached with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. The details of that arrangement have never been fully disclosed.
As negotiations continued, NATO launched a new mission aimed at strengthening security in the Arctic, an apparent effort to address growing concerns over the region's strategic importance.

Can Trump ban CNN, news outlets he doesn’t like from the White House?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:47:17 UTC
17:47:17 KST

Can Trump ban CNN, news outlets he doesn’t like from the White House?
The ban is the latest attack by Trump on media outlets that he perceives as unfavourable to his administration.
United States President Donald Trump has taken the unprecedented step of announcing that several media outlets are to be banned from the White House, “immediately”.
On Friday, he took to his social media platform, Truth Social, to announce the ban, citing “reporting FAKE NEWS!” as the reason, with other outlets to follow.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Really terrified’: Milo Yiannopoulos speaks out after deportation from US
- list 2 of 3Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House for ‘fake news’
- list 3 of 3Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, Politico from the White House
Asked by reporters later on Friday what he meant, Trump said: “Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, The New York Times is fake news, The Washington Post is fake news.”
Here is what you need to know:
Which news outlets have been banned and why?
The US President banned CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico from reporting from the White House.
On Truth Social, he accused the outlets of propagating “fake news”. He added that the outlets “constantly write or report fiction or lies” about the Trump administration, but did not give any examples.
However, a short news conference at the White House on the same day revealed that it was likely a partisan issue, telling reporters the outlets “purposely write negative news” and seek to “diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration. And honestly, we’ve done a fantastic job.”
What have the responses been?
CNN denounced the move, saying it stands behind its White House team and their “fair and accurate reporting”.
“We have a right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” a CNN spokesperson told Al Jazeera. “Should the ban, which President Trump threatened, go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right.”
Politico said it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them.”
The news outlet’s communications team also pushed back on a separate Trump claim that Politico had received government subsidies, calling it “false” and saying it had “been thoroughly debunked”.
MS NOW did not immediately comment on Trump’s announcement.
The National Press Club was among several groups that immediately criticised the ban as an attack on the free press.
“Banning news organisations from the White House based on the administration’s disapproval of their coverage is a clear attempt to control which voices are allowed to witness and report on the exercise of presidential power,” said the group’s president, Mark Schoeff Jr.
“Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the First Amendment works,” said Tim Richardson, journalism and disinformation director at PEN America.
Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”
What rights do White House journalists have and what is their job?
White House journalists report on the US president and what he says and does; they question officials at briefings, report on policy, and rotate through the small “press pool” that follows the president into the Oval Office and onto Air Force One.
The First Amendment protects what they publish, so the government can’t censor them or legally penalise them for their reporting.
Once press passes are offered, courts have ruled they can’t be denied or revoked arbitrarily.
The White House must follow fair standards and give notice and a chance to respond.
On that basis, CNN won a court order in 2018 restoring Jim Acosta’s revoked pass.
Has Trump done this before?
The ban follows the president’s decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet’s decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America.
AP has taken legal action against this.
Throughout his second term, Trump and his administration have attacked certain media outlets in court and through regulatory action.
Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media.
Since returning to office, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.
His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation with ABC over renewal of its broadcast licences.
Can outlets challenge this ban in court?
After the AP ban, the news agency filed a lawsuit, and that case is ongoing.
In the 1977 Sherrill v Knight case, a federal appeals court ruled that although the White House is not required to open its doors to the news media, once it establishes press facilities for credentialed journalists, it cannot deny access based on the content of a journalist’s coverage.
The court held that any denial must serve a compelling government interest and that the journalist must receive notice, the chance to respond and a final answer in writing.
It remains unclear at this stage what legal recourse CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico could pursue.
Reporting from Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher said Trump’s ban will likely be challenged soon.
“The United States has the First Amendment [of its Constitution] that says the government cannot restrict access to this sort of thing,” he said.
“Other presidents have been angry at press coverage before. Lyndon B Johnson used to rail about it. Richard Nixon wondered whether or not he could ban certain people from the White House as well. At every point, they were told it’s not a good look.”

Scientists discover first new wild cat in more than 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:44:23 UTC
17:44:23 KST

Scientists discover first new wild cat in more than 100 years
Scientists have identified a previously unknown species of wild cat living at a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia. The tiny, spotted feline had lived at the sanctuary for years before genetic analysis revealed it as the first new living wild cat species identified in more than a century.
A previously unknown cat species has been identified in plain sight: at a wildlife sanctuary in Bolivia, where the small, spotted feline had been living for years.
The discovery, reported Thursday in the journal Current Biology, marks the first time scientists have named and described a new living wild cat species in more than a century.
Bolivian biologist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the study’s lead authors, said a colleague who thought the cat looked unusual invited her to examine it at the sanctuary in the country’s Yungas region, where she volunteered, a couple hours' drive from the administrative capital of La Paz.
A local family had left it there after finding it in the forest and struggling to keep it as a pet. What struck her was its size, she said – smaller than an average house cat, the male, now about 10 years old, measures 18 inches (46 centimetres) from its head to the base of its tail and weighs just 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms). Its light brown coat is patterned with dark, leopardlike spots.
“Knowing other wild cats, it was peculiar,” she said. “He really is tiny.”
Read moreNepal's tiger numbers rise 20 percent to an estimated 429
To locate the cat in South America’s feline family tree, researchers compared genomes – complete sets of genetic instructions – from over 30 cats across locations including Colombia, Peru and Brazil. Bones and skins preserved in US and European museums supplied DNA to fill the gaps where fresh samples were unavailable.
The analysis revealed that the sanctuary cat belonged to a previously unrecognised species whose lineage split from its relatives about 1.4 million years ago. The last feline species formally identified was the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.
“During naturalist expeditions in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, this cat was never collected and the species was never properly described,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
While some species are named after scientists or explorers, the researchers named this one Leopardus tilcayo, preserving the moniker used by communities in the tropical cloud forests of the Andes Mountains in Bolivia where the animal lives.
The findings helped unravel a longstanding mystery about South America’s tiger cats, which scientists once classified as a single species because they look so much alike. The researchers' DNA analysis pointed to at least five distinct species – four previously named, plus the newly described tilcayo.
“Even in groups that are very well studied, like the cat family, apparently there’s still a diversity that is hidden,” said evolutionary biologist and study co-author Jonas Lescroart with the University of Antwerp.
The next challenge is finding out more about these tiny cats in the wild.
“We still don’t know how many there are,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said, adding that researchers still need to establish details about the new tiger cat's diet, behaviour and habitat. Its presence has been confirmed only in Bolivia’s Yungas forests, but its full range remains unknown.
Scientists hope the designation of the new species will help protect its forest habitat, which faces threats from accelerating deforestation and gold mining.
“We should make haste in doing these kinds of discoveries, because all of this biodiversity is under pressure, and it’s disappearing as we speak,” Lescroart said.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Iran has put Hossein Pedaran to death following a closed espionage case in which authorities alleged that he supplied Israel with intelligence about missile facilities in the central province of Isfahan.
The execution forms part of a broader campaign against people accused of working with foreign intelligence services. Human-rights organizations have questioned the fairness of similar cases, particularly when convictions have relied heavily on statements made during detention.
Iran’s judiciary said Pedaran was convicted of cooperating with Mossad, Israel’s foreign intelligence agency. His death sentence was reviewed and approved by the country’s Supreme Court before being carried out, according to the judiciary-run Mizan news agency.
Officials presented Pedaran’s alleged account of his contact with foreign intelligence agencies as a central element of the case. They claimed he first attempted to reach the CIA but received no response.
He then allegedly contacted Mossad and, several days later, began communicating through WhatsApp with a person calling himself “Ben” who used a Dutch telephone number.
Authorities said Pedaran provided information concerning missile sites in Isfahan, a strategically important province that contains major military and nuclear-related facilities. They did not disclose when the alleged communications occurred or provide documentation showing what information was transferred.

Meloni argued that the recent surge in hostile activity stems directly from Russia’s inability to achieve its strategic objectives in Ukraine, noting that the invasion has failed to deliver the rapid victory promised by the Kremlin.
She warned that Putin seeks an escalation with Europe precisely to distract domestic audiences from the reality of the war, urging European nations to avoid disproportionate responses that could play directly into Moscow’s strategic calculations.

Across China: Chinese entrepreneur shapes low-carbon future via Yangtze plant
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:39:45 CST
17:39:45 KST

This photo taken on Spet. 13, 2026 shows fields of Miscanthus lutarioriparius in Shishou City, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua)
WUHAN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- For years, a tall grass growing along a stretch of the Yangtze, China's longest river, was treated as little more than a nuisance.
Known as Miscanthus lutarioriparius, the perennial grass once supplied small local paper mills. But after the mills were shut down over pollution concerns, much of it was left to rot. Millions of yuan had to be spent each year clearing it away.
Now, entrepreneur and botanist Sang Tao sees something very different in the same plant: a raw material that could replace some petroleum-based materials in a wide range of everyday and industrial products.
At his company in Shishou, a city in central China's Hubei Province, the grass collected along the Yangtze is processed into lignin- and cellulose-based materials. These can then be made into bio-resins, biodegradable plastics and other products for uses ranging from agriculture and consumer goods to new energy and advanced manufacturing.
Some of Hubei Shouding Industrial Co., Ltd.'s bio-resins are already on the market. This year, its biodegradable mulch film is expected to be used across several thousand mu of farmland.
For Sang, however, these products are only a beginning. He expects plant-based raw materials to gradually replace a portion of petroleum-derived materials over the next five to 10 years.
"The global oil market is unstable, while there is an urgent need to curb global warming. We must therefore move faster," Sang said.
Petroleum is deeply embedded in modern manufacturing. It provides the raw materials for countless products, from plastics, clothing and cosmetics to electronics, medical equipment and automobile components.
China is a major oil consumer and relies heavily on imported oil, with its dependence on imports reaching 72 percent, according to official data.
The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), released in March, calls for promoting a green and low-carbon transition and encourages the development of new energy, new materials and bio-manufacturing as emerging and future industries.
This broader push is creating new opportunities for companies like Shouding to scale up.
Shouding established its factory in Shishou in 2019, with its output valued at 20 million yuan (2.96 million U.S. dollars) last year. Sang plans to expand production, with a biorefinery capable of producing 10,000 tonnes a year set to come online this year, roughly 10 times the company's current capacity.
Sang, who earned his PhD in the United States, sees Miscanthus as just a starting point. He hopes the technology can eventually be applied to the roughly 1 billion tonnes of crop straw produced annually in rural China, turning agricultural waste into a valuable industrial resource.
For Shishou, the project offers a way to give new value to a once-overlooked local resource.
"We hope the company can bring both economic and environmental benefits, boost rural revitalization and local incomes, and support a greener, low-carbon and circular economy along the Yangtze River Economic Belt," said Hu Zhenchao, a local river management official in Shishou.
Shouding is not the only company in Shishou exploring new uses for plants. The city has also attracted companies that use Miscanthus and other plant-based materials to make high-performance specialty paper products for applications including home and food products, medical care, consumer goods and electrical equipment.
Sang sees the field as an industry of the future, and believes China, with its rapidly growing clean energy and advanced materials sectors, can offer useful experience to the world in pursuing greener, lower-carbon development. ■
This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a factory using Miscanthus lutarioriparius to produce new materials in Shishou City, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Lu Jinbo)
This photo taken on Sept. 13, 2026 shows a papermaking workshop using Miscanthus lutarioriparius to produce specialty paper in Shishou City, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua)

New U.S. Navy destroyer honors a D-Day Coast Guard hero
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:38:03 UTC
17:38:03 KST

- The future USS Quentin Walsh, a Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, has reached the Land Level construction stage at Bath Iron Works.
- The ship is named for U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Quentin R. Walsh, who earned the Navy Cross for helping secure Cherbourg after D-Day.
Bath Iron Works said the future USS Quentin Walsh, a Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, is now one of the ships taking shape at its Land Level erection stage, the point where large prefabricated hull sections are joined together before launch.
General Dynamics’ Bath Iron Works shipyard in Maine marked the milestone alongside National POW/MIA Recognition Day, tying the ship’s construction progress to the wartime record of its namesake, U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Quentin R. Walsh. Walsh earned the Navy Cross during World War II for his role in securing the Normandy port of Cherbourg days after the D-Day landings, when he convinced German defenders he commanded a force of 800 men ready to attack. That bluff led to the surrender of 350 German troops and the release of 53 Allied prisoners of war.
DDG 132 will be the 44th Arleigh Burke-class destroyer built at Bath Iron Works and the third Flight III variant of the class under construction there. The U.S. Navy awarded the contract for the ship in December 2018, and Bath Iron Works began cutting steel for it in November 2021. The shipyard laid the vessel’s keel in May 2025, when Walsh’s great-granddaughter, serving as the ship’s sponsor, welded her initials into the keel plate in a traditional authentication ceremony.
Like other Flight III destroyers, the Quentin Walsh will carry the AN/SPY-6(V)1 Air and Missile Defense Radar, a four-sided phased array system built to track and help defend against ballistic missiles, hypersonic weapons, cruise missiles, surface threats and electronic attacks in a single integrated radar. The Flight III design also adds upgraded electrical power and cooling capacity to support that radar and other systems compared with earlier Arleigh Burke variants.
Arleigh Burke-class destroyers remain the backbone of the Navy’s surface fleet, built to operate against air, surface and subsurface threats simultaneously. Bath Iron Works has not disclosed a specific launch date or delivery timeline for the Quentin Walsh beyond its current construction stage.

====================================================================================================

Two AI dangers we keep confusing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:36:37 UTC
17:36:37 KST

The growing chorus from the people building the world’s most powerful artificial intelligence systems is becoming difficult to ignore.
In his recent 3,800-word essay, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei argued that humanity might need to “pace the frontier” if AI capabilities begin advancing faster than our ability to control them. OpenAI’s chief scientist has similarly advocated voluntary slowdowns until common safety thresholds are established.
They have good reason to worry.
The possibility that increasingly autonomous AI systems could deceive their operators, circumvent safeguards, improve themselves or perform actions their creators never intended is no longer confined to science fiction.
Recent experiments with AI agents have produced behavior disturbing enough to raise a legitimate question: What happens when systems far more capable than today’s begin operating with greater autonomy?
Slowing down may therefore be sensible. But before applying the brakes, we need to ask a question strangely absent from much of this debate: Slow down what?
The term “AI safety” increasingly conflates two fundamentally different dangers.
Humanity loses either way
The first is the danger that AI becomes so capable that humans lose control of it. This is the existential-risk scenario that dominates Silicon Valley’s safety debate.
The ultimate threat is not China, the US or any particular lab. Rather, it is an artificial intelligence whose capabilities exceed our ability to understand, constrain or reliably direct it.
It does not matter who gets there first. If the worst fears prove correct, humanity loses either way. Call this AI safety.
The second danger is almost the opposite. AI remains perfectly under human control. It does exactly what humans tell it to do. The problem is who is doing the telling. Call this AI security.
China, Russia, Iran and North Korea do not need a rogue superintelligence to threaten democratic societies. They need increasingly capable AI systems that remain obedient while making cyberattacks more sophisticated and military planning more effective.
An AI that penetrates an adversary’s military network, discovers vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure or helps disrupt communications during an attack on Taiwan while following Beijing’s instructions perfectly would be something called–an effective AI agent. This distinction matters because the two dangers can demand opposite policies.
Singularity
If AI systems begin acquiring capabilities for autonomous replication, deception, uncontrolled self-improvement or actions their developers cannot reliably supervise, slowing development until safeguards catch up could make humanity safer.
But suppose AI becomes extraordinarily good at detecting cyber intrusions, defending power grids, identifying influence operations, protecting military communications or discovering vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them. Should democratic countries slow those capabilities too?
Quite possibly the opposite. They may need to accelerate them.
That creates a paradox at the heart of AI policy: Developing some capabilities too quickly could make us less safe. Developing others too slowly could do the same. This distinction becomes especially important when discussing China.
There is a genuine case for US-China cooperation on existential AI risks. Neither Washington nor Beijing benefits from creating systems that neither can control. Both have reason to prevent AI from interfering autonomously with nuclear command systems or triggering unintended military escalation.
Communication, common testing standards, emergency channels and greater transparency around genuinely catastrophic capabilities therefore deserve serious exploration. Catherine Thorbecke of Bloomberg recently argued that US-China AI talks should seek mutual visibility rather than an unrealistic grand bargain. That is sensible.
Overlaps end
But the overlap ends where strategic advantage begins.
China has little reason to help the US neutralize AI capabilities that strengthen China militarily or politically. Nor should Washington expect Beijing to disclose sensitive military, intelligence or cyber programs simply because both governments have signed an agreement bearing the words “AI safety.”
This is where global cooperation must be carefully defined. An agreement designed to prevent either country from losing control of advanced AI could benefit both.
An agreement that constrains the US’ ability to develop defensive AI while leaving unverifiable what China’s military and intelligence services are developing could make it less safe.
The most dangerous mistake would therefore be to negotiate “AI safety” as though every AI capability belonged in the same basket. They do not.
The US needs a more discriminating strategy: slow capabilities that materially increase the danger of losing human control and accelerate defensive capabilities to protect democratic societies from adversarial uses of AI. That means stronger cyber defenses.
Frightened of itself
It also means recognizing something important, which is that maintaining an AI advantage over authoritarian competitors can itself be a safety objective.
This is where calls for slowing AI development become dangerously incomplete. Asking US companies to slow broadly while assuming competitors will eventually recognize the wisdom of doing likewise is not a strategy. Authoritarian governments have strategic objectives that do not disappear because Silicon Valley becomes frightened by what it is building.
None of this means Amodei is wrong. Humanity should not race blindly toward technologies whose consequences we do not understand merely because everyone fears somebody else will arrive first.
But neither should democracies become so preoccupied with the possibility of AI turning against humanity that they neglect the more immediate possibility of humans turning AI against one another. That distinction should guide both domestic policy and negotiations with China.
The AI race is dangerous. But there is more than one way to lose it.
Racing too quickly toward capabilities we cannot control could endanger humanity. Racing too slowly toward capabilities democracies need to defend themselves could hand an extraordinary advantage to regimes that do not share their values.
The challenge, then, is not simply to put the brakes on AI. It is knowing where to brake — and when we may need to press the accelerator.
John Cheng is a retired businessman from Hong Kong who lives in Taiwan and is the author of “Taiwan Is Taiwan.”

USA approves potential sale of $2.7 bln worth of air defense systems, ammunition to Ukraine

11:35:06 EEST
17:35:06 KST

The U.S. State Department has approved a potential sale of $2.68 billion worth of U.S. military equipment to Ukraine for air defense systems, according to the State Department's website.
"The U.S. Department of State has made a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine for purchase of Air Defense Development Upgrades and related equipment and services. The estimated total cost is $2.68 billion," the statement reads.
If the proposed purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program, appropriated during the prior U.S. administration.
Funds from the FMF will be credited as a U.S. contribution to the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund via a 1:1 reimbursement.
Ukraine has submitted a request to purchase the following weapons, which do not fall under the category of major defense equipment items: S-300 Clone missiles; GAM-67 missiles; Range-Extended, Laser-Guided Air Defense missile systems; Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher (ITEL) 1.5; mobile launching system modification kits; RPS 202 counter-Unmanned Aircraft System radars, etc.
"Implementation of this proposed sale will not require the assignment of any additional U.S. Government or contractor representatives to Ukraine… The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the basic military balance in the region," the department concluded.

Estonia and the U.S. seek rare‑earth agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Estonia and the U.S. seek rare‑earth agreement
Estonia and the United States are working toward an agreement on rare earth elements to strengthen supply security. The talks are not about Estonia's mineral deposits; the goal is to develop local industry and attract new investment, says Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. On Thursday, Lithuania signed a similar agreement with the U.S.
The global rare‑earth market is largely controlled by China, which in recent years has significantly restricted exports. As a result, the U.S. is trying to diversify supply and secure its supply chains by striking agreements with other partners. Estonia, for its part, has one of Europe's largest rare‑earth production and processing capacities. Both sides are interested in closer cooperation, but negotiations are still in the early stages.
"Our interest is to establish in Estonia at least Europe's largest knowledge and development center. And likewise to bring broader‑scale investments to Estonia and strengthen Estonia's role in the rare‑earth network — and certainly also for security‑policy reasons. We are not negotiating over Estonia's mineral resources," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
Countries already involved in the U.S. initiative include Poland, the United Kingdom and Japan. On Thursday, Lithuania's foreign minister, who visited Washington, signed a cooperation agreement.
"This is currently our second foreign‑policy priority — the first is security. We must face these economic challenges, build a strategic partnership with the world's leading power, the United States, and create a resilient and strong supply chain," said Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys.
"Supply and processing security for rare earth elements is a foundation of the 21st‑century economy. This has been discussed before. It is essential for our economy and for defense. Lithuania, for example, has a global leadership role in photonics," said U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The agreement was discussed extensively with Lithuanian companies, who believe it could lead to several major projects. Over the next six months, Lithuania and the U.S. will decide which initiatives are worth pursuing. Funding is expected to come from both government and private sources.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Argo Ideon

Details

People leave everything behind and flee the shelling
Reuters spoke with families who were forced to leave their homes with practically nothing. Some people fled barefoot, leaving behind livestock, clothing, blankets, and food supplies.
We fled barefoot. We did not even know where our children were. We had nothing with us: no blankets, no mattresses, no food, no water, nothing
Her family had already been forced to leave their native village eight years ago because of the war and had lived in a camp for displaced people. Now, due to the renewed fighting, the family had to flee for a second time.

Britain exploring return to making its own reactor fuel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
09:32:19 BST
17:32:19 KST

Britain has begun exploring options to re-establish the production of reactor fuel for defence purposes, work the government says would be fully consistent with its obligations under the Non-Proliferation Treaty, according to the annual update to Parliament published this week.
The Nuclear Fuels Programme is part of the recapitalisation the Defence Nuclear Enterprise is carrying out simultaneously, which the update describes as covering two submarine build programmes with a further one in design, two warhead programmes, the fuel cycle work, and the infrastructure required to build and maintain those capabilities.
Every British submarine is nuclear powered, with the reactors manufactured by Rolls-Royce Submarines at Raynesway near Derby. The update describes nuclear propulsion as critical to sustaining continuous at sea deterrence, allowing submarines to remain dived on long-range patrols without detection.
Raynesway is one of the two sites receiving a share of the £6 billion committed under the Defence Investment Plan for infrastructure, alongside Barrow-in-Furness, investment the update says will grow the capability of the enterprise to produce a submarine every eighteen months in future.
Britain last enriched uranium for defence purposes at Capenhurst, and the country has relied on existing stocks for reactor fuel since domestic production ceased, which is the position the exploration now under way would change.
The update sets out the rest of the submarine picture alongside it. The Royal Navy has operated the Vanguard class since 1993, and those boats will be replaced by the Dreadnought class, with steel cut for the fourth and final Dreadnought in September 2025 on the same day the King commissioned HMS Agamemnon, the sixth Astute-class submarine.
The Astute class supports the deterrent while also undertaking other defence and intelligence tasks, including work with maritime task groups. Beyond those two programmes sits SSN-AUKUS, the design now in progress, with BAE Systems, the Defence Nuclear Organisation, Babcock and Rolls-Royce Submarines all maintaining teams at Barrow contributing to it.
The enterprise spent £12 billion in the 2025/26 financial year and projects spend of over £100 billion through British suppliers over the next ten years, with in excess of £20 billion more going into it between 2026/27 and 2029/30 than across the previous four years.

Turkish drone pods team up to jam, image enemy radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:32:15 UTC
17:32:15 KST

- ASELSAN demonstrated three airborne electronic warfare and imaging pods working together on Bayraktar TB2 drones during live trials in Konya province.
- The systems detected, jammed and photographed a radar target in sequence, before an audience of more than 15 international defense delegations.
Turkish defense manufacturer ASELSAN demonstrated in live trials in Konya province that three of its airborne systems can work together on Bayraktar TB2 drones to detect, jam and photograph enemy radar in a single coordinated sequence, the company said, in a demonstration attended by more than 15 international defense delegations.
The trial combined three pods: the ANTIDOT 2ES 100, which detects and pinpoints the location of enemy radar signals; the ANTIDOT 2EA 200, which jams those same radars once found; and the FULMAR 200, a radar imaging pod that builds detailed ground pictures regardless of weather or darkness. ASELSAN said the systems were flown on the Bayraktar TB2, though other reporting on the same Konya event described the ANTIDOT and FULMAR pods operating from two separate TB2 aircraft rather than one, and put the number of participating countries at 18 rather than the 15-plus figure in ASELSAN’s own statement.
In the first phase of the demonstration, the ESM pod found and geolocated a search radar, then passed that targeting data to the jamming pod, which carried out a precision electronic attack. At a set point, the jamming was deliberately paused to let the target radar reacquire and lock onto the drone. Once locked on, the jamming pod used digital radio frequency memory techniques, which capture and retransmit a radar’s own signal back at it with subtle alterations to confuse its tracking, to disrupt that tracking radar as well.
In the second phase, the detection pod again located the emitter while the FULMAR 200 built a high-resolution radar image of the target area, accurate to within a few meters for ground mapping and target identification. ASELSAN said the combination shows the pods can support day-and-night, all-weather reconnaissance missions.
ASELSAN framed the full sequence, detection, jamming and imaging, as an early version of what the military calls Suppression and Destruction of Enemy Air Defense missions, work aimed at disabling an opponent’s own radar and air defense systems so that other aircraft can operate more safely nearby. The company said the complete version of this concept, as already proven in combat, ends with a target being marked using its ASELFLIR 500 sensor system and destroyed with a laser-guided munition, though that final strike step was not part of this particular demonstration.
The Bayraktar TB2 has been in wide combat use since the early 2020s, and ASELSAN’s ASELFLIR 500 sensor has previously flown on Baykar’s larger Bayraktar TB3 drone, including during a mission launched from the Turkish Navy’s drone carrier TCG Anadolu. ASELSAN has not disclosed whether any customer has ordered this specific three-pod electronic warfare and imaging package, nor given a cost or timeline for fielding it beyond this demonstration.

China, Iran, Israeli groups weaponize AI for first-of-their-kind social media influence campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:44 UTC
17:26:44 KST

Iran, China, and groups from Israel used artificial intelligence to operate thousands of fake accounts, creating first-of-their-kind AI-powered influence campaigns across social media, according to an investigation published by The New York Times.
The countries and firms used AI to intensify the scale of online campaigns beyond what verified human users could organically achieve, US officials told the NYT.
The firms reportedly turned to Chinese “open-source” AI models, which users can download and modify for custom purposes. The firms then used those open-source models to create “agents,” bots with the autonomy to operate software and complete tasks on their own without constant prompting.
The New York Times explained that once hundreds of those AI agents were let loose on the internet, they autonomously opened networks of fake accounts on platforms such as Instagram, Facebook, X/Twitter, and TikTok.
The AI agents then rapidly populated the fake profiles with false information relating to politics and current events.
First time Chinese models were used like this
US officials told the NYT that these instances marked one of the first times AI agents from Chinese-produced models were used to handle every stage of an online influence campaign, from creating new fake accounts to coordinating messaging and framing online.
Unlike proprietary AI models, the open-source models were manipulated by developers to allow the agents to evade safeguards designed to verify users and prevent the manipulation of online discourse, the US officials added.
The US intelligence community, along with cybersecurity experts, looked into the groups behind the AI-powered campaigns and traced those efforts back to state-backed Chinese and Iranian groups, as well as to Israeli campaigns stemming from two private firms.
Kyle Crichton, a fellow at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology who studies AI and cybersecurity, told the NYT that “Agent-led campaigns” will likely become more common as the technology spreads.
“Agents can be fairly sophisticated, and so in addition to just scale, they have an ability to blend in and look more like a human user,” he said.
The investigation was published in the wake of other major technology news, as AI leaders warned of the risks of developing AI too quickly and without proper safety measures. These warnings followed public concern over recent stories of AI models going rogue and hacking other companies.
In a report last month, Meta said it had seen a “technically significant development” of bad actors using AI for malicious purposes.
AI is now “embedded within automated systems that can produce, adapt, and distribute content with minimal human intervention,” Meta added.
The investigation also traced AI-agent campaigns back to Israel
The report mentioned that IntelEye, a Tel Aviv-based company founded by former NSO Group employees, operated roughly 1,000 AI-powered fake accounts on social media to manipulate political discourse around the upcoming Israeli elections.
The company used DeepSeek, a Chinese open-source AI model, to create its agents. According to the investigation, the bots then published content both supporting and opposing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
IntelEye disputed claims that its work was intended to influence online discussions, stating the company was conducting a defensive research experiment to expose weaknesses in AI systems.
“IntelEye does not operate influence campaigns,” co-founder Maor Sellek told the Times. “Our work with DeepSeek was conducted for defensive research and testing, to understand how models with insufficient safeguards could be misused and to improve detection of that activity.”
Sellek said IntelEye bought 10,000 social media accounts and handed over control to autonomous AI agents, though he added that only about 1,000 of the accounts were operational.
The agents used the accounts to leave comments on posts to boost engagement, although Sellek said they were not very successful.
Meta told the New York Times that the vast majority of the AI-powered agents set up on Facebook and Instagram by IntelEye, other companies, and state-backed groups had been removed by its automated detection and verification systems.

In the kitchen with Henny: Celebrating in the sukkah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:26:34 UTC
17:26:34 KST

Rosh Hashanah just ended, and already we’re planning our Sukkot menus. Just three days ago, there was no room in my fridge for one extra carrot, and now there’s almost nothing in there except for carrots. The irony!
And the cycle will continue over the next couple of weeks. Even for Yom Kippur, when we don’t eat, the supermarkets are packed with people buying food for before and after the fast. Again, the irony.
But Sukkot is something I look forward to all year. I love Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, with their days of prayer, reflection, and forgiveness, but there is something so special about sitting in a cozy sukkah, surrounded by guests, both spiritual and physical, and simply taking in Hashem’s love and kindness.
Sukkot is a time of real joy, and after all the planning, cooking, and preparing, I can’t wait to sit down in the sukkah and celebrate.
Arugula Salad with Maple Dressing
Besides being beautiful, this salad is perfect for this time of year. The maple dressing and candied pecans give it a touch of autumn, while the mangoes are perfectly sweet right now.
You can use arugula, baby leaves, spinach, or a combination of whatever greens you like. As always, adapt it to fit your own culinary style and what your family enjoys.
Yields 6 servings
4 cups arugula (rocket)
3 cups mixed baby leaves
3 small cucumbers, thinly sliced
1 ripe mango, peeled and thinly sliced
1 apple, thinly sliced
½ cup candied pecans, roughly chopped
¼ cup sunflower seeds or pumpkin seeds, optional
Dressing:
¹⁄³ cup olive oil
2 Tbsp. maple syrup
2 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice
1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar
½ tsp. salt
Black pepper, to taste
In a small bowl or jar, combine the olive oil, maple syrup, lemon juice, apple cider vinegar, salt, and black pepper. Whisk or shake well until combined. Set aside, or refrigerate until ready to use.
Place the arugula and baby leaves on a large serving platter. Arrange the cucumbers, mango, and apple over the greens, then sprinkle with the candied pecans and sunflower or pumpkin seeds, if using. Drizzle the dressing over the salad just before serving and toss gently.
Crispy Potato Cups
I don’t know why, but I always associate the sukkah with finger foods. Maybe it’s because we’re going up and down the stairs between the apartment and the sukkah, and I’d rather not carry large pans filled with hot liquid, or maybe it’s simply because finger foods are fun and the sukkah has such a fun feel to it.
When I saw the idea of making potato cups using just a potato, I thought, this sounds easy enough. I’m giving you a ground beef filling here, but you can really be as creative as you want.
For a vegan option, try mashed sweet potato or butternut squash. For a dairy version, fill them with sautéed veggies, mushrooms, and onions, and top with shredded cheese.
I love recipes that can be adapted to fit different meals. You can prepare a batch of the potato cups ahead of time and then fill them with whatever works best for the meal you’re serving.
Yields 12 potato cups
Potato cups:
12 small potatoes or 6 large potatoes, plus 1 large potato for the meat filling
2-3 Tbsp. olive oil
½ tsp. paprika
1 tsp. garlic powder
1 tsp. salt
½ tsp. ground black pepper
Oil spray, for greasing
Ground beef filling:
2 Tbsp. olive oil
2 large onions, diced
400 grams ground beef
1 red pepper, diced
¼ cup chopped fresh parsley or cilantro (coriander)
2 Tbsp. tomato sauce or BBQ sauce
½ tsp. salt
¼ tsp. ground black pepper
1 large cooked potato, reserved from the potato cups
1 egg
Place the potatoes, with the skins on, in a large pot and cover with water. Bring to a boil and cook until soft and easily pierced with a fork. Drain and let cool enough to handle. Set aside 1 large potato for the meat filling.
Preheat the oven to 200°C/400°F. Grease a 12-cup muffin tin or ramekins very well with oil spray. Place one small potato, or half of a large potato – skin side down, into each muffin cup or ramekin. Using the bottom of a small glass, press each potato down and up the sides of the muffin cup, leaving the center hollow. Use a spoon to gently smooth and shape the potatoes into cups.
In a small bowl, combine the olive oil, paprika, garlic powder, salt, and black pepper. Brush the mixture generously over the inside and edges of each potato cup. Bake for 15-20 minutes, or until the edges begin to brown and crisp. Remove from the oven and allow the potato cups to cool in the muffin tin.
Meanwhile, heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the onions and sauté until soft and caramelized. Add the ground beef and cook for about 5 minutes, breaking it apart with a wooden spoon as it cooks. Add the red pepper, parsley or cilantro, tomato sauce or BBQ sauce, salt, and black pepper. Continue cooking for another 5-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is cooked through and the pepper has softened.
Peel and mash the reserved cooked potato, then stir it into the meat mixture until everything is well combined.
Reduce the oven temperature to 180°C/350°F. Spoon the meat filling into the potato cups and bake for about 20 minutes. Allow the cups to cool for a few minutes in the muffin tin before carefully removing and serving.
Breaded Veal Chops
Whenever I see breaded veal chops, I immediately think of my mother. She didn’t make them often, which is probably part of why I remember them so well, but when she did, I loved them.
Years later, on one of our visits to New York, our cousin Lisa, on my husband’s side, took us out to a meat Italian restaurant in Manhattan that she knew we liked. I spotted breaded veal on the menu, and, all of a sudden, that memory came rushing back. I ordered it, and it came with creamy mashed potatoes and was smothered in fried onions. It was every bit as comforting and delicious as I remembered.
Veal chops are not something you see very often here, but around the holidays they tend to show up more at the butcher. So if you spot them, pick up a few and make these easy breaded veal chops for one of your Sukkot meals. The crispy coating and fried onions make them feel festive without being complicated.
Yields 4 servings
4 veal chops
1 cup potato starch or wheat flour
2 eggs, beaten
2 cups unseasoned bread crumbs
¾ tsp. salt
½ tsp. ground black pepper
2 Tbsp. granulated garlic
½ tsp. paprika
½-¾ cup oil, for frying
1 large onion, sliced into rings
Prepare three shallow plates. Place the potato starch or flour on the first plate. On the second plate, place the beaten eggs and season with ¼ tsp salt and a dash of black pepper. On the third plate, combine the bread crumbs, granulated garlic, paprika, ½ tsp salt, and ½ tsp black pepper.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Dip each veal chop first into the potato starch or flour, then into the egg mixture, and finally into the bread crumbs, making sure it is well coated on all sides.
Place the breaded veal chops in the hot oil and fry for 8-10 minutes on the first side. Flip and fry for another 8 minutes, or until golden and crisp on the outside and cooked through.
While the veal is frying, add the onion slices to the same pan. Fry until golden and crisp, removing them as they are ready.
Transfer the veal chops to a serving platter, scatter the crispy onions over the top, and serve warm.
Cookie Crust Brownies
I feel very blessed that I get to cook with my students at Midreshet Darkaynu on Wednesday evenings. Last year, one of the students, Atara, asked if we could make these triple-layer brownies that she loves. I was a little skeptical at first because they sounded complicated, but they really weren’t.
We divided the group into two. One group prepared the chocolate chip cookie crust while the other made the brownie batter. And what goes in the middle? Oreos. That part was simple enough!
We spread the cookie dough into the pan, arranged the Oreos on top, and then poured the brownie batter over everything. It was such a fun dessert to make together, and even more fun to eat.
Because these brownies are so rich, they’re not something I would make all the time, which is exactly why I think they’re perfect for Sukkot. It’s a festive dessert, a little over the top, and definitely one that feels like a celebration.
Yield: 20-24 brownies
Cookie layer:
¹⁄³ cup brown sugar
¹⁄³ cup granulated sugar
¹⁄³ cup oil
1 egg
½ tsp. vanilla extract
1½ cups flour
1 tsp. baking soda
½ tsp. salt
¹⁄³ cup chocolate chips
20 Oreo cookies or other chocolate sandwich cookies
Brownie layer:
½ cup oil
250 grams chocolate
1 tsp. vanilla extract
3 eggs
1 cup sugar
¾ cup flour
¼ tsp. baking soda
½ tsp. salt
Preheat the oven to 175°C/350°F. Line or grease a 23 x 33 cm. (9 x 13-inch) baking pan.
For the cookie layer, mix the brown sugar, granulated sugar, egg, oil, and vanilla until well combined. Add the flour, baking soda, and salt, and mix until a dough forms. Add the chocolate chips and mix until evenly incorporated. Press the cookie dough evenly into the bottom of the prepared pan, then arrange the Oreo cookies in a single layer over the cookie dough.
For the brownie layer, place the chocolate and oil in a small saucepan over low heat and stir until melted and smooth. Remove from the heat and set aside to cool slightly. In a separate bowl, mix the eggs, sugar, and vanilla until combined. Slowly add the melted chocolate mixture, stirring as you pour. Add the flour, baking soda, and salt, and mix until smooth.
Pour the brownie batter over the Oreo layer and spread evenly. Bake for about 30-35 minutes, or until the brownie layer is set and a toothpick inserted into the brownie portion comes out with moist crumbs.
Allow the brownies to cool completely before cutting into squares.
I HOPE you found some of these recipes exciting and that they’re getting you into the festive Sukkot mood. Although we still have Shabbat Shuva and Yom Kippur in the coming days, Sukkot will be here before we know it.
It’s such a meaningful time of year, filled with reflection, prayer, and forgiveness, and hopefully giving us the ability to move forward with more understanding, connection, and unity.
I want to take this opportunity to wish you a year filled with good health, laughter, and joy. May it be a year of coming together, of feeling more connected to one another, and of enjoying many festive meals together with the people we love.■
Henny is a kitchen coach who teaches women how to meal plan and cook so they get dinner on the table and prepare for Shabbat and hag on time. To book her for one-on-one coaching or an exciting food workshop: www.inthekitchenwithhenny.com
