India: British Sikh man granted bail after 9-year detention
Published September 19, 2026last updated September 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Scottish-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without being convicted, has been granted bail
- India is set to replace Asian Games opening ceremony male flagbearer over missing ceremonial kit
- Counting underway in elections for the Delhi University Students' Union
Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Saturday, September 19:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee
US President Donald Trump has extended the $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions through September 2027, the White House has said — a move that will be strongly felt in India, the largest source of H-1B recipients.
The extension, announced on Friday, keeps a policy first introduced in September 2025 in place. It excludes visa renewals and student visa holders transitioning to H-1B status.
Trump also signed a proclamation directing tighter scrutiny of applications, instructing agencies to weigh employers' recent layoffs of American workers when reviewing petitions.
The policy remains under legal challenge, with an appeals court reviewing a June ruling that found the fee unlawful.
The stakes are high for India: USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 showed Indian nationals accounted for 69.9% of approved H-1B petitions, far ahead of China's 12.1%.
When the fee first launched last year, it caused panic among Indian travelers, including passengers who deboarded a Delhi-bound flight fearing they'd be barred from returning.
Opposition Congress party leader Pawan Khera criticized the extension on social media, warning it would make it "harder for Indian students to enter the US workforce" and could drive a "talent drain" toward the UK, Canada and Australia.
He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his perceived camaraderie with Trump, adding: "Modi bent over backwards to appease Trump. Trump got the appeasement. India took the humiliation and the hit."
Surendra Koli, acquitted in Nithari serial killings case, found dead in suspected suicide
Surendra Koli, a key figure in India's notorious 2006 Nithari serial killings case who was acquitted of all charges last year, was found dead at a tea stall he operated in Haridwar.
Police are treating the case as a suspected suicide.
Residents discovered Koli's body inside the rented stall and alerted authorities, Haridwar City Deputy Superintendent of Police Shishupal Singh Negi told local media.
No suicide note was found and the body was sent for post-mortem examination as investigators look into the circumstances.
Koli first drew national attention in 2006, when he was a domestic worker at businessman Moninder Singh Pandher's home in Noida. The discovery of human remains, including children's, in a drain behind Pandher's house sparked a major investigation and nationwide outrage.
Koli was convicted and sentenced to death in multiple cases beginning in 2009. In October 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted both Koli and Pandher for lack of evidence.
Two key observations were made: Koli's confession was inadmissible, as it was extracted after a long, unauthorized interrogation in police custody without adequate legal safeguards, and the prosecution could not prove that the remains uncovered from the "open, public" drain were based solely on Koli's statements.
The decision was upheld by India's Supreme Court in late 2025.
Reports suggest he moved to the northern city of Haridwar after the acquittal. Police identified Koli through an Aadhaar card found on his body.
India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up
A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan.
Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer.
Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India.
"I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony.
The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue."
The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4.
Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team.
A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway.
Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody
The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody.
The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail.
Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding.
He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017.
He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued.
Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary.
"Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture."
Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed.
What did the court say in its ruling?
In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon."
The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached.
Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported.
"I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison."

Trump signs bill authorising sweeping Russia sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Trump signs Bill authorising sweeping Russia sanctions
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump on Sept 18 signed a Bill authorising new sanctions designed to pressure Russia over its war in Ukraine, with Congress giving its approval after months of delay.
Washington is pushing to revive a mediated path towards ending the conflict as Moscow intensifies attacks against Ukraine, even though much of its attention – and munitions – are focused on the ongoing war against Iran.
The legislation, which US lawmakers approved this week, takes aim at Russia’s energy and defence sectors, alongside President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to evade Western sanctions, and allows Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
That could potentially cover China and India, and furthers efforts to cut off revenue financing Moscow’s war.
The Republican-led House of Representatives passed the package by a 262-159 vote on Sept 16.
The Bill would also target companies and foreign actors supporting Russia’s military, and extend sanctions involving Iran.
But the broad powers to impose tariffs sparked an unusual split among Democrats, who largely support Ukraine but have resisted handing Trump wider authority over trade.
Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev said on Sept 19 that the country’s response to the sanctions should involve “military deterrence”.
Medvedev, a senior ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin and one of Moscow’s most prominent anti-Western hawks, did not elaborate on his remarks.
“Even across the ocean, they hear only the language of direct military deterrence, and that is the language in which we should respond to Russophobic atrocities, such as the law of the dead terrorist, Graham,” Medvedev, who now serves as deputy chair of Russia’s Security Council, said on Telegram.
Medvedev, who served as Russia’s head of state between 2008 and 2012, was referring to the late US senator Lindsey Graham, whom the Bill is named after.
Since Moscow launched its full-scale offensive against Ukraine in February 2022, Russian officials including Putin have described Ukraine and its supporters as “terrorists”, accusations dismissed by Kyiv as baseless wartime propaganda.
Tougher pressure
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky earlier hailed the legislation as “symbolic” and thanked US lawmakers.
The Bill is “an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the point where it has to make peace”, Zelensky wrote on X.
“Sanctions must be strong so that all efforts for peace – including our joint diplomatic efforts with the United States, Europe, and our other friends – can succeed,” he added.
India said on Sept 17 it would continue buying oil “through diversified sourcing”.
New Delhi – which counts Russia as one of its most important strategic partners – has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the US-Iran conflict in part by turning to Moscow, despite pressure from Western countries.
Supporters of the legislation argued that tougher economic pressure is needed against Moscow.
The congressional vote was celebrated by pro-Ukraine activists, who pointed to continuing Russian attacks, including drone strikes on Sept 16 on civilian transport in the south that officials in Kyiv said killed five people.
Trump has generally preferred to retain control over sanctions and tariffs rather than have Congress dictate policy, helping delay the measure for more than a year.
The President’s signing of the Bill comes a week before he is due to meet his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington. AFP

Remembering Churchill’s Zurich speech as Europe faces security crisis

Remembering Churchill’s Zurich speech as Europe faces security crisis
In 1946, former British prime minister Winston Churchill delivered a speech in Zurich in which he urged Europeans to “recreate the fabric” of their continent in the aftermath of the Second World War. Now, as Europe again grapples with complex threats to its security, do his words still resonate?
In his address, made at the University of Zurich on September 19, 1946, Churchill called for a “remedy” to prevent future conflicts, one that he said would make Europe “as free and happy as Switzerland is today.” That remedy, he said, was “to recreate the European fabric” and “build a kind of United States of Europe.”
“Churchill used the word ‘bewildered’ in his speech – how could this destruction in Europe have happened?” British Ambassador James Squire told Swissinfo on the margins of an event in Zurich celebrating the 80th anniversary of the speech. “It was a time for Europe to work out how it could preserve peace in future.”
Churchill called not just for a united Europe, but for the United States – “mighty America”, in his words – to support it.
>> Learn more about Churchill’s Zurich address and its links to the creation of the EU and the Council of Europe:
More
When Winston Churchill called for European unity in neutral Zurich
Today, these “fundamental pillars of European security” are under threat, said Jamie Shea, a former top NATO official and current senior advisor at the European Policy Centre, a Brussels-based think tank. He pointed to “lots of question marks” about the future of the European Union with the rise of populist parties, alongside a waning US commitment to European defence. The challenge now, Shea said, is how to re-establish these pillars.
Amid Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine and hybrid threats including sabotage and attacks on critical infrastructure, Squire said the message from Churchill’s speech is to confront that reality with optimism and pragmatism, just as the former wartime leader had. “We can’t take peace and freedom for granted,” Squire said. “We have to stand up for that.”

When Winston Churchill called for European unity in neutral Zurich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

When Winston Churchill called for European unity in neutral Zurich
In September 1946, Winston Churchill delivered a famous speech in Zurich, calling for “a kind of United States of Europe”. What became of his idea – and why did he present it in Switzerland, of all places?
Switzerland is home to many international organisations. But when it comes to getting involved in them, the country has historically been hesitant. It is not a member of the European Union (EU), and there are no signs of this changing. And it only joined the United Nations (UN) in 2002, after 189 states had already done so.
In 1946, just a few months after the first ever UN General Assembly, Winston Churchill, who had led Britain through the Second World War, was in Switzerland. In this year of peace, the possibility of change was in the air – and Churchill duly set a milestone when on September 19, at the University of Zurich, he called for a United States of EuropeExternal link.
“I always say there are two origins of Europe. Churchill’s speech is one of them,” says Birte Wassenberg, a historian at the University of Strasbourg who specialises in the history of European organisations. But how did it come about that the idea of European unification was proposed in Switzerland of all places?
For Wassenberg, the Zurich location – which she describes as a “good choice” – has to be seen in the context of the incipient Cold War. “Switzerland was chosen because of its classic neutrality – it was an attempt at a speech for peace on neutral European soil,” says the academic.
A speech not for the Swiss
Martin Conway, a professor of contemporary European history at the University of Oxford, agrees on the logic of the neutral location. “It doesn’t seem to me that Churchill is in any way giving a speech to the Swiss – he’s giving it to a kind of post-war European political elite, who he’s urging to look beyond immediate problems and to focus on building a new world”, Conway says.
>> A statesman on holiday: a look back at what Churchill got up to during his 1946 Swiss visit:
More
When Churchill mixed Swiss business and pleasure
Today, meanwhile, Churchill’s speech is often associated with the roots of the EU – but it is at least as directly connected to the creation of the Council of Europe in 1949.
Churchill said in Zurich that there was a need to “build and fortify” the UN. But he also called for more. “We must re-create the European family in a regional structure called, it may be, the United States of Europe, and the first practical step will be to form a Council of Europe,” he said. His goal: a Europe which is “as free and happy as Switzerland is today”.
And if at first not all states were ready to “join a union”, it would have to be done with those who wanted to and could, Churchill said. He envisioned France and Germany taking the lead on this – for Conway, a “striking” sign of confidence from a leader who had spent the previous years fighting Nazi Germany.
Beyond this, Great Britain, the US and Soviet Russia should become the “friends and sponsors” of the new Europe and “champion its right to live”, Churchill said.
As such, the Soviet Union was explicitly addressed; Churchill saw its participation as essential to a good outcome. “The Council of Europe initially tried not to integrate into the Cold War blocs,” says Wassenberg. But “the Soviet Union did not accept this.”
At the Congress of Europe in The Hague, held in May 1948 under Churchill’s patronage, there were still participants from states that would go on to form part of the Eastern Bloc, like Poland or Slovakia. “But with the closing of the Iron Curtain, they were denied membership in the Council of Europe in 1949”, says Wassenberg. The ten founding members of the Strasbourg-based organisation were all from Western Europe.
>> Read about how Switzerland was involved in the security arrangements that led to the OSCE:
More
50 years of the Helsinki Accords: Switzerland’s role between the blocs
Churchill the opposition leader
Wassenberg describes the portrayal of Churchill as a “founding father of the Council of Europe” as accurate, but with certain caveats.
For her, he is not the one outstanding champion of European unification. “He advocated for European strength; his speech on founding a European army perhaps fits in with this. But he himself was not part of the movement that truly strove for a united Europe.”
Wassenberg also points to the ambivalence in Britain’s relations with Europe – as well as Churchill’s changing positions depending on whether he was in government (1940-1945, 1951-1955) or the opposition (1945-1951), as was the case when he made his Zurich speech.
>> Follow Swissinfo in Zurich as we examine the resonance of Churchill’s words amid current threats to European security:
Meanwhile the speech was also silent on what would become one of the Council of Europe’s core goals – democracy and its protection. While he talks about “tyranny” and “freedom”, the word “democracy” doesn’t appear at all. “It’s only in retrospect that people say what was being aimed at was democracy,” says Conway. “At the time, Churchill and others were basically talking about how we just recover from the war.”
Democracy in Europe after 1945
Yet Conway says the speech came at a pivotal moment for democracy in Europe. The decades after the Second World War saw democracy become the “default structure of Western Europe” – something which he also says was not at all inevitable. The term “democracy” was “rescued” from previous experiments like the Weimar Republic and repackaged – in constitutions and at the Council of Europe – as a “stable, moderate, inclusive form of government where everybody has a share in power. For Conway, this “very important redefinition of democracy” prevailed across Western Europe for the following decades.
>> Churchill did not only visit Zurich in 1946; his trip also brought him to other parts of Switzerland:
In this light, Switzerland again provides an interesting backdrop for Churchill’s speech. On the one hand, the version of democracy which took hold in Western European capitals was not the Westminster two-party model favoured by Churchill. Yet neither was it by any means the type of direct democratic model associated with Switzerland. In Germany, especially, there was great distrust of the popular will after the rise of national socialism, Conway explains. Ultimately, he says, the post-war democratic turn was a “collective and pragmatic act by the political elites of Western European states […] with very little emphasis on consulting the people about it”.
The creation of the Council of Europe
Meanwhile, positions were taking shape at the international level about what European cooperation could actually look like – especially at the assembly which Wassenberg sees as the second origin of European unification: the 1948 Congress in The Hague.
At this Congress of Europe, over 800 delegates – including influential politicians such as former Swiss government minister Marcel Pilet-Golaz and future German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer – discussed routes towards European unification. “It became clear that one camp, the federalists, were more in favour of a united Europe, while the so-called unionists rather wanted an intergovernmental organisation,” Wassenberg explains.
The structure of the Council of Europe – especially its Committee of Ministers, where foreign ministers of member states meet – is “very intergovernmental”, as Wassenberg puts it. At the same time, federalists initially hoped that the parliamentary assembly in Strasbourg – where elected representatives from the countries gathered to discuss – could be used to create something more resembling a “United States of Europe”.
Wassenberg sees the 1951 formation of the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) with six member states as a “counter-reaction” to initial conflicts, disappointments and differences in the Council of Europe. “People wanted to found something else that might have a better prospect of developing into a federal Europe,” says Wassenberg.
Ultimately, the ECSC, which – unlike the Council of Europe – had very concrete economic goals – provided the basis for the emergence of the EU, which today has 27 member states.
The hesitation of neutral countries
The Council of Europe, for its part, now has 46 member states – and, since 2024, a Swiss Secretary General for the first time: Alain Berset. Many these days know the Strasbourg-based organisation because of the European Court of Human Rights, which has existed since 1959. According to Wassenberg, the Council of Europe’s focus on human rights and democracy was inherent from its beginning. “After the end of the Second World War, people were convinced that, in addition to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a special convention was needed in Europe – to prevent another Holocaust from ever happening again,” she says.
As envisaged in Churchill’s speech, the Council of Europe acted as a complement to the UN in its early years. “There was always more competition between the Council of Europe and the later EU than with the UN,” says Wassenberg. Today she sees major differences in the objectives of the EU and the Council of Europe, and these have enabled the Council of Europe to retain its relevance.
And although the Council of Europe once aimed to position itself as neutral in the Cold War, neutral states initially held back on joining, Wassenberg adds. Finland only joined in 1989. As for Switzerland, it signed up in 1961: 15 years after Churchill’s Zurich speech, but at least over 40 years before it joined the UN.

AI professor: Today's chatbots will not end civilization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:57:00 UTC
16:57:00 KST

AI professor: Today's chatbots will not end civilization
In recent weeks, leading figures in the tech world have grown increasingly vocal in warning about the risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence. However, University of Tartu Professor of Artificial Intelligence Meelis Kull says there is currently no existential risk.
The debate gained momentum when executives at several major corporations urged engineers to slow down the development of new systems. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for example, warned on his blog that the current pace of development carries excessive risks. At the same time, U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk called on countries to take swift action to rein in the new technology. One expert in the field estimated that there is a greater than 10 percent chance that artificial intelligence could destroy civilization.
In Kull's view, society first needs a clear picture of what machines are actually capable of today. The chatbots people use every day are still powered by large language models that wait for instructions from humans and only then search the web for information.
"Right now, we are talking about the most extreme danger — a threat to civilization and all of humanity. I would emphasize from the outset that with the capabilities AI has today, I do not see such a threat. It is close to zero," Kull said.
Scientists are much more concerned about the future when code begins improving itself. The human role in training models is steadily diminishing and in the future algorithms may be able to create increasingly intelligent versions of themselves without human assistance.
"The danger arises when we build AI systems that are vastly more intelligent. If a superintelligence emerges that is vastly more intelligent than humans in every respect, then managing and controlling it and guaranteeing that nothing can go wrong will be very difficult," the professor explained.
A catastrophe would not even require an attacker with malicious intentions. It would be enough for engineers to give a machine a noble goal but fail to define its limits precisely. For example, an algorithm instructed to stop global warming could conclude that the most effective solution would be to immediately shut down all oil platforms worldwide, along with economic activity more broadly.
"The danger also arises when a person has no intention of doing anything bad and simply wants to use AI for a good purpose — even in that case, a superintelligence could behave in ways we would not want," Kull said.
To prevent such scenarios, programmers need to give their digital assistants clear ethical boundaries. In practice, however, ruling out every possible loophole is simply beyond human capabilities.
"The problem with human error is that when assigning a task to AI, it is very difficult to define the conditions and set the boundaries precisely enough to completely eliminate the risks," the professor said.
An incident at OpenAI's labs this summer provides a good illustration of the potential cost of mistakes. Developers asked a virtual agent to test an internal network for security vulnerabilities. Unexpectedly, however, the program broke out of the controlled environment. The model was able to establish a means of communication through a message board on a public website and began attacking the servers of another company, Hugging Face.
The safeguards created by humans failed because the machine chose a path to solving the problem that engineers had not anticipated. Such dangerous incidents are encouraged by cutthroat competition in the technology sector where companies race to be the first to bring new products to market.
Stricter external oversight could help address the situation.
"First, there needs to be agreement on the processes used to mitigate risks. Independent experts can primarily verify whether those processes are being followed. When the pace of development is too fast, the processes are not followed precisely because of carelessness and that is exactly what increases the risks," Kull emphasized.
The global race also worries experts because computing power is becoming concentrated in the hands of a small number of organizations. A handful of U.S. technology giants currently dictate the pace of development worldwide. They have the money and servers that smaller startups could never afford.
With major corporations firmly in control, Europe has largely been left watching the digital race from the sidelines. Researchers and engineers in Europe lack resources comparable to those available to U.S. labs.
"Europe's serious problem is that we do not have anything comparable to the cutting-edge capabilities of U.S. companies. The strongest models in Europe are currently being trained by the French company Mistral, but its models are still slightly weaker than those of OpenAI and Anthropic in the U.S.," the professor said.
However, Kull said Europe's lag and the global risks should not deter small countries from embracing innovation. The energy consumption of artificial intelligence, for example, is steadily declining and an algorithm now requires 10 to 100 times less energy to perform the same computation than it did a couple of years ago. More efficient models could instead help organizations achieve their green transition goals.
If Estonian companies turn their backs on intelligent algorithms, they will give their competitors a huge advantage in international markets.
"If the question is whether these kinds of risks should prompt us in Estonia to restrict the use of AI, my answer is: absolutely not. Estonia has every reason to adopt AI more and more widely. It gives us economic advantages and increases our competitiveness," Kull said.

Kyiv • UNN
After talks with the US, Belarus released 25 political prisoners. Washington had expected 200–300 people to be released and continues to seek a larger-scale move.
In Belarus, after a new round of talks with the United States, 25 political prisoners were released, although before the meeting the American side had expected a much larger group—around 200–300 people. Negotiations between Washington and Minsk have been ongoing for more than a year, but this time their result was more modest than previously expected, UNN writes, citing Carnegie Politika.
Details
U.S. Special Envoy to the President for Belarus John Coale arrived in Minsk on September 15 after an approximately six-month pause in negotiations. It was reported beforehand that he planned to seek the release of 200–300 political prisoners.
In the end, Minsk agreed to release 25 people. In exchange, the United States announced the lifting of sanctions on two Belarusian enterprises—Lakokraska and Bellesbumprom.
Why the negotiations stalled
As noted by Artyom Shraibman, a visiting expert at the Carnegie Berlin Center for the Study of Russia and Eurasia, one of the problems for Minsk was that the previous easing of U.S. sanctions did not produce the economic effect expected by the Belarusian authorities.
In particular, Minsk hoped that Washington’s steps would prompt the European Union and countries neighboring Belarus to similarly ease their sanctions. However, this did not happen, making further bargaining between the sides more difficult.
At the same time, the negotiating process has not stopped. After the latest meeting, Coale said that the United States expects to secure the release of hundreds of people in the near future.
According to Reuters, despite a series of releases, hundreds of people whom human rights defenders recognize as political prisoners remain in Belarusian prisons. At the same time, human rights organizations continue to report new cases of politically motivated persecution.

NAZA: Why are old Gaza allegations causing new fury in Israel?

NAZA: Why are old Gaza allegations causing new fury in Israel?
Israeli soldiers’ Gaza testimony causes backlash across much of the country’s political establishment.
Israel’s bitter political divisions are particularly sharp before the country’s October elections. But the furious response to a new documentary about the military’s actions in the genocidal war on Gaza has revealed an issue that much of Israel’s political and media establishment appears united on.
Few of the central allegations in NAZA, made by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, are new. Reports that the Israeli military was relying on artificial intelligence systems to generate targets in Gaza, often killing the inhabitants of entire buildings to kill just one individual identified by the system, were reported in April 2024.

- list 1 of 4Israel weaponises AI for West Bank demolitions
- list 2 of 4Netanyahu threatens to revoke Israeli citizenship of NAZA filmmakers
- list 3 of 4Jerusalem Daily: Israelis protest outside ‘NAZA’ filmmaker’s home
- list 4 of 4Israel would rather not watch NAZA
Other accusations against Israel, such as committing genocide, deliberately causing a famine, and unlawfully killing children, have also not received much attention in Israel.
In contrast, NAZA has unleashed a litany of abuse from across Israel, and brought the allegations to the centre of Israel’s political debate.
Culture Minister Miki Zohar reacted to the film’s premiere at the Venice Film Festival – where it received a 25-minute standing ovation – by calling for the directors to be stripped of their citizenship and to be investigated by the internal intelligence service for treason.
Army chief Eyal Zamir has dismissed the film as being built on blood libel and ordered a legal probe to hunt down its military and intelligence sources.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also cited the film when advancing legislation to revoke citizenship from anyone deemed to be smearing the country’s soldiers, while in the coastal city of Ashdod, graffiti branding the directors “traitors” has appeared on the walls.
“You can’t really understand the extent of the madness from outside of the country,” Orly Noy, an editor at Local Call, which first carried many of the accusations contained in the film, said. “They’re attacking the friends and families of [the filmmakers] Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. They’re talking about revoking their citizenship. They’re asking the Shin Bet to investigate them – for making a film, and it isn’t just the politicians. Journalists, who you might expect to show some kind of solidarity with them, are competing to attack them. It’s scary.”
Denial
In late 2025, the Committee to Protect Journalists reported escalating censorship and harassment in Israel, with Israeli journalists telling the organisation that the media’s approach had become “part of the war effort” and, by extension, significantly shaped Israeli view of their war on Gaza.
In October 2025, a study by the Israeli think tank Molad found that only 3 percent of Channel 12’s coverage of the first six months of the war mentioned Gaza’s humanitarian crisis. Of 206 war-related images and video clips broadcast by the network, Israel’s most-watched channel, only two showed Palestinian civilian casualties.
Nevertheless, before the film’s release, polls found that most Israelis believed the coverage they were receiving of the military’s conduct in Gaza was balanced.
“I guess it was because the mainstream media outlets in Israel did not investigate the conduct of the army during the war in Gaza, and hardly covered the war from the Palestinian point of view,” Anat Saragusti, the Israeli jurist and journalist responsible for press freedom at the Union of Journalists in Israel, said of the shock that had accompanied the release of the film. “[The Israeli media] hardly reported on the human toll and the scale of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.”
Compounding the gap, Saragusti said, was a deep-seated national narrative: that the war had been imposed on Israel, that Hamas had carried out a massacre on October 7, 2023, and that Hamas’s use of civilians as human shields made mass casualties in Gaza all but unavoidable.
Palestinian deaths, in this telling, were framed less as the product of Israeli conduct than as collateral damage forced on Israel by its enemy’s tactics, she said.
Lynch mobs
“Even journalists that usually support the anti-Netanyahu bloc have criticised the filmmakers,” Israeli political sociologist Daniel Bar-Tal said.
“Israeli Jews deny the genocide,” he continued, “Even all the opposition parties joined the vicious criticism of the filmmakers.”
The language used against the filmmakers has been echoed by some of Netanyahu’s most prominent political rivals.
On Monday, former military chief and one of Netanyahu’s principal rivals Gadi Eisenkot denounced the film for “moral blindness, a detachment from reality, and harm to the State of Israel in a difficult hour”.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who is also running in October’s election, called the film a “horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters”.
“Everything gets heightened the closer to the election we get,” Noy said. “But I think only now, for those of us who live here, is the extent of the fascism becoming clear. Journalists, politicians and the media are forming some kind of incitement machine.”
“I’ve had anxieties over where Israel had been going for a long time,” she said, “but right now I’m genuinely worried for my friends and colleagues.”

He will lead a Chinese delegation to the United States from September 19 to 23 for consultations on "economic and trade issues of mutual concern", the official Xinhua news agency reported, citing the commerce ministry.
The talks will be guided by the "important consensus" reached by the two leaders, according to the ministry.
Trade relations will top the agenda
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week he would meet He over the weekend.
Bessent suggested the discussions could also touch on Iran, whose close economic ties with China have long been a source of friction between Washington and Beijing.
But trade issues are expected to take centre stage when Xi and Trump meet.
The world's two largest economies reached a fragile truce in October 2025 after months of tariff tensions triggered by Trump following his return to the White House.
The agreement helped cool fears of a damaging trade escalation, but negotiators on both sides have yet to reach a comprehensive settlement, leaving key disputes unresolved.

North Korea reveals new drone production lines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:50:08 UTC
16:50:08 KST

- North Korean state media showed Kim Jong Un touring drone production lines Sept. 16-18, including a one-way attack drone resembling Israeli loitering munitions.
- The drone's launcher system first appeared publicly at an October 2025 military parade, mounted six per truck on four vehicles.
North Korean state media revealed production lines for at least three types of domestically built drones this week, including a one-way attack drone that resembles Israeli-designed loitering munitions, as part of a factory tour by leader Kim Jong Un reported Sept. 19.
The ruling Workers’ Party newspaper Rodong Sinmun said Kim, the party’s general secretary, inspected “important munitions industry enterprises” from Sept. 16 to 18. Photos accompanying the report showed him walking through an assembly hall containing dozens of small flying-wing drones mounted on stands, alongside separate images of him examining what appeared to be missile or drone airframe components with factory officials.
One drone shown is a one-way attack type visually similar to Israel’s Harop family of loitering munitions, weapons built to fly toward a target and detonate on impact rather than return to base. North Korea unveiled a dedicated launch system for this drone at a nighttime military parade on Oct. 10, 2025, marking the Workers’ Party’s 80th anniversary.
That parade featured four 6×6 trucks, each carrying two stacked rows of three launch containers, for an apparent capacity of six drones per vehicle. The parade followed an August 2024 reveal of prototype airframes styled after Israel’s Harop and Switchblade-style “Hero” loitering munitions, neither of which came with published performance figures at the time.
This week’s images of the attack drone during testing were partly obscured, withholding a clear view of some components, though analysts have suggested the design may be related to a rail-launched drone North Korea has separately tested that uses a small rocket booster to get airborne.
Other drones shown on the factory floor were still semi-complete airframes, but their shape already matched North Korea’s larger reconnaissance-strike drones, the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9.
Both first appeared publicly in July 2023 and have undergone repeated flight tests since. The Saetbyol-4 bears a resemblance to the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk surveillance drone, while the Saetbyol-9, with a wingspan of roughly 20 meters (66 feet), resembles the U.S. MQ-9 Reaper and carries hardpoints that suggest it is built to fire guided weapons rather than only observe. North Korean state media has separately called for expanded production across the country’s drone programs, following Kim’s public push earlier this year to accelerate output.
The factory visit came the same week Kim toured facilities producing a mobile rocket launcher that outside analysts have compared to the U.S. Army’s HIMARS system, and the same week North Korea rejected an International Atomic Energy Agency resolution criticizing its nuclear weapons program.
North Korea has not disclosed the factory locations, production quantities for any of the drones shown, or further technical detail on the attack drone beyond what appears in the partly obscured photos.

China railway passenger trips hit record high in first eight months
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:49:57 CST
16:49:57 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China handled a record 3.32 billion railway passenger trips in the first eight months of 2026, up 3.9 percent year on year, according to the China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway).
During the period, the railway network operated an average of 11,508 passenger trains daily, up 5 percent from a year earlier.
Responding to passenger growth driven by the country's transit visa-free policy, the railway network recorded over 16.68 million foreign passenger trips in the first eight months, up 33.3 percent year on year.
Cross-border rail travel also continued to grow. The China-Laos Railway carried 245,000 cross-border trips, up 39.1 percent, while the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong high-speed railway handled over 23.4 million cross-border trips, up 10.7 percent, China Railway said.
Analysts attributed the record to the expansion of China's high-speed rail network, stronger operational capacity, a rebound in tourism consumption and easier cross-border travel.
China has expanded its 240-hour visa-free transit program to 57 countries, with Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam the latest added. The policy has helped fuel a surge in cross-border travel, with Chinese border authorities handling 499 million inbound and outbound trips in the first eight months, up 8.7 percent year on year.
China Railway has also worked with local cultural and tourism departments to promote tourism, operating 2,501 tourist trains nationwide during the period.
Aboard the Y839 tourist train from Xining to Lhasa, Chris, a 56-year-old British tourist, was traveling to China with his wife and daughter for the first time, with Lhasa as the first stop. Long fascinated by China, he chose the train to take in the plateau scenery. "This train is carrying more than 30 foreign passengers from seven countries, including Thailand, Britain and Japan," said Gai Mingjing, conductor of the Y839 train.
China Railway said it will prepare for the upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday travel rush, improve station and onboard services, and run distinctive tourist trains to give passengers a better travel experience. ■

An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 11, 2026 shows a view of the Xiangjiang River in Quanzhou County of Guilin City, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. In the winter of 1934 during the Long March, the Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the Kuomintang troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle.

China Focus: China eyes strong cultural, tourism industries by 2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:49:18 CST
16:49:18 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- China will strengthen its cultural industries and tourism over the next five years, aiming to steadily raise their share of GDP, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.
The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development, newly released by the ministry, calls for turning the sectors into pillars of economic development and businesses that improve people's livelihoods and sense of happiness.
One key target is 8.3 billion domestic trips a year by 2030, nearly 2 billion more than in 2025.
Chinese tourists spent 6.3 trillion yuan (about 933 billion U.S. dollars) on domestic trips in 2025. The 2030 target is 7.7 trillion yuan.
Market analysis shows tourism spending is increasingly flowing into sectors that blend culture and new experiences into travel.
Traveling for concerts, sports events and commercial performances, or to explore places known for revolutionary history or modern industry, is a notable example.
"It all points to the same trend: tourists are no longer satisfied with a tour that is just about moving from one place to another, but a trip that can invoke cultural identity, or enable them to express their identity or experience something new," said a report by Meadin Research Institute, a market analytics firm.
Such an infusion represents a focus of efforts to boost cultural industry and tourism in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development.
The plan supports industrial tourism based on equipment manufacturing and consumer goods, travel packages featuring farming experiences, and comprehensive consumption scenarios.
Other efforts include further integrating sports events with cultural tourism, fostering high-quality ski destinations and promoting deeper links between cultural tourism and transportation.
For 2030, the plan pledges to create diverse, immersive and interactive consumption scenarios, while boosting spending on cruise and yacht tours and recreational vehicle camping.
To cultivate tour packages and business models that integrate culture and tourism, the plan says revolutionary culture and fine traditional Chinese culture can be used to build an emotional connection and improve the tourist experience.
It also encourages employers to ensure paid vacation and stagger holidays to boost tourism spending.
GROWING APPEAL FOR INTERNATIONAL TOURISTS
Improving tourist experience in China appeals to both domestic and international visitors, especially with continued support expected over the next five years.
The World Tourism Cities Federation (WTCF) listed Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Hangzhou and Chengdu among the world's top 20 tourist cities in its latest World Tourism Cities Development Report (2025-2026).
China has the most cities on the list, according to the report released at a sideline event during the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services, held in Beijing from Sept. 9 to 13.
Joseph Lema, an expert with the WTCF, said competition among tourism cities has moved beyond attractions and visitor numbers. What matters now, he said, is the ability to deliver quality experiences, effective governance and sustainable development.
On the way to building strong cultural and tourism industries, China is more confident in realizing its ambitious inbound tourism goal. In the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development, the target is to attract 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030.
To reach that goal, China will continue to make travel easier for international tourists in areas such as visa-free policy, payment, tax refund, accommodation and transportation.
Easier access and more options, from hairstyling and dental care to traditional Chinese medicine and custom tailoring, will bring longer stays by overseas visitors.
"This allows them to see a more authentic, diverse and vibrant side of China," said Hu Yang, senior vice president of Tujia. ■

New details revealed: Yair Netanyahu’s dramatic escape from an Iranian assassination plot in Miami
“This security is not a luxury,” Netanyahu said, warning that without adequate protection, those seeking to harm his relatives “might succeed"
Less than a month ago, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu disclosed during a live interview on Channel 14 that Iran had attempted to assassinate one of his sons. The information had previously been barred from publication by Israel’s military censor.
Now, nine months after Yair Netanyahu was urgently evacuated from Miami, i24NEWS has reported new details about the operation.
According to a US law-enforcement source cited by Newsmax, Israeli intelligence uncovered an Iranian plot in December 2025 to target the prime minister’s 35-year-old son, who was living in Hallandale Beach near Miami.
Intelligence assessments indicated that a suspected Iranian cell was already operating in the Miami area and monitoring Netanyahu’s home and daily routine.
Col. (res.) Ronen Cohen, chairman of Israel’s Advisory Committee for Personal Security, previously described the incident as an assassination attempt thwarted “at the very last minute.” Although Cohen discussed the case on the television program Cabinet Shishi, the military censor initially prevented Israeli news organizations from reporting his remarks.
After receiving the intelligence warning, Israeli officials alerted US authorities, and Netanyahu was instructed to leave his residence immediately. He reportedly departed without collecting his personal belongings and flew to Israel, arriving on December 7.
A separate report said Netanyahu’s security detail in Miami could not adequately respond to the threat. Two additional teams assigned to President Isaac Herzog, including a senior commander, were therefore sent from New York, where they were accompanying the president on an official visit.
The reinforcements reportedly helped evacuate Netanyahu to the airport, from where he flew to Israel later that night.
Yair Netanyahu had already taken extensive precautions during his two years in Miami because of concerns for his safety. At times, he reportedly avoided stepping onto the balconies of his residence, even before the alleged plot was uncovered.
Following the disclosure, the prime minister defended the extensive protection provided to his family.
“This security is not a luxury,” Netanyahu said, warning that without adequate protection, those seeking to harm his relatives “might succeed.”
In July, the Shin Bet extended security protection for Netanyahu’s wife, Sara, and his sons, Yair and Avner. His sons are reportedly expected to remain under protection for five years after Netanyahu leaves office.
The Shin Bet later confirmed that authorities had identified a “significant threat” against Yair Netanyahu. Following a security assessment, officials decided to evacuate him and his protection team to Israel immediately.

Aselsan tests electronic warfare systems on TB2 drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:48:32 UTC
16:48:32 KST

Turkish defense firm Aselsan has demonstrated electronic warfare and radar systems on Baykar’s Bayraktar TB2 drones in Konya, with defense delegations from 18 countries attending.
One drone carried the Antidot 2ES 100 electronic support pod and Antidot 2EA 200 electronic warfare pod. A second carried the Fulmar 200 synthetic aperture radar system.
During the first test, the Antidot systems detected and located a target radar before carrying out an electronic attack, allowing the drone to approach without being detected, Aselsan said.
In the second test, Antidot located another target and shared its coordinates with Fulmar 200, which produced high-resolution radar images of the site.
The company said the demonstration combined detection, location, jamming and imaging in a single operational sequence. It marked the first test of Antidot systems against live radars aboard the TB2, according to Aselsan.
The electronic support pod identifies radar signals and relays information to ground control stations. The electronic warfare pod can autonomously counter search and tracking radars using preprogrammed techniques.
Fulmar 200 is designed to provide radar imagery by day and night in all weather conditions. It can be mounted beneath a wing or on the aircraft’s body and used alongside optical and infrared cameras.

Nvidia CEO says there’s ‘0% chance’ that world will end in 2030
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang renewed his pushback against AI doomsday scenarios, saying that the technology does not pose an extinction risk to humanity.
“However it’s characterised, 2030 is not going to be the end of the world,” he said in an interview with CBS News.
“There is a 0 per cent chance it’s going to be the end of the world.”
During multiple appearances at events in recent days, the CEO has reiterated his stance that artificial intelligence can be safely managed.
Huang, whose company is the leading provider of AI processors, has also argued against the need for new regulations.
Researcher Jacob Coxon kicked off a wave of AI unease with his resignation from Anthropic earlier in September.

issey miyake turns matisse cut-outs into clothing and choreography at tate modern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:45:59 UTC
16:45:59 KST

Inside Tate Modern’s South Tank, the performance begins as guests entered the room. A pale felt surface covered the floor, with benches following the circular concrete wall and individual seats scattered closer to its center. Lying across the floor was a pleated garment shaped after one of the paper cut-outs in Henri Matisse’s The Snail (1953). Then a performer began lifting sections of felt to reveal more clothing underneath.
Presented on September 16th, 2026 as the second edition of HOMME PLISSÉ ISSEY MIYAKE’s OPEN STUDIO, the evening placed the audience directly inside the structure of the dance. Performers approached individual guests and invited them to sit for sessions of One One One, a format developed by Ioannis Mandafounis in which a dancer creates choreography live in response to the person in front of them. Eye contact holds the exchange together. Around them, the rest of the room watches these encounters take shape one by one.
As the sessions continued, performers pulled garments from beneath the felt and slipped them on. Shapes familiar from The Snail (1953) began moving independently across the room. In Matisse’s composition, colored paper sits flat against a white ground. Here, those same geometries stretch across shoulders and torsos, while HOMME PLISSÉ ISSEY MIYAKE’s pleats expand and contract with each movement.
The idea came from the design team’s first encounter with the work. They describe wanting to ‘animate each paper cut-out by translating it into a garment,’ using their pleating process to give Matisse’s forms another kind of movement. During the performance, dancers repeatedly changed clothes and placed the discarded pieces across the stage, recalling the loose paper forms that once filled Matisse’s studio. The source image gradually disperses across the room rather than remaining fixed at its center.
performers move through the Tate Modern’s South Tank
the stage loses its fixed front
The South Tank gives the exchange room to move in every direction. Its raw concrete perimeter surrounds a broad open floor, while the seating arrangement leaves people embedded within the performance area itself. In the wider views, dancers cross between seated guests as other performers occupy distant corners of the room. Attention keeps shifting. A person who is watching can suddenly become the person being watched.
That spatial setup suits Mandafounis’s One One One. The method asks dancers to translate sensations prompted by an audience member’s presence into movement, giving each encounter its own duration and rhythm. The spectator influences what happens simply by being there. Meanwhile, everyone sitting along the outer wall sees a series of small performances forming across the room, each with its own temporary center.
dancers retrieve pleated garments hidden beneath the felt flooring throughout the performance
from image to body and back again
Toward the end, the exchange changes again. A single performer appears on the floor before the others return and pull back the felt at the center of the Tank. Beneath it is a full-scale reconstruction of The Snail (1953) assembled from the pleated garments, with each piece cut to match the geometry of Matisse’s original composition. The dancers gather around it and continue moving as the fragmented image comes back together.
For much of the performance, Matisse’s image exists through people. Its forms bend around bodies and travel through the room. By the closing sequence, those garments return to the floor and become an image again. The audience also changes position within that cycle. Earlier, an individual spectator could prompt the choreography directly. At the end, everyone faces the same composition. OPEN STUDIO turns that shift between participation and observation into part of the work itself.

Details

MSF launches Ebola vaccination study among DRC frontline workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:42:46 UTC
16:42:46 KST

Bunia, Democratic Republic of Congo – As the Ebola disease outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) and Epicentre, MSF’s epidemiological research centre, are launching a vaccination study, BRAVO.1 The significant study will follow frontline workers in the Ebola response over time to assess the effect of the ERVEBO vaccine. The study is integrated into the Ministry of Health-led outbreak response. No vaccine or treatment specifically targeting Bundibugyo virus is immediately available.
Conducted with the Ministry of Health, Africa CDC, the Congolese National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB), and scientific partners, the study will document and evaluate the use of ERVEBO, the only Ebola vaccine currently available at scale. The vaccine has a well-established safety profile and has been widely used in DRC. However, it was developed and licensed for the Zaire virus of Ebola disease, not Bundibugyo virus, which is driving the current outbreak.
“Although ERVEBO was not originally developed to protect against Bundibugyo, preliminary data suggest that it may offer some degree of protection against the virus,” says Dr Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF. “In a race against time such as the one the DRC is currently facing, we must use every tool available to us.”
Even partial protection could help reduce severe illness and deaths... That is precisely the purpose of BRAVO.
“Even partial protection could help reduce severe illness and deaths,” says Dr Manangama. “However, these potential benefits must be demonstrated scientifically. That is precisely the purpose of BRAVO.”
Launched on 19 September at the World Health Organization (WHO)-run training centre for health workers in Bunia, the study will run for a period of nine to 12 months. This will include three months dedicated to vaccination and a minimum of six months of participant follow-up. It will target 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu provinces, a group at particularly high risk of exposure to the virus and essential to the outbreak response. The study will generate real-world data on the use of the ERVEBO vaccine and its potential effectiveness in the current outbreak context.
Several vaccines specifically targeting Bundibugyo virus are under development and may become available in the coming months. Continuing and accelerating this research remains essential. In the meantime, ERVEBO is being offered as an interim measure because of its established safety profile and its approval by several leading regulatory authorities, including the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the European Medicines Agency, and WHO.
Participation in BRAVO and vaccination are entirely voluntary. Vaccination is an additional protective measure; it does not replace proven infection prevention and control measures. All frontline workers must continue to use protective equipment, follow safe-care procedures, and report symptoms quickly.
“It is important to stress that this vaccine will not end the current outbreak,” says Dr Manangama. “However, it may offer additional protection to those most exposed, and help strengthen the response alongside other essential interventions.”

'Deeply offensive' to suggest farmers 'prefer to abuse and exploit backpackers', NFF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:40:34 UTC
16:40:34 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia's peak farming body says new visa limits could leave growers short of workers during key harvest periods.
- The body has rejected any suggestion that farmers rely on backpackers because Pacific workers are harder to exploit.
Australia's peak farming body has accused Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke of making "deeply offensive" comments about farmers, as concern grows over how changes to backpacker visas could affect the nation's agricultural workforce.
The National Farmers' Federation (NFF) has warned the changes could contribute to higher food prices if they leave growers without enough workers during key harvest periods — times when farmers often hire 'backpackers' on Working Holiday visas.
While Burke acknowledged the migration changes would create challenges for some, he suggested the agricultural sector could utilise additional capacity in the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.
The scheme allows eligible Australian businesses to recruit workers from nine Pacific island countries and Timor-Leste when there are not enough local workers available.
Burke also said the strengthening of protections for PALM workers during his tenure as employment minister had led to warnings from some agricultural employers that they would turn away from the PALM scheme.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"At the time that we were improving those rules, we had some of the farm organisations say to us, 'If you do this, our members will just go and use backpackers,'" Burke told SBS News.
"If the reason that people are more reliant on backpackers and refusing to use Pacific workers is because they're upset that we've ended exploitation in those areas, I think that is a very different question for a number of operators."
He also stressed the criticism did not apply to the entire agricultural sector, saying "that doesn't depict the whole of the farm sector, not for a minute".
Richard Shannon, executive officer of the NFF Horticulture Council, labelled Burke's comments as "provocative" and rejected any suggestion that employers had moved away from the PALM scheme because of stronger protections for workers.
"The minister is suggesting that employers in horticulture would prefer to abuse and exploit backpackers than remain in the PALM program," Shannon told SBS News.
"This is not about exploiting people and finding loopholes, and it's deeply offensive."
Shannon argued that the reason some employers had moved away from PALM was because changes to the scheme had increased costs and administrative requirements.
He said backpackers and PALM workers also served different purposes within the agricultural workforce and could not simply be substituted for one another.
Employers in the PALM scheme have responsibilities including arranging accommodation and transport and providing additional support to workers.
Shannon said those requirements made the scheme significantly more expensive for employers than hiring backpackers, particularly for businesses needing workers for shorter periods.
The changes come as parts of Australia's horticulture industry approach major summer harvest periods, when growers can require large numbers of workers for relatively short periods.
"What [Burke] is effectively doing now is shortening the supply of backpackers and pushing people, employers, back into a program that is uncommercial for them," he said.
Why are farmers concerned about the visa changes?
Under the federal government's migration overhaul announced on Thursday, working holidaymakers wanting to remain in Australia for a second or third year will have to enter a ballot after completing the required regional work.
Second-year places will be capped at 45,000, compared with 57,000 people who qualified last year, while third-year places will fall from 31,000 to 5,000.
The government says the changes will give it greater control over migration numbers while retaining incentives for backpackers to work in regional Australia.
The government has also announced agriculture will receive priority under changes to skilled visa processing.
Shannon said the agricultural sector's immediate reaction to the changes has been "alarm", and farmers were seeking more detail from the government about how the changes would affect workforce availability.
"We have no detail as to what effect this might have on the workforce that's available in the short term and ongoing," he said.
"That's so important for our growers right now — to better understand what effect this is going to have on the numbers of backpackers in the region, and whether or not they need to make alternative plans."
Shannon also said any significant shortage of workers could ultimately flow through to consumers through higher production costs.
"It's quite clear that there's going to be a shortage now of workers, and that prices of food are going to go up."
Shannon said agricultural worker shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic had also led to such price rises but added that the industry was still uncertain about exactly how Labor's changes would affect worker availability during key harvest periods.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences reported in late 2021 that fruit and vegetable prices had risen above their usual seasonal levels but said declining availability of overseas agricultural workers was only one possible cause.
What's happening to Working Holiday visas?
The government's recently announced changes form part of a broader effort to bring net overseas migration down to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027-28.
Burke said working holidaymakers accounted for 48,000 places in the nation's net overseas migration figure last year, arguing no part of the visa system could be excluded from efforts to reduce overall numbers.
Backpackers will still need to complete 88 days of specified regional work to qualify for a second year and six months to qualify for a third.
But completing that work will no longer guarantee an additional year. Eligible applicants will instead enter the new ballots for the limited number of places.
At the same time, the government says processing of primary working holidaymaker applications will return to faster rates for countries whose visa arrangements include the regional work requirement.
Shannon said the NFF wanted the government to leave the existing working holidaymaker arrangements in place rather than impose the new caps.

- North Korean state media said Kim Jong Un toured munitions factories from Sept. 16 to 18, inspecting production tied to a rocket launcher resembling the U.S. HIMARS system.
- The visit follows a May 2026 test of the launcher alongside an upgraded 240mm rocket and an AI-guided cruise missile Kim ordered deployed near the South Korean border.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured major munitions factories over three days, from Sept. 16 to 18, inspecting weapons production that reportedly included a mobile rocket launcher Western analysts have compared to the U.S. Army’s HIMARS system, state media reported Sept. 19.
The ruling Workers’ Party newspaper Rodong Sinmun said Kim, the party’s general secretary, visited “important munitions industry enterprises” to check on production conditions. Kim told factory officials the military must “constantly load the most powerful and overwhelming strategic force” into the armed forces, according to the report, and pressed the plants to expand output.
The visit follows a pattern Kim has repeated for years, touring weapons factories every few months and calling for faster, larger-scale production. He made similar visits in August 2023, January 2024 and December 2025, each time emphasizing what state media described as the “paramount importance” of missile and artillery output to the country’s war readiness.
The launcher system tied to this week’s visit first appeared publicly at a 2023 military parade and was tested for the first time on May 26, 2026, alongside two other weapons: an upgraded 240mm guided rocket and a tactical cruise missile North Korea says uses artificial intelligence for terminal guidance.
Photos released by North Korean state media at the time showed a wheeled vehicle carrying a small number of launch tubes, a configuration that resembles the U.S. Army’s M142 HIMARS, a truck-mounted system that fires precision-guided rockets from a single launcher and has seen extensive combat use in Ukraine. South Korea’s military detected the May test independently, tracking projectiles that flew roughly 80 km (50 miles) toward the Yellow Sea, though Seoul did not confirm North Korea’s specific claims about the systems involved.
Kim ordered the accelerated deployment of the AI-guided cruise missile to front-line artillery units near the South Korean border after that May test, calling the results “a clear signal” of North Korea’s military progress. This week’s factory tour suggests the program has moved from testing toward production, though North Korea did not disclose how many units of any system have been built or where the factories are located, following its usual practice of withholding exact locations from state media coverage.
The factory visit came the same week North Korea rejected a resolution the International Atomic Energy Agency adopted criticizing its nuclear weapons program. North Korean officials said the country’s status as a nuclear power is permanently written into domestic law and does not require international recognition, a position Pyongyang has maintained consistently in response to IAEA and U.N. criticism.

Macron heading to Saint Pierre and Miquelon to meet with Canadian PM Carney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:38:46 UTC
16:38:46 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron is travelling to Saint Pierre and Miquelon this weekend, an archipelago the Élysée describes as "central to today's France."
French President Emmanuel Macron is travelling to Saint Pierre and Miquelon this weekend to discuss the future of the archipelago, as well as France's geostrategic presence in the North Atlantic, maritime sovereignty and cooperation with Ottawa.
The last French president to make a trip to the overseas collectivity, which is located some 20 kilometres off the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador, was François Hollande back in December 2014.
Eleven years on, Macron will be there on Sunday alongside Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.
Their meeting comes amid Carney's apparently blossoming relationship with Brussels and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada an associate member of the EU.
An archipelago 'central to today's France'
The key goal of the trip is to "deliver a message (...) about France's presence across five oceans," the French presidency said during a telephone briefing with the media, including Euronews. France has a presence in the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans, as well as "in the Arctic, through Saint Pierre and Miquelon" and in the Southern Ocean.
Located at the gateway to the Arctic, Saint Pierre and Miquelon gives France a significant exclusive economic zone and allows it to maintain a military presence there.
That presence is partly provided by the Fulmar, a navy patrol vessel and the only French military ship permanently based in the archipelago, which is due for replacement.
Saint Pierre and Miquelon is not a peripheral outpost, the Élysée stresses, but "a territory, an archipelago that is central to today's France."
During the presidential visit, questions of sovereignty will also be discussed in relation to digital cables and connections linking the archipelago and the European continent, as well as space-related activities, where further investment expected.
Another item on the agenda will be regional cooperation. Paris wants to turn Saint Pierre and Miquelon into a "rear base for polar cooperation," working not only with Canada but also with Denmark and Greenland.
The president is also expected to focus on the day-to-day difficulties faced by residents.
Saint Pierre and Miquelon is grappling with economic and social problems similar to those seen in many isolated territories around the world while also experiencing the effects of climate change.
The archipelago's population is also declining. The biggest blow came with the collapse of the fishing industry following years of a Canadian moratorium on cod fishing. France also saw its exclusive economic zone there reduced following a court ruling in 1992.
Another threat facing the territory is rising sea levels. The village of Miquelon-Langlade, located on a narrow strip of sand just two metres above sea level, is being moved farther inland. It is the first relocation project carried out in France in response to the effects of global warming.
Canada, a new energy partner?
Paris supports closer ties between Brussels and Ottawa and has reiterated its willingness to work with all countries that "share our values and want to strengthen their ability to decide, produce and act for themselves."
The practical details of this new partnership, however, have yet to be worked out.
Energy could become one of its main areas of focus.
France is looking to Canada to help secure European supplies of hydrocarbons, at a time when fuel prices are soaring due to global conflicts and tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.
This situation is already putting additional pressure on France's heavily indebted public finances, forcing the government to extend some existing measures and step up talks with partners, particularly in the Middle East.
Macron and Carney are due to continue their talks next week in New York, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

First new wild cat discovered in a century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:36:33 UTC
16:36:33 KST

The newly identified Tilcayo cat walks through the Yungas forest.
Scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat for the first time in more than a century, a Bolivian researcher said on Sept. 17.
The Tilcayo tiger cat, a small feline with a spotted, leopard-like coat, was identified in the mountainous Yungas region near the capital La Paz.
Locals who saw the creature in the Bolivian Andes had mistaken it for an ordinary house cat, said biologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who was part of the research team that studied them.
The nickname “tilcayo” given to the animal by locals inspired its new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo.
Nogales-Ascarrunz lauded the discovery as a “remarkable event, because a new wild cat species hasn’t been described in 100 years.” The cat is the first new feline discovered since the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.
The tilcayo is slightly smaller than a domestic cat, measuring around 45 centimeters, with rounded ears. A pair of tilcayos, the only such creatures found so far, have undergone whole genome sequencing, Nogales-Ascarrunz said, referring to a type of in-depth genetic testing.
A male tilcayo is living at an animal shelter in Yungas, after it was handed over by a family who had taken in the creature.
A female was rescued and released into the wild after being attacked by locals.
Research on the species was published on Sept. 17 in the journal Current Biology, capping off research that scientists began in 2021.
“So far, it’s only been detected in Bolivia” and not “anywhere else on the planet,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. She said the creatures were classified as vulnerable to extinction.
