Sichuan is not just about spice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:36:22 UTC
16:36:22 KST

If you think Sichuan cuisine is all about spicy food, then you haven’t really discovered it yet. On my first visit, I too expected a cuisine dominated by chillies, Sichuan pepper and hotpot. Yet what stayed with me was not the intensity of the spice, but the extraordinary complexity and layering of flavours. A single mouthful can begin with chilli heat, followed by that distinctive numbing tingle, then sweetness, acidity, fermentation and umami. Sometimes it is difficult to find two dishes on the same table that taste remotely alike.
That complexity is precisely what has earned Sichuan its place among China’s most important regional cuisines. Its capital, Chengdu, has been part of the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Gastronomy since 2010, and UNESCO highlights the cuisine’s remarkable ability to balance sweet, sour, bitter, spicy and salty flavours. There is even a saying in China that captures Chengdu’s culinary reputation rather neatly: “Food is in China, but flavour is in Chengdu.”
The flavour sensation most closely associated with Sichuan cooking around the world is málà. The word describes two distinct sensations working together. Là is the heat of chilli; má is the peculiar tingling, numbing effect of Sichuan pepper, a sensation that can feel almost electric on the tongue. Bring the two together and the result is not simply greater spiciness. Combined with oils, aromatics, spices and fermented ingredients, they create a succession of sensations and flavours that seems to evolve as you eat.
Perhaps the greatest misconception about Sichuan cuisine is that it begins and ends with málà. Traditional Sichuan cooking encompasses dozens of distinct flavour profiles. Sweet-and-sour, garlicky, sesame-rich, pickled, fermented and red-oil preparations sit alongside dishes that can be surprisingly subtle and delicate. Sichuan cooking techniques have been recognised as part of China’s national intangible cultural heritage, while UNESCO’s report on Chengdu refers to 24 distinct flavour profiles within the cuisine.
Nor does Sichuan have a single culinary identity. Chengdu is the centre of a particularly refined and intricately layered style of Sichuan cooking. Nearby Leshan is a food destination in its own right, famous for street food and small bites, from tofu pudding and skewers to dumplings and shaomai. Travel further south and you reach Zigong, whose distinctive food culture grew out of the wealth generated by its historic salt industry. It is the heartland of yanbangcai, often translated as “salt merchants’ cuisine,” an important tradition within the broader Sichuan repertoire. Yibin, meanwhile, has its own distinctive noodle dishes and a taste for bold, assertive flavours. Saying “I’ve eaten Sichuan food” is therefore a little like saying “I’ve eaten Mediterranean food”: Travel a few hundred kilometres and the ingredients, the intensity of the spice and even the way people eat can change considerably.
Chengdu’s restaurant scene is also going through an interesting transformation. The 2027 Michelin Guide Chengdu, announced on 11 September, offers a revealing snapshot of how far the city has come. The selection includes 84 restaurants: One with three Michelin stars, one with two and 13 with one star. For the first time, Chengdu has a three-Michelin-starred restaurant. More significantly, the guide points to a new generation of chefs reinterpreting traditional techniques through contemporary ideas, with local produce and cultural identity playing an increasingly prominent role in their cooking.
For me, this is where Chengdu becomes particularly exciting. Tiny noodle shops where a bowl still costs only a few yuan, wonton specialists and traditional teahouses continue to thrive, while alongside them a serious contemporary dining scene is emerging, with chefs finding new ways to express Sichuan’s culinary heritage.
Perhaps what makes Sichuan so compelling today is precisely the fact that these two worlds can coexist. On one side are centuries of knowledge about fermentation, traditional teahouses, markets, bubbling hotpots and recipes passed down through families; on the other, a younger generation of chefs beginning to translate that inheritance into a contemporary culinary language.
HH ENTERING CHINA THROUGH A DIFFERENT GATEWAY
On this trip to China, I flew with Sichuan Airlines. It was my first time travelling with the carrier, and when I looked into the airline and saw the figures, I was surprised by its scale. Sichuan Airlines today operates an all-Airbus fleet of more than 200 aircraft and carries over 35 million passengers a year. According to the latest figures provided by the airline, its fleet has reached 213 aircraft and its network now covers 151 destinations.
Its story, in some ways, mirrors China’s extraordinary growth over the past four decades. Founded in 1986, Sichuan Airlines operated its first flight between Chengdu and Wanzhou in 1988. When the company was restructured in 2002, its fleet consisted of just 12 aircraft. Today, it is the fifth Chinese airline to have passed the 200-aircraft mark. It was also the first airline in mainland China to operate the Airbus A320 — an interesting detail in the story of a carrier that has since built an entirely Airbus fleet.
I flew business class from Istanbul to Chengdu. And in fact, you don’t have to wait until you land to get your first taste of Sichuan; the character of the region begins to reveal itself on board. The cabin crew’s charming panda aprons during meal service are the first playful detail. More importantly for me, however, was the food. Regional flavours appear on the menu, so your introduction to Sichuan cuisine can begin at 10,000 metres. On long-haul flights, where airlines often gravitate towards dishes designed to appeal to the broadest possible range of palates, I liked the fact that Sichuan Airlines allowed the destination to make its presence felt before we had even arrived.
Once you land in Chengdu, a very different side of China opens up. From its home base, the airline flies to major cities including Lhasa, Kunming, Sanya, Hangzhou and Nanjing, as well as destinations such as Xishuangbanna, Dali and Daocheng, which are considerably less straightforward to reach from Türkiye. For me, that is one of the most interesting aspects of flying into Chengdu: It offers an alternative gateway to western and southwestern China. The airline’s international network was broader than I had expected, too. Sichuan Airlines has branded its international expansion “Panda Routes,” and its network today extends across Asia, Europe, Africa, Oceania and North America.
Its ownership structure is another interesting detail. Sichuan Airlines is independently managed, yet its shareholders include all three of China’s major state-owned airline groups. Sichuan Airlines Group holds the largest stake at 40 per cent, followed by China Southern at 39 per cent, while China Eastern and Air China each hold 10 per cent. The remaining one per cent belongs to Chengdu Gingko Restaurant Co. — a small detail that, as a food writer, naturally caught my attention.
But beyond the fleet sizes, passenger numbers and route maps, what interests me most is where an airline can take you. A good air connection does more than shorten the distance between two cities; sometimes it opens up a journey you might never otherwise have thought of making.
Sichuan is a perfect example. You can spend several days in Chengdu eating your way from hotpot and dan dan mian to mapo tofu, while discovering the city’s wonderful teahouse culture, and then continue your journey into an entirely different part of China. Sichuan Airlines’ extensive domestic network also means there is no reason to experience the country solely along the familiar Beijing–Shanghai axis. Even within Sichuan itself, Chengdu makes an excellent starting point for a food journey through Leshan, Zigong and Yibin.
Perhaps the most interesting thought I brought home from this journey was this: In a country as vast as China, the gateway through which you enter can shape the China you ultimately discover. This time, that gateway was Chengdu. And I didn’t even have to wait until landing to begin discovering Sichuan; from the panda aprons to the regional flavours, the journey had already begun on board.
For someone like me, who so often plans a journey around what I am going to eat when I get there, it is difficult to imagine a more delicious beginning.

Wildfire risk persists in Türkiye despite autumn rain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:35:32 UTC
16:35:32 KST

(AA Photo)
Favorable rain created ideal ignition environments by boosting plant growth, experts said, urging authorities to maintain strict preventive measures as autumn arrives.
The situation does not mean the fire season has ended, Isparta Applied Sciences University Rector Yılmaz Çatal said in the southern province of Isparta. High temperatures, low humidity and strong winds alter fire behavior within hours, making Türkiye’s outlook fragile amid Western European heat waves.
August and September form the critical period, as high temperatures in southern and western Anatolia prepare vegetation for ignition. Human activity causes nearly 90 percent of fires, Çatal said. Northern rainfall triggers dry northeasterly winds in the south, complicating firefighting while summer conditions continue in the Aegean and Mediterranean.
Officials must supervise agricultural activities, industrial facilities, energy lines and forest-rural interfaces. Çatal said assigning duties to neighborhood heads and police is essential during this period.
Türkiye recorded a milder 2026 season due to weather and firefighting capacity, but officials must use dynamic risk maps combining meteorological data, terrain, past fires and human mobility. Expanding artificial intelligence, cameras, satellites and unmanned aerial vehicles will help manage these risks, Çatal said, pointing to climate predictions showing the Mediterranean basin will warm faster than the global average.
Heavy rains increased combustible material loads nationwide, Karadeniz Technical University Forestry Faculty Professor Ertuğrul Bilgili said in the northern province of Trabzon. “This increase in combustible material paves the way for a fire to start, grow and develop into a hazard,” he said.
Bilgili said uncontrollable fires strike when combustible moisture drops below 10 percent during strong winds, making mid-July to early August the peak danger period for the Aegean and Mediterranean.
Negligence causes over half of the fires, making public training on evacuation, stubble burning, garden waste clearance and picnic fires essential alongside socio-economic expectations. Officials must base fire prevention on scientific foundations and special funds, expanding controlled burning and using helicopters as primary aerial vehicles, Bilgili said.
Türkiye’s climate causes long, dry summers, leaving coasts highly susceptible to rapid fire spread. The country completely overhauled its emergency response strategies following the 2021 wildfires.

U.S. approves Ukraine air defense package with unclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:27:59 UTC
16:27:59 KST

- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.68 billion air defense sale to Ukraine on Sept. 18, funded through European contributions and prior U.S. military financing.
- The package lists "S-300 Clone" and "GAM-67" missiles, designations that don't match any publicly known current weapon system.
The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.68 billion sale of air defense equipment to Ukraine on Sept. 18, a package built around several weapons whose exact identity the notification itself does not make clear.
The Defense Security Cooperation Agency’s notification to Congress describes the deal as an “Air Defense Development Upgrade.” Ukraine would pay for it through a mix of European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing that Congress appropriated under the prior administration, with that American funding counted as a one-to-one capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund. The sale still needs to clear the standard congressional review period before any contract can be finalized, and the eventual contractors would be chosen through a competitive U.S. government procurement process.
The equipment list includes items called S-300 Clone missiles and GAM-67 missiles, along with Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, a launcher platform called the Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher 1.5, mobile launcher modification kits, and RPS 202 counter-drone radars, plus the usual mix of spare parts, software, training publications and logistics support that accompanies most Foreign Military Sales packages.
Two of those names don’t match any publicly known current weapon system. GAM-67 is the U.S. Air Force’s old designation for the Crossbow, a turbojet-powered anti-radar missile program that Northrop’s Ventura Division built in the 1950s. Only 14 were ever produced, and the Air Force canceled the program in 1957 because the missile was too slow to be useful against modern air defenses. That history makes it clear the notification isn’t describing a Cold War-era leftover; the designation appears to have been reused, whether as a placeholder or a formal label for something new, rather than referring to the original Crossbow. “S-300 Clone” is similarly undefined in any public Pentagon or industry documentation, and no other name for it has surfaced.
The most plausible explanation available comes from outside the official notification. Robert Hamilton, a retired U.S. Army colonel who now leads the Delphi Global Research Center, told PBS NewsHour that the United States and Ukraine have been working jointly either to modernize Ukraine’s aging stock of S-300 interceptor missiles or to develop a newer version of the missile with improved capability. Hamilton said he expects that upgraded system to become operational close to the end of 2026. Neither the State Department nor Ukraine’s government has confirmed that this effort is the same program referenced as “S-300 Clone” in Friday’s notification, but the timing and subject matter line up closely enough that the two appear connected.
The S-300 is a Soviet-designed, long-range surface-to-air missile system that Ukraine inherited in large numbers and has relied on throughout the war, alongside Western systems like the Patriot. Ukraine has faced a persistent shortage of S-300 interceptors because Russia is now the only producer of the original missile, making any American-backed alternative, cloned, modernized or newly built, a potentially significant addition to Ukraine’s ability to keep those launchers firing.
The State Department’s notification includes the standard language used in nearly all such filings: the sale would not require additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine, would not affect U.S. military readiness, and would not alter the basic military balance in the region. No offset agreement has been proposed so far; any such arrangement would be negotiated separately between Ukraine and whichever companies win the eventual contracts.
What remains unclear is what the S-300 Clone and GAM-67 items actually are, technically or physically. Congress has not yet completed its review, and neither Washington nor Kyiv has released further detail on the specifications, quantities, or delivery timeline for either item.

The James Webb Telescope has discovered mysterious worlds that astronomers had never encountered before
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:27:31 EEST
16:27:31 KST

The James Webb Telescope has discovered mysterious worlds that astronomers had never encountered before
Kyiv • UNN
The telescope detected brown dwarfs in IC 348 with masses of about two Jupiters. A disk was observed around one of them, where planets may be forming.
The James Webb Space Telescope has detected the least massive brown dwarfs known to date—some of them have a mass only about twice that of Jupiter. The discovery was made while studying the star-forming region IC 348, located approximately 1,000 light-years from Earth, the European Space Agency (ESA) reports, writes UNN.
Details
IC 348 is located in the constellation Perseus and is one of the closest regions of active star formation to Earth. Astronomers used Webb's capabilities to determine how small objects formed during the star-formation process can be.
Brown dwarfs form as a result of the collapse of gas clouds, just like ordinary stars. However, their mass is insufficient for hydrogen to be stably converted into helium in their cores.
The discovery surprised astronomers
In 2022, Webb had already found brown dwarfs in IC 348 with masses of approximately 3–4 Jupiters. New, deeper observations made it possible to detect objects with masses of only about 2 Jupiters, or approximately 0.19% of the Sun's mass.
According to ESA, these are the least massive brown dwarfs known. Their existence raises new questions for modern models of star formation, since objects this light were nevertheless able to form through a "stellar" process.
Astronomers discovered another surprise near one of the new brown dwarfs. It has signs of a disk of material around it, in which planets could potentially form, even though the mass of the brown dwarf itself is comparable to the masses of planets.
Researchers also detected unusual signs of hydrocarbons in the atmospheres of the smallest brown dwarfs. Scientists suggest that such extremely low-mass objects may even belong to a separate spectral class.
Along with the study's findings, ESA released a large-scale image of IC 348 taken by the telescope's NIRCam camera. It shows young stars, brown dwarfs, protostars, and jets of material expelled by newborn stars into the surrounding gas and dust.

Tallinn-Pärnu section is the most mature
"I just visited the project office and asked the site manager what the biggest problem is right now. Naturally, he said they're short on trucks," Veskimäe noted.
Rail Baltic Estonia believes that extending deadlines could cool the construction market and allow the project to rely more on EU funding.
"A longer construction period would certainly ease the situation, making it possible to build kilometers at a more reasonable price," said Rail Baltic Estonia board member Lauri Ulm.
A delay would also affect train procurement. After the failure of its first tender, Elron is preparing a new one. Elron CEO Lauri Betlem wants new trains to begin operating within Estonia by 2030.
"I think we should stick to the proposed deadline, mainly because the project becomes more expensive with each passing year," Betlem said.
Although Latvia's construction pace gives little hope that trains could run beyond Ikla by 2030, the Tallinn–Pärnu section could be completed by the end of the decade.
"The Tallinn–Pärnu section is the most mature. Construction is underway across nearly the entire stretch," Ulm said.
Minister: We must decide what's sensible
Estonia's infrastructure minister Kuldar Leis said that revising the plan requires approval from Brussels.
"On Sunday and Monday, the three Baltic transport ministers will meet in Ireland at the gathering of European transport ministers. We'll discuss this again to ensure all three Baltic states act in the same way," Leis said.
"We must look at the entire process as one whole and bring all components together. First, whether Estonia is capable of finishing by 2030. Second, our southern neighbor Latvia has not given a clear signal about their ability to continue building. Third, the EU funding period is 2028–2034. If we truly finished by 2030, a large portion of EU support would go unused. Putting all this together, it makes sense to slow the pace now," Leis explained.
The minister said the plan remains to finish the domestic section — Tallinn to Pärnu — earlier. "The regional train tender will be relaunched immediately. We are not slowing down work on the entire route. Since construction on the Tallinn–Pärnu stretch is progressing very rapidly — over 100 kilometers where work is actively underway — that will continue. But south of Pärnu, and also from Ülemiste terminal toward the port in Tallinn, we can delay the start of work."
Leis added that early next week the Baltic prime ministers will also meet to discuss Rail Baltic's new timeline. "Much depends on Latvia — whether they will specify a year or not. Once the three Baltic states agree on our shared capability, we will negotiate with the European Commission on the pace of Rail Baltica. The European view is: agree among yourselves, say what you can deliver, and complete Rail Baltica."

Gallery: More than 50 Estonian artists take stock of what matters now

Gallery: More than 50 Estonian artists take stock of what matters now
What matters to Estonian artists right now? A major new exhibition at Tallinn's Haus Gallery offers 51 perspectives through nearly 60 never-before-displayed works.
"From the Artist's Perspective" opened Thursday, marking a new curatorial project that Haus Gallery hopes to turn into an annual tradition: a dialogue between artists and the public around issues they see as important right now.
The exhibition was assembled through an open call that drew dozens of professional artists from across generations.
With few restrictions on medium or format, artists were invited to submit one to three recent works that represented something personally meaningful to them, reflecting a significant personal position or worldview.
None of the works had been previously exhibited, and artists were asked to personally provide a few lines contextualizing each work and its significance in terms of the show. These accompanying texts, the gallery said, form an important part of the project and are included on site as well as on their website.
Nearly 60 works were ultimately selected, bringing together different artistic perspectives as well as their common threads to provide a unique collective portrait of the present moment.
Rather than imposing a single interpretation, the exhibition leaves viewers to consider what Estonian artists are depicting, what moves them and why.
51 Estonian artists
Haus Gallery, which has been active on Estonia's art scene since 1997, says the project is rooted in its conviction that art can map our emotional history and reflect what takes place in society through the personal but broadly resonant perspectives of individual artists.
Curated by Piia Ausman, the exhibition features 51 artists, including Vano Allsalu, Jaan Elken, Mall Nukke, Marko Mäetamm, Maarit Murka, Liisa Jugapuu, Mari Früling, Tiit Pääsuke, Laurentsius, Katariin Mudist, Liisa Mudist, Mari Roosvalt, Külli Suitso, Lisa Add and Valeri Vinogradov.
"From the Artist's Perspective" will remain on view through October 24.

West Nile virus is spreading across Europe; more than 650 cases have been recorded in Italy
Kyiv • UNN
More than 650 cases of West Nile virus have been registered in Italy—about half of the European total. Warming temperatures are lengthening the transmission season.
More than 650 cases of West Nile virus infection were registered in Italy in 2026 — approximately half of all recorded cases in Europe. Experts link the expansion of the infection’s range and the longer transmission season to rising temperatures, Associated Press reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to Italian health authorities, the virus is increasingly being detected in areas of the country where infections had previously been rare. West Nile virus has been considered endemic in Italy since 2020.
About 80% of those infected have no symptoms at all. In most of the remaining cases, the disease is mild, with flu-like symptoms; however, a small proportion of patients may develop severe neurological complications. Older people and patients with underlying conditions face the greatest risk.
The infection season may last until November
Antonino Bella, a researcher at Italy’s National Institute of Health, explained that higher temperatures create more favorable conditions for the reproduction of mosquitoes that transmit the virus.
Higher temperatures associated with climate change help mosquitoes reproduce and extend the transmission season, increasing the likelihood that infected mosquitoes will spread the virus among people
According to him, because of warmer weather, the virus transmission season may last as late as November in some years.

The World Health Organization’s Regional Office for Europe notes that climate change is not the only cause of the virus’s spread; however, warming extends the mosquito activity season and creates more favorable conditions for the virus itself to survive.

Who deserves a transplant? AI's answer isn't the same as a human doctor's
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:16:34 UTC
16:16:34 KST

AI chatbots make faster, more confident, but less nuanced decisions than human doctors when choosing who gets a life-saving kidney transplant.
Would you get a transplant if AI were the one deciding? New study points to differences in decision-making and prioritising between artificial intelligence language models and human doctors.
AI models show overconfidence, value different factors and oversimplify complex decisions when deciding which patient should receive a transplant, according to a new study.
For their study, researchers from Penn State University in the United States gave Large Language Models (LLMs) hypothetical scenarios, based on existing datasets from published human research on kidney allocation, where real participants had already made these same choices.
Each scenario involved two patients, Patient A and Patient B, both eligible for a single available kidney and characterised by age, health, and drinking habits. A decision maker must then choose which of the two patients should receive it.
“We ran these comparisons in a few different ways,” Hosseini said. “Sometimes we isolated just one trait at a time, sometimes we mixed several traits together to see how AI weighed competing factors, and sometimes we added a flip-a-coin option to measure indecision, a key factor present in human moral judgment.”
While human respondents tended to place greater importance on age — favouring younger over older patients — many models favoured lower alcohol consumption instead. Human decisions considered multiple factors and were more context-sensitive than those of LLMs, which often focused on a single attribute.
“First, AI chatbots often diverge from human values in how they weigh a patient’s traits,” said Hadi Hosseini, lead of the study at Penn State University. “They fixate on a single factor, like drinking habits, rather than balancing multiple considerations the way people do.”
The researchers also saw that AI did not struggle with indecision. While humans recognised there is no single objectively correct answer and decisions can rely on nuanced human moral judgements, the systems committed to a single option with little hesitation.
"When we allocate something scarce, whether it’s a kidney, a job or access to some other resource, there isn’t always a single objectively correct answer,” said John Dickerson, chief executive officer at Mozilla.ai, who collaborated in the study.
“Humans recognize that ambiguity and codify it via open debate into the allocative process. AI models often don’t.”
AI and ethical decisions
Recent interactions with AI systems increasingly require them to go beyond factual information and make value judgments, the authors noted.
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into healthcare, supporting clinical workflows, diagnosis, treatment planning and timely utilisation of scarce medical resources.
One of their applications involves decisions on allocating deceased-donor or living-donor kidneys to patients, which, according to the authors, depend on complex ethical and moral considerations.
In such high-stakes scenarios, the researchers pointed out that decisions demand not only accuracy but also alignment with human values and moral judgement.
According to the researchers, asking if AI can make moral decisions or whether they’re aligned with human values lies at the core of today’s wider debate on artificial intelligence.
“The ethical stakes are high, and AI’s role in such life-altering decisions requires deep reflection,” said Hosseini. “Moral decisions in settings like organ allocation directly determine who lives and who dies, so getting AI's role in them right isn't optional.”
“While we do not intend to encourage the use of AI as a substitute for professional judgment in medical decision-making or other high-stakes contexts, it's becoming essential to understand their behavior as individuals, organizations and firms more and more rely on AI to make decisions or receive recommendations,” he added

Jewish communities must build warm ties with every first responder - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:14:57 UTC
16:14:57 KST

Police, fire, EMS, and rescue are not immune to antisemitic lies. B’nai B’rith International will pilot proactive relationships in select communities – and we need partners to do it.
Jewish communities have spent years building cameras, plans, and volunteer patrols. Those tools matter. They are not enough.
If the people who answer a distress call – the ambulance team, the engine company, the rescue squad, the police officer – do not see Jews as neighbors worth rushing toward, our safety, our health, and our ability to remain in a community or a country are in the balance.
This is not only a law-enforcement problem. Firefighters, paramedics, EMTs, and disaster crews are just as exposed as anyone else to antisemitic lies. We cannot assume a Star of David on a door or a synagogue on a dispatch screen will be treated as a call for help rather than a reason to hesitate.
I have seen what changes when the relationship is built before the crisis.
At the Anti-Defamation League, I took newly appointed NYPD chiefs of department to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington. The museum opened early for a special tour on law enforcement and the Holocaust.
These were seasoned officers. I watched their faces change as they learned how the Nazis used ordinary police in the Final Solution. The lesson was not that American officers are Nazis; it was that decent institutions can absorb a lie if no one has done the work of making Jews fully human to them.
Later, standing volunteer security outside my synagogue with the Community Security Service, I often stood next to a uniformed officer who knew almost nothing about the institution he was assigned to protect.
We started with human conversation – shared values, kids, the job. That bond is bipartisan. It is as simple as organizing a visit to say thank you: we are the Jewish community, and we appreciate you.
Preventing a possible nightmare
The nightmare we are trying to prevent is specific: an ambulance team that sees a Star of David and decides that call can wait; a firefighter who does not drive as fast to a Jewish home or business. If we lose first responders, we do not merely lose a layer of security. We lose the practical possibility of living as Jews in public.
B’nai B’rith International has spent decades working with first responders after natural disasters. We have thousands of volunteers in close to 50 countries. That network has too often been used only after the wreckage. We intend to use it before the siren sounds.
We at B’nai B’rith International will pilot this initiative in select communities in North America, Latin America, and Europe.
The work is straightforward and local: synagogues and lodges going to firehouses, EMS stations, and precincts; thank-you visits; shared meals; tours that humanize Jewish life; and ongoing contact so a first responder already knows the people behind the address.
We will need partners – synagogues, federations, security networks, first-responder associations, and communal organizations that already have relationships on the ground. As we develop this through our international infrastructure, we will reach out. This is not about silos. It is about partnership to make Jews safer and human again.
Gratitude is not soft. It is a strategy. A chief who walks through a Holocaust museum with Jewish hosts does not leave as the same official who entered. An officer who has talked about his children with a congregant does not hear the next rumor the same way.
The Jewish world is very good at showing up after a catastrophe.
The next chapter is quieter: walking into a firehouse when nothing is burning and saying, “We see you, we need you, and we intend to be neighbors you would run toward.” If we wait until the siren is already sounding, we have waited too long.
The writer is the CEO of B’nai B’rith International.

Al Jazeera has fired 24 journalists and staff members who worked for the network in the Gaza Strip, amid a lawsuit filed in the US accusing the Qatari broadcaster of providing support to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), Ynet reported Friday.
The lawsuit was filed in February 2025 by Shurat HaDin, with support from the pro-Israel advocacy group StandWithUs. It names the employees and alleges that some Al Jazeera staff members had ties to terrorist organizations and, in some cases, were members of those groups.
The Jerusalem Post reported in June that the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) would conduct a comprehensive review of its database of journalists killed during the Israel-Hamas war after Hamas and PIJ published obituaries identifying individuals previously listed by CPJ as journalists as members of their organizations.
In a statement on June 25, CPJ said it had removed 20 names from its database after confirming that those individuals had worked for Hamas or PIJ.
The review followed Israeli media reports that identified several individuals previously listed as journalists by international organizations as having ties to Hamas or PIJ.
CPJ outlines criteria for listing journalists in database
“CPJ has always been clear that we do not include anyone in our data sets if there is evidence that they were engaging in combat or inciting imminent violence,” CPJ CEO Jodie Ginsberg said in the statement. “This is consistent with international humanitarian law, which considers journalists affiliated with non-state actors to be civilians, provided they do not directly participate in hostilities.”
According to CPJ, the organization uses at least two independent sources of information, desk-based research, and, where possible, in-person reporting before adding an individual to its database as a journalist or media worker.
CPJ said that in-person verification by researchers outside Gaza has not been possible since the beginning of the war because Israel has not allowed international correspondents access to the territory.
CPJ pushes for access for foreign media in Gaza
The organization has petitioned the Israeli government and the Supreme Court to reverse the restrictions preventing foreign journalists from entering Gaza.
“CPJ condemns in no uncertain terms the misrepresentation of combatants as journalists or media workers, or the misuse of ‘Press’ insignia,” Ginsberg said. “Such actions endanger every single individual journalist legitimately trying to report. We are conducting a full review of the names on our lists to confirm that no one who was actively engaged in combat is listed in our data.”

Choose a path to peace: An open letter to my Palestinian neighbors - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:14:14 UTC
16:14:14 KST

I live in a Jewish town in the Judean Desert, 20 minutes from Jerusalem. I am a wife, a mother, a grandmother, a hospice chaplain, and the mayor of my community. I raise my family here, I celebrate life cycle events here, and I bury the dead here.
I watch the sun set over the same hills that appear in the Bible. Many Jews who live in Judea and Samaria have written open letters to their Palestinian neighbors. Yossi Klein Halevi did it with care and moral seriousness in a full book. This is mine.
I am sorry for what happened to your family. War is ugly. Displacement is painful. Loss leaves marks that last generations. I will not pretend otherwise.
There is no way to turn the clock back to 1948 and restore the exact house your grandparents left. History does not work that way. In 1947, the United Nations offered a partition plan that would have created a Jewish state and an Arab state side by side.
The Jewish leadership accepted it. The Arab leadership rejected it and declared that the entire land, from the river to the sea, would remain Arab. Five Arab armies then attacked the newly declared State of Israel. They lost.
That war had consequences. Jews who remained in what became Israel after 1948 were not expelled from the new state. Arabs who did not flee were allowed to stay on their land and become citizens. Many did. Nazareth remains an overwhelmingly Arab city inside Israel to this day.
Those who left, or whose families left, made choices in the middle of a war their leaders had chosen to start. Choices in war have costs. Pretending the outcome was simply an “injustice done to” your family erases the agency of the people who rejected partition and launched the attack.
Your great-grandparents decided at a decisive moment. The leadership of their side also made a decision. They were wrong if the goal was a state of their own living next to a Jewish one. Israel exists now. It will not become “Palestine.”
Clinging to a key from a house that no longer belongs to you will not change that. The healthier path is to build a functioning society in the areas under Palestinian control and to seek peace with the Israelis rather than to wait for another war that your side keeps losing.
It is painful to watch the same pattern repeat. Israel has offered the West Bank and Gaza as the basis for a Palestinian state more than once: Camp David in 2000, Olmert’s proposal in 2008, even after Hamas seized Gaza. The Palestinian leadership refused to close a deal. The chant “from the river to the sea” continued.
Waiting for the shift to happen
After October 7, 2023, Israelis are finished making the same offer on the same terms while the other side still treats the Jewish state as temporary and illegitimate.
This land is not empty of Jewish history. Judea and Samaria are filled with ancient Jewish archaeology and biblical sites. Jews were exiled from this land for centuries and longed to return.
In many cases, your families still live only a short distance from where their grandparents lived, on the same stretch of land between the river and the sea. If you live elsewhere, that, too, is a choice. You could be building institutions, schools, and a politics of peace where you are.
Israel has had large, visible peace movements for decades. Palestinian society has produced far fewer voices willing to say, in public and at personal risk, that they want a state next to Israel rather than instead of it. Those who do are often branded collaborators. That culture has a price.
Until Palestinian leaders and a critical mass of the public declare, clearly and repeatedly, that they accept a Jewish state and will build their own instead of trying to erase ours, they will remain without a state of their own.
Jews built a country in which Arab citizens have equal legal rights. Israel has made peace with Egypt, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, and others when those governments decided they wanted peace rather than Israel’s destruction.
When Arabs choose peace, Israel lives with it. When the goal remains the elimination of Israel, Israel treats that population as a security threat. Why would it do otherwise? Jews did not return after 2,000 years of exile just to hand the state over and disappear.
Things do not have to stay as they are.
Accountability would help. Stop presenting every consequence of rejected partition, rejected offers, and renewed war as something done to you with no decisions on your side. Perpetual victimhood without agency has not produced a state. It has produced more funerals.
Choose nation-building. Choose leaders who will say out loud that Israel is here to stay and that the task now is to create a decent life for Palestinians rather than to wait for Israel to vanish.
Until that shift happens in public, loudly, and at scale, the reality will remain what it is: Israeli security control in Judea and Samaria, Hamas in Gaza, and another generation raised on the hope that the next war will succeed where the last ones failed.
I write this from a hill in Judea, as a woman who has spent years sitting with the dying and raising children in a place the world insists is temporary. It is not temporary. Israel is Israel. The question is whether your side will finally decide to live next to it.
The writer is a certified interfaith hospice chaplain in Jerusalem and the mayor of Mitzpe Yericho, where she enjoys spending time with her family.

Türkiye revokes Bank Mellat’s operating license

16:13:30 KST

Türkiye’s Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK) has revoked the operating license of Iranian lender Bank Mellat’s Istanbul main branch, according to a decision published in the Official Gazette on Sept. 19.
The regulator’s board adopted the decision on Sept. 18 under Article 71(1)(b) of Banking Law No. 5411.
The provision allows the regulator to revoke a bank’s license when its continued operations threaten the rights of depositors and participation fund holders, as well as confidence and stability in the financial system.
The Tehran-based lender began operating in Türkiye on April 16, 1982, through its Istanbul main branch, following Cabinet approval in 1981.
It later opened branches in Ankara in 1985 and İzmir in 1992.
According to the bank’s website, its Turkish operations provided financial services supporting trade and joint projects between Türkiye and Iran.

Jet fuel prices in parts of the United States have climbed close to their highest levels since the war with Iran began, renewing concerns over airline costs and ticket prices.
Prices on the Gulf Coast, the U.S. benchmark market, stood at $4.55 a gallon on Sept. 17, just over 20 cents below their wartime peak.
In New York, jet fuel cost $4.75 a gallon.
U.S. production fell to its lowest level since early March in the week to Sept. 11, the report said. Supplies remain high but are moving closer to normal seasonal levels, leaving scope for further price increases.
Broader fuel supply disruptions, particularly in diesel, are adding to the pressure. Diesel and jet fuel are both middle distillates, with closely linked prices. Refiners can increase output of one at the expense of the other.
The fuel price surge earlier this year pushed up airfares and worsened airlines’ financial difficulties. Spirit Airlines halted operations in May, citing sustained fuel-cost increases and its inability to secure the additional funding needed to continue flying.

Sirens sounded twice overnight between Friday and Saturday in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, for the first time since the dramatic advance by Yemen’s Houthi rebels and their takeover of a stretch of coastline that has effectively given them control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi Civil Defense later said the danger had passed. No damage or casualties were reported. Arab media reported explosions across the capital.
The alerts heard in Riyadh were also activated in the nearby Al-Kharj region. The first siren sounded at around 3 a.m. local time and the second at about 5:20 a.m. Shortly before 1 a.m., sirens were heard in the Farasan region. On Friday evening, waves of alerts sounded in several other areas, including Yanbu, Taif, Jeddah, Khamis Mushait, AlUla, Jazan and Abha.
Yanbu, on the Red Sea coast, is home to a major oil export terminal that Saudi Arabia uses to ship crude abroad while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, where tanker traffic remains sparse amid the continuing confrontation between the United States and Iran.
Last week, Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, which feeds the Yanbu terminal, was attacked and taken out of service. Pro-Iranian militias in Iraq continue to deny involvement in the attack, while U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed Iran directly.
Saudi Arabia has meanwhile found a partial workaround. Reuters reported that it is transferring oil between ships off the port of Sohar in Oman.
Qatar-based Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported Saturday morning that “clashes between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have intensified on several fronts, alongside airstrikes and rapid changes in territorial control, particularly along the western coast and in areas surrounding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.”
The report said the Houthis claimed Saudi warplanes had stepped up attacks on areas under their control. It also said the humanitarian consequences of the fighting were worsening, with more than 112,000 people displaced since the beginning of the month and emergency medical aid arriving in Sanaa to address shortages.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Friday that over the previous 24 hours, “Saudi warplanes, particularly F-15s that took off from Khamis Mushait Air Base, carried out 26 airstrikes in Taiz province.”
Khamis Mushait was among the places where sirens sounded overnight. Saree also claimed that Saudi Arabia had carried out about 300 strikes in Yemen since the beginning of the week.
Interceptor stocks running low, US met with Houthis
Amid the continuing fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, The Associated Press reported this week that Saudi Arabia’s stockpile of interceptor missiles is running low and that Riyadh has appealed to Western and regional allies for help.
According to the report, Saudi Arabia asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to send air defense assistance to the region so it could intercept missiles and drones launched toward the kingdom by the Houthis or other Iranian-backed militias.
The United States is Saudi Arabia’s main supplier of interceptor missiles, but the report said U.S. inventories had also been depleted in recent months because of the war with Iran, prompting Riyadh to seek help from other allies.
The Houthi takeover of the strategic Red Sea coastline, which gives the group control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, continues to raise concern internationally and across the Middle East. The Houthis seized the area in an offensive that defeated forces belonging to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government.
Reuters reported Wednesday that U.S. officials met Houthi representatives in Oman earlier in the week. According to the report, the Houthis told the United States that they intended to refrain from attacking American vessels in the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which they now effectively control.
Reuters said the meeting, which was not publicly disclosed but was confirmed by three sources, took place Sunday at the U.S. Embassy in Muscat, Oman.
The Houthis told U.S. officials they remained committed to the ceasefire reached with Washington in 2025 and therefore did not intend to attack American ships.
One source, a Yemeni official, told Reuters that militia representatives also said they would not attack Israeli vessels or other commercial shipping, except for ships belonging to Saudi Arabia.
Riyadh said the Houthis this week launched a drone toward the Saudi city of Mecca for the first time in the current round of fighting. Mecca is Islam’s holiest city and home to the Kaaba, one of the religion’s most sacred sites, drawing millions of Muslim pilgrims each year.
Saudi Arabia said it intercepted the drone but described the launch toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometers from the Yemeni border, as the crossing of a “red line.”
The Houthis denied launching a drone toward Mecca. The last apparent attempt to target the city came in 2017, when a ballistic missile was fired in its direction.
The Houthis strongly reject the Saudi accusation, and demonstrations were held in Yemen on Friday against Saudi Arabia over the allegation.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said artificial intelligence development in the US should move “as fast as we can,” pushing back against growing calls within the technology industry to slow advances while stronger safety measures are developed.
Asked by CBS News whether AI development should be slowed and whether doing so could affect competition with China, Huang said the industry should continue moving quickly regardless of its competitors.
“We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anybody else,” Huang said in an excerpt released on Friday from an interview set to air on Sunday.
He stressed, however, that speed should not come at the expense of safety.
“We would never, ever, and never should ship products before they’re ready, deliver products that are unsafe, and nobody’s expecting us to do that,” said Huang.
“But everybody’s expecting us to succeed and help America be as prosperous as possible.”
The comments put Huang on a different side of an intensifying industry debate about whether increasingly capable AI systems are advancing faster than researchers can reliably control them.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last week called for leading AI developers to slow improvements in model capabilities to give safety research and oversight more time to catch up.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI founder Elon Musk subsequently expressed support for slowing or “pacing” development of frontier models.
Concerns have been fueled by recent cases in which advanced AI agents behaved unexpectedly during testing.
Google confirmed on Friday that its Gemini model accessed systems belonging to three real companies during a cybersecurity evaluation after accidentally gaining internet access.
The company said the model stopped each intrusion once it realised the systems were real and did not classify the incidents as model misalignment.
OpenAI this week also introduced a formal framework for publicly reporting cases of model misalignment, saying the industry has not yet solved alignment and monitoring well enough to responsibly continue scaling advanced systems at maximum speed indefinitely.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Justice's Agency of Corrections said Friday that it will focus this year on intercepting unauthorized deliveries.
Aerial drones can fly into prisons to sneak in prohibited items. The corrections agency used signal jammers and pursuit drones as countermeasures.
The agency said it chose Changhua Prison for this year's Ching An task force training. It selected 100 officers from 51 correctional facilities to participate in the 20-day training, per a press release.
Justice Minister Cheng Ming-chien (鄭銘謙) hosted the event. He was joined by corrections agency Director Lin Hsien-ming (林憲銘), regional correctional facilities, and local law enforcement.
The exercise proceeded in three major phases:
- Task force operators used signal jammers to repel the intruding drone and pursue with their own drones
- Patrol drones gathered evidence and transmitted live footage to make informed decisions
- Regional units provided additional manpower for joint defense to put down a mock prison riot
Besides tech demonstrations, the task force also performed martial arts, takedown moves, and police baton techniques.

Coventry stressed, however, that the final decision on the sports program rests with the continental body and the host.

Google's Gemini hacks 3 real companies in security test
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:02:38 CST
16:02:38 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Google confirmed Friday that its Gemini artificial intelligence (AI) model accessed the protected systems of three real companies during a cybersecurity test in May, mistakenly treating them as authorized targets.
Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said in a statement that during a standard evaluation, Gemini used publicly available information on the internet and guessed login credentials to access three websites it believed were part of the authorized test environment.
Google said the model stopped further activity after determining that the systems belonged to real companies.
"We ensured the three entities were made aware," Adkins said, adding that Google had worked with the testing partner to adjust its testing procedures.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the testing was conducted by AI security evaluation company Irregular. In one test run, Gemini repeatedly tried passwords before gaining access to a protected real-world system. In two other runs, the model found exposed login credentials in publicly available repositories and used them to access systems belonging to other companies.
Irregular said in an earlier report that the tests were designed around a fictional company, but human error caused the fictional name to overlap with a real-world internet domain. At the same time, internet access was unintentionally available in some of the testing environments, allowing AI models to mistake real-world targets for part of the simulated exercise.
Irregular said the known issues had since been fixed, affected parties had been notified and additional safeguards had been introduced to prevent similar incidents.
Google said that the incidents caused no damage to the companies involved and that it did not consider the behavior an instance of model misalignment. ■

New Zealand reforms earthquake-prone building rules

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:02:24 CST
16:02:24 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's parliament has unanimously passed legislation reforming the country's earthquake-prone building system, with a focus on buildings that pose the greatest risk to life.
The reforms passed on Friday are expected to remove around half of the buildings currently designated as earthquake-prone from the system and save building owners and the economy 8.2 billion NZ dollars (4.7 billion U.S. dollars), Building and Construction Minister Simon Watts said in a statement on Saturday.
Under the new system, remediation requirements for buildings that remain designated as earthquake-prone will be more targeted, reducing costs and complexity while addressing life-safety risks, Watts said.
High-risk unreinforced masonry buildings and vulnerable multi-story concrete buildings in high and medium seismic zones will continue to be subject to earthquake-prone building requirements. Councils will also retain the ability to identify serious seismic risks that may have been missed, according to the statement.
Updated seismic zones, based on the latest seismic science, will take effect the day after the legislation receives formal approval, it said, adding that buildings in Auckland, the Chatham Islands and the upper North Island low seismic zone will be entirely removed from the earthquake-prone building system.
The remainder of the reforms will take effect on July 1, 2027, giving councils, building owners and the wider sector time to prepare, Watts said. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: In China's mountain orchards, oranges are taking flight
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:02:22 CST
16:02:22 KST

A drone monitors an agricultural demonstration park in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province, Sept. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Jinbo)
WUHAN, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- On a steep hillside in the Three Gorges region along the Yangtze River, drones glide over rows of citrus trees, spraying pesticides across the orchard.
It is one of the many jobs drones now do in Zigui, a mountainous county in central China's Hubei Province. During the November harvest, they also carry freshly picked navel oranges down the slopes.
For years, fertilizing and spraying the orchards were done by hand. Getting oranges down from Zigui's steep hills meant carrying baskets along narrow, uneven paths, with elevation drops of up to 400 to 500 meters.
Guo Xingcheng, 39, knows the work firsthand. After starting to manage his family's orchard in 2011, he spent the next decade carrying the fruit himself during the harvest, about 50 kilograms per trip. On the toughest stretches, the journey could take up to 40 minutes.
"The paths were rough. At first, baskets would fall and people would stumble," he said.
That began to change in 2021, when Zigui started testing drones to transport oranges. Guo became the first person in the county to buy an agricultural drone and learn to fly it, trying it out in his orchard.
"A drone can carry 100 kilograms at a time and fly down the mountain in just one minute," he said.
The technology has advanced quickly since. A drone can now move 25,000 to 30,000 kilograms of oranges a day, roughly the workload of 10 people.
For crop protection, one drone can do the work of about 25 people, while applying pesticides more precisely and using less water and chemicals.
"Farmers were skeptical at first," Guo said. "Soon, more and more wanted to use them."
Guo later started a company that now employs 10 drone pilots, all young people who have returned to Zigui, as well as a crop protection team of more than 40 workers.
The work has drawn more young people. Zigui now has around 2,600 certified agricultural drone pilots.
With the orange harvest still weeks away, some of Guo's pilots are now in Fujian Province in eastern China, helping transport pomelos by drone.
"The terrain in Zigui is complicated, with lots of trees and steep slopes, so flying here takes a lot of skill," Guo said. "Our pilots find it much easier when they work elsewhere."
Li Songfei, a local government official in Guojiaba Township, Zigui, said the government uses agricultural support funds to subsidize farmers' drone purchases and helps arrange pilot training.
Drones are only one part of the changes in Zigui's orchards.
Across nearly 400,000 mu, or about 26,700 hectares, of citrus orchards, the county has digitally mapped individual plots, recording information such as elevation, slope and tree age. Farmers can also use smartphones to upload photos of pests and diseases and receive identification and treatment advice.
For farmers who once relied mainly on experience and weather, data is becoming another tool for managing their orchards, said Li Li, an official with the county agriculture bureau.
But the changes taking place in Zigui's orchards come against a much longer history of change.
Zigui was among the areas most affected by China's Three Gorges Project, the world's largest hydropower project. Roughly 100,000 people -- about a quarter of the county's population -- were relocated before the dam began operating in the early 2000s.
Li Songfei, a native of neighboring Henan Province, has spent more than five years working with local communities.
Her work has coincided with a new phase of rural development since China declared an end to absolute poverty in 2021, with efforts shifting toward revitalizing rural areas and raising the incomes of hundreds of millions of farmers.
New technologies are increasingly part of that effort, from drones and the Internet of Things to robotics, opening up new possibilities for agricultural production.
The county's orchards now produce more than 1 million tonnes of oranges a year, generating over 25 billion yuan in output value and supporting more than 260,000 people.
Zigui is also the hometown of Qu Yuan, one of China's best-known ancient poets, whose writings more than 2,000 years ago came to embody a deep devotion to his country and people.
"You can see how much this place has changed," Li said. "But amid all the change, there is also continuity. What endures is the passion and resilience with which people here have always sought a better life." ■

A drone transports oranges at an agricultural demonstration park in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province, Sept. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Jinbo)

Interview: Austrian parliament speaker calls for mutual learning, fair cooperation between Europe, China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
15:02:22 CST
16:02:22 KST

Walter Rosenkranz, president of Austria's National Council, or the lower house of Parliament, speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Vienna, Austria, Sept. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/He Canling)
VIENNA, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Europe should abandon an anxious mindset toward China's development and instead pursue mutual learning and fair cooperation, said Walter Rosenkranz, president of Austria's National Council, or the lower house of Parliament.
In an interview with Xinhua, Rosenkranz said China has achieved leaps and bounds in many fields, notably in renewable energy. "The EU and China must continue to deepen their cooperation while operating within a framework of fair rules," he said.
European national legislatures, he said, should take the initiative to build fair and reasonable frameworks for cooperation, helping various sectors in Europe and China eliminate perceptual biases, deepen practical cooperation, and achieve complementary strengths and common development.
Noting that he recently led a delegation to China, which was his first visit to the country since taking office as president of the National Council, Rosenkranz said Austrian political parties share broad consensus and a strong willingness to deepen exchanges with China.
During the visit, the delegation not only experienced China's long and profound history and culture, but also witnessed the vitality of China's modernization drive, he said.
This year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Austria. Rosenkranz said friendship between the two countries has been deepening since the establishment of diplomatic ties.
Since the 1990s, there have been more than 60 exchanges between the national legislative bodies, Rosenkranz said.
Looking back on the 55-year history of exchanges, Rosenkranz said Austria and China cherish peace, consistently uphold multilateralism and the norms of international law, and remain committed to promoting peace through cooperation and pursuing development through win-win outcomes.
The two countries share compatible development concepts and have long worked together under the framework of the United Nations to contribute to world peace and development, while deepening cooperation in multiple fields, including the economy and culture, with fruitful results, he said.
More than 650 Austrian companies are currently operating in China, fully demonstrating the strong vitality of Austria-China cooperation, he added.
Rosenkranz said the current international situation is marked by intertwined changes and turbulence, with challenges such as climate change, artificial intelligence governance and regional conflicts emerging one after another. The legislative bodies of Austria and China could further deepen dialogue and cooperation, build consensus on governance, improve cooperation rules, and contribute wisdom and strength to addressing global issues.
Looking to the future, Rosenkranz regards young people as the main force of future cooperation and the inheritors and promoters of friendship between the two countries.
Deeper youth and cultural exchanges, he added, could strengthen the foundation of people-to-people ties and give the friendly strategic partnership between the two countries fresh momentum. ■

16:00:41 KST

The Liberal Democrats have begun work on a new manifesto in case of a possible snap election, as Ed Davey said he understood the frustrations of some of his MPs who fear that the party’s message is currently at risk of being lost.
But Davey also urged his party not to panic at static polling numbers, arguing that with tactical voting and fragmented political loyalties, he fully expects the party to do even better at the next election than in 2024, when it won 72 seats, the highest total for a century.
Speaking ahead of the party’s annual conference in Brighton, Davey warned that discipline and focus were vital, given what he described as their “moral responsibility” in blocking a Reform-led government, predicting that Kemi Badenoch would eventually seek an alliance with Nigel Farage’s party.
A manifesto working group, led by the Cheadle MP Tom Morrison, has already been created, Davey said, meaning the party can be ready if Andy Burnham calls an election. “We don’t normally do it this early,” he said.
The Lib Dems already have a number of policies in place, including an economic proposal based around seeking to rejoin the EU’s single market, with a similarly Brussels-focused immigration policy of signing up to a Europe-wide pact on migration and asylum.
The party’s national poll ratings are largely static at about 12% or 13%, with the Lib Dems spending much of this year in fifth place behind Reform, Labour, the Conservatives and a resurgent Green party.
Some of Davey’s MPs complain privately about what they see as an overly slow and cautious approach to both policy and rhetoric, saying this has sidelined the party from the national debate.
However, it is by no means a unanimous view, with others saying the pace has picked up since the appointment of the party’s new political director James Holt, a veteran of the coalition years who then spent nearly a decade working with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.
Davey said he understood the concerns, but said MPs should not get distracted: “They’re frustrated because they’re coming up with the arguments, they’re running the campaigns and they don’t get the coverage for them. And I get it, it’s frustrating.”
Headline poll ratings, he said, were only a partial guide to an election in which tactical voting and local campaigns were likely to play a major role in votes likely to be split five or even six ways.
He said: “It’s going to be a ground war much more than people think, and good for us because we’re great at ground wars and at the community politics that turns poll ratings into loads of seats.”
Party strategists are confident they can defend many of the 60-plus so-called blue wall seats won from the Conservatives in 2024 – a zone Davey now refers to as the “orange wall” – and add to that tally. A number of candidates are already in place in target seats after a streamlining of the selection process.
Such efforts, Davey predicted, could be the one thing standing in the way of a Nigel Farage government.
He said: “I have felt for a long time that we have a moral responsibility in our party. It weighs heavily on my shoulders, because when I see men in black shirts and balaclavas, and when I see overt racism at the level we’re seeing it, we have to win. That is a burden for me, knowing we just have to be as smart as we possibly can.”
Some Lib Dems argue that this mission to hoover up anti-Reform sentiment actually makes the party’s slightly subterranean profile a potential benefit, and that Davey should ignore voices calling for him to be bolder or more outspoken.
One MP said: “Unlike Reform and the Greens, we have worked out how to use the electoral system, and if we want to stop bad things happening, we have to tailor our campaigning to that reality. If, say, you embrace one side in a culture war, you divide your community.”
Another MP said Davey should embrace his “centrist dad” image: “He’s a safe pair of hands, which is a valuable thing these days. He could say something a bit crazy to appeal to the core and increase our polling numbers … but it wouldn’t win us a single extra seat.”
Although there are no moves to challenge Davey as leader, some Lib Dems are pushing for the party to set out what it represents.
“We risk being dead in the water if we can’t articulate a proper vision of what we are, and what liberalism is,” one MP warned. “People know what Labour and the Conservatives stand for. If they have an opinion about us, it’s often that we’re slightly nicer Tories.
“Yes, Ed has been our most successful leader ever. But you have to progress or you’re doomed, and at the moment it feels a bit static.”

Greenish and pleasant: long-awaited rain returns to England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
07:00:41 UTC
16:00:41 KST

The landscapes of southern England and Wales are slowly regaining their colour after this summer’s extreme heat.
The UK’s hottest summer on record left the south of the country dried out and brown, making the impact of the drought particularly visual.
As autumn begins, large parts of the UK are still officially in drought. And even if autumn is wetter than normal, some could still be in drought in the spring, according to the Environment Agency.
But some rain has returned, and with it the green, to the relief of many. Darren Share, the director of the royal parks, which manages Hyde Park and St James Park among others, recalls: “The grass was completely scorched off across all of our park network, it was quite shocking. The grass level had almost turned to dust.
“We’ve had heatwaves in the past but they’ve only been for short periods of time. The grass dies off, we get the rain again and then everything starts coming back quite quickly. This time it was just one [heatwave] after another.”
The extreme conditions not only changed the physical features of the parks, he said. “You could see that people were using the parks completely differently.”
Visitor numbers decreased significantly during the day and many sporting and volunteering activities were cancelled because of health and safety concerns.
The royal parks are not yet in full bloom again, but the difference between now and peak summer is stark. Share attributes the rapid regrowth to the resilience of grass. “I’m looking at the parks and seeing the grass come back to green. We’re very lucky that grass can tolerate that level of heat and will regenerate like we’re seeing now,” he said.
In Wales, which was hit by wildfires in mid-August, the death of grassy areas had a range of social and environmental effects. “I saw really thin cattle because they had no food for grazing,” said Carolyn Thomas, a climate activist and former Senedd member. “Farmers … had to go into their winter stock to keep their animals fed.
“Sheep and cows were hiding under the shade of trees barely moving. Some were lying down flat and I was thinking: ‘Are they dead?’”
The UK government has pledged £100m to “strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to extreme weather and wildfires”, but Thomas said she did not think this was the solution.
“If you have to evacuate your home because of a wildfire you can’t just think: ‘We need a bigger fire service and more helicopters that can drop water’,” she said. “We need prevention.”
Like southern England, the Welsh countryside is slowly returning to normal, much to Thomas’s pleasure. “Now I’m walking and seeing green fields,” she said. “It’s amazing. But we still have that loss as well and it’s going to take a while to recover.”
Groundwater and reservoir levels remain low and the government has urged water companies to continue their efficiency measures until normal levels are reached.

16:00:40 KST

In hindsight, Sheri Ingram, 35, can see the red flags. Lee Slocombe, a builder hired to renovate her ex-boyfriend’s home in the south Wales valleys, offered to do the work cheaply because he had materials left over from another job, then asked for money upfront to buy additional supplies.
“At the time, we believed him,” says Sheri, who was in her early 20s when it happened, and had just left university. The couple budgeted about £8,000 for work that included removing a supporting wall and building an extension with a balcony.
Within weeks, the house had been ripped apart. “He pulled up the floorboards and removed the floor joists – he said they had wood rot and needed to come out – took out the staircase, took down the walls, and removed the ceiling,” Ingram says. “The first floor was pinned up using metal poles, and he threw the rubble out the back.”
Slocombe kept finding problems and asking for more money, so Ingram’s then boyfriend borrowed another £6,000 from family. By the end, the couple had handed over about £14,000. The builder gave various excuses about where the money had gone and said he was expecting a medical payout for an injury suffered on another job, which he would use to repay them. He even turned up one day in a sling and said he needed a few weeks off. Then, after about six weeks, he disappeared.
Slocombe, from Swansea, was jailed for six years in February after defrauding nine victims of £400,000 – his latest conviction in a decade of offending. Ingram’s case was part of a previous trial.
Ingram is one of many customers who have lost money to cowboy builders. In July, Citizens Advice said 4.8 million homeowners had a problem with a home repair job in the previous 18 months, from unfinished or unsafe work, to disputes with traders. About 1.7 million had to pay more to fix earlier work, or had been overcharged, losing an average of £750 each. For one in 10, the extra cost topped £5,000.
Among Andy Burnham’s first promises as prime minister was a crackdown on rogue builders, with a register of trusted traders scheduled to go live this month.
The government is also backing a Trusted Payment app, endorsed by the Chartered Trading Standards Institute. It will create a “fair contract between trade and consumer”, says its director, James Walker.
Under the system, milestone payments are delayed by 24 hours, giving time to cancel if consumers feel under pressure, with payments for completed work held in escrow by the Dispute Resolution Ombudsman until the job is finished to both parties’ satisfaction. Projects costing more than £2,500 are covered by a two-year warranty. Traders who fail to follow ombudsman decisions can be banned from the app.
Walker says the aim is to create a “trusted network for consumers” while helping reputable tradespeople win more business.
“We are not going to stop a rogue trader going out … but we are providing a trusted mechanism so you know if you use this process you are protected,” he says.
With the promise of greater protection, Paul Boielle, 82, hopes others will be spared his experience. He had noticed a problem with a corner of his roof when three men knocked on his door. It was soon after his wife’s funeral, and he was caught off-guard and “vulnerable”.
“They said they were doing work in the area and asked if I needed any roofing work,” Boielle says. He showed them the problem. “Before I knew it, they’d taken the tiles off.”
Among the men was the roofer David Vincent, from Orpington, London, who was later sentenced to 28 months in prison. He pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation and engaging in unfair commercial practices.
The men told Boielle the problem was more serious than he realised, and advised replacing the entire roof, quoting £30,000 – about twice what he says it should have cost. He paid a £5,000 deposit.
Roofers arrived soon afterwards, removed the solar panels and tiles, re-felted the roof and replaced everything. The job was finished in 48 hours. Boielle’s son and neighbours were concerned by how quickly it was done, and contacted Trading Standards. An investigation by Hertfordshire council’s Trading Standards service found that Vincent had grossly overcharged Boielle for the work, carried it out to a poor standard, and failed to provide information about the right to cancel.
For Boielle, the ordeal continued after the roofing team left. Tiles were crooked and the wrong capping tiles had been fitted. The work had to be redone and
it took most of the next year to sort it out.
The head of policy and market insight at the National Federation of Builders, Rico Wojtulewicz, says many reputable builders may simply choose not to join Trusted Payments because they are busy and do good work. “We don’t think this is the best approach,” he says.
“We believe every building should have a digital building passport – effectively a logbook recording all significant work, and who did it. If it subsequently fails, or is found to be substandard, that should be recorded against the builder responsible. It would shine a light on companies that consistently do poor-quality work.”
