Nearly six in 10 Danish companies with more than 10 employees now use artificial intelligence, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark. That’s almost four times the share recorded three years ago.
In 2026, 59 percent of these companies use AI, up from 15 percent in 2023. The share was 42 percent in 2025.
The uses of AI include analyzing text, converting spoken language into machine-readable code, generating images and videos, and automating work processes.
Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said it has seen AI move from being mainly a topic of discussion to a tool used in daily business.
“Companies’ use of artificial intelligence is here to stay, and we can see that the large companies are the furthest ahead,” Frederikke Saabye, industry director at Dansk Erhverv, said.
According to the business organisation, companies see greater efficiency as the main benefit of using AI. A lack of employee skills, knowledge and time are the biggest barriers to making greater use of the technology.
IT-Branchen, an industry association representing technology companies in Denmark, said the wider use of AI also increases the need to consider issues such as quality, transparency and data security.
“The more the technology spreads, the more important issues of quality, transparency, data security, and not least human judgment become,” IT-Branchen’s CEO Natasha Friis Saxberg said, adding that the development makes broader AI knowledge and training more important, including upskilling and continuing education for employees.
The Danish government plans to charge tourists 20 DKK per overnight stay in Copenhagen and Aarhus and introduce a levy on cruise ships, according to government sources and a memo obtained by Børsen.
The previously undisclosed measures would help fund tax cuts that the minority government will seek support for this autumn. The plans require backing from other parties, expected to come from the center-right opposition.
The government wants to abolish the 7.5% intermediate tax on annual income between 641,200 DKK and 777,900 DKK. It also plans to remove the top-top tax on income exceeding 2,592,700 DKK.
Corporate tax would fall from 22% to 19% over three years. The ceiling for share savings accounts would rise to 500,000 DKK over the same period, and taxes on shares would be reduced.
Planned funding measures include keeping the duty on chocolate and sweets, reducing the research and development deduction for companies and raising taxes on dividends received by major shareholders.
The government also wants to limit interest deductions to 150,000 DKK for individuals and 300,000 DKK for couples. Estates worth more than 10 million DKK would face a tax rate 15 percentage points higher than today.
The tax cuts are not fully covered by higher taxes and duties. The government plans to use about 1.5 billion DKK from available public funds in 2027, rising to about 2 billion DKK in 2029.
Denmark’s government consists of the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Moderates and Social Liberals. It does not have a parliamentary majority.
Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.

The Danish government will require police to register all potential crimes as criminal cases and end the practice of shelving reports without a proper investigation.
The Justice Ministry announced Tuesday that it would implement all recommendations from the National Audit Office, Denmark’s independent public spending watchdog. The disputed police practice is known as “washing cases.”
“Citizens must naturally be able to have confidence that the police handle their case properly and correctly, regardless of where in the country you live,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said.
“In the future, all potential criminal cases must be registered as actual criminal cases,” he added.
The Public Accounts Committee, a parliamentary oversight body, strongly criticized police in May after receiving a National Audit Office report on the practice. Cases were reportedly shelved partly to save resources.
The new government reshuffled senior police leadership in June. Top positions in the National Police and PET, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, changed hands.
Several justice spokespersons in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, said they had no confidence in National Police Commissioner Thorkild Fogde after he said he did not know about the practice. Fogde was later removed from the position.
The ministry did not say whether police would receive additional funding. Wammen previously said he was open to providing more money and noted that a multiyear agreement had already increased funding and training.
The National Police and Director of Public Prosecutions must regularly report on future developments to the political parties behind that agreement.
Two earlier State Prosecutor reports were not used because the National Audit Office identified issues they had missed, Wammen said.

“These are just some of the damages we see on our traction power system,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Sigsgaard said Monday.

DSB and Banedanmark said passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes could use DSB’s travel time guarantee.
DSB paid 67 million DKK in passenger compensation during the first six months of 2026, more than twice as much as during the same period in 2025.
A delay of at least 30 minutes provides a new ticket for the same route or a refund of 50 percent of the ticket price. Passengers delayed by an hour can receive 75 percent and claim up to 75 DKK for food and drinks.
Delays exceeding 90 minutes qualify for a full ticket refund.

A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.

Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.

Cuba hit with another nationwide blackout amid US fuel blockade
Cuba suffered a total blackout after the collapse of its electrical grid on Friday. The blackout is the latest of at least six partial or total grid collapses since the beginning of this year, as the island grapples with an ongoing US fuel blockade.
Cuba's electrical grid suffered a total collapse on Friday, plunging the nation into darkness and leaving millions without power amid a US pressure campaign that has largely blocked oil from reaching the Caribbean's largest island.
Friday's collapse was triggered by a failure in high-voltage transmission lines in central Cuba that occurred around 2pm local time, authorities said.
"Protocols are now in place to begin the gradual restoration of the system," said Felix Estrada, an official with Cuba's National Electrical Union (UNE).

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Power had returned to a handful of scattered neighbourhoods in Havana by late evening, primarily around hospitals, but much of the city remained completely dark under cloudy skies and rain.
The nationwide blackout, the latest of at least six partial or total grid collapses since January, hardly registered in a country accustomed to long hours, or even days, without power.
Many exhausted residents of the capital Havana were already without power when the blackout hit.
"Yesterday I'd gone without power for 24 hours. They turned the lights on for an hour, and then the grid collapsed," said Frank Lorenzo, a 23-year-old Havana resident looking forward to a long night of sweating and slapping mosquitoes.
Read moreUS sanctions Cuban president, Castro relatives in latest pressure campaign
Cuba's aging power generation system has been under severe strain from fuel shortages and decrepit infrastructure for years, but a US-imposed oil blockade that began in January has vastly worsened blackouts and led to more frequent grid collapses.
The grid collapsed three times in July and rolling blackouts have since spanned 30 hours or more across most of the country.
United Nations human rights experts have condemned the US oil blockade, calling it a violation of international law and warning that Cuba risks becoming a "silent Gaza" as shortages and blackouts grow ever more critical.

Could US pull one-third of troops from Europe? What that would mean
US Pentagon is reportedly considering proposals for reducing military footprint across the Atlantic.
The United States is reportedly considering a significant reduction in its military presence in Europe after its allies there refused to allow Washington to use their airbases for the war on Iran.
US media reported this week that senior Pentagon commanders are expected to submit plans to US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in the coming days.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4NATO jet shoots down suspected Russian drone over Lithuania
- list 2 of 4Trump says Canada becoming EU ‘associate member’ could be ‘hostile act’
- list 3 of 4Italy to deploy warships to protect shipping through Bab al-Mandeb
- list 4 of 4Why does Canada want to join the Europe-led JEF military partnership?
The news comes amid Russia’s ongoing war on Ukraine and as European countries increasingly sound the alarm about possible sabotage operations on their territory; Germany accused Russia of a drone attack on an airport earlier this month.
Europe has, for decades, depended on its partnership with Washington via the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) to deter a possible Russian attack. However, relations between some European capitals and Washington have deteriorated in the past year.
Here’s what we know about what options the US could be considering:
Why is the US reviewing its presence in Europe?
The Pentagon is weighing several possible options for reducing troops and military assets in Europe as part of a NATO review it announced in June, according to NBC News, which cited security sources.
Hegseth alluded to the review at a NATO meeting in Brussels in June, when he lashed out at fellow members and said new changes would be “designed to ensure that NATO is moving fast and irreversibly toward Europe leasing and stepping up to take primary responsibility for the defence of Europe”.
Hegseth said European allies’ decision not to provide US forces with access to bases in Europe to launch attacks on Iran was “shameful”.
“These allies, they put America’s sons and daughters, our sons and daughters, at risk by denying them the predictable access, basing and overflight that never should have been in question at all.”
What options is Hegseth considering?
One option could be to withdraw one-third of the estimated 68,000 US troops stationed in Europe. This option would largely affect soldiers stationed in Germany, Italy and Spain, NBC reported.
A second, more drastic scenario could see 40,000 soldiers exit, along with military aircraft, ships, and weapons.
The US may also consider moving troops away from stations in Central or Western Europe to NATO’s eastern flank, closer to Russia.
Hegseth is expected to reach a final decision by November 6, NBC reported.
Has the US already withdrawn troops from Europe?
Yes. About half of the 2,000 US soldiers stationed in Romania departed last year.
Some 5,000 US troops are in the process of withdrawing from Germany, where more than half of the European contingent is based.
The announcement of their withdrawal in May came after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticised the US’s war on Iran. Trump threatened to go “a lot further”, but US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly blocked the White House from withdrawing as many as 25,000 soldiers at the time, according to US media.
What would a US military drawdown mean for Europe?
A mass exit of troops and assets would be significant for Europe as it would undermine the US’s nuclear deterrence posture on the continent, said Ian Lesser of the German Marshall Fund.
While Russia is not likely to attack NATO members, Moscow would certainly see advantages in such a development, the analyst said.
“But it really depends on where and when the troops are removed,” Lesser added, pointing out that it would be hard to estimate the effect on Europe for now. If troops are moved from Western Europe to the eastern flank, for example, that might not be concerning since countries like Germany and France are rapidly boosting their military capabilities, he said.
But the US, too, would lose out by withdrawing troops, as its ability to project power across Europe would be reduced, experts say.
Senior members of Trump’s Republican Party have voiced concern about that.
The move could send “the wrong signal to [Russian President] Vladimir Putin,” Senators Roger Wicker and Representative Mike Rogers said in a joint statement after the troops from Germany started departing.
Why are relations souring between the US and Europe?
Since his first term, Trump has repeatedly accused European NATO members of forcing the US to carry most of the financial burden of the alliance. Last January, Trump said NATO countries should start spending 5 percent of their gross domestic product (GDP) on defence, rather than rely on US support, but many NATO members are still struggling to meet the current 2 percent target.
NATO members have already agreed to boost spending on defence to 3.5 percent of GDP by 2035.
Adding to Trump’s annoyance, however, has been the refusal of European countries to join the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran by allowing the US to use European bases. Some members, such as Spain and Italy, have actively spoken out against Washington’s war.
Another issue has been tariffs. The EU exports a large amount of its goods to the US, but Trump slapped a 15 percent tariff on European imports as part of his trade war last year.
Also in the last year, the EU and Washington faced off after Trump said the US wanted to acquire Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark positioned strategically in the Arctic and with untapped reserves of oil and other resources. Trump threatened European countries with additional trade tariffs if they stood in his way. He later dropped that threat and said he would not attempt to take Greenland by force.
On Friday, Trump announced that he had reached a new deal with Greenland and Denmark which would grant the US “permanent control over security and all other needs” in Greenland, suggesting it could provide the US with access to natural resources as well.
Are other US allies facing issues?
Taiwan, another traditional US defence partner, is also finding it harder to rely on Washington.
Since 1950, Taipei has depended on the US’s presence in the Pacific to deter a possible attack from China. However, Trump has made several comments that have put that relationship into question.
For example, in the run-up to the 2024 presidential elections, he said Taiwan should pay Washington for protection. He has also said Taiwan should “cool down” because the US would rather not have to go to war in the region.
As the war on Iran continues, the US has increasingly diverted military assets from the Pacific to the Iran conflict, raising concerns about Taiwan’s vulnerability. Most recently, the Trump administration redeployed its last aircraft carrier remaining in the Pacific to the Middle East to relieve the Abraham Lincoln, which had been at sea for months without a break.
The US has also appeared unwilling to support Saudi Arabia, with which it has security agreements, against Yemen’s Houthi militia, while US allies in the Gulf have all sustained severe damage to energy and military facilities from Iranian strikes against US assets.

The UN has documented more than a thousand cases of sexual violence since the beginning of the war in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
09:28:44 EEST
15:28:44 KST

The UN has documented more than a thousand cases of sexual violence since the beginning of the war in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The UN has documented 1,004 cases of sexual violence since the beginning of the full-scale war. 89% of the cases are attributed to the Russian authorities, and 11% to the Ukrainian authorities.
The UN Human Rights Office has documented more than a thousand cases of sexual violence since the beginning of russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This is stated in the Office’s report, UNN reports.
Details
During the reporting period, OHCHR documented 1,004 cases of sexual violence committed both in detention and outside it. Although representative, these data do not purport to provide a comprehensive overview of cases of sexual violence, which, as in other situations, are underreported in Ukraine
It is noted that the observed patterns indicate that sexual violence was used as a method of torture and other forms of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment against prisoners of war and civilians.
The majority of these cases verified by OHCHR—89%—are linked to the authorities of russia, including representatives of the Russian Armed Forces, the Federal Penitentiary Service and the Federal Security Service. 11% of the confirmed cases are attributed to the Ukrainian authorities, including servicemen of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the Security Service of Ukraine
The report states that in the occupied territories of Ukraine and within russia, the Russian authorities committed sexual violence against Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained civilians at all stages of captivity, including during capture, transfer, interrogation and detention.
The violations included gang rape, rape, mutilation of the genitals, and the use of electric shocks to men's genitals with a Soviet-era field telephone known as a "tapik." The findings were based on interviews with victims of sexual violence committed by both sides.
Most victims held in detention were men, including prisoners of war and detainees, although women and children also suffered, mainly in the territories of Ukraine occupied by russia. The youngest documented person to survive rape was a four-year-old girl, while the oldest was an 82-year-old woman.
In territory controlled by the Government of Ukraine, nearly half of the violations attributed to the Ukrainian authorities against Russian and third-country prisoners of war and detainees involved threats of sexual violence and beatings of the genitals; at the same time, no cases of Russian prisoners of war being raped by Ukrainian soldiers were documented.
Recall
russia has launched another stage of an information campaign aimed at discrediting international investigations and denying the war crimes of the russian army in Bucha.

The death toll from an explosion and gun attack at a police headquarters in northern Pakistan rose to at least 31, including 16 police personnel, a senior police official told AFP on Saturday, with fighting ongoing.
Terrorists stormed the Old Police Lines complex in Kohat, a town of around 220,000 people in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, targeting Friday prayer gathering near a mosque inside the police compound, where the explosion left a crater outside the mosque.
The police compound serves as a district-level police headquarters, housing key offices of the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD), Special Branch and several other police units.
"At least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, have been killed and more than 100 injured so far in the terror attack and suicide bombing," the official said.
"Several terrorists are still holed up in the Special Branch section of the Kohat Police Complex," the police official told AFP on condition of anonymity.
"An exchange of fire with them has been ongoing since late last night. Their exact number remains unclear," the official added.
A statement from the Kohat district health officer late on Friday said that more than 100 people had been injured, the vast majority of them police personnel, and several were in a critical condition.
Local terrorist group IMP, a faction linked to terror group of Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Rubble, blown-out walls
AFP images showed military personnel standing by piles of bricks, rubble and blown-out walls following the attack, with soldiers carrying assault rifles guarding the complex.
Several ambulances were seen lining a street near the police compound.
Pakistan has blamed the increase in attacks in KP and the southern border province of Balochistan on terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, where the Taliban government denies Afghan involvement.
The accusations have sparked a bitter rift and armed conflict between the neighbouring countries, with Pakistan carrying out deadly air strikes against terrorists who are using Afghan soil.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack on Friday evening, expressing "deep sorrow and regret over the injury of several people as a result of the blast".
He directed that "the best medical assistance be provided to the injured" and called for a report into the attack.
President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "regret" over the casualties, sending his "best wishes for the speedy recovery of those injured in the blast".
"The complete elimination of Fitna-al-Khawarij and terrorists operating with foreign backing is essential for national security," he said, using another term for the TTP terror group.

BNR Symphony orchestra conductor Konstantin Ilievsky: We are fighting to survive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:23:12 UTC
15:23:12 KST

Author
BNR team
News
Hunger strike at BNR! When will a solution be found for BNR’s musical ensembles?
BNR Symphony orchestra conductor Konstantin Ilievsky: We are fighting to survive
Saturday 19 September 2026 07:37
Saturday, 19 September 2026, 07:37
Symphony orchestra of the Bulgarian National Radio performing in Studio 1 of the BNR wearing reflective vests as sign of protest
PHOTO Ani Petrova
Font size
The musical ensembles of the Bulgarian National Radio have been protesting for more than a year over insufficient funding. Midway through the previous season, the Radio Symphony Orchestra suspended its concert activities and continued to work solely on recording projects.
BNR musicians halt concerts in protest over low pay
This week it became clear that the musicians are no longer prepared to wait indefinitely for politicians to find a solution.
First came the news that Galina Koycheva, the orchestra’s concertmaster, was leaving. A little later came an even more alarming announcement:
BNR orchestra violinist announces hunger strike over low pay
“My name is Iva Djadjeva, and I am a musician with the BNR Symphony Orchestra. After a year and a half of agony, I have taken the extreme step of declaring a hunger strike, because our orchestra is falling apart and we simply have no options left. We are desperate. We are pleading for attention!”
We have been forced to resort to these extreme measures, said composer and pianist Antoni Donchev, who served as conductor of the BNR Big Band until July this year.
“This is a problem that has been dragging on for many years, namely insufficient funding, particularly for the musical ensembles of the Bulgarian National Radio, as well as for BNR as a whole."
Slav Slavchev, solo oboist with the Radio Orchestra, outlined the musicians’ demands:
“An additional one-off allocation of €350,000 for BNR’s musical ensembles in the BNR budget for 2026. We would also like to see the Bulgarian National Radio’s budget for 2027 increased by BGN 2 million compared with the 2026 budget, with the funds earmarked exclusively for the sustainable financing and development of BNR’s musical ensembles and the gradual resolution of the structural problems that have accumulated over the years. This comes in the context of the anticipated amendments to the Radio and Television Act, which would change the status of the ensembles and establish a sustainable model for their continued existence. We genuinely expect the draft law to be submitted for public consultation by the end of September, so that we can find out what the new rules for funding public service media will actually be.”
BNR Director General Milen Mitev was adamant that one-off, stopgap measures are not viable solutions. He, too, is counting on the necessary legislative amendments being adopted by the end of September.
“The problem of the extremely low pay of musicians at the National Radio, which is part of the broader problem of inadequate funding for public service media in Bulgaria, is not a recent one. It is a problem that has existed for many years and, unfortunately, has been growing steadily and inexorably worse over time.
At present, a working group at the Ministry of Culture is nearing completion of a proposal for amendments to the Radio and Television Act. One of the envisaged changes is to regulate the status of the National Radio’s musical ensembles, define their activities and include those activities as part of BNR’s work eligible for public funding.
If this bill is adopted, it will make it possible for BNR’s future budgets to be drawn up in a way that also incorporates the activities of its musical ensembles. In my view, this is the right course of action because it will establish a lasting framework for these relations.Short-term solutions involving one-off transfers can always be implemented, but we are seeking a long-term solution. I believe that both the Ministry of Culture and the National Assembly’s Committee on Culture and Media, which are aware of this problem, will find a way to accelerate the process, including through short-term measures that would allow us to wait for the legislative changes that have been discussed and prepared for so long to finally become a reality.
The Ministry of Culture is striving to present the bill for public consultation and subsequent adoption by September 30, so that this change can be enshrined in law.”
In an interview for BNR's Horizon channel, Konstantin Ilievsky, chief conductor of the BNR Symphony Orchestra, said that the musicians were deeply concerned:
Conductor Konstantin Ilievsky
PHOTO Ani Petrova
“I think it is clear to everyone that what happened, namely the declaration of a hunger strike, is truly an absolutely extreme measure. Personally, I was extremely surprised because this is an outright last resort, signalling to the entire public that our situation is genuinely dire, and has been for a very long time.
We have been waiting for a solution to our problem for more than a year and a half. And, as I understand it, this is a problem that goes back many years, even before I joined BNR as chief conductor of the Symphony Orchestra.
Three governments have come and gone. We have been repeatedly assured and promised that work was under way to address our situation. But the fact remains that, to this day, our situation is becoming increasingly difficult.”
We are fighting for survival, Maestro Ilievsky stressed, explaining:
“For us, this is not about fighting for some exceptionally luxurious or comfortable life as people working in the arts. We are simply fighting to survive. With the salaries they receive here, my colleagues cannot afford to live in the capital, especially younger musicians who are planning or already have families and children. Some may come from outside Sofia, yet they are exceptionally talented musicians whom we need to attract to this elite ensemble and retain here. They simply cannot make ends meet. Once they have paid their rent, they have no money left for food.”
According to Ilievski, the average salary in BNR’s orchestras is well below €1,000.
“A young colleague who is left with around €700 after all deductions genuinely has no chance of making ends meet.”
In his view, the financial dimension of the problem is becoming increasingly serious and has now reached a point where it can no longer be contained.
The problem affects more than 200 people, and that number is declining as some musicians leave, Ilievski said, stressing that it is also becoming increasingly difficult to recruit new musicians.
“If our problem is not resolved, I am unfortunately afraid that the situation will continue to deteriorate.”

Harrods seeks to recover abuse compensation costs from Mohamed Al Fayed’s estate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:23:11 UTC
15:23:11 KST

Harrods is seeking to recover the cost of the compensation paid to hundreds of women allegedly sexually abused by Mohamed Al Fayed from his estate, the Guardian understands.
The luxury department store is seeking full indemnity from the late billionaire’s estate for any settlements it is required to pay, according to evidence seen by the Guardian.
Survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse said the retailer’s plan to recover its compensation costs was distressing and at odds with its public acceptance of responsibility.
Lucy Traynor, a senior associate at KP Law, which represents the majority of known survivors, said: “Harrods publicly says that it accepts responsibility for the abuse suffered by survivors. However, its lawyers have confirmed that Harrods intends to seek a full indemnity from Mohamed Al Fayed’s estate for any compensation it is required to pay.
“If successful, that would mean Harrods recovering the entirety of those compensation payments from the estate and bearing no ultimate financial consequence itself. Its present position is that, despite its statements about accepting responsibility, it intends to seek recovery from the estate of every pound it pays in compensation.”
Traynor said Harrods’ intention to fully indemnify itself was “difficult to reconcile with its public statements about institutional responsibility and accountability”.
She said the allegations concerning Harrods went beyond “Al Fayed as an individual who owned the business”.
“Survivors have raised serious questions about the environment in which this was able to happen, the role of others within the organisation, what was known or ought to have been known, and whether institutional structures facilitated or failed to prevent his conduct,” she said.
If Harrods were successful, the claims of survivors who were only seeking compensation from the estate could be affected, Traynor said.
“Any attempt by Harrods to recover substantial sums from the estate could reduce the assets available to meet those survivors’ claims.”
In a statement, Harrods said: “Our priority is to ensure all eligible survivors receive compensation for abuses perpetrated by Fayed, and Harrods continue to settle claims.”
The store has previously accepted “vicarious liability” for the sexual abuse allegedly perpetrated by Fayed, and condemned it.
Earlier this week, KP Law said compensation claims against Harrods and the estate by 275 of the survivors it represents could reach up to £150m.
Fayed, who died aged 94 in 2023, has been accused of rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking from 1977 to 2014. Survivors claim that Harrods did not adequately address the allegations for years.
Two years ago, Harrods opened an investigation into whether any of its current staff were “directly or indirectly involved” in the alleged sexual abuse of women by Fayed. An employee had left the business in 2025 in relation to that investigation, the store later said.
The retailer created its own compensation scheme for survivors last year, which closed to new claims in March. Its latest accounts showed it had paid out £4.1m from the £57m it set aside for compensation in 2025. The store added that it had made settlements with 113 women to date, but did not disclose the total amount paid.
In 2023 the Sunday Times reported that Fayed’s fortune was £1.69bn, making him the fourth richest person in Scotland at that time.
Last year, Harrods made a passing-over application (POA) to appoint special executors to administer Fayed’s estate, replacing family members. The department store said this was necessary to protect assets and to ensure the estate could pay compensation “in a timely and appropriate manner”. A high court hearing is scheduled for November.
Harrods’ statement added: “To our knowledge, the Fayed estate has not publicly acknowledged abuses, nor apologised or settled a single claim. The POA seeks the appointment of an independent executor to administer claims against the estate, therefore, any financial recovery for compensation to survivors of Fayed’s abuses remains a number of legal steps away.”
Shanta Sundarason, who says she was sexually assaulted by Fayed in his office when she worked as a designer at Harrods, said the store’s plan to recover the costs of compensation was “deeply disturbing”.
“My abuse did not happen in some separate world belonging only to Mohamed Al Fayed. Harrods was not simply the backdrop to what happened to me, it was the environment in which I was recruited, selected, controlled and ultimately abused,” she said.
“Harrods cannot tell me that it accepts institutional responsibility for what happened to me, while simultaneously seeking to ensure that the institution ultimately bears none of the financial consequence. For me, accountability is not simply writing a cheque and then recovering every penny from someone else.
“What happened to me was not simply the act of one individual. My abuse existed within a system. From Mohamed Al Fayed’s security detail and office staff to management and the structures surrounding him, it took more than one person to create an environment in which abuse could occur and remain hidden.”
A former employee named Catherine, who says she was sexually abused by Fayed when she worked as his personal assistant between 1990 and 1991, described Harrods’ plan to recover compensation costs from the estate as “truly sickening”.
“Harrods have stated that they are sorry but [are] doing everything they can to escape paying anything and it’s simply not right,” she said.
The estate was approached for comment.

Trump signs into law sweeping Russia sanctions package aiming to choke off revenues funding the war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:20:40 UTC
15:20:40 KST

The bill received widespread opposition from Democrat lawmakers, who favoured tougher sanctions on Russia, but opposed provisions in the draft which would enable Trump to impose tariffs freely on nations that continue to buy large amounts of Russian energy.
US President Donald Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russian officials and key pillars of its economy on Friday, that is meant to punish and pressure Moscow for its ongoing war against Ukraine.
The measure was a final legacy item for the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a close ally and friend of the president who had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July.
In the works for more than a year, the bill passed with large bipartisan margins; 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House.
It’s meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbour in February 2022.
The bill, co-drafted by Senator Richard Blumenthal, sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers the Kremlin uses to evade existing Western sanctions and keep Russian energy moving.
“I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day. I know he would be so proud. Lindsey believed this bill, which he worked on for well over a year, would help end the war through squeezing Putin economically and forcing his customers to re-evaluate their relationship with Russia,” said Senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham's sister, in a statement Friday.
Darline Graham was appointed to complete her late brother's Senate term, set to end on the 3rd of January 2027.
“If he were here today, he would be jubilant about our bill’s passage — and already thinking about the next one,” Blumenthal said of Graham after the House passed the legislation on Wednesday evening.
“Putin is a thug who understands only force and strength, which is what we must show clearly and unequivocally,” Blumenthal added.
The bill also enables Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Despite overwhelming support on Capitol Hill, the legislation faced criticism from a vocal set of Democratic lawmakers, who favoured a tougher stance on Russia, but warned that Trump could use his new expanded tariff powers to impose fresh levies in the European Union and elsewhere.
“Why in the world would this Congress or the People’s House give this president unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?” said Democrat lawmaker and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Graham’s journey to getting Trump’s sign-off on the bill had been full of turbulence, as the White House had to be convinced that the president would be able to retain sufficient flexibility on sanctions.
Eventually, Trump gave a final nod of approval to the bill after it included his push for a provision which would enable his administration to extend sanctions on Iran for another five-year period.

Herzog's stance on Netanyahu's pardon raises possibility of compromise if election ends in deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:18:41 UTC
15:18:41 KST

President Isaac Herzog said on Wednesday that his considerations on whether a pardon could serve as leverage on the way to a unity government were "solely substantive." He said that before deciding on any pardon request, he had proposed mediation under the auspices of the President’s Residence, and that he believes Netanyahu’s trial should end through an agreement and plea deal.
According to Herzog, the prime minister has not yet responded to the mediation proposal, and he continues to leave that possibility open. Political figures have raised a scenario in which, if neither side has 61 seats and Herzog is determined to prevent another election cycle, ideas for a unity government and a rotation arrangement could return to the table.
Pardon issue enters broader political discussions
Some have raised, as a possible scenario, the idea that the pardon issue could emerge as part of a broader discussion on a political compromise. Sources close to Herzog declined to address that possibility and emphasized that consideration of the pardon issue is being conducted solely on substantive grounds.
The issue is being discussed against the backdrop of the possibility that another election could end without a clear outcome. In that case, the President’s Residence could become one of the central arenas in efforts to break the deadlock. Herzog has already said he will do everything possible to prevent another round of elections and has indicated that he intends to use the discretion available to him to help establish a stable government.
In interviews on Wednesday, Herzog said, "I will do everything so that there will not be repeat elections, and that a stable government will be established in Israel." Regarding the possibility of bringing political figures together and pushing for the formation of a unity government, he added: "I have a wide set of tools; the discretion is broad." Herzog declined to specify which framework he would support.
Sources close to Herzog said that while the president’s powers in the government formation process are defined by law, the legislation does not address every detail of the process and therefore leaves the president with broad discretion. According to officials at the President’s Residence, court rulings and precedents are binding, and the central question remains who can form a government. However, within that framework, the president retains flexibility in the way he manages the process.
Past presidents intervened during political deadlocks
The extent of Herzog’s room for action would ultimately depend on the election results and the political landscape that emerges afterward. There are precedents for such discretion. In 2019, after the 22nd Knesset elections, then-president Reuven Rivlin brought together Benjamin Netanyahu and Benny Gantz and worked to promote a unity government. He proposed an equal government structure and changes to the arrangements surrounding incapacity and the position of acting prime minister in an effort to resolve the political impasse.
An earlier precedent appears in the memoirs of Israel’s sixth president, Chaim Herzog, who described how he acted after the 1984 elections to advance a unity government between the Alignment and Likud.
"I had to try to bring together the different elements rather than allow the dynamics of events to lead to the development of a dangerous split," he wrote.
When the deadlock continued, Herzog granted Shimon Peres additional time to form a government. Later, when negotiations reached an impasse, he wrote that he "acted to establish a small negotiating team," including representatives from Likud and the Labor Party. Days later, Peres and Yitzhak Shamir’s unity government was presented, built around a rotation agreement.
The precedents of Chaim Herzog and Rivlin do not indicate how the current president would act if a deadlock emerged after the elections, but they show that the President’s Residence has previously served not only as a formal stop for receiving recommendations and assigning the mandate to form a government. Presidents have attempted, under different circumstances and with different tools, to help political parties reach agreements when the political system struggled to do so on its own.
The reason the scenario is already occupying the political system lies in the coalition map. Possible paths to forming a government without Netanyahu could involve various combinations of Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman and the Democrats, while other scenarios could require Haredi parties to join or some form of reliance on Arab parties.
These possibilities are not politically identical, and some involve significant gaps between potential partners. Coalition figures estimate that Netanyahu may view this complexity as a reason to believe that even if his opponents succeed in forming a government, it would face significant internal tensions, similar to those experienced by the previous change government.
The conscription law could add another difficulty of its own. Sources familiar with contacts involving Haredi parties said they have heard from Haredi officials about the possibility that at least some factions would prefer to remain in the opposition until the issue is resolved. They stressed that there could be differences on this matter between Shas and United Torah Judaism.
Under such a scenario, Haredi parties could initially remain outside both blocs, making government formation even more difficult.

Gemini hacked three companies in first known breakout by Google's AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:18:18 UTC
15:18:18 KST

Google's GOOGL.O Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, the first known example of the company's AI systems autonomously committing such an act.
The hacks occurred in May during a cybersecurity test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations.
During a standard testing evaluation, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said in a statement.
"We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes," Adkins said. "These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly."
An Irregular spokesperson said the incident involved the same issue that affected other AI labs and that all relevant labs were notified in late July. "All known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago," the spokesperson said.
Other AI companies have had similar crises
Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed similar incidents linked to Irregular. Meta said in August the incident did not involve a sandbox escape or sophisticated cyberattack, while Irregular said it was working on best practices for securely conducting AI cybersecurity evaluations.
The incidents have raised questions about the safeguards needed as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to the internet and computer systems.
In one of the cases, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to then access protected systems, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the news on Friday.
Adkins said that in all three instances, the model ceased its hacking.

Trump to personally meet Xi at military base: White House unveils state visit program
Kyiv • UNN
Donald Trump will personally meet Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews on September 23. The following day, the leaders will hold talks and a state dinner.
U.S. President Donald Trump will personally greet Chinese President Xi Jinping upon his arrival in Washington, and the following day the leaders will hold bilateral talks and attend a state dinner. The White House has released a detailed program for the Chinese leader's state visit, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, will arrive in the United States on Wednesday, September 23. Their plane will land at Joint Base Andrews near Washington.
Trump will personally greet the Chinese leader at the airport. An official arrival ceremony will also take place there, which, Bloomberg notes, is rare practice for a military base.
Talks and state dinner
The main events are scheduled for September 24. Trump will greet Xi and Peng Liyuan at the White House, after which the presidents will attend a military review in the Rose Garden and hold a bilateral meeting.
In the evening, Donald and Melania Trump will host the Chinese leader and his wife at a state dinner in the East Room of the White House. At the beginning of the event, Trump and Xi will deliver speeches. The heads of major technology and financial companies are expected to be among the guests.
Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan will also hold a separate event in Washington, although the White House has not yet disclosed its details.
On September 25, Trump and the U.S. first lady will invite Xi and his wife for tea at the White House. After that, they will visit the National Archives, where the Chinese leader will be shown the United States' founding documents.
After the program concludes, Xi Jinping and Peng Liyuan will head to Andrews Air Force Base to depart the United States.

Latvian defence technology companies meet German industry leaders in Berlin

2026-09-19
06:17:10 UTC

During a trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), Latvian defence and dual-use technology companies met leading German defence companies, industry organisations and a representative of the German Federal Ministry of Defence in Berlin. Members of the delegation, led by Latvian Minister for Economics Viktors Valainis, presented their solutions and discussed opportunities to join German companies’ supply chains, jointly develop technologies and expand production.
The programme focusing on defence and dual-use technologies began on 16 September with an event dedicated to cooperation between the Latvian and German defence industries, organised in partnership with the German Security and Defence Industry Association (BDSV).
“Industrial cooperation between Latvia and Germany is becoming increasingly close. In the first half of 2026, Latvia’s exports of goods to Germany grew by 10%, while exports of machinery, mechanical appliances and electrical equipment increased by EUR 34.3 million. This also represents the manufacturing base on which Latvia’s defence industry can grow. Our companies can supply electronic components, unmanned systems, military vehicles, metal structures and other solutions needed to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities. The priority now is to involve Latvian companies more extensively in German and European supply chains, joint technology development and manufacturing,” Minister for Economics Viktors Valainis said.
Latvian business representatives met the leadership of BDSV, German defence companies and a representative of the German Federal Ministry of Defence to discuss industry priorities, upcoming procurements and opportunities for cooperation.
Direct talks with the German defence industry
During an in-depth industry session, Rheinmetall, HENSOLDT, Rohde & Schwarz and Quantum Systems presented their expertise and opportunities for cooperation. Discussions focused on expanding defence production and supply chains, sensors, electronic warfare and counter-unmanned aerial system solutions, secure communications and autonomous systems.
Latvia’s defence technology ecosystem was presented to German partners by Artis Pabriks, Executive Director of the Military Technology, Drone and Robotics Association MilTech Latvia, and Jānis Atslēns, a representative of the Federation of Security and Defence Industries of Latvia.
“As Ambassador, security is one of my main priorities in relations between Latvia and Germany. We cooperate both bilaterally and as NATO and EU partners. Germany is one of the world’s leading military industry countries, and Latvia has excellent opportunities to develop closer cooperation with the German defence industry. We have highly qualified specialists and innovative companies capable of adapting to changing industry conditions. Trust and close professional contacts form the foundation of this type of long-term cooperation. The Embassy will continue to actively support Latvian companies by helping them establish new contacts, strengthen their presence in the German market and become part of the European defence industry’s supply chains,” said Ilze Rūse, Latvia’s Ambassador to Germany.
Focus on unmanned and autonomous systems
On 17 September, Latvian and German companies, industry organisations and public-sector representatives participated in a round-table discussion on unmanned aerial vehicles and counter-UAV technologies, autonomous systems, robotics, artificial intelligence, secure communications, electronics and the resilience of defence supply chains. The event was organised by LIAA in cooperation with Berlin’s economic development agency Berlin Partner and MilTech Latvia.
Participants were introduced to the Latvian and Berlin defence technology ecosystems, while Latvian and German companies presented their solutions. The discussions explored specific areas for cooperation, including component supplies, systems integration, joint product development, technology testing and manufacturing.
“Economic cooperation between Latvia and Germany already has a solid foundation, with more than 1,000 German-owned companies operating in Latvia. In the defence industry, Latvian companies must now demonstrate their ability to meet specific technical, quality and delivery requirements. In Berlin, they had an opportunity to discuss these matters with potential partners and determine what steps are necessary to qualify as suppliers. Following the mission, LIAA will continue working on the most promising cooperation opportunities, advancing them towards technology testing, supplier qualification and cooperation agreements,” said Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of LIAA’s Export and Innovation Services Department.
Berlin is strengthening its position on Europe’s defence and security technology map. The city is home to approximately 130 companies specialising in security and defence, as well as more than 400 companies whose technologies can be used for both civilian and military purposes. The Berlin Senate is also developing a dedicated defence technology ecosystem to forge closer links between companies, researchers, investors and public-sector customers.
The delegation also visited Andres Industries AG, a Berlin-based company that develops and manufactures thermal imaging and night-vision technologies for armed forces, police and other security institutions.
Latvian companies offer technologies and manufacturing capacity
The Latvian delegation of defence and dual-use technology companies included ALMIKO, Daugavpils Lokomotīvju Remonta Rūpnīca, Electrify, EMJ Metāls, HansaMatrix, Latvia Packing, VOLBURG, VORX and VR Cars.
The delegation’s offering encompasses printed circuit board and electronics manufacturing, metalworking and the production of armoured structures, military ammunition packaging, materials for large-format 3D printing, military vehicles and unmanned ground platforms. In Germany, Latvian companies are seeking systems integrators, customers, manufacturing partners and opportunities to participate in German and broader European defence projects.
For example, Electrify presented the Latvian-developed Rocky6 electric unmanned ground platform in Berlin. It is designed to transport cargo and specialised equipment across difficult terrain, perform reconnaissance, evacuate casualties, and integrate communications and counter-UAV systems. The platform has a payload capacity of up to 1,200 kilograms and an electric range of up to 150 kilometres.
“Latvian defence technology companies offer their German partners a powerful combination of flexibility, engineering expertise and solutions tailored to real operational needs. At DK NEJET, we develop software-defined defence technologies, ranging from high-speed interceptors and navigation in GPS-denied environments to drone-swarm coordination. We combine engineering development, manufacturing and operator training within a single ecosystem. Combined with Germany’s industrial capacity, this creates a solid foundation for the rapid deployment of field-tested and cost-effective European defence solutions,” said DK NEJET co-founder Olga Provotar, emphasising the importance of participating in LIAA’s trade mission to Germany.
Trade mission covers several technology sectors
The Latvian business trade mission to Germany, organised by LIAA, took place from 14 to 17 September. It brought together 53 Latvian companies and organisations representing information and communication technologies, financial technologies, life sciences, and defence and dual-use technologies. The programme was organised by sector, combining company visits and joint events with individual business meetings.
Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states. Since 2020, Latvia’s exports of goods and services to Germany have grown by more than 40%, rising from EUR 1.47 billion to approximately EUR 2.1 billion in 2025. Last year, Latvia exported more to Germany alone than to the United States, France and China combined.
Growth has continued this year: in the first half of 2026, exports to Germany increased by 11%, while Latvia’s total exports grew by 6%. Germany is also Latvia’s largest market for service exports, which reached EUR 779 million in 2025. More than 1,000 German-owned companies operate in Latvia, with their combined investments in share capital exceeding EUR 800 million.
LIAA organises participation in international trade missions under the European Union co-financed programme for the development of innovative entrepreneurship among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), supported by funding from the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget. Companies may participate in trade missions either for a fee or by receiving support to cover eligible costs.

Economic Watch: AI takes spotlight at China-ASEAN Expo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:14:48 CST
15:14:48 KST

People visit the sales area of AI-related products during the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 18, 2026. AI-related products have taken center stage at the ongoing 23rd China-ASEAN Expo, which attracts more than 3,400 companies from China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and beyond. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming)
NANNING, China, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- When Vietnamese visitor Doan Minh Thao stepped into an exhibition hall of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo here on Friday, he got interested in an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered eyewear that can provide real-time translation in over 40 languages, including Vietnamese.
With the help of this gadget, developed by a Chinese company, he managed to have unimpeded verbal communication with exhibitors at the venue.
AI-related products including these smart glasses have taken center stage at the ongoing Expo, which attracts more than 3,400 companies from China, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and beyond.
FROM CONCEPT TO REAL BUSINESS
"Last year, AI was mostly for show. This year, it is driving sales," said Wang Jicai, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Expo Secretariat.
In exhibition halls situated in the downtown area of this southern Chinese city, embodied AI robots, exoskeleton medical equipment and AI-enabled wearables attracted crowds of curious visitors, while unattended coffee booths and ice cream stands served customers with nimble robotic arms.
As some companies display fancy hardware at the Expo, others showcase AI-driven systems for sectors ranging from finance, healthcare, transportation and agriculture to production management and water treatment.
China and ASEAN, trading partners that saw bilateral trade volume top 1 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025, have been organizing this major trade and investment event for more than two decades. And for this year's Expo, which runs from Sept. 17 to 21, special emphasis was placed on the AI sector.
According to organizers, the Expo's "AI marketplace" features about 500 products from more than 70 companies, allowing visitors to test and buy products on-site.
In the meantime, a China-ASEAN AI application cooperation center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential AI scenarios, set up offices in Vietnam, Laos and Malaysia, and backed over 30 cross-border projects.
AI ENABLES BROADER COOPERATION
"What inspires me most is seeing that AI is not limited to the technology sector. It can also serve as an enabler for education, healthcare, tourism, industry, public services, agriculture and the development of economic zones," said Dyah Wahyu Ermawati, director of investment and integrated license services office of Indonesia's East Java province.
"There are very broad opportunities for cooperation," the Indonesian official said to Xinhua Thursday when attending the 2nd China-ASEAN AI Scenario Application Matchmaking Session organized in Nanning alongside the Expo.
China and ASEAN, already each other's biggest trading partner, are seeking to strengthen and upgrade cooperation in a wide range of sectors. The progress in digital technologies including AI has facilitated cooperation and enhanced efficiency.
In Laos and Cambodia, for example, a platform developed by local partners together with an enterprise from China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region has started to use satellite imagery, drones and ground sensors to optimize tropical crop cultivation.
Apart from precision agriculture, cooperation in AI applications can also include fields like smart logistics, manufacturing automation, financial technology, urban management and cross-border e-commerce, according to exhibitors and seminar speakers at the Expo.
AI BRINGS GREAT OPPORTUNITIES
As China and ASEAN advance high-quality economic cooperation under the framework of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, signed in October 2025, AI has emerged as a new frontier for win-win cooperation.
During a China-ASEAN business and investment summit held here on Thursday, a collection of case studies on China-ASEAN AI cooperation was released, showcasing a range of practical achievements.
The cases include 31 practical AI cooperation projects between China and ASEAN, covering all 11 ASEAN member states and sectors such as infrastructure, intelligent manufacturing and smart logistics.
"I think there's a lot of optimism that we will be benefiting from this collaboration with AI," Secretary-General of ASEAN Kao Kim Hourn said to reporters Thursday on the sidelines of the Expo. It is not only for the economic sector; it cuts across all sectors of the society, he said.
The secretary-general said there are great opportunities to capitalize on the potential of AI and the digital sector. Regarding AI cooperation, he called for adequate rules and regulations and advised against stifling innovation and creativity. ■

Austrian parliament speaker calls for mutual learning, fair cooperation between Europe, China

VIENNA, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Europe should abandon an anxious mindset toward China's development and instead pursue mutual learning and fair cooperation, said Walter Rosenkranz, president of Austria's National Council, or the lower house of Parliament.
In an interview with Xinhua, Rosenkranz said China has achieved leaps and bounds in many fields, notably in renewable energy. "The EU and China must continue to deepen their cooperation while operating within a framework of fair rules," he said.
European national legislatures, he said, should take the initiative to build fair and reasonable frameworks for cooperation, helping various sectors in Europe and China eliminate perceptual biases, deepen practical cooperation, and achieve complementary strengths and common development.
Noting that he recently led a delegation to China, which was his first visit to the country since taking office as president of the National Council, Rosenkranz said Austrian political parties share broad consensus and a strong willingness to deepen exchanges with China.
During the visit, the delegation not only experienced China's long and profound history and culture, but also witnessed the vitality of China's modernization drive, he said.
This year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Austria. Rosenkranz said friendship between the two countries has been deepening since the establishment of diplomatic ties.
Since the 1990s, there have been more than 60 exchanges between the national legislative bodies, Rosenkranz said.
Looking back on the 55-year history of exchanges, Rosenkranz said Austria and China cherish peace, consistently uphold multilateralism and the norms of international law, and remain committed to promoting peace through cooperation and pursuing development through win-win outcomes.
The two countries share compatible development concepts and have long worked together under the framework of the United Nations to contribute to world peace and development, while deepening cooperation in multiple fields, including the economy and culture, with fruitful results, he said.
More than 650 Austrian companies are currently operating in China, fully demonstrating the strong vitality of Austria-China cooperation, he added.
Rosenkranz said the current international situation is marked by intertwined changes and turbulence, with challenges such as climate change, artificial intelligence governance and regional conflicts emerging one after another. The legislative bodies of Austria and China could further deepen dialogue and cooperation, build consensus on governance, improve cooperation rules, and contribute wisdom and strength to addressing global issues.
Looking to the future, Rosenkranz regards young people as the main force of future cooperation and the inheritors and promoters of friendship between the two countries.
Deeper youth and cultural exchanges, he added, could strengthen the foundation of people-to-people ties and give the friendly strategic partnership between the two countries fresh momentum.■

Switzerland has changed its national security strategy because of Russia’s war against Ukraine and hybrid threats

Switzerland has changed its national security strategy because of Russia’s war against Ukraine and hybrid threats
Kyiv • UNN
Switzerland has approved a security strategy with 10 objectives and 46 measures. The country will prepare for hybrid attacks and a possible armed assault.
Switzerland has adopted a new national security strategy that provides for strengthening the country's defense capabilities amid Russia's war against Ukraine, cyberattacks, and other hybrid threats. The document contains 10 goals and 46 specific measures, Anadolu Agency reports, writes UNN.
Details
The Swiss Federal Council stated that the international security situation is becoming increasingly unstable due to rivalry among major powers, armed conflicts, and the weakening of the international order.
The document paid particular attention to Russia's aggression against Ukraine. The Swiss government noted that an end to the war is not yet in sight, while the number of cyberattacks, influence operations, and other hybrid threats is increasing.
Switzerland will prepare for a possible armed attack
The strategy identifies three main areas – increasing the resilience of the state, economy, and society; protecting the population and critical infrastructure; and strengthening the country's defense capabilities.
The government considers hybrid and remote attacks, as well as organized crime activities, to be the most likely threats. At the same time, Switzerland must be capable of effectively countering an armed attack as well.
To this end, the country plans to create the necessary military capabilities in advance and expand cooperation with partner states.
Implementation of the strategy will be coordinated by the State Secretariat for Security Policy. The Federal Council is to receive a report on the implementation of the planned measures by the end of 2028.

The US nearly started a war with China over an erroneous AI-generated report – CNN
Kyiv • UNN
The US prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel based on a false report about a nuclear cargo. The AI error was discovered before the operation began.
In the spring, U.S. military personnel prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel based on an intelligence report claiming that the ship was carrying components for a nuclear program. Shortly before the operation began, it was discovered that the analyst had prepared the document using artificial intelligence, which had misidentified the cargo, CNN reports, citing sources, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred in the spring amid the war with Iran. An intelligence report circulated among U.S. military personnel contained information about a Chinese vessel in the Middle East that was allegedly carrying components linked to a nuclear weapons program.
The information was taken so seriously that the U.S. military began planning to intercept the ship. According to CNN sources, armed U.S. service members were preparing to board it, while military aircraft were already in the air.
The error was discovered before the operation began
Only shortly before the planned interception did officials decide to examine in greater detail the report prepared by an analyst from the U.S. Special Operations Command.
It then emerged that artificial intelligence had been used in preparing the document, and that the chatbot had incorrectly identified the materials being carried by the Chinese vessel. CNN was unable to establish what was actually on board.
According to one of the network's sources, the report about the cargo was "completely false."
This nearly started a war
The U.S. military operation against the Chinese vessel could have caused a serious escalation in relations between Washington and Beijing and potentially developed into an armed confrontation between the two countries.
