Gemini hacked 3 companies in first known breakout by Google’s AI
Google’s Gemini model accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities, the first known example of the company’s AI systems autonomously committing such an act.
The hacks occurred in May during a test conducted by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity evaluations.
During a standard evaluation, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Google’s vice-president of security engineering Heather Adkins said in a statement.
In one of the cases, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system.
In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to access protected systems, according to The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the news on Sept 18.
Adkins said that in all three instances, the model ceased its hacking when it realised it had accessed real companiess.
“We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes,” she said. 
“These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”
An Irregular spokesperson said the incident involved the same issue that affected other AI labs and that all relevant labs were notified in late July.
“All known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago,” the spokesperson said.
Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed similar incidents linked to Irregular. 
Meta said in August that the incident did not involve a sandbox escape or sophisticated cyberattack, while Irregular said it was working on best practices for securely conducting AI cybersecurity evaluations.
The incidents have raised questions about the safeguards needed as AI agents gain greater autonomy and access to the internet and computer systems. REUTERS

President Donald Trump on Friday announced an agreement with Greenland and Denmark that gives the U.S. what he described as "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the Danish island territory.
"We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many," Trump said in a Truth Social post.
Greenland already has a U.S. military presence under a decades-old defense agreement with Denmark.
The deal as described in Trump's post appears to stop far short of his prior insistence that Greenland must be made a part of the United States.
Greenland has maintained it is not for sale, and the European Union earlier this year united to rebuke Trump over his push to acquire the island.
But Trump signaled Friday that he was satisfied by the new deal, claiming that it addresses "ALL of our many U.S. concerns."
"There will be NO COST to the United States," he wrote.
The Danish prime minister's office in a press release later Friday said that the three governments expect to sign the agreement at the United Nations General Assembly next week.
Greenland Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in an included statement that the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area and therefore is great for NATO and Europe as well."
He added that it "recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination."
"We welcome the announcement that an agreement will soon be signed by the United States, Denmark, and Greenland," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said in a statement. "The Arctic and the North Atlantic are essential for our collective security, and this agreement will help advance security, stability, and cooperation in this vital region. NATO will continue to do its part to strengthen security in the Arctic."
Trump's post included some vague claims about the agreement, including that it guarantees that the U.S. "will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland."
The official text of any deal was not immediately available. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information on the deal.

====================================================================================================

Maths doesn't add up for Australian parents juggling work and school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:22:05 UTC
08:22:05 KST

The lost time of modern parenthood
Australian families are living in work, school and care systems designed for another era. And the math ain't mathing.
Morning scramble. Uniform. Lunch box. Breakfast. Hair. Teeth. Socks. Socks! Drop off. Commute to work. Work. Pick-up. After school sport. The assemblies. The parades. The homework. The appointments. The pings of parent WhatsApp groups. The bottomless laundry basket. The shopping. The dinner. The never-ending list of unpaid work. The endless worry and guilt.
When it comes to working and being a modern-day parent, the juggle is real.
If we look back to family life in the 1960s, or even the 1990s, so much has changed.
In most two-parent families these days, both parents are employed, but the work and school systems are largely set up for a bygone era.
"The maths does not add up," says Kate Harrison Brennan, director of the Sydney Policy Lab at The University of Sydney.
To help us put the numbers in context and talk about real solutions, alongside Dr Harrison Brennan we've enlisted these experts:
- Elizabeth Hill from The University of Sydney Department of Political Economy
- Georgie Dent, CEO of advocacy organisation The Parenthood
- Lyndall Strazdins from the ANU National Centre of Epidemiology and Population Health
- Rowena Ditzell, lecturer at the University of Technology Sydney
So with the introductions out of the way, let's do some rough sums.
The maths
Parents can feel like there aren't enough hours in the day. And when you stop to work out just how much overlap there is between the hours that your children need you, and the hours that you're expected to devote to work, it's easy to see why.
We know that every family arrangement is different.
Let's assume there are two parents at home, and both parents work full-time.
We're going to look specifically at parents of primary school-aged children and compare the average work year with the average school year.
7.5 hours per week
Is the gap between the full-time work week and average primary school hours.
Read more
School often starts about 9am and finishes between 3pm and 3:30pm. The traditional full-time work day is 9am to 5pm or 8 hours. Assuming school finishes at 3:30pm, that's 300 hours per year parents need to find across the 40-week school year.
"What becomes immediately obvious for any parent in the first week of their child being at school is that suddenly there is a cliff when you get to 2 something in the afternoon … and kids need to get picked up," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
After-school care is often relied upon to cover the gap, but that's if parents can afford it. It gets expensive if you have multiple children.
And many people don't have access to it at all.
"I'd say you're part of a lucky one in five in Australia," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
"The reality is: places in subsidised after-school-hours care are incredibly concentrated in Australia's major cities."
"The gap between care and work, and school hours and work hours, isn't an inconvenience; it's a structural tax that parents, most often mums, pay every single day," says The Parenthood CEO Georgie Dent.
The average daily commute is 52 minutes, or about 56 minutes in capital cities. On average, Australians spend 3.8 hours commuting to work each week, which is about 182 hours per year.
While many Australians are now able to work from home, or work a hybrid arrangement, most Australian workers still commute to work.
"For those who work at a distance from their workplace and from their school drop-off, the degree of difficulty in completing that task every day, five days a week, for four terms a year is really, really high," Professor Hill says.
The COVID-19 pandemic did make working from home much more common.
It's one of the things that's made the workplace happier for many women, Dr Strazdins says.
"They're finding that time by cutting back on a commute from work, from home and dovetailing tasks a bit better," she says.
"I think the ferocity with which we embrace work from home and protected it when it looked like it was going to be threatened speaks to how desperate families are to find every last minute because they need them."
But when you throw in the difference between the workday and school day, the commute time makes a lot of work completely inaccessible to many Australians.
"Once you factor in things like the time at which children can be dropped at school and what that's like for a young child in early primary years when they are dropped at school leads to whether that's actually even a solution for parents to be able to drop off when the school gates open," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
"Factor in commute times to an office, and increasingly families needing to move further out in our major cities in Australia.
"As soon as you get out into some of the kind of commuter suburbs, it makes actually commuting into a job in the city or somewhere else in a metropolitan city just not even a thing for families."
While distances are much greater in rural or regional areas, most (78 per cent) primary school-aged parents live within 2 kilometres of their school.
That may be a 2-minute drive or a 15-minute walk.
But if we're conservative and allow 10 minutes for each drop-off and pick-up, which realistically, doesn't also account for the time it takes to get everyone out of the house, settle the kids at school and get back, that's roughly 1.7 hours per week.
Professor Hill says for workers who work a "typical" workday of 9am-5pm or 8am-6pm, the school pick-up is a real problem.
"It's a hard stop, and it typically happens when you're kind of reaching peak productivity in your working day."
It's hard to get the exact figures on how many activities children do and how much time parents spend attending them, but increasingly Australian families are feeling the pressure to enrol their kids in sports, arts, swimming and tutoring.
The last Australian Bureau of Statistics survey into children's participation in cultural and leisure activities found 35 per cent of kids aged 5 to 14 did a cultural activity outside of school hours. About 60 per cent did an organised sport and spent about 5 hours a fortnight training or playing outside of school hours.
Let's be conservative and allow 1 hour of the working week for dropping off and attending extracurricular activities, (even though it's likely to be more for most families).
Often this involves working parents coming up with creative solutions like carpooling, working from the sidelines or logging back on when the children are in bed.
Professor Hill says some parents feel penalised for accessing flexibility for this.
"Just because they pick up their kids from daycare or from school or take them to netball practice, or to piano lessons, does not mean that they're any less committed as an employee and any less deserving of access to training opportunities or promotion opportunities."
24 days per year
For school holidays. And that's if parents take all of their annual leave separately.
Read more
The average Australian worker gets four weeks of annual leave, but there are 12 weeks of school holidays. Then there are at least four pupil-free or curriculum days to cover (in some states there are up to eight).
Even if there are two parents at home who each have four weeks of annual leave and they choose to take all of their leave separately, which means no family holiday time, there's still a gap of more than four weeks.
There are sometimes school holiday program options, but they can be costly.
Dr Harrison Brennan says kids often need this time for downtime at home and with family and friends.
"Many parents, they look to the school holidays and think, 'Oh, finally, this is going to be a chance to regroup.'
"And then the realisation comes in that first year of school, 'Oh no, now we have to look at holiday care options', because even if you have four weeks of annual leave and two parents in a household, that's only going to cover about two-thirds of a child's annual school holidays."
She says it's an outdated set-up we're dealing with.
"It's just such a clear example of our models for the purposes of annual leave for workers and the purpose of school holidays for children being at complete odds with one another.
"It's affecting kids, it's affecting families and extended families as well as grandparents being asked to do more. And sometimes that's possible, sometimes it's simply not."
At least 814 hours
That's how much time parents have to find each year if both parents are working full-time and have primary school children.
Read more
That overlap, when your job and your children need your attention, works out to be about 34 full days every year.
And we know this is being conservative.
Obviously it doesn't take into account the many variables in different family situations.
It doesn't reflect families that have only one parent and/or children with additional needs.
It's not counting the huge amount of unpaid work, cooking, cleaning, washing, planning, maintenance or day-to-day caregiving, that needs to be done for a family to run smoothly.
It also doesn't factor in the assemblies, the medical appointments, the early pick-up days, the school events or homework.
"The numbers are damning but they're not surprising," Georgie Dent says.
"Those additional hours, they're so unseen until you're in the midst of it," Dr Harrison Brennan says.
"Parents are trying to find another 800 hours and they're facing impossible job demands," Dr Strazdins says.
Dr Strazdins says it's time to talk about the broken system.
"We've got lots of reasons why we do need to have this conversation," she says.
"If you're trying to find an extra 800 hours a year, well, what are you actually doing to do that? I mean, what actually are people trying to do if they're trying to find those extra hours?"
There is a lot of evidence to show that time pressure changes how people behave, Dr Strazdins says.
"They're rushing, they're feeling incredibly anxious, they're cutting back on other things that they really need to do.
"It's really a social problem to put this much pressure on citizens."
Professor Hill says society needs to recognise that intensive child care does not end when young kids start school.
"I think it's really good to name it and to shine a light on the quantum of hours that require some form of adult supervision, whether it's parents, whether it's grandparents, whether it's other community members."
Mums are in paid work more, but still carry larger portion of unpaid workload
Between 1990 and 2025, the proportion of two-parent families in which both partners worked rose from 55 per cent to 71-73 per cent, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.
Over the past 20 years, the hours of paid work has grown for women.
This chart shows the hours worked when there is a child under 15 in the home, broken down by men and women.
Median hours of working men haven't changed much.
Across the past 20 years, they've sat at about 40 hours per week.
For quite some time, working hours of women hovered between 24 and 25 hours a week.
But since about 2016, those hours have been rising.
ABS data shows the median hours for mums is currently about 30 hours.
And that's the same whether they are in a two-parent or single-parent home.
But the data also shows historically those hours fluctuate a lot and continue to do so.
The dips in hours show that women's work has been more flexible to accommodate the school holidays.
All of the notable downward spikes in this chart appear to align with the four school holiday periods in summer, autumn, winter and spring.
The biggest drop shows a holiday period in 2012/2013 known as the "Angry Summer".
Catastrophic bushfires, extreme heat and devastating floods were simultaneously happening across the country, which may explain the dramatic dip in hours for both men and women employees at this time.
But it hasn't been the norm for both men's and women's hours to change during the holidays.
If we look at 2014 as an example, we can see that men's hours remained unchanged throughout the year, while women's hours zigzag during the school holiday periods.
However, that is changing.
In more recent years, men's hours have been fluctuating during these periods too.
If we fast-forward to 2024, men's hours reduce across the four holiday periods.
This may indicate that more dads are reducing hours to accommodate the school holiday juggle.
However the size of the dips indicate that women are still having their hours disrupted more dramatically.
Increasing financial pressures mean families often don't have a choice about whether or not both parents should work, or work more.
In homes where there is a couple and children aged 0-14 years, about 36 per cent have both parents working full-time.
The way society is built has not kept up with the reality of modern family life, Georgie Dent says.
"There are more parents than ever in paid work, not as a lifestyle choice, but out of necessity, yet so many of our systems, from schools to workplaces to paid parental leave and child care, still reflect an outdated assumption that there's a parent at home to readily absorb the care and domestic load of raising a family."
And not only that, the economy wants women to work more.
Australian women work part-time at higher rates than many other advanced economies.
In an economic roundtable a year ago, economists highlighted that women were an untapped resource for our nation's productivity.
"We've got women working shorter hours, doing the rest, helping men work the long hours and making the money … but it's not in the country's interests and it's certainly not equal," Dr Strazdins says.
This is reflected in the amount of unpaid work mums do, compared to dads.
An ABS survey reveals mothers do more than 2 hours of extra unpaid work and have 24 minutes less leisure time each day than fathers.
Georgie Dent says our economy relies on the unpaid work of women.
"We've built an economy and society that runs on the invisible labour of parents, particularly mums, and called it a 'work-life balance problem' instead of a policy failure."
A flood of comments in a recent ABC social media post highlighted that many mums felt like they weren't juggling, they were struggling.
"Working hours and school hours do not make sense … this is structural inequality that guarantees failings for all parents, but especially mums. We've lost before we even walk out the front door." - @lauren_affairs_and_trade
Another commenter said: "We're not juggling, we're sacrificing our own mental, physical and emotional health to meet the structures of a system designed for a different time." - @otto.von.gram
What society needs to do to keep up
The majority of our workforce are 'worker-carers' — people who have responsibilities at both work and home.
Experts say there is no silver-bullet solution to overhaul the system, but propose a suite of changes to better support modern families.
This can come in many different forms, says Rowena Ditzell, who specialises in the future of work.
"People are talking about working from home and that's certainly a really common way of flexible working, but there's many other ways, whether it's flexible start and finish times, which can really help parents with school-aged children, whether it's term hours, you know, things like that can make a real difference for working parents."
A four-day work week is one possible solution to a more flexible work environment, Dr Ditzell says.
"Certainly in my research I have spoken to women who have told me that because they have been able to do a relatively important role, but been able to do it in four days, they wouldn't have been able to access that role beforehand.
"Rather than thinking to be successful or to be taking your career seriously, you need to be in the office five days a week, it's about: to be successful you need to be delivering your outcomes."
Dr Ditzell says while more Australians are able to access workplace flexibility, it needs to come without the worry of being overlooked for pay increases or promotions.
"We still see what we call either flexibility stigma or flexibility bias and that is the situation where people who use flexibility actually feel that they are disadvantaged as a result of that and they feel that they are judged differently."
Experts say for the gender pay gap to shrink and the glass ceiling to break, more men need to take up the flexibility too and employers need to recognise that mums and dads have equal responsibility for children.
Professor Hill says research suggests men can suffer from flexibility stigma in more extreme ways than women.
"If flexible work arrangements are not taken up by men as well, then they risk becoming just another reason for women to continue doing a disproportionate amount of unpaid care work," she says.
Dr Strazdins says flexibility should no longer be seen as a nice to have under Australian Work Health and Safety laws.
"There's legislation now, and it's called psychosocial hazards … parents are trying to find another 800 hours and they're facing impossible job demands."
She also argues it's time to crack down on working hours beyond the mandated 38-hour work week.
"While we allow long-hour jobs to be so well incentivised and earned, households have to make a really tough choice: who earns the big bucks and works the long hours and then who does the rest?"
Kate Harrison Brennan says reliable after-school care, ideally in the same location the child goes to school, is the backbone to stable employment.
"Quality, affordable care is crucial, particularly for workers who aren't able to be flexible with their working hours."
This could look like extra leave for parents of young children, beyond when they're babies, to give families more time together.
"I think this mismatch between the hours that we are at work and the hours that they are at school really demands that we think in new ways around paid leave away from work in order to provide those supports," Professor Hill says.
"We've always thought about 'paid parental leave' as being something only relevant to the first year of a child's life, but there are countries where there's an expectation that parents have access to paid leave throughout the early years of a child's schooling as well."
In Sweden parents get 480 days of paid parental leave per child, shared between the parents. That can be banked and used flexibly throughout their childhood.
Dr Strazdins says legislating against excessive work hours can level the playing field and reduce the gender pay gap.
"There's a review of the National Employment Standards right now. I would say there's very few employment standards which are so routinely ignored as the work hours per week.
"I'm trying to get people to see that it's really not right for workplaces to expect people to work these excessive hours – even if they reward them for it."
Men need to step up and do more of the unpaid work, and society needs to make that more possible, Professor Hill says.
"It's a big task. It's mostly invisible. It's squeezed in around everything else. It creates huge cognitive, emotional and logistical pressure that is primarily borne by mothers and grandmothers, and we need community and workplace supports that recognise that and allow it to be distributed more equally between all caregivers.
"Importantly, in offering and providing that flexibility, it's really critical that employers don't penalise dads for contributing to the unpaid care load."
We can’t expect families to keep patching over the gaps, Georgie Dent says.
"We're effectively asking parents to run a marathon in shoes designed for someone else and then wondering why they're not keeping up."
She says sytems that don't match modern-day realities are not only leaving parents scrambling, but they're failing children.
And perhaps, one of the biggest changes required is an attitude one.
“Supporting parents isn’t a concession to adult convenience: it’s one of the most powerful things we can do for the next generation," Ms Dent says.
“When we invest in parents, we invest in children."

Trump says he's struck deal for "permanent control over security" in Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:16:27 UTC
08:16:27 KST

Trump says he's struck deal to give U.S. "permanent control over security" in Greenland
President Trump said Friday he has struck a deal to give the United States "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," following a push by the president to boost the U.S.' influence over the Arctic island — or, if possible, take it over.
The governments of Greenland and Denmark, which oversees the semi-autonomous island, confirmed they reached a deal with the United States. The agreement is expected to be signed in New York City on Tuesday, when scores of world leaders will be in town for the United Nations General Assembly, two U.S. officials told CBS News.
Details are sparse, but the deal does not appear to constitute an outright U.S. takeover of the territory — an idea Mr. Trump had previously backed, rattling Denmark and other NATO members.
A State Department official told CBS News the U.S. was guaranteed permanent access to the island and overflight rights, allowing the military to potentially increase the number of bases. The deal also blocks non-NATO members from establishing military bases, and restricts American adversaries from making sensitive investments in Greenland, the official said.
The deal is set to remain in place permanently, "even if Greenland becomes a fully independent country," the State Department official said.
Mr. Trump said in a Truth Social post that he plans to boost the U.S.' presence in Greenland. The island has hosted a U.S. base on its western coast since the 1950s.
"We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many," Mr. Trump said. "We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the deal a "huge win."
"Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area," he said in a statement. "This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland."
Mr. Trump has argued since his first term that the U.S. needs control over Greenland, citing its position in a strategically important corner of the world, in between North America and Europe and across the thawing Arctic Ocean from Russia. He has pushed to buy the territory from Denmark, an idea officials in Denmark and Greenland have long rejected.
The president dramatically escalated those takeover efforts earlier this year, threatening steep tariffs on Denmark and any other countries that don't "go along with" his efforts to buy Greenland. His administration did not rule out using military force to assume U.S. control of the island.
The gambit came shortly after Mr. Trump ordered the military to remove Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from power, and before he launched a war against Iran and blocked most of Cuba's oil imports, signaling an increasingly assertive approach to foreign policy.
Denmark warned a U.S. takeover would effectively mark the end of the NATO alliance, and Greenland rejected the idea. Other NATO member states sided with Denmark, opposing Mr. Trump's annexation push.
Mr. Trump called off the tariffs in January and took military action in Greenland off the table, announcing that he and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte had formed "the framework of a future deal with respect to Greenland." It's not clear whether the agreement announced Friday stemmed from those discussions with NATO.
In a statement Friday, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen's office said the U.S., Danish and Greenlandic governments are planning to sign the deal next week. It will also need to go through "necessary parliamentary procedures" in Denmark.
"I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," Frederiksen said. She added that the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area and is thus also good for NATO and Europe," and "recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."
Greenland's prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, called the deal "gratifying."
"The agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in international cooperation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said in a statement shared by Frederiksen's office.

Yemen’s government, backed by Saudi Arabia, said on Friday its forces had killed 30 Houthi rebels and wounded more than 60 in clashes in the al-Waziiyah district of Taiz province, one of several fronts where combat has picked up this week.
The exchange has come on the heels of a widening escalation of fighting in Yemen between the government’s military and the Houthi fighters.
Tens of thousands marched through Sanaa on Friday in a show of support for the Iran-backed Houthis and against Saudi Arabia, as the rebels press gains that have brought large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, under their control.
Earlier this week, the intensifying attacks between the Yemeni government and the Houthi rebels killed at least five people, including three children, according to reports from both sides.
Saudi Arabia said one person was killed in the Taif governorate after a Houthi drone was intercepted, while Houthi-linked media reported deaths from Saudi attacks in Taiz and the town of Abs.

The escalation has drawn in Washington, though reluctantly.
United States officials met Houthi representatives at the US embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat, over the weekend after the group’s rapid territorial gains raised concern over shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, a vital corridor for global trade.
The Houthis reportedly assured Washington that vessels not linked to Saudi Arabia would not be targeted.
Despite appeals from Riyadh for US President Donald Trump to strike the Houthis directly, Washington has so far held back, wary of opening a new front while still fighting a costly war with Iran.
Meanwhile, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday the bloc’s Red Sea naval mission, Operation Aspides, had raised its alert level as the situation in the region worsened, the Reuters news agency reported.
“Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are unacceptable and sabotage the global economy,” Kallas said in a post on X.
She added that she had spoken with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about diplomatic efforts to end the fighting in Yemen and restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

Putin says Ukraine interfering in Russian parliamentary election
MOSCOW – Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sept 18 that Ukraine was deliberately hindering talks aimed at ending the 4 ½-year-old war and accused Kyiv of interfering in Russia’s parliamentary election.
Putin, in comments to Russia’s Military-Industrial commission, also reasserted Moscow’s main defence aim of relying on its “nuclear triad” of weapons and said Moscow also had to move towards improving its anti-missile defences.
In comments reported by Russian news agencies, Putin said Ukraine had “long degenerated into a dictatorship”, referring to the country not holding a new presidential election despite the expiry of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s mandate.
“The Ukrainian leadership is in no hurry to hold elections, as you know, but they are also trying to interfere with us,” Putin was quoted as saying, without providing evidence.
Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials say no election can be held in their country while a state of emergency, in place since Russia’s February 2022 invasion, remains in effect.
Kyiv derides the Russian vote as a “pseudo election” with the result never in doubt.
Election ongoing
Russians began voting on Sept 18 in a three-day parliamentary election that Putin has said will show that millions of people back his army fighting in Ukraine, even though most anti-war candidates were not allowed to run.
The result is likely to be held up by the Kremlin as evidence of widespread public support for Putin’s policies and, in particular, for his prosecution of Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War Two, now in its fifth year.
Putin said Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets meant Kyiv’s offers to hold negotiations to end the war were disingenuous.
He said one recent Ukrainian strike had hit a home in a village in a Russian-occupied part of Zaporizhzhia, killing the head of a local election commission, who had been presented posthumously with a Russian state honour.
“By committing crimes of this kind, they are doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin was quoted as telling the commission.
In other comments to the commission, Putin said Russia was continuing to rely on the nuclear triad of land-based, sea-based and aircraft-launched weapons, but that it also needed to improve air defence systems.
Ukraine has rapidly developed its drone capabilities and has launched strikes against Russian industrial targets up to 3,000km from its border, disrupting fuel supplies and other aspect of Russian daily life. REUTERS

Presumption of guilt doesn't make prosecution case 'gospel truth': SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:55:22 UTC
07:55:22 KST

A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and NV Anjaria gave this ruling
NEW DELHI: In a judgment that will impact as many as nine penal laws, Supreme Court has ruled that the stringent provisions of Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Pocso) Act providing for presumption of guilt of the accused must not persuade trial courts to believe the prosecution's case to be the "gospel truth".A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and N V Anjaria gave this ruling while setting aside concurrent judgments of a Delhi court and Delhi HC convicting a man, whom a woman had falsely accused of sexually assaulting her minor daughter in a Kalkaji slum in south Delhi in 2015. It said the accusation was part of a long-standing feud over water the woman had with him.The bench said both the trial court and HC appeared to have been swayed by the presumption of guilt provision in Pocso Act and overlooked glaring discrepancies and loopholes in the mother's testimony despite these being highlighted by the accused during cross-examination. Writing the judgment, Justice Anjaria said presumption of guilt in Pocso Act did not operate to eliminate evidence standing in favour of the accused.The statutory presumptions cannot be read to mean that the prosecution version is liable to be treated as gospel truth in every case," he said.The presumptive provision cannot unburden courts from "discharging their essential duty to analyse the evidence on record in light of the features emerging in a particular case", he added.
This ruling will potentially impact provisions of presumption of guilt against the accused, or casting reverse burden on them, in eight other laws - Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, Prevention of Corruption Act, Wild Life (Protection) Act, Essential Commodities Act, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, Customs Act, Foreign Exchange Management Act, and Negotiable Instruments Act, which were specifically mentioned in the 42-page judgment.
Justices Mishra and Anjaria said, "The court should not mechanically accept the ipse dixit of the prosecution riding on the provisions regarding presumption of guilt to give a stamp of approval to every prosecution even if they are absurd or improbable in its story."It said the provision, or the rule of reverse burden requiring the accused to prove his innocence, did not change the rule of standard of proof as normally applied in criminal cases.

US President Donald Trump on Friday signed a new sanctions bill into law that targets Russia’s leading energy buyers – China and India – just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for a state visit.

US and Denmark reach deal on Greenland, Trump says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:41:06 UTC
07:41:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump claims 'infinite' Greenland security deal with Denmark
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington "permanent control" over Greenland's security that would bar Russia and China from setting up bases in the Arctic territory.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
Denmark and Greenland -- an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen -- both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week.
"I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
"From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."
The 80-year-old said it was an "'Infinite Life' Agreement, there is no end!" and said Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory.
'Good agreement'
Trump has repeatedly warned about Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland amid a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic, and the State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so.
"This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors," a State Department official said.
At the Davos economic forum this past January, Trump reached a purported deal with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte over the future of Greenland, the terms of which have remained vague.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen had said Monday that she was "optimistic" that ongoing discussions with the United States and Greenland since January could resolve the dispute.
On Friday, she said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," adding that it was "good for NATO and Europe."
Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the United States "strengthens" the territory's security.
NATO tensions
Trump gave no details about how the deal would work, and it was not clear if it was linked to or substantially different from the Rutte deal.
But several media outlets have reported that the United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.
A 1951 defense pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance.
At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.
Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Gazans face critical shelter conditions as rainy season arrives: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:28:46 CST
07:28:46 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Shelter conditions for the majority of Gazans range from critical to catastrophic as the rainy season arrives, UN humanitarians said on Friday.
Humanitarian partners continue to warn that families are living amid widespread destruction, immense humanitarian needs, and ongoing restrictions on access and the entry of essential supplies, said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
"An estimated 1.2 million people, or 58 percent of the population, face shelter conditions ranging from critical to catastrophic," said OCHA.
As the first rains of the season fell over Gaza on Friday, humanitarian partners stress that more than 65 percent of families they have assessed are living in tents or makeshift shelters, with over half of those described as being in poor or very poor condition, said the office.
Parts of a war-damaged residential building collapsed on Friday in Gaza City, the second such incident this week. Emergency teams were able to rescue children who were underneath the building, and only minor injuries have been reported, said OCHA.
The first collapse, which occurred on Wednesday, has killed at least 21, including 11 children.
OCHA said that, with its partners, it reached 200 households with rapid assistance last week and provided nearly 6,600 families with routine shelter support, including hundreds of new tents, tarpaulins, kitchen sets, solar lights, sleeping mats and blankets.
Once again, the UN urged Israeli authorities to approve the entry of heavy equipment, engine oil, durable shelter materials and other items necessary to repair damaged buildings and help people secure safer living conditions. ■

Economic Watch: European investors grow wary of U.S. Treasury risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:28:44 CST
07:28:44 KST

BELGRADE, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- European financial institutions are increasingly reassessing risks associated with U.S. government debt, as Treasury yields remain near multi-year highs and U.S. federal debt has surpassed 40 trillion U.S. dollars.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield hovered around 5 percent on Friday after hitting its highest level since 2007 earlier this week. Despite the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hike in more than three years and the U.S. Treasury's expanded buybacks of longer-dated securities, long-term borrowing costs have remained elevated.
Against this backdrop, some European investors have moved to reduce exposure to U.S. government bonds, while others have raised concerns over the country's fiscal outlook and the traditional perception of Treasuries as virtually risk-free assets.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages Norway's sovereign wealth fund, proposed earlier this month reducing the share of government bonds in the fund's fixed-income benchmark to 50 percent from 70 percent, while increasing exposure to non-government debt, including mortgage-backed securities.
Under the proposal, the weighting of U.S. government bonds in the benchmark would fall to 21.9 percent from 34.1 percent.
Other European asset managers have also adjusted their positioning toward U.S. government debt.
Swisscanto Asset Management said in its September asset allocation update that interventions by the U.S. Treasury in bond and currency markets had unsettled investors. The Swiss asset manager said it was reducing exposure to long-dated U.S. Treasuries after the 30-year yield broke above its previous trading range, while finding Australian government bonds more attractive.
British private bank and wealth manager Brown Shipley has, meanwhile, maintained a tactical underweight position in U.S. Treasuries, citing higher energy prices, elevated government borrowing and persistent geopolitical uncertainty. It said an expansion of U.S. Treasury buybacks of longer-dated debt could provide some technical support to bond prices but would not address underlying fiscal concerns.
The debate has also extended to the traditional status of government bonds as safe assets.
James Turner, head of global fixed income for Europe, the Middle East and Africa for BlackRock, recently told the Financial Times that government bonds were "not as risk-free as they used to be." He noted that a company with a fiscal position comparable to that of the U.S. government would be unlikely to be regarded by investors as risk-free.
Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at London-based global investment manager Man Group, has also identified reduced exposure to U.S. Treasuries among the market trends to watch this autumn. She said uncertainty surrounding U.S. policy was contributing to unease among international investors, while moves by some U.S. allies to relocate part of their gold reserves also reflected broader concerns.
BNP Paribas Wealth Management said in its September fixed-income outlook that the recent rise in Treasury yields had been driven in part by increased capital demand and a higher term premium amid uncertainty over Federal Reserve policy.
The institution said the U.S. Treasury's decision to expand buybacks of longer-dated securities was unlikely to have a lasting impact on yields. It maintained a 12-month target of 4.50 percent for the 10-year Treasury yield, while saying yields could temporarily approach 5 percent in the coming months. ■

NAIROBI, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Kenya has launched a counter-terrorism hotline to give citizens a confidential channel to report concerns linked to radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism.

Mudavadi said the toll-free channel allows Kenyans to share confidential tips anonymously without fear of exposure, removing barriers to intelligence reporting and strengthening public safety nationwide.
"Communities and security agencies should closely monitor the activities of such gangs, given the risk of radicalization and their potential evolution into violent extremism and terrorism," he said during the launch of the hotline on Thursday evening in Nairobi.

"The hotline provides an essential platform for enhanced cooperation between communities and security agencies in making Kenya a country in which all people can live together safely and peacefully," he said.
Mudavadi urged Kenyans to use the platform responsibly and clarified that it was intended specifically for counter-terrorism reports, rather than general police complaints.
He called for heightened public vigilance ahead of the 2027 general election, warning that political gatherings could be targeted by extremist groups.
He emphasized that vigilance must extend online to counter emerging cyber-terrorism and ransom-seeking attacks.
Mudavadi stated that regional instability across the Horn of Africa continues to heighten security risks, making close cooperation between the public and security agencies vital for identifying and disrupting potential threats.
He warned that organized criminal gangs, including groups involved in violence and intimidation, could evolve into violent extremist and terrorist organizations if their activities are not closely monitored.
Mudavadi said communities and security agencies must increase vigilance to prevent criminal gangs from expanding, becoming entrenched and threatening national security.
The Kenyan official also emphasized that authorities must closely scrutinize organized criminal gangs that terrorize communities, undermine state institutions and threaten democratic processes. ■

Higher energy costs have also added to inflationary pressure. Germany's inflation rose to 2.9 percent in August from 2.8 percent in July, while energy prices jumped 10.5 percent year-on-year, their sharpest increase in more than three years, official data showed. ■

Feature: The last 7 dunams -- a farmer's struggle in Gaza
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
06:28:08 CST
07:28:08 KST

GAZA, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- On a seven-dunam plot near the "Yellow Line," 55-year-old Mohammed Al-Dahdouh bends over a small field of potatoes, a fraction of the more than 40 dunams he once cultivated.
The military demarcation line established under a ceasefire arrangement separates Israeli-deployed areas from the rest of the Gaza Strip, making every planting season a gamble.
Since the war began on Oct. 7, 2023, Gaza's farmland has shrunk dramatically. Water, electricity, fuel, and agricultural supplies are scarce or unaffordable. Yet Al-Dahdouh, a father of six, refuses to abandon the soil.
When shelling nears, he flees; when it stops, he returns.
His struggle mirrors that of farmers across the enclave. In Beit Lahia town in northern Gaza, 42-year-old farmer Ibrahim Abu Samhadana grows strawberries, zucchini, and eggplant while living in a tent beside the ruins of his home.
His family's 22 dunams are gone.
"The war has completely devastated the agricultural sector," Abu Samhadana said.
Still, he plants on.
"I am determined to rely on agriculture, as it is the profession we have known since childhood," the farmer, also a father of six, added.
In southern Gaza, the guava season, normally from September through December, tells a similar story.
Farmer Hani Al-Qudra's land in Khan Yunis has shrunk from about 1,350 dunams before the war to around 200 dunams, and his workforce from about 100 to 15.
"Guava is one of the most important crops in the Gaza Strip; both residents and farmers depend on it for food and employment opportunities," Al-Qudra said.
Consumers feel the loss too. In a Khan Yunis market, 45-year-old Ahmed Al-Najjar, a father of three, said guava, once an affordable seasonal fruit, is now beyond reach for many families.
"It saddens me when my children ask for it, and I cannot buy it," Al-Najjar said.
Experts paint a grim picture. Agricultural specialist Mohammed Abu Shamala said guava cultivation had fallen from about 1,700 dunams before the war to less than 100 in Gaza, while damage to farmland and irrigation systems and rising water salinity have degraded crop quality and limited the cultivation of some varieties.
A Food and Agriculture Organization assessment issued in August found that only about 448 hectares, or roughly 3 percent, of Gaza's cropland remained both accessible and undamaged. Gaza's Hamas-run agriculture authorities have put agricultural losses at about 3.49 billion U.S. dollars.
Before the war, agriculture accounted for about 10 percent of Gaza's economy and supported more than 560,000 people. Today, for farmers like Al-Dahdouh, Abu Samhadana, and Al-Qudra, insisting on cultivating potatoes, vegetables, and guavas has become a struggle to preserve both their livelihoods and what remains of Gaza's agricultural sector.
When shelling subsides, Al-Dahdouh returns to his seven dunams, tending his potatoes and preparing to plant tomatoes in the coming season.
"I insist on farming and earning an income for the sake of my children," he said. ■

Trump says he’s banning media outlets CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House
US President Donald Trump said on Sept 18 he was banning three major news outlets – CNN, MS NOW and Politico – from the White House, in his latest move to crack down on the independent press.
He wrote that he was banning the outlets for allegedly “reporting FAKE NEWS” in a move that is likely to be challenged as conflicting with the US Constitution’s First Amendment guarantees of free speech and a free press.
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
CNN, MS NOW, Politico and the National Press Club did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNN’s team remains at the White House working as if it were a normal Friday afternoon, CNN reporter Brian Stelter said on air.

OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York for the UN General Assembly, an OpenAI spokesperson said on Sept 18.
The 15-member Security Council is due to meet on Sept 23 on artificial intelligence and international security, just weeks after several AI industry leaders called for a coordinated slowdown of the development of the increasingly powerful technology, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.
“Sam Altman will brief an open UN Security Council meeting in person next week,” an OpenAI spokesperson told Reuters. “His remarks are expected to focus on the steps OpenAI is taking to ensure AI is safe and benefits people globally, along with the need for international coordination and shared safety standards.”

Karandeep Anand will join Disney on Oct 2 as senior executive vice-president and CTO, reporting directly to chief executive Josh D’Amaro.
Anand will oversee enterprise technology, infrastructure, data management and AI platforms, product and engineering, Disney said in a statement.
Bayern star Harry Kane becomes fastest player to score 100 Bundesliga goals
Harry Kane scored twice in Bayern Munich’s 7-0 demolition of Union Berlin on Sept 18, becoming the fastest player to reach 100 Bundesliga goals.
Kane scored his 100th and 101st goals in just 98 domestic games, obliterating the previous record set by Cologne’s Dieter Mueller in 1977 by 31 games.
It’s the latest record that the England captain has torn up during his time in Munich, having already become the fastest Bayern player to reach 75, 100 and 150 goals in all competitions.

"I built knesset2026.com to help olim (immigrants) understand Israeli politics. Users can answer 16 questions to discover the candidate that best matches their views, then receive a daily news email about Israel in their language,” said Dan Finel, a recent French immigrant.
The free, user-friendly online questionnaire is available in English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, and even in Hebrew.
“On October 27, I will be voting for the first time in Israel, and I wanted to understand the different candidates and their opinions,” he explained. “There are many candidates I don’t know much about, and I couldn’t find enough information in French or English. I spoke with many olim from different countries, and they told me it’s difficult to find information online in foreign languages.
“So, for those who cannot follow the news in Hebrew, I decided to create a quiz where you answer easy questions about your views. At the end, we tell you the candidate most aligned with your thinking. We update the questions often. And then, every day, you receive curated news about Israeli politics in your preferred language, in an easy-to-understand format. At the end of each newsletter, which is also free, is a review of the latest election polling results.”
Finel, 27, is learning to perfect his Hebrew on the job as a data scientist at Similarweb. Meanwhile, his knesset2026.com platform has attracted more than 50,000 users, mainly between the ages of 25 and 40. (I’m much older than the average user, but I found the website helpful in confirming my choice of candidate.)
Growing up in Paris in a traditional, Zionist family, Finel visited Israel annually from the time he was six years old. Although he is the first in his immediate family to make aliyah, his grandparents live in Ashdod, and he has aunts and uncles in Givat Shmuel and Tel Aviv.
While finishing his studies at a top business school in France, he had the option to do a six-month internship abroad and decided to do it in the start-up nation through the Jewish Agency’s Masa Israel Journey career development program.
The track he chose was Israel Tech Challenge (ITC), a Jewish Agency and Israeli National Cyber Bureau initiative connecting young professionals and students from overseas with the tools they need to break into careers in Israel’s hi-tech industry.
“I loved the country, and I wanted to see what it was like to live in Tel Aviv,” he said.
Originally, his flight had been scheduled for October 9, 2023. For obvious reasons, that flight was postponed, and instead he arrived in November. Despite the wartime situation, his ITC experience cemented his decision to move here.
“I really loved meeting Israelis and people from around the world; in Paris you were only with French people,” he said.
Part of the present and the future
ONE OF THE people he met during his six-month internship, Susana Arditti, was from his past and she’s now part of his present and future – they’re getting married in October.
“Susana and I met in kindergarten in Paris, and we were basically in love,” said Finel. “Then her family moved to London, and we didn’t see each other for 20 years until we met again in Masa. She was going to make aliyah, and I said, ‘I love life in Israel, and I want to leave Paris, so let’s do it.’” Arditti works as a corporate brand designer.
Finel officially made aliyah in September 2024. “Now I’ve been here for more than two years, and I have lived through war and bombings. It’s been quite challenging. Sometimes you can’t sleep at night,” he said.
“One regret I have is that I didn’t do the army; I arrived at 24, a bit too late. But I have friends in the army, and they say it’s hard, but they feel proud to defend the country.”
When asked his favorite aspect of Israeli life, Finel didn’t hesitate to answer: “The people.”
“You feel that even if you don’t know anyone, if something happens to you, people will help. I felt it at work the moment I arrived. I’m a French guy; nobody knew me, and I didn’t speak Hebrew well, but I immediately felt they were like family. They told me if I needed anything, they’d be there for me. And that’s been true.”
The biggest difference he notices between French and Israeli culture is the Israeli directness in communication.
'The sun, the beach, the restaurants, the food'
“Relations between people are much more authentic and honest,” he said. “In France, you don’t say exactly what you think, and there are many topics you don’t talk about. In Israel, nothing is off limits. If you think something, you can discuss it openly. At the beginning that was difficult for me, but you get used to it.”
In addition to the warm culture, he enjoys “the quality of life, the sun, the beach, the restaurants, the food.”
One of Finel’s favorite hobbies is cooking and baking, everything from pasta and fish to chocolate cake. “I love learning and trying new stuff,” he said. He’s also an avid runner and all-around sportsman.
With everything he has going on in his life, he still felt the need to contribute his skills voluntarily toward greater unity among Israelis. Using his favorite Hebrew word, bekitzur (in short), he phrased it like this:
“The country is a bit broken, very divided, and that’s difficult. This is why the election is so important. I feel we should all be together, going in the same direction and helping each other get there, even if we don’t all think the same way. We have so many enemies; we need to be together.” ■
Dan Finel, 27
From Paris to Tel Aviv, 2024

Putting conversation first: Jerusalem ulpan founder reflects on 18 years of teaching Hebrew to olim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:22 UTC
07:10:22 KST

Any immigrant who ever struggled to become conversant in Hebrew could rightfully feel a bit jealous of Ami Steinberger.
He grew up in a bilingual home in Los Angeles, speaking English with his mother and Hebrew with his Israeli father. That gave him a huge advantage when he relocated to Israel.
Steinberger felt he could help those without prior Hebrew fluency reach a conversational level that most could not achieve in existing ulpan classes. (“Ulpan” means “studio” but is also used to describe an intensive school for learning Hebrew.)
On August 18, 2008, he held his first ulpan class in his living room in Katamon. He had four students. Two months later, he was asked to hold two simultaneous classes at AACI and had to hire another teacher.
Today, Steinberger’s Ulpan La-Inyan (ulpan.com) employs 80 to 90 teachers in a variety of time zones, teaching private lessons and group courses to roughly 2,000 students annually, online and in person. Companies, embassies, and gap-year programs are among its clients.
In celebration of Ulpan La-Inyan’s 18th anniversary, Steinberger talked with the Magazine about the history of his ulpan, current trends and methodologies for teaching Hebrew, and how Hebrew is increasingly pivotal to Jewish identity outside of Israel.
A new kind of ulpan
Although he officially made aliyah in 1994 at age 14, when his family lived in Ra’anana for a year, and came back for a year after high school and two years after college, Steinberger permanently relocated in 2007. He had earned an undergraduate degree in English literature from Yeshiva University and a master’s degree in clinical psychology.
Ulpan La-Inyan was born of his interest in languages – he had searched for an effective method for mastering Arabic, French, and Spanish as a hobby – combined with his realization that the free ulpan courses offered by the government for new immigrants weren’t always successful.
“I noticed that although some English-speakers would come out of a traditional government ulpan with strong Hebrew, many of them would come out understanding the difference between verb forms but not being able to open their mouths and speak,” he said. “These ulpan classes are too large for the teachers to engage each student, so they rely more on theory than on practice. They’re teaching language as if it’s an academic discipline rather than a social skill.”
He saw this as a gap that needed filling.
“I decided to open my own language school based on the method that had helped me learn foreign languages. And it turned out that the need was real. People would come to me and say, ‘I’ve been to five ulpanim, and this was the first one that worked.’
“Traditional ulpan, for many people, is like taking a horse and buggy to your destination; our ulpan gets you there in a car.”
Grammar drills vs speaking skills
Steinberger creates scripted lessons based on research into how the brain absorbs and processes language. Without going into detail, this method teaches words by repeating them at very specific intervals.
“All of this takes place in a conversation which is relevant and useful, where you feel as if you’re actually participating. We don’t teach words with flashcards but through natural conversation.”
In the past decade, additional private ulpanim in Israel have followed suit, radically shifting the emphasis from grammar drills to speaking skills.
“I like to think we started that trend,” Steinberger said. “However, none of them use our exact method, our secret sauce.”
Along with online quizzes and games, ulpan homework these days might include watching a contemporary Israeli TV show and discussing it in the next class, or meeting up in a Hebrew-speaking environment like a café.
Another trend is online learning. Ulpan La-Inyan is still headquartered in Jerusalem with a branch in Tel Aviv, but the physical location doesn’t matter as much anymore.
“Before corona, we offered only private lessons online, not group lessons, and that segment constituted no more than 10% of our clientele. Since corona, 50% of our students participate online, in private and group classes,” Steinberger said.
Students come from North America, South America, Mexico, and Europe. Not all students are Jewish. For example, clientele includes Jerusalem Arabs seeking to improve their Hebrew for easier integration into academia or the workplace.
Hebrew via AI?
The growing preference for long-distance learning comes in tandem with many options for language acquisition – for example, the popular Duolingo digital language-learning platform and app. Steinberger said Duolingo is fun but not very effective for Hebrew, Arabic, and other non-European languages.
“Then there are AI language-training apps with an avatar acting like a language coach; the learner speaks, and the avatar corrects them.
“However, if someone really wants to progress in a language, it requires discipline. If you have good self-discipline to engage with the app on a consistent basis, AI is great. If you’re somebody who needs a structured learning environment where you feel accountable to the teacher and classmates to show up, that is what will help you progress,” he said.
“Either way, AI is not human, and it’s the human element in conversation that really drives communication.”
Ulpan La-Inyan is developing a hybrid option: a digital course combined with human interaction in real time.
“This enables you to experience fadihot, those embarrassing mistakes, together and get past them,” Steinberger said. “AI can be helpful, but people will always need a sense of human connection because language is ultimately a social activity.”
Pitfalls, pet words, and identity
What are the most common difficulties for new Hebrew-speakers?
“Pronunciation can be difficult to master,” said Steinberger. “English-speakers often confuse the pronunciation of the Hebrew letters hay and het, while French-speakers often confuse raish and het.”
Aside from that, he said, “mostly it’s the verb conjugations that trip people up.”
Steinberger noted that shaky Hebrew skills lead many a new immigrant to feel a frustrating loss of self-esteem. “They may have a PhD, but their Hebrew is on a first-grade level.”
It helps to inject some basic everyday expressions into your vocabulary from day one. Handy exclamations such as sababa, ahla, and yalla – all of which, ironically enough, are borrowed from Arabic – lend ease to daily interactions even if your ability to put a full sentence together isn’t yet up to speed.
Steinberger believes that the ability to interact with Israelis in their own tongue is increasingly essential to Jewish identity formation in the Diaspora, particularly in non-Orthodox streams.
It’s true that many graduates of Orthodox and ultra-Orthodox schools lack conversational Hebrew fluency because Hebrew is often taught as a subject and not a language, he says. But their Jewish identity is tied to Torah values and lifestyle rather than spoken Hebrew.
“However, in the non-Orthodox world, the educational emphasis is on creating a link with peers in Israel. Hebrew could be that bridge, especially in times when Israel’s reputation is in question and Jewish identity becomes complex,” Steinberger said.
“If someone opts to say ‘I stand with Israel,’ then learning the language becomes their opportunity to connect with Israelis. Many people with a strong feeling of Jewish identity abroad feel they don’t belong at all when they’re in Israel because they can’t really have a conversation.”
And that brings us back to the question of how best to acquire a comfortable command of Hebrew.
Studies back up Steinberger’s contention that the old-style approach of memorizing grammatical rules and vocabulary word lists is not nearly as effective as the way babies learn to talk, by listening and speaking.
So, if you haven’t progressed as well as you’d like in a public or traditional ulpan, don’t despair – Ulpan La-Inyan or similar programs may be just the ticket for a faster ride to fluency.■
To sign up for Steinberger’s Daily Dose of Hebrew via WhatsApp or email, or book a 15-minute trial lesson: ulpan.com/your-daily-dose-of-hebrew

Pentagon's US-Iran war fatality accounting may be inaccurate - report

The Pentagon's public account of US service member casualties in the Iran war excludes at least four service members killed in the Middle East since the war began on February 28, The Washington Post reported on Friday, citing six US officials familiar with the Defense Department's internal casualty accounting data.
While the Pentagon's public database, the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), lists 18 US military fatalities, five of the officials told WaPo that there had been at least 22 fatalities, with an additional official saying there had been 23.
The official said that while not all of the undisclosed deaths were directly tied to the conflict, all involved US personnel in the region during the war.
Three US contractors based in the region have also died since the start of the conflict, the official added.
Officials expressed their frustration with the excluded deaths to the Washington Post.
Proper accounting of military deaths essential for families
In addition to public transparency, the proper accounting of military fatalities is essential for service members' families who receive survivor benefits based on whether the death occurred while performing official duties.
As of Friday, 14 fatalities are listed in the system as occurring during Operation Epic Fury, with an additional four categorized under Overseas Operations, referring to the July ceasefire between the US and Iran, which later collapsed, the Washington Post wrote.
Pentagon releases two additional names of service members killed in region
The Pentagon also released the names of two service members who died in the Middle East since February while assigned to missions unrelated to the Iran war, although both deaths occurred at bases attacked by Iranian forces.
Sgt. Devin Seibel died in Irbil, Iraq, during a training accident on May 31 while assigned to the ongoing campaign against Islamic State terrorists, Operation Inherent Resolve, according to a Pentagon press release.
In addition, Maj. Sorffly Davius died on March 6 after suffering an unspecified medical emergency, having been deployed under Operation Spartan Shield, which involved partnerships with regional militaries, according to the Washington Post.

‘Checkout,' ‘Fauda’ test the appetite for Israeli spy stories after October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:10:13 UTC
07:10:13 KST

Is there still an appetite for Israeli spy stories?
Two productions arriving in the United States this month are testing that question: Checkout, a dark Israeli comedy about an aging Mossad operative, and the fifth season of Fauda, the Israeli action thriller about undercover counterterrorism agents.
One is an indie film that spent years getting to the screen; the other is a global Netflix hit whose new season plunges directly into the trauma of the October 7 massacre.
The two projects are seeking audiences in a challenging climate. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in March found that 60% of Americans had an unfavorable view of Israel, compared with 37% who viewed the country favorably. And Israeli cultural exports have faced increasing scrutiny abroad over the country’s conduct since October 7.
Yet Fauda has returned to Netflix with considerable international attention, while Checkout opened in Manhattan to a sold-out audience.
“It’s hard for Israeli movies right now to find an audience because everything translates to, you know, the ‘P’ [Palestinian] problem,” Jonathan Dekel, the writer, director and executive producer of Checkout, said in an interview. “It’s problematic.”
Checkout premieres to sold-out theater
Checkout opened September 17 to a sold-out audience at the Quad Cinema in Greenwich Village, which Dekel described as a “stalwart of indie cinema.”
Dekel has said the film’s six-year production was almost as difficult as the journey of its protagonist. They shot in Ukraine in November 2020, at the height of the pandemic, and barely escaped with the film’s hard drive after the set was bombed when Russia invaded. They had just finished editing when October 7, 2023, arrived, and Dekel was called up for military service.
Dekel knew that the movie would debut in a world transformed by the war and its aftermath.
“Trying to find a good time to put out a movie, a satire - a dark comedy about the Israeli special forces - was very, very touch and go until we finally decided to go for it,” he told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Checkout is not a conventional spy thriller. Its protagonist, Dov, is an American-born New Yorker who moved to Israel and is now about to retire from the Mossad.
“The day he checks out of his hotel to retire, someone else checks in, and it turns out it’s Mossad’s number one target - an arch terrorist [code-]named Gilgamesh,” Dekel said. “The entire movie is this weird weekend in a hotel where these two middle-aged men, spy-versus-spy, try to figure out who they are. They’re trying to find out about each other, but they find themselves.”
Josh Pais, who plays Dov, said his character is a man searching for meaning in his life - and comes to believe he can find it by tracking down and stopping a terrorist.
“He is possibly stepping into delusion,” said Pais. “What was appealing to me was that this is a story of what really happens to spies. So many movies tap into, you know, the James Bond of being a spy. Those movies are awesome, but this movie is about what it’s really like to be sent to a distant land, to be on location and to pretend that you’re someone else. Over a certain amount of time these guys start to lose touch with reality because, in truth, the vast majority of time as a spy nothing happens.”
Shai Satran, the movie’s co-writer, said he believes this is the “perfect moment for a movie about the Israeli intelligence community and an operation gone bad.”
“His driving force is not really to catch that guy - he doesn’t care about that guy. The driving force is to be accepted by his peers, the people who sent him - that’s at the core,” said Satran. “I don’t want to be crude about this, but there was something pre-October 7 about the Israeli security forces, maybe the special forces: There’s a certain arrogance in being only worried about your peers and not being aware of” the wider mission. In the lead-up to the Hamas attacks of October 7, “Israel, in a sense, thought that they were more in control of the situation than they were,” he said
Fauda's international success rewarded with fifth season
That idea - of intelligence work as something more complicated than heroic missions and exotic adventures - also runs through Fauda, though in a much more conventional action-thriller format.
The Israeli series has been an international success since its Netflix debut in 2016, and its fifth season, which arrived on Netflix September 8, is now testing whether audiences will follow its characters into a story shaped directly by and set two years after October 7.
Lior Raz, the show’s creator, co-writer and star, said last month at a fundraiser in Lenox, Massachusetts, for Israel’s Magen David Adom emergency service that he was genuinely surprised by the show’s reception in unlikely places: Previous seasons of the show hit No. 1 in popularity in Lebanon and the United Arab Emirates, and it was No. 2 in Qatar.
Season four ran in 2022 in Israel and early the next year on Netflix. The show’s creators had originally begun writing a different fifth season. But after the October 7 Hamas attack, Raz said those scripts were discarded. The new season deals directly with the aftermath of the attack and what Raz described as the nature of revenge. One reviewer called it “gripping, emotionally exhausting and often deeply difficult to watch,” particularly because of its depiction, in flashbacks, of October 7.
Raz, in his MDA talk, said the backlash against Israel was a campaign orchestrated by radical activists and Israel’s enemies. The latest season of Fauda is in part an attempt to depict the Israeli perspective for those open to nuance. “I want them to look in my character’s eyes, and to see what we felt on those days,” he told the New York Times. “If it would happen in their countries, they would feel exactly like we felt and how we feel about the world. So I hope it would open people’s eyes to see what happened on October 7.”
Although its reception abroad is hard to gauge, the latest season was a hit in Israel: The Times reported that it had already been the most-watched season of any show in the history of Israel’s Yes network.
Lacking the backing of a streaming giant, Checkout will have to work harder to find an audience. The Sundance Screenwriters Lab supported the Checkout script, Dekel said, but that was before October 7. Since then, “finding a distributor, finding a Netflix, Amazon or Hulu was pretty much crickets [silence] all over. It might be our movie, but looking around [at] movies from my colleagues - Israelis - I think it’s pretty much a broad phenomenon.”
Asked if he believed the difficulty he faced was because it is an Israeli movie or because it involved Jews, Dekel replied, “Is there a difference?”
