Archbishop of Canterbury revokes award from Pakistani cleric who praised Osama bin Laden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:09:58 UTC
07:09:58 KST

The Archbishop of Canterbury withdrew on Thursday an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden in comments he made in 2007.
Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi, a Muslim cleric from Pakistan, received the Hubert Walter Award for Reconciliation and Interfaith Cooperation at Lambeth Palace, the residence of the Archbishop of Canterbury, last Friday.
Ashrafi serves as the chairman of the Pakistan Ulema Council, an Islamic umbrella group composed of Islamic scholars from a wide spectrum of Islamic traditions.
The Archbishop’s office said that Ashrafi was being honored for “his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance.”
The statement continued to praise Ashrafi’s role in supporting “religious minorities in Pakistan, particularly the Christian community.”
Bin Laden was 'fighting for Islam'
The ceremony coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. Lambeth Palace announced the withdrawal of the award after Ashrafi's comments resurfaced.
Comments made by Ashrafi emerged from 2007, in which he praised bin Laden, the architect of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, as someone who had “been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans, and British,” and in a different instance said he would give bin Laden the title “Saifullah,” meaning “sword of God.”
Lambeth Palace faced backlash over the resurfaced comments and announced it would withdraw the award.
“It is a longstanding principle of interfaith dialogue and co-operation that we must engage with one another across deeply held differences, and that remains the case,” Lambeth Palace announced.
“However, previous comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led Lambeth Palace to reconsider this award, and we can now confirm today that the award has been withdrawn. We have contacted Imam Ashrafi to make him aware of this decision,” the statement continued.
'An unfair campaign' against him
In a statement to the BBC, Ashrafi told reporters that his comments from 2007 had been “totally taken out of context” and the subsequent outcry was “an unfair campaign” aimed at smearing him.
Ashrafi said he made the comments in response to “the hurt felt by many Muslims” after the British government’s decision to knight the “Satanic Verses” author Salman Rushdie.
Ashrafi has also been criticized since the award was first announced for his support of the Pakistani blasphemy laws, which have been criticized by human rights groups.
Ashrafi claimed the laws actually “save lives” by stopping people from taking matters of religious offenses into their own hands.
Human Rights Watch said last year that “the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs.”
The group also called on Pakistan’s government to reform the laws to prevent them from “being weaponized” against any of Pakistan's minority communities.

US granted permanent control over all security needs in Greenland, Trump announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:09:54 UTC
07:09:54 KST

WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump announced that the United States has reached what he described as a permanent agreement with Denmark and Greenland, granting Washington sweeping and indefinite security rights in Greenland, including the ability to expand its military presence and prevent adversaries from establishing bases, deploying forces, or making sensitive investments there.
Trump said the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” while fully addressing what he described as longstanding American concerns in the strategically important territory.
“There will be NO COST to the United States!” Trump wrote in announcing the agreement.
“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” he said.
Trump also said that under the agreement, no US adversary would be permitted to establish a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without express written American approval.
“For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it,” Trump said. “I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation.”
He described the arrangement as an “Infinite Life” agreement, declaring that “there is no end.”
Permanent access, bases, and overflight rights
A US State Department official provided additional details on the agreement, describing it as an unprecedented arrangement that permanently guarantees US security interests in the Arctic at no cost to the American taxpayer.
According to the official, the deal gives the United States permanent security control over Greenland and ensures that the territory will remain part of what Washington describes as the strategic defense area of North America.
The agreement explicitly guarantees the United States “the complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent,” the official said.
Those authorities include permanent access, basing and overflight rights.
The agreement also allows the US military to increase the number of bases in Greenland as necessary, according to the State Department official.
Trump said the United States would “immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” adding that Washington would work with the people of Greenland on development and construction.
“This solution is a great one for the United States of America, Denmark, Greenland, and all of our Allies,” Trump said.
Non-NATO countries prohibited from building bases in Greenland
The State Department official said the agreement explicitly prohibits any non-NATO country from building a military base in Greenland or maintaining a troop presence there.
The official contrasted that with what the administration described as the previous status quo, under which countries outside NATO could potentially have been allowed to establish military facilities or send forces to Greenland.
The official singled out China and Russia, saying the agreement guarantees that neither country can establish a base in Greenland or deploy troops there.
It also creates mechanisms designed to prevent adversaries from investing in sensitive sectors.
According to the official, only the United States and its allies will be able to make sensitive investments in Greenland under the agreement, replacing what the administration described as a previous system under which adversaries could invest in sensitive areas without investment screening.
The deal, the official said, is intended to remain fully in force even if Greenland one day becomes a fully independent country.
Rubio: ‘A huge win’
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the agreement “a huge win for the United States and the American people.”
“Thanks to President Trump’s vision and leadership, this historic agreement permanently guarantees US security interests in the Arctic at zero cost to the US taxpayer,” Rubio said.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he added.
Rubio said the agreement “permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.”
Trump framed the deal in similarly sweeping terms, calling it “a dream come true for the United States of America” and describing it as “very important, historic, and special.”
“We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land,” Trump said. “We will be very protective of it.”

Trump claims deal with Denmark gives US ‘permanent control’ over Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:01:35 UTC
07:01:35 KST

Trump says deal with Denmark gives US ‘permanent control’ over Greenland
Denmark and Greenland plan to sign a US defence pact next week, pending approval from both parliaments.
United States President Donald Trump has said Washington has entered into an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the US “permanent control over security and all other needs”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, Trump said, “At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the US will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump threatens Spain trade, demands US take over Greenland at NATO summit
- list 2 of 3Russia warns Denmark after near miss in Baltic Sea
- list 3 of 3EU pledges more than $200m to Greenland amid Trump annexation threats
He added that US adversaries will be barred from establishing military bases or stationing personnel in Greenland unless they receive written authorisation from the US.
Trump, who had previously threatened to annex the Arctic island for what he said were national security reasons, announced that plans will begin immediately to build a significant US military footprint in suitable areas across Greenland, adding that there are numerous potential locations. He called the development “a dream come true for the United States of America”.
The US already holds nearly total overflight and basing rights in Greenland under a 1951 treaty, but Trump’s announcement suggests he was nonetheless pleased with the outcome of the negotiations and might not revive his territorial claims, at least in the near future.
While he offered few specifics on the upcoming rollout beyond mentioning the island’s existing Space Force base in the remote northwest, his setup hints at larger strategic ambitions.
Signing expected next week
Denmark and Greenland also released a joint statement on Friday indicating that a pact with the US is set to be signed during next week’s United Nations General Assembly session.
The statement added that the deal remains subject to parliamentary approval in Nuuk and Copenhagen.
Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement “recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination”.
On Saturday, Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said on social media that “a long period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic and thereby also our shared security in NATO and Europe”.
Also on Saturday, NATO welcomed the announcement, with its spokesperson saying “the agreement will help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region”.
Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the US “strengthens” the territory’s security.
In a separate statement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the deal “permanently and completely” addressed Washington’s national security concerns with respect to the island.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defence area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” Rubio wrote.
Observers say the agreement could offer a path out of prolonged diplomatic tension.
Mikkel Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, said that while full details remain undisclosed, the deal provides an opening to end a standoff that has dragged on for more than a year and a half.
“It also has to do with excluding Russia and China from Greenland, excluding them, barring them from having military bases,” Olesen said.
“This is a stipulation that I think the Danes and the Greenlanders will have less trouble with because the Danes and the Greenlanders have no wish for Russia or China to have bases in Greenland.
“So, there are a lot of things we don’t know,” Olesen added. “But overall, I think the positive thing to zoom in on here is that it has the potential to end the crisis, and also, I see that, without the loss of sovereignty for Denmark and Greenland.”
Reporting from Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher noted that Trump views the agreement as a key strategic victory.
“It’s thought that Donald Trump will look to expand the number of US bases in Greenland. He sees it as an important step in his Golden Dome missile programme. He wanted to place interceptors and also trackers there,” he said.
“What is interesting is that all the time Donald Trump has been talking about what he wanted to do with Greenland and take over Greenland, he talked a lot about rare earth minerals,” added Fisher.
“This isn’t mentioned in either the statement from the Danish and the Greenlandic side, or indeed from Donald Trump, on his social media platform.”
Richard Weitz, a senior fellow at the NATO Defense College, said Trump “settled for less” with the Denmark-Greenland pact.
“This seems to be a pattern. He wanted to annex Canada and the Panama Canal, and raised the idea of annexing Venezuela and Greenland as well. But in each case, there was local opposition, so he’s backed down and settled for less, and in this case, he got pretty much everything he wanted, except formal annexation,” Weitz told Al Jazeera.
“The most immediate and very great contribution is this diffuses perhaps the most severe sources of internal tension between the alliance,” said Weitz, adding that resolving this issue allows NATO allies to focus on “common threats”, the most paramount one being Russia’s war on Ukraine.

Screen time isn’t linked to language delays in autistic children, large U.S. study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:00:57 UTC
07:00:57 KST

A recent study suggests that reading books together at home is associated with better language abilities in young autistic children. The research provides evidence that this shared reading time helps explain why children from higher-income families tend to have stronger communication skills, but finds that screen time does not have a negative impact on these abilities. The findings were published in Autism Research.
Language skills vary widely among children on the autism spectrum. Autism is a developmental condition characterized by differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors. Some autistic children experience challenges producing or understanding spoken language, whereas others develop abilities similar to or exceeding those of their neurotypical peers. To understand this variation, scientists are increasingly looking at environmental influences that shape early development.
Human development is shaped by different layers of a child’s environment. Broad, distant factors include a family’s socioeconomic status, which generally refers to household income and the parents’ education levels. Closer, everyday factors include the specific activities a child experiences at home, such as shared book reading and screen time. Shared book reading involves an adult caregiver looking at and reading a story with a child, encouraging them to actively participate.
Screen time refers to the hours a child spends in front of televisions, tablets, computers, or smartphones. In the general population, researchers have observed that reading together provides benefits for communication skills. For example, a 2026 study of early childhood development indicated that interactive home literacy routines, like reading books and discussing past events, directly promote language growth over time.
However, reading with an autistic child might look different. In fact, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that autistic children tend to focus their attention differently during shared reading than neurotypical children, looking less at the reader’s face and more at background objects. Because autistic children might engage with their environment in unique ways, scientists wanted to see if the typical patterns seen in other children hold true for them.
“Children with autism are likely to experience language delays and other challenges using and/or understanding spoken language that emerge early in childhood and sometimes persist into adulthood,” said lead author Meredith Pecukonis, an assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at Smith College and director of the Autism & Neurodevelopment (AND) Lab. “Identifying how certain aspects of the home environment relate to language abilities in autistic children is an important first step towards understanding how children’s experiences at home are shaping their language development, and developing interventions that lead to stronger language outcomes for autistic children.”
“Prior to publication of our study, only three studies had looked at the association between screen time and language abilities in autistic children,” Pecukonis told PsyPost. “All of these studies were conducted in China, and therefore no studies had been done in the U.S. on this topic. This gap in the literature was surprising to us, given that several studies have linked excessive screen time to language delays in neurotypical children, and autistic children engage in more screen time than their neurotypical peers.”
To address this gap, the researchers aimed to map out how socioeconomic status, reading habits, and screen use connect to language development. They wanted to see if the broader impact of a family’s income and education might operate through the daily routines children experience at home. To investigate this, the researchers analyzed data from the National Survey of Children’s Health collected between 2018 and 2022.
They focused on a nationally representative group of 1,217 autistic children living in the United States. The children in the sample were between the ages of two and five. Data was collected through surveys completed by parents or adult caregivers who lived with the children.
The survey assessed socioeconomic status by recording the highest level of parent education and calculating the family’s poverty ratio based on their income. It also tracked daily habits, asking parents how many days per week they read to their child and how many hours per weekday the child spent on electronic devices. To measure language, the researchers looked at both expressive and receptive skills.
Expressive language included abilities like speaking single words, asking questions, and telling a story. Receptive language involved understanding instructions, pointing to objects, and recognizing the beginning sounds of words. The statistical models accounted for both the age and sex of the children.
The results showed that autistic children from households with a higher socioeconomic status tended to have higher expressive and receptive language skills. These children were also read to more often and spent less time using screens. The researchers found a direct association between reading frequency and communication abilities. Autistic children who experienced more shared book reading at home demonstrated better language skills across the board.
When analyzing the connections between these variables, the researchers found that shared book reading partially explained the link between socioeconomic status and language skills. This suggests that children from higher-income families experience more frequent shared reading, which in turn helps build their communication abilities. The daily habit of reading acts as a bridge connecting a family’s broader resources to a child’s specific developmental gains.
“Effect sizes are small, meaning that the environment has a small yet significant impact on language development in autism,” Pecukonis said. “Parents raising children in lower SES households may have less time and energy to devote to shared book reading if they are working multiple jobs to pay their bills. Lower SES households may also have reduced access to books in the home.”
“If we want to support autistic children’s language development, we need to acknowledge that children are shaped by various aspects of their environments,” she continued. While some aspects can be addressed through direct family interventions, she noted that others “will likely require systemic change through public policy (e.g., providing greater financial support and services to lower SES families).”
The study found that screen time was not statistically associated with expressive or receptive language skills in autistic children. This means that the amount of time these children spent on devices did not predict better or worse communication abilities. This lack of an association stood out to the researchers, as previous studies of neurotypical children frequently link heavy screen use to developmental delays.
“We were really surprised that the association between amount of screen time and children’s language abilities was non-significant,” Pecukonis said. “This contradicts with what has been reported in the literature on neurotypical children.”
“The non-significant association between screen time and language abilities doesn’t suggest that screen time is ‘good’ or ‘bad’ for autistic children… it just shows that there is no association,” she added.
The results are in tension with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that replacing shared reading with screen time was linked to lower developmental scores. However, that earlier study looked at neurotypical preschoolers, whereas the new study focused exclusively on autistic children. Similarly, a 2024 study linked higher screen time to poorer language skills in the general population, which contrasts with the neutral effect observed here for autistic children.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relied on parent surveys, which can sometimes be subject to reporting biases, such as overestimating reading time or underestimating screen use. The data also captured a single snapshot in time rather than tracking the children over many years. Because of this, it is not possible to declare that reading directly causes better language skills in this group.
“We only looked at two household activities (shared book reading and screen time) as our measures of the environment when in reality there are probably hundreds, if not thousands, of other aspects of the environment that are shaping language development in autism that we just didn’t measure here,” Pecukonis explained.
“The purpose of this work isn’t to ‘blame’ parents for their children’s language delays, but rather to document trends, show that the environment does matter for language development, and find ways to support autistic children through modifications to their environment,” she emphasized. “Our hope is that these findings will ultimately help autistic children and their families by showing that there is a need for greater support for those from lower SES households.”
The study also measured the sheer quantity of screen time and reading without looking at the quality of those activities. It is entirely possible that autistic children with stronger language skills are more likely to request story time, leading to more frequent reading sessions. Future studies could use direct observation to see how the types of digital media and the specific reading strategies parents use shape language development.
“We just applied for funding to run a longitudinal study to see how screen time measured early in development relates to language abilities measured later in development,” Pecukonis noted. “This study will also measure both the quantity and quality of screen time.”
The study, “Socioeconomic Status and Quantity of Shared Book Reading, But Not Screen Time, are Positively Associated With Language Skills in a Nationally Representative Sample of Autistic Children,” was authored by M. Pecukonis and A. Geffin.

ExclusiveWord to the wise on organising a Chinese leader’s US visit
Ex-senior US intelligence official Dennis Wilder reflects on his experience of Hu Jintao’s 2006 White House visit ahead of Xi-Trump meeting
Let me begin by wishing those planning Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US on September 24 the best of luck, something I didn’t have in 2006, when president George W. Bush invited president Hu Jintao to the White House. After you read this, you may wonder how I was able to keep my job. All I can say is, Bush was a very forgiving boss.
This story begins in January 2006. I had just been elevated from China director to acting special assistant to the president and senior director for Asian affairs on the National Security Council. My predecessor Michael Green had returned to his position as a professor at Georgetown University. To say I was wet behind the ears is an understatement.
As 2006 began, Beijing was pressing for a state visit by Hu to Washington. Bush had made a highly successful visit to China just two months earlier as part of a four-nation Asian tour. China was playing a key role as host of the six-party talks on North Korea and not standing in the way of the war on terrorism.
On that trip, the US president had made his strongly held views on religious tolerance clear not by haranguing Beijing but by attending a Protestant church service. He also participated in an extraordinary mountain bike ride with young Chinese Olympic aspirants that was heralded in the Chinese press and supplanted the boring men-in-suits images so typical of US-China summits.

Trump signs Graham sanctions bill targeting Russia

Source: White House
Quote: "HH.R. 5334, the 'Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,' which authorises and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran."

Trump says US, Denmark reach deal to expand military presence in Greenland
US President Donald Trump said on Friday he had reached a deal with Denmark to expand the US military presence in Greenland, while respecting Danish and Greenlandic sovereignty. Denmark said the agreement would be signed next week during the UN General Assembly but still requires parliamentary approval.

President Donald Trump said Friday he has a deal with Denmark to bolster the US military presence in Greenland after months of threatening to take island by force from the NATO ally.
Trump in a social media post announcing the deal said the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.”
He added that with the agreement his administration would “immediately” begin the process of developing a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory.
The office of Denmark's prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said the deal will be signed by three governments next week during the United Nations General Assembly, but parliamentary action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced.
In a statement she said “the agreement recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Greenland and Denmark and upholds both people's right "to self-determination.”
Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the emerging deal benefits all three governments and “recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation.”
With his return to the White House last year, Trump called on Denmark to sell the island to the United States, while insisting that Greenland is crucial for US security. He pointedly wouldn't rule out taking the island by military force, even though Denmark is a NATO ally of the US.
Denmark and Greenland repeatedly said the island is not for sale and condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there. The US push for Greenland is also opposed by Russia and much of Europe.
Read moreLeaders urge EU to expand Arctic presence amid Russia 'threat'
But Trump in his social media post Friday suggested an understanding may been reached that could bring an end to what was viewed as an existential crisis by Denmark.
“We look forward to working with the wonderful people of Denmark and Greenland toward a magnificent future with respect to this large, and highly strategic, parcel of land,” Trump said in his post. “We will be very protective of it!”
Trump had raised concerns that Russia and China had become more active in the Arctic, making the need for the US to take control of Greenland necessary.
But the agreement bans any non-NATO base in Greenland, limits adversaries from being able to make investments in Greenland and guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, according to a State Department official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio cheered the statement as a “historic deal” and “huge win” for the United States.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” Rubio said. “This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.”
Despite Trump's repeated aggressive comments toward Denmark about Greenland, Danish officials had repeatedly made clear that they stood ready to work with the US to expand the American military presence and strengthen US commercial interests in Greenland.
Still, Trump’s repeated demands for Greenland and threats to take it by force rattled the NATO alliance and discomfited European allies, said Imran Bayoumi, an associate director at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.
“I think Americans really underestimate how damaging it was for the image of the United States in Europe,” he said. “I think Greenlanders, Danes, Europeans saw this as a real attack on their sovereignty, and it’s going to take a lot of work to repair.”

US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:45:36 UTC
06:45:36 KST

US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortage
The US has warned allies to expect delays of as much as five years in key weapons deliveries as it rebuilds its own depleted munitions stocks.
Multiple European nations are expecting deliveries of key missile and air defence capabilities to be pushed back as a result of the US military exhausting its own arsenal in the Iran war, officials said.
Germany has asked the US to speed up delivery of the long-range Tomahawk cruise missile and the ground-based Typhon launcher, but depleted US stocks of the powerful weapon means its manufacturer, RTX Corp’s Raytheon, is unlikely to fulfil the order in the next five years.
Two other officials said some Eastern European nations also reliant on US weapons systems have experienced delays since soon after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb 28.
The Defense Department didn’t immediately return a call seeking comment.
The Pentagon’s decision to prioritise its own stockpiles is also straining Ukraine’s push for the US to send it more Patriot air defence interceptors ahead of what is expected to be a difficult winter for the war-torn nation. The issue of Ukraine’s badly needed air defense will be a key topic at next week’s United Nations meetings in New York.
President Donald Trump earlier this week told reporters that he’s talking to Ukraine about either sending them a “far less sophisticated version” of the Patriot system, or granting licences for Europeans to build the weapons.
The US is estimated to have used more than half of its most advanced Patriot missile variants, a third of its Tomahawk missiles and almost half of its precision strike missiles and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptors in Iran. The Congressional Budget Office said the US had probably used as much as two-thirds of its inventory of missile defence interceptors since June 2025.
The military fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of the war that it “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Pentagon officials acknowledged to its inspector general.
Officials are now working to stockpile critical components and selected munitions, as well as streamline production lead times, the watchdog office said in a report released this week.
Defence firms are ramping up production, with Lockheed Martin Corp working to increase annual capacity from around 600 to 2,000 of the most advanced PAC-3 MSE, or Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement.
The stockpile shortages aren’t just impacting the US and Europe. In April the US told Japan its Tomahawk deliveries would be delayed by as much as two years. Saudi Arabia has also urged allies, including the US, to provide military support to help counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen. Washington has not said if it will provide extra assistance.
Still, the US continues to deliver weapons bought by European allies for Ukraine through NATO and European Union initiatives, the people said.
Europe’s main concern is that the US continues to provide Ukraine with battlefield support.
European leaders plan to lobby Trump on providing Ukraine with more Patriots next week as world leaders attend United Nations meetings. EU officials also hope to push the US to grant European nations licences to build their own Patriots that could eventually be provided to Kyiv. BLOOMBERG

PM Koretskyi orders action to eliminate delays in identifying repatriated bodies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

PM Koretskyi orders action to eliminate delays in identifying repatriated bodies
He announced this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
“The state must speed up the identification of the bodies of repatriated military personnel and civilians. We must eliminate unnecessary delays and strengthen coordination and information sharing between government agencies. I have instructed officials to prepare a clear plan for improvements within a week,” the statement said.
According to the report, the Prime Minister held a joint meeting with the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the Ministry of Defense, during which the entire process was examined in detail, from forensic medical examinations to the steps that follow. Coordination between agencies must be strengthened at every stage to ensure that all procedures are completed more promptly.
At the same time, Ukraine is strengthening its forensic examination capacity. Currently, examinations are conducted at 21 regional forensic medical bureaus under the Ministry of Health. The draft 2027 budget allocates more than UAH 600 million, including funding to equip the bureaus with the necessary equipment.
“We must ensure that families receive accurate information as quickly as possible and can say a dignified farewell to their loved ones,” Koretskyi added.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 17, following repatriation efforts, the Russian side returned the bodies of 252 fallen Ukrainians. Law enforcement investigators, together with expert institutions of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, will conduct all necessary examinations and identify the repatriated bodies.

How a New Trump Administration Rule Could Restrict Access to Green Cards—and Confront Immigrants With a Tough Choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:35:45 UTC
06:35:45 KST

President Donald Trump’s Administration is rolling out a new rule that experts predict will make it more difficult for immigrants to get green cards if they access public assistance programs, such as Medicaid and food stamps—and could deter those hoping to obtain the status from enrolling in public benefits.
The rule, which goes into effect on Friday, updates a policy dating back to the 19th century that the U.S. has long used to prohibit immigrants who are believed to be likely to become a “public charge” from getting green cards.
Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has argued that the change “is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves,” adding that it is “reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers.”
The rule marks the latest move in Trump’s efforts to sharply restrict both illegal and legal immigration. The President enacted a similar change during his first Administration, but the effort was subjected to court challenges and ultimately rescinded by his successor, Joe Biden.
The new rule has already been challenged in court by a coalition of more than a dozen states, including New York and California. It’s unclear at this point how the ongoing litigation will affect the rollout of the rule.
Here’s what to know about the new rule and how it could affect immigrants.
What is the “public charge” rule?
With its new policy, the Trump Administration is implementing a change to what’s known as the “public charge” rule, a policy first established under the Immigration Act of 1882. Since then, one factor that the U.S. government has considered when reviewing green card applications is whether the applicant is likely to become dependent on government assistance.
Historically, officials reviewing these types of applications have only taken into account cash benefit programs—for instance, Supplemental Security Income from Social Security—as “public benefits” that could lead to an immigrant being deemed a “public charge” and having their green card application denied. They have usually not deemed non-cash public benefits, such as Medicaid and food stamps, as programs that would disqualify an immigrant from obtaining permanent resident status.
During his first term in the White House, Trump tried to expand the programs that could result in an immigrant being deemed a “public charge,” but a federal judge ruled that the policy had to be vacated, saying it had “numerous unexplained flaws” that made it “arbitrary and capricious.”
When former President Joe Biden was in office, he officially rescinded Trump’s rule and stipulated that non-cash benefits would not result in an immigrant being considered a “public charge.”
How is the Trump Administration’s new policy different from the long-standing “public charge” rule?
In July, the Trump Administration revealed that it was revoking the Biden-era policy and was rolling out a change similar to the one that faced legal challeges during Trump’s first term. Under the new rule, officials reviewing green card applications are able to consider a broader scope of public benefit programs. The Trump Administration has noted that the new “public charge” rule does not apply to some immigrants—for instance, refugees.
The guidance, though, is vague—it doesn’t include a full list of the benefits that can be taken into consideration, saying only that immigration officers will be “using good judgment and discretion” and will be “making individualized, fact-specific public charge inadmissibility determinations, based on a totality of the alien’s circumstances.”
“Now, the officers who are reviewing and adjudicating these cases have much more discretion in how they make that determination—whether they believe the person is likely to become a public charge,” says Melissa Shepard, the legal services director at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center. “The difference now is that it’s a much broader analysis, whereas before it was a little more limited.”
Adriana Cadena, the executive director of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, says she worries that, because the new policy is so broad, it “opens the door for abuses by immigration officials” during the green card application process.
“It’s going from having guidance and clarity and understanding to opening the door to any kinds of programs,” she says.
How could the Trump Administration’s new rule affect immigrants?
Immigration experts say that the new policy could result in more green card applications being rejected, as well as cause many immigrants to delay seeking permanent resident status.
Charles Kuck, an immigration lawyer and former national president of the American immigration Lawyers Association, says that he expects there will be “massive numbers of denials” of green card applications as this new policy is rolled out. He adds that he and his colleagues have heard from some of their clients that they plan to wait until after Trump leaves the White House before filing their green card applications.
People who do not have permanent resident status in the U.S. are not eligible for many public assistance programs, but experts also warn that the new rule could result in immigrants disenrolling from public benefit programs that they or their children are eligible for because they are afraid of potentially harming their chances of obtaining a green card in the future.
Experts are additionally concerned that the Trump Administration’s new rule opens the door to immigration officials taking into account whether a green card applicant’s family member used a public benefit. The new rule stipulates that “if there is evidence in the record the alien’s family members whom the alien is legally obligated to support receive means-tested public benefits based on the alien’s income falling below the designated threshold, DHS would consider that fact.”
Kuck says he fears that this could lead to a situation where, for example, if a green card applicant’s child who is a U.S. citizen receives a public benefit, such as a free school lunch program, that could lead to their parent’s application being denied.
According to Shepard, it’s not yet clear how exactly the new policy will be applied in practice because it is so broad and gives immigration officers “so much discretion.” But she says she believes the change will cause people to be “a lot more cautious” and potentially fearful to access public assistance programs.
Cadena says the new rule is “forcing families to choose between either being able to adjust their status in the future or be able to have access to essential programs like food and child care.”
“In the current environment that we are in, where immigrant family safety is constantly being threatened, immigrant families … want to be able to keep their families together,” Cadena says. “And if keeping their child enrolled in an important program like Medicaid is going to threaten that, then they would more than likely disenroll their children from these programs.”
DHS has previously estimated that the rollout of the “public charge” change could lead to more than 950,000 people disenrolling from or choosing not to enroll in public assistance programs.
The change is the latest action the Trump Administration has taken to restrict immigration, including ramping up efforts to limit several legal pathways to immigration and proposing raising the fees associated with applying for citizenship.
“This is just one small factor or small piece of the entire immigration system, I think, that is under attack,” Shepard says.

US, Denmark reach 'infinite' Greenland security deal: Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:34:00 UTC
06:34:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that Washington had reached what he called an "infinite" agreement with Denmark granting the United States control over Greenland's security while preventing foreign adversaries from establishing bases on the Arctic island.
"I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
"From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."
While gaining independence from Denmark remains consistently popular in Greenland, Danish polling in January 2025 showed that 85% of Greenlanders opposed joining America. That month, Trump said the U.S. needed to control Greenland. He has since said that if the U.S. doesn’t occupy the island then China or Russia will. Both Beijing and Moscow have dismissed the claims. The president’s repeated comments about acquiring Greenland - and his refusal to rule out military force to do so - sparked months of tension between the U.S., Greenland and Denmark, and more broadly within the NATO alliance. Ultimately, Trump backed off and the issue moved to a diplomatic track. In March, a U.S. general told a Senate committee the administration was negotiating new bases in Greenland.

US and Denmark reach deal on Greenland, Trump says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:18:38 UTC
06:18:38 KST

US, Denmark reach ‘binding’ security deal on Greenland
WASHINGTON – The United States, Denmark and Greenland have entered into an agreement that will see the US develop a significant military presence on the island, while prohibiting its adversaries from building their own bases there, US President Donald Trump said on Sept 18.
In a Truth Social post, Trump wrote that America’s enemies would not be able to make sensitive investments on the island without US approval, and that the agreement had no expiry date.
“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will forever have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” he wrote.
“Additionally, from now on, no US adversary can ever have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”
Earlier on Sept 18, Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Greenland were closing in on a deal for the island that would result in an increased US military presence, but would stop well short of Trump’s long-held dream of acquiring the island for the US.
The US already has nearly total overflight and basing rights in Greenland due to a 1951 treaty.
Trump’s announcement suggests that he was nonetheless pleased with the outcome of the negotiations, and that he may not revive his territorial claims, at least in the near future.
He said, without elaborating, that the US would soon be rolling out a large military presence on the island, which already hosts one Space Force base in its remote north-west. “This is a dream come true for the United States of America,” he wrote.
Extent of agreement unclear
Denmark hailed the “binding” deal. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said on Sept 19 that the potential signing meant “next week could be a good week”.
“A long period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic,” he said in a social media post.
He added that the deal, which he said respected Denmark’s “red lines”, was “important” in the light of a changed security situation.
In a statement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the deal as “an agreement which at the same time recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”.
Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement that the agreement recognised Greenlandic interests and the Arctic island’s place in international cooperation.
“This benefits us all,” he said.
Much remained unclear late on Sept 18, including whether any new US bases would be constructed as a result of the agreement. Trump’s Truth Social posts about negotiations or agreements often lack context or specifics.
Imran Bayoumi, a former Pentagon official now with the Atlantic Council think-tank, said it would be new if the US can build bases without the approval of Greenland or Denmark, but that largely, “it seems that Washington could have achieved a lot of these objectives through diplomacy and dialogue without straining the broader US-NATO relationship”.
It was also unclear how the agreement would be received in Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark. The island’s residents aspire to independence and have bristled at US attempts to assert hegemony.
In a separate statement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the deal “permanently and completely” addressed Washington’s national security concerns with respect to the island.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defence area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he wrote.
A State Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss specific terms, said the deal prohibits non-NATO countries from building a base in Greenland, and will allow only the US and its allies to make unspecified “sensitive investments”. The official said the agreement grants the US permanent access, basing and overflight rights, and would continue to apply even if Greenland becomes independent. REUTERS

Why the Outcome of Russia's First Parliamentary Elections in Years Is All But Assured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:18:06 UTC
06:18:06 KST

Russia is just one day into three-day elections that will determine the makeup of the lower house of the country’s parliament, the State Duma. But the outcome of the vote has been all but guaranteed since before the first ballots were cast.
The elections, the first parliamentary vote the country has held since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, are widely expected to result in the Kremlin-aligned United Russia party maintaining its overwhelming dominance in the Duma.
The party currently holds 310 of the 450 seats in the chamber, giving it a supermajority and the power to make major legislative decisions without the input of other parties. It needs to keep at least 300 seats to retain that supermajority.
Four other political parties are also expected to be represented in the Duma following the election, all of which generally vote in line with United Russia and support the war in Ukraine. They are the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, the A Just Russia party, and the New People party.
Democracy watchdogs and foreign governments have denounced Russia’s elections as being neither free nor fair. Russian officials have rejected such claims in the past, saying that the country carries out its voting process in line with the law.
But experts tell TIME that the Russian government exerts its influence in ways that all but predetermine the results of elections and ensure that President Vladimir Putin and United Russia maintain control.
And this year’s vote, says David Szakonyi, an expert on Russia and election fraud who is professor at George Washington University, is “occurring in the most repressive political environment in Russia's post-Soviet history.”
Here's what experts have to say about how the Kremlin ensures elections result in its desired outcome—and why it continues to hold them.
Restricting opposition
The Kremlin uses multiple levers to influence elections on the government level, at the polls, and in daily civilian life, according to Szakonyi.
“Without a doubt, the most powerful tool” in the Kremlin’s arsenal, Szakonyi says, is limiting which candidates appear on the ballot in the first place.
In the case of the ongoing parliamentary vote, the one anti-war party that was registered by the Central Election Commission, the Yabloko party, was prohibited from participating in the election by Russia’s Supreme Court. The high court ordered that the party be removed from the ballot last month in response to a lawsuit from the pro-Kremlin Rodina party that accused the Yabloko party, which has garnered support from young Russians and those opposed to the war in Ukraine, of copyright infringement, receiving foreign funding, and extremism.
Szakoni says that the Kremlin has the ability to “harness the judicial system to pass rulings” such as the Supreme Court’s decision against the Yabloko party, which it uses as a “legal veneer” that shields the influence of Putin’s government over the ballot.
This screening of anti-war and other opposition parties, he says, comes months in advance of elections, creating a list of candidates that includes little or no meaningful opposition at all.
The Kremlin has also labeled opposition figures who oppose the war as “foreign agents,” a designation that prevents them from holding public office. In other instances, opposition leaders and activists such as Alexei Navalny have been prosecuted and imprisoned. Still others have fled the country.
The vote count
Experts tell TIME that the Russian government has also exercised its influence more directly on vote counts to achieve its desired election results.
“Historically,” Szakonyi says, Russian electoral officials have “intervened regularly to deliver votes to the ruling party and take them away from competitors.”
In the past, this was done via “crude ballot box stuffing,” he says; now, he asserts it is also performed by altering the results of online votes.
Online voting is used in more than a third of Russia’s regions, which Szakonyi asserts puts more power in the government’s hands since it eliminates the physical tally represented by paper ballots.
“The way that the electronic votes are being counted is almost completely a black box for the rest of society,” he says.
Regina Smyth, an expert on Russia and authoritarian regimes who is a professor at Indiana University, says that “falsification,” or the practice of altering the number of votes that are counted, occurs at precinct election commissions, of which there are over 90,000, all across Russia, that she says are “mostly staffed by loyalists, and they will simply report false numbers.”
There is also fraud, Smyth alleges, in “mobile voting,” when officials deliver and pick up ballots from people in their homes who are, for example, disabled or ill and unable to vote otherwise.
‘Implicit threat’
On a deeper level, an “implicit threat” stemming from the Russian government sways countless votes each election cycle, Szakonyi contends.
“Many Russian voters do not have the autonomy to cast an independent vote. They work for the state,” he says. He argues that many university students, healthcare workers, and teachers, whose livelihoods depend on state-run organizations, belong to a “block of captive, vulnerable voters” who fear prosecution by the Kremlin more than they value the influence of their ballot.
Voting is also taking place this year in Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine: in Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014, and in the Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
“In the occupied territories of Ukraine, where the elections are being held in these illegally occupied territories, soldiers, heavily armed soldiers, travel from house to house coercing people to vote,” Smyth tells TIME.
A lack of independent election oversight
On top of the various methods the Kremlin allegedly uses to achieve the voting results it wants, there are slim to no oversight mechanisms in place to document election interference in the country.
Golos, which was the only independent election watchdog within Russia, shuttered in 2025 following years of governmental pressure after its chairman was found guilty of working with an "undesirable organization" and imprisoned in a penal colony.
Szakonyi describes Golos’ loss as the “biggest blow toward any type of accountability” for the Kremlin, saying it was “the biggest tool that civil society had to identify, uncover, and publicize the fraud that was basically happening in every single electoral cycle.”
Russia has also refused to invite international election monitors from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), the world’s largest regional security organization, to observe this year’s elections.
Maria Telalian, director of the OSCE’s election-monitoring office, the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, said in a statement last month that the decision not to invite any OSCE monitors was “deeply regrettable, particularly as it continues a pattern of not implementing the commitments that every OSCE participating State has undertaken towards its own citizens and the international community.”
The ongoing vote marks the third nationwide election in Russia to take place without OSCE observation. Russia previously imposed severe limits on OSCE election observation in 2021 that the organization said made monitoring that year’s parliamentary elections in the country impossible. It did not invite the group’s monitors to the 2024 presidential election at all.
So why is Russia holding elections at all?
Despite the results of the parliamentary elections being all but determined, they carry a symbolic weight crucial to Putin’s legitimacy in the public eye and his desire to continue the war against Ukraine, experts tell TIME.
“There's lots of reasons to have elections. First and foremost, the Russian population expects elections,” Szakonyi says. “Putin's legitimacy depends on his ability to win election votes to the presidency and have his ruling party win on a regular interval, and demonstrate that they're popular and that their policies are in demand from the citizenry.”
During an address in which Putin urged Russians to vote days before the elections began, the leader said that “your choice and resolve will show once again that millions of people stand behind our fighters” and that “participating in the elections is our shared contribution to Russia’s victory.”
“This is a way for him to theoretically show that the Russian population is united behind his war and wants to continue fighting, and that Russia has had this referendum and will continue to push harder,” Szakonyi says.

AI cloud provider Nscale files to go public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:08:28 UTC
06:08:28 KST

Nscale, a cloud provider specializing in infrastructure for artificial intelligence models, has filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol "NSCL."
The company had a $1.02 billion net loss on $140.6 million in revenue in the six months ended June 30, 2026, according to its prospectus for an initial public offering. The net loss over the same time period a year earlier was $368.9 million, while revenue was up 1,252% from $10.4 million.
Nscale pointed to $56.4 billion in remaining performance obligations.
Competitors include market-leading cloud providers such as Amazon, as well as younger AI-centric suppliers like CoreWeave and Nebius that are known as neoclouds.
OpenAI, Anthropic and other labs have had seemingly endless thirst for more computing capacity since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, as people tap generative AI products for coding, productivity and general chat. As a result, Anthropic and OpenAI have required impressive amounts of cash to pay its computing bills, and both are planning to go public.
Both of those labs have struck deals with Nscale, which rents out Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) for training and running models. Microsoft, itself a cloud provider, has also signed up with Nscale. One unnamed customer accounted for over half of revenue in the first half of 2026.
Nscale has sought to diversify. It now offers to handle inference requests for a slew of models. In July it announced plans to acquire statup Anyscale, whose software helps with the construction of AI models.
Last week Nscale said Fidji Simo, a former OpenAI, Instacart and Meta executive, was joining its board. In July she stepped down from her post as OpenAI's product and business chief after taking medical leave. Other board members include former Meta leaders Nick Clegg and Sheryl Sandberg.
London-based Nscale had over 1,000 full-time employees as of Aug. 31.
As of Aug. 31, Nscale held 25,000 active GPUs and 461,000 that were either active or contracted, with five active and 12 contracted data center sites. It has line of sight to 10 gigawatts' worth of computing power, while sitting on more than $8 billion in debt, excluding a financing arrangement with AI server maker Dell.
The company emerged from stealth mode in 2024, spinning out of cryptocurrency mining firm Arkon Energy. Investors include Blue Owl, Dell, Nvidia, Fidelity and Point72. In March the company said investors had valued it at $14.6 billion in a funding round. Nvidia agreed to guarantee up to $860 million on Nscale's obligations for a data center lease agreement in Texas, according to the filing.
"From inception, we built Nscale with an infrastructure-first thesis, building against contracted customer demand, underwriting projects to attractive long-term returns, maintaining prudent leverage and seeking to match the duration of our capital commitments with the strong revenues supporting them," Josh Payne, Nscale's 32-year-old founder, chair and CEO, wrote in a letter to prospective investors included with the filing. "That discipline remains central to how we scale."

US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:07:35 UTC
06:07:35 KST

Breadcrumb
US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
The US military's price tag for the Iran war has grown to $43.6 billion as of 3 September, according to a new estimate provided this week to lawmakers.
The figure from US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched by the United States and Israel on 28 February.
A Congressional Budget Office report released Tuesday said the war had cost $38 billion through 1 August and will continue to rack up expenses of around $3 billion a month depending on the conflict's intensity.
The new breakdown, seen by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Punchbowl News, also showed the continued use of expensive munitions by American forces.
Weapons costs jumped by more than $6 billion in just over a month, from $21.7 billion listed in the CBO report to $28.1 billion in US Central Command’s estimate.
The financial cost is just one measure of the impact of the Iran war, which also is affecting oil prices and the stock market and has led to deaths and injuries of American troops.
The political costs will be calculated in November's midterm congressional elections, with Republicans facing increasing headwinds from the war's unpopularity.
The US military's one-page breakdown to Congress includes costs for operating warships, planes and bases as well as for equipment losses and medical support for troops.
Casualties tallied by the Pentagon have included 18 dead and more than 830 wounded, according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System.
The report does not include damage to US bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released Monday said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
In the new report to Congress, the figure for munitions was by far the largest, constituting well over half of all costs. The advanced weapons that have been in the most demand are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army's Patriot and THAAD systems.
The diminished stockpiles also have caused alarm in Europe, where U.S. and NATO officials have told the AP that there is a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors.
Saudi Arabia also is running low on interceptors and has turned to regional and Western allies for assistance as its standoff with Houthi rebels in Yemen drags on.
(The Associated Press)

Where thinking beats mugging up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:54 UTC
06:06:54 KST

(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
(Top row, R-L): AM/NS India CSR head Vikas Yadvendu, Uttar Pradesh deputy CM Brajesh Pathak, Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka, and DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar with some of the winners of Times Critical Thinking Championship in Delhi
NEW DELHI: Hands hovered over buzzers as students listened intently to each question, ready to hit the button before their competitors. Every few moments, a buzzer broke the silence and another answer was put to the test. But points were not won through recall alone, as the questions pushed students to reason, judge, analyse and think beyond the obvious.The questions came thick and fast. "If a meteor crashes on the Moon and an astronaut is 1,000km away, when will they hear the sound?" A student quickly buzzed in with the answer: they wouldn't - sound cannot travel through the vacuum of space.Then came a word puzzle: "Which word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?" Buzzers went off again. The answer was "short" - add "er" and it becomes "shorter".That was the scene at the auditorium of DPS RK Puram on Friday as students went head to head in the semi-final and final rounds of the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship 2026, conceived and conducted by Times Foundation. The Nav Ratna prize distribution ceremony was held soon after, during which chief guest Brajesh Pathak, deputy chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, handed over certificates to the winners.
Pathak, who spoke of the "immense effort" involved in reaching so many schools and students, urged participants to never stop asking questions. "Human beings are not machines meant to follow the same routine. We have the ability to think, understand and show the world a new direction," he said.The championship has been designed to encourage students to move beyond rote memorisation and develop the ability to question, analyse information and arrive at conclusions independently. The students who reached Friday's rounds had already made their way through a much larger field. From thousands of participants, 140 were shortlisted for written and oral assessments. The field was then narrowed to 36 students for the buzzer rounds, with nine winners emerging. The gathering included their parents, DPS teachers and other representatives."Critical thinking is very important for the younger generation because students need to learn to ask questions, reason and analyse before reaching conclusions. We see this initiative not as a one-off event but as a long-term process," said Vikas Yadvendu, head, CSR, AM/NS India.Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka said, "Critical thinking is the need of the hour. With young people exposed to so much information through social media, they can sometimes lose sight of their own judgement or be misled. So, such initiatives are important."DPS RK Puram principal Anil Kumar said, "This initiative encourages children to think, reason and analyse. Over 10 lakh students have participated across languages, and next year, we aim to reach one crore."Over the past six months, TCTC reached more than one million students from over 20,000 schools, spanning Grades III to XII across 28 states and eight Union Territories, with the programme conducted in 14 languages.
But amid those numbers were students from different corners of the country, each with their own interpretation of what it meant to think critically.Bhanvi, a Class V student from Kerala, summed it up simply: "Critical thinking is not agreeing with something just because everyone thinks it is right. Don't always listen to others. Use your own mind." Aaryahi Hazarika, a Class IV student from Assam, said it helped people find solutions carefully, while Sarah from Kashmir described it as the ability to "think out of the box". Divisha, a Class IV student of DPS East of Kailash, described it as "finding solutions by thinking with our own minds" rather than blindly following others.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story Has Nothing New to Say About Female Rage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
21:06:45 UTC
06:06:45 KST

This article discusses the full season of Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story
Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is about female rage and repression. That isn’t my personal interpretation of the latest installment of Ian Brennan and Ryan Murphy’s Netflix true-crime anthology. It’s the talking point that the show’s makers have been leading with, in publicity materials and in multiple interviews. These are fine themes for the first season of Monster with a female subject, even if they’re not exactly unique within a post-Big-Little-Lies, #MeToo-informed TV landscape where so many dramas aimed at women double as amplifiers for gendered frustrations. The well of misogyny isn’t in danger of running dry anytime soon. But if we must keep diving into it, each descent should at least leave us with some new insight or nuance.
Lizzie Borden, now streaming, fails to clear even that bar. Perhaps the least historically accurate Monster yet—and that’s saying something—the season uses the infamous tale of a Fall River, Mass. woman who probably hacked her wealthy father and stepmother to death with an axe in 1892 as a conduit to just about every plague on womankind you can imagine, past, present, and perennial. Rape. Domestic violence. Pregnancy and childbirth. Housework. Menstrual maladies. Pressure to marry. The premium put on physical beauty. The perils of sex work. Confinement in the home and subjugation to male relatives. By tying together Lizzie’s story with the legends of supposed forerunner Elizabeth Báthory and descendent Aileen Wuornos, Brennan, who wrote every episode, suggests a simplistic kinship between all female killers.
There’s no use fretting over the extremely purposeful anachronisms and inaccuracies in this retelling, which plays as fast and loose with the Borden family as that classic nursery rhyme. With 26-year-old Ella Beatty starring as a dreamy, blank-screen Lizzie, who ages from 32 to her 60s by the end of the season, and Charlie Hunnam and Rebecca Hall cast as parents who were really a couple of decades the actors’ seniors, everyone is much younger and prettier than their real-life counterparts. And more shocking, in some ways, than the hyperspeed double murder reenactment that opens the premiere, is what immediately follows it: a flashback to four months earlier, when Lizzie scares off a suitor by passing a bucket of menstrual blood on the white sofa where they’re sitting. As it turns out, what the fictionalized Bordens refer to as her “lady time” had some relevance to the actual case. But Lizzie Borden is such a massive remix, mingling facts with half-truths and rumors and fabrications, it barely matters which detail is which.
Because its source material is not especially extensive—one double homicide, as opposed to the lengthy and lurid sagas of most past Monster subjects—the show is forced to stretch. The series is padded with Fall River horror scenes that either never happened (the oyster poisoning that leads to so much operatic barfing) or didn’t transpire remotely the way they’re shown (the murder of Bertha Manchester, played by Linda Reiter). Brennan also adds queer love to Lizzie’s life, in the form of the family’s maid, Bridget Sullivan, who they really did call Maggie, after a former servant. He is far from the first to investigate this angle; the 2018 film Lizzie, to take just one example, is also built around a romance, between Chloë Sevigny’s Lizzie and Kristen Stewart’s Bridget.
Monster is, however, the first dramatization to make such imaginative use of the character. Phantom Thread breakout Vicky Krieps, who played ‘Bitch of Buchenwald’ Ilse Koch in Monster’s Ed Gein season, is a conspicuously Germanic Irish maid, with an ahistorical shag haircut dyed a series of shades reminiscent of, by turns, Wuornos and Ziggy Stardust. She has picked up skills in everything from cooking and cleaning to pharmacology in the course of her global travels. It’s no mystery why the awkward, sheltered Lizzie, who craves a bigger life, is enchanted by this glamorous, androgynous outsider. Maggie is easily the best part of the season, thanks in no small part to Krieps’ at once humane and otherworldly performance.
She’s also the unstuck-in-time character who first connects Lizzie to murderesses from other eras. As Maggie reads from a French book about Báthory, a 16th century Hungarian noblewoman said to have killed hundreds of young women and bathed in their blood in pursuit of eternal youth, we see Krieps—with hair and makeup straight out of the goth club—as the so-called Blood Countess. The Runaways’ anthem of teen-girl rebellion “Cherry Bomb” blares. And Lizzie is electrified by the story. She feels a kinship with Báthory. Never mind that killing your cruel parents to free yourself and massacring a village’s worth of peasant girls because La Mer has yet to be invented are about as different as murder motives get. The fact that each woman is acting in response to some form of sexism is, I guess, supposed to bridge that gulf.
It takes almost half the season for the third member of the deadly trio, played by Murphyverse MVP Sarah Paulson, to show up. Often framed as America’s first female serial killer, Wuornos, a Florida sex worker who killed seven johns between 1989 and 1990, is, in this telling, as inspired by Lizzie as Lizzie is by Báthory. Her presence, and her unsuccessful attempt to claim in court that she acted in self-defense against rape, allows the show to take on—and force us to watch—sexual violence. I’m not sure it needed to be shoehorned into the rare true-crime drama where it doesn’t have an obvious place. Brennan also connects Aileen’s well-documented queerness with the speculative relationship between Lizzie and Maggie. On a pilgrimage to the Borden home, now a bed and breakfast, Aileen and her girlfriend (Jessie Lee) have public sex. A fantasy sequence has the two couples dancing side-by-side in Lizzie’s sacred garden shed. But it’s never clear what Monster is trying to say about lesbians and murder, and this is a case where ambiguity leaves space to insert some pretty dark assumptions.
The outcomes for each of the three female killers are as different as their motivations. Lizzie is acquitted and buys a mansion with her inheritance, presumably because sexist men can’t conceive of a woman committing such physical murders—and because she learns to correctly perform femininity, crying and fainting at appropriate moments, during the trial. Despite wrenching testimony, coarse, unfeminine Aileen is convicted and executed. This might lead you to conclude that privilege and falling in line with patriarchal expectations are what it takes for a woman to get away with murder. But then there’s the rich, powerful, and apparently quite appearance-obsessed Báthory. Our last glimpse of the countess is as a rotting corpse, bricked up in her castle for her sins. So what is really being said here?
Not much, as far as I can tell. Lizzie Borden certainly makes a strong case that women have always been repressed, that rage is the obvious product of that repression, and that liberation is the only antidote. (Of course we get a scene in the finale where Lizzie celebrates suffrage.) But if you didn’t know that, it’s probably also news to you that water is wet and the pope is Catholic. The show’s obsession with women’s bodies as the sites of unending horrors reminds me of House of the Dragon’s repeated depictions of traumatic childbirth. It’s as though viewers are expected to go in completely ignorant of basic hardships afflicting half the human population and must see them reproduced over and over again in gory detail to be enlightened, much less empathetic. And in that case, I suppose it’s also necessary to render interchangeable three notorious women defined by actions rooted in a near-universal form of rage.
But theirs are old stories, already told and retold in every conceivable media, and often, effectively, by women. Wuornos was, of course, most famously portrayed by Charlize Theron, in writer-director Patty Jenkins’ career-making, Oscar-winning 2003 film also titled Monster. Isabelle Huppert stars as Báthory in The Blood Countess, a new feature by German experimental cinema legend Ulrike Ottinger, which is earning praise on the festival circuit for its strangeness and sense of humor. Meanwhile, on TV, creator Liz Meriwether just gave us Furious—another story of female rage, female repression, and yes, even a (fictional) female serial killer. While Krieps is mesmerizing in Monster and frequent Murphy production designer Matthew Flood Ferguson has outdone himself with lavishly suffocating Gilded Age interiors, Furious is the superior show because it takes “being a woman is hard” as the given it is rather than as the endpoint of many repetitive episodes. It has dark, lived-in comedy and real stakes, posing the question of what can realistically be done about systemic misogyny and the anger over it that stains women’s lives.
“All your books are written by men,” Maggie scolds Lizzie in Monster’s season premiere. When you consider how heavily male the creative team behind Lizzie Borden is (executive producer Max Winkler directed six episodes and Sarah Adina Smith, two), this kind of has to be a self-aware line. But whether it’s intended as a wry apology or a small joke, I couldn’t tell you.
