India’s New Eye in the Sky: EOS-05 Satellite and What It Means for South Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:18:00 UTC
04:18:00 KST

The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) recently launched a new surveillance satellite designated as EOS-05 into geosynchronous earth orbit (GEO). The launch was carried out with the GSLV-F17 rocket.
The satellite – launched on September 4 – is the first earth observation satellite deployed in GEO by India. The satellite will allow New Delhi to continuously observe the subcontinent from an altitude ranging between 34,903 km and 35,884 km. The chairman of ISRO, V. Narayanan, said that “EOS-05 will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo orbit providing important strategic data for the country.”
The launch of the satellite is part of India’s long-term plan to strengthen its intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities. The satellite will provide India with the capability to persistently track military movements in the subcontinent – especially Pakistan’s naval warships, aircraft, strategic assets movements, and force mobilization during crisis time. A new eye in the sky is an important military asset for India and can increase its counterforce capabilities in the age of emerging and disruptive technologies.
India’s current space architecture consists of navigation, communication, ISR, and scientific satellites. For the purpose of communication, India has three dedicated military satellites – two of which are used by the Indian Navy and one by the Indian Air Force. Besides this, India has around 10 satellites that are dual-capable and can be used for military communication. The Indian navigation satellitessystem – known as Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) – has three operational satellites, IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I , and NVS-01. However, for basic positioning service four satellites are required in orbit ; the next satellite NVS-03 would be launched soon. The Indian ISR architecture consists of the CROSAT series for Optical purposes, the RISAT and NISAR series for SAR purposes, and the EMISAT satellite for Electronic ISR. The newly launched EOS-05 would be India’s first ISR satellite that would give real-time persistent observation of the subcontinent.
In 2024, India’s Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approved the Space Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-III) program that aimed to deploy 52 defense satellites into low-earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary orbit for surveillance. Under this project, ISRO will deploy 21 satellites and the private sector will develop 31 satellites.
After the May 2025 crisis, there have been calls within the Indian strategic community to further strengthen Indian military capabilities in the space domain. For example, former Indian Chief of Defense Staff General Anil Chauhan, speaking at the Indian Defense Space Symposium (IDS) 2026, stressed the importance of military space based assets. He said, “If we fail in space, we will be forced to fight blind. However, if we dominate in space, we will fight with foresight.”
The statement reflects a transformation in India’s strategic thinking vis-à-vis the military utility of space. The evolving character of warfare necessitates strengthening ISR architecture for maintaining persistent surveillance of strategically important areas both during peacetime and crisis situations.
The newly launched EOS-05 satellite is particularly important as it adds to the persistent surveillance layer of India’s existing ISR architecture. Currently, India’s satellites are mainly in LEO, where they provide high-resolution imagery but have limitations because of rapid movement across the earth’s surface. EOS-05 being in geosynchronous orbit will provide prolonged observation of the subcontinent. This capability will strengthen India’s precision-strike capacity, as precision-strike missiles not only depend on range and accuracy but also timely information regarding the location of targets. Thus, in the broader sensor-to-shooter chain of network-centric warfare, space-based surveillance would play an important role.
Moreover, persistent eyes in the sky can also strengthen India’s counterforce capabilities for both conventional and strategic purposes. For Pakistan, the implications of India strengthening ISR architecture and enhanced counterforce capabilities are direct. A persistent Indian eye in the sky would give its tri-services a near real-time picture of Pakistani naval deployments in the Arabian Sea, aircraft movements, and the dispersal of mobile missile launchers. As the survivability of mobile systems rests largely on their concealment, continuous wide-area surveillance, combined with high-resolution follow-up, shortens the time between detecting a target and striking it. India’s growing arsenal of long-range precision-strike missiles may become far more threatening with an added eye in space.
Moreover, there are also benefits to India of the new satellite system for defensive purposes. It can also help India be better prepared for a counterstrike by Pakistan, especially with an advanced missile defense system. Having persistent capability to monitor movements of Pakistan’s troops, India can be more prepared to defend itself.
However, this can have implications for South Asian deterrence dynamics. Faster detection, enhanced targeting information, and better precision-strike capabilities would lead to a compression of decision-making timelines during crisis. Because of territorial contiguity between India and Pakistan, decision-making timelines are already very short. Thus, increasing vulnerability of strategic assets to detection can induce Pakistan to early dispersal, mobilization, and further concealment of its military assets. This can also create a “use-it-or-lose-it dilemma” and further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation. Thus, enhanced space-based ISR capabilities can help in increasing situational awareness but would present new challenges for crisis stability and escalation management in South Asia.
In conclusion, EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader imitative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities under the SBS-III program. However, its launching points toward an Indian strategic shift from periodic snapshots to persistent watch, and this enhancement of capability can have implications on how the next crisis between India and Pakistan will unfold. Islamabad has to further strengthen survivability of its conventional and strategic assets through concealment, deception, and mobility practices.

Elon Musk talks up AI safety while fighting regulation in wild week of strange alliances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:15:24 UTC
04:15:24 KST

Elon Musk had a head-spinning week in AI.
After agreeing with bitter rivals Dario Amodei and Sam Altman in their call for foundation model labs to slow the pace of development, Musk was contradicted by President Donald Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said AI companies actually need to go faster.
Trump, whose stock portfolio includes shares of Nvidia and SpaceX according to his most recent disclosure, called fears of runaway AI a "hoax."
Speaking on a panel at the All-In Summit on Tuesday that included longtime friend and former White House AI czar David Sacks, Musk took a more middle-of-the-road approach. He urged companies to test each other's new models to identify and fix safety issues before they get released, an option he sees as preferable to the government taking a heavy-handed regulatory position in AI.
"You can always escalate the amount of regulatory oversight, but it is very difficult to reduce it," Musk said in a virtual appearance at the event. "It does tend to be very much a one-way ratchet."
Behind the scenes, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that Musk had joined Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg in advising President Trump to oppose an industry-funded regulator.
Musk didn't immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.
The back and forth in just the past week is a microcosm of Musk's history in artificial intelligence, dating back to an early check he wrote to fund DeepMind, which Google acquired in 2014. The year after that deal, Musk co-founded OpenAI with Altman and others as a nonprofit research lab.
While Musk has long expressed controversial and often conflicting views in AI, torching friendships along the way with the likes of Google co-founder Larry Page and Altman, the stakes now are higher than ever. Model developers are rolling out technology that has industry insiders sounding the alarm about the potentially existential threats of AI, while internet giants spend hundreds of billions of dollars a year on the infrastructure to power it.
Musk's SpaceX is heavily invested in the technology's growth. The company merged with xAI, Musk's AI startup, in February, and completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding tools provider Cursor in August. In between those two events, SpaceX went public in the largest IPO on record, briefly turning Musk into a trillionaire.
Meanwhile, Musk's other public company, Tesla, continues work on so-called physical AI, including driverless cars and humanoid robots.
"Tesla is arguably the world's biggest robotics company," Musk said at Tesla's "AI Day" in 2021. "Because our cars are semi-sentient robots on wheels."
'Some scary outcomes'
Since Musk's early days in AI, he's simultaneously drummed up public fears of world-ending threats from AI "superintelligence" while building out his own AI businesses and fighting off regulation. He told CNBC's "Closing Bell" in 2014, "I like to just keep an eye on what's going on with artificial intelligence," adding, "There have been movies about this, you know, like '[The] Terminator.' There are some scary outcomes."
His fear-plus-optimism campaign is part of a strategy documented by AI ethics and computer science researchers Timnit Gebru and Emile Torres in a March 2024 paper.
The paper mentions Musk more than 30 times and concludes that he and a small group of elite players in AI have claimed they are, "safeguarding humanity's future, while simultaneously creating unsafe products, centralizing power, and evading accountability," and disproportionately harming marginalized groups.
In late 2014, Musk told students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology that AI development was like "summoning the demon." Around that time, he donated $10 million through his foundation to seed the Future of Life Institute (FLI), a nonprofit led by MIT researcher Max Tegmark, who aimed to raise awareness of AI's terrifying potential and to steer the technology in a manner that would avoid driving humans to extinction.
Speaking at a keynote at the 2015 Effective Altruism conference, Musk said the threat of AI advancements spinning out of human control was the biggest existential risk that he could envision. He soon signed an open letter from FLI calling to "pause AI."
That same year, Musk co-founded OpenAI with a mission to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return."
His rift with Altman came in 2018, when Musk privately pressured his OpenAI co-founders to give him control of the lab and to make OpenAI a for-profit subsidiary of Tesla. Musk poached key talent from OpenAI for Tesla, and resigned from the organization's board that year.
It was another four years before the magnitude of that breakup would start to become apparent. In November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, kicking off the generative AI boom, with Musk largely on the sidelines.
A few months later, in March 2023, Musk signed another "pause AI letter" from FLI.
"AI systems with human-competitive intelligence can pose profound risks to society and humanity, as shown by extensive research and acknowledged by top AI labs," the letter began.
At roughly the same time, Musk was incorporating his new AI venture, xAI, in Nevada, but he kept it quiet from Tesla investors and the public until July.
Musk v. Altman
Then came the legal battle with Altman.
In August 2024, Musk filed a suit against OpenAI and its co-founders, claiming they had violated a promise to keep the lab a nonprofit. Musk lost the high-profile California trial in May, when a jury and federal judge determined his claims were filed outside of the statute of limitations. Musk said he would appeal but has yet to do so.
Correspondence brought to light in the case showed that Musk's obsession with creating OpenAI was built on fears that Google would control the technology after acquiring DeepMind, though in public he and Altman touted more altruistic aspects of their mission.
Now, Musk is back to calling for safety. Following Amodei's essay last weekend imploring the industry to "pace the frontier," Musk posted on X, "Dario is right."
That's quite the contrast from February, when Musk called Anthropic "misanthropic and evil" and said it "hates Western civilization." Things changed dramatically in May, when Anthropic agreed to pay SpaceX up to $1.25 billion a month to rent computing infrastructure in Memphis, giving Musk's company a hefty dose of sorely needed AI revenue before SpaceX's IPO.
"I was clearly wrong about Anthropic," Musk wrote on X in July. "They are obviously currently the leader in AI."
Musk's recent track record on AI safety has been rocky.
He's built out data centers in and around Memphis, Tennessee, while fighting off litigation from residents nearby suffering from air and noise pollution from the operations.
At SpaceX, Musk sold a version of xAI's Grok models to the U.S. military which "enabled U.S. forces to deploy over 2,000 munitions to 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours," according to DOJ legal filings.
And at xAI — now known as SpaceXAI — Musk sued to stop state regulations that would ban Grok's "nudify" features in Minnesota, and that would require his company to be transparent about the data used to train its models in California.
As Musk and his peers and rivals debate the right approach to AI safety, and whether the government should have a big role or no role at all, lawmakers and third-party researchers are growing increasingly skeptical of the industry's ability to police itself.
Tyler Whitmer, CEO of the nonprofit Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST), told CNBC that self-regulation won't be enough to protect the public from existing and future harms enabled by AI systems.
"We need real regulation that creates a level playing field for companies but also protects the public, and the companies just can't do that themselves," Whitmer said. "There needs to be a government-enforceable requirement that third-party evaluators be involved, not just the companies themselves."

AI is giving scientists more ideas than they can test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:10:36 UTC
04:10:36 KST

Ask any mathematician where artificial intelligence stands in their field, and you’ll hear it moved into the office down the hall, knocked off a few open problems and is elbowing in on the credit. Ask a biologist or chemist, and you’ll hear it’s still circling the parking lot. People have spent years expecting AI to change how new medicines are discovered, for example. So why hasn’t it?
In recent months, AI companies have turned to generating proofs, including results that have prompted accusations that they scooped academics, to put notches in their models’ belts and showcase scientific capability. Meanwhile the U.S. government has repeatedly stressed, including in a National Science Foundation (NSF) memo last week, that AI will “transform the questions researchers can answer” and the way science is done, highlighting it as a research priority. But those advances haven’t translated into anything like the same acceleration for drug discovery or experimental biological research.
A report out this week from Google, Google DeepMind and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s MIT FutureTech quantifies some of the gaps. The researchers set out to measure how AI is changing the economics of science in a variety of fields and, in the process, pointed to places where it still stalls. The study combines a survey of 637 scientists with analyses of 15 million Gemini conversations and an inventory of more than 2,600 specialized models. (The scientists were recruited through specialist panels, so frequent AI users may have been overrepresented.) About 44 percent of those scientists said that, over the past two years, their main research bottleneck had shifted downstream, toward later stages such as physical experimentation and data collection. Forty-one percent said their backlog of untested hypotheses had grown.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Eight-nine percent of those who save time using AI spend more than a 10th of the time that they’re saving actually checking AI outputs,” says Mihai Codreanu, a research economist at Google and co-lead author of the report. “Forty-six percent spend more than a quarter.”
Codreanu says the time spent checking whether responses and predictions are correct affects which types of work AI can do—and how useful it can be in different fields. “There is a lot of heterogeneity,” he says. A mathematical proof can be checked against formal rules, for instance, but a predicted protein function has to be built in a lab and tested in a living system.
The people building and studying these systems point to different causes for the jam.
At Stanford University, biomedical data scientist James Zou has built methods for handing research over to both large language models (LLMs) and specialized tools such as DeepMind’s AlphaFold, including fully virtual automated labs. He says extending that automation to the real world has a lot of hurdles to overcome. “They’re still fairly limited in the kinds of experiments that can be automated, mostly some chemistry experiments,” Zou says. “But [with] things that involve, let’s say, animals, it becomes much harder.”
As the experiments become larger or more complex, so, too, do the models that simulate them, and the data to train those models is hard to come by. Robots handling real-world materials raise safety questions that are unknown to software. And, as Zou points out, the existing automated labs can be prohibitively expensive.
Others think the problem comes down to the type of questions different scientists ask. “When you look at the tasks where AI has made much progress, they are the ones where you have ground truth,” says Daron Acemoglu, an economics Nobel laureate at M.I.T., who studies AI’s labor impacts. “In most of medicine, there is no ground truth.
The slowness can be deliberate. Clinical trials move at the pace of regulatory review, and any experiment involving people is constrained by safety checks before, during and after. Nobody has explained how AI would compress that or why we’d want it to.
Some scientists are trying to clear the hurdles anyway. Julius B. Lucks, principal investigator of the AI-Driven, Rapid, Experimental Automation Machine (DREAM) Cloud Lab for Protein Engineering at Northwestern University, is trying to automate more of the protein-engineering cycle. His lab, which received $20 million from the NSF over the summer as part of a new national network of programmable cloud laboratories, is building systems that let researchers remotely design, build and test proteins with automated equipment. Lucks says he’s taking it one step at a time. But he’s also thinking past it. “We’ll learn,” he says. “We’ll figure out what makes sense: What is the thing that we need to automate next?”

What does OpenAI’s blockbuster Navier-Stokes proof mean for the real world?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:10:32 UTC
04:10:32 KST

OpenAI may have claimed to have solved a million-dollar math problem that’s fundamental to lots of modern technology, but don’t expect anything to change—at least, not immediately.
Earlier this month OpenAI claimed one of its internal models had proved that the Navier-Stokes equations, which are used to model the motions of fluids, break down and yield nonsensical answers in certain scenarios. The equations can be thought of as “essentially Newton’s second law, applied to a little fluid parcel,” says Justin Beroz, CEO of ReynKo, an engineering company that specializes in turbulence.
Regardless of whether OpenAI can actually take the credit for solving the problem, the notion that an artificial intelligence has apparently succeeded where humans have, for so long, failed is earth-shattering for mathematicians. That isn’t the case for engineers, however, say several experts working in fluid dynamics.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The Navier-Stokes equations are used to great success in a wide array of applications, such as calculating airflow over a jet’s wings, forecasting weather patterns and determining how blood flows through biomedical devices. Even so, mathematicians have spent nearly 200 years struggling to prove that the models fully correspond with reality. At very small scales, they have suspected, the equations might predict something physically impossible: fluids that accelerate to infinite speeds.
Still, as to how much this affects engineering, Beroz says, in short, “not much.”
“The longer answer is a bit more nuanced,” he says.
The knowledge that the equations break down at a certain point doesn’t really change how they will be used because the equations themselves are only an approximation of how a fluid will react, says Florian Schäfer, an assistant professor at New York University. What really matters, he says, is that this approximation is good enough that any flaws are trivial.
“The Navier-Stokes equations have a certain regime of validity in which we think that they're basically enough at describing what the physics will do,” Schäfer says.
OpenAI’s proof does provide an example in which the equations allow a fluid to hit an infinite velocity, but the scenario is so contrived that it’s almost certainly unlikely to have any direct relevance to any physical system in the real world. The methods the large language model (LLM) marshaled to achieve its result could in principle, offer fresh insights for engineers and mathematicians alike, says Spencer Bryngelson, an adjunct professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology.
Proving a breakdown in Navier-Stokes could “have many knock-on effects that are useful, even though it’s unclear sometimes how those knock-on effects will happen,” Bryngelson says.
One place where those effects could eventually be felt is in improved computer simulations, Beroz says.
“We have plenty of things where we deal with drag and lift and design these things, but the key thing is: it’s always done experimentally,” he says, because the mathematics of fluid dynamics are notoriously complicated. “We don’t have good computational tools to simulate these things in advance, and this really separates fluid engineering from other kinds of engineering.”
As an example, Beroz points to aerospace design, in which the development cycle of a new airplane can take a decade and cost billions of dollars.
“The kicker is that roughly half the time and half the cost is spent building, testing or finding physical prototypes in the wind tunnel—and the only reason you’re doing that is that the software sucks,” he says.
The upshot is that, while any formal proof of a breakdown in Navier-Stokes may not have any immediate effects on engineers, it’s hard to predict how this knowledge will be implemented in the future. Basic scientific research can lead to dramatic and unforeseen applications and technologies years down the line.
“This is clearly an example where the equations do not do what the physics would do, and then that might guide us to a new way of understanding in what sense and in what regimes these equations are incomplete,” Schäfer says.

Labor's migration target comes with a political catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Labor's migration target comes with a political catch: an auction it can't win
Labor has made a lasting concession to a migration debate that shows little sign of rewarding them for joining it.
A Treasury forecast for net overseas migration (NOM) to fall to 225,000 had already become a political benchmark to judge the federal government against.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has now gone further by formally accepting the figure as a target and effectively turning it into a guarantee.
Most Labor MPs will be glad to see the end of constant speculation about Labor's temporary migration policy, sparked by the six-week delay in unveiling the plan.
Burke certainly delighted in dispelling some of the inaccurate reporting when he finally announced the tighter visa rules aimed at bringing down arrivals and increasing departures.
He has ended the uncertainty of what the government intends to do, but Labor is now in a fight where the terms have been set by its political opponents.
Failure is not an option
Fronting the National Press Club on Thursday, Burke declared the NOM forecast "must be met" and was unequivocal when pressed on the possibility of failure.
He said that "won't happen".
The distinction was essentially academic, but future governments may wish Labor had never formally accepted NOM as a "target".
It was not quite a year ago that Burke was at the press club describing the figure as a "guide" and declining to nominate an optimal number.
"I won't give you a magic number," he said. "I don't think there is a magic number."
Burke argued NOM's predictability would "always be uncertain" partly because of Australian citizens' behaviour.
But under pressure from political opponents, who argue they have the public on their side, Labor gave up what wriggle room remained.
Migration votes are hard to find
There is no doubt Australians are concerned about migration.
Ask voters if levels are too high and many will say yes, just as they would complain about congestion, housing or pressure on services.
But pollster Kos Samaras argues there is a difference between disliking something and voting on it.
Research conducted by his firm Redbridge over the past year has found migration is a salient issue for only about 10 per cent of voters, with most already supporting One Nation.
"I do not know why the political class keeps talking about migration," Samaras told this column. "There are no votes in it for anyone except One Nation."
Even on housing, only about 30 per cent of Australians believe migration has contributed in some way.
Samaras said the main vote drivers remain the economy and health.
Reducing migration might be popular in isolation, but the voters most likely to reward a government for doing it are already parked with the one party promising to go much further.
Pinning down the numbers
The other difficulty for Labor with fixing on 225,000 is how the number was arrived at in the first place.
Treasury does not start with a desired number deemed optimal for the economy and work backwards. It forecasts movements into and out of Australia based on observed behaviour, visa data and government policy.
Lately the predictions haven't been great, largely because it has proved difficult to pin down when temporary migrants already here will leave.
Still, Labor has adopted the destination already sitting in the budget and promised to make policy conform to it.
But that doesn't settle whether a number calculated as the likely outcome of existing settings should become the basis for future policy.
How low is low enough?
In embracing NOM as a target, Burke argued the post-COVID migration peak had been too high and housing supply needed time to catch up. But there is no guarantee Labor will get any political dividend from hitting 225,000, particularly when its opponents are promising to go much lower.
That would be why Burke has been trying to make the case against deeper cuts, warning they would "trash" the economy and services.
Burke rejected the idea of Australia as a nation of "mass migration" — a term used by One Nation and many in the Coalition — as "absurd". And yet Labor has accepted the premise of that debate, that there should be a publicly nominated migration number for which government is accountable.
Once everyone is bidding on NOM, the argument naturally becomes who will go lower.
One Nation want to plunge into the negative before settling at 130,000 in three years' time, while the Coalition will tie its target to housing completion rates and likely settle on a NOM of between 150,000 and 170,000.
Loading
Political control over migration
Labor may want the argument to be about how migration is managed, but in fixing on a target it has given greater legitimacy to the numbers contest.
Every time housing gets tighter, unemployment rises, infrastructure strains or the NOM overshoots, there would be political pressure to revise the number down.
There would be much less political reward for arguing it should go back up.
It's hard to imagine anyone outbidding One Nation leader Pauline Hanson in this auction.
And Labor spends its time explaining why its own reduction is sufficient, then the argument has already moved away from whether cuts are the right response to the underlying problems.
Burke's policy package is largely about gaining control over parts of the migration system that are demand driven like backpacker extensions, student dependants, visa-hopping and overstayers.
But as no one knows better than him, greater control over the system is not the same thing as precise control over NOM.

Police capture suspected serial killer disguised as woman, carrying baby in Brazil
Brazilian police said Friday they had captured a suspected serial killer linked to at least 16 deaths since May, who was arrested while disguised as a woman and carrying a baby.
He claims to have killed more than four times that number.
The suspect was arrested Sunday after a 30-hour police manhunt in a forested area of Paraiba state in northeastern Brazil.
He was wearing a dress and long black wig, which police described as a disguise to evade capture. In a statement, they said he had been carrying a baby in his arms.
Images and video published by local media, including O Globo, showed the suspect with painted nails wearing a striped dress, a dark wig, women's sandals and sunglasses.
Police said the child he was carrying was not related to him. Police did not release details on the baby's condition.
"Although the suspect claimed involvement in 80 homicides, civil police have confirmed his participation in 16 killings in the region, 11 of which he confessed to during questioning," police told AFP.
The 16 homicides all took place since May. The identities of the victims and details of the killings have not been made public.
The suspect was identified by authorities as 33-year-old Jorlan Lopes da Silva, Record R7 reported.
The suspect evaded an earlier attempt to arrest him a few weeks ago after a confrontation with security forces, who consider him a member of an "ultra-violent" criminal group.
In a video of his interrogation obtained by AFP, the man said he acted alone and denied having ties to organized crime.
Instead, he claimed all his victims were "linked to the criminal world" and he was taking justice into his own hands in response to threats against himself and his family.
"I never acted against any family man, mother or working person," he said, denying being a "psychopath."
He said he had committed his first homicide at the age of 13.
After the earlier attempt to arrest the suspect, police seized bulletproof vests, the stock of a submachine gun and over 100 rounds of ammunition, which the man acknowledged were his during questioning. Two other men were arrested during the operation on suspicion of involvement in the crime, according to iG Último Segundo.
Under Brazilian law, he faces a maximum sentence of 40 years in prison, according to Record R7.
The region of Mulungu, where the killings took place, lies 1,553 miles north of Rio de Janeiro.

Air Force Retires EC-130H, Embraces EA-37B, as Davis-Monthan Transitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:56:00 UTC
03:56:00 KST

The 55th Wing officially retired the EC-130H Compass Call aircraft in a ceremony Sept. 18 at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, Ariz., while the 355th Wing there inactivated its A-10 Warthog units, another major transition for the base.
The Compass Call mission is transitioning from the old propeller-driven EC-130s to the sleek EA-37B, which packs the electronic warfare mission into a modified Gulfstream 550 jet. The 55th Electronic Combat Group at Davis-Monthan has five of the new jets on hand, en route to a planned dozen by 2028 and 22 by 2031.
Meanwhile, the 355th is transitioning to a rescue mission as the base prepares to host a new special operations wing.
The new Compass Call jets compress the targeting, jamming, and other electronic warfare missions into a tighter space. About 70 percent of the equipment is unchanged, but instead of 13 Airmen performing Compass Call functions in the EC-130H, the E-37 B needs only nine.
“Its ‘plug-and-play’ architecture allows for rapid software updates and the integration of new capabilities to counter emerging threats and technologies without costly redesigns,” Maj. Claire Fitle, 355th Wing spokesperson, told Air & Space Forces Magazine by email.
The jet has “significantly increased speed, altitude, and range compared with the legacy EC-130H,” Fitle wrote. The equipment can also detect and jam a wider range of enemy systems from farther distances.
The new system is software-driven, allowing rapid updates via software rather than hardware modifications, “dramatically reducing response time … [to] evolving electromagnetic threats,” Fitle wrote.
Decade-long Road to Upgrade
The Air Force began seeking a replacement for the EC-130H in 2014, then awarded L3 Technologies a contract in 2017 to engineer the capability into a smaller airframe. Congress sped up the procurement program two years later, originally expecting to complete procurement in 2026.
The first five aircraft lack some low-band capability, which is anticipated in the remaining aircraft.
BAE Systems and L3Harris delivered the first EA-37B for developmental testing in 2023, and Air Combat Command received the first two airframes in 2024. Initial training sorties began in 2025 and operational testing wrapped up within the year. Contractors will be primarily responsible for maintaining the EA-37Bs at Davis-Monthan, Fitle wrote.
During Operation Epic Fury, they got their first combat exposure—even before the Air Force declared full operational capability.
The EC-130H saw combat action during Operation Just Cause in Panama, 1989, Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Operation Allied Force in Kosovo in 1999, and throughout the Global War on Terror in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria over the past 25 years. It was a workhorse to the end, making its final mission in the early stages of Operation Epic Fury.
The first legacy EC-130H retired in 2021, while the last aircraft conducted its final flight Sept. 2.
The 355th, 492nd, and the A-10
In a parallel event, the 355th inactivated its A-10 Warthog units as well Sept. 18. While the larger Air Force is keeping the popular close air support platform around until the 2030s, the 355th is becoming a “rescue hub,” Fitle wrote.
“Close air support is an enduring mission rather than a single airframe, and the Air Force will continue providing responsive CAS across the joint battlespace through a flexible mix of fifth- and fourth-generation multirole aircraft,” she wrote. “Experienced A-10 aircrew and maintainers are transitioning their close-support expertise directly into these platforms to ensure seamless coverage.”
The wing will continue its CSAR and personnel recovery mission through the 563rd Rescue Group using the HH-60W Jolly Green II helicopter and the HC-130J Combat King II aircraft.
Meanwhile, the 492nd Special Operations Wing is moving to Davis-Monthan, with full operational capability expected between 2028-29. The move comes as the USAF has restructured the former training wing.
The special ops wing will backfill the 355th’s A-10 capabilities by basing its OA-1K Skyraider II and CV-22 Ospreys at Davis-Monthan as well, expanding strike and specialized operational capabilities.
The former “high-end” strike missions will be absorbed by fifth-generation aircraft across USAF.

How Zach Cregger's Resident Evil Delivers a Subversive and Shocking Ending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:54:38 UTC
03:54:38 KST

Warning: This post contains spoilers for Resident Evil.
For a movie based on a video game series that's made a name for itself as a testament to human resilience and survival against impossible odds, Zach Cregger's Resident Evil sure serves up a brutal kick in the teeth of an ending. For fans of the video games' traditionally triumphant resolutions, it's a narrative decision that's likely to be divisive. But if you're willing to lean in to the Weapons filmmaker's penchant for expectations-upending final acts, it's one that offers some good old fashioned horror nihilism.
Cregger's adaptation tells an original story in the Resident Evil universe rather than faithfully adapting any of the games, building on previous films, or pulling in legacy characters. Still, the movie manages to successfully capture the atmosphere and experience of playing through a new installment in gaming’s most storied survival horror franchise, first launched in 1996 by Japanese developer Capcom. Like a fair share of Resident Evil leads who came before him, our protagonist, medical courier Bryan Hodukavich (Austin Abrams), finds himself thrown into a nightmarish fight for survival against uber-aggressive biological monstrosities. Ammo is scarce, obstacles are everywhere, and perhaps most relatably, Bryan has no real idea how to operate the progression of increasingly high-caliber guns he picks up along the way.
The film opens with Bryan—whose newly pregnant girlfriend Michele is waiting at home to discuss their future—accepting a last-minute double-pay delivery job transporting a high-priority Schedule A organ carrier case up through the snowy mountains to Raccoon City General Hospital.
Unfortunately, Bryan's situation quickly turns from dangerous to unbelievable to dire after he accidentally hits a woman with his car who turns out to have been infected by a mutating zombie virus that the shadowy Umbrella Corporation accidentally unleashed on the city a few hours prior.
By the time Bryan learns he is actually carrying the final ingredient needed to synthesize a cure to the virus, he has already fought off several infected individuals, who, to his horror, didn't exactly die after being shot in the head. Instead, their remains fused together to transform into a grotesque, Cronenberg-esque amalgamation of limbs and tentacles intent on hunting Bryan down. Not to mention Bryan was also been bitten by one of the aforementioned infected, making his race for an antidote all the more pressing.
How does Resident Evil end?
Despite having to face off with a horde of dive-bombing zombies, an acid-vomiting monster, and a heavily infected maternity ward, among other horrors, Bryan does eventually make it to the secure lab on the 28th floor of Raccoon City General Hospital. However, by the time he hands the key to the cure over to a team led by Umbrella Corporation scientist Carl (Zach Cherry), he has already started to transform.
Just as the team completes the antidote, which they plan to hand over to a unit of National Guard soldiers set to land on the roof at any minute, Bryan's grotesquely mutated limbs start lashing out and savagely killing the scientists before dragging their corpses in to meld with Bryan's body. Bryan begs for one of the scientists to simply stick him with the syringe of cure and end it, but they're all either quickly incapacitated or too frightened. Eventually, monster Bryan crashes through a window with the last-surviving scientist in his grip and there's a final chance for the technician to inject him with the antidote. It seems like he's about to succeed, but in a bleak twist, Bryan knocks the syringe from his hand and it goes crashing down dozens of stories into the darkness below. Bryan roars as the National Guard helicopters circle, and it seems like all hope of preventing a total zombie apocalypse are gone.
There is no moment of triumph or last-minute turn of the tide. Instead, the screen cuts to black and the movie is over, leaving you contemplating just how futile all of Bryan's efforts were. To fans who were hoping for a more conventional Resident Evil final boss battle, it's an ending that may come off as a bit mean-spirited. But according to Cregger, he felt just as assured about this choice of kicker as he did about the much-discussed climax of Weapons.
"I remember when I thought of that moment and that was an 'aha' moment. I was excited. I was like, 'That is perfect,'" he told Men's Health. "There's a similar thing at the end of Resident Evil and I remember, when I had the idea of how this movie should end, I was like, 'That is it.' And it feels good when you know you can stop searching. I'm always looking for the next, 'How can I improve every idea?' and sometimes when you get an idea where you're like, 'Nope, that's what it is,' that's a good feeling. It's like, 'That is a solid table with four legs. Leave it alone.' It's nice when that's the end of the movie too. If you know that you can stick the landing, then you're in good shape."
However, Bryan dying an agonizing and untimely death apparently doesn't necessarily mean Cregger is done with Resident Evil as a whole. "I can’t help thinking about other places this story could go. I’ve got ideas," he told the Playlist. "Let’s see what happens."

Hegseth has promoted a heavy focus on policies that he says are necessary to maximise military preparedness but that critics say are importing right-wing culture war issues into the military.

Chinese man sentenced to prison for 2024 Switzerland knife attack on children
GENEVA - A Chinese man who in 2024 knifed a group of children on their way to a daycare centre in Switzerland, wounding three of them, was on Sept 18 sentenced to 15 years in prison.
The man, whose identity was not disclosed by Swiss media, was found guilty of attempted murder by a court in Zurich, the city where the crime happened, the Keystone-ATS news agency reported. He is to lodge an appeal.
The Chinese man, aged 23 at the time, attacked the children on Oct 1, 2024 as they were walking along a residential street to the daycare centre. Three boys aged five were wounded and had to be hospitalised.
A daycare worker accompanying the children, with the help of a passerby, overpowered the man, who was arrested at the scene.
Prosecutors said the man, who was studying in Switzerland, confessed under questioning.
The court’s judge said the man acted “coldly” and “without scruple”.
His defence lawyer had argued for an acquittal on the basis of a psychiatric report suggesting that his client had mental issues and was not responsible for his actions at the time of the attack.
On Sept 17 during his trial, the man told the court that three weeks before the attack he heard a voice in his head telling him to kill children, according to Keystone-ATS.
The prosecution dismissed the testimony, saying he had not previously told investigators about that.
Instead, the prosecution insisted that the man had carefully planned the attack over weeks.
Prosecutors alleged that, in August 2024, the man had asked ChatGPT what criminal consequences he would face for randomly stabbing victims and issued prompts about human anatomy, Keystone-ATS reported. AFP

Sources say Australia withdrew from West Bank sanctions talks ahead of statement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:47:19 UTC
03:47:19 KST

Sources say Australia withdrew from West Bank sanctions talks ahead of statement
In short:
A coalition of 12 countries that released a statement on the West Bank last week were "disappointed" when Australia did not join them.
Australia was involved in discussions but withdrew late in the process, sources said.
The Australian government said it was "working closely together towards the same objective" with international partners.
European diplomats say they were surprised and disappointed that Australia baulked at joining a UK-led move to impose trade sanctions on West Bank Israeli businesses.
Last week the United Kingdom announced a major policy shift by targeting Israeli settlements with sanctions, declaring that ethnic cleansing was taking place in the West Bank and declaring Israel's occupation of the territory unlawful.
The move was followed by a collective statement from 12 governments — the UK, France, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden — which said they would also either commit to or consider targeting trade with illegal settlements.
In the lead-up to the statement's release, EU officials had been working to try and build a wide coalition of countries to ramp up pressure on Israel.
Australia had been involved in those discussions — and had indicated it was open to taking more action on the West Bank — only to ultimately decide it would not join the action reasonably late in proceedings, multiple diplomatic sources from different countries told the ABC.
According to four diplomatic sources, Australia was involved in the discussions around the sanctions until close to the statement's finalisation.
Canada was the only country outside Europe to put its name to the statement, despite those efforts to bring in a wider coalition.
Why Australia did not join coordinated move
In the past year, Australia has acted in concert with a large group of countries to try to press Israel over Gaza and over its treatment of Palestinians, including the joint push for countries to recognise the State of Palestine at the UN General Assembly in New York one year ago.
But its absence from the collective statement has created a gap in foreign policy between allies that had been moving in step.
The ABC spoke to eight diplomatic sources, based across Sydney, Canberra, Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, who said the coalition of countries had hoped Australia would join the statement and were disappointed when it did not.
The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly on the issue.
In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Australia and international partners were "working closely together towards the same objective, even if we are not all taking exactly the same measures at the same time".
"We are concerned blanket import bans present practical challenges, including how to ensure they do not inadvertently harm Palestinian businesses, workers and livelihoods. The UK government has acknowledged these challenges as they work on their legislation over the next year," they said.
"In the meantime, Australia is pursuing further targeted measures, in coordination with international partners, to deter illegal settlements and settler violence."
EU allies expected Australia to join action
One official from a Nordic country that joined the statement said they believed Australia was "likely" to sign on. They said Canberra had "missed an opportunity" to apply meaningful pressure on Israel by backing away from it.
Another official said they were "disappointed" that Australia did not sign the statement.
They said the Albanese government clearly had reservations about the impacts of the sanctions and their enforceability, but speculated that the government was also worried about the domestic political impact.
A different EU official said they had seen some text for an earlier version of the statement, which had included Australia.
It was not clear whether Australia had ever agreed to be part of the statement or was just written into a draft.
It was only on the day the statement was released that two sources involved in the negotiations realised Australia had not joined, they told the ABC.
Two EU officials said they were "surprised" Australia did not sign on.
But another official from a different country also involved with negotiations painted a different picture, saying that while Australia had signalled it was open to signing on, Canberra had never given a concrete commitment to join it.
The prospects of Australia following the UK may have also been complicated by local Australian politics, multiple sources suggested.
Some sources speculated the pressure Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been under since the Bondi terror attacks, and the criticism from Jewish groups that the federal government has not been strong enough on antisemitism, may have played a part in Australia's decision not to announce sanctions last week.
Other sources suggested internal politics meant the federal government could not pull together an aligned position in time to join the statement.
Just two months ago, at the Labor Party's national conference, MP and former Albanese government cabinet minister Ed Husic had pushed — unsuccessfully — for the party to take almost identical measures to those announced by the United Kingdom.
UK 'ethnic cleansing' statement caught officials off guard
Multiple sources from signatory countries also said they were caught off guard by UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's announcement that preceded the joint statement.
Mr Miliband told the British parliament there was "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank and that Israel was turning a "blind eye" to it.
Loading...
He also announced the British government's formal position was that the occupation of the West Bank was illegal, bringing the UK in line with the International Court of Justice 2024 advisory opinion.
His statement was a departure from the language agreed upon in the final joint statement, one EU source said.
Mr Miliband became the first UK foreign secretary to declare the West Bank occupation illegal and describe settlers' actions as "ethnic cleansing", marking a shift in the country's policy on Israel.
Australia 'ready to take more action'
Israel has been facing increasing international pressure over intensifying settler violence in the West Bank and its rapid expansion of settlements in the territory.
In August, four European countries released a joint statement condemning Israel's plans to move forward with a controversial development that would effectively split the West Bank in two.
Israel's occupation of the West Bank, and settlements in the territory, are considered illegal under international law.
Israeli human rights organisation B'Tselem this week released a report that concluded Israeli policies in the West Bank were "eliminating Palestinian collective existence".
Israel has denied accusations of ethnic cleansing and rejects that its occupation of the West Bank, or its settlements, are illegal.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the Senate last week that Australia would not be taking the same action as the UK, saying the government was instead "pursuing further targeted measures in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence".
In June, Australia joined the UK, Canada, France and Norway in coordinated sanctions against Israeli networks involved in financing, enabling and carrying out violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
At the time, in a statement, Australia said it stood "ready to take more action if the Government of Israel does not take urgent steps to address the situation on the ground".

The measure comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Managua following constitutional reforms approved by Nicaragua's National Assembly in the first of two required legislative votes earlier this month.
The reforms extend the presidential term from six to seven years and allow authorities to bar individuals deemed to have acted against the country from participating in elections. The changes would also further strengthen the powers of Ortega and his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo.
Rubio has separately urged US partners to stop “business as usual” with the Ortega-Murillo government, saying Washington would work through the Organization of American States to increase pressure on Managua.
The move comes as Washington increases pressure on the Ortega-Murillo government, with US officials calling for greater international pressure on Managua and measures aimed at supporting a democratic transition.

AICS Project on Heritage Conservation in Cartagena de Indias Gets Underway
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
20:40:33 CEST
03:40:33 KST

With the start of renovation and waterproofing work on the roof of the Cathedral of Saint Catherine of Alexandria in Cartagena de Indias, the project “Sustainable Tourism and Enhancement of the Walls of Cartagena de Indias,” promoted by the Italian government through the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS). The announcement was made by the Italian Ambassador to Colombia, Giancarlo Maria Curcio, and the municipal administration of Cartagena de Indias. “This necessary preventive measure aims to ensure the sustainability of future efforts to preserve and enhance the historical, cultural, and religious heritage represented by the Cathedral. Once the physical integrity of the building has been secured, we will be able to proceed with the enhancement of the elements that tell our history and identity, as well as the important contributions made by Italian clergy and artists. The project therefore sets out a clear roadmap: first, to protect the structure, and then to proceed with the enhancement of its heritage features,” the Ambassador stated in a press release. This initial phase is part of a much broader and more ambitious initiative promoted by Italy, which integrates three components—“conservation and restoration, sustainable tourism, and training”— — with the goal of safeguarding the city’s heritage and ensuring that it “remains a living element, connected to its history, its identity, and opportunities for development.” The Cathedral project represents the first step in this comprehensive strategy, which includes other planned interventions in the fortified area of the Caribbean city—such as the La Tenaza Bastion, the “Murallita del Diablo” (Little Devil’s Wall), and a future elevated walkway connecting the bastions of San Ignacio and San Francisco Javier—all aimed at creating new pedestrian tourist routes in the historic center. These initiatives are part of the largest international cooperation project ever undertaken by Cartagena de Indias in the areas of “heritage conservation, promotion of sustainable tourism, and strengthening of the local economy” and were made possible thanks to a 3-million-euro donation from the Italian government, coordinated by the Italian Embassy and AICS. “This project demonstrates how international cooperation can translate into concrete actions for our city,” noted María Mercedes Abondano, director of international cooperation for the Municipality of Cartagena de Indias.

Carpathian Summit participants sign declaration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:40:00 UTC
03:40:00 KST

Carpathian Summit participants sign declaration
The Office of the President reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
At Ukraine’s initiative, the participants established the Carpathian Integration Initiative as a platform for coordinating joint efforts aimed at deepening European integration.
The participating countries intend to facilitate cooperation among the states of the region, EU institutions, and other interested partners, including through annual summits and other events. They also plan to coordinate efforts to strengthen good-neighborly relations, cross-border cooperation, economic ties, security, and sustainable development in the Carpathian region.
The countries agreed to strengthen energy resilience by developing electricity, heating, and gas infrastructure, while actively expanding distributed generation, renewable energy sources, and energy efficiency.
In addition, the countries will support the restoration and modernization of critical infrastructure to enhance resilience, security, and adaptability to long-term threats, attract investment in energy facilities, and develop new generation capacity and energy storage systems.
The participating states also intend to pay particular attention to protecting the unique biodiversity of the Carpathians, preserving cultural landscapes, the traditional way of life of mountain communities and their cultural heritage. They will also promote joint infrastructure projects to integrate the region’s transport and logistics infrastructure into the European transport network, modernize border infrastructure, and develop modern transport corridors.
The parties plan to promote tourism opportunities in the Carpathian region, showcase its natural, historical, and cultural heritage, create joint cultural and tourism routes, support local cultural initiatives and traditional crafts, foster the development of creative industries in the region, and encourage the exchange of experience and best practices among the countries in the areas of veterans’ policy and support for veterans.
The Summit participants noted that the Carpathian Initiative can be a tool for supporting the gradual integration of candidates on their path to EU membership. The leaders of the participating states believe that successful implementation of the Initiative will strengthen the stability and resilience of the countries in the region and make an additional contribution to joint efforts to ensure lasting peace on the European continent.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced today the launch of a new format, the Carpathian Eight (C8), comprising Ukraine, Romania, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Austria, and Serbia.

SRINAGAR: A trade facilitation centre (TFC) at Salamabad in border town Uri, which once facilitated duty-free, cashless barter trade between J&K and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), will now be used for border tourism, ending speculation about resumption of trade through the route.A senior tourism department official confirmed the govt had authorised the department to utilise the TFC located in Baramulla district for tourism-related activities. “The larger objective is to use Salamabad as a gateway to the wider Uri border tourism circuit,” the official said. He added that the emphasis will be on “regulated, responsible and curated border tourism”, ensuring that these remain fully aligned with security and administrative requirements.Salamabad TFC, around 100 km north of Srinagar, was originally established for cross-LoC trade. Following the suspension of such trade in 2019, the facility has remained unutilised for its original purpose.After improved relations in 2008, both India and Pakistan decided to allow cross-LoC trade and travel on certain conditions as part of confidence-building measures (CBMs). However, in April 2019, the Centre suspended the facilities saying the trade routes were being misused for funneling illegal weapons, narcotics, and fake currency.
“During ongoing investigations of certain cases by NIA, it has been brought out that a significant number of trading concerns engaged in LoC trade are operated by persons closely associated with banned terrorist organisations involved in fuelling terrorism/separatism,” a Union home ministry (MHA) release had said then. The statement also mentioned that some individuals, who had crossed over and joined terror outfits, had opened trading firms in Pakistan.
The cross-LoC travel (bus service) and trade were seen as two of the biggest CBMs between the neighbours in decades. Then PM Manmohan Singh flagged off Karwaan-e-Aman (peace caravan), the first cross-LoC bus service that connected Srinagar with Muzaffarabad in PoK, on April 7, 2005.
Cross-LoC barter trade began on Oct 21, 2008, through two routes -- Salamabad (Uri)-Muzaffarabad (PoK) and Poonch-Rawalakot (PoK). Traders on either side were permitted to exchange 21 mutually agreed items.Both sides constructed TFCs 5km inside LoC. In J&K, one TFC came up at Salamabad and the other at Chakan da bagh in Jammu’s Poonch district. Trade was allowed through both routes four days a week.

Now Back in Uniform: At Least 134 Airmen, Guardians Who Refused COVID Vaccine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:33:18 UTC
03:33:18 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—More than 130 Airmen and Guardians have returned to service after leaving the military rather than receive the COVID-19 vaccine. And more could follow, an Air Force official said.
Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs Richard Anderson said that, as of Sept. 15, 137 individuals have applied for reinstatement so far, and 48 have been accepted. Another 86 have returned through the reaccession process, for a total of 134 service members have already rejoined the ranks.
The two routes back are distinct: Reinstatement is slower, requiring interested veterans to apply to the Air Force Board for Correction of Military Records. If successful, the payoff is they will be eligible for back pay and other benefits—offset by whatever they earned in civilian jobs while separated. Reaccession, which is faster, skips the board process but also does not include back pay. A third option is to go through reaccession and only then apply for reinstatement after they have rejoined the ranks.
The Air Force and Space Force involuntarily separated about 600 Airmen and Guardsians for refusing the COVID shot: then-Undersecretary of the Air Force Gina Ortiz Jones pegged the number at 610 in early 2023, and the Air Force Review Boards Agency said it identified 595 cases in a review earlier this year.
But others chose to leave when their service commitment was up rather than be vaccinated, and they are eligible to rejoin as well. Thousands of Airmen and Guardians sought medical and religious exemptions and refused the mandatory shots in 2021 and 2022. But the number that left voluntarily before the mandate was lifted in early 2023 is unclear.
Since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the Pentagon has made a concerted effort to make good on a campaign promise to restore those to service who departed because of the mandate, which was ordered by then-Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin. Current Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in April 2025 that his department was “welcoming actively back those warriors of conscience.”
Since then, the Pentagon has extended the deadline for applying until April 2027, and has reduced the minimum service obligation for those returning from four years to two.
Anderson and his team have also taken steps to ease the process for those who wish to return. In August, they announced medical processing and board reviews would take place simultaneously to speed the reinstatement process, and they hired case managers to help those seeking to return to service.
“We now, I think, have stabilized criteria and expectations,” Anderson said. “We have done a very sustained comms program to tell the affected universe that they are welcome back and welcome to apply … and we’ll continue to to advertise very heavily to get worthy Airmen and Guardians back in uniform.”
According to statistics compiled by the Department of the Air Force in December 2022, just before the COVID vaccine mandate was lifted by an act of Congress, 97.6 percent of the 490,000 members of the Active-Duty Air Force and Space Force, Air National Guard, and Air Force Reserve got fully vaccinated, leaving about 11,700 unvaccinated. The department noted approximately 1,080 religious and administration exemptions to the mandate at the time.

Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:32:24 UTC
03:32:24 KST

Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
Buffett will become chairman emeritus immediately and his son Howard will become chairman.
Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway in the next step of the transition at the top of the $1 trillion conglomerate he led for more than six decades.
Buffett, 96, will become chairman emeritus and will take on his new role immediately, nine months after handing the CEO reins to longtime lieutenant Greg Abel, the company said Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why does Canada want to join the Europe-led JEF military partnership?
- list 2 of 4Asian Games 2026: All to know about the dates, venues and sports
- list 3 of 4US voter opposition to war on Iran grows to new highs: Poll
- list 4 of 4UEFA, CONCACAF challenge FIFA on reserves and demand $10m payout to members
His son, Howard, will become Berkshire Hathaway’s new chairman, part of a long-planned succession. Howard Buffett has been on the Berkshire Hathaway board since 1993.
Warren Buffett is credited with transforming Berkshire from a failing textile company into a $1.1 trillion conglomerate while building an investment philosophy that influenced generations of investors and executives, making him one of the most consequential figures in the modern corporate United States.
Berkshire’s Class B shares were last down 0.3 percent in premarket trading. Buffett’s reputation has also been reflected in the company’s valuation, with investors for years ascribing a “Buffett premium” to its shares.
Berkshire remains the only financial firm in the trillion-dollar market-value club dominated by technology giants.
“It was always a matter of when, not if. Buffett has made a graceful exit,” said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
“Berkshire has had years to prepare for this transition, so this feels more like the completion of a carefully planned succession than a sudden changing of the guard.”
A six-decade legacy
“Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me,” Buffett, 96, who has been with Berkshire since 1965, wrote in a letter to shareholders on Friday.
Buffett’s influence has extended far beyond Berkshire, shaping generations of corporate leaders and investors with his emphasis on long-term thinking, disciplined capital allocation and straightforward management.
“The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian,” Abel said in a statement on Friday.
CEOs have looked to Buffett, often known as the Oracle of Omaha in a nod to the city he lives in, as a sounding board on everything from acquisitions and succession to navigating periods of market turmoil. His annual shareholder meetings became a gathering point for investors.
“As Chairman Emeritus, Mr Buffett will remain a member of the Board of Directors and will continue to offer his valued judgment and perspective,” Berkshire said in a statement.
Buffett first announced plans to step away from the conglomerate in May 2025, surprising shareholders and analysts despite his age. After decades at the helm, he had become synonymous with the company, making his succession one of the most closely watched in the US corporate world.
Berkshire’s businesses include Geico car insurance, the BNSF railroad, many energy and industrial companies, Dairy Queen ice cream, and grizzled brands such as the World Book Encyclopedia. It also owns hundreds of billions of dollars of both stocks and US Treasuries.
In the second quarter, its operating profit rose 16 percent to $12.98bn, topping analyst forecasts. Net income more than doubled to $25.67bn, including unrealised gains and losses on stocks that Omaha, Nebraska-based Berkshire still owns.
‘It’s not rocket science’
Unlike his father, Howard Buffett, known as Howie, would not have a management role as chairman, and his main responsibility would be to preserve Berkshire’s culture.
That culture includes letting Berkshire’s operating businesses handle their day-to-day affairs without interference from upper management, though Abel is widely seen as more eager than Warren Buffett to address performance shortfalls.
“Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet,” Buffett said. “Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against.”
Abel has direct oversight of several Berkshire business lines, while Vice Chairman Ajit Jain oversees insurance and newly installed President Adam Johnson oversees consumer, services and retail subsidiaries.
Howard Buffett had his own definition of Berkshire’s culture.
“It’s not rocket science,” he told the Wall Street Journal in January 2025. “The culture is to keep things simple, to do what you need to do, but don’t do a lot of things you don’t need to do, treat people fairly, respect your managers, respect your shareholders. Tell them the bad news upfront; be honest.”

====================================================================================================

In a world of conflict and terrifying new weapons, where is the UN?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

analysis
The UN often feels damned to irrelevance, but it is needed now more than ever
When Anthony Albanese and Penny Wong attended the United Nations General Assembly 12 months ago, it felt like something significant might be happening.
Australia joined a number of other nations in recognising the state of Palestine. The world was scrabbling to regroup around the chaos unleashed by Donald Trump. The UN was itself fighting for survival amid Trump's hostile assault on it.
This year, things feel like they will be a bit more… prosaic. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is due to finish his term at the end of the year so lobbying is in full swing on the question of his replacement.
Australia is lobbying for a non-permanent place on the Security Council for the 2029-30 term.
That's something that Australia has always taken reasonably seriously — though outsiders might wonder why, given veto powers of the permanent members of the Council (the US, Russia, China, France and the UK) means it rarely makes significant decisions.
The Security Council is still seen as an important platform for smaller countries.
Australian leadership "of the Council's response to the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17, and the first Council resolution on small arms and light weapons are prominent examples" of what occasional membership of the Security Council can achieve, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade website says.
And there is a particularly long history for Australia with the Security Council, given the significant role the country, and External Affairs Minister HV 'Doc' Evatt, played in the establishment of the UN in the first place. It was one of the first members of the Council in 1946 in acknowledgement of that role, and in fact even chaired its first session.
What's on the UN's agenda?
The hostility of the Trump administration to the UN — and for that matter many multinational institutions — often feels it damns it to irrelevance.
(In July, the US also reportedly attempted to enlist its NATO allies in a campaign to "systematically dismantle" the International Criminal Court.)
But the UN continues to play important roles, to the extent its much reduced funding allows, in humanitarian work and peacekeeping.
Those activities would only seem more important just now, given the increasingly intractable and widening conflicts in the Middle East and Europe.
Yet strangely the escalation of those conflicts doesn't seem to be reflected in any material actions contemplated by the UN when leaders meet there next week.
There will be a "two state" conference where leaders will discuss events in Israel.
But there are no signs of any further movement to try to address the lack of progress in Gaza, nor the increasing settler violence and land grabs by Israel in the occupied West Bank.
This is despite the fact that the Trump Board of Peace proposal for Gaza — to which the Security Council gave its blessing last year — has gone absolutely nowhere since then.
There seems to be no talk of any further UN resolutions on these issues. Or of Australia pushing for them, even as it now finds itself at odds over West Bank trade sanctions with the countries it acted with on the recognition of Palestine last year.
Last year's meeting of the UN happened before the US and Israel attacked Iran, and before events seemed to turn for a while in Ukraine's favour before, in more recent times, looking as if they may have turned in Russia's favour.
And it happened before the closure of the Strait of Hormuz gave a whole new impetus to the long conflict in Yemen by increasing the strategic importance of the Red Sea.
These developments feel to have only tipped the scales determining world events further towards those possessing weapons and away from those pursuing diplomacy and multilateral action.
Drone warfare in Ukraine
The wars in Ukraine and in the Middle East are now being transformed by defensive weapons being depleted, or running out altogether, while new forms of offensive weapons are arriving.
In Ukraine, analysts note the arrival of the newest iteration of drone warfare — but this time it is not drone innovation on the Ukrainian side as it has so often been this past year.
Instead, Russia is using Iranian-sourced attack drones with a terrifying new feature: the capacity to travel at jet speed, thanks to turbojet engines rather than propellers, carrying large payloads, at considerable distance. For all intents and purposes, these are likened to a cruise missile, but much cheaper to build.
It was one of these Shahed 136 drones — a new version called the Geran 5 — that hit a train station near the Ukrainian-Polish border, well to the west of Kyiv, just after a train carrying a range of European officials had passed through and while former Central Intelligence Agency chief David Petraeus was in the station.
The managing editor of Foreign Policy, Ravi Agrawal, sketched a bleak picture this week after returning from Kyiv.
"We're coming up against the cold months now, and Russia's been developing about maybe 3,000 of these jet-powered drones a week", he said.
"That means that, come the winter season, it'll probably have tens of thousands of these drones ready to go. And it could shoot them at all forms of civilian and energy infrastructure."
What this is going to end up meaning, Agrawal said, "is that Ukraine could lose energy supplies, power supplies. It could get very cold, very dark for the Ukrainian people."
Agrawal observed that "one could have made the case a few months ago that Ukraine was in the ascendancy".
"It was really beginning to attack Russian energy installations. They had made Putin fearful to the extent that he low keyed his Victory Day parade, which he cares about a lot."
Loading
Germany's weapons transformation
But Russia can now target passenger trains on Ukraine's western borders, as well as penetrate the airspace of Lithuania, Poland and Germany.
While analysts vainly searched for signals about what had been achieved at the recent meeting in Moscow between Donald Trump's envoys and Vladimir Putin, you have to assume that they were prompted by Trump altering his assessment of who may come out a winner from this war, after briefly putting the case that Ukraine had the upper hand.
The same drones being fired at Ukraine can be used by the Iranians, of course, in their assault on Gulf states and US facilities located there.
Like Ukraine, the Gulf states have run out of interceptors, making them increasingly vulnerable to attacks, including those on Saudi Arabia from Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen.
Donald Trump was this week dismissing calls for the US to give more immediate assistance to Saudi Arabia in fighting the Houthis, despite the threat their move along the coast of Yemen now poses to global oil markets.
The sudden urgent need for armaments — and the transformation of many economies into weapons manufacturers — notably Türkiye, Poland and now Germany — changes many geopolitical equations.
Two more states in Germany, in the old East, will have elections this weekend, with uncertain outcomes. But German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is concerned enough — and worried enough about his own future — that he cancelled his trip to the UN.
Just consider the spectre of a Germany run by a far-right party, openly sympathetic to Moscow, that has been transforming itself into one of the world's major weapons manufacturing hubs.
It casts manoeuvring at the UN headquarters in a rather irrelevant light.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.
