US prosecutors accuse Huawei of ‘far-reaching criminal scheme’ spanning decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:28:45 UTC
02:28:45 KST

CHINA CAPITAL
US prosecutors accuse Huawei of ‘far-reaching criminal scheme’ spanning decades
The Chinese tech giant is on trial in New York for allegedly violating U.S. sanctions on Iran and stealing trade secrets as it built its global telecommunications empire.
The U.S. government has long warned, in sweeping terms, that the Chinese tech giant Huawei is effectively an arm of the Chinese state that acts with impunity on the global stage, including allegedly violating U.S. sanctions. Over the last two weeks, U.S. prosecutors have begun to make that case, labeling Huawei a “criminal enterprise,” in what could be a lengthy trial in a New York federal court.
Huawei enacted “a far-reaching criminal scheme extending over twenty years,” according to Department of Justice prosecutor Taylor Stout. “Crime was an important business strategy.”
Nearly eight years after the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed its indictment against Huawei, the company is facing 12 felony charges, including that it conspired to steal technologies from U.S. competitors and business partners. The federal government also alleges that Huawei lied to its Western banking partners about doing business in Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions. No individuals have been charged.
Huawei’s lawyers rejected the government’s characterization, with Brian Heberlig, one of at least a dozen attorneys working for the defense, arguing that the charges concerned “disconnected incidents.”
“It’s about competition, not conspiracy,” Heberlig said.
In December 2018, Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Vancouver at the request of U.S. officials and charged with fraud. After a lengthy period of house arrest, Meng reached a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. authorities in 2021 in which she admitted to lying to HSBC and other banks about a Huawei subsidiary’s business in Iran. That admission will likely be introduced during the trial.
As reported in China Capital, ICIJ’s recent investigation into Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Huawei had leaned on its close relations with the state-owned bank to insulate itself from the fallout of Meng’s arrest. After the Justice Department unveiled its indictment, the company’s bankers at ICBC’s London branch facilitated a transfer of $1.3 billion in “emergency cash” from London to a branch in China without informing compliance staff.
The federal government’s investigations of Huawei go back to at least the Obama administration. Some of the alleged crimes occurred around the turn of the century. The allegations include that Huawei stole technology from U.S. companies like the cell service provider T-Mobile and the networking giant Cisco. Prosecutors have claimed that Huawei paid bounties to employees for recruiting workers to leave rivals, bringing their trade secrets to Huawei, which employs about 210,000 people in more than 170 countries and regions. In one incident raised at trial, a Huawei employee allegedly snuck into a booth at a trade show to take photos of Fujitsu network equipment and was spotted by a security guard.
For years, U.S. intelligence and government officials have expressed concern that, along with being a dominant player in global telecommunications, Huawei is a tool of Chinese statecraft, enabling espionage and repression in autocratic countries like North Korea. Huawei’s global expansion, officials warned, might allow the Chinese government to eavesdrop on numerous countries.
In the first days of the current trial, Parham Baheshti, a former engineer at Mobinet, an Iranian telecommunications firm, testified that Huawei, working with Iranian intelligence, built a domestic surveillance system that could spy on users of Mobinet’s wireless network. “They help a dictatorship to rule and suppress people,” Baheshti said.
Huawei’s defense lawyers argued that the company furnished a so-called lawful interception program similar to the ones found in many other countries, both democratic and otherwise, which sometimes run on equipment from Western tech companies.
Judge Ann Donnelly told jurors last week China and the Chinese Communist Party “are not on trial.” But the backdrop of great power competition, especially in a trial that began with a focus on Huawei’s business in Iran in alleged violation of U.S. sanctions, is hard to ignore. Jurors were asked if they had any family ties to China and scrutinized for their opinions on the tech industry.
The trial is one of the biggest in the history of the Eastern District of New York, with hundreds of pieces of evidence expected to be introduced, along with numerous witnesses who have worked for or with Huawei in the U.S., Iran, and other countries. Judge Donnelly said she hopes that proceedings will conclude by Christmas, but the trial may run into next year.
“What is so remarkable is that the case is going to trial,” Duke University Law Professor Brandon Garrett said in an email to ICIJ. “The vast bulk of criminal cases, including corporate cases, are resolved through negotiated settlements. Here, the company has already been sanctioned and may have had little incentive to settle.”
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet with President Donald Trump on Sept. 24 in Washington, D.C., where they will discuss issues such as AI safety and American citizens imprisoned in China. President Xi has championed Huawei, which just last month reached a potential agreement with the Egyptian government to build AI data centers. The State Department, hoping to stymie a potential victory for China’s tech industry, has reportedly encouraged U.S. companies to outbid Huawei’s offer.
If the world’s largest telecoms firm is eventually found guilty, it’s not clear what the Justice Department, or the Trump administration, may want as restitution.
“Should the government prevail, what consequences can be imposed on top of existing sanctions?” Garrett, the law professor, said. “What assets are available to pay fines, for example, if the company is found liable?”

That is the message Irish Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister (Tánaiste), Simon Harris, shared with Euronews in an exclusive interview
Harris pushed back against recent remarks made by US President Donald Trump, who blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian diesel refineries for creating a shortage. Oil prices are hovering around $108 per barrel.
"The reason there's a major energy crisis in the world right now is because the Strait of Hormuz is closed," Harris said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes With. "I always make the point, and I would make it again today, that the greatest economic intervention we could see is de-escalation in the Middle East," he added.
He noted that this became evident during the summer, when there was a brief moment of respite in the conflict. "We saw a very rapid fall in the commodity markets and therefore a benefit at the pump."
Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil and gas facilities are squeezing Moscow’s oil output and having an impact globally, as Russia is one of the world’s largest oil producers, but experts agree the current energy crisis is primarily caused by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz – the transit route for 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies.
The situation has escalated after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, following drone attacks earlier this month from Iran-backed allied Houthis and Iraq.
"From an economic perspective, I'm very concerned [after] what we've seen on oil markets in recent days," Harris said. "I'm also very concerned about the fact that we aren't seeing de-escalation; we're actually seeing an escalation and indeed more fronts in terms of complications opening up regarding energy."
Windfall tax on the table
It is against the backdrop of mounting energy costs that finance ministers from eurozone countries gathered in Dublin on Friday, rushing to mitigate the rising prices and discussing measures to mitigate the impact on citizens.
One of the ideas circulating among EU ministers at the meeting is a windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility, following calls from several member states to consider this measure.
"Some energy companies are making extraordinarily large profits on the back of this energy crisis," Harris said, noting that they are not doing so by "being innovative," but "because of the chaos that we're seeing in the energy markets as a result of the Strait of Hormuz being closed."
Without pre-empting possible outcomes of the talks, Harris said he would be having an initial conversation on such a tax with ministers in Dublin. Ireland currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency, allowing it to set the work programme and Council meeting agenda.
"It's likely that we will ask the European Commission to further examine this and that we would formally discuss it in Brussels at the next formal [Economic and Finance Council] meeting in October."
World 'cannot become numb to loss of life'
Harris stressed that, aside from the economic importance of ending the Middle East conflict, the world can not turn a blind eye to the human toll either.
"I think while I'm obviously speaking in the capacity of a finance minister, we should never become numb to the loss of life in war, whether that's the loss of life in Ukraine, whether it's the horrific genocide we've seen in Gaza, whether it's a situation in the Middle East more broadly," he said. "We need to see a de-escalation of conflict more broadly in the world."
On settler violence seen in the West Bank against Palestinians, the Tánaiste argued in favour of a tougher stance on Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law.
"I'm massively pro-European, but I think when it comes to Gaza, it's been disappointing, to put it mildly, that more hasn't been done at that coordinated level," Harris said.
Several European countries, including Ireland and more recently the United Kingdom, have announced national bans on the import of all goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
"Member states are listening to their public and are moving ahead, but we would always rather see action at an EU level because we think it's more impactful."
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, recently put forward an EU-wide ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as a "principled stance" for the bloc, comparing illegal settlements in the West Bank to Russia’s occupation of Crimea.

From Symbolism to Strategy: The Expanding Operational Role of Women in Baloch Militancy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:23:00 UTC
02:23:00 KST

On May 22, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), one of the principal armed groups in Pakistan’s Baloch insurgency, announced the formation of a dedicated women’s wing and named Shaynaz Baloch as its commander. The announcement was significant not simply because it placed a woman in a more visible position within the organization, but because it appeared to formalize a trend that has been developing since 2022: the expansion of women’s participation in Baloch militancy from largely symbolic and support roles into direct operational activity.
The development raises a broader question: Why are Baloch militant organizations expanding women’s roles now, and what does this mean for an insurgency historically dominated by men?
The shift can be traced most clearly to April 2022, when Shari Baloch carried out a suicide attack at the Confucius Institute at the University of Karachi, killing three Chinese teachers and their Pakistani driver. The BLA claimed responsibility and presented her as its first female suicide operative. Since then, several other women have been linked to suicide operations attributed to BLA factions. In June 2023, Sumaiya Qalandrani Baloch carried out a suicide attack targeting a military convoy in Turbat. In August 2024, a woman identified by the BLA as Mahal Baloch conducted a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Bela. In March 2025, Mahikhan Baloch carried out another suicide attack against a paramilitary convoy in Kalat.
In November 2025, the trend extended to another major Baloch armed group, the Baloch Liberation Front (BLF), when Zareena Rafiq carried out a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Nokundi. The pattern suggests that the use of women is no longer confined to an isolated form of militant propaganda. It is becoming part of how some Baloch armed groups recruit, operate, and present themselves.
The development became even more visible during the BLA’s January-February 2026 offensive, which the organization called Operation Herof 2.0. The BLA publicized the participation of several women in the coordinated attacks, including female suicide operatives.
Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province by area and one of its least densely populated, has experienced successive waves of Baloch nationalist insurgency, with the current conflict emerging in the early 2000s. The BLA and BLF are among the principal separatist organizations involved. They frame their campaigns around grievances including political marginalization, resource distribution, and alleged abuses by the Pakistani state. Pakistani authorities classify the groups as terrorist organizations and have attributed aspects of the insurgency to external support. The conflict has also acquired a significant international dimension. Balochistan hosts Gwadar Port and other major infrastructure associated with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), making Chinese nationals and projects recurring targets for Baloch militants.
For much of the current insurgency, however, women associated with Baloch nationalism were more visible in political activism, advocacy, and community mobilization than in armed operations. Organizations such as the Baloch Students Organization-Azad (BSO-A) and the Baloch Yakjehti Committee have provided platforms for campaigns concerning enforced disappearances, alleged extrajudicial killings, and other grievances involving the Pakistani state. Women such as Mahrang Baloch and Sammi Deen Baloch have subsequently become prominent advocates on these issues. Karima Mehrab Baloch, who became the first woman to chair BSO-A, was another prominent figure in Baloch nationalist activism before she died in Toronto in December 2020.
This established a largely political role for women within the broader Baloch nationalist movement. But the emergence of women in militant operations since 2022 marks a departure from that pattern. The May announcement of a dedicated women’s wing in the BLA represents a potential further step in this evolution, from individual female participation in militant operations toward a more formal organizational role.
The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. Political grievances, personal experiences, family or social networks, ideological commitment, trauma, and the search for purpose can all influence recruitment. These factors differ from one individual to another.
The organizational incentives are easier to identify. Women can provide militant groups with additional operational flexibility. Gendered assumptions about who constitutes a security threat can affect how individuals are screened, monitored, or approached by security personnel. This does not make women inherently better operatives. Rather, it gives organizations another category of personnel through which they can attempt to exploit gaps in security practices. Female participation can also broaden the pool from which militant organizations recruit. It allows groups to portray their struggle as extending beyond young male fighters and into families and communities.
The propaganda value may be even more important. A female militant challenges the conventional image of an insurgent as a young man carrying a weapon. Baloch militant groups have used photographs, videos, and biographies of female operatives to portray their participation as evidence that the conflict has reached across gender and social boundaries.
However, reducing female militants to passive victims of manipulation obscures their agency and the possibility that some make deliberate ideological or political choices. At the same time, focusing exclusively on agency can obscure the organizational structures that recruit, train, indoctrinate, and deploy them. The analytical challenge is to account for both.
The Baloch case is part of a much broader history of women’s participation in political violence. Research on female suicide bombers has documented substantial participation by women in conflicts ranging from the Middle East to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Secular separatist organizations such as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) were among the groups that developed significant roles for women in their military structures. The LTTE incorporated women into combat units and became particularly associated with female suicide operations. The PKK likewise developed extensive female military and organizational structures.
Later, jihadist organizations including Boko Haram, al-Shabaab, and the Islamic State expanded women’s roles in different ways, including recruitment, propaganda, logistics, and, in some cases, direct participation in attacks. The comparison should not be overstated, however. These organizations differ substantially in ideology, structure, social environment, and strategic objectives. Baloch armed groups are primarily ethno-nationalist and separatist organizations rather than transnational jihadist movements.
The expansion of women’s participation comes amid a broader deterioration in Pakistan’s security environment. The Baloch insurgency is only one component of that deterioration; the resurgence of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), particularly along the Afghan border, has also contributed substantially to the country’s terrorism burden.
The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism in 2025, recording 1,139 terrorism-related deaths and 1,045 incidents. Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa together accounted for more than 74 percent of terrorist attacks and 67 percent of terrorism-related deaths recorded in Pakistan that year. This wider context matters because the emergence of female militants could tempt security institutions toward an overly broad response.
The answer is not simply increased surveillance of women. A poorly designed response could stigmatize women participating in legitimate political activity and further blur the distinction between peaceful activism and militancy. Instead, intelligence assessments should account for women as potential participants across the spectrum of militant activity, including recruitment, propaganda, financing, logistics, and direct operations. At the same time, investigators must distinguish genuine indicators of militant involvement from political dissent, human rights activism, and ordinary civic activity.
That distinction is particularly important in Balochistan, where a significant political and human rights movement exists alongside an armed insurgency. Conflating the two would not only threaten civil liberties; it could also make counterterrorism less effective by expanding the pool of people who feel alienated from the state. The strategic challenge is therefore twofold: prevent militant organizations from turning women’s visibility into an operational advantage, while ensuring that the state’s response does not itself deepen the alienation that those organizations seek to capitalize on. That means combining intelligence-led counterterrorism with community engagement, strategic communication, and efforts to address the grievances that militant organizations seek to exploit.
The shift from symbolic female participation to a more structured operational role is still developing, but the direction is increasingly difficult to ignore.

China Coast Guard rams Philippine ship near Palawan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:16:59 UTC
02:16:59 KST

- A China Coast Guard vessel rammed the Philippine ship BRP Datu Magat Salamat on Sept. 18 during a fuel subsidy mission for Filipino fishermen.
- The Philippine Coast Guard said the collision caused structural damage but no injuries, while China blamed the Philippine vessel for the incident.
A Philippine government ship carrying fuel to Filipino fishermen was struck by a Chinese Coast Guard vessel on Friday, the latest collision in a South China Sea dispute that has grown more dangerous and more frequent throughout 2026.
The Philippine ship, BRP Datu Magat Salamat, belongs to the country’s Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources. It was on what the Philippine Coast Guard called a humanitarian and livelihood mission: bringing fuel subsidies to Filipino fishing boats so they could keep working in waters the Philippines considers its own. The ship was about 54 nautical miles, roughly 100 kilometers, off the coast of Palawan province when the encounter happened, well within the country’s exclusive economic zone.
According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the Chinese vessel, identified as CCG-21585, first cut across the stern of the Filipino ship at around 11:04 a.m. local time, passing within about 10 meters, or 33 feet. Nine minutes later, it repeated the maneuver, this time making contact. Video released by the Philippine Coast Guard captured the moments before impact, with crew members shouting “brace for impact.” The collision left the ship’s starboard side damaged: railings bent and torn loose, metal support structures deformed, and equipment and debris scattered across the deck. No one was hurt, but Philippine Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan ordered additional ships and aircraft to the area to check on the crew and make sure the vessel could continue safely.
The Philippine Coast Guard did not mince words in its account, calling the incident a deliberate strike on a civilian government ship and accusing China of violating international rules for avoiding collisions at sea, a 2016 international tribunal ruling on the South China Sea, and the broader United Nations treaty that governs the world’s oceans.
China’s version of events looks very different. Its coast guard said it was carrying out routine law enforcement work near Sabina Shoal, an area both countries claim, when the Philippine vessel ignored repeated warnings, suddenly changed course, and sped up in a way that put it in the path of the Chinese ship. Beijing said its own crew acted professionally throughout and that responsibility for the collision rests with the Philippine side.
It is a familiar back-and-forth for anyone who has followed the increasingly tense standoff in these waters. China claims sovereignty over nearly the entire South China Sea, a claim so broad that it overlaps with waters the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, and other countries consider their own. In 2016, an international tribunal ruled that China’s claim had no basis under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, but Beijing has never accepted that decision and has continued to assert control through its coast guard and, at times, its navy.
This year alone has brought several similar flashpoints. In July, the Philippines accused Chinese ships of firing water cannons at government vessels near Scarborough Shoal on back-to-back days, and separately said a Philippine Navy crew member was struck on the head with a wooden baton during a tense encounter at Second Thomas Shoal. In March, a Chinese navy frigate closed in dangerously on a Philippine landing ship near Thitu Island in the Spratly Islands, coming close enough that the two vessels nearly collided. And in August 2025, a Chinese coast guard cutter and a Chinese navy destroyer actually collided with each other while chasing a Philippine patrol boat near Scarborough Shoal, a mishap that Manila said badly damaged the Chinese cutter.
What makes Friday’s incident notable isn’t that it’s unprecedented. It’s that the pattern keeps repeating, almost predictably, even as both sides know the world is watching. Fishing boats and government resupply vessels have become the recurring flashpoint, because they represent the practical, everyday reality of who actually controls these waters, regardless of what treaties or tribunals say on paper. Every time a fuel delivery mission turns into a shoving match at sea, it becomes another data point in a dispute that has resisted years of diplomacy.
For now, neither country has signaled a change in approach. The Philippines has continued sending its fisheries and coast guard vessels into the disputed areas as a way of asserting its rights, even knowing confrontations are likely. China has continued treating those missions as intrusions into its own waters. Friday’s collision caused property damage but no injuries, and the Philippine vessel was still able to receive help from other ships sent to the scene. Whether the next encounter ends the same way is, as always in these waters, an open question.

Shipki La and the Battle Over the History of China-India Trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:14:00 UTC
02:14:00 KST

After a six-year hiatus, the China-India border trade via Shipki Pass, a 3,930-meter pass in Himachal Pradesh’s Kinnaur district, resumed on August 1, 2026. After the 2020 Galwan military standoff, the border trade from this pass, often called the “Gateway to Tibet,” was suspended. With limited operations and economic scope but significant political symbolism, the resumption of border trade has also rejuvenated interest in the competing legitimacy narratives over the Tibet question.
According to China’s state-affiliated think tanks and media, border trade via the Shipki L Pass dates to the 7th to 9th centuries when the Tubo Empire reigned over the plateau. China frames trade along this route as a sub-set of the Silk Road. Between the 14th and early 20th centuries, Chinese tellings claim Tibet as a commercial bridge between China and South Asia, while in the late 18th century, the Qing Dynasty of China took measures to standardize trade activities between Tibet and its neighboring countries, for “better management” of Tibet.
As per the Chinese accounts, the “peaceful liberation” of Tibet in 1951 and the signing of the Panchsheel Pact led to the abolishment of India’s trade “privileges” in Tibet and the formalization of a new paradigm for Indo-Tibetan trade.
China claims to have set Sino-Indian border trade free from unequal terms set by colonial rule, ushering in an era of normalized development. Cut to the present: the reopening of Shipki La Pass, despite the minuscule trade volume, is received by Chinese media as a welcome move toward improving China-India strategic ties.
Every aspect of the Chinese reading of history sidelines the Tibetan side of the story. For starters, what the Chinese narrative misses is the independent agency Tibet exercised before 1951.
By contrast, Tibetan scholars characterize Shipki Pass as a major route for trade and cultural exchange between Indian territories and Tibet, independent of Chinese involvement. Consistent with Tibet’s claim to political and commercial autonomy, historical records describe Shipki Pass as a crucial route connecting Tibet with the Kingdom of Bushahar, Ladakh, and Kashmir. The exchange across the regions, involving a variety of products, was governed by gamgya, a traditional informal oath of mutual trust that was respected and maintained across generations.
However, with the development of modern state infrastructure on either side of Shipki Pass and growing geopolitical disputes culminating in the Sino-Indian War in 1962, the centuries-old trade system was fractured.
The Tibetan accounts also challenge the Chinese manipulation of history to appropriate the Shipki Pass trade route into a meta-narrative of the Silk Road. The commentaries consistent with the Tibetan narrative challenge the engulfing of Tibet in Chinese historical narratives as a simple commercial bridge, stripping it of its agency and independent existence.
Tibetan scholars argue that it was the PRC’s administrative and military consolidation post 1951 that led to the dismantling of traditional trade and transit networks, not the British colonial disruption. The PRC’s normalization with India involved the isolation of Tibet and the enforcement of new restrictions on previously autonomous trade practices between India and Tibet
This is not a dispute over mere historical fact-checking. It leads to the question of who holds legitimacy over Tibet, and the framing of the India-China-Tibet relationship since the 1950s.
The re-opening of Shipki Pass – often framed in terms of the overall China-India relationship – is seeing one version of history eclipse the other. Popular media crowds out the complicated, contesting narratives and historical claims by constructing a more attractive narrative around boosting local trade, development, and restoration of ancient ties. Given the meager economic value of this barter-driven border trade, the Chinese media has woven the narrative around regional livelihood, the possibility of infrastructure development, and building mutual trust. The Chinese commentary construes the opening as a “revival” of ancient Sino-Indian border trade, with Tibet as a commercial bridge, and part of efforts to eliminate the colonial inequalities after the “liberation of Tibet.”
Over the last few years, the construction of border village resettlement projects, combining civilian housing with military and surveillance infrastructure, in the Tibet Autonomous Region near the Shipki Pass has gained momentum. These villages help give physical form to China’s version of the story, elevating ancient Sino-Indian trade ties over India-Tibet exchanges. Expanding beyond academic and journalistic narratives, Beijing is consolidating its rendition of Tibet as a commercial bridge through trade resumption and border infrastructure.
The reopening of Shipki Pass matters for reasons beyond trade resumption and China-India diplomacy. It highlights the disputes over sovereignty, history, and measures to consolidate control over the border. As it turns out, the trade diplomacy along the Sino-Indian border is less about trade and more about whose history triumphs.

The American automotive industry wants President Donald Trump to maintain policies that make it difficult for Chinese automakers to operate in the U.S. — or even ban them altogether.
In a letter to Trump dated Thursday and viewed by CNBC, groups representing major facets of the U.S. automotive industry — from franchised dealers and suppliers to domestic and foreign automakers — urged the president to "maintain policies that keep the door firmly shut to Chinese automakers seeking to sell, import or manufacture vehicles inside the U.S."
"The automotive sector is foundational to our advanced manufacturing and defense base, with the capacity and workforce to respond during a national emergency. Once that base is hollowed out, it can't be rebuilt overnight," the letter reads.
The letter comes ahead of Trump's expected visit next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, as well as Trump last week saying he would permit Chinese automakers to move manufacturing to the U.S.
"If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I'd be OK with it," Trump said Sept. 11 on Fox News' "The Ingraham Angle."
The letter argues that allowing Chinese automakers to manufacture in the U.S. would "undermine fair competition and jeopardize the progress" the administration has made in preventing "Chinese dominance in key industries." Chinese automakers are heavily subsidized by their government and are rapidly expanding outside of China to other countries.
The letter is the latest in a string of messages from the automotive industry to the Trump administration, but this time represented a more unified coalition.
It was signed by leaders of six trade associations that represent every major automaker operating in the U.S., including Tesla and foreign automakers, as well as the nation's roughly 17,000 franchised dealers.

US-Israel arms transfers: 2,000 pound bombs, destruction in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:04:27 UTC
02:04:27 KST

Breadcrumb
US-Israel arms transfers: 2,000 pound bombs, destruction in Gaza
The United States' approval of a $2.8bn arms deal with Israel has renewed criticism of US policy towards Tel Aviv, with the package set to include 2,000-pound bombs that have frequently been used in both Gaza and Lebanon to devastating effect.
The approval, which could bypass Congress, is set to replenish the stockpile of heavy munitions, according to reporting from the New York Times.
What are these munitions, where have they been used, and why have they spurred controversy? The New Arab takes a look.
Heavy munitions
The arms package consists of 40,000 heavy bombs developed and made by the US, including 20,000 MK-84 bombs and 20,000 BLU-117 bombs.
The bombs are nearly identical, weighing 2,000 pounds (907kg), creating up to 50 feet (15 metres) deep craters in use, as well as being programmed to detonate above ground as well as underground.
Detonation above ground can send shrapnel 1,000 feet (300 metres) in any direction.
Alongside the bombs, the US will also be supplying 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads. These bombs are also 2,000 pounds but are reinforced and explode on delay, allowing them to punch through surfaces before exploding underground.
Where have they been used?
These bombs have been extensively used by Israel in its wars on Gaza and Lebanon, to deadly effect.
Israel’s war on Gaza has killed over 73,000 Palestinians in a dense urban environment that saw Israeli strikes sometimes killing hundreds at a time in built-up areas, particularly during the first months of the war.
Their repeated use in Gaza, and Israel’s other wars, has seen the US resupply Israeli stockpiles several times in the last three years. In 2024, the Biden administration blocked the transfer of 2,000-pound bombs amid public pressure urging Washington to stop Israel’s invasion of Rafah, which occurred anyway.
US President Donald Trump later unblocked the transfer of the weapons, just a few days into his administration.
According to the New York Times, it has identified 208 craters at least 40 feet across in an area of southern Gaza where Israel told civilians to move to safety.
One such incident in the Jabaliya Refugee Camp at the start of the war killed around 195 Palestinians and wounded a further 777, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, which has since seen the systematic destruction of infrastructure in Israeli-occupied areas of the enclave, has destroyed most of Gaza’s housing and other infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, roads, water and sewage.
Though Israel has launched campaigns against seven Middle Eastern countries since the outbreak of its war on Gaza -- including Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iran, Iraq and Qatar – MK-84 bombs are not deep-strike munitions, meaning they have a minimum range that’s limited to the aircraft's operational range, limiting their usage to areas where Israeli aircraft can directly fly over.
Where is the backlash?
The sale has generated backlash from parts of the US political scene, which has seen figures from both sides of the aisle become increasingly wary of the partnership with Israel.
The most vocal critic of the deal among the Democrats has been Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and supporter of Israel, who said he would not clear Trump’s proposal.
In a press release published on Wednesday, Meeks said that though he is committed to Israel’s security, “the Trump administration’s proposed sale of 40,000 2,000-pound bombs, some of the most destructive munitions in our arsenal, raises grave, unresolved concerns about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon".
“The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with U.S. law and with appropriate protections for civilians. I therefore will not clear this sale at this time,” he added.
Democrat Senator Chris Van Hollen also weighed in on X, saying he would work to stop the transfer.
Within the Republican political commentariat, Tucker Carlson, who in recent years has distinguished himself as a staunch critic of Israel’s wars in the region, also hit out against the decision.
“By definition, what the Netanyahu government has done in Gaza is genocide. The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region.
“If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do,” he added.
It is unlikely that Congress will be able to stop the transfer, as it would require a resolution of disapproval with a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate, which has never happened before, according to the New York Times.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations have also bypassed congressional reviews when selling and transferring arms to Israel since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza by invoking emergency authority.

Ahead of Morocco's elections, young voters ask what will change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:04:27 UTC
02:04:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco's youth are looking for a way forward as upcoming elections expose a crisis of trust
On July 30, over 70,000 people abruptly fled their home country to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, leaving many Moroccans stunned as they were drenched by incessant live feeds of the crossing.
At least 145 died in the resulting stampedes or were submerged by the sea currents.
For days, the Ceuta crisis was on everyone's lips, with the same question on a loop. What could possibly have driven these young people to leave their homes to the peril of their lives, sometimes without informing their loved ones, in the search for a fancied future in an unwelcoming territory?
Nabila Mounib, a 66-year-old endocrinology professor and candidate of the Unified Socialist Party (PSU) for the September 23 legislative elections in the highly disputed district of Casablanca Anfa, provides us with a hint.
While leading the party from 2012 to 2023, Nabila has seen defeatism and despair grow among the youth, who lost confidence in the ability of class to improve their daily lives.
"When they throw themselves into the sea, they look elsewhere to obtain the dignity they cannot get in their country," she said.
"They are politicised in their own way. Rejecting everything is, in itself, a stance that can be considered political."
Over time, the Ceuta tragedy has quietly faded from public discussion. Yet the difficulties encountered by Morocco’s youth haven’t.
According to the High Commission for Planning (HCP), the country’s economy grew by 3.8% in real terms in 2024. Yet young Moroccans continue to face significant barriers to entering the labour market, with unemployment among those aged 15 to 24 reaching 36.7%.
Youth exclusion from employment and education is also substantial: HCP estimates that 1.5 million Moroccans aged 15 to 24 were neither in employment nor in education or training (NEET) in 2023, representing 25.6% of that age group.
Political participation has also varied considerably, with turnout in legislative elections ranging from 37% in 2007 to 50.18% in 2021, highlighting fluctuations in electoral participation and political engagement.
Despite its marginal electoral weight, the leftist alliance of the PSU and the Federation of the Democratic Left (FGD) aims to shake up the public debate by presenting candidates in most regions.
An MP since 2021, Nabila has been vocal about the powerlessness of Morocco’s parliament and has relentlessly called on the country’s political leaders for their inability to initiate genuine political reforms.
"We are the ones raising the only fundamental debate. The other parties have always focused on a socio-economic approach. We take a multifaceted approach, both political and socio-economic. The primary economic reform is a political one: the fight against corruption, the separation of powers, and accountability," she asserts.
The trust gap
Two weeks before the vote, the central siege of the PSU, located on a quiet alley behind the crowded jabber of Casablanca, feels like a bubble of optimism.
Safaa Benmasoud, a 39-year-old biology professor and member of the political bureau, is training a group of volunteers who showed up to carry out the campaign.
Safaa grew up with the leftist ideals of her elders, close to Mohamed Bensaid Ait Idder, a revered figure of Morocco’s left, joining the PSU as a sympathiser in 2006 and eventually becoming a party member five years later.
She refutes the idea that the youth aren’t interested in or informed about politics. The issue lies in their lack of trust, she insists. "They consciously don’t believe in politics. They think, ‘Why should I be involved in politics’?" she tells The New Arab.
The first leaflet session in the Maarif district confirmed the general defiance of Moroccans towards political actors.
Many recognised Nabila from social networks, knew her orientations and even agreed with her assessment of the state of affairs.
Yet that didn't mean they would translate that vocal support into a vote. Several youngsters seemed quite excited to meet her, before some of them realised they weren’t registered on the voting lists.
Hanane, a member of the PSU national council, instructed a few on how to verify if they could vote and know where their voting booth would be located.
While the youth aged 18 to 24 number 3.85 million, only 632,000 are registered, representing a mere 4% of the electorate.
A few days into the campaign, the competing parties didn’t seem to have succeeded in reaching out to youngsters through their political programmes.
Rather, they hired them to distribute leaflets, as they had done for previous elections.
Those who shared them were generally unfamiliar with activism and ignored the basics of the political programmes they handed to passersby, who, in turn, often immediately threw them onto the sidewalks.
However, most knew the popular president of the Royal Football Federation, Faouzi Lekjaa, who has been Morocco’s budget minister in the outgoing government.
A generation losing faith in politics
Despite recently joining the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), part of the ruling coalition, he isn’t running for a seat.
Yet he has monopolised the local media’s attention in his campaign for the party and was put forward as a possible chief of government.
Nevertheless, the hubbub around him seems so far to have done little to convince the sceptical voters dragging their feet to set their sights on a candidate.
Despite recent declarations from Lekjaa setting aside his future participation in government, the lack of a clear definition of political parties has kept numerous Moroccan citizens away.
The campaign has a sense of déjà vu.
For several years, Aziz Akhanouche, Morocco’s chief of government since 2021 and a major business figure, had served in government as a non-partisan technocratic minister before taking the helm of the National Rally of Independents party in October 2016.
Political party-switching and the non-linear career paths of politicians have severely eroded voter trust, leading citizens to feel that political interests take precedence over them.
Last year, the GENZ212 demonstrations clearly expressed the youth’s concerns.
Created online, the group called for educational and health reforms, in opposition to the rising budgets devoted to Morocco’s organisation of the 2030 World Cup.
The protesters were met with state repression. Since the eruption of the movement in September 2025, about 2,500 people have been prosecuted, of whom 950 were placed on provisional release and 1,550 kept in pretrial detention, according to AMDH activist Omar Arbib, leaving over 580 people currently in Morocco’s jails.
That response only further deterred youngsters from political involvement.
Over the last decade, the spaces for political debate have already dramatically shrunk. Several organisations, trade unions, and political parties, including those that took part in the government, such as the PJD, have encountered organisational complications.
Summer camps that have mentored youth for decades have become increasingly difficult for non-governmental organisations to hold.
More importantly, the Union Nationale des Étudiants du Maroc (UNEM), a pivotal student union, has been progressively stripped of its role as an opposition force.
The pressure suddenly grew in 2014, explained Tayeb Madmad, a member of the AMDH central bureau in Rabat, when the Interior Minister, Mohammed Hassad, made a statement in parliament, claiming that certain organisations were pursuing foreign agendas and could jeopardise the country's security.
At the AMDH, Morocco’s biggest human rights organisation, most of the 102 bureaux across the country have been denied official documents. Because of that, in order to organise any public event, activists have had to overcome a series of hurdles.
This drained their already limited financial resources, creating new difficulties, such as being unable to rent public rooms or organise public events.
Tayeb said the organisation couldn’t address youngsters as it used to through educational meetings in schools.
As he distributed his party’s programme in the Bourgogne district of Casablanca with a group of activists, 23-year-old Mohamed Zakaria Elaski, a candidate and university student who joined the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS) two years ago, acknowledged the youth's disenchantment.
"The political class failed to convince the youth. For them, voting has no impact," he regretted.
"The election period comes late [to raise their interest]. They should have convinced them to register to vote."
But as he went on, he added, "Either you participate, or you are subjected to politics."

The Story Behind Netflix's Rousing Bollywood Dance Comedy Best of the Best
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:03:17 UTC
02:03:17 KST

Maitreyi Ramakrishnan wants to make this clear: She had to audition for Best of the Best, the coming-of-age comedy playing out against the world of collegiate Bollywood dance competitions.
“Please include that Maitreyi Ramakrishan was not just offered this role,” she says, her almighty finger pointing hard at my notebook. “Maitreyi Ramakrishnan worked!”
She’s responding, in her beguilingly animated way, to my suggestion that her character, Maya, feels as though she were written for Ramakrishnan, the Never Have I Ever star who was introduced to us in 2020 as the fabulously temperamental teen Devi in Mindy Kaling and Lang Fisher’s Netflix dramedy. Maya was actually conceived around the same time, when Patriot Act host Hasan Minhaj and his writing and producing partner Prashanth Venkataramanujam spent their time in lockdown cooking up Best of the Best, their answer to the Step Up franchise, which is finally hitting Netflix on Sept. 18.
For some fans, who were eager to see Devi go to college, Best of the Best might serve as a suitable replacement for a continuation of the show, which ended in 2023 after four seasons. The movie reunites Ramakrishnan with one of her Never Have I Ever directors, Lena Khan, and co-choreographer Joya Kazi, who appeared in its first season, performing a Bollywood-style routine to the song “Nagada Sang Dhol.” In that scene, Kazi fluidly blended India's traditional Kathak dance with the swirling and romantic poses choreographed specifically for the big screen in Mumbai. That fusion, in a nutshell, is what Bollywood dance is all about.
Devi, who harbored complicated insecurities about her cultural identity, scoffed at the performance. Ramakrishnan’s Maya, on the other hand, would scoff at anyone challenging her Bollywood-style supremacy. “Maya is that bitch,” says Ramakrishnan.
A clear casting choice
We’re at dinner, discussing Ramakrishnan’s leap from leading a TV show to carrying a movie, a conversation we will pick up again a week later on a Zoom call with Minhaj. I meet up with Ramakrishnan at East Tea Can, a restaurant in her Mississauga neighbourhood, west of Toronto. She orders the cardamom black tea for us to share but insists she could finish off the entire pot by herself, and introduces me to mana’eesh, a stone-baked Middle Eastern pizza served with minced beef and lamb.
I’ve interviewed Ramakrishnan on several occasions, witnessing how young fans would swarm her in the wild. This time, she avoids all that by strategically choosing a table in the back and facing away from the diners, though our server recognizes her instantaneously, even behind her large burgundy frames. Her nose ring and traditional bell-shaped earrings are less flash and more a reminder that Ramakrishnan, 24, has always been more at home with South Asian culture than Devi was in that first season. That’s one of the many reasons Minhaj felt she was just right to play Maya, the UCLA freshman thrust into competition with her childhood best friend Anjali.
The latter is played by Priyanka Kedia, a fresh-faced Indian-American actor originally from the Bay area, who joined Best of the Best after graduating from NYU and catching a breakthrough part in Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day. Her Anjali is the more poised social butterfly to the headstrong and rebellious Maya, their lifelong relationship tested when they both make the school’s esteemed Bollywood dance team and must jockey for parts while adjusting to campus life, rigorous academics, and new relationships. Their story draws from Minhaj and co-writer Venkataramanujam’s own college experiences.
“I'll be honest with you,” says Minhaj later, on that Zoom call. “I for real felt, we would be so lucky to have Maitreyi. She was the person that I felt had the two things that I think Maya needed. Everybody knows that Maitreyi naturally is comedically brilliant. She has that ‘It’ factor that you can't teach. Your Amy Poehlers, your Kristen Wiigs, your Kate McKinnons.” But her comedic talents would also need to be balanced with something deeper. “If you look at Maitreyi’s work, especially in Seasons 3 and 4 of Never Have I Ever, there is an emotional depth, that pathos that she has. I was like, there's no other number one for this film than her.”
Despite, Minhaj’s confidence in her, Ramakrishnan auditioned to reassure the whole team she was ready to transition from the snappy sitcom pacing of Never Have I Ever to the more considered emotional stakes of a feature film.
Even Kazi, who went to college with Minhaj, had to jump through similar hoops. “She was a dance Superstar at UC Davis,” says Minhaj. “Even when we were interviewing, I had to recuse myself. I needed her LinkedIn profile to speak for itself. The friendship is real. It goes back to the second Bush Administration.”
Minhaj is at his parent’s home in Sacramento, dressed in a blue and white baseball jersey. He’s immediately heartened to see my daughter’s bedroom, where I set up shop, in the background, pointing out the kids’ toys scattered on the floor around him. He pulls out framed photos of baby Hasan, clearly taken at some department store photo studio. The space feels familiar, if only because you could immediately imagine it filled with the characters he’s intimately described in his semi-autobiographical standup specials like Homecoming King and The King’s Jester.
Small talk with Minhaj includes some history on the Punjabi community in Northern California, the early 19th century immigrant farmers who would later hide their identity after the Chinese Exclusion Act. “This becomes the milieu of South Asian identity, specifically in Northern California,” says Minhaj, who just unpacked the context behind where his family resides as if he were freestyling a Patriot Act segment for an audience of two.
Long before they met, Ramakrishnan was a huge fan of Patriot Act, a Netflix series in which Minhaj wielded punchlines and PowerPoint presentations to unpack politics and the perils of unchecked capitalism.
“The first time I met you was way later at one of your first ever performances of Hasan Hates Ronnie / Ronnie Hates Hasan,” she tells Minhaj, referring to his live comedy tour with Ronny Chieng.
“And you were in full costume, right? You were dressed as Princess Leia or something like that?”
“It wasn’t a costume,” says Maitreyi. You can hear the eyeroll in her voice. “It was fashion.”
“Wait wait,” Minhaj says, shrinking.
“But it’s fine. Whatever. Wouldn’t expect you to know, Minhaj.”
“You had a full hood.”
“It was sick.”
“It was a karate gi meets Obi-Wan Kenobi up top.”
This jabbing rapport reads as a playful generational tete-a-tete between millennial and Gen Z, but it also speaks to the exchange of perspectives that informed their collaboration on Best of the Best. “What you're seeing in the movie,” says Minhaj, “is Maitreyi and Lena coming together, and really masterminding and creating the tone and the feeling of the film.”
A fusion of many styles of dance
During weekly script sessions, Ramakrishnan would join Khan, Minhaj, and Venkataramanujam to share her input on drafts, and her character. These workshops would come at the end of the day for Ramakrishnan, who had a jam-packed training schedule to ensure she could convincingly play the part of a teen who’s been dancing all her life.
Ramakrishnan is the first to admit she’s not a dancer. She spent a year as a child learning Bharatnatyam, the traditional 3,000-year-old dance originating from Tamil Nadu in India, but decided that all that ballet-like discipline wasn’t for her. “The structure of being told, ‘This is what you have to do in this order,’ over and over again, didn't work for my child brain,” says Ramakrishnan. “I just wanted to run around.”
She was in her nerves about signing on to do a dance movie and potentially misrepresenting a community that she admires. “Dancers are no joke,” she says. But she says her mother offered the objective perspective she needed to face the job: “You read the script. You don’t need to be a great dancer. You just need to be good at seven dances.”
Choreographers Phillip & McKenzie, who tapped Kazi’s cultural expertise, organized a two-month boot camp for Ramakrishnan in L.A. She attended six classes a day, six days a week, training in everything from Bharatnatyam and Kathak to contemporary, hip-hop, heels, and groove. Then it was off to New Jersey, where she joined the rest of the cast and dancers for another two months. That’s four months of training for an eight-week shoot that left Ramakrishan physically broken but with an even deeper appreciation for the commitment and the craft.
“I got to witness so many great talents,” she says. “I noticed the dancers that have this sparkle. There’s many that can nail the choreo, be on time with the counts, understand musicality, do the trick and the flip. But then there’s some dancers that can do it all in a way that makes an audience member, who has never danced before in their life, want to get up and dance with them, because you’re as intimidated and impressed by their dancing as you are welcomed and invited.”
That welcoming and invitational vibe can be applied to the movie’s diverse approach to the dances, as well. The term “Bollywood dance” is a bit misleading. Best of the Best boasts a fusion of styles, reflecting trends within Bollywood dance competitions, and the culture online. In the same way that Save The Last Dance folded hip-hop into the ballet space, young classically trained Bharatnatyam dancers in North America have been blending traditional movements with krumping and breaking.
The real-life sister dance duo Poonam and Priyanka Shah went viral a decade ago, performing butterflies and splits to the Bollywood song Ramta Jogi, taking their “Bfusion” routines from the collegiate circuit to the internet. In recent years, French-Tamil dancer Usha Jey broke the internet busting moves in a saree to Lil’ Wayne. These children of South Asian immigrants have been using fusion dance to broker a new cultural identity for themselves, with one foot in their ancestral lands and another in the place they call home.
Best of the Best is the first popular movie to explore that fusion, and its evolution. There’s storytelling in the dance sequences that shift between Bharatnatyam and Brooklyn styles like bone breaking. That intentionality extends to the soundtrack, which at one point tips its hat to the music that got this cultural exchange started, the early-2000s hip-hop produced by Timbaland and Dr. Dre sampling Bollywood. One extravagant Bollywood musical number features the Truth Hurts song “Addictive,” produced by Dre, battling with the iconic 1969 Hindi song that it famously sampled, “Thoda Resham Lagta Hai.”
“The beautiful thing that we wanted to do in this film,” says Minhaj, “is to take all of these things that make our identity and create something new with it.” He turns his attention to the varied identities spread across South Asia. “This is a rare opportunity where all of us from the diaspora can reconcile a lot of paradoxes that we couldn’t necessarily participate in if we were to do this film in India. There are all these other social, political and language barriers that separate Pakistan, Bangladesh, India, and Sri Lanka. They become sequestered to their own cinema. In the States, all of that becomes kind of irrelevant.”
Best of the Best breaks up monolithic representations of being South Asian, with a cast hailing from all regions, and a dance troupe composed of cheeky character types. These go beyond the nerd, the heartthrob, the Paul Rudd in Clueless sensitive type and the mean girl, to include the rich slick-haired wealthy “FOBs” (meaning “fresh off the boat”), and even a token white guy (Nico Greetham) so hilariously obsessed with Indian culture that he speaks fluent Hindi.
Prioritizing cultural specificity
The filmmakers also accounted for Ramakrishnan, and the very specific Eelam Tamil identity she brings to the film, with all its fraught political connotations. When Maya introduces herself at one point, she says, “I'm Tamil. My family's from Sri Lanka.” The wording is precise. Ramakrishnan’s family is not, for instance, from Tamil Nadu in India, like Devi’s in Never Have I Ever. Nor do they identify as Sri Lankan. The state, which her family fled, stands accused of perpetrating a genocide against the Eelam Tamil population in 2009, after a 25-year civil war. For Ramakrishnan’s family, calling themselves Sri Lankan would be akin to a Palestinian identifying as Israeli.
“Is it something that I expect everyone to catch?” asks Ramakrishnan. “No. Everyone will catch that she's saying she's Tamil. She doesn't understand Hindi, because not every South Asian person understands Hindi. But I think the Tamil Eelam folks, like yourself, will catch that.”
Ramakrishnan has never shied away from discussing her identity and that history, and how both have shaped her. As a child, she joined her activist parents at protests in Toronto, calling for a ceasefire and an end to the genocide in Sri Lanka. She kept that spirit alive last year, at a “No Tyrants” rally in Vancouver, holding up a sign that said, “Never Have I Ever Thought Genocide Was OK."
“Maitreyi has such a strong sense of self, and such a strong sense of pride in her culture,” says Minhaj. He describes one of his favorite moments on set, seeing that cultural pride pour out of her when Ramakrishnan and Kedia’s characters perform a Kuthu dance at a frat party. Kuthu is a high energy, high impact Tamil folk dance that can appear like jumping jacks and aggressive pelvic thrusts colliding. It’s the kind of dance that isn’t taught in professional studios. “A lot of people over time have seen Kuthu as lower-class rowdy street dance,” says Ramakrishnan,
She likens Kuthu to Bhangra, which started as a dance for Punjab farmers, and is now a common sight at Indian weddings. The best place to learn both Bhangra and Kuthu? “At the function,” she says. Regarding Bhangra, “You learn it at the wedding. You learn it with the vibes. You get the beat in your shoulders and you're going.” As for Kuthu: “It’s at whatever banquet hall birthday party, for some 2-year-old kid who will never remember any of this, because he’s passed out in the corner while all the uncles and aunties are going off on the dance floor.”
The Kuthu sequence is riotous, befitting the chaos of the frat-party environment. Ramakrishnan and Kedia bound over lawn furniture and kick up grass. Ramakrishnan gets all the background actors hyped while she tugs at the collar of her blue checkered shirt, a nod to the red flannel that Prabhu Deva wears during the dance number in the 2007 gangster movie Pokkiri.
A grand and meaningful finale
Minhaj also says that he and Venkataramanujam leaned into Ramakrishnan’s identity for the film’s spectacular finale, which plays out on a stage decorated like a museum, a playground of colonial artifacts. The climactic dance number, according to Minhaj, is meant to inhabit and challenge the South Asian literary discourse on colonial reparations. Did you expect anything less from the duo behind Patriot Act?
The finale incorporates the Koh-i-Noor, the 105-carat diamond recorded to be from India that had changed hands across Asian empires for centuries before being surrendered to the British during the Victorian-era. It’s currently set in the Queen Mother’s crown and housed in the Tower of London. Indian politician Shashi Tharoor and British MP Kieth Vaz are among the voices who have called for the diamond’s return. New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani echoed their sentiments earlier this year when pressed about what he would discuss if given the opportunity to meet with King Charles.
Minhaj questions whether such a symbolic reparation is useful, especially when it could sow further division in a region torn apart over centuries. Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan all lay claim to the diamond of obscure origin, which, as Minhaj points out, could just be an anchor tying a new generation down to a complicated colonial history as opposed to encouraging us to flourish.
“Even if the Koh-i-Noor diamond would be returned to us,” he asks, “What does that change for us today? How does it shape our tomorrow? The uncomfortable reality is that it's up to us to shape that, irrespective of that diamond ever coming back to us."
I won’t spoil how, but it’s Ramakrishnan, as Maya, who steps up to embody what Minhaj has in mind as the way forward.
“Maitreyi is the actor for this moment because she comes from very special cloth. Her parents are incredible activists and academics. She understands her political and social place in history and in time. It only feels right that she's the lead of our film, and the voice of what is new and what is to come.”

Anthropic and OpenAI need truly independent safety evaluators, experts say in public letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:02:32 UTC
02:02:32 KST

Over 100 artificial intelligence experts and evaluators are banding together to warn they won't have the necessary resources and protections to test the safety of AI technology, which is facing heightened scrutiny due to concerns from insiders about the potential dangers of frontier models.
"We're just trying to really demonstrate a shared common ground on basic principles and ensure that independent oversight can be a meaningful tool for managing AI risk broadly," said Conrad Stosz, chair of the AI Evaluator Forum consortium that organized the letter, in an interview.
The group published a public letter on the matter on Friday, and shared it exclusively with CNBC. The signatories include AI luminaries like Geoffrey Hinton and members of organizations such as Johns Hopkins University, Stanford University and the nonprofit evaluator METR. They want to compel foundation model providers to ensure that third-party AI evaluators are allowed the necessary "scientific objectivity, transparency, independence, and robust protections" to do their jobs effectively and credibly, the letter said.
Stosz said it's part of an effort to hold the foundation model companies accountable to their recent pledges to support more thorough third-party AI safety testing.
The niche community of evaluators has been catapulted into the limelight since Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei floated the idea over the weekend of providing some of them "employee-like access" to inspect and audit bleeding-edge foundation models and their development processes. While some industry leaders have called on the government to regulate AI development to ensure it's not spinning out of control, President Donald Trump and his former AI czar, David Sacks, have adamantly opposed such efforts.
Stosz said that the coalition doesn't "advocate for one particular way" to ensure that AI models are developed safely, but wants to ensure that "basic principles" and "greater standardization" are at least established for evaluators and others who work independently of the major labs.
Amodei's proposal, Stosz said, appears to involve providing significantly more access than evaluators have previously enjoyed. Such a scenario, Stosz said, could involve foundation model makers giving third-party evaluators access to company computers, allowing them to talk to employees candidly and letting them "see sensitive internal data and unreleased systems."
"That type of access would give us much greater confidence and certainty about the actual risk, particularly for systems that they're using internally and not releasing," Stosz said. He cited the unreleased OpenAI model used in the Hugging Face attack.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella have publicly supported Amodei's proposal, but they've yet to address the logistical issues with such an undertaking, such as which AI evaluators will be selected and how deeply they would get to inspect closely guarded technologies.
The signatories want the work of evaluators to be conducted independent from the businesses, with more transparency about the technologies, and "to be shielded from retaliation from the companies they embed with," the letter said.
Consolidated power
Vinh Nguyen, a Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow for AI and former chief AI officer of the National Security Agency, said independent evaluators are needed to help unearth crucial information that could help mitigate potential security failures and economic calamities.
"When a few powerful labs control capabilities that can endanger the cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, and the systems our national security and economy run on, the government and the public cannot be dependent on those labs' own account of what's secure and safe," Nguyen, who signed the letter, said in a statement.
Stosz said third-party evaluators are not intended to "be a replacement for any internal efforts to evaluate, let alone mitigate issues that that developers find." He acknowledged that it's possible the foundation model companies ignore the public letter and the call to action, but said their credibility is at stake.
"There's a very small number of groups that are actually sufficiently technically credible and have the scale and the ability" to perform the kind of work, he said.
Read the full letter below, and click here for a link to the list of signees:
Minimum Conditions for Embedding Evaluators
We, the undersigned, are encouraged to see frontier AI companies call for embedding third-party organizations to evaluate rapidly escalating AI capabilities and risks. We believe that all frontier AI companies should embed evaluators to independently assess AI risks, including evaluating the systems themselves and any significant incidents of real-world harm, as well as the companies' training, deployment, oversight, operational, and safeguard practices.
To be credible, embedded third-party evaluations must have scientific objectivity, transparency, independence, and robust protections against interference from the evaluated companies, including at least:
-  Frontier AI companies should rely on evaluators that are meaningfully independent, that maintain full editorial control, and that disclose and mitigate potential conflicts of interest. This includes at a minimum that embedded evaluation organizations should not be owned or governed by frontier AI companies, should not have other significant commercial business with them, and should not accept any form of payment or other reward contingent on the evaluator's findings. 
- Frontier AI companies should incorporate differing viewpoints and areas of expertise, including by embedding multiple evaluation organizations across a range of priority risk areas, each with deep relevant technical expertise, as well as by allowing and encouraging evaluators to share how conclusions differ among evaluators and between evaluators and company employees. 
- Embedded evaluators should be transparent, including transparency about their methods and findings, the nature of their access, and the broader terms of the evaluation. Frontier AI companies should actively facilitate this transparency, including limiting the scope of non-disclosure agreements. They should also allow evaluators prompt and unfiltered communication with the companies' boards and other privileged oversight bodies, as well as public release of findings and evidence, subject only to a time-limited redaction process restricted to protecting critical interests in intellectual property, customers' sensitive information, individual privacy, security, and public safety. 
- Embedded evaluators should be shielded from retaliation from the companies they embed with for choosing reasonable evaluation methods, discovering information, or drawing conclusions that are unflattering to those companies. This includes reasonable protections against retaliatory litigation, as well as funding mechanisms that give them confidence they will remain funded even in these cases. 
- Frontier AI companies should grant embedded evaluators access equivalent to that of their own highly privileged employees for the purposes of their evaluations, and with exceptions to protect sensitive data belonging to the company's customers and other third parties. This includes access to the same relevant systems, data, tools, and physical spaces as those available to senior internal company employees responsible for carrying out comparable risk assessments, as well as candid and direct one-on-one communication with relevant staff.
This list is not comprehensive, and conditions like these to ensure credible evaluations should be increasingly standardized, codified, and enforced. One example is the set of terms defined in the AEF-1 standard, which has already seen early adoption, but far more work will be necessary to ensure that embedded evaluators are effective and meaningful. 
Embedded evaluations cannot address all oversight needs and should be treated as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, broader efforts by frontier AI companies to expand external oversight, including greater public transparency and additional, broader forms of access for independent researchers.

Ukraine destroys Russian S-400 launcher in Bryansk region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:01:58 UTC
02:01:58 KST

- Ukraine's Defense Forces destroyed a Russian S-400 launcher near Poroshino, Bryansk Oblast, on Sept. 17 using Fire Point's FP-1 drones.
- Fire Point said the launcher had been modified to strike ground targets, including Kyiv, and Ukraine's General Staff separately reported striking two S-400 launchers in the same region.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces destroyed a Russian S-400 air defense launcher in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast on Sept. 17, using FP-1 drones, according to Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that builds the drone.
Fire Point said the launcher had been modified by Russian forces to strike ground targets and had previously been used against Kyiv. The company said the strike hit the launcher near the village of Poroshino, along highway 15K-303. The open-source monitoring group CyberBoroshno said it geolocated the destroyed vehicle from photos of the wreckage, pinning the site at coordinates 53.134224, 33.944510.
Ukraine’s General Staff separately reported that its forces struck two S-400 launchers overnight into Sept. 17 in the Vygonychi area of Bryansk Oblast, a location close to Poroshino, though it is not clear whether that report describes the same launcher Fire Point identified or a separate one. Russia has not confirmed any S-400 losses. Bryansk’s acting governor, Alexander Bogomaz’s successor Yegor Kovalchuk, said Russian air defenses shot down 82 drones over the region in 24 hours but made no mention of losses among the region’s own air defense systems.
The S-400 Triumf is Russia’s long- and medium-range surface-to-air missile system, built to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles, and Russia has claimed it can also intercept some ballistic targets. Since 2024, Russia has adapted some of the system’s interceptor missiles for a secondary role, firing them at ground targets in Ukraine on a quasi-ballistic trajectory. That dual use is why destroying individual launchers has become a specific target set for Ukraine, since a single system removed from service can eliminate both an air-defense asset and a launcher capable of hitting cities like Kyiv.
Fire Point introduced the FP-1 in late 2024 as a long-range, one-way attack drone built for deep strikes into Russian territory, with a payload of 60 to 120 kilograms (130 to 265 pounds) and a publicly stated range that has grown over time, from roughly 1,600 km (994 miles) at introduction to as much as 3,400 km (2,110 miles) in extended-range configurations the company began advertising in mid-2026.
The drone has previously been used against Russian refineries and other high-value sites well beyond the front line, including a strike on the Omsk refinery in July and a facility in the Yamalo-Nenets region on Sept. 9.

Sudanese army says it killed RSF fighters, destroyed 9 vehicles in Blue Nile

2026-09-18
17:00:33 UTC
02:00:33 KST

Adel Abdelrheem and Lina Altawell
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
The Sudanese army said Friday that it carried out a “well-planned” preemptive attack south of the Al-Keili area in southeastern Blue Nile state, killing a number of Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters and destroying nine combat vehicles along with their equipment.
Sudan’s Defense Ministry said in a statement that the armed forces and allied units carried out the operation “based on precise intelligence.”
“The swift operation inflicted heavy losses on the enemy, including the destruction of nine combat vehicles with all their equipment and the elimination of a number of Rapid Support Forces militia mercenaries,” the ministry said.
It added that the operation had destroyed the force’s main combat capability and left the RSF presence in the area “completely paralyzed.”
There was no immediate comment from the RSF on the army’s claims.
The development came a day after the army announced that it had taken control of 11 areas in North Kordofan state following clashes with the RSF.
On Tuesday, the RSF carried out drone attacks on Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile state.
The Blue Nile front has remained active, with the Sudanese army saying Sunday that it shot down an RSF drone in the Balanq area of the state.
The army also announced that it had taken control of the strategic Jabal Kadam area in Blue Nile and repelled an attack by the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N).
On Sept. 2, Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan visited Damazin, where he inspected the army’s 4th Infantry Division and reviewed its combat readiness.
The visit came after the arrival of the Joint Forces of armed movements allied with the army and an elite brigade from the General Intelligence Service to participate in military operations in Blue Nile.
Alongside Blue Nile and Darfur, Sudan’s three Kordofan states, North, West and South Kordofan, have witnessed fighting between the army and the RSF since Oct. 25 last year.
Sudan has been engulfed in a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, which has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Syrian security forces arrested five senior air force officers and commanders who served under the deposed Bashar al-Assad regime over involvement in airstrikes on populated areas, the Syrian Arab News Agency SANA reported Friday.
Col. Abdul Aal Mohammad Abdul Aal, head of Internal Security in the coastal Tartous province, said specialized units, in cooperation with the Anti-Terrorism Directorate, carried out a series of security operations that led to the arrests.
Abdul Aal said the detainees included pilots, field commanders and officers who served in operations rooms under the former regime.
Those detained were identified as Maj. Gen. Mohammad Fajr Ali, Brig. Gen. pilot Abdullah Ali Mualla, Col. pilot Nidal Hussein Saleh, Col. Mohammad Ali Salim and Lt. Col. pilot Talib Abdul Karim Hassan.
Investigations and military records indicated that the five, each according to his position and responsibilities, were involved in planning, directing and carrying out airstrikes, he added.
According to the security chief, aircraft, air bases and field command centers were used to conduct intensive strikes on populated areas, resulting in the destruction of residential neighborhoods and infrastructure, forced displacement and extensive casualties.
On Sept. 10, Latakia Internal Security Commander Abdulaziz al-Ahmad said a series of security operations led to the arrest of the nine pilots after surveillance, tracking, intelligence gathering, and investigations.
He said the detainees had participated, according to the investigations and available information, in “numerous crimes and violations against the Syrian people,” exploiting their military positions and expertise in combat and helicopter aviation.
The statement said the operations they took part in included bombardment and attacks that caused large numbers of deaths and injuries, inflicted extensive damage on cities and towns, displaced residents and destroyed homes, facilities and civilian infrastructure.
Syrian authorities periodically announce the arrest of people accused of committing violations against civilians during the years of the revolution, which began in March 2011 before opposition forces entered Damascus and toppled the Assad regime on Dec. 8, 2024.
