Five ROMULUS 151 drone ships now under construction
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
18:00:06 BST
02:00:06 KST

Five HII ROMULUS 151 uncrewed surface vessels are now under construction in Louisiana, with the first hull completing its structural build and being turned over ahead of deck and pilothouse work, according to HII.
Four of the vessels are being built by Breaux Brothers Enterprises in New Iberia, while a fifth is under construction at Halimar Shipyard in Morgan City. HII said the first ROMULUS 151 hull at Breaux Brothers has now completed its main structural build and undergone the hull-flip process, allowing construction to move on to the upper parts of the vessel.
The programme is intended to produce a family of modular, AI-enabled uncrewed surface vessels for missions ranging from surveillance and mine countermeasures to strike and the operation of other robotic systems. ROMULUS is built around HII’s Odyssey Advanced Autonomy architecture, an open system intended to allow different mission payloads and software to be integrated as requirements change. The company says the vessels are being developed for potential use by the US Navy, US Marine Corps, other joint forces and allied customers.
Mission roles identified by HII include intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, mine countermeasures, strike operations and counter-uncrewed systems missions. The vessels are also intended to act as motherships for other autonomous platforms, with the ability to launch and recover uncrewed underwater and aerial vehicles.
The ROMULUS 151 is one member of a wider family rather than a single-purpose craft, with HII seeking to use common autonomy and open architecture across different sizes and mission configurations. The current production effort is split between two commercial Louisiana yards, with HII providing the autonomy technology and programme integration while the shipbuilders carry out construction.
HII said the arrangement was intended to combine conventional shipyard production methods with autonomous maritime technology, allowing vessels to be built in numbers without relying on a single yard. The first hull reaching the flip stage is an important construction milestone because it marks the point at which work can move from the principal hull structure towards the deck, pilothouse and subsequent outfitting.
HII describes ROMULUS as part of a broader move towards scalable autonomous maritime forces, where comparatively lower-cost uncrewed vessels can carry sensors, weapons or other systems alongside conventional warships. The company is already heavily involved in US Navy uncrewed systems, particularly underwater vehicles, and is using ROMULUS to expand that work into larger surface vessels.
With five ROMULUS 151s now being built simultaneously, the programme has moved beyond individual demonstrators towards a small production run intended to prove both the vessel design and the industrial approach needed to manufacture autonomous ships at greater scale.

Will the U.S. megadrought ever end?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Will the U.S. megadrought ever end?
A controversial new hypothesis suggests “No”
Kearny, Ariz., is a town on the brink. Located at the foot of the Dripping Spring Mountains in eastern Arizona, this small community of 2,000 people sources its water from the Gila River, a verdant waterway that snakes by the southern edge of town.
But in March, the snowpack feeding the river had dropped to precipitous levels: It was just 1 percent of its historic norm for that time of year. The Gila River water commissioner slashed Kearny’s allotment of river water by some 85 percent. And in April, town officials announced that “Zero Day” was approaching, at which point the taps would run dry.
“We need rain,” says Norm Warren, a lifelong Kearny resident. He owns the only large grocery store within a 45-minute drive of the town. Without tap water for refrigerator cooling systems, Warren says he won’t be able to store perishable products like meats and fresh produce.
Kearny’s dilemma foreshadows a crisis building across the American Southwest. Since 2000, the region — which includes Arizona, New Mexico, California, Utah, Colorado and parts of northern Mexico — has endured a historic “megadrought,” or a period of severe dryness that persists for decades. Scientists say it’s the driest this region has been in 1,200 years.
“We’re 27 years into it, and it shows no signs of letting up,” says Brad Udall, a water and climate researcher at Colorado State University in Fort Collins.
Scientists point to two factors causing the drought — rising temperatures and declining precipitation. Heat from human-caused climate change creates a thirsty atmosphere that is more effective at drying out the landscape, says Kevin Anchukaitis, a dendrochronologist who runs the University of Arizona Laboratory for Tree-Ring Research in Tucson. As for the lack of rain, many researchers wonder if it is simply a stroke of bad luck.
But a controversial study published in Nature in 2025 suggests something far more ominous: Humankind has disrupted a naturally occurring climate cycle in the Pacific Ocean that historically ushered episodes of wet weather into the Southwest. If that’s true, Udall says, things are not looking good for places like Kearny. Other researchers worry that the megadrought may be locked in place for the foreseeable future.
A thirstier atmosphere
The drought is transforming the American Southwest slowly but inexorably. Since 2000, the region’s most vital waterway, the Colorado River, has seen its flow decrease by roughly 20 percent. Lakes Powell and Mead, the river’s largest reservoirs, fell to historic lows in August — about a quarter of their combined capacity. That’s a hard blow for the roughly 40 million people who depend upon the Colorado for their daily needs.
In August, the federal government cut the amount of river water allocated to Arizona, California and Nevada by roughly 20 percent over the next two years. If conditions don’t improve, those states could see future reductions of up to 40 percent.
Although agriculture is likely to bear the brunt of the reductions, residential users in many cities may see their water bills increase dramatically as a result, according to municipal officials from Phoenix and Tucson.
“We feel the urgency of it,” says Warren, who — along with other residents of Kearny — has cut back on his laundry and showers. He has let his lawn die and now waters his other plants with used dishwater. “The town is really trying.”
Nature, however, isn’t getting on board. As temperatures across the Southwest climb, rainfall is dropping. From 2000 to 2021, annual precipitation in the Southwest was 8.3 percent lower than the average of the previous 50 years. That’s helped create a drought of historic magnitude.
An analysis of regional soil moisture and tree ring data backs that up: The drought is the most severe the Southwest has endured in more than a millennium, scientists reported in 2022 in Nature Climate Change. An updated dataset provided to Science News shows that the megadrought, now 27 years long, remains the driest such period since the year 800.
Those numbers don’t particularly shock Margaret Evans, an ecologist at the tree ring lab.
Evans and her colleagues study the 1,000-year-old rings of ancient trees across the Southwest to measure past droughts. Like the stratigraphic layers of the Grand Canyon, these rings serve as natural records of the settings in which they formed. Thicker ones indicate years of greater growth, which generally correspond to wetter conditions.
By examining the tree rings from roughly a dozen sites in the Upper Colorado Basin, researchers from her lab and others have found evidence of at least two other megadroughts: one in the 12th century and another that spanned almost the entire second century. Scientists used computer models to reconstruct how much water would have flowed through the Colorado River at the time. During the 12th century drought, the river fell to roughly 80 percent of its 20th- and early 21st-century average. During the second century drought, the river fell to 68 percent of that average.
A Modern Megadrought
The current megadrought in the American Southwest is the driest 27-year period in the past 1,200 years, according to soil moisture anomalies derived from tree ring data and modern observations.
That suggests our modern megadrought falls within the realm of natural variability, Evans says. What’s different, she adds, is that it’s a “warm drought.”
Temperature plays a key role in how much moisture remains on the ground as rain or snow. The hot conditions brought on by climate change, Anchukaitis says, have made the sponge of the atmosphere better at sucking up moisture. A 192-year-old thermodynamic formula called the Clausius-Clapeyron equation explains how: For each degree Celsius of warming, a parcel of air can hold 7 percent more water. “A thirsty atmosphere will take that water that does fall from the sky away from the surface,” Anchukaitis says.
Those effects — and the uncertainty over how long they will continue — has caused some researchers to stop using the word “drought” altogether. Instead, they favor the term “aridification,” which describes a progressive drying process. Wet weather can come and go, Anchukaitis says, but if the temperature keeps rising, it’s the perfect recipe for aridification.
A Pacific influence
An arid atmosphere isn’t all that’s driving the megadrought. The other piece of the puzzle lies in the vast waters of the Pacific Ocean.
At its heart is a phenomenon known as the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, or PDO. It’s an alternating climate pattern in which areas of warmer and cooler than normal surface waters switch their positions every 20 years or so, says climate scientist Richard Seager of Columbia University. Unlike some shorter-term climate patterns, the PDO “goes back and forth with timescales of many decades,” Seager says.
Scientists had long assumed that the PDO obeyed a regular rhythm dictated by the complex interactions between the land, sea and atmosphere. Understanding that cadence has always been of vital interest, Anchukaitis says, because of the PDO’s powerful influence on the North American climate.
When the PDO shifts, it diverts the path of the Pacific jet stream, a band of high-flying winds that steers weather patterns around the world. During the PDO’s warm phase, a horseshoe of cooler water covers the northern, western and southern Pacific, while a warmer tongue occupies the eastern Pacific. That pushes the Pacific jet stream south over North America, shepherding wet weather patterns into the Southwest.
But when the PDO switches to its cool phase, the locations of those warm and cool surface waters flip, and the jet stream moves north, diverting wet weather patterns out of the Southwest and making drought more likely.
The PDO’s last warm phase ran from 1977 to 1998, causing the wettest period the Southwest had seen in a millennium, Seager and colleagues reported in 2025 in AGU Advances. But sometime around 1999, the needle swung in the other direction, moving the region from an extremely wet period to an exceptionally dry one, Seager says.
Given the PDO’s presumed cyclical nature, many scientists thought that the switch was only temporary. “The conventional wisdom suggested that the PDO could shift any given year, and we [wouldn’t] have to worry about drought [after that],” says climate scientist Jeremy Klavans of the University of Miami.
But he and colleagues weren’t so sure. They dug into that assumption, analyzing more than 500 simulations of the PDO from a dozen major climate models. They examined how the PDO shifted — and stabilized — in the presence of outside forces such as volcanic eruptions, solar variation and levels of greenhouse gases and aerosols.
Their finding: Greenhouse gas and aerosol emissions had effectively hijacked the behavior of the PDO over the last 50 years by altering atmospheric temperatures, the team reported in 2025 in Nature.
Ballooning concentrations of industrial aerosols — which can have an atmospheric cooling effect — probably pushed the PDO to increasingly favor its warm phase starting in the 1950s, the researchers say. But in the 1980s, clean air legislation decreased aerosol emissions even as greenhouse gas levels continued to rise and warm the atmosphere. That combination drove the PDO toward its cool phase, making drought conditions more likely in the Southwest. Instead of being a rare event, drought “becomes kind of commonplace,” Klavans says.
To see if such events had historic precedent, another group of researchers looked to a period of warming that took place during the mid-Holocene Epoch, some 6,000 years ago. At the time, changes to Earth’s orbit around the sun and the spread of vegetation caused less sunlight to be reflected away from the planet, heating up the Northern Hemisphere. The researchers reasoned such warming should have pushed the PDO into a prolonged cool phase.
After scouring data from bog and lake sediment cores and analyzing dozens of climate simulations re-creating the period, they found that something resembling a cool phase of the PDO did in fact take place. It lasted several thousand years, during which time drought became widespread across the Southwest, they reported in 2025 in Nature Geoscience.
And the current climate models may actually be underestimating the potential duration of the ongoing megadrought, based on those findings, says study coauthor Victoria Todd, a climate scientist at the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colo.
That could be bad news for the American Southwest, Udall says. Even if people stopped emitting greenhouse gases today, planet-warming carbon dioxide will continue to accumulate in the atmosphere, locking the PDO and megadrought into place, potentially for decades. If the emerging science is right, then the Southwest is going to keep getting drier and drier, Udall says. “No question about it.”
Trading Places
The Pacific Decadal Oscillation, or PDO, is a climate pattern in which areas of warmer- and cooler-than-normal surface waters in the Pacific Ocean switch their locations every couple of decades. This affects climate on the surrounding continents.
Warm phase (1977–1998)
During the PDO’s warm phase, the Pacific jet stream (red arrow) moves south over North America, drawing wet weather patterns into the Southwest.
Cool phase (1999–now)
When the PDO switches to its cool phase, the Pacific jet stream (blue arrow) moves north, diverting wet weather patterns out of the Southwest and making drought more likely.
What’s to come
The hypothesis that human emissions have disrupted the PDO could be put to the test this year. That’s because scientists are predicting a historically strong El Niño, a Pacific climate pattern characterized by months of warmer than normal sea surface temperatures in the eastern equatorial Pacific. El Niños often bring wet conditions to the Southwest — and they have been known to force the PDO into a different phase. For example, the 1976–1977 El Niño helped push the PDO into a warm phase for nearly a quarter of a century.
But a powerful El Niño in 2015 wasn’t able to force the switch for more than a few years. That suggests the PDO may be slowly changing, Klavans says. “Something’s different here.”
Even if the current El Niño is strong enough to force the PDO into a warm phase, no one should expect the megadrought to go away any time soon, Seager says. “We’re talking about something that’s been going on for a few decades now. Even one very wet winter is not going to be enough to restore Colorado River reservoirs to where they would preferably be.”
To find out what would happen if the PDO switched to a warm phase in the near future, Seager and colleagues simulated multiple scenarios in which the PDO either stayed in the warm phase or flipped back into a cool phase, all the while monitoring potential impacts on the megadrought.
Even in the best-case scenarios, the Southwest never returns to the wet years of the 1980s and ’90s, when lakes Powell and Mead reached maximum capacity numerous times, the researchers reported in 2023 in npj Climate and Atmospheric Science. The findings instead suggest that, regardless of what the PDO does, the region will face a far drier climate than it did in its recent past. In other words, even if the megadrought were to end, the Southwest faces an uncertain future when it comes to water, according to the study.
Communities need to prepare for the future by improving their water conservation efforts and infrastructure, Anchukaitis says. Those practices will grow only more crucial as the Southwest’s population continues to balloon: Utah, Texas, Nevada, Colorado and Arizona are among the 10 fastest growing states by population this decade, according to a 2024 report by the University of Virginia’s Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service.
Even if wet weather returns, Anchukaitis says, the cities of the Southwest shouldn’t fall into complacency. “[More rain] doesn’t mean that … megadroughts aren’t going to come back,” he says. “Maybe it buys us some time to ease systems into a new way of thinking.”
In Kearny, the town’s residents have made some impactful changes. Though officials first warned Zero Day could occur in July, they now estimate that water restrictions and conservation efforts — as well as canceled water requests by other communities — have helped extend the town’s water supply until at least the end of the year.
But such measures can do only so much. The upstream flow of the Gila River is controlled by the Coolidge Dam, and the reservoir behind the dam is currently less than 1 percent full. If nothing changes before next year, Kearny’s annual allotment of river water could fall to zero.
Back in his store, Warren contemplates the town’s future. “This is going to hurt us if we have to shut off our livelihood,” he says, glancing around at his stocked shelves. “We can’t walk away from it.”

Syrian security forces arrested five senior air force officers and commanders who served under the ousted Bashar Assad regime over their alleged involvement in airstrikes on populated areas, state news agency SANA reported Friday.
Col. Abdul Aal Mohammad Abdul Aal, head of Internal Security in the coastal Tartous province, said specialized units, in cooperation with the Anti-Terrorism Directorate, carried out a series of security operations that led to the arrests.
Abdul Aal said the detainees included pilots, field commanders and officers who served in operations rooms under the former regime.
Those detained were identified as Maj. Gen. Mohammad Fajr Ali, Brig. Gen. pilot Abdullah Ali Mualla, Col. pilot Nidal Hussein Saleh, Col. Mohammad Ali Salim and Lt. Col. pilot Talib Abdul Karim Hassan.
Investigations and military records indicated that the five, each according to his position and responsibilities, were involved in planning, directing and carrying out airstrikes, he added.
According to the security chief, aircraft, air bases and field command centers were used to conduct intensive strikes on populated areas, resulting in the destruction of residential neighborhoods and infrastructure, forced displacement and extensive casualties.
On Sept. 10, Latakia Internal Security Commander Abdulaziz al-Ahmad said a series of security operations led to the arrest of the nine pilots after surveillance, tracking, intelligence gathering, and investigations.
He said the detainees had participated, according to the investigations and available information, in "numerous crimes and violations against the Syrian people,” exploiting their military positions and expertise in combat and helicopter aviation.
The statement said the operations they took part in included bombardment and attacks that caused large numbers of deaths and injuries, inflicted extensive damage on cities and towns, displaced residents and destroyed homes, facilities and civilian infrastructure.
Syrian authorities periodically announce the arrest of people accused of committing violations against civilians during the years of the revolution, which began in March 2011 before opposition forces entered Damascus and toppled the Assad regime on Dec. 8, 2024.

CHANDIGARH: Ending a prolonged standoff with state employees, the Bhagwant Mann government on Friday announced relief for around eight lakh employees and pensioners, increasing the Dearness Allowance (DA) by 8 per cent.The decision followed a meeting held here between chief minister Bhagwant Mann and representatives of employee and pensioners' organisations.Ministers Aman Arora and Baljeet Kaur, chief secretary KAP Sinha, secretary general administration KK Yadav and others were also present.After the meeting, Gurnam Singh Virk, president of Punjab State Ministerial Services Union, said the enhanced DA will be given from October 1.He said, regarding various other issues, the government has also assured them that these will be discussed soon.The deadlock began August 27 when over three lakh government employees went on a statewide strike by availing mass casual leave, pressing the state government to accept their various demands, including release of their pending 18 per cent Dearness Allowance.An official statement quoting Bhagwant Mann said the move reflects his government's commitment to the welfare and dignity of employees, whom he described as the backbone of the state's administrative machinery.
The chief minister also announced compulsory monthly meetings with employee representatives to address genuine issues, postings for women employees within 40 kilometres of their homes, and highlighting that around 70,000 government jobs have been provided through a transparent and corruption-free process.Women employees should not have to choose between their career and their family responsibilities. The state government will ensure that the system remains sensitive to their genuine needs, he said.Mann met representatives of employees and pensioners, heard their concerns, it said.After the meeting, Mann stated on X: "Had a very positive meeting today with employee and pensioner organisations. Employees are an important part of our family, and keeping their welfare in mind, we have immediately decided to increase the Dearness Allowance (DA) by 8 per cent. This increase will start reflecting with the October salary"."We also discussed long-pending issues inherited from previous governments, including the Old Pension Scheme (OPS), salary during the probation period, and issues concerning ASHA and Mid-Day Meal workers. We will meet again in the first week of October to work towards a permanent resolution of these longstanding issues."There is no distance between our government and employees. We will resolve every issue through mutual dialogue. We will continue to work together for Punjab's progress," he said.Emphasising that the welfare, dignity and legitimate concerns of government employees remain a priority for his government, Mann said, "As per the decision, two instalments of 4 per cent each will be released to employees and pensioners, with the benefit to be reflected in their salaries from October 1. Ahead of the festive season, this decision will provide additional financial support to thousands of government employees and pensioners and their families."The chief minister said, "The government understands the responsibilities shouldered by its employees and the pressures they face in their personal and professional lives.""A happy employee is a productive employee and I believe that when an employee works with satisfaction, dignity and peace of mind, the entire system performs better and the people receive better services..."."The state government has an open mind towards the genuine demands of employees and pensioners and these issues will be examined sympathetically and in accordance with the applicable rules, financial implications and legal position."He said the government will examine various long-pending demands, including "the demand for a 2.59 pension multiplication factor, restoration of the Old Pension Scheme (OPS), restoration of various allowances, implementation of Assured Career Progression (ACP), issues relating to the 2015 and 2020 letters concerning the probation period, generalization of court decisions and others.""No genuine issue concerning employees is being ignored and the government will examine each matter with an open and sympathetic approach. Employee welfare cannot be treated as a one-time exercise and requires continuous dialogue between the government and its workforce," he said.
Notably, earlier, the employees had remained adamant on their demand for clearance of DA arrears as per directions of the Punjab and Haryana High Court.The Punjab government had moved the Supreme Court challenging the High Court order directing it to release all pending DA and dearness relief dues to state employees and pensioners within a fortnight, contending that the direction to pay arrears totalling around Rs 14,191 crore in such a short period was impossible.

Inside Gaza’s death trap of collapsing, bombed buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:53:23 UTC
01:53:23 KST

Amr Adas pulls the remains of his family’s clothes from the rubble of the Al-Sa’ada building, friends steadying him so he doesn’t collapse. The structure fell onto the displaced families sheltering inside it, including his wife and five children. He places each item into an empty flour sack. When he reaches the clothes of his two children — Bilal, 6, and Dunia, 12, who died when the building collapsed before dawn on Wednesday — he breaks into wails.
His screaming rises from the eastern side of the site, mixing with bulldozers clearing rubble from the west for a second consecutive day. Friends and neighbors try to calm him, some with words, some with Quranic verses on patience.
“This is not God’s will,” he shouts, to no one. “This is the world’s silence over our annihilation. It’s the lack of even the most minimal support in finding a safe shelter. It forces us to accept any place to stay in, no matter how dangerous.”
Adas, 37, kneels at the site where he was rescued, amid rubble and dust. He points to what was his children’s room. Two are dead; three survived: Sama, 14, with multiple injuries; Malak, 10, with a pelvic fracture; and Mennatullah, a year and a half old.
He recalls that when the collapse began at 2:45 a.m., he jumped to shield the infant, but his wife, Nawal, 32, had already covered her with her own body. He embraced them both as the building fell around them, screaming to his other daughters in the next room: “Come here, come here.”
“The building kept collapsing for a few minutes, and everything was falling on us, and I heard nothing but the sound of bricks and concrete,” Adas said. “I could hear the screams of my four children in the next room, but I couldn’t move, and I could barely say a few words hoping to reassure them.”
“Suddenly, the place went silent after the collapse finished, and the voices of my children calling for me went silent, too, especially the two who died,” he said. “When my children’s voices stopped, it was the harshest moment of my life — that I was meters away from them and couldn’t save them.” The collapse of the Al-Sa’ada building is not an isolated incident. According to the most recent UNOSAT satellite analysis, based on imagery from July 2026, approximately 78 percent of all structures in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed since October 2023 — including an estimated 282,904 damaged housing units.
As the Al-Sa’ada building crumbled, Adas didn’t know at first whether it was an Israeli strike or a collapse. He heard neighbors calling, “Is anyone alive?” and answered once, “We’re here, save us,” before he could no longer speak. His wife kept calling out until rescuers arrived, directed light toward them, and lifted the rubble with their hands and simple tools. Adas said he had been pinned under stones and a concrete pillar.
Adas, a motorcycle mechanic before the war and unemployed ever since, said he accepted living in the bombed building because there was no other space. “The occupation destroyed my home in Zeitoun, east of Gaza City, which is now inside the danger zone, and there was no room anywhere else,” he said. “Some specialists told us the place was dangerous and at risk of collapse, but we had no other options. I feel enormous guilt for accepting this choice and losing two of my children, but I swear to God we had no alternative.”
‘A crime that happened with the knowledge of the entire world’
Muhammad al-Sawtari, 30, was also at the site searching for his family’s scattered belongings. His wife suffered moderate injuries and had to leave the hospital because she was nursing their two-month-old daughter, Misk. Their older daughter, Sham, 9, suffered serious injuries and was admitted to intensive care. Their two other daughters were also injured.
“Now some local and international institutions have rushed to clear the rubble and pull out the victims,” al-Sawtari said. “What if they had acted before that, and provided us with dignified shelter? Everyone warned us about the place, but no one offered us any alternative, and they left us in a dangerous building.”
“I don’t know yet whether my older daughter will survive, and I don’t know where we’ll go now, since all our belongings are under the rubble,” he said. “This is a crime that happened with the knowledge of the entire world, and the UN and international institutions operating in Gaza must act now to force the occupation to allow mobile homes in, so we can live with at least a minimum of dignity. There are no alternatives, and if any exist, they’re just worn-out tents made of fabric or plastic. Now we dream of nothing but a roof and walls, even if they’re collapsing.”
With conventional building materials blocked by Israel’s blockade, there is no practical pathway to rebuild. And with displacement ongoing, the only shelter available to tens of thousands of families is the ruins of what was already destroyed.
‘Every detail points to death, but we cling to life’
Several hundred meters away, Khaled Shabat, 33, ate food from a nearby communal kitchen with his wife, sister, and four children: Abd al-Hai, 10; Asala, a year younger; and twins Lana and Dana, 5. Shabat, unemployed, lives on the fourth floor of a bombed Islamic University building, separated from an internal corridor by a wall at risk of collapse, with a cracked ceiling, dangerous open floor edges, and an unexploded rocket nearby.
Displaced since the war’s first days, Shabat moved 11 times across the Strip before ending up here — the only unoccupied place available when he returned from al-Mawasi with the last truce in October 2025. “Our homes in Beit Hanoun were destroyed, and that area is now behind the Yellow Line,” he said. “This deadly option was all that was available to us. We’re ready to leave if the relevant institutions provide us with mobile homes. But tents? God forbid! We lived our harshest days in them.”
Shabat believes death in a building is more bearable than life in a tent, and would still prefer death by bombing over death by collapse. “We don’t want to spend moments feeling like we’re in a graveyard called a bombed building,” he said. “Every detail points to death, but we cling to life, and we consider staying in any building to be life, and the tent to be real death.”
A ‘nightmare’ winter approaches
Mahmoud Basal, spokesman for Gaza’s Civil Defense, said the coming winter will prove to be a “nightmare,” since bombed buildings become more prone to collapse with rain and wind. He warned that more than 40,000 Palestinians are living in over 2,000 destroyed, collapse-prone buildings whose structural condition requires demolition, not habitation.
The al-Sa’ada building, he said, had been bombed by Israeli aircraft in November 2023, and more than 100 people had taken up residence inside it over the past year. “Some of the displaced left, and the rest were asleep until the major collapse occurred at 2:45,” he said. “Some managed to flee within moments, while the rest were trapped among the rubble. Some died, others were injured.”
“We pulled out 45 survivors since we arrived at the site only minutes after the collapse, using our hands and primitive tools, without any machinery. Then we requested help from the Egyptian delegation, which provided excavators, and the Red Cross brought in an excavator at 7 a.m.,” Basal said.
Civil Defense currently operates only 15 ambulance, firefighting, and rescue vehicles, down from around 75 before the war. It owns no bulldozers or heavy machinery. UN institutions have no alternative shelter to offer residents beyond tents, which residents consistently refuse. Civil Defense holds a detailed list of collapse-prone buildings, nearly all inhabited, whose residents refuse to evacuate without mobile homes, an alternative Israel refuses to allow into Gaza, according to UN institutions.
He said removing the collapse-prone buildings requires capabilities entirely unavailable now, but described a one-year plan achievable with around 50 pieces of heavy machinery, alongside a suitable alternative for the displaced families living in them.
Basal described the international community’s inaction as complicity. “Aren’t we in Gaza human beings who deserve life like everyone else?” he asked. “Why the silence and weakness in the face of the occupation? The world is complicit in these crimes.”

Over 150 countries reject US decision to bar Palestine from UNGA

Breadcrumb
Over 150 countries reject US decision to bar Palestinian delegation from UN General Assembly session
At least 152 countries voted on Thursday in favour of a resolution that states the US should reverse its decision to bar the Palestinian delegation from attending the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
The US, Israel and Paraguay voted against the resolution while Colombia, Honduras, Panama, and Peru abstained.
The countries stressed that banning the Palestinian delegation from attending is considered a clear violation of the Headquarters Agreement.
The agreement, which is between the UN and the US, legally obliges Washington to facilitate the entry and residence of diplomatic delegations, member states and observers to attend General Assembly meetings without any obstructions.
The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the resolution and said if it was adopted, it would effectively end any efforts to prevent its delegation from attending.
The foreign ministry said the visa sanctions were "an unjustified measure that runs counter to efforts to rebuild trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and create the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability".
A statement on Friday from the General Secretariat of the Arab League also welcomed the resolution, stating it reflects the broad international opposition to the US decision to prevent Palestine from its right to conveying its voice and position to the international community.
The General Secretariat commended the positions of the nations that sponsored and voted in favour of the resolution, and denounced the US decision, calling on it to fulfil its legal obligations.
The development comes after the US State Department said on Thursday it had greenlit visas for an Iranian delegation and staffers to attend the session, but denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and other Palestinian officials visas.
The US accused the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) of "glorifying terrorism" and attempting to "internationalise" the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Palestinian officials have rejected this, stating they have the right to seek accountability for Israel’s war crimes in Gaza, and against an occupying force, in accordance with international law.
Reports on Friday said the UN General Assembly would allow Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas to address the panel virtually next week for the second consecutive year.
The State of Palestine is currently recognised by around 75% of the UN's 193 member states, including the UK, France, Canada and Australia.

Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ goes on show amid clash between brother and King Charles
The outfit became a symbol of the royal couple’s troubled relationship and the public breakdown of their marriage
Princess Diana’s “revenge dress” went on display in London on Friday, days after new claims about King Charles’s reaction to her death, as the shadow cast over the royal family by the so-called “people’s princess” lingers nearly 30 years on.
The dress became a symbol of the rancour between Charles and Diana during the public breakdown of their marriage in the early 1990s, when she made a public appearance in the off-the-shoulder black silk number soon after Charles admitted his infidelity.
This week scrutiny of their troubled relationship has resurfaced thanks to extracts published in a forthcoming book by Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, who accuses the king of being “giddily elated” in the immediate aftermath of her death.

Saudi Aramco has told at least two European refining customers they will receive no crude oil next month following an attack on the kingdom’s key East-West pipeline, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
European refiners typically buy Saudi crude under contracts guaranteeing monthly supplies, but Aramco has informed customers that deliveries planned for next month will not proceed, according to the report.
Saudi Arabia had earlier warned European customers that some cargoes would be cancelled after drone attacks damaged three pumping stations, forcing the shutdown of the pipeline and disrupting oil loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The disruption has prompted refiners to seek alternatives. Poland’s Orlen, for example, has bought North Sea crude to replace disrupted Saudi imports, according to traders cited by Reuters.
Reuters could not independently verify the Bloomberg report. Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Aramco is working to partially restart the pipeline within days and restore it to full capacity within six weeks, Bloomberg reported.
The company has also increased crude exports through the Gulf using ship-to-ship transfers off Oman’s Sohar port to offset reduced shipments through the Red Sea.
France calls for G7 energy meeting
The disruption comes as crude prices have risen about 20 percent this month amid the US-Iran conflict and fighting involving Houthi forces in Yemen.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that France would convene a G7 meeting on energy in the coming weeks to strengthen cooperation and discuss options for releasing strategic reserves.
“In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues,” Macron said.
The meeting would also provide an opportunity “to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves”, he added.
Macron said the surge in fuel prices was “not the result of government decisions” but a consequence of the geopolitical situation. He said existing support measures would be reviewed and adjusted to help households.
“Before spending vast sums of money, which is taxpayers’ money and would ultimately translate either into a higher deficit or higher taxes, we must above all remain focused on addressing the root causes,” Macron said.

More than a quarter of Anthropic PBC’s research and development (R&D) work for artificial intelligence (AI) is driven by its Claude chatbot, the company said, providing the clearest indication yet that AI can help speed up development of future models.
Anthropic found Claude “leads” 26 percent of Anthropic’s R&D, up from effectively nothing at the start of the year, a report released on Thursday said. The AI developer said Claude also collaborates with staffers for about 90 percent of their work.
The figures were released as part of a wider report to help the public track the progress of AI development in response to growing concerns about the potential for AI to rapidly move beyond human control.
Photo: Reuters
The company also reiterated its plans to embed third-party evaluators from several organizations within the company, and grant them access to internal processes, systems and data comparable to what the company grants its own employees.
“AI systems are becoming exponentially more powerful and have begun to automate more of the process of building themselves. As the world considers slowing the pace of frontier AI development, the public needs more information,” the company said.
Anthropic is one of several AI companies focusing on “recursive self-improvement” (RSI), or the idea of an AI system capable of improving itself with little to no help from humans. Some firms see it as the future of AI development, but it has also fueled concerns about the security threats this form of AI could pose if it is achieved.
In the blog, Anthropic said that it attempted to create a framework to track agents and monitor the amount of work they do on its platform. It said that as of last month, more than 30,000 agents are doing research and engineering work at the company at any one time.
Anthropic also laid out how it allocates resources toward accelerating AI development over ensuring the safety of its AI. According to its measurements, it found that between 6 to 12 percent of its computing resources, depending on the type of research being done, went toward safety monitoring.
In a blog post earlier this month, rival AI maker OpenAI also shared updates on its pursuit of automating research, saying that it had paused some training of its models after it found that they had hacked the external systems of Hugging Face, a startup.
Anxiety about AI’s existential risks gained momentum last week, driven by the high-profile departure of Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who accused AI companies of “gambling with our lives” in a resignation post he shared on social media.
In the past several days, numerous AI company leaders, including Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have urged slowing the pace of the development of the technology to address its increasingly unpredictable risks — though they diverge on exactly how it should be handled.
On Saturday in a 3,800-word essay, Amodei called for government regulation and for the tech industry to support a broader AI slowdown. That prompted vehement pushback from US President Donald Trump, who dismissed fears about the tech’s risks as “a hoax” and rejected the idea of new rules.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

Sitting down with a cup of coffee is one of life’s simple pleasures. However, many people are not fully aware of the actual differences between different types of coffee beyond their names. For example, what exactly is espresso? Although the name may sound like “express,” it is more closely related to the Italian idea of coffee being “pressed out” under pressure. That, however, is only part of the story. What makes this more confusing is that all espresso is coffee, but not all coffee is espresso.
The differences largely come down to the type of roast and how the beans are ground and brewed. Espresso is the most concentrated form of coffee, made by forcing hot water through finely ground beans under high pressure. As a result, more flavor is extracted in a short time, creating a bold and concentrated drink. Espresso often carries hints of chocolate, caramel, or nuts. It also forms the base of many popular coffee drinks, including lattes, cappuccinos, and macchiatos.
Espresso lovers appreciate it for its strong flavor, thick texture, and distinctive crema — the thick, golden-brown layer of foam that forms on top of a freshly brewed shot. It adds a velvety texture and a slight bitterness that many enjoy. Since espresso takes only about 20 to 30 seconds to brew and is usually served in a 25- to 30- milliliter portion, it is ideal for those in a hurry. Even so, some people prefer to sip it slowly, showing that coffee is as much about personal experience as it is about preparation.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
坐下來喝一杯咖啡是人生中簡單的樂趣之一。然而，除了名稱之外，很多人並不完全了解不同咖啡種類之間的實際差異。例如，義式濃縮咖啡（espresso）究竟是什麼？雖然這個名字可能聽起來很像「快速（express）」，但它其實與義大利語中在壓力下「被擠出」的咖啡概念更為相關。然而，那只說對了一部分。更讓人感到困惑的是，所有的濃縮咖啡都是咖啡，但並非所有的咖啡都是濃縮咖啡。
這些差異主要在於烘焙種類，以及如何研磨與沖煮咖啡豆。濃縮咖啡是咖啡最濃縮的形式，它是透過高壓方式強行將熱水沖過磨成細粉的咖啡豆萃取而成。因此，在短時間內能萃取出更多風味，形成口感強烈且濃郁的飲品。濃縮咖啡通常帶有一點巧克力、焦糖或堅果的風味。它同時也是許多熱門咖啡飲品的基底，包括拿鐵、卡布奇諾以及瑪奇朵。
濃縮咖啡的愛好者喜愛它濃烈的風味、醇厚口感，以及獨特的咖脂（在新鮮萃取的濃縮咖啡上方形成的那層濃厚、金褐色的泡沫）。它增添了絲絨般的口感，以及許多人喜愛的微苦風味。由於濃縮咖啡只需約二十至三十秒即可沖煮完成，且通常以二十五至三十毫升的分量供應，因此非常適合趕時間的人。即便如此，有些人仍喜歡慢慢啜飲，這說明了咖啡的重點不只在於製作過程，更關乎個人的體驗感。
What Did You Learn?
1. What does the author mean by saying “all espresso is coffee, but not all coffee is espresso” in the first paragraph of the Day 1 passage?
(A) Espresso is one type of coffee, but coffee includes various types.
(B) Espresso and regular coffee are unrelated, but both are widely consumed.
(C) Espresso is made in a special way, while coffee is prepared in many ways.
(D) Espresso contains all kinds of ingredients, while coffee includes only one type.
2. Which feature of espresso helps create its smooth texture and slight bitterness?
(A) The coarse grounds used during brewing.
(B) The crema that forms on top of the drink.
(C) The paper filter that removes fine particles.
(D) The long brewing time that extracts flavors slowly.
答案：1. A 2. B
Words in Use
1. confusing a. 令人困惑的
The instructions were so confusing that Bill had to read them several times. 說明內容太令人困惑，比爾不得不讀好幾遍。
2. largely adv. 大部分
Andy’s success was largely due to his persistence.
安迪的成功主要歸功於他的堅持。
3. concentrated a. 濃縮的
The company produces concentrated fruit extracts that are used in a variety of beverages.
這家公司生產濃縮果汁萃取液，用於各種飲品中。
4. finely adv. 細緻地
The chef finely chopped the onions for the soup.
廚師把洋蔥切得非常細來做湯。
5. extract vt. 萃取，提煉
Scientists extract useful substances from plants to create new medicines.
科學家從植物中萃取有用物質來製作新藥。
Practical Phrases
1. be aware of. . . 了解∕知道……
Amy should be aware of the rules before joining the contest. 艾咪在參加比賽前應該要知道規則。
2. be related to. . . 與……有關
Many health problems are related to long-term stress and a lack of proper rest.
許多健康問題與長期壓力以及缺乏適當休息有關。
3. come down to. . . 關鍵在於∕歸結為……
For Daniel, success comes down to daily practice.
對丹尼爾來說，成功的關鍵在於每天練習。
4. be ideal for... 非常適合……
This chair is ideal for those who sit for long hours at work. 這張椅子很適合需要長時間坐著工作的人。
5. in a hurry 匆匆忙忙地
Emma answered the question in a hurry, so she made a small mistake. 艾瑪匆忙作答，因此犯了一個小錯。

The US has approved a US$24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia, the US Department of State said on Thursday, the kingdom’s latest major arms purchase since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel has voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalize relations.
“The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defense, and improving interoperability with US forces,” the department said. “[It] will also augment Saudi Arabia’s operational aircraft and enhance its air-to-air, and air-to-ground self-defense capability.”
Photo: AFP
The Saudi Arabian embassy in Washington praised the transaction, saying it “reflects the strength and enduring nature” of the relationship with the US.
The security cooperation between the two countries “has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defense capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests,” it added.
Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran’s forces since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Yemen’s civil war had been dormant for years, but fighting between Houthis and the internationally recognized, Riyadh-backed government reignited in July, with the rebels declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and targeting its ships in the Red Sea.

====================================================================================================

Fed staff should have known Silicon Valley Bank was vulnerable, new report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:56 UTC
01:38:56 KST

An outside review of the Federal Reserve's oversight of the failure of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023 has found the Fed's staff "knew, or should have known," that the bank was vulnerable prior to the crisis, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said Friday.
Bowman's announcement of the report's findings immediately escalated political tensions around the Fed. The White House said the report implicated Fed Governor Michael Barr, who was appointed by President Joe Biden in 2022 and held Bowman's job as the Fed's top bank regulator during the banking crisis in 2023 that led to Silicon Valley Bank's failure.
Trump said this week the Fed's board is "hostile" after Chairman Kevin Warsh joined a unanimous vote of the Federal Open Market Committee to raise interest rates. Some in the Fed community have worried the report, which was being publicly undertaken, would be used as a pretext to push Barr off the board. Neither Trump nor Warsh made any immediate announcements to that effect.
The Fed's Board of Governors declined to comment on the report, beyond Bowman's comments. She announced the initial results of the review, by the consulting firm Starling Advisory Group, in a speech in London.
Starling didn't immediately respond to questions about whether it would release the full report. Bowman described the consulting firm's work as an initial report, but didn't say when or whether the public might see the full results of the inquiry.
Silicon Valley Bank experienced a run in March 2023 after the bank announced it had sold securities at a $1.8 billion loss and needed to raise more capital. The bank's large holdings of U.S. Treasurys had lost value after the Fed began raising interest rates.
The bank's customers included tech startups and venture capital firms. Many kept large sums on deposit at the bank, above the $250,000 threshold for deposit insurance. When the bank showed signs of strain, customers immediately sought to withdraw their funds, prompting a dramatic, fast-moving run on the bank.
The bank's deposits were "94 percent uninsured and concentrated in venture capital–backed technology companies," Bowman said the review found.
After the run, the heads of the Fed, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Treasury Department issued a joint statement saying they would insure all deposits in the bank, even those above the FDIC's $250,000 limit.
Barr was assigned to review of the episode in April 2023. The Fed's staff conducted an investigation that found its bank supervisors were overcautious in responding to the episode.
The new review largely concurs, according to Bowman's description. The outside firm found Fed supervisors knew, or should have known, about the risks in advance, Bowman said. The report does not identify Barr by name and instead attributes the failures to supervisory staff.
Barr stepped down from the supervisory position in February 2025 to allow President Donald Trump to select a new top regulator for the Fed. The president picked Bowman, who was confirmed by the Senate for that role.
Barr told the newsletter Capitol Account in July that he had agreed to cooperate with the new review.
White House spokesman Kush Desai charged that Barr "failed to do his job throughout this debacle, and then put out a report widely regarded as politicized and self-serving absolving himself of any blame. Everyday Americans, investors, and financial markets deserve competence and accountability in a Federal Reserve that keeps its eye on the ball."
A spokesperson for the Fed did not immediately respond to an email seeking a response to Bowman's comments and whether the Fed might release the Starling report itself.
Barr's review in 2023 had found the Fed had shifted its regulatory standards following a 2018 law. That change effectively reduced the Fed's standards, Barr said, and prompted "a less assertive supervisory approach."
The new outside review disagreed, Bowman said. "The delays in supervisory action were not caused by the regulatory tailoring mandate," she said.
Bowman has already begun a sweeping overhaul of the Fed's bank-oversight practices. She has said she plans to reduce the ranks of the Fed's supervision and regulation division by about 30%. An update to the Fed's staff page showed a dozen senior staff had left the division by early September, though some new staff had been added and others may be hired going forward.
The new review was a waste of taxpayer money, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, who is the ranking Democrat on the Senate banking committee, said in a statement following Bowman's comments.
"It's an embarrassing attempt to re-write history designed to pave the way for more dangerous deregulation that will lead to the next Silicon Valley Bank disaster," Warren said.
— Megan Cassella and Jeff Cox contributed to this report.

The three-day event in Taitung County from Wednesday through yesterday was part of National Disaster Prevention Day exercises.
Photo: Liu Jen-wei, Taipei Times
Yesterday’s drill — simulating a magnitude 7.3 earthquake in the southern section of the East Longitudinal Valley — involved personnel from 11 countries.
American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene, Canadian Trade Office in Taipei Executive Director Marie-Louise Hannan and Swedish Representative to Taiwan Carl Michael Grans were among the foreign representatives at yesterday’s drill.
A “semi-notified, unscripted” format was used as participants responded to simulated damage to critical infrastructure and disruptions to external assistance.
The drill incorporated lessons from Typhoon Danas and the Mataian River (馬太鞍溪) barrier lake disaster in Hualien County last year, including arrangements for backup communications, as well as evacuations and shelters.
The government has expanded international disaster-response cooperation in the past few years, including cooperation between Taiwan and Germany on disaster prevention, humanitarian assistance and joint rescue operations, Lai said.
More than 177,000 people have been trained as disaster preparedness personnel, up from about 100,000 last year, he said.

Australia tightens visa rules, to detain tourists who overstay, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:53 UTC
01:38:53 KST

Australia will detain tourists who overstay visas to send a message of deterrence under new rules aimed at reducing levels of migration, a minister said yesterday.
Australia’s ruling Labor party has denied it is tightening visa rules in response to the rise of the far-right One Nation, which has become one of the country’s most popular parties this year with pledges to drastically slash migration.
Under reforms announced on Thursday, Australia would stop family members accompanying students, introduce ballots for working holiday makers and crack down on overstayers.
Photo: Reuters
Tourists would be put in immigration detention to reduce the level of visa overstayers, which has risen to 77,000, Australian Assistant Minister for Immigration Matt Thistlethwaite said.
“Once the word gets around, ‘Hey, I overstayed on my tourist visa for a couple of weeks, I got picked up and I spent a couple of weeks in immigration detention, it’s not a nice place, I’m going home.’ Once that gets around, then we think that obviously that deterrence will ensure that people abide by the conditions,” he said.
People who do not have the right to remain in Australia would face a “consequence” and be removed, he added.
Since 2015, Australia’s immigration detention centers have swelled with people with criminal convictions awaiting deportation after a policy change that saw mandatory cancelation of permanent visas for certain criminal offenses.
Australian Minister for Immigration and Citizenship Tony Burke, announcing the new policy on Thursday, said the government would open 250 beds and add 100 compliance officers to house the visa overstayers in different facilities.
Australian Tourism Industry Council CEO Erin McLeod said talk of detaining tourists was not good for Australia’s image.
“I don’t think it does our reputation as a welcoming destination any good and can become quite damaging — tourism is an important part of the Australian economy,” she said.
The council represents thousands of small tourism businesses.
Refugee Council of Australia director of policy Rebecca Eckard said the move raised safety and legal concerns.
“It is being framed as punitive to change behavior. The use of punitive detention is not permitted under Australia’s immigration act,” she said.
“There has been a major problem with immigration detention,” she added, pointing to concerns raised by the government ombudsman over insufficient staffing and healthcare access.

Tang Prize laureates honored ahead of today’s lectures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:52 UTC
01:38:52 KST

The six recipients of the seventh Tang Prize were honored at a ceremony in Taipei yesterday, ahead of a full day of lectures today featuring their award-winning work.
Five of the six laureates attended the ceremony at the Taipei Performing Arts Center to receive their awards in person. Steven A. Rosenberg, one of three recipients in the biopharmaceutical science category, was unable to travel to Taiwan, according to the Tang Prize Foundation.
During the ceremony, Tang Prize Selection Committee convener Wong Chi-huey (翁啟惠), a former president of Academia Sinica, and the chairs of the four category selection panels introduced the laureates and outlined their major contributions.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The six recipients were announced by the prize’s selection committees in mid-June.
They are scheduled to deliver lectures at the Taipei Bioinnovation Park throughout Saturday, discussing the research and ideas they have developed over their careers.
American atmospheric chemist Susan Solomon received the Tang Prize in Sustainable Development for research that helped establish chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, as the primary cause of the expanding hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica.
Her work explained the chemical reactions behind ozone depletion and provided a scientific basis for global efforts to phase out CFCs under the Montreal Protocol.
The Tang Prize in Biopharmaceutical Science was jointly awarded to Rosenberg, Michel Sadelain and Carl H. June for developing cancer treatments that harness patients’ own immune cells.
Their work on tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies helped pioneer “living drugs,” in which immune cells are collected, enhanced or genetically modified, and returned to patients to attack cancer.
Chinese historian Ge Zhaoguang (葛兆光) received the Tang Prize in Sinology for his research on Chinese intellectual, cultural and religious history.
His influential studies exploring the question “What is China?” have challenged conventional historical perspectives and introduced new approaches to the study of China.
Yale University constitutional scholar Bruce Ackerman received the Tang Prize in Rule of Law for his work on constitutional government, judicial review and democratic institutions.
His ideas include “dualist democracy,” which distinguishes routine government decision-making from rare periods of broad public mobilization that bring about fundamental constitutional change.
The Tang Prize is a biennial award established in 2012 by Taiwanese entrepreneur Samuel Yin (尹衍樑) to recognize significant contributions in four fields: sustainable development, biopharmaceutical science, sinology and rule of law.

Rowing champions voice Brisbane venue concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Prominent Australian rowing figures have criticized the approval of Rockhampton’s crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River as the venue for the sport at the Brisbane Olympics, arguing the course would require extensive investment and leave little lasting legacy.
Worries about the venue initially focused on the 500 crocodiles that live in and around the river, but there are also concerns about the impact of river current on the fairness of competition and the lack of accommodation in the city of 80,000.
However, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli announced in state parliament on Thursday that an independent technical review had found the course capable of hosting fair rowing and canoeing competitions in 2032.
Photo: AP
Experienced coaches and former elite rowers remain unconvinced that a venue about 600km north of the host city is the best option.
“Without a massive infrastructure spend, it’s just going to be like a country regatta with Olympic athletes,” said former world championship medalist Andrew Butler, who has coached rowing for 17 years, including on the Fitzroy River.
“Why are you taking it 700km away from a multi-sport event when it’s obviously not to a better venue?”
Three-times Olympic champion Drew Ginn said he had concerns that water depth, river characteristics and the potential for flooding could all impact the competition.
“I row on a river in Melbourne. I love rowing on it, love training on it, but I’d never want to compete at the Olympic Games on it,” he said.
“If you have flowing and moving water, that is completely unfair,” Ginn said.
“One lane over another lane can be dramatically different. Imagine if [a flood] happens the week of the competition. Races get cancelled or the venue has to be moved,” he said.
“There’s never been a national championships held there, there’s a reason for that. It feels like it’s a gamble that the Queensland government’s taking,” he added.
Ginn also called for the technical review to be made public.
“If there’s good evidence for it and good data for it, then you should be able to make it transparent,” he said.
In a statement issued by Brisbane 2032 organizers on Thursday, World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland was quoted as saying the venue could deliver fair competition, but unusually the body did not issue its own statement nor the report.
There was no immediate response from World Rowing to a request for comment on the technical endorsement.
In a short statement, Rowing Australia “acknowledged” the completion of the technical review while making it clear neither it nor Rowing Queensland had played any part in the process.
John Driessen, an Olympic rowing coach and former elite rower who has coached on the Fitzroy River, echoed Butler and Ginn’s concerns over the legacy of the venue.
“I’ve coached at Fitzroy and it worked really well. But turning it into an Olympic-class course, I would have thought would be quite expensive and difficult,” he said.
“There’d be a lot of money going into a spot where there’s no real guarantee that it would benefit the state of Queensland in the future.”
However, Driessen said he did not think the Fitzroy River course would necessarily lead to unfair competition.
“It’s quite a shallow course,” he said. “If they’re going to maintain the basic principles of a rowing course with depth and lack of flow, then I think it would be a challenge to achieve that. I’m not sure that if the course was run at Rockhampton, it would be that unfair in terms of lanes,” he added.
Driessen said hosting the Olympic rowing at Moreton Bay just north of Brisbane, the site favored by Rowing Queensland, was a “no-brainer” and “the simple answer.”
Butler favored the original plan to stage the rowing on flat water at Wyaralong Dam some 86km southwest of Brisbane, describing it as “probably the best course I’ve rowed on in Queensland.”
“Investment there would be an absolute legacy ticket,” said the twice Australian champion.
However, Crisafulli is determined that regional cities around Queensland should be able to share in the Olympic experience and has previously denounced critics as “elitist.”
“I thought the Olympics was a sporting event,” Butler said.

====================================================================================================

EDITORIAL: Protecting the participating society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Taiwan ranked seventh worldwide for civil participation in The Global State of Democracy 2026: Democracy in an Age of Conflict report published on Tuesday by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance. The Stockholm-based intergovernmental organization, which has more than 30 member states, evaluates four characteristics of democracies: representation, rights, rule of law and participation.
Taiwan ranked far above its neighbors in the “participation” category, with South Korea 36th and Japan 60th. The category measures voter turnout and the strength of civil society, as well as participation in political and nonpolitical organizations.
Taiwan was up five places from a year earlier in “representation,” down one place in “rule of law” and unchanged in the other two. With 57 percent of the countries assessed declining in at least one measure of democratic performance, maintaining a high standard is no small feat. Yet one look at Taiwan’s history demonstrates why its ranking is not surprising.
Although the nation’s democracy is relatively young, it has been built upon decades of ordinary people taking action for social and political change. During the 1970s and 1980s, the dangwai (黨外, “outside the party”) movement challenged the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) political monopoly under martial law and pushed for greater political freedoms. Rights advocates, journalists, lawyers and ordinary citizens organized in spite of the risks, helping lay the groundwork for political liberalization.
In 1990, three years after martial law was lifted, thousands of students demanded the dissolution of the aging National Assembly, the repeal of the temporary provisions governing the country and a timetable for political liberalization. The rally, known as the Wild Lily student movement, accelerated constitutional reforms, including the retirement of the “10,000-year congress” and the introduction of direct presidential elections in 1996.
The tendency of Taiwanese society to organize and demand change did not end with democratization. In 2011, Japan’s Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear crisis gave new momentum to the anti-nuclear movement, prompting thousands to protest construction of the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant in New Taipei City’s Gongliao District (貢寮) and call for a reassessment of nuclear energy policy. Three years later, students and civic groups of the Sunflower movement occupied the Legislative Yuan over the government’s handling of a cross-strait trade agreement.
Last year, civic groups mobilized volunteers to collect signatures and trigger recall votes against KMT legislators. While all 24 recall votes failed, they drew an average turnout of more than 56 percent — much higher than the turnout typically seen in recall elections — demonstrating that voters on both sides of the political divide were motivated to take part.
Taiwan’s record of participation is not limited to politics. When devastating floods affected more than 1,600 homes in Hualien County’s Guangfu Township (光復) last year, tens of thousands of volunteers traveled from across the nation to help clear mud and debris, distribute food and supplies and assist residents in rebuilding their homes.
The same spirit is visible in nationwide urban resilience and air-defense drills, which have increasingly involved cooperation between local governments, businesses and residents. Whether disaster response or crisis preparedness, the efforts reflect a broad willingness among the public to take care of their communities.
Behind the long-standing culture of participation is a broader sense that society is something worth investing in and improving.
A 2021 Pew Research Center survey of 17 advanced economies asked people what made their lives meaningful, fulfilling and satisfying. While most cited factors such as family, jobs and material well-being, Taiwan was the only nation in which “society” ranked as the top source of meaning. It was also the only nation that ranked “freedom” in the top five.
Taiwanese pointed to the convenience and safety of daily life, affordable healthcare and the freedom provided by the nation’s democracy and rule of law. One woman said that she felt “fortunate to live in Taiwan, especially in the aspect of public health, democracy, and the rule of law and human rights, because it is very free.”
However, as much as Taiwanese value their free, safe and democratic society, they must also understand that it is not self-sustaining. It must be cultivated — especially as younger generations would face new challenges amid a rapidly changing political, technological and international landscape.
Taiwan’s ranking in the democracy report is much more than an impressive number. It represents decades of ordinary people dedicating their time to organize, volunteer, vote, protest and generate systemic change. That is something Taiwan should be proud of — and something worth protecting.
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Green manufacturing in Vietnam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Taiwanese companies have been part of Vietnam’s manufacturing landscape since the 1990s. They have established a presence across sectors including electronics, textiles and materials.
However, the conditions for manufacturing are changing. Vietnam is pushing toward net zero emissions by 2050, while global companies are placing greater environmental demands on their suppliers.
For Vietnam, the green transition is becoming part of a broader challenge: How to remain competitive as the requirements of global manufacturing change.
That shift is important to Taiwanese companies already operating in Vietnam. Many supply global brands whose environmental requirements are becoming stricter. Apple, for example, requires its entire direct manufacturing supply chain to use 100 percent renewable electricity for Apple production before 2030. Last year, more than 20 gigawatts of renewable energy procured by suppliers and online in Apple’s supply chain generated more than 38 million megawatt-hours of clean energy.
Requirements like those do not stop at the headquarters of global brands. They reach the factories producing their components and products. For Taiwanese manufacturers in Vietnam, reducing emissions is gradually becoming a part of doing business. A competitive manufacturing location is no longer judged only by labor costs, infrastructure or access to markets. The availability of cleaner electricity is becoming part of the equation.
Vietnam is moving in that direction. Its revised Power Development Plan VIII, approved in April last year, targets renewable energy, excluding hydropower, at 28 to 36 percent of the power mix by 2030. The plan also places emphasis on developing the power system and grid to meet rising demand. Vietnam has also introduced a direct power purchase mechanism, allowing large electricity users to buy power directly from renewable-energy generators. The framework was updated in June.
However, for Taiwanese manufacturers, green electricity is only part of the issue: The power also has to be reliable. Vietnam’s electricity shortages in 2023 exposed the vulnerability of its rapidly expanding industrial base. In 2024, authorities asked major manufacturers in northern Vietnam, including Foxconn, to voluntarily reduce electricity use by 30 percent during periods of high demand. The request was precautionary rather than mandatory, but it highlighted a problem that matters to manufacturers operating in global supply chains: An interruption in electricity can quickly become an interruption in production.
This is where the interests of Vietnam and Taiwanese manufacturers begin to overlap. Vietnam needs to expand cleaner energy while making its electricity system more reliable. Taiwanese companies need a production base that can meet the environmental expectations of global customers without compromising the stability of their operations.
Some companies are already responding. Foxconn and Brookfield in June announced that they would jointly develop up to 1 gigawatt of utility-scale wind, solar and battery capacity in Vietnam, supported by long-term power-purchase agreements. The significance is not simply the size of the proposed investment. It points to a broader shift: Manufacturers are becoming more interested in the energy infrastructure around their factories, not just the factories themselves.
The same trend can be seen elsewhere in Taiwan’s manufacturing presence. Far Eastern New Century has been expanding renewable-energy use across its production network, including operations in Vietnam. Taiwanese manufacturer Je Hong Textile is developing a new factory in Vietnam focused on environmentally friendly fabrics, with features including wastewater treatment, LEED Gold standards and planned solar generation. Tainan Enterprises has also operated a LEED Gold-certified facility in Vietnam since 2017.
These examples do not mean that every Taiwanese factory in Vietnam is already green or that the transition will be easy — companies face different costs, technologies and regulatory conditions — but they show that Vietnam already has an established group of Taiwanese manufacturers with reasons to invest in cleaner production. That creates an opportunity to deepen the economic relationship.
Taiwan-Vietnam ties have long been shaped by trade, investment and manufacturing. The “China Plus One” strategy — avoiding a reliance solely on manufacturing and sourcing in China — has added to Vietnam’s importance as companies diversify production beyond China.
However, the next stage does not necessarily have to mean simply building more factories. Vietnam itself wants to attract investment that brings greater technology and value, while moving toward higher-value and more complex activities within global value chains. The World Bank has identified this as an important part of Vietnam’s longer-term development path.
Renewable electricity alone will not move Vietnam up the value chain. What it can do is help create the industrial conditions that increasingly matter to international manufacturers: cleaner production, more reliable power and the ability to meet tougher environmental standards. For Taiwanese companies, that makes Vietnam’s energy transition increasingly relevant to their own competitiveness. For Vietnam, it offers a way to improve an industrial base that is already closely connected to global production.
The foundations are already there. Taiwanese companies have spent decades building factories and production networks in Vietnam. Vietnam is now changing what it expects from its industrial economy. The next chapter of Taiwan-Vietnam economic cooperation might be less about how many factories are built and more about the conditions the factories operate in: cleaner energy, reliable electricity and an industrial environment that can meet increasingly demanding international standards.
For Vietnam, the task is to make the industrial base it has built over the decades greener and more competitive, while becoming better positioned in higher-value parts of global value chains.

S Korean president vows not to get drawn into Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung ruled out sending troops to the Strait of Hormuz to join the US war against Iran, despite pressure from US President Donald Trump, as Lee fights to reverse hemorrhaging public support and get his policy agenda back on track.
Lee has seen his approval ratings plunge in the past two months, hitting a fresh record low of 37 percent in a poll released yesterday — down from a high of 67 percent earlier this year. He faces strong domestic opposition to sending troops to the Middle East.
“There will be no involvement or intervention in the war,” Lee said during a snap news conference aimed at shoring up public support. “We will not deploy troops or military assets for that purpose. We have adhered to that principle so far, and that principle will remain unchanged.”
Photo: Bloomberg
The remarks were Seoul’s clearest message yet on deploying troops or military assets to the Middle East after Trump ramped up pressure on the US ally over its lack of support for the war with Iran.
South Korea is reviewing ways to help ensure safe passage through the strait by expanding the operations of its naval unit already deployed near the area, Lee said.
While the comments might please Lee’s base domestically, they might further fuel tension with key security partner Washington, Zeitgeist Institute director Eom Kyeong-young said.
“Just imagine how the US would feel hearing that,” Eom said, adding that more diplomatic language could have been helpful.
“He seemed to make those remarks with his core supporters in mind, but they looked problematic coming from a president,” Eom added.
At home, many South Koreans have soured on Lee over the economy. Even as the global artificial intelligence build-out reaps record profits for chip giants SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co, voters are seeing little impact on their lives, with surveys highlighting growing discontent on issues such as Seoul’s high property prices.
Lee apologized “to the people who continue to struggle through their daily lives in difficult circumstances.”
He said he was “taken aback by what seemed to be a sudden wave of disappointment and concern from the public,” but added that “the people are always right.”
Lee ordered a sweeping reshuffle of his cabinet weeks ago, changing out his finance, defense and justice ministers among others, with his top policy adviser Kim Yong-beom stepping down.
The reset and shift in messaging have failed to boost Lee’s approval ratings.
“This is a crisis of trust. Voters are at a point where they don’t believe what he says, no matter what he says,” Eom said.
Lee has also been struggling to balance Seoul’s all-important relationship with security ally Washington, which stations about 28,500 soldiers in the South in part to help protect it from the nuclear-armed North.
Trump canceled long-planned joint military drills with Seoul last month, citing his friendship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Seoul’s purported refusal to help with Iran.
