Syria's abolition of Assad-era terrorism court 'welcomed'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:56:09 UTC
00:56:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria's abolition of Assad-era terrorism court 'welcome'
The abolition of an Assad-era terrorism court by Syria's parliament has been described as a "welcome and necessary step", rights advocates told The New Arab, though warned that without effective implementation, the decision risks becoming a symbolic announcement.
Syria's parliament abolished the court, founded through the passing of Law No. 22 in 2012 during the height of Syria's civil uprising, on Wednesday. The abolition of the court also saw the abolition of its legal rulings.
The court's purpose was to issue legal verdicts in line with Law No. 19, which pertained to counter-terrorism, used by the Assad regime to prosecute activists and dissidents in a bid to stifle the uprising against the regime.
Fadel Abdul-Ghany, Director of the Syrian Network for Human Rights, told Syria's state news agency SANA that 90,560 cases were brought before the court, alongside 10,767 people, since its founding.
This includes 3,970 cases of property seizure, and 40,602 cases of seizure and confiscation orders affecting 320,000 people between 2012 and 2024.
Kholoud Helmi, a non-resident Fellow at TIMEP, told The New Arab that the move is a "welcome and necessary step."
"This court was never an instrument of justice; it was used to criminalise peaceful opposition, legitimise arbitrary detention and confiscate Syrian's property, often on the basis of confessions extracted under torture."
However, Helmi said that Article 48 of the constitutional declaration already required the abolition of exceptional laws, unjust rulings by the Terrorism Court and a restitution of property.
"Parliament's decision should therefore be understood as the implementation of an existing constitutional obligation, rather than an entirely new measure."
She added that the significance of the ruling will depend on several things, including, "whether it establishes clear, accessible and time-bound procedures for reviewing judgements, restoring property and providing remedies when restitution is impossible".
If this is done, it could become a significant step in the country's transitional justice process that is key to moving the country away from the period under Assad, as well as healing it from the traumas of dictatorship and civil war.
"If it merely repeats Article 48 without delivering tangible remedies, it risks becoming a symbolic announcement," Helmi said.

NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Telescope glimpses its first cosmic light
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:55:52 UTC
00:55:52 KST

Say cheese, universe. NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has caught its first glimpses of cosmic light—a major step on the road to beaming back unprecedented images and data about our galaxy and the wider universe.
The telescope activated its Wide Field Instrument (WFI) on September 11, initiating the preliminary setup for Roman’s highly sensitive 300-megapixel camera. This is the first step in the telescope’s mission of looking for dark matter and energy and studying the Milky Way, as well as discovering new exoplanets in distant star systems.
After Roman’s launch on August 30, it spent 10 days drying out to prevent damage to its highly sensitive systems. With that done, the heaters were turned off, and the telescope was cooled down to –225 degrees Fahrenheit (–143 degrees Celsius)—at that point, its 18 infrared instruments could be activated.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Among the systems that came online for the first time were Roman’s calibration system, which NASA put through some testing, as well as light filtering devices and the WFI’s focus mechanism. Meanwhile the telescope continued to cool down to a frigid –300 degrees F (–183 degrees C).
After it is fully operational, the WFI will be used to capture extremely detailed patches of the sky, each bigger than the apparent size of a full moon. That will allow the telescope to study more than 50 times as much of the sky in its planned five years of operation as the Hubble Space Telescope has in 30 years of work.
“After years of effort to build and test the instrument on the ground, we now have confirmation that it is operational in space,” said WFI scientist Josh Schlieder in a statement. “There is much to do, but we are on our way to groundbreaking science.”
Along with the WFI, NASA engineers tested out communications with the telescope’s coronagraph—a complicated series of mirrors, sensors and other instruments that will be used to directly image exoplanets orbiting distant stars.
All the systems are working as expected—good news as we wait for Roman to become fully operational. The first images are expected around the holiday season, while science operations are scheduled to start in January 2027.

Early voting for the Nov. 3 US midterm elections got underway Friday in several states, beginning a process that will spread across most of the country in the coming weeks.
Minnesota and South Dakota allow voters to begin casting absentee ballots in person 46 days before Election Day, while Virginia also opened its early in-person voting period Friday.
Pennsylvania can make mail-in or absentee ballots available in person as early as 50 days before an election, although the timing varies by county and depends on certification of the candidate list.
Early voting rules differ significantly across the US.

Alabama, Mississippi and New Hampshire do not offer universal early in-person voting, though some voters may qualify for absentee options.
Early voting periods nationwide range from three to 46 days, with the average lasting about 20 days. Most states will begin offering early voting later in September or October.

Digital services making up over half of global services exports, serve to reshape trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:54:32 UTC
00:54:32 KST

Yunus Turk, Fahri Aksut, and Emir Yildirim
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Digitally deliverable services (DDS) rose to make up 56% of global service exports, outperforming broader service trade growth over the past 10 years, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
A new UNCTAD report showed that global services exports grew 6.7% over the past 10 years, while posting 8.3% growth in 2025.
Trade in DDS surged faster than the rest of the sector, posting an average of 7.1% annual growth over the past decade, driven by the proliferation of cloud computing, digital platforms, and improved connectivity infrastructure.
Insurance, finance, telecommunications, computing, research and development (R&D), management consulting, and architectural, engineering, and scientific services are included in this expanding category.
The report showed a stark technological divide as digital services made up around 61% of total service exports in developed countries versus 16% in least developed countries.
Total service exports from the least developed countries grew by an average of 3% per year over the past 10 years, while their share of total global service exports shrank from under 1% in 2010 to 0.6% in 2025, the data showed.
This gap between developed and least developed countries was further quantified in the report’s artificial intelligence (AI) readiness index, in which advanced economies scored an average of 0.65, while developing economies reached 0.41, and least developed countries lagged at 0.31.
Fewer than one-third of all developing countries have reportedly established a national AI strategy.
The UNCTAD urged emerging economies to focus on cross-border digital payment systems investments to prevent advanced AI from furthering existing inequalities, while also investing in regulatory frameworks and targeted workforce skills.
Competitive edge from added technological and service value
Erdem Erkul, chair of the digital tech business council at Türkiye’s Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK), told Anadolu that the UNCTAD data shows how the structure of global trade has transformed over the past 10 years, with physical manufacturing no longer being enough as modern products in almost every sector are integrated with supplementing software, data, and digital services.
“A country’s competitive edge will be determined by the extent to which it can add technological and service value to the goods it produces,” he said.
Erkul said AI risks widening the global wealth gap but it also offers developing nations an opportunity to lower the cost of producing and exporting digital services.
“AI can boost efficiency in many sectors and facilitate small companies’ accession to global markets,” he said.
He mentioned that key inputs for AI, such as data, financing, expert human resources, and high computing capacity, are concentrated in a small number of countries and firms, advising developing countries to focus their AI development on their already established areas of expertise.
“In Türkiye, we can bring solutions developed for quality control, energy management, and maintenance in our factories to global markets to transform our expertise into exportable digital products and services,” he added.

UN chief urges governments to honor sustainable development pledges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:54:22 UTC
00:54:22 KST

Diyar Guldogan
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday urged governments to honor their commitments to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), warning that conflicts, climate change, inequality and mounting debt are undermining global development.
Addressing the SDG Moment at the UN headquarters in New York, Guterres said the goals represented a shared commitment by governments to build healthier, safer and more prosperous societies.
"The promises governments made in adopting the Goals are not being kept. It is time to keep them," he said.
Guterres highlighted progress made since the SDGs were adopted, including reductions in child and maternal mortality, the prevention of millions of HIV infections and expanded access to education, social protection, safe drinking water, sanitation, electricity, renewable energy and the Internet.
But he said the gains had been accompanied by profound setbacks, most notably the global COVID-19 pandemic, which “erased years of progress and exposed deep vulnerabilities.”
“Through every crisis, we adapted. We learned. And we kept moving forward,” he said, emphasizing that development progress had been achieved through the determination of people, communities and countries.
 
- ‘Development faces powerful headwinds’
Guterres said development now faces “powerful headwinds,” citing conflicts, divisions and mistrust that are weakening international cooperation.
He pointed to continuing crises in the Middle East and elsewhere that are driving economic insecurity and disrupting the flow of food, energy and trade.
The UN chief also raised concerns over threats to the rights of women and girls, as well as the financial pressures facing developing countries.
Guterres outlined four areas where governments should intensify efforts to meet their SDG commitments.
The first is tackling inequality through investment in quality education, food security, decent work, universal health coverage and strong social protection systems.
The second priority is protecting the planet.
He said renewable energy has become the cheapest and fastest-growing source of new power across much of the world and called for countries rich in renewable resources to receive the tools needed to produce clean energy, manufacture clean technologies and create decent jobs.
Guterres identified sustainable development financing as the third priority.
"Countries have pledged to strengthen domestic resource mobilization and channel resources to the areas of greatest need. But much more is needed," he said.
The fourth priority is accelerating progress through better data, strategic foresight, technology and connectivity, Guterres said.
Guterres acknowledged that the SDGs are ambitious because of the scale of the challenges facing the world, but said ambition must be matched by action.
“Commitments must be matched with transformative action,” he said.
“That is the promise governments made. Keeping that promise is an obligation. It’s also our greatest opportunity to build a fairer, safer and more sustainable world.”
The SDGs, adopted by UN member states as a shared global framework, aim to address poverty, hunger, inequality, health, education, climate change and other development challenges while ensuring that no one is left behind.

AI boom pushes Belgium’s data center power demand toward eightfold increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:54:19 UTC
00:54:19 KST

Melike Pala
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Electricity consumption by large data centers in Belgium is expected to increase nearly eightfold by 2034 as demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and digital services accelerates, according to figures from Belgian transmission system operator Elia.
The country's 47 large data centers currently consume about 3.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity annually, equivalent to roughly 1 million households and about 4% of Belgium's total electricity use, figures broadcaster VRT cited Friday.
Elia forecasts that electricity demand from large data centers could reach 27.3 TWh by 2034.
Data centers are expected to become an increasingly important driver of electricity demand in Belgium, alongside the growing use of electric vehicles and heat pumps.
The increase raises questions about how Belgium and neighboring countries will meet rising electricity demand, particularly when domestic generation is constrained.
Belgium has increasingly relied on electricity imports during periods of high demand or reduced domestic generation.
The rapid expansion of data centers is also putting pressure on electricity networks elsewhere in Europe.
The Netherlands has faced grid congestion in several regions, limiting the ability of companies and other customers to obtain new electricity connections.
Other major European data center hubs, including Frankfurt, Paris and London, are also experiencing growing constraints on available grid capacity.
Ireland has taken measures to limit the expansion of data centers in areas where new facilities could place additional pressure on the electricity system.

Local council elections are also scheduled in the administrative centers of 10 regions.
111 million people eligible to vote
According to Russia's Central Election Commission, about 111 million people, including approximately 1.8 million registered voters abroad, are eligible to vote in the parliamentary polls.
Voting is taking place at polling stations, as well as through Russia’s remote electronic voting system, and will conclude at 8 pm local time on Sunday in the country’s numerous time zones.
Russia stretches across 11 different time zones, so in different regions the local time will vary from GMT+2 to GMT+12.
Eleven political parties are competing in the State Duma election, including the country's ruling United Russia party and the four parties currently represented in the Duma — the Communist Party, Liberal Democratic Party, A Just Russia—For Truth, and New People.

“The timing is right to complete the transition,” Warren Buffett said in a letter to shareholders accompanying Friday’s announcement.
Warren Buffett described serving as chairman as the “privilege of a lifetime” and expressed confidence in Berkshire’s future leadership.
Abel said Warren Buffett’s impact on Berkshire and its shareholders was unparalleled in US business history, adding that the culture and values he established would remain central to the company.
Howard Buffett, 71, has chaired the Howard G. Buffett Foundation since 1999. The foundation focuses on global food security and conflict mitigation.
He previously served on Coca-Cola's board.
‘Oracle of Omaha’
Born in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1930, Warren Buffett began investing as a child and later studied under Benjamin Graham, a leading proponent of value investing, at Columbia Business School.
He took control of Berkshire Hathaway, then a struggling textile manufacturer, in 1965 and transformed it into one of the world’s largest conglomerates.
Berkshire expanded through acquisitions and investments into insurance, rail transportation, energy, manufacturing, services and retail. Its businesses include insurer Geico, railroad operator BNSF, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and confectioner See’s Candies.
The company also became known for its major stakes in publicly traded companies, including Apple, Coca-Cola and American Express.
Warren Buffett’s strategy of buying high-quality businesses at attractive prices and holding them for the long term earned him the nickname the “Oracle of Omaha” and made Berkshire’s annual shareholder meeting one of the most closely watched events in global finance.
One of the world’s wealthiest people, Warren Buffett has pledged to donate 99% of his fortune to philanthropic causes. He co-founded the Giving Pledge with Bill and Melinda Gates in 2010.
Forbes estimated his net worth at $144.7 billion as of Friday, ranking him as the world’s 10th-richest person.

Aid agency officials said the boost in celebrity attention could help bring more support to Gaza, where nearly all residents rely on aid for food, water, medical care and shelter.
“But what’s really most important is that people who have been so generous keep fighting over a sustained time,” said Toby Fricker, a local official with UNICEF. “That’s why we really call for sustained support, not one-off peaks, but sustained.”
Hussein Murtaja, who runs a Gaza humanitarian group that provides mental health support to children, said Macklemore’s solidarity matters more than the money he donated.

Russia labels acclaimed filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev a 'foreign agent'
MOSCOW, Sept 18 - Acclaimed Russian film director Andrey Zvyagintsev, who has repeatedly criticised Moscow's war in Ukraine, was designated on Friday as a "foreign agent", state news agency TASS said.
Russia has applied the label, which has connotations of espionage, to numerous people, including public figures, who it deems to be engaging in anti-Russian activity with support from abroad.
Zvyagintsev won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival this year for "Minotaur", a film depicting a Russian businessman who is forced to decide which of his employees should be mobilised to go and fight in Ukraine.
"Millions of people on both sides of the front line dream of only one thing: for the massacres to stop," Zvyagintsev said in his acceptance speech, adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin was the only person capable of ending the war.
Critics described "Minotaur" as one of Zvyagintsev's most openly critical commentaries on Russia's political and moral condition.
The director, who has lived outside Russia since the COVID pandemic, is known for a series of other films including "The Return", "The Banishment" and "Leviathan", a bleak portrayal of life in rural Russia.
People listed as foreign agents are subjected to onerous bureaucratic requirements and restrictions on their income in Russia.
They have to warn in capital letters on everything they publish, including on social media, that the content was produced by a foreign agent.
Among other cultural figures to be labelled in this way are writer Boris Akunin and rock musician Boris Grebenshchikov. REUTERS

Nigerian forces fire at protesters rallying over deaths of detained miners
Government has promised to fully investigate after 37 miners died while being held in police custody in Niger state.
Security forces in Nigeria have opened fire and deployed tear gas during protests over the deaths in detention of 37 miners.
Demonstrators rallied in their hundreds in the mineral-rich city of Minna in Niger State during a second day of protests on Friday, with some attacking government facilities.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3When does a family meal become a luxury in Nigeria?
- list 2 of 3Nigeria suspends official visits to South Africa over anti-migrant violence
- list 3 of 3Nigerian police probe death in custody of 37 illegal mining suspects
It was not immediately clear whether troops fired live ammunition or anti-riot pellets, but a witness told the Reuters news agency that bullets had been used and the body of one person lay on the ground.
Officials announced on Thursday that the 37 miners had died while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), a paramilitary agency. The miners were arrested earlier this week during raids in the Wushishi-Lukoto area, west of Minna, on suspicion of illegal mining.
A 24-hour curfew was imposed by state governor Umar Bago on Friday, while the government promised to fully investigate the 37 deaths.
Al Jazeera’s Ahmed Idris, reporting from Abuja, said Friday’s protest violence targeted mostly government facilities in the state capital. But it “died down” after the imposition of the curfew.
“There were violent outbreaks across many parts of the country’s Niger State. There were attacks on government buildings and officials in the capital of the state,” Idris said.
“One of the areas that was targeted was the transport agency where buses and other vehicles were damaged by protesters who were angry at what happened in the Security and Civil Defence Corps detention centre.”
The NSCDC initially suggested that the miners may have been killed by an outbreak of disease, but has since clarified that the cause of death is yet to be confirmed. The NSCDC said further investigations will be conducted, including medical examinations.
However, all of the deceased were buried on Thursday evening, raising questions about whether post-mortems will still be possible.
The AFP news agency said it had seen an intelligence report suggesting that the deaths may have been caused by poor ventilation in the cells and overcrowding. Some protesters also told the Associated Press that the miners had suffocated.
Some survivors recounted their panic on Friday, saying they struggled to breathe inside the cell.
“We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well,” Dauda Shehu told journalists at a central Nigerian hospital. “All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”
The NSCDC’s commandant in Niger State, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, has been suspended by Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, pending a full investigation.
“It is an unfortunate incident, however, a full investigation will be conducted while the commandant under whose watch this happened remains suspended,” the Interior Ministry said in a statement.
Niger State is home to vast deposits of mineral resources, including gold and uranium and mining is a core part of the economy.
Illegal mining is common in Nigeria and has been blamed for fuelling violence among armed groups competing for control of the lucrative trade.

Shakira launches 12-concert Madrid run to close world tour after 8-year absence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:45:23 UTC
00:45:23 KST

Shakira returns to Spain this Friday with 12 shows in Madrid, wrapping up her world tour after eight years away, playing to about 50,000 fans a night until 11 October.
Shakira kicks off in Madrid this Friday night a marathon of 12 concerts that will bring her world tour to a close and end an eight-year absence from Spanish stages.
The Colombian singer, 49, will perform until 11 October in a temporary venue with capacity for 50,000 spectators, erected in the south of the capital and dubbed "Shakira stadium", according to Live Nation, the promoter of the shows.
With no new European dates announced, Madrid’s authorities are expecting a major economic impact from her return to Spain. In May and June the city already hosted ten concerts by Bad Bunny, another of Latin music’s biggest stars.
Shakira had not performed in Spain since 2018, several years before her separation from former Spanish footballer Gerard Piqué, a legendary Barcelona defender, became public in 2022.
The artist embarked in February 2025 on a world tour to present "Las mujeres ya no lloran", an album inspired by her break-up with the former Barcelona player and which earned her a fourth Grammy Award.
Over a career spanning several decades, Shakira has sold more than 95 million records worldwide and has performed at both the opening ceremony and the final of the 2026 football World Cup. "Waka Waka (This Time for Africa)" was also the official song of the 2010 World Cup, held in South Africa, the first ever staged on the African continent.
Shakira’s return to Madrid also comes after, in November 2023, she paid a fine of 7.3 million euros as part of a settlement with the Spanish justice system. The singer pleaded guilty to avoid having to stand trial for tax fraud.
In that high-profile case, Shakira also paid 17.45 million euros to the Spanish tax authorities to regularise her tax affairs in the country.

====================================================================================================

Xi Focus: Steering China's strides toward manufacturing powerhouse
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:39:27 CST
00:39:27 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Defying intense pressures at home and abroad, China's manufacturing sector has forged ahead, accelerating the construction of a modern industrial system with advanced manufacturing as its backbone, and solidifying the foundations for high-quality development.
China's manufacturing value-added accounts for nearly 30 percent of the global total, topping the world for over a decade.
That is no accident. It is the result of the insight and leadership of Chinese President Xi Jinping over the past years. As early as 2018, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said that China was experiencing a decline in manufacturing's share of the economy that was too fast, and the problem demanded close attention.
At a national conference on advanced manufacturing recently held in Beijing, Xi stressed the need to accelerate the development of a modernized industrial system with advanced manufacturing as its backbone and to reinforce the foundations of the real economy.
ANCHORING REAL ECONOMY
In May 2025, Xi visited Luoyang Bearing Group in Henan Province. Bearings are the joints of the entire manufacturing body, setting the performance ceiling for high-speed rail, wind turbines and aerospace alike.
Standing on the factory floor, Xi reflected on China's industrial journey. "From importing matches, soaps and iron products to becoming the world's largest manufacturing country with the most complete industrial sectors and categories, China has always adhered to the path of developing the real economy, which has proven to be the right path."
Over the years, Xi has walked the length and breadth of China's manufacturing landscape, and each stop has reinforced the same conviction that for a country of China's size, developing the real economy is non-negotiable.
At Gree Electric Appliances in 2018, he noted that advanced manufacturing is a key component of the real economy and that at no time should economic development become decoupled from the real economy and shift toward the virtual. At Zhengzhou Coal Mining Machinery the following year, he called manufacturing "the foundation of the real economy" and the real economy "the bedrock of the country's development." And at a "little giant" firm, Yangquan Valve, in 2025, Xi emphasized that the real economy should not be neglected, nor should the traditional industries within it.
Behind these instructions lies a profound reading of global economic history. International experience shows that manufacturing's share of GDP typically peaks and then declines as industrialization matures. When the decline goes too far, it hollows out industries and leaves an economy vulnerable to risks.
Under Xi's strategic vision, the country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) explicitly proposes moving faster to strengthen manufacturing, calling for maintaining a reasonable share of manufacturing in the economy and building a modern industrial system led by advanced manufacturing.
The president has also clarified the direction: high-end, intelligent, and green manufacturing.
China's manufacturing sector has been remarkably successful. In 2013, China sold just 17,600 new energy vehicles (NEVs), with market penetration at 0.08 percent. By 2025, annual sales had surged to 16.49 million units, with penetration reaching 47.9 percent.
In shipbuilding, China had held the top spot globally for 16 consecutive years by 2025, completing 56 percent of the world's ships and holding two-thirds of global orders last year. The same year, China's industrial robot exports grew 48.7 percent over 2024, surpassing imports for the first time and making China a net exporter of industrial robots.
BREAKING BOTTLENECKS THROUGH INNOVATION
While inspecting Wuhan HGLaser Engineering Co., Ltd. in June 2022, Xi attentively watched a display of innovative achievements in the chip industry and said earnestly: "With our country's further development, it is urgent to address the bottlenecks in core technologies in key fields."
For Xi, self-reliance and independent innovation are not slogans -- they are the fundamental guarantee for China's manufacturing to stand firm over the long run.
In the spring of 2023, a moment at the "two sessions," the annual meetings of China's top legislature and political advisory body, vividly showcased the confidence of China's manufacturing sector as it strides toward innovation and strength.
Shan Zenghai, a deputy from Xuzhou Construction Machinery Group (XCMG), a leading heavy machinery manufacturer, said that the company's 220-tonne all-terrain crane can now be 100 percent domestically produced, during a deliberation of deputies from Jiangsu Province.
"What about the chips in the cranes? Are they also homegrown?" Xi inquired.
The answer was affirmative. Shan said that XCMG manufactured 91 percent of all components in its products, up from 62 percent previously. Xi commended the company's achievements in making world-class engineering machinery. "We need to upgrade to medium- and high-end manufacturing. This is a hallmark of high-quality development."
The Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee has repeatedly dedicated study sessions to frontier technologies. Concrete measures have followed. China has established national manufacturing innovation centers, launched major science and technology projects, rolled out a decade-long action plan for basic research, and focused on full-chain breakthroughs in critical sectors, including integrated circuits and industrial machine tools.
In the first half of this year, China's major industrial enterprises produced 279.8 billion integrated circuit units, surging 23.1 percent year on year.
POWERING THE WORLD
From solar panels harvesting sunlight in Egypt's deserts to China-Europe freight trains carrying equipment across Eurasia, China's manufacturing has become deeply embedded in global supply chains, powering the world with affordable, high-quality products and technologies.
"As we further modernize our industrial system, we will provide the world with more and better products made and created in China, and with a Chinese market of a larger scale and stronger demand," Xi said at a meeting in 2023.
This pledge is being translated into concrete action. Today, China has fully eliminated market access restrictions for foreign investment in the manufacturing sector. The updated catalog of encouraged foreign investment industries channels foreign capital into advanced manufacturing and other high-end fields, while international standards exchanges in areas such as NEVs and artificial intelligence continue to deepen.
As the world's largest manufacturing country, China has built extensive, well-integrated production capacity across a wide range of industrial goods, allowing producers worldwide to access key equipment, components and intermediate goods at lower cost and with greater efficiency.
Through technological innovation and intense market competition, China has built the world's largest and most integrated supply chains for the new energy industry. Chinese solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and NEVs have made energy transition more affordable.
Attending the BRICS summit in New Delhi last week, Xi proposed five initiatives, including an intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative. He said China stands ready to help fellow BRICS countries build smart factories, develop standards and norms, and jointly promote manufacturing transformation and upgrading.
Experts noted that Chinese products have won markets with their proven strength, and Chinese manufacturing has built deep confidence with its remarkable resilience. This is a powerful testament to the strategic vision of developing advanced manufacturing, and a vivid display of the broad horizons of innovation-driven progress. ■

Interview: Indian experts see stronger future role for BRICS
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
23:39:08 CST
00:39:08 KST

by Xinhua writer Chen Dongshu
COLOMBO, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- After two decades of development, BRICS has evolved from a grouping of rising economies into a more institutionalized cooperation platform capable of representing the interests of the Global South, Indian experts said.
Aravind Yelery, associate professor at the Center for East Asian Studies of Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the momentum of BRICS has changed significantly over the past 20 years.
When the BRICS concept was first envisaged in the early 2000s, its members were largely viewed as rising economic forces that could serve as a counterweight in the global economy, he said.
Since then, BRICS has undergone "a tremendous transition," moving "from a grouping which was reacting to the volatilities" toward a more institutionalized mechanism in responding to global challenges, Yelery said.
He also highlighted the grouping's growing role in representing developing countries.
"BRICS represents most of the common interest and agenda of those who are left out," Yelery said, adding that successive rounds of expansion have demonstrated its capacity to represent the Global South and distinguished it from many other groupings.
Nayanima Basu, adjunct fellow at Gateway House, an Indian foreign policy think tank, said greater cohesion among BRICS members could unlock further opportunities for developing countries.
"BRICS needs to be more cohesive," she said, noting that the trend has become increasingly evident from the Kazan summit to the latest summit in New Delhi.
Basu also advocated stronger trade and economic ties among members. "It does not have to be anti-West, but a BRICS free trade agreement will always be good when all these countries do trading amongst each other," she said.
Looking ahead to China's BRICS presidency in 2027, Yelery said the grouping's next stage of development should focus not only on further institutionalization, but also on bringing tangible benefits to the Global South through greater access to finance and technologies, as well as exchanges of best practices and governance experience.
He expressed confidence that China will carry forward the achievements and lessons accumulated by BRICS, while linking previous cooperation with the priorities emerging today and the development agenda for the grouping's next decade. ■

Asian Games | Mishap, lodging complaints cast shadow on Games opening

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games set to open on Saturday are overshadowed amid a series of organizational issues and mishaps as the latest occurred to the men's field hockey match between South Korea and Bangladesh on Friday.
The organizers mistakenly played the DPR Korean national anthem ahead of the kickoff of South Korea's hockey match against Bangladesh at the Kakamigahara Green Stadium.
As the South Korean players lined up for the pre-match ceremony, the DPR Korean anthem was played instead of their national anthem. The players looked at each other in confusion, with some standing at attention, some running their hands through their hair and others placing their right hands over their hearts.
Organizers later corrected the mistake and played the South Korean anthem. However, the referee instructed players from both teams to shake hands and prepare for the match while the anthem was still playing, according to South Korea's Yonhap News Agency.
A stadium announcer apologized for the mistake, but South Korean coach Min Tae-seok expressed strong dissatisfaction.
"This is a really serious problem. When we protested, they said, 'We're sorry. It wasn't that it wasn't prepared, there was a mistake on the part of those responsible for playing it'," he said. "But this is something that simply should never happen."
A South Korean Olympic committee official said the organization was looking into the incident.
The anthem mishap came after other issues the had happened during the build-up to the Games.
Accommodation has been a major focus of attention, with the Games not providing a traditional athletes' village. Instead, athletes and officials are staying in hotels, temporary container-style accommodation and a cruise ship at Nagoya Port.
Some teams have criticized the quality of their accommodation, including beds that were too short. There have also been complaints about a shortage of rooms.
The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) defended the decision not to build a traditional athletes' village, saying organizers needed to take into account the circumstances of the host country and the use of facilities after the Games.
"We wish that we have an athlete village, number one. But, number two, we also have to be flexible," OCA Director General Husain AHZ Al-Musallam said at a press conference on Friday.
He said the approach could vary from one Asian Games to another, citing previous Games where athletes' villages were converted to other uses or sold after the event.
Mohammad Tayyab Ikram, chairman of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games Coordination Committee, said organizers did not want to leave a "white elephant" after the Games.
Complaints also came from transportation for some delegations.
Chinese gymnast Zhang Boheng, who won two silver medals at the Paris Olympics and two world championship titles, said he and some teammates were left waiting for six hours after arriving here on Wednesday. He said the delay was caused by registration and paperwork before they headed to the cruise ship, while heavy rain later prevented them from boarding.
Indian delegation also reported long queues and delays in obtaining athlete accreditation at the airport, while some South Korean athletes reportedly waited for more than five hours after arriving on Thursday.
Weather has added another uncertainty to Games preparations. On Friday, Ikram said organizers had been preparing for a possible typhoon expected to affect the region on Monday.
He said disaster management, particularly typhoon preparedness, had been discussed at coordination meetings over the past three to four years. Every competition and non-competition venue had its own emergency plan, while large shelters had been prepared near Garden Pier, where 3,000 to 4,000 Games participants are staying, as well as for those accommodated on the cruise ship.
A controversy arose after South Korea's Olympic committee filed a complaint with Games organizers over the appearance of a person dressed as Japanese warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi at the welcoming ceremony.
Hideyoshi led Japan's invasions of Korea in 1592-1598, making the appearance a sensitive issue in South Korea. Korean Sport & Olympic Committee President Ryu Seung-min sent a letter to the local organizing committee and the OCA expressing regret and calling for measures to prevent a recurrence.
Some sports have already begun competitions ahead of Saturday's opening ceremony of the Games, which will run through Oct. 4. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Friday chaired a State Council executive meeting, which heard a report on the work on population aging and discussed matters concerning the healthy development of sports events.
The meeting also made arrangements for the work to expand and upgrade medical rehabilitation and nursing care services, adopted a draft regulation on the protection of traditional knowledge of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), and discussed draft amendments to 15 laws.
Regarding the work on population aging, the meeting called for improving services and support for the elderly, and making sustained efforts in elderly care, health promotion and social security.
It also called for developing silver economy products and services tailored to the elderly, fostering new consumption scenarios, and better meeting elderly people's consumption needs.
On promoting the healthy development of sports events, the meeting stressed the need to increase the supply of high-quality sports events, make better use of various sports venues, facilities and event-related resources, and advance the coordinated development of competitive, professional and mass-participation sports events.
It also urged the integrated development of sports events with culture, tourism and commerce, faster application of new technologies, and improved spectator experience.
Regarding the sector of medical rehabilitation and nursing care, the meeting emphasized strengthening the service system with a focus on community-level services, extending rehabilitation and nursing resources to communities and families, and improving the accessibility of rehabilitation and nursing services for urban and rural residents.
It called for leveraging scientific and technological innovation to improve medical rehabilitation and nursing care, developing more intelligent technologies and equipment, optimizing the review and approval of new technologies and products, and enriching service scenarios.
The meeting also said that TCM theories, technologies and prescriptions are important resources for China's independent innovation. It called for comprehensively strengthening the protection and management of traditional knowledge of TCM to safeguard the foundation for the development of TCM, coordinating protection and utilization of TCM resources, and strengthening international exchanges.
The meeting discussed and approved, in principle, draft amendments to the 15 laws, including the Emergency Response Law, and decided to submit them to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for review. ■

BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China urges Japan to face up to and deeply reflect on its history of aggression, and gain the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community with concrete actions, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a press briefing on Friday.
The September 18th Incident 95 years ago marked the start of Japan's 14-year invasion of China.
Ninety-five years ago today, Guo said, Japanese militarists launched aggression against China, and they were met by the courageous resistance of the Chinese people, which lifted the curtain of the eastern theater of the World Anti-Fascist War.

The increasingly prevalent historical denialism in Japan is truly troubling, and the danger is self-evident, Guo noted.
Denialism not just reflects serious regression in Japan's perception of history, but also indicates alarmingly an organized attempt to turn back the wheel of history with clear political motives, said Guo, adding that the real purpose is to keep the Japanese public from the truth, and clear the path for Japan to escape the straitjacket of the postwar system and rearm itself.
Denying the crime of aggression is to challenge historical conclusions and undermine the post-war international order, Guo said, stressing that all countries in the region, including China, must remain highly vigilant, not allow Japanese militarism to resurface, and not let historical tragedies repeat themselves.
"We must work together to uphold the outcomes of the World War II victory and jointly safeguard peace", Guo added. ■

====================================================================================================

Likud files petition demanding Eisenkot's Yashar remove anti-Netanyahu campaign ads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:35 UTC
00:38:35 KST

Likud filed a petition against Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar party, demanding the removal of three election campaign videos about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct in the period leading up to the October 7 massacre.
The petition was submitted to Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, chairman of Israel’s Central Elections Committee.
Likud claims the videos present journalistic sources and Netanyahu’s remarks in a partial and misleading manner, amounting to “unfair interference” with the party’s election campaign.
Attorneys Ilan Bombach and Inbal Amit filed the petition on Likud’s behalf. The party is also seeking an interim order requiring the videos to be removed while the case is under consideration.
Likud’s allegations focus largely on how the videos edited and presented the sources they relied on.
According to the petition, the three videos were posted on Eisenkot’s Facebook, Instagram, X/Twitter, and TikTok accounts. Each opens with an image of Netanyahu and the question, “Netanyahu, tell us, do you remember this?” The Yashar party’s logo appears at the end against a background featuring the color associated with its campaign.
Likud claims clips taken out of context
Likud cites the distribution of the videos across four social media platforms as one of the factors demonstrating what it describes as its campaign nature.
The first video displays a headline stating, “Two months before the massacre: Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief gave Netanyahu ‘a warning of war,’” alongside a reference to a report published by Ynet News.
Likud argues that the words “two months before the massacre” do not appear in the original source and that the reference to “a warning of war” appeared there in a different context.
The video is based on a column that stated: “After all, if Ronen Bar truly believed what he told Netanyahu, ‘I am giving you a warning of war today.’”
The petition claims the video reworded the statement, while the website’s name and publication date appeared alongside it. Likud argues that this could give viewers the impression that the wording shown in the video appeared in the original article.
The second video displays the text, “Netanyahu two weeks before the massacre: The goal is a quiet holiday period,” alongside a reference to a report by N12 News.
Likud claims this wording also does not appear in the original report and that the statement was not presented there as a direct quote from Netanyahu.
The petition also raises questions about the timeline. Likud claims the original source refers to discussions held in September 2023 that do not correspond with the framing of “two weeks before the massacre.” According to the party, the video includes wording that did not appear in the report, alongside its identifying details.
The third video uses a clip from a 2023 Netanyahu interview on the Israeli television program “The Patriots.” Netanyahu was asked about a Military Intelligence assessment that the threat of war was increasing and responded: “I think this is being exaggerated.” The excerpt in the video ends there.
The petition quotes part of Netanyahu’s later response, which the video omitted. Netanyahu said Israel “always prepares for this possibility” and was prepared “to deal with it from all directions.”
“I think they understand that it is not a good idea to start a war with the State of Israel,” he later added.
Likud argues that ending the clip immediately after the words “I think this is being exaggerated” leaves viewers with a partial response that excludes Netanyahu’s remarks immediately afterward.
Based on these three examples, Likud claims the external sources were edited in a way that changed how their content was presented to viewers. The petition argues that the wording created for the videos appears to have been taken directly from the original sources, creating what Likud describes as an “alternative reality.”
Likud’s legal argument centers on whether the videos accurately presented their sources. The petition states that “truth in advertising is not the standard” in this case.
According to the party, altered wording presented as though it appeared in a news report, or the editing of a source in a way that changes the meaning of the material, could be considered “unfair interference” with a rival party’s campaign under Section 13 of Israel’s Elections Law governing campaign methods.
Likud added that reasonable voters cannot be expected to locate the original reports and interviews and compare them with the videos. The party argues that displaying the name of the news outlet, the publication date, and the original footage gives the wording used in the videos a factual and credible appearance.
Sohlberg must determine whether the use of external sources in this case exceeds the permissible limits of editing in an election campaign. At this stage, the claims remain Likud’s allegations, and no ruling has been issued.
Likud asks for immediate removal of videos
Likud is asking Sohlberg to order the removal of the videos while the petition is being considered. The party based its request on the nature of social media distribution, arguing that videos can accumulate views, be widely shared, and continue circulating online.
It maintains that removing the videos later would not reverse the effects of their distribution. The petition notes that if the case ends with its rejection, Eisenkot and his party would still be able to republish the videos.
Before filing the petition, Likud contacted Eisenkot and demanded that he remove the videos by 10 a.m. on September 17. Eisenkot’s attorney responded at 9:23 that morning: “Confirming receipt. We will respond, but not by 10 a.m.”
Likud claimed it had received no substantive response by the time it filed the petition and that the videos remained online.
The petition also criticizes the response to Likud’s earlier demand. Likud described the reply, which was sent shortly before its deadline, as “unacceptable” and argued that it carried “an unpleasant scent of an attempt to neutralize the risk that an interim order would be issued.”
The party asked Sohlberg to consider ordering the respondents to pay its legal expenses because of how they handled the request, regardless of the case’s final outcome.
The central question is whether the editing and framing of the three videos amount to “unfair interference” with Likud’s election campaign under the Elections Law. The ruling could also affect how news reports, quotations, and interviews may be used in Israeli election campaigns.

Saudi Aramco suspends European crude deliveries after East-West pipeline attack - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:30 UTC
00:38:30 KST

Saudi Aramco has told at least two European oil refining customers they will receive no Saudi crude shipments next month after an attack on the kingdom’s key East-West pipeline, Bloomberg reported Friday.
The customers typically receive Saudi crude through long-term supply agreements, which provide regular monthly deliveries. People familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that those allocations will not be provided next month.
Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Saudi Arabia shut down its East-West pipeline last week after drones targeted the facility. The pipeline is expected to resume partial operations within days and return to full capacity within six weeks, according to a person familiar with the situation who spoke on Wednesday.
While oil and security sources previously said two pumping stations were damaged in the attack, a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery identified damage at three stations, sources confirmed in a Reuters report on Thursday.
European refineries that purchase Saudi crude typically receive shipments through Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, which is linked to the Red Sea by pipeline infrastructure.
Aramco customers seek alternative oil sources
The disruption has prompted some Aramco customers to seek alternative sources of supply. Poland’s Orlen SA has issued more than 10 tenders since Friday as it looks to secure replacement crude shipments.
European countries belonging to the OECD imported 577,000 barrels per day of Saudi crude in June, according to the International Energy Agency’s monthly Oil Market Report.
The pipeline has provided Saudi Arabia with a vital alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, reducing reliance on a narrow maritime chokepoint through which a significant share of global energy supplies passes.
Any further decline in Saudi crude exports could add pressure to an already strained global energy market, potentially driving higher fuel prices, increasing inflation concerns, and contributing to greater volatility in financial markets.

====================================================================================================

President Trump, stand with Palestinian democracy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:22 UTC
00:38:22 KST

The United States has the sovereign right to deny entry to particular individuals on legitimate security or legal grounds, whether they are Palestinian, Israeli, or of any other nationality. Yet a broad restriction directed at an entire people would be neither wise nor constructive.
Such a policy would silence precisely the Palestinian voices America should want to hear: those who reject violence, seek peaceful engagement, support political reform, and believe that ballots - not bullets - must determine the future of the Palestinian people.
Regarding PA President Mahmoud Abbas specifically, I understand that denying him a visa may be intended to exert pressure on the Palestinian leadership to undertake long-overdue reforms. Yet pressure is effective only when it is paired with a clear, constructive policy that supports democratic change.
Today, the most meaningful opportunity for Palestinian reform is already before us.
Abbas has called legislative elections for November 28 - the first such elections in two decades. Several powerful figures within the Palestinian political establishment are now seeking to postpone or cancel them. Some are reportedly attempting to enlist the US or influential regional countries, including Saudi Arabia, as ones asking to close the democratic door once again.
Washington should not allow its name to be used for this purpose.
Abbas only senior Palestinian leader committed to November 28 election date
Abbas currently stands almost alone among senior Palestinian leaders in keeping the election date. On this issue, he deserves international support. A clear public statement from US President Donald Trump endorsing free, inclusive, and credible Palestinian elections on its determined date, November 28, could be decisive. It could prevent those who fear change from claiming that America demands cancellation or that regional circumstances require it.
If Washington genuinely wants Palestinian reform, it must do more than punish the failures of the existing leadership. It should empower the Palestinian people to choose a new one.
We have already seen the consequences of closing this door.
Palestinian elections scheduled for 2021 were postponed indefinitely. Their cancellation did not create the catastrophe of October 7, 2023, and it would be irresponsible to draw such a simple line of causation. But it deepened the political vacuum, weakened moderate voices, destroyed public confidence, and reinforced Hamas’s argument that change could never be achieved through democratic or peaceful means.
When ballot boxes are closed, extremists offer other boxes - filled with weapons, funerals, and false promises.
We must not repeat that mistake.
A new Palestinian generation is now searching for a different path. Our political movement, Masar Jadid - New Path - was created to answer that demand. In approximately one month, more than 1,200 Palestinians from Jerusalem, Gaza, the West Bank, and the diaspora joined our movement. Most are young. Many are women, students, professionals, academics, entrepreneurs, and people entering political life for the first time.
They are joining because New Path offers ideas rarely stated so clearly in Palestinian politics: democracy, transparency, peaceful transfer of power, an independent judiciary, and one legitimate authority governed by one law and possessing one weapon.
We reject both corruption and extremism. We believe Palestinian interests are better served by dialogue and persuasion than by violence. We support a demilitarized Palestinian state, regional economic integration, and a negotiated two-state solution that provides Palestinians with freedom and dignity while ensuring security for Israelis.
These ideas are attracting support because hundreds of thousands of Palestinians have lost confidence in everything around them but have not yet lost their desire for a better future. They no longer trust the traditional factions. They are tired of being asked to choose between failed government and endless resistance, between stagnation and destruction. They want a third choice: democratic change.
Trump’s recently announced peace initiative has awakened genuine hope that the region may finally move from managing conflict to building a new future. Yet no regional peace architecture can endure if Palestinians remain politically excluded and denied the right to renew their own leadership.
Reconstruction, investment, demilitarization, and regional cooperation all require legitimate Palestinian institutions. Foreign governments cannot impose legitimacy, and aging political elites cannot inherit it indefinitely. It must come from the people.
Trump understands the political power of a mandate from the voters. He also understands that peace requires breaking with failed formulas and confronting entrenched interests. Supporting Palestinian elections would not be a concession to the PA. It would be an investment in a new Palestinian leadership capable of becoming a credible partner for peace.
Trump should therefore state clearly that the US supports holding the November 28 elections on time; that it expects all Palestinian institutions and regional partners to facilitate them; that Jerusalemites and Gazans must be included; and that Washington will judge emerging Palestinian forces by their commitment to democracy, nonviolence, reform, and peace.
Such a declaration could save the election. It could also save lives.
Upcoming Palestinian elections must not be canceled
Canceling elections would tell another generation of Palestinians that peaceful political change is impossible. That message would open the gates of despair and accelerate the next regional earthquake. Supporting elections would send the opposite message: that moderation has allies, peaceful change is possible, and Palestinian society will not remain permanently trapped between authoritarian stagnation and armed extremism.
I continue to believe that Trump can achieve a historic peace in the Middle East - and that the world may one day remember him for doing so. Perhaps such an achievement would even earn the recognition of the Nobel Peace Prize.
But the most meaningful prize would be a generation of Palestinian and Israeli children who grow up knowing politics instead of war, ballots instead of bullets, and hope instead of fear.
Mr. President, do not allow the door to Palestinian democracy to be closed again. Your public support can keep it open - and help change the future of the Middle East.
Samer Sinijlawi is a Palestinian political figure from Jerusalem and the founder and president of Masar Jadid (New Path), a Palestinian political movement advocating democracy, nonviolence, reform, and regional peace.

Haifa International Film Festival brings celebrated cinema and classics to the Carmel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:11 UTC
00:38:11 KST

The 42nd Haifa International Film Festival will bring the most celebrated movies from the world’s major festivals to Haifa alongside new Israeli films, documentaries, genre movies, and classics. Originally scheduled for September 26 to October 3 during Sukkot, the organizers added an extra day of screenings on September 25 due to demand.
The festival will open with the Israeli premiere of Avi Nesher’s Our Loves, fresh from its warmly received world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival earlier this month. Nesher will also receive the Haifa festival’s Lifetime Achievement Award for cinematic excellence and his contribution to Israeli culture at the opening-night ceremony, hosted by Lior Ashkenazi.
Our Loves’ narrative begins on October 6, 2023, focusing on several characters who think they are having the worst day of their lives, and blends drama, romance, and comedy as they cope with a situation worse than their worst nightmares.
Artistic director Yaron Shamir has made sure that the international program is extremely strong, featuring many of the most talked-about movies of the year. Danny Boyle, the director of Trainspotting, 28 Days Later, and Slumdog Millionaire, has made a movie set in the cutthroat world of UK tabloid journalism with Ink. The film, which opened the Venice Film Festival, is set in 1969 and dramatizes the transformation of Britain’s Sun newspaper under Rupert Murdoch, played by Guy Pearce.
Olivier Assayas’s The Wizard of the Kremlin spotlights a different kind of political history, starring Paul Dano as Vadim Baranov, an artist and television producer who becomes a political strategist for a rising Vladimir Putin, played by Jude Law. Based on Giuliano da Empoli’s novel, it follows the creation of the political mythology surrounding the Russian leader.
Pierre Salvadori’s 'The Electric Kiss' gives viewers an escape from politics
For viewers who would rather escape politics altogether, Pierre Salvadori’s The Electric Kiss, which opened Cannes this year, offers a Parisian romantic comedy set in 1928 about a grieving painter, a fake psychic, and a series of fraudulent séances.
If you have enjoyed eating Hershey bars, you can now learn the story of the founder of the iconic chocolate company in Hershey: Mark Waters’s biopic about Milton Hershey. Finn Wittrock plays the famous chocolatier, with Alexandra Daddario (who may be the next on-screen Wonder Woman) as his wife.
The Panorama section includes All About Corinne, Marc Fitoussi’s comedy starring Isabelle Huppert as Corinne, an eternal movie extra who dreams of finally getting a substantial role. When she befriends a famous actress, played by Sandrine Kiberlain, she sees a possible route into the inner circle of French cinema. The supporting cast includes Diane Kruger, Anne Marivin, and Emmanuelle Bercot.
Romanian director Tudor Giurgiu’s 3 Days in September tells the story of a heroine whose wedding is wrecked when her fiancé’s mistress appears, sending her fleeing aboard a train and into an all-night journey through an off-season seaside resort. It features a single take lasting more than an hour and shifts between comedy and drama.
Everyone who loves the Big Apple will want to see The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, directed by Noah Segan and starring John Turturro as Harry, an old-school thief trying to survive in the digital age. Steve Buscemi, Giancarlo Esposito, and Tatiana Maslany co-star in what is both a crime story and a lament for a city that is changing faster than many of its residents can handle.
Another very different American story is told in The Weight, Padraic McKinley’s Depression-era thriller. Ethan Hawke plays a prisoner offered a chance at freedom by a warden, played by Russell Crowe, if he will help smuggle stolen gold from a remote mine.
One of the most important titles in the Carmel International Competition this year is Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur. The director of Leviathan and Loveless focuses on a successful Russian businessman whose orderly existence begins collapsing in 2022 amid professional, personal, and political pressures. The film won the Grand Prix at Cannes, and additional Haifa screenings have already been added to meet demand.
Also in the competition is François Ozon’s The Stranger, a new adaptation of Albert Camus’s classic novel. Set in French-colonial Algeria in 1938 and starring Benjamin Voisin as Meursault, the film returns to Camus’s story of alienation, murder, and the absurd while giving particular visual weight to the North African setting that forms the novel’s background.
A highlight of the festival will be the Israeli Cinema section, which features Marco Carmel’s much-anticipated Double Panther, based on the true story of Yaakov Elbaz, a criminal recruited by the police to infiltrate the Israeli Black Panthers, a political group that fought for the rights of Mizrahi Jews.
The assignment becomes complicated when Elbaz begins to sympathize with the people he is supposed to betray. Based on police files and archival material that remained confidential for decades, it turns a chapter of Israeli social history into an undercover crime drama, and stars Yaakov Zada-Daniel in the lead role.
Many Waters, written and directed by Imri Matalon, features Lihi Kornowski as a young woman who is paralyzed after an accident in the sea and meets Yosef, played by Alaa Daka, an aide at the rehabilitation center where she receives treatment. An intimate relationship develops between them, but outside pressures threaten it.
The leading director, Nitzan Gilady, passed away earlier this year; his final film, Thou Shalt Love, will be shown. It stars Yael Elkana as Naomi, a 28-year-old haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yoga teacher whose marriage is thrown into crisis when she discovers why her husband failed to appear at an important meeting with their rabbi. Michael Moshonov and Lena Fraifeld co-star.
Tomer Heymann's 'I Want to Tell My Story' is a fresh approach to Holocaust history
Tomer Heymann is one of Israel’s most celebrated documentary filmmakers, and his latest film, I Want to Tell My Story, has an unusual approach to Holocaust history. As Shimon Rothschild approaches his 100th birthday, he reconstructs his own life on a studio set, directing actors portraying relatives who were murdered and restaging episodes including Auschwitz, medical experiments at Sachsenhausen, a death march, and his life after the war. Rather than simply recounting his memories, Rothschild becomes, in effect, the director, which floods him with conflicting emotions.
Uri Levi’s documentary Peace 2030 follows Maoz Inon, whose parents were killed on October 7, and Aziz Abu-Sarah, a Palestinian from Jerusalem who has suffered his own family loss. Together, they embark on an ambitious campaign the achieve Israeli-Palestinian peace by 2030.
Among the Haifa Docs selections is Boaz Dvir’s To Kill a Nazi, an investigation into the extraordinary story of Michel Cojot, a French Jew who sought the truth about his father’s murder at Auschwitz. His pursuit eventually led him to Klaus Barbie in Bolivia and unexpectedly connected him to the events surrounding the Entebbe rescue operation. Jason Alexander of Seinfeld narrates.
Music lovers will want to see Broken English, Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard’s documentary about iconic singer Marianne Faithfull. Made with Faithfull’s participation, it looks back at a six-decade career defined as much by survival and reinvention as by music.
A special Japanese cinema program, From Mishima to Oshima, includes Paul Schrader’s typically unconventional 1985 movie, Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters. Schrader weaves the final day in writer Yukio Mishima’s life with flashbacks and highly stylized dramatizations of his fiction, accompanied by a score by Philip Glass.
The program also includes Kon Ichikawa’s 1958 Conflagration, adapted from Mishima’s novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion. Its story of an alienated young man whose obsession with the purity and beauty of a Kyoto temple takes a destructive turn remains one of the landmarks of postwar Japanese cinema and literature.
Haifa’s Wildest Nights section offers Hille Norden’s German film Easy Girl, about Nore, an uninhibited young woman who befriends a medical student and gradually reveals her dark past.
Haifa Classics is always a wonderful section, and this year it provides a welcome opportunity to see Barbra Streisand as she was meant to be seen: larger than life, on a movie screen.
The Streisand tribute will include William Wyler’s Funny Girl, the 1968 film that gave Streisand her first movie role, and an Oscar, for her portrayal of vaudeville and Broadway star Fanny Brice, a movie that holds up remarkably well, and features Omar Sharif as her husband, Jewish gambler Nick Arnstein; Gene Kelly’s lavish 1969 musical Hello, Dolly!; and Frank Pierson’s 1976 version of A Star Is Born, in which Streisand stars opposite Kris Kristofferson, with a screenplay by the director and acclaimed authors Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne.
It isn’t the best version of this story, but it will be interesting to see how it holds up after 50 years. Yentl, the classic gender-bending story of shtetl life based on an Isaac Bashevis Singer story, will also be shown.
The Israeli premieres of major new films by Boyle, Assayas, Ozon, Zvyagintsev, and Salvadori, along with a strong Israeli lineup, ambitious documentaries, Japanese masterpieces, and Streisand singing her heart out, make this year’s Haifa International Film Festival an event every cinephile will want to attend.

EU Operation Aspides raised alert level of its ships after Houthi attacks, Kallas says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:10 UTC
00:38:10 KST

The European Union's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said on Friday that the EU naval mission in the Red Sea, Operation Aspides, has raised the alert level for its vessels after the situation in the area worsened.
"Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are unacceptable and sabotage the global economy," she said in a post on X.
She added that she had spoken with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al-Saud about diplomatic efforts to end the fighting in Yemen and restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis have expanded their foothold around the Red Sea in recent weeks, capturing several strategically important locations near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Perim Island, which sits at the center of the narrow waterway.
The Iran-backed group has also taken control of the Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish islands, giving it additional positions from which to observe activity around one of the world's most vital maritime routes.
Houthi positions increase risks for vessels crossing Bab al-Mandab
The Bab al-Mandab remains open to commercial shipping, and the Houthis do not currently have the ability to completely shut down traffic through the strait. Their growing presence in the area, however, gives them better surveillance capabilities and more opportunities to threaten specific vessels.
The strait, which separates the Red Sea from the Gulf of Aden, is only around 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. It serves as a key connection between the Indian Ocean and the Suez Canal, with energy shipments equivalent to roughly 7% of global oil consumption typically passing through the route.
By controlling areas including Mocha, Dhubab, Perim Island, and the Hanish islands, the Houthis have increased their ability to track maritime movement and create uncertainty for commercial operators. Shipping firms and insurers factor these risks into their decisions, sometimes raising costs or avoiding routes altogether when they believe a vessel could become a target.
Houthis use growing foothold to pressure Saudi Arabia
The Houthis have also sought to use their strengthened position to pressure Saudi Arabia, including through attacks targeting the kingdom’s infrastructure and renewed threats against Saudi territory, including remarks involving Mecca.
The situation illustrates the broader impact of the Houthi threat, even without the group fully controlling the maritime passage. The risk of attack alone was enough to influence decisions by shipping companies, insurers, financial institutions, and logistics operators.
Anna Barsky contributed to this report.
