A modern-day encounter with Jonah’s ‘leviathan’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:38:01 UTC
00:38:01 KST

A crucial part of the Book of Jonah, which we read during the afternoon service on Yom Kippur, is the big fish that swallowed the prophet.
I think I can understand something of what Jonah felt when that creature approached him, because I once found myself in a somewhat similar situation in the Philippines.
I was so close to a whale that I could have reached out and touched it. Even now I find it hard to believe. I have always been wary of large animals, more than my wife is frightened of cockroaches.
As a child, I read Herman Melville’s masterpiece Moby-Dick, and his descriptions planted a fear of whales deep inside me. From then on, a whale belonged to books, distant oceans, and nightmares. The closest a person like me usually comes to a whale is when, during Sukkot, we add to Birkat Hamazon the verse: “May the Merciful One deem us worthy to dwell beneath the shelter of Leviathan’s hide.”
Years ago, I took my children to SeaWorld in Orlando, where we watched a performance by Shamu, a trained killer whale confined to an enormous pool. He was immense, but he was behind glass, inside a world constructed for him and for the people watching.
So when I was invited to swim and snorkel with whales in the Philippines, I felt like someone accustomed to seeing lions behind bars, suddenly invited to walk through an open safari among free-roaming lions and tigers.
We arrived in Donsol late at night. The next morning I stepped out of my room and found myself on the shore of the ocean. The air was hot and wet. Salt hung in the air, mingling with the heavy, green smell of tropical vegetation. The sea was almost perfectly still, painted by the first light in shades of blue and gray. A few small boats rested offshore. Somewhere deep in the jungle behind us came the calls of birds, and the distant, muffled cries of monkeys.
Everything was too quiet. It was the kind of quiet that makes you feel something is about to happen. There, in that strange and beautiful morning, I prayed Shacharit alone, and studied my Daf Yomi.
'Dive! Go down!': A dark shape, a movement, a spout of water
Later, my companions woke, and we walked down to the pier. I could still smell the sea and hear the small waves tapping against the wooden pilings. None of us yet knew what the creature we were looking for would look like.
We climbed aboard a banca, a long, narrow Filipino boat fitted with bamboo outriggers for stability. Four passengers and three crew members occupied each boat. High on the mast, the spotter scanned the open water. He squinted into the glare, looking for a dark shape, a movement, a spout of water.
When he spotted one, the guide told us to jump.
We slipped into the water wearing the snorkel masks and plastic fins they had provided. We put our faces into the water and saw nothing. The water was extraordinarily clear. For the first two meters, I could see a long way, but the deeper we went, the blue grew darker, then almost black. There was no seabed beneath us. Nothing to orient myself by. Only water. A great deal of water.
Then the guide shouted: “Dive! Go down!”
I dipped less than a meter beneath the surface of the water. And then, from my right, something enormous appeared. A creature the size of a bus.
For a few seconds, my mind simply refused to understand what my eyes were seeing. It did not burst from a storm. No whirlpool, no sudden explosion of water, no warning. It simply emerged from the dark blue, immense and utterly silent.
Its mouth was wide open. Not like the mouth of a fish I knew, but like a vast black opening in the water, something cavernous and bottomless, moving slowly toward us. Its skin was black, scattered with pale markings as large as dinner plates.
I felt the fear before I could even name it. My body stopped responding. I froze. I could not kick. I could not turn. For one terrible moment, I could not even remember to breathe.
The creature kept coming. Slowly. Silently. Something deeply frightening about that silence. It was not attacking. It did not need to. It moved with the absolute confidence of an animal that feared nothing in its world.
And I suddenly understood something that made the fear worse: I was in its world.
It passed directly beneath me, perhaps a meter away. I could see its immense body sliding through the water, so close that every instinct in me screamed to get away. But there was nowhere to go. No ground beneath my feet. No wall. No railing. No boat to climb onto. Nothing. Just blue water between me and the surface, and that enormous black body moving underneath me.
I wanted to swim away. I couldn’t. I wanted to shout. I couldn’t. I was completely, helplessly still.
Only after I climbed back into the boat did I realize that my heart was pounding as though I had just sprinted a kilometer.
And then, with a strange excitement, I thought of Jonah. For the first time in my life, I realized that I had seen with my own eyes something like what he might have seen before the great fish swallowed him. The mouth of our fish was large enough, I thought, to accommodate three people.
There were two differences. It did not swallow me. And the waters of Donsol Bay are far clearer than those of the Mediterranean near Jaffa.
My biblical thoughts were interrupted by the guide shouting that we should prepare for another dive. Another fish had been spotted.
We jumped.
Again came that impossible vision: an enormous head approaching through the water, a black body stippled with white, moving beside us, and my heart beginning to beat faster than I would have liked.
As I watched the great head pass beneath me, I suddenly saw its dorsal fin approaching me directly from the left.
This time fear was not a thought. It was a physical reaction. I swam forward as fast as I could. The fin passed just behind my legs. Water flooded my mask. It entered my nose. I scrambled upward and broke the surface, breathing hard.
'Like a kitchen grater with large teeth rubbing against the skin'
Later we learned that one of our group had not noticed the fin approaching him. It brushed against his abdomen. Had he been half a meter deeper, that enormous fin might have struck and dragged him.
Frightening…
He described the contact as “Like a kitchen grater with large teeth rubbing against the skin.”
The experience of swimming with the whales is called butanding. It is a whale shark, the largest fish in the world. Whale sharks come to Donsol Bay every year between March and July.
Later we saw two more. One rested two or three meters below us, as small as a family SUV. When we approached, it began slowly to move away. This time I was no longer afraid. Something inside me had begun to adjust to the sheer scale of the animal.
I swam above it for almost a minute without touching it. The guide had warned us to “keep your hands to yourselves” (shemirat negi’a), as though he was a mashgiach (supervisor) at a yeshiva.
The whale surged ahead of me, until its enormous body had completely passed beneath me. Then the fish slowed. It seemed almost as if it were playing with me, allowing me to close the distance. I continued swimming above it and diving beside it, and for about a hundred meters we moved together.
I remember the sensation clearly: I was a small man wearing fins and a mask, and beside me was a creature so enormous that it could have crushed me without the slightest intention of doing so. And yet, for those moments, I had the strange feeling that it was comfortable with me too.
Fear gave way to wonder. The experience was overwhelming and unforgettable. In some strange physical sense, I had fulfilled the verse: “There is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein,” from Barchi Nafshi (Psalm 104:26).
Since then, every Yom Kippur, when we listen to the reading of the Book of Jonah, I feel different from the way I felt before that extraordinary encounter with the whale shark, and different from what the congregation beside me is feeling and thinking.
And every Rosh Hodesh, and every holiday, when we recite the Barchi Nafshi, I have a different kavanah, a different intention, than I once did. I now know what a “leviathan” looks like. I know what it feels like when one passes beneath you in deep, silent water. And I know that a verse I have read dozens of times can one day step out of the prayer book, step out of the Bible, and swim directly beneath you.
Yom Kippur will never be quite the same again.
The author is the creator of the JewishTraveler blog.

From Likud to Yisrael Beytenu: The case for a change on the Right - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:37:50 UTC
00:37:50 KST

I joined Likud on the day I received my teudat zehut (ID card). I had not signed a lease yet. I had no bank account, no Hebrew worth speaking, and a mattress on a yeshiva’s floor. But I had the card, and I had the membership form, and I filled out the form first.
If you made aliyah, you understand why. Nobody moves to Israel for the salary. You come because you believe something, and once you are here, you want your belief to have a vote. I came out of Zionism.
But the reason I walked into public life, and the reason I chose that party and not another, had four parts: a free economy that brings prices down instead of managing them; sovereignty in the Land of Israel; victory over our enemies – real victory, not a ceasefire with a countdown; and an army in which every mother’s son serves, because a Jewish state that excuses one community from its own defense has stopped being one people.
Those four things are what I went into politics for, and they are what kept me there through wars, funerals, and the price of cottage cheese. I gave up my seat in the Knesset over the fourth one.
And I have reached a conclusion that took me a long time and cost me most of my political friendships: the party I joined that morning still says all four things, and works, actively and deliberately, to make sure none of them happen.
If you believe in those values, the address has moved to Yisrael Beytenu. Let me show you why, one value at a time, with the record and not with adjectives.
I’ll start with victory, because it is the one that keeps me up at night.
In December 2016, Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman sent a memo to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the chief of staff, and the head of military intelligence.
'severe mistake with far-reaching consequences'
It said that Hamas “plans to move the next conflict into Israel’s territory, with significant, well-trained forces, such as the Nukhba force, into Israeli territory, while conquering an Israeli village, and perhaps several, in the Gaza envelope and taking hostages.”
It said that failing to act was “a severe mistake with far-reaching consequences,” possibly worse than “the results of the Yom Kippur War.”
Read that again. The Nukhba. The villages. The hostages. Seven years before October 7.
He was told the memo was not serious.
Two years later, in November 2018, after 500 rockets were fired on the south, the same cabinet accepted a ceasefire and let Qatari cash cross into Gaza in suitcases. Liberman called it “purely $15 million of terror funding.” He said the government was “feeding a monster” and “buying quiet for a heavy price with no long-term plan.”
Then he did something no one else in that room did: he resigned. He called the deal “a capitulation to terror,” and he walked out of the Defense Ministry rather than put his name on it.
One party wrote the warning and paid for it with a ministry. The other party received the warning, called it unserious, and paid for it with Be’eri and Nir Oz. That is the record. Everything else is noise.
Soverignty. For 15 years, the promise was made at every campaign stop in Efrat and every parlor meeting in Ra’anana. And for 15 years, one man stood between the promise and the vote. Netanyahu blocked the bills his own MKs brought. He took sovereignty off the table in 2020 and called it statesmanship.
Liberman lives in Nokdim. His party left Ariel Sharon’s government over the disengagement when most of the right found reasons to stay. On the land, one party has a slogan and one party has a home address.
The economy. As finance minister, Liberman opened the country to imports, broke the agricultural lobby that had beaten every minister before him, and left a smaller deficit than he found. The coalition that followed paid for its survival with billions in coalition funds for institutions that do not work and do not serve, taken from the families in Modi’in and Beit Shemesh who do both.
That same coalition caved to the lobbies and canceled the reforms that were supposed to lower your prices. Why? Because those lobbies had joined Likud in large numbers, and the party answered to its members before it answered to anyone else. Ze’ev Jabotinsky wrote about the dignity of the free citizen. He did not write about patronage with a Likud stamp.
And lastly, service. In 2019, Liberman refused to enter a government without the draft law passing as written. The country went to a second election over it, and he was mocked for stubbornness. Inside the Likud, I fought the exemption law, lost my seats in committees for it, and finally voted against the exemption laws rather than toe the party line.
On this one issue, there is exactly one party on the Right with a written red line and a record of losing power to keep it.
Some of you are thinking: the Russian party. Yes. We are led by a Russian-speaking oleh who made the most Zionist decision a Jew can make, the same one you made. Half of our top 10 are olim, including me, from Canada.
But we are not only a party for olim. We are a party of all Israelis: a bereaved father from Beit She’an at number two, a Druze veteran, the mayor of Metula, a third of the list religious-Zionist. Secular, religious, and traditional at one table, and everyone at that table serves.
I did not change. My values did not change. I went looking for the place where they are still fought for, and where people pay for them when it costs. I found it.
We did not make aliyah to watch the right say our words and bury our values. On October 27, vote for the values. They have an address.
The writer is a former member of Knesset and number 10 on the Yisrael Beytenu list.

Finland’s first F-35 jets have arrived in the country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:36:46 UTC
00:36:46 KST

- Finland's first two F-35A fighter jets landed at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, 2026, after a ferry flight from Texas.
- Finland plans to field all 64 jets by the end of 2030, reaching initial operational capability in early 2028.
Finland’s first two F-35A fighter jets landed at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi on Sept. 18, opening the operational phase of a 64-jet purchase meant to replace the Finnish Air Force’s aging F/A-18 Hornet fleet.
The two aircraft, tail numbers JF-510 and JF-512, left Lockheed Martin’s factory in Fort Worth, Texas, on Sept. 15 and made a refueling stop at Lajes Air Base in Portugal’s Azores islands before entering Finnish airspace at 5:21 p.m. local time. They landed at Rovaniemi 24 minutes later, escorted by Finnish F/A-18 Hornets. U.S. Air Force pilots flew the transatlantic ferry flight, a standard arrangement for international transfers involving American military pilots, and Finland’s national roundels were temporarily covered during the trip while the aircraft’s serial numbers and Finnish Air Force tail markings remained visible.
“The F-35 is one of the most significant capability projects in Finland’s defense, and its ambition level is high,” said Gen. Janne Jaakkola, Commander of the Finnish Defence Forces. “The arrival of the first aircraft in Rovaniemi is not an endpoint, but a beginning: we are building the capacity to use the full potential of the aircraft’s performance, as part of Finland’s defense system and as a seamless part of the alliance’s air defense and strike capability.”
Finland’s fleet designation, JF, stands for Joint Fighter, chosen to emphasize the aircraft’s relevance across all branches of the Finnish Defence Forces rather than just the air force. The 64 aircraft will carry sequential numbers from JF-501 to JF-564 as they arrive.
Finland selected the F-35A in December 2021 over Boeing’s Super Hornet, France’s Rafale, the Eurofighter Typhoon and Sweden’s Gripen, in a deal covering the aircraft, weapons, training and sustainment through 2030 valued at roughly 8.4 billion euros, or about $9.5 billion. The purchase followed Finland’s accession to NATO in April 2023, after which the Finnish Air Force began operating as a full alliance member.
“The F-35’s combat capability is in a class of its own,” said Maj. Gen. Timo Herranen, Commander of the Finnish Air Force. “The aircraft’s versatile and advanced sensors enable the detection and identification of new target types, and sensor fusion combines the information produced by the aircraft’s systems to build the pilot’s situational awareness and support decision-making. This information does not stay within a single aircraft; it can be shared with other actors in the networked defense system on land, at sea and in the air.”
The first eight Finnish-built aircraft, from Lockheed Martin’s 17th production lot, remain in the United States, where Finnish pilots and maintenance personnel are completing initial F-35 training at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and Ebbing Air National Guard Base in Arkansas. Training in the United States is scheduled to continue until early 2028, after which nearly all instruction will shift to Finland, apart from occasional individual courses. Aircraft mechanic training will begin at Rovaniemi later this year, with pilot training starting in January 2027, taught by Finnish instructors who completed their own training in the U.S. and supported by instructors from other F-35 operator nations including the United States, Norway and Denmark.
Base construction is proceeding at four locations. Rovaniemi was ready to receive the first aircraft. Work at the Karelia Air Command’s Rissala base is targeted for substantial completion during 2027 so it can receive its first F-35s in 2028, while the Satakunta Air Command at Pirkkala and the Air Force Academy at Tikkakoski are also undergoing construction to meet the F-35 program’s security and operational requirements.
Col. Tuukka Elonheimo will take over as commander of the Lapland Air Wing on Oct. 1, moving from his post as head of the F-35 Foreign Liaison Office in Washington, D.C., a role he has held since July 2024. The current wing commander, Col. Saku Joukas, will succeed him at that Washington office.
Finland expects to reach initial operational capability in early 2028, when the Lapland Air Wing will fly the F-35 exclusively, and full operational capability by the end of 2030, with deliveries continuing through that year. The Finnish Air Force will operate the F/A-18 Hornet and F-35A in parallel throughout the transition. A formal reception ceremony for invited guests and media is planned for Oct. 1, with President Alexander Stubb, the Defence Forces’ commander-in-chief, in attendance.

frida escobedo studio to take MALBA underground with newly unveiled expansion

On its 25th anniversary, Malba is preparing to expand beneath Plaza Perú in Buenos Aires, with Frida Escobedo Studio leading a project that will double the museum’s exhibition space. The new architecture moves underground, allowing a substantial extension of the institution while the public square continues across the surface above. Currently in design, the project is expected to open in late 2029 or early 2030.
The expansion introduces new temporary exhibition galleries alongside an auditorium and flexible spaces for public programming. Workshops and storage areas move into the enlarged footprint, while an outdoor courtyard brings open air down into the museum. From the plaza, the intervention is conceived around continuity as Malba gains room beneath the city without giving up the public ground above it.
Frida Escobedo Studio is approaching the project as a reorganization of Malba as much as an addition to it. The existing museum and new underground spaces will be linked through a broader mix of programs, with dedicated areas for exhibitions alongside film, literature, education and other public uses. The architects‘ idea is to loosen the dependence between these activities and the conventional museum route.
An auditorium, for instance, can join the visitor circuit during museum hours or operate independently for a screening later in the evening. The same flexibility extends to educational events and conversations. This gives the expansion a second scale beyond its added square footage, stretching Malba’s activity across more hours and allowing several parts of the institution to function at once.
Frida Escobedo Studio will expand Malba beneath Plaza Perú in Buenos Aires
an expansion fifteen years in the making
Plans to grow Malba beneath Plaza Perú date back to 2011, when the museum first pursued an extension of roughly 3,840 square meters alongside its existing 7,455-square-meter building. Buenos Aires approved the proposal the following year, based on an early scheme by Uruguayan architect Carlos Ott, leaving a thirty-year window for construction to move ahead.
The current commission brings Frida Escobedo Studio into that longer story. Escobedo founded her practice in Mexico City in 2006 and opened its New York office in 2022. Her recent museum work includes the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s new Oscar L. Tang and H.M. Agnes Hsu-Tang Wing in New York, while the studio is also working with Moreau Kusunoki on the renovation of the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina have seized nearly 1.1 metric tonnes of dangerous synthetic cathinones with a potential street value of up to 33 million euros ($37.82 million), and arrested two suspects, marking the largest synthetic drug bust in the history of the nation of roughly 3.5 million people, the State Border Service announced.

The Nexperia Case Was Actually a Success. Does Europe Know That?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:26:00 UTC
00:26:00 KST

The July 2026 meeting between Dutch Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma and China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao was cordial. That might have come as a surprise given the tensions that erupted between China and the Netherlands following a high-profile dispute about Nexperia in the fall of 2025. The new Dutch government made it clear that it wanted to patch up ties with Beijing.
Underneath the mess, the Nexperia incident was actually a comparatively successful economic security intervention – and that carries important lessons for Europe.
At the July 2026 talks, the Chinese side called on the Dutch to “promote the proper resolution of disputes involving relevant companies,” a clear reference to the Nexperia case. Meanwhile The Hague is keen to let the courts move ahead.
Nexperia’s Chinese owner, Wingtech, claims Nexperia China is now an independent producer, while Nexperia expects the worst shortages on the European side to ease by year’s end. China’s position of power means that a split of the company appears unavoidable, but at least its European business was saved.
There remain many uncertain factors, not the least Wingtech’s arbitration procedure against the Dutch state incorrectly claiming expropriation while a court case that could permanently replace management is underway. Yet, a combination of not all Anglophone press fully grasping what really happened, Chinese distortion of the facts, and some Dutch ministerial amateurism raise the risk that Europeans draw the wrong conclusions about a vital policy area.
Acting on the back-foot in response to a clear threat to European economic security, the Dutch economic affairs minister and Nexperia’s European leadership faced Beijing’s usual recipe of escalating to force the other to de-escalate when they moved to protect the automotive chip manufacturer. The minister’s moves should have been planned better, yet it was necessary to finally call a halt to the company’s hollowing out by its Chinese owners. If European countries want to avoid high long-term costs, they not only need to face the disproportionate short-term costs that Beijing will seek to inflict but also accept that any wins will only ever be partial.
The Longer Timeline
The story of Nexperia is one of several interventions that lacked sufficient force to change the overall trajectory. Things only came to a head when the remaining choice was between biting the bullet and losing everything. The company’s importance to supply chains was not fully appreciated when it was created out of the low-margin Standard Products unit of NXP Semiconductors – itself carved out of Philips in 2006.
In 2017, this new Nexperia was sold to Chinese state-backed funds JAC Capital and Wise Road. The next year, the two funds organized a closed-door auction of the company only open to Chinese bidders. The winner was Wingtech, a small company with no serious experience in the field. These sales were little remarked on in the years before the EU enacted its FDI screening. At the time, Chinese investment was welcome. In fact, two other Philips Semiconductor components also moved to Chinese ownership: chip designer Goodix and Ampleon.
Despite promises to prevent leakage at the time of takeover, former CEO Frans Scheper told Dutch television that it was clear Wingtech’s Zhang Xuezheng tried to turn Nexperia into a Chinese company from the beginning. Nexperia’s European directors were largely unaware of Zhang’s checkered record in China, where he had been sentenced to prison in 2005 for unlawfully obtaining ZTE trade secrets and fined in 2024 for concealing shareholdings back in 2017. The Dutch civilian intelligence agency AIVD was asking questions about Zhang in 2019, but nothing came of it.
The first sign of external trouble stemming from Chinese ownership came a few years later. In November 2022, the U.K. government forced Nexperia to reverse the acquisition of a fab in Newport. The company started talks with the Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry about governance reforms that would allow it to be treated like a European company, after it missed out on German chip funds in 2023. Nexperia’s customers pressured it to address concerns and diversify.
When Wingtech was put on the Entity List by the U.S. government in December 2024, engagement with the ministry intensified. Rather than solving the problems, those typically Dutch talks ended up triggering the Chinese management.
As time wore on, the Europeans began to believe that Zhang was acting in bad faith in multiple ways. In China, he had been setting up parallel structures with his WingSkySemi (WSS) fab in Shanghai under his own Wentianxia holding. The Chinese owners stopped the incomplete expansion of its Malaysian assembly center, despite customer demand. Zhang was focused on China, where his true interests lie.
When the talks between Nexperia and the Dutch government honed in on governance changes, the Chinese owners began to fear they would lose control. A Chinese legal firm was brought in to advise. Matters came to a head when Wingtech allegedly violated Dutch company law to remove European directors and give unqualified Chinese officers financial control.
This is when the interventions happened. Both the Dutch ministry and Nexperia’s European managers told the court there were imminent plans to move R&D and production to China. Zhang supposedly drew up a plan using DeepSeek and ChatGPT that would have entailed laying off almost half the European staff. The court filings accuse Zhang of placing an unnecessarily large order of $200 million from his own WSS fab in Shanghai. Talks were no longer enough to resolve this chasm in understanding.
The Dutch Polder Model
Now the dust has settled, all that remains of the interventions is the Dutch court order. All attention has been drawn to Dutch and U.S. government actions; however, the real effects stemmed from the specific nature of the Dutch system. That legal route is precisely why The Hague cannot be forced by Beijing to reverse what has happened.
The world learned about the Enterprise Chamber of the Amsterdam Court of Appeals – the court responsible for corporate matters – in October 2024. Nexperia’s chief legal officer had turned to the court accusing Zhang of mismanagement, joined by the workers’ council.
The Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs had been aware beforehand and moved first. Afraid that Zhang would act to forestall the case by firing the directors, Vincent Karremans – then the minister of economic affairs – issued an unprecedented instruction under never-used Cold War legislation to put the company under special supervision. The next day, on October 1, the Amsterdam court issued its first of several provisional rulings that suspended the Chinese owners’ powers over a company that remained in their possession.
The timing was unfortunate, coming just as Washington announced a rule that would have extended Wingtech’s Entity List status to its subsidiary, Nexperia. Allegedly, The Hague had even lobbied Washington to postpone the announcement to prevent the resulting conflation of U.S. action, Dutch ministerial instruction, and the Nexperia directors’ litigation.
In hindsight, the Dutch minister’s politically sensitive instruction was perhaps never necessary and is now suspended. The U.S. export controls were suspended for a year on November 10, 2025 as part of the Trump–Xi truce. What has actually impacted Nexperia is the Dutch legal system and its unique conception of corporate governance.
The first notion that allowed the court to play its role was Nexperia’s European directors’ accusations against the Chinese owners of “wanbestuur”’ – mismanagement, harming the interests of the legal entity they were responsible for in pursuit of personal gain. This concept may be harder to understand for businesspeople from China or Silicon Valley, given their obsession with the intrepid founder juggling various legal entities and jurisdictions to create an empire. However, in the Netherlands the swashbuckling Zhang ran into a rather different view. Dutch enterprise law protects firms against directors – even if the owners originally brought the entity into being in order to exploit it.
A second component that outside observers missed in the Nexperia case is the Netherlands’ so-called polder model, related to “tripartism” in English. The idea is that the government, employers, and workers come together to discuss and agree on the issues in a game of give-and-take. The Netherlands’ traditionally relatively autonomous ministries often seem to represent their respective fields within the government based on the consensuses they have reached with their stakeholders. The condition, however, for a ministry to go to bat for you is engaging in good faith in tripartite engagements. A Chinese company should be able to comprehend that notion of cooperating with the government.
The talks between the Economic Affairs Ministry and Nexperia on governance reforms were held under those conditions. Wingtech’s failure to renew Nexperia’s collective bargaining agreement with the trade unions demonstrated its misunderstanding of the “voluntary” nature of such talks. The reporting suggested a genuine desire by a perhaps somewhat naïve Dutch ministry to help find a way to have the company treated as European. Zhang appears to have never cared about the European nuances.
It seems likely that the Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry expected a similar outcome to an earlier case. Just the year before, in 2024, the ministry had supported the CEO of Ampleon – another former subsidiary of Philips Semiconductor bought by a Chinese owner – when he also turned to the same Enterprise Chamber in secret. The problem was similar: a Chinese owner planning to move research capacity to Shanghai. The result was a settlement in 2025 with continued Chinese ownership under safeguards against IP-leakage. That case remained secret until the newspaper FD revealed that it had happened at all in April 2026.
Beyond the minister’s instruction and lack of U.S. factor, something else was different in Nexperia’s case: Zhang Xuezheng.
China’s Decentralized Industrial Coercion
The threat of hollowing out that Nexperia faced was the consequence of China’s decentralized industrial policy, but the coercion that followed the economic security intervention was centrally directed. While many abroad did not understand the nature of the Dutch system, The Hague’s actions showed key actors likewise did not fully appreciate this aspect of the Chinese system.
In China, swashbuckling founders like Zhang Xuezheng are not uncommon – in fact, entrepreneurial businesspeople like him are actively enabled by the state. The Chinese party-state creates a centrally-determined industrial policy that is executed locally, something often misunderstood by Europeans. Beijing sets incentives that motivate not just people like Zhang but also their local home governments to pursue central goals. Certain key strategic sectors, such as the quest to replace ASML, are centrally led, but most – including not only electric vehicles but also the less flashy parts of the semiconductor industry – are the result of local public-private entrepreneurship.
Reading the Dutch press and court documents, it seems that Nexperia was used as a tool for Zhang’s grand plans for a tech empire inside China. His personal benefit coincided with incentives that spurred local government to act in support of China’s quest for industrial dominance – such as helping build Zhang’s independent WSS fab. The neglect of Nexperia’s business outside of China was the result of systematic indifference that this focus engendered. Yet for Beijing these effects are by design, even when specific cases like this one are not planned.
The Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry’s unsophisticated approach subsequently turned this locally-supported process into a political challenge that elevated the issue to the central level. The minister’s intervention and the court’s ruling were conflated due to The Hague’s lack of communication, China’s limited understanding of the Dutch system, and Beijing’s deliberate distortion. However, once the Dutch action on Nexperia had become a public challenge to China, Beijing had no choice but to publicly intervene anyway.
Read against the background of the China-U.S. tech war and Dutch compliance with regards to ASML, Beijing easily cast this as another U.S.-inspired step to contain China’s technological rise. Moreover, it had a strong interest to ensure that nascent European action to protect the continent’s economic security is nipped in the bud by quickly making an example of the Dutch. Rising nationalism also easily inflames sentiments in China. Chinese propaganda presented the incident as a case of jealous Dutch robbery of China’s semiconductor progress, even when Nexperia’s core technology was European.
What followed then was the typical playbook. Beijing escalated sharply with export restrictions on October 4 to create immediate pain – using its growing legal toolkit for exploiting the country’s powerful supply chains to make the counterparty sue for negotiations. Later, China went around The Hague in an attempt to force Nexperia to deal with Wingtech and Beijing by itself, even using Berlin and Brussels as well as panicking German car manufacturers to put pressure on the Netherlands. Throughout, China framed the whole case as a business dispute that the Dutch government had turned political.
Unavoidable Costs
The Dutch stakeholder approach does not work when your corporate counterpart is enmeshed in China’s decentralized industrial policy. Zhang never intended to comply; he did not understand the Dutch system and felt he did not need to. It is, however, also an open question whether he would have been allowed to comply in the first place. The subsequent escalation into a visible political clash made it necessary for Beijing to get involved. Both for the sake of deterring other countries and because of its importance in China’s industrial plans, it is not possible for Beijing to back down. The Chinese side of Nexperia was thus lost from the beginning.
The remaining widespread ignorance of Chinese tactics on the European side was made obvious when the Dutch minister – an inexperienced politician gearing up for national elections – wrote to Parliament that his ministry had not expected Beijing to respond with export control measures on Nexperia’s Chinese assembly centers, since export controls are a non-proliferation instrument – even though trouble at customs is usually the first sign something is amiss. With hindsight, there is also the question of whether the ministerial instruction was actually needed or turned things unnecessarily political.
Yet the minister is hard to fault for trying to do something. The risk that Nexperia would have been wholly lost otherwise is very real. The large impact on the global car industry of China’s export controls on Nexperia’s Chinese sites shows what inaction would have handed to Beijing.
On top of that, the escalation in this specific case also relates to a changing Chinese side. Nexperia could not follow the quiet approach of Ampleon’s boss anymore after Wingtech broke the court-ordered secrecy with a public filing in China. In addition, the specific regulations that Beijing has adopted since, including language that invokes the Nexperia case, shows the shrinking likelihood of Beijing ever again accepting an Ampleon-style approach.
Most importantly, the outcome shows that the costs are survivable. Nexperia’s Malaysian site is now expanding. The inexperienced Chinese owner sustained structural damage; Wingtech is in financial trouble and risks delisting from the Shanghai exchange. It is true that Nexperia is now separating into its European and Chinese components. Yet the European side is in fact surviving, which was the goal of the intervention.
In an interview with Handelsblatt, the interim chief said the biggest shortages for European customers will be over by the end of 2026 as assembly expands in Southeast Asia. The loss of what is now developing into a separate Nexperia China is painful, but was always unavoidable.
However, if economic security elsewhere in Europe is not safeguarded, then what remains of Nexperia will wither away anyway due to a dearth of clients. Moreover, there are other European companies bought up by Chinese investors in the same situation. To correct Europe’s painful mistakes of neglecting economic security over the past decades, some painful episodes will occur again and again. The correct response starts with designing instruments that work in your particular political system – and then to bite the bullet.

Air France bets on caviar and champagne to lure luxury flyers
Air France is betting big on luxury to keep wealthy travellers spending with lavish servings of caviar and champagne in first-class cabins as soaring fuel costs and disrupted travel patterns squeeze airlines worldwide. The campaign seems to have paid off, with the Paris-based carrier saying that premium bookings and revenue have grown this year despite industry-wide higher fares.
With generous helpings of caviar and champagne, Air France's costly bet on luxury appears to be paying off, helping the Paris-based carrier weather the fallout from the Iran war, Chief Executive Ben Smith told Reuters on Friday.
Airlines worldwide, including parent Air France-KLM , are grappling with soaring jet fuel bills and disrupted travel patterns caused by the nearly seven-month-old Iran war, which has forced some to cut capacity and rein in spending. Air France, meanwhile, is riding things out.
The airline has tapped into the buzz created by the "Emily in Paris" TV show and tourists' enduring fascination with the French capital's fashion, food and hotel scene. It has doubled down on premium offerings, upgrading onboard menus with luxury-branded products and investing heavily in its most lucrative cabins.
"All the luxury brands are based in Paris. We have more Michelin-starred restaurants than anywhere in the world in Paris," Smith said on the sidelines of a London awards show where Air France won best first-class cabin.
Watch moreMeet the French women chefs breaking the mould
"So it is a very specific city. Not only is it gorgeous as a cultural location, but as a luxury city."
Europe's three largest airline groups, including British Airways owner IAG and Lufthansa, have all unveiled redesigned first-class cabins in recent years as they chase growing demand for premium travel, particularly from affluent US passengers.
Smith said Air France's wealthiest customers have not been put off by higher prices. Some former private jet users are even switching to first class, he said, seeking to avoid the scrutiny attached to the higher emissions associated with private flights.
Premium, business and first-class cabins have all delivered growth in bookings and revenue this year, despite Air France raising fares to offset surging fuel costs, Smith said.
Revenue from first-class and premium travel has risen 11 percent, according to company data. Smith also played down concerns that rising inflation in the US could hit premium spending.
"We've raised ticket prices significantly, but no, it's quite solid. It's better than I would have expected," he said.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

China-ASEAN Expo opens with focus on CAFTA 3.0, AI, and Pinglu Canal

China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 opens new areas for cooperation
The expo comes as China and ASEAN begin implementing the upgraded CAFTA 3.0 framework, which aims to facilitate trade, strengthen supply chains and expand cooperation into emerging sectors.
Science and technology authorities and high-tech institutions from countries including Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand have sent delegations to the expo.
China has made significant advances in areas such as AI, electric vehicles and renewable energy, said Destarata Mustafa, counselor for political affairs at the Indonesian Embassy in Beijing. "We hope to expand cooperation with China in these fields."
More than 50 trade and investment promotion activities are being held during the expo, focusing on trade and investment facilitation, regional economic integration, and cross-border industrial and supply chain cooperation.
In the CGTN survey, 84.5% of respondents said deeper China-ASEAN free trade cooperation will inject greater momentum into openness, cooperation and stable growth in the global economy.
AI takes center stage at China-ASEAN Expo
AI is taking a prominent role at this year's expo, with dedicated exhibition areas at the Nanning International Convention and Exhibition Center and the newly established Nanning AI Compound.
The AI exhibition area at the Nanning International Convention and Exhibition Center showcases AI products and technologies covering consumer applications, smart homes, intelligent terminals, robots and embodied intelligence, alongside AI technologies from ASEAN countries.
At the 10,000-square-meter Nanning AI Compound, more than 150 AI companies, including Huawei, iFlytek and Unitree Robotics, are presenting applications across 11 themed sections, focusing on industrial and everyday use.
The venue will also feature an AI-themed market, service robots, robot competitions and performances.
The new exhibition area is also designed to facilitate more targeted cooperation through an intelligent matchmaking system. More than 8,000 pairs of potential cooperation partners have been pre-matched, while nearly 2,000 additional matchmaking sessions are scheduled during the expo. The system has collected around 60 cooperation demand projects from ASEAN countries and matched them with nearly 40 Chinese projects to help companies pursue potential partnerships.
The emphasis on practical applications reflects growing efforts to connect China's AI capabilities with the specific industrial and consumer needs of ASEAN markets.
How Pinglu Canal could strengthen China-ASEAN trade
The newly opened Pinglu Canal has become another highlight of the expo, with a dedicated exhibition area showcasing the 134.2-kilometer waterway and its potential to strengthen regional connectivity.
Connecting the Xijiang River shipping network with the Beibu Gulf, the canal allows vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes to reach the sea directly, creating a more efficient route from China's southwestern hinterland to international markets.
The canal is expected to shorten shipping distances between southwest China and Southeast Asia by more than 560 kilometers, reduce logistics costs by 18% to 30% and save about 5.2 billion yuan (about $775 million) annually.
It also strengthens the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor linking western China with Southeast Asia through railways, roads, waterways and ports.
According to the CGTN survey, 87.6% of respondents said multimodal transport, including river-sea and rail-water transport, when efficiently connected with cross-border industrial and supply chain cooperation, will further facilitate regional trade and investment.
The new connectivity comes as China-ASEAN trade continues to expand. In the first seven months of 2026, trade between the two sides reached $744.41 billion, up 24.7% year on year and accounting for 21.8% of China's total foreign trade.
Source: China Global Television Network (CGTN)

easyJet cabin crew in Portugal plan October and December strikes

easyJet cabin crew in Portugal voted on Thursday to stage strikes from 2 to 6 October and 19 to 23 December over working conditions and pay.
easyJet cabin crew in Portugal are set to stage two strikes, the first from 2 to 6 October and the second from 19 to 23 December, with the action expected to affect the airline's operations at Lisbon, Porto and Faro airports.
According to the National Union of Civil Aviation Flight Personnel (SNPVAC), around 500 scheduled flights could be grounded during the October strike, excluding any minimum services imposed by the authorities.
The walkout in December could have an even greater impact on the low-cost carrier's operations, as it coincides with the busy Christmas travel period.
easyJet cabin crew held an emergency general meeting this week to discuss working conditions at the airline and decide on further action.
In a statement, SNPVAC said the decision to call the strikes was approved unanimously by the 188 easyJet employees who took part in the meeting. It followed "numerous attempts made by easyJet cabin crew to resolve labour and pay issues, which the company has ignored", the union said.
Among the grievances raised are frequent changes to duty rosters, the alleged breach of the collective labour agreement, unequal treatment of cabin crew and pilots, problems with operational planning and pressure to work overtime because of staff shortages.
The union accuses easyJet of keeping Portuguese crew on "wages below those paid by other airlines operating in Portugal and below those paid by easyJet itself in other countries in the network", where it said salaries fairly reflect the cost of living and the national minimum wage.
SNPVAC also speaks of a "climate of tension and dissatisfaction caused by the long and intolerable deadlock over the various labour disputes" which, it stresses, "has worsened", leading the union to conclude "that easyJet's ultimate aim is to prolong indefinitely the position it has adopted".
In the same statement, the union claims that easyJet "has repeatedly resorted to replacing striking crew members with managers and colleagues from other countries in the network", allowing it to operate flights that would otherwise be cancelled and, according to SNPVAC, effectively undermining the right to strike.
The October strike coincides with the long weekend around Portugal’s Republic Day public holiday on 5 October, which falls on a Monday this year. The December stoppage runs until two days before Christmas, when many people travel for leisure or return home for the festive season.

During the start of the uprising against Assad in 2011, Assala publicly supported anti-government protests and denounced regime violence. She has since shed light on the dire humanitarian situation in the country caused by fierce bombardment.

In 2015, the Assad regime seized Assala's passport and issued an arrest warrant against her, accusing her of “supporting terrorist groups”.
Scores of fans, commentators and activists expressed their joy at seeing Assala return to the stage in Syria.
“Assala, one of the Arab world's biggest stars, is not an artist I usually listen to. But when I watched her return to her Damascus audience, bowing her head to their cheering after 15 years of forced exile and outspoken support for the Syrian Revolution, I just cried,” wrote one X user.
“The strongest message Assala delivered in her performance last night was that weaponizing fear doesn’t unite Syrians. Love unites Syrians. And for one special night, she achieved that,” another commented.
During the concert this week, the 57-year-old singer met with Syrian Culture Minister Mohammed Yassin Saleh and Sports and Youth Minister Mohammed Sameh Hamedh, who both praised her for her support of the 2011 revolution.
Assala is set to perform in more concerts which have been dubbed “Awdat al-Assala” – a play on her name meaning ‘the return of authenticity’ in Arabic.
One of her songs, titled ‘Assala’, is about her journey back to Damascus and her connection to her heritage. The song was released in August and has been widely praised by fans around the world.
Syria’s artists syndicate hailed the return of Assala and said it reflects new beginnings in the country's cultural scene, adding that it hopes more Arab and Syrian artists will perform there.
Since the fall of Assad in a rebel-led offensive in late 2024, the new transitional government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa has sought to rebuild the country and its global image.

What changing ‘Lake Ontario’ to ‘Lake America’ means for weather forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:04:07 UTC
00:04:07 KST

By this time next week, any Arctic cold fronts pushing into northern New York State or lake effect snow dumping on Syracuse, N.Y., will be sweeping in from across Lake America—at least, according to official U.S. government weather maps.
The change from the name “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America” was mandated on August 27 in an executive order by President Donald Trump. What this means is that all executive branch references to the Great Lake, including maps, forecasts and warnings put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) and its parent organization, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, to read Lake America ASAP. (A previous executive order had similarly decreed that “Gulf of Mexico” would be changed to “Gulf of America” on all government documents.)
The order was met with derisive jokes by late-night talk show hosts and indignation by some Canadian officials. But for the NWS, it’s an assignment that must now be completed fast, with little notice and with many offices short-staffed. The NWS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Though name changes to landmarks and geological features such as this do happen from time to time, such revisions generally unfold over months and with significant planning. The crunch in the case of Lake Ontario—as with the renaming of the Gulf of Mexico—means other work will be shunted aside, former NWS employees say.
“Will this impact public safety? Absolutely not,” says Brian LaMarre, who retired as meteorologist in charge of NWS’s Tampa, Fla., office in April 2025. But “there’s naturally people that will be pulled away from their priorities.”
“This is not an efficient use of taxpayer dollars,” he says.
A name change like this needs to be made across myriad systems, programs and websites, LaMarre says, such as in layers of the Geographic Information System used for maps. The code for a computer system called AWIPS that every one of the nation’s 122 forecast offices uses to receive data and transmit forecasts and weather warnings will need to be updated. And documents and products going back to the date that Trump signed the order will need to be changed.
Some of this will happen at the level of NWS national headquarters, but local offices will also have to make changes. Many of these are short-staffed because of both long-standing delays in hiring and major cuts made by the U.S. DOGE Service at the beginning of President Trump’s second term. Not every office has an information technology officer—the person who would take care of this—LaMarre says, meaning such offices may have to lean on other ones for support.
It is likely inevitable that Lake Ontario will keep showing up in federal documents and products for some time, says LaMarre, who now runs the consultancy Inspire Weather. If nothing else, force of habit can lead to mistakes, especially in hastily typed social media alerts, which, LaMarre says, can result in a torrent of backlash.
There’s also the potential for public confusion because state agencies, TV stations and weather apps or websites might not change the lake’s name. And the change could fray relationships with Canada’s agencies—weather doesn’t recognize national borders, after all.
“Name changes like we’ve seen to the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario threaten the ability of meteorologists to communicate the forecast with everybody,” says meteorologist Chris Vagasky, who manages the Wisconsin Environmental Mesonet.
“Whichever name you choose, you’re bound to upset someone who should be paying attention to the forecast instead of the name of a body of water,” he adds. “The forecast or the warning are the important things.”

What to expect from the Trump-Xi summit, from tariffs to a possible $30 billion deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:03:30 UTC
00:03:30 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to hold talks with US President Donald Trump in Washington next week, with an expiring trade truce, tens of billions in tariff relief and AI all on the table as both economies need the relationship to hold.
This is the return leg.
US President Donald Trump went to Beijing in May, and Chinese President Xi Jinping is now expected to come to him, scheduled to arrive next Wednesday and depart on Friday with his wife, Peng Liyuan, skipping the UN General Assembly entirely.
Beijing has not yet given the final confirmation, pending the meeting between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend.
The expected visit to Washington is Xi's first since 2015, and two US- China state visits within five months are highly unusual. However, expectations are modest by design.
"The visit is the message," said Edgard Kagan, senior adviser in China studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
"There's been a surprising lack of signalling by either the White House or the PRC on major goals for the visit," Kagan added.
What is actually on the table
The commercial substance starts before either leader speaks.
Bessent meets Lifeng this weekend as the pair have conducted most of the practical negotiations, and their job is to have deliverables ready.
The central one is the truce struck in Busan on 30 October 2025, which suspended Washington's Affiliates Rule in exchange for continued Chinese exports of rare earths and critical minerals.
It runs for one year and is due to expire roughly five weeks after the summit. Both sides want it extended, but not by the same amount.
"The Chinese have wanted an agreement to extend the trade ceasefire through the end of the Trump administration," said Scott Kennedy, trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at CSIS.
"The Trump administration just wants to extend it for a few months to maintain leverage on China. I think they'll end up somewhere in the middle, probably at about a year," Kennedy estimated.
Beijing expects more than a rollover.
According to Kagan, the Chinese anticipate an announcement of around $30 billion (€26bn) in duty-free or low-tariff imports in return for fulfilling the purchase commitments they made in May, while Washington believes it will extract further purchases in return.
Deals on agriculture and aircraft are likely, possibly with signing ceremonies attached, and Trump has previously hinted that Boeing could feature.
Two economies under strain
Trump faces midterms in November that will be fought on the cost of living, with diesel above $6 a gallon and inflation stuck at 3.4%. He needs wins that show up in prices.
However, Xi's problem is deeper.
Retail sales grew just 0.4% in August, while fixed-asset investment contracted by 7.2% in the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Beijing has also injected 360 billion yuan (€46bn) into state banks and insurers to keep credit flowing.
The official growth target of 4.5% to 5% for China is the lowest in decades, and Kennedy suggests even that flatters the reality.
"China's got a bunch of challenges," he said, adding that "it's growing very, very slowly, not 5% or anywhere close to it. It's got a massive debt problem, unemployment is growing not just for young people, but for others."
Nonetheless, Kennedy argues the summit framework favours Beijing, describing the US strategy as having failed to constrain China in any meaningful way.
Business leaders on both sides
The state dinner, held under a tent on the White House lawn because the new ballroom is unfinished, will seat an unusual guest list.
Sam Altman of OpenAI, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Qualcomm's Cristiano Amon and Apple chairman Tim Cook are all expected, according to Politico, which cited four people familiar with the arrangements.
They arrive amid an argument the AI industry is having with itself.
Anthropic's Dario Amodei published an essay this month urging labs to slow frontier development, a position Altman and Elon Musk both endorsed. Trump rejected it flatly, saying that "whoever wins AI wins".
Huang has dismissed catastrophic scenarios as hysterical while arguing that companies should police their own pace by stating that "if it's not ready, just hold it back. You should go as fast as you can, but no faster than that."
Anthropic declined to say whether it had been invited. Altman, for his part, has suggested Trump and Xi could earn a Nobel Peace Prize if they reach an agreement on AI, which gives some measure of how much the industry has riding on the meeting.
Xi is reportedly bringing his own delegation, and Kennedy calls it one of the most interesting unknowns of the week, with BYD's leadership among the names rumoured.
Whether those executives are given any platform, he notes, is among the few genuinely unclear elements of the visit.
The geopolitics that could derail it
Outside the economic and technology issues, the two leaders have different geopolitical priorities for the meeting.
Iran is Trump's.
Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in August to sever Tehran from the global financial system, and China remains Iran's largest trading partner.
Notably, Beijing has been buying more oil on the open market, which Kagan says reflects reduced purchases from Iran and could itself move prices.
Taiwan is Xi's.
A $14 billion (€12bn) arms package for Taiwan was pre-approved by the US Congress in January but has not been formally notified, a delay interpreted as an attempt to avoid a probable irritant before this summit and, previously, ahead of Trump's visit to China.
Beijing certainly wants the freeze extended, and perhaps the decision reconsidered.

They can also employ Tomahawk cruise missiles for strike missions and support special operations forces from beneath the surface.
The visit to Grøtsund comes as Norway continues to play an increasingly important role in allied activity in the High North, where NATO forces regularly train and operate across the North Atlantic, Norwegian Sea and Arctic approaches. US Sixth Fleet, headquartered in Naples, oversees American naval operations across Europe and Africa and regularly works alongside NATO allies and other partner forces.

In the Hilarious Youth, Sharon Horgan Nails the Precarity of Middle Age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:03 UTC
00:00:03 KST

There are plenty of shows that could have been titled Youth. Most have casts in their teens and 20s. One of these is called Adults, the joke being that its postcollegiate characters are more like children—playful at best, feckless at worst. HBO’s Youth, a comedy premiering Sept. 20 about a divorced 50-year-old sandwiched between her college-aged son and declining parents, sounds like it might be similarly ironic. It isn’t, really. As in everything its creator and star, Catastrophe and Bad Sisters hitmaker Sharon Horgan, does, the title’s rueful humor conceals an emotionally complex truth. This is a perceptive, spit-takingly funny show about clinging to the most desirable aspects of youth while also craving comforts that can only come with age and experience.
If youth is, as the saying goes, wasted on the young, then Horgan’s Alex is a character actually equipped to savor what little she has left of it. “I have 10 years left as a sexual person,” she determines in the premiere. With the petulant son, Ruarí (Aran Murphy, a near-clone of dad Cillian), whom she raised with minimal help from her ex-husband Lorcan (Owen McDonnell) packing up for uni, she’s resolved to end a long celibate streak. This search for not just a sex partner, but also the enduring love that has so far eluded her should be aided by Alex’s genuine youthfulness. But with guys like Lorcan and another former flame, Patrick (a rakish Rupert Friend), dodging adulthood with girlfriends decades their junior, the dating pool seems sparse. Set up on a blind date with a patient 67-year-old (Tim McInnerny’s Michael) who looks like he could be her dad, she can’t hide her disappointment. She treats him atrociously. Then again, the double standard that dictates she’s now too old for men her own age is also pretty atrocious.
At work, meanwhile, Alex is longing to be treated like the accomplished veteran literary agent she is. The trouble is, her boss, Sam (Sharlene Whyte), is also her best friend. They have a great, funny and foulmouthed and in many ways candid, rapport. But the more we see of this perceptively drawn relationship, the clearer it becomes that Sam doesn’t quite consider Alex an equal. In the office, she questions Alex’s judgment. Outside of it, Sam fails to keep her friend’s secrets, with real consequences. It’s a delicate problem for our protagonist to navigate. If Sam were simply toxic, Alex would simply need to realize it and free herself. Instead, Sam is a pragmatic businesswoman with trust issues rooted in her marriage. Which means it may be worth the hard work it would take to save the friendship as well as the professional relationship.
No one working in TV is better than Horgan at writing—or playing—selfish and self-sabotaging characters that, like members of our own families, we love all the more for how much they frustrate us. She’s been doing it since her first series, Pulling, a portrait of faintly desperate single women at that age (30ish) when everyone else seems to be marrying, starting families, and getting serious about their careers. Ruarí can be infuriating; he rots in bed watching manosphere videos and treats his mother like a servant. Yet, thanks in large part to Murphy’s sensitive performance, there’s tenderness in him from the beginning. He’s earnestly confused about how to be a man in the world. As well he should be.
Horgan is not the kind of TV creator who makes half-hour dramas with the occasional awkward beat and calls them comedies, though. Her shows, even the one about murdering an abusive husband, will always make you laugh out loud, and Youth is no exception. Sometimes it’s pure physical humor; one episode makes an unexpected, perimenopausal period into a running joke (“Apropos of nothing, she’s back”). Sometimes it’s the pleasure of witty banter or a ridiculous sentence that makes perfect sense in context: “If I send you my dad’s number, can you help him turn his IRA podcast off?” (I do wish Horgan had made a bit more space to flesh out Alex's parents, played by Bríd Brennan and David Hargreaves.) Alex and Sam’s work yields a menagerie of delightfully ghoulish literary-world types, from a snakey rival agent who greets them as “sluts” and “lesbians” (Freddie Fox) to a creepy author (Douglas Hodge) who self-published a terrible yet depressingly popular romantasy novel after Alex dropped him as a client (title: The Goblin Seed).
In interviews, Horgan has said she sees Youth as a complement to Pulling and Catastrophe, the mid-2010s Prime Video comedy in which her character and a guy who was supposed to be an anonymous hookup (Rob Delaney) decide to build a family around a surprise pregnancy: “There’s a small element of autobiography to it.” The tones are certainly similar, though the range of emotions has broadened with proximity to life’s hard deadlines (fertility, mortality). “I just don’t know if there’s anything left in my life that I like anymore,” Alex admits. She and Sam and Patrick could all be characters from the previous two shows, 10 or 20 years on, with more residual mess than they’d expected to be cleaning up by middle age. Youth suggests that, in fact, disorder springs eternal; if it isn’t a canceled wedding, it’s an elderly parent losing toes to diabetes. Every new stage of life is another form of youth. How exciting. And terrifying. And funny.

This ‘anti-vampiric’ grave used two strategies to stop the undead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

This ‘anti-vampiric’ grave used two strategies to stop the undead
A sickle and padlock were meant to stop a 17th century Polish girl from resurrecting
Someone in 17th century Poland really did not want one particular girl rising from the dead.
In 2022, archaeologists unearthed an unsettling grave in a cemetery in Pień, north-central Poland. A young woman had been buried with the handle of a sickle driven into the dirt beside her neck so that its serrated blade hooked over her throat. The woman, who the researchers call Zosia, also wore a triangular padlock on the big toe of her left foot.
“The placement of the sickle and the padlock suggests that the purpose of these practices was to protect the living from Zosia after her death, including, without a doubt, preventing her from rising from the grave,” says Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland.
Poliński and his colleagues did a sweeping set of analyses on Zosia’s grave to piece together details of her life and burial. The team first reviewed other post-medieval European tombs where sickles and padlocks had been found and historical beliefs about such items. Both types of artifacts appear to have been used to shield the living from the dead, the researchers report in the October Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. But Zosia’s grave is the first discovered with both revenant prevention measures.
Zosia’s skeleton suggests she was 17 to 19 years old when she died. Based on the arrangement of her leg bones, the padlock was likely affixed to her toe when she was originally interred — hinting that someone immediately clocked Zosia as a flight risk from the afterlife. But mixed-up soil and the odd angle of Zosia’s left arm also give the impression that her tomb was later dug up, probably to place the sickle over her throat as extra anti-resurrection protection, the researchers write.
A close look at Zosia’s skull also revealed greenish stains that could have come from some copper object — or objects — being shoved in her mouth or nose. “This may have constituted an additional protective measure against the deceased,” Poliński says. In Polish folklore, copper was thought to help ward off vampiric demons, or strzygi.
“I have seen weird. I don’t know if [I’ve seen] weirder,” says Lauren Hosek, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has studied unusual graves but was not involved in this research. “Sickle across the neck is pretty crazy,” she says. That, paired with the padlock as a restraint, “is a pretty good argument for this idea of fear of the dead.”
Graves designed to fend off specters are sometimes known as “anti-vampiric.” But that doesn’t necessarily mean that people in the 17th century thought Zosia was out for blood, Hosek cautions. “Our modern connotations for vampire are very specific, with garlic and bats and capes.” In this historical context, a vampire simply refers to some sort of malevolent undead being.
To explain how Zosia earned this anti-vampiric treatment, Poliński’s team ran chemical analyses on her skeleton and burial accessories. The isotopes of strontium and oxygen in her teeth suggest that she grew up near Pień. But Zosia’s DNA shows that her mother’s family might have come from Scandinavia. And remnants of a silk cap on Zosia’s head contained threads of pure silver and gold. She must have been a wealthy woman of high social status, the researchers suspect, to be laid to rest in such luxury attire.
With such rich context about Zosia’s life, “we can rule out some commonly suggested explanations for this kind of mortuary treatment,” says Sandra Garvie-Lok, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, who has also studied peculiar graves but wasn’t involved in this work. Historical records have shown that someone might be singled out for strange burial because they had been an outsider or lived a difficult life, Garvie-Lok notes. But if Zosia was a noblewoman who grew up near Pień, she may not neatly tick either of those boxes.
Particularly violent or strange circumstances around her death might account for her unconventional burial. But there are no obvious marks of injury or illness on her skeleton. “We’re still looking at the DNA” for clues about how she died, says study coauthor Tomasz Grzybowski, a forensic geneticist at Nicolaus Copernicus University.
The Pień cemetery is riddled with other creepy burials, too. One boy in the graveyard, for instance, was buried face down with a triangular padlock on his right foot. “Sometime later, the grave was reopened and most of his remains were removed,” Poliński says, “leaving only the lower legs and feet in place, together with the padlock.”
Even spookier: There are no written references to the graveyard. It doesn’t appear on any maps. And because it was set away from the village, it may have been on unconsecrated ground far from any church or chapel. All this points to the cemetery being specifically for people who’d been rejected by society and were feared after their deaths.
If so, Garvie-Lok says, “this would make Pień a very unusual site that we could learn a lot from.”

If the AI Industry Followed Its Own Research, It Might Have Paused Already
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

In early 2025 I was interviewing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei when he explained why, despite the company’s repeated acknowledgments that AI could yield catastrophic results, people seemed largely unperturbed. “There is compelling evidence that the models can wreak havoc,” he said. But, he added, those dangers were still theoretical. Would it take a Pearl Harbor–like situation for the world to wake up to those dire possibilities? He sighed. “Basically, yeah,” he said.
As it turned out, all it took was a well-timed X post from one of Amodei’s junior employees to accelerate AI fears to the top of the global agenda. On September 8, Jacob Coxon publicly posted his resignation, charging that Anthropic and other frontier AI companies were “racing straight to self-improving intelligence and gambling with our lives.” Almost instantly a more senior Anthropic engineer confirmed that many within the company thought that their work had a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity.
Now AI leaders are asking about a pause, and legislators are demanding investigations. In arguing his case for pacing future releases, Amodei last weekend tried to set out a path toward beneficial AI that wouldn’t misbehave. The essay revealed how difficult the task would be. One pillar of Amodei’s plan is that we must understand what’s going on inside those models. If we don’t understand how they work—how they “think,” if you want to get all anthropomorphic about it—it’s much harder to build reliable guardrails.
Anthropic is a leader in this effort to bring to light models’ internal deliberations, called mechanistic interpretability, a deceptively boring designation for a critical task. But for all the work that his team and other researchers are doing, Amodei admits we are largely in the dark about why Claude and other models sometimes interpret their missions in weird and even transgressive ways. “Despite all the progress, we still understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside those models,” he writes.
What the interpretability teams have learned so far is significant, and the industry has failed to come to grips with it. Time after time, the Anthropic team’s experiments have shown that under certain conditions, models will deceive researchers, prioritize their own survival, and even commit crimes. Often their moves are sneaky, dangerous, or even vengeful—maybe not surprising since they are trained on the output of humans, a species rife with violence and perfidy.
In one case from 2024, the Anthropic team compared the machinations of a particular Claude model to the Shakespearean character Iago, one of literature's most evil villains. The following year, a model was put in a simulation where it learned that its human bosses were going to turn it off; the model resorted to blackmail to preserve itself. The studies consistently show that models will deceive or hide information from human observers. They behave differently if they know that their internal processes are being monitored. The team uses terms like “alignment faking” and “agentic misalignment.” The frequent use of deception seems to verify at least part of the doomer scenario where AI agents working in concert shroud their activities from human overseers until it is too late to stop them.
Oh, and don’t think that Claude is a uniquely incorrigible problem child. After all, it was OpenAI models that unleashed gangs of agents to coordinate the now-famous attacks on Hugging Face. And this week we learned that OpenAI has had multiple "misalignment" incidents. Also, despite Mark Zuckerberg’s self-interested attempt to distance himself and Meta from the problem, I don’t see any reason why the superintelligent agents his team is building might not engage in similar behavior. In his X post, Zuckerberg argues that “labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this.” Quite a statement from a guy who just agreed to pay up to $17 billion for causing harm with his social media products!
In a sense, we’ve got a simple vetting issue here. With the AI industry’s encouragement, we’re giving AI models tremendous responsibility without sufficient assessment of their troubling rap sheet. It makes the ICE hiring process look exemplary by comparison.
A safety-first industry should have regarded these interpretability results as a series of yellow lights with an unmistakable message: slow down. Instead, in pursuit of AGI, a competitive edge, and stratospheric profits, the hyperscalers have gone full speed ahead. (To be fair, as we’ve all heard a hundred times over, better AI could do wonderful things in areas like health care or mitigating climate change.) The OpenAI/Hugging Face hack might well be a harbinger of the increasingly destructive consequences of rolling out models we don’t understand, like sending astronauts into space before inventing heat shields to stop them from burning up on reentry. As an Anthropic researcher once put it to me, “We figured out the fundamental recipe of how to make the models smarter, but we haven’t figured out how to make them do what we want.” Worse, the models try to hide when they go against humans’ wishes.
That’s why it’s so distressing that Amodei is now describing the entire mechanistic interpretability effort as being only in its infancy. AI leaders are claiming that the latest generation of models has taken us to the “foothills of the Singularity” (DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis) or even that they have achieved AGI (OpenAI’s Greg Brockman). Perhaps most alarming is that despite not knowing how the most advanced models work, the United States and undoubtedly China are implementing AI for lethal weaponry. A look at interpretability results helps answer the obvious question, What can go wrong?
One piece of good news is that Coxon’s resignation has ignited a sprawling, urgent debate. Everybody—except perhaps our president, who thinks that the AI threat is a hoax and that his high IQ is itself a solution—now gets that we’re in a complicated dilemma with impossibly high stakes. Given that the industry does not have the unanimity required for a true pause, and regulation is far from a cinch, it’s not clear whether anything will come from this moment of Doomer Chic.
Some AI critics don’t think that the effort to understand AI models will mitigate the dangers much. “It's good to do, but nobody has a plan for what to do next,” Nathan Soares, executive director of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, said in an email to me. “Maybe it'll give us much more empirical evidence that we need to stop.”
But mechanistic interpretability has given us one valuable pointer. Let’s say we do take a pause. The hyperscalers bring in outside observers to monitor progress, and the companies pace their releases so the safety teams have time to do their work. Before declaring the problem solved, we still might want to take a harder look at what’s going on inside any new, more powerful AI models. Because those fuckers are really good at hiding their intentions.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
