Making the Most Out of Growing US-Uzbekistan Trade and Investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

The purchase of U.S.-made commercial aircraft and an Uzbek company’s historic opening of a manufacturing facility in Kentucky demonstrate the dynamic and growing economic relations between the United States and Uzbekistan. As U.S. diplomatic engagement with Tashkent increases – new contracts and trade and investment frameworks signed – understanding each country’s priorities and objectives will help explain this new chapter of the partnership. Moreover, stronger trade and investment numbers must translate into employment opportunities and an improved quality of life for the Uzbek population.
Relations between Washington and Tashkent have generally strengthened over the past couple of years. U.S. President Donald Trump and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev will next meet in December, as Trump has invited the Uzbek leader to be a guest at the G-20 summit in Miami.
Stronger diplomatic links are translating into trade and investment deals. In June, the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Ambassador Jamieson Greer visited Tashkent and signed “an early harvest of trade commitments to strengthen the bilateral economic and investment relationship.” Specifically, Tashkent committed “to eliminate or reduce tariffs” on U.S. industrial goods and agricultural products. In contrast, Washington committed “to provide favorable consideration” in tariff actions for Uzbekistan’s industrial goods and agricultural products. The two sides are also working to conclude an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment.
Also in June, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) launched the U.S.-Uzbekistan Joint Investment Platform, which will “aim to identify strategic investments in Uzbekistan for U.S.” in areas like energy, infrastructure, critical minerals, transportation and logistics infrastructure.
The topic of investment in critical minerals, energy, and transportation was also reportedly discussed during a meeting between Mirziyoyev and Sergio Gor, the U.S. special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs, on the sidelines of the recent Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
This activity builds upon the momentum of earlier deals. In 2025, Tashkent announced a $8.5 billion deal to buy as many as 22 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft to modernize the country’s commercial aviation industry. The aircraft will allow direct, long-distance flights with the United States, increasing connectivity and tourism.
Investment now goes both ways, breaking stereotypes and assumptions of the U.S. being the only actor in the Central Asia-U.S. relationships that invests on the other side. The Uzbek company AFKA is building a manufacturing facility in Bowling Green, Kentucky. It will be the first Uzbek manufacturing company to operate in the U.S. The groundbreaking ceremony took place in July, and when complete, the AFKA Aluminum Solutions plant will employ 331 people, supporting the local economy and strengthening bilateral commercial ties.
Stronger economic links between the two governments occur at a time when Tashkent is looking to develop the entire country, not just the capital. For example, the historic city of Khiva is getting a face-lift through the expected construction of a conference hall, a 3-star hotel, and a reception house, which will create jobs and attract tourism. Plans also include building a toll road and a railway to connect the Urgench airport with Khiva. Other plans include modernizing regional airports to improve domestic and international connectivity.
As for Nukus, the capital of the Republic of Karakalpakstan, the goal is to upgrade the city’s public transportation via a loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
From Washington’s perspective, there is a new race on to access resources like oil, gas, and especially critical minerals. Central Asia has been blessed with many of the resources that the world’s great powers desire. Central Asian governments like Uzbekistan view this situation not as a game or a race but as an opportunity to build new commercial partnerships and attract investors. While the Trump administration continues to focus on energy, minerals, and transportation infrastructure as vital areas for future investment and trade, Tashkent can hopefully also redirect U.S. interest to other projects and industries.
For example, during the November 2025 summit between Trump and the five Central Asian leaders, Washington pledged to explore “the expansion of a partnership in the upcoming sale and privatization of UzAuto Motors” in addition to a potential $3 billion investment from Air Products for a methanol production facility in Uzbekistan. The Uzbek government aims to generate 54 percent of its power from renewable sources by 2030. Washington and Tashkent hope to encourage U.S. companies to invest in this field.
There are limitations to consider, specifically the Jackson-Vanik Amendment, which denies permanent normal trade relations to Uzbekistan. To be fair, while the amendment irritates political relations, its impact on bilateral trade and investment is negligible. Tashkent has, for decades, received temporary normal trade relations through annual presidential waivers.
Moreover, even if U.S.-Uzbek trade grows considerably, it will still be dwarfed by trade between Uzbekistan and China, which reached between $7.7 and $8.9 billion in the first half of the year. Simply put, stronger U.S.-Uzbek trade and investment ties will not dramatically create a new architecture of priority partners for Uzbekistan.
There is also a domestic component to consider: Uzbekistan has the region’s largest population, with around 39 million (according to a new census), and a vast young workforce who deserve jobs and a future in their homeland. Unfortunately, a significant portion of the population lives below the poverty line, and unemployment is still problematic, more than a million Uzbeks migrate abroad for work every year.
As in many countries, wealth and development concentrate in the capital. While the examples of regional infrastructure development mentioned in this commentary are positive, a 2025 study conducted by the National Statistics Committee of Uzbekistan in collaboration with the World Bank showed that the largest numbers of poor residents were recorded in the Samarkand region (265,000 people), as well as in Fergana (239,000), Kashkadarya (238,000), and Andijan (214,000) regions.
In other words, Uzbekistan must invest more in infrastructure projects and economic growth across its regions, not just the capital.
In a September 3 speech, Mirziyoyev said a new system to reduce poverty and unemployment across the country will be introduced. This new strategy must be monitored to ensure it promotes employment and helps low-income individuals, rather than falling victim to bureaucratic incompetence or corruption.
As interest in Central Asia’s natural resources continues to grow, it is also important to understand the priorities of the five Central Asian governments. In Uzbekistan, the momentum is to diversify the country’s energy production and bring development to areas outside Tashkent. Washington and American industries must keep Tashkent’s priorities and objectives in mind to secure win-win contracts and agreements and ensure this partnership continues as the so-called race for critical minerals heats up.
For Uzbekistan’s population, particularly those living outside Tashkent, this stronger partnership must mean more jobs, economic growth, and a better quality of life.

Saudi Aramco will not supply European oil refiners with crude in October: Sources

Saudi Aramco will not supply European oil refiners with crude in October: Sources
NEW YORK – Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no crude in October under long-term agreements after the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea was attacked, people informed of the decision said.
European customers normally receive Saudi Arabian crude on so-called term contracts, ensuring a steady flow of supply every month. Those deliveries will not take place in October, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public. The decision applies to all European buyers, they said.
Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment made outside normal working hours.
The absence of Saudi flows in October will heighten the need for European buyers to secure replacements. Already, Poland’s Orlen SA has been hunting for shipments, helping propel the prices of regional oil grades higher. Dated Brent, which is the benchmark for real-world barrels in Europe, topped US$130 this week at one point.
Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West pipeline last week after it was attacked by drones. Aramco is working to partially restart within days and ramp up to full capacity within six weeks, a person familiar with the matter said on Sept 16.
The shutdown has forced Aramco to make the rare move to offer customers in Asia cargoes on a so-called spot basis – agreements for immediate delivery. Once the pipeline restarts, traders will focus on whether Aramco offers refiners in Europe similar terms.
Those supplies to Asia are going through the Persian Gulf, which means Aramco has once again pivoted towards the embattled Strait of Hormuz. The company has sold tens of millions of barrels to customers for collection just outside the waterway this week, a route it had largely shunned during the conflict in the Middle East as regular attacks of ships made the journey risky.
The increased flows towards the Persian Gulf, however, brings little relief to Europe’s refiners. In order to get to buyers in the continent, those shipments would either have to sail through the Red Sea, where Yemen’s Houthi militants have been attacking Saudi ships, or sail almost five weeks around Africa.
European refineries typically lift Saudi crude from Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, which is connected to the Red Sea via a pipeline.
European countries in the OECD imported 577,000 barrels a day of crude from Saudi Arabia in June, according to the International Energy Agency. BLOOMBERG

Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:34 UTC
23:53:34 KST

Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
MOSCOW, Sept 18 - Russians are voting in a three-day parliamentary election which is widely expected to see the ruling United Russia party retain its dominance in what is a tightly controlled political system that has excluded most candidates who oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Even though the overall outcome is not in doubt, here are some of the reasons why the vote may be useful to President Vladimir Putin.
A MANDATE FOR MORE WAR?
As president or prime minister for more than a quarter of a century, Putin's grip on Russia has never been tighter. But the war has lasted much longer than many Russians expected and fallout from the conflict is now being felt much more sharply on the home front.
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia itself have escalated, and while civilian casualties are far lower than in Ukraine, they have sharply increased this year. Strikes on oil refineries have caused fuel shortages, while businesses are grappling with drone attacks on their warehouses and polls suggest some Russians are increasingly anxious.
Having framed the election as a test of support for the war, Putin is likely to point to the results to say that most people back his decision to fight on until key war aims are met.
CREATION OF A 'NEW ELITE'
Putin has said that those who fought in Ukraine are "warriors", part of a new "elite" he has promised will have prestigious careers. Should the some 200 veterans standing from a range of parties do well, Putin is expected to point to their success at the ballot box as an example of how Moscow looks after those who risked their lives for the motherland and to show how distinguishing oneself on the battlefield can lead to a high-profile political career. It's a development that could also encourage more people to sign up to fight in Ukraine.
CONTRAST WITH UKRAINE
Putin has repeatedly suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is illegitimate, pointing to the fact that his five-year term ran out in May 2024 and that Zelenskiy has refused to hold a new election since. Martial law, introduced in Ukraine in 2022, bans any wartime election and the constitution says the president serves until a newly elected one takes office. But Putin - who has faced criticism from Western politicians about Russia's own political system - may use the vote to say that Russia - unlike Ukraine - has stuck to its electoral timetable regardless of the war and is giving people a chance to vote.
SENSE OF NORMALCY
Putin has been keen to show Russians that despite the conflict and everything associated with it they can largely carry on life as before. Increasingly deep and destructive Ukrainian drone strikes have made that harder to achieve in what is the fifth year of the war. But holding a relatively smooth parliamentary election across 11 time zones in what is the world's largest country, whilst also waging war in Ukraine, could help Putin reassure Russians that pre-war traditions are being respected and that life - up to a point - goes on despite the conflict.
MOBILISATION/CENSORSHIP
Putin this month dismissed suggestions by Ukraine and Western media pundits that Russia would carry out a post-election mobilisation to expand the ranks of its army in Ukraine as "nonsense," suggesting it was a malicious suggestion designed to sow panic.
However, domestic and foreign critics of the war fear he could use the outcome of the election to justify such a move, given what Western intelligence agencies say are heavy Russian losses on the battlefield and what they say is Moscow's desire to urgently speed up the pace of its territorial gains with more manpower.
Those same critics fear that the authorities may move ahead with more repressive measures once the election results are in and a pre-election feel-good mood is no longer required.
They point in particular to plans previously floated by the authorities to have mobile service providers charge customers extra for using more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data in a month, a move seen as targeting people who use VPNs or virtual private networks to access websites and apps banned inside Russia. The authorities have given no public indication they intend to imminently resurrect the plan. REUTERS

Your Shoe Size Can Change as You Age. Here's Why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:32 UTC
23:53:32 KST

If you’ve always worn the same size shoe but your sneakers and boots feel tighter now that you’re in, say, your 40s or beyond, you’re not alone. People on TikTok are also sharing their experiences with growing feet as they’re getting older. But do your feet really get bigger with age?
“Yes, but ‘bigger’ is somewhat misleading,” says Dr. Kimberly Koury, an orthopedic surgeon at Atlantic Health. “Adult feet do not continue to grow in the same way they do during childhood. Instead, the shape of the foot can gradually change with age.”
This can happen for a variety of reasons and cause feet to become wider, flatter, and slightly longer, she explains. “Someone may notice that a shoe that fit well when they were younger now feels too tight, even though their actual foot bones have not continued to grow.”
Here’s what to know about why your feet may get bigger with age and what to do about it.
What causes feet to get bigger?
The main reason is that over time, your arch “flattens and spreads,” says Lesly Robinson, a podiatrist and interim dean of the Temple University School of Podiatric Medicine.
This is often due to decreased collagen—the protein that provides strength and elasticity to your skin, muscles, bones, tendons, and ligaments—that naturally happens with age. This can cause the ligaments supporting your arches to become lax, Robinson says. “When the arch falls, the foot both widens and lengthens,” adds Dr. Alexis Dixon, an orthopedic surgeon and foot and ankle specialist in Marina Del Ray, Calif.
Another reason feet may change in shape and size is a foot deformity, like a bunion or hammertoe, which become more prevalent as you get older. A bunion is a bump that forms on the inside of your big toe joint, but it’s not an extra bone growth. Instead, it’s a change in alignment, where the big toe moves toward the other toes, Koury says. “That makes the forefoot wider and can make previously comfortable shoes feel too narrow.” This can also contribute to flattening arches, Robinson says. Hammertoes happen when the tissue of your toes weakens, causing the muscles and tendons to buckle and curve, Dixon says.
Bunions and hammertoes can be genetic or result from wearing tight, narrow shoes over a lifetime, she says. They’re more common for women.
Arthritis is also common in feet and ankles, especially in the big-toe joint, Dixon says. It can cause bone spurs (extra growths of bone tissue) on top of the foot or at the back of the heel, which may rub against your shoe and make it feel too tight.
When do these changes happen, and who’s most affected?
People may notice foot changes starting in their 30s, but there’s no specific age when they happen, says Sindhu Srinivas, a podiatrist in Atlanta.
Age-related foot changes are generally more common for women, Koury says. The hormonal fluctuations in pregnancy and menopause affect collagen, and years of wearing high heels or narrow or ill-fitting shoes may contribute to structural changes in the feet.
People with previous foot injuries, flat feet or bunions (or a family history of these conditions), and a higher body weight are more at risk, Koury adds.
Being overweight puts pressure and stress on the feet, Srinivas says. “Over time, this increased load can contribute to changes in the foot's supporting structures and overall biomechanics.”
How much bigger will your feet get?
The changes happen gradually and can affect your foot’s length, width, and arch height, Srinivas says. But how much bigger your feet can get varies.
A study published in 2016 examined the foot measurements of 68 women aged 20 to over 80. It found that the widths of the balls of the feet increased by 3 to 4 millimeters per decade, while ball circumferences increased by about 5 to 7 millimeters, high-step circumferences 0.4 to 4.8 millimeters, and heel instep circumferences up to 2 millimeters.
“That may sound small, but these changes accumulate over several decades and can become enough to affect shoe fit,” Koury says.
Some people may need a wider shoe, while others might need one a half size larger, Dixon says.
When to see a doctor
If your feet seem to be getting wider or longer and you’re experiencing pain, swelling, numbness, tingling, or difficulty walking or doing other activities, see your doctor, Koury says. Also, talk to your doctor if you’re getting recurrent calluses, blisters, or skin breakdown, or if your bunions, hammertoes, or flatfoot are worsening. Sudden foot changes, especially if they only affect one foot, should also get checked, Srinivas says.
Pay extra attention to your feet if you have diabetes, neuropathy, or circulation problems, as even minor changes in your shoes’ fit can cause more serious problems, Koury says.
Doctors will recommend the best treatment for your feet. This may include orthotics to improve arch support, Robinson says. It’s also possible to modify footwear for bunions or hammertoes, Dixon adds. Physical therapy or exercises may be helpful for some, Koury says. Surgery may be necessary for some foot issues if other treatments don’t help.
How to protect your feet as you age
You can’t necessarily prevent age-related foot changes, but you can take steps to keep your feet healthy as you get older, Koury says.
Most important: wear shoes that fit well. Avoid footwear with narrow toe boxes, which compress your toes (and may cause bunions), and limit high heels, which put stress on the front of the foot and may even cause a deformity, Koury says. Shoes should be supportive and have a wider toe box, Robinson says. “It’s helpful to have your feet measured periodically, including the width, not just the length,” Koury says.
Maintaining a healthy weight can “help reduce unnecessary stress on the tendons, ligaments, and bones,” Sirinivas says.
Regular physical activity strengthens your feet and ankles. Low-impact, weight-bearing activities can maintain foot function and stability, improve balance, and prevent falls, Dixon says. Also try foot exercises, such as standing on one foot while holding onto a counter, or toe scrunches, which involves curling your toes to pick up a washcloth or other object off of the floor.
Treat bunions, flattening feet, or other foot problems as early as possible to avoid problems later, Koury says. “The goal is to accommodate the new foot shape and prevent the changes from becoming painful or functionally limiting.”

Volkswagen recalls over 208,000 vehicles in US over steering defect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:13 UTC
23:53:13 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
German automaker Volkswagen is recalling 208,724 vehicles in the US due to a steering system defect, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).
The recall covers certain 2018 Volkswagen Tiguan, 2018-2019 Volkswagen Atlas and 2019-2021 Audi Q3 models.
One of the bolts attaching the steering rack to the subframe may corrode and break, potentially causing the steering rack housing to fracture, the regulator said.
A broken steering rack housing could result in a loss of steering control, increasing the risk of a crash.
Authorized dealers will replace the right-side mounting bolt on the steering rack free of charge.
Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed on Nov. 10.
The recall was filed under NHTSA campaign number 26V590000, while Volkswagen’s recall codes are 48LG and 48VT.

Red Cross spokesperson: ‘Death and destruction for Palestinians in Gaza continues every day’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:08 UTC
23:53:08 KST

Death and destruction continue to affect Palestinians in Gaza every day despite a decrease in the intensity of hostilities since last year's ceasefire, according to Pat Griffiths, a spokesperson for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
“Let’s be clear: death and destruction for Palestinians in Gaza continues every day. The suffering is real, present and here every day – even when Gaza isn’t in the headlines,” Griffiths told Anadolu.
“Life for Palestinians here is disrupted in ways that are hard to imagine. Children go without education. People go without access to specialist or chronic medical care. Families have lost homes, livelihoods – many are still missing loved ones, not knowing if they are detained or deceased," he said.
Griffiths, who is currently in Gaza City on a weeklong visit, said urgent humanitarian needs remain across the enclave, particularly for food, water, shelter and health care.
“At the ICRC, we adapt our humanitarian response to changing needs and conflict dynamics. But make no mistake: urgent humanitarian needs remain. In terms of food, water, shelter, health, family connection - so much more needs to be done,” she said.
Griffiths said humanitarian access remains one of the biggest challenges facing ICRC teams working in Gaza.
“To help people in need, we need to be able to reach them – wherever they are, including in places of detention. That’s not always possible,” he said.
She said access can be restricted because of security concerns or because those with the authority to grant access do not do so.
“Granting humanitarian access is something that is an obligation for parties to armed conflict and occupying powers. It’s also something this is outside our control as humanitarians,” he said.
“And it’s why working towards improving our humanitarian access is a continuous conversation with those who have influence over it.”
Griffiths added that the problem extends beyond reaching people to ensuring that essential supplies can enter Gaza.
“People still desperately need better access to quality and nutritious food. Hospitals and primary healthcare centres still face shortages of medicines and medical items,” he said.
“Heavy machinery and materials that could be used to safely clear rubble, search for human remains or repair broken water and wastewater systems face restrictions on entry.”
He also pointed to shortages of fuel and engine oil needed to keep generators operating.
“Everyone in Gaza faces challenges in terms of sustained access to electricity, relying on generators that are themselves reliant on enough fuel and engine oil being able to enter so they can function. And there’s not enough fuel and engine oil entering.”
According to Griffiths, shortages are also driving up prices at a time when many displaced Palestinians have lost their homes and livelihoods.
“These shortages in Gaza disrupt essential services and drive prices up. And when people are displaced and lose their homes – they also lose their livelihoods. So, cash is scarce, and people can’t afford what might be available on the market.”
“All of these things make life harder for Palestinians in Gaza right now. It’s why we continue to call for the unrestricted entry and access to those who need it of essential food, goods, medicines and other items.”
She said the ICRC continues to call for international humanitarian law to be upheld in its dialogue with Israeli authorities.
“That’s why, in our dialogue with Israeli authorities, we continue to call for international humanitarian law, which seeks to reduce the suffering of civilians in times of armed conflict, to be upheld.”
“It’s why we continue to call for the political will that is necessary to seek dialogue and sustainable solutions to improve the lives of Palestinians in Gaza. Too many lives are at stake for anything less.”
Impossible choice between tents and unsafe damaged buildings
Griffiths said thousands of Palestinians in Gaza continue to live in tents after being displaced or losing their homes, with many having been forced to move multiple times.
After three years of living in tents through extreme heat and cold, some families are returning to damaged buildings despite the risk of collapse because they have few alternatives.
She recalled the recent collapse of a damaged building in Gaza City where more than 100 people were sheltering. Many were rescued, but others, including children, were killed.
“Choosing between life in a tent … or a building that is damaged and at risk of collapse, just to have a roof over one’s head, is not a choice any family should have to make,” she said.
With winter approaching, Griffiths warned that heavy rain and winds could increase the risk of further collapses and called for heavy machinery to clear rubble and for durable shelter materials to enter Gaza.
'The desire for a normal life'
Despite the destruction and hardship, Griffiths said Palestinians in Gaza continue to express “the desire for a normal life” — to go to school, see friends, work, be with family and return home.
He acknowledged that the ceasefire in October last year reduced the intensity of hostilities and allowed more food and goods into Gaza, but said the humanitarian crisis remains severe.
“Death and destruction for Palestinians in Gaza continues every day,” he said, warning that suffering persists even when Gaza is no longer in the headlines.
Griffiths said Palestinians’ “dreams and hopes” for the future are often missing from international coverage. He also highlighted the kindness and solidarity he has witnessed among people helping their families, communities and even strangers despite years of hardship.
He said the desire for a dignified, normal life reflects the purpose of international humanitarian law: protecting civilians and reducing suffering during conflict.
A Palestinian journalist's poem about freedom
Griffiths recalled a meeting with a Palestinian journalist during a previous visit to Gaza that has remained with her.
“When I was last in Gaza, I met a Palestinian journalist who read to me a poem that he had written,” she said.
“The poem was about a bird that spread its wings and flew. After he finished reading the poem, the journalist told me that he was the bird. He told me that all he wanted to do was to experience the freedom of being able to spread his wings.”
“He was telling me that he wanted to live a life of dignity, with choice and agency.”
Griffiths said the journalist’s aspirations reflected those of many Palestinians in Gaza.
“So many people in Gaza are like him. They have dreams and hopes and fears for their future. They want to spread their wings and live, but they can’t.”

Switzerland adopts new security strategy amid Russia war, rising hybrid threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:53:01 UTC
23:53:01 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Switzerland's Federal Council on Friday adopted a new national security strategy aimed at preparing the country for an "increasingly unstable" international environment, citing Russia's war against Ukraine, hybrid threats and critical dependencies.
The 2026 Security Policy Strategy establishes three main priorities: strengthening the resilience of the state, economy and society; improving the protection of civilians, institutions and critical infrastructure; and bolstering Switzerland's defense capabilities.
The government said in a statement that the international security situation has become "increasingly unstable and volatile," pointing to intensifying rivalries between major powers, armed conflicts and a weakening international order.
It said there is "still no end in sight" to Russia's war against Ukraine, while cyberattacks, influence operations and other hybrid threats are increasing. Switzerland must also address domestic security risks, natural hazards and pandemics, the statement added.
The strategy contains 10 objectives and 46 measures, prioritizing efforts against what the government considers the most likely threats: hybrid and remote attacks and organized crime within Switzerland.
On defense, the Federal Council said the country must be capable of effectively countering an armed attack, including by establishing the necessary capabilities and cooperation with partner states in advance.
"In view of the current threat situation, the Federal Council had instructed the relevant departments to implement the proposed measures right from the start of the consultation process, and to plan a monitoring system for this purpose," it said.
The State Secretariat for Security Policy will coordinate the work, with the Federal Council due to receive a progress report by the end of 2028.

Russia said Friday that it had demanded Japan withdraw US Typhon land-based missile systems deployed on its southwestern Kyushu island.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow sent a protest note to Japan on Sept. 3 over the deployment of the US-made systems, which are designed to launch medium- and shorter-range missiles.
She said Russia had repeatedly raised concerns with Tokyo that the deployment of such weapons on Japanese territory poses threats to Russian national security, regional peace, and stability.
Russia “emphasized the inadmissibility of advanced deployment by Japan on its territory under any proposal of the above-mentioned installations, regardless of the duration and methods of their placement,” Zakharova said.

‘Pray for Gaza’: Is Drake cynically jumping on the bandwagon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:51:33 UTC
23:51:33 KST

Breadcrumb
‘Pray for Gaza’: Is Drake’s new song pro-Palestine, or a publicity stunt?
Canadian rapper and singer Drake, born Aubrey Drake Graham, on Tuesday made headlines again after he premiered his hour-long ‘not so short film’ FOMO, which included an unreleased song titled “Pray for Gaza”
The Genius website, which hosts one of the world’s largest collections of song lyrics and music insights, revealed the lyrics this week.
“I'm a big bad boy in the ends right now, wallah,” Drake says in one verse, using the Arabic-language word for 'by God'.
However, some of the most striking lyrics that have stirred debate are the ones that appear to mention the besieged Gaza enclave.
“Inna di worl, we ah pray for Gaza. Worl' Boss home when I pay with cards. My brand new nickname Baby Gaza. Yuh dun know di killydem crazy, baba. Yeah, Baby Gaza, your opp ma dropped, save the drama,” the lyrics say.
Shahla Omar, freelance culture journalist and The New Arab contributor, describes Drake as an "unserious artist", but doesn't believe the mention of Gaza was an intentional decision to boost his new tracks, as it was likely in the works for a long time.
She noted, however, that Drake and other artists must do more to highlight the plight of Palestinians, considering the scale of their platforms and the impact it would have.
"There are so many musicians today who model themselves on Drake. I think if he were to make more meaningful stances on issues like the genocide in Palestine, at least some of the artists that look up to him would follow suit, less afraid of the repercussions they might face," she said.
"Drake actually has a big tour coming up next year, so it will be interesting to see if he uses that stage to make a stronger expression of solidarity with Palestine than he has so far," she added.
The lyrics have also prompted conversations on social media.
“Drake is using the murder of innocent men, women, and children as a trend to score brownie points with his fanbase, and they’ve all fallen for it,” one person commented on X.
“The suffering and mass extermination of a group of people is now being used as a trendy weapon for social popularity to steer people away from being actual political participants. They would rather stream a Drake song that says “pray for Gaza” than actually do something for Gaza,” another commented.
Calls for a ceasefire
Drake signed an open letter by Artists4Ceasefire in late 2023, urging for a ceasefire after Israel launched a brutal offensive on Gaza, which has since killed over 73,000 people.
In May, Drake also released three albums, with one of them containing lyrics taking aim at music producer DJ Khaled over his silence on Israel’s war on Gaza.
At the time, the lyrics divided opinion, with some praising him for shedding light on the onslaught, while others called him hypocritical for failing to be more vocal on the atrocities taking place.
Some also accused Drake of using alleged war crimes, and what has been determined to be a genocide by leading rights groups, in a song, claiming that he has reduced it to a pop culture moment.
"Your people are still waiting for a ‘Free Palestine,’ but apparently, everything isn't black and white and red and green. I'm seeing everyone's true colours, for real," the song titled 'Make Them Pay' says.
Further questions have now arisen over the Pray For Gaza track, and whether it is indeed a further show of support for Palestinian victims of Israeli occupation, or if it is a reference to singer Vybz Kartel, who popularized "Gaza" as a nickname for Waterford, a neighbourhood in the Jamaican city of Portmore.
"I do think there is an element of bandwagoning here, but Drake is quite a consistent bandwagoner — you can hear it in his frequent switches in musical styles, or the creeping habibification of his lyrics," Omar said.
"I do agree that lyrics like these contribute to a trivialisation of the genocide, whether that trivialisation is intentional or not. We’re seeing it everywhere I think, not just in music. I think that will only get worse the longer this genocide is allowed to continue," she added.
Drake's 'Pray for Gaza' comes amid widespread music-related controversy over the past week, after rapper Macklemore revealed he was removed as a supporting act from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after his call for a “Free Palestine”.
Macklemore said pro-Israel billionaire and Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft told Sheeran he would have to choose between using his stadium and having Macklemore on stage, and that he also pressured other venues to do the same.
Sheeran has faced mounting criticism for what activists said was succumbing to pressure and prioritising money rather than taking an ethical stance on the matter.
Many fans have also dubbed the ordeal a watershed moment in terms of pop culture figures speaking out in support of Palestine.
"To declare yourself an apolitical artist, as Ed Sheeran did in response to the backlash he was facing — we’ve seen in the public roasting he’s gotten since then that such a claim about oneself as an artist simply will not fly anymore. I think there is a growing public understanding that art and politics cannot be separated from each other, and that expressions of solidarity with Palestine are penalised to an absurd extreme," Omar explained.
"I think the cumulative effect of lots of musicians making reference to Palestine and Gaza can build up into something powerful — it’s a kind of immortalisation or time capsule-ing of what the social and political conscience was in a particular moment of time. That includes lyrics and songs that are powerful and poignant, but also the borderline ridiculous," she concluded.

Feature: From digital recipes to AI menus, food gets tech touch in Poland
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
22:51:02 CST
23:51:02 KST

A visitor selects ice cream at Warsaw Sweet Tech in Warsaw, Poland, on Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Yue Yuanyuan)
WARSAW, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Following instructions on a screen, chefs from across Poland worked through the steps of making gelato, using a digital tool to balance their recipes as they turned natural ingredients into the frozen dessert.
The demonstration at Warsaw Sweet Tech, a trade fair held from Tuesday to Thursday, brought digital precision into the craft of gelato making.
On the screen, users could fine-tune the recipe's sweetness, fat content and the gelato's firmness, while an automatic balancing function helped calculate the proportions of ingredients.
In the mind of Aleksander Pitura, co-creator of the website myGelato.eu, the goal is to give makers greater freedom to develop their own recipes using natural ingredients, without artificial coloring or flavoring.
For Pitura, the idea grew out of a practical difficulty: making gelato from scratch required knowledge that ready-made mixes did little to teach.
Following instructions on a packet could produce a dessert, he explained, but it did not necessarily help makers understand how to balance ingredients or develop a recipe of their own.
He teamed up with a friend to develop a website that would help gelato makers with those calculations, creating what he described as the first platform of its kind in Poland.
Alongside recipe balancing, the website provides step-by-step production guidance, helping users put their formulations into practice.
That flexibility also matters when recipes cross borders. Pitura said some of his Asian customers preferred less sweetness, requiring formulations to be adjusted for different tastes. His clients include users in Shanghai and Hong Kong.
Innovation in kitchen technology is also changing how food is decorated and presented.
Elsewhere at the fair, Lithuanian family business JetLt showed how a customer's photograph or design could become part of the dessert itself.
The company manufactures flatbed printers that apply edible ink directly to cakes, chocolate and other confectionery, transferring images from a computer onto the treats to give them a personal finishing touch.
The founder's son, representing the company at the fair, said the family began manufacturing the printers in 2016 and had been selling them in Poland for seven years.
At the time production began, he said, theirs was one of only three companies in Europe known to him to be making such printers.
A simple name or logo can take about 30 seconds to print, while a complicated image on a large cake may take up to two minutes, he said. The machines can also decorate several items, such as macarons, in one batch.
For confectioners, the technology offers a way to combine personalized orders with repeatable production. The cake or chocolate still has to be made; printing adds another option for how it is presented.
The family's move into food decoration itself grew out of an earlier craft. The representative recalled his father's work printing on CDs and DVDs before adapting that experience to a very different surface.
"We're always trying something new," he said.
While technology is opening up new possibilities for how food is made and presented, a restaurant's appeal also depends on what happens around the plate.
That part of the experience was the focus of Zuzana AI, a Polish venture exhibiting at the concurrent ProKitchen Expo.
Co-founder Miron Blacerzak said many restaurant QR codes in Poland simply direct diners to static PDF menus, offering little opportunity for interaction.
His team developed a platform designed to turn that familiar code into an interactive assistant. Customers would scan it to open a chat interface, ask for recommendations based on the menu, and then order and pay without installing an app.
For restaurant operators, the system is also designed to answer questions about stock levels and compare the performance of different dishes, connecting the customer-facing service with work behind the scenes.
The project had been under development for three years and was due to launch in about two weeks, Blacerzak said.
The intention, he said, is to help waiters focus on delivering food and making guests feel comfortable, including the small exchanges that can turn a visit into a relationship.
For culinary historian Bogdan Galazka, who holds a doctorate in history from Nicolaus Copernicus University in Torun, Poland, preserving tradition goes hand in hand with embracing the possibilities offered by new technology.
"Modern technology is entering the kitchen, and that is wonderful. A robot waiter can be a pleasant attraction for our guests," he said. "But we must not forget tradition, which safeguards historical and national memory." ■
A confectionery with printed patterns is seen at Warsaw Sweet Tech in Warsaw, Poland, on Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Du Zhiqian)

More than 100,000 people have also been displaced inside Yemen as fighting intensifies, particularly along the western coast, Desamours said.
Health system under pressure
Meanwhile, only 60 percent of 5,415 assessed health facilities in Yemen are fully functioning, WHO spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic told reporters in Geneva on Friday.
Only 6 percent provide a full package of trauma care despite growing emergency needs.
More than 18,000 suspected measles cases and 106 deaths have been reported this year, alongside 390 diphtheria cases and 13 deaths.
Around 30,000 children experience severe acute malnutrition with complications each year, while some therapeutic feeding centres are operating at 120 percent of bed capacity, Jasarevic said.
Access remains particularly difficult in northern Yemen, where UN operations have been suspended in 90 priority districts.
Jasarevic said only $490,000 had so far been secured through WHO’s Contingency Fund for Emergencies, leaving a “significant funding gap” to sustain and expand the health response.

====================================================================================================

4 Fault Lines that Could Shape the Trump-Xi Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:32:00 UTC
23:32:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet next week at the White House in Washington, D.C., provided that the “conditionalities” attached to the summit are met. This will be the second leaders’ summit between Trump and Xi this year, following the U.S. president’s visit to Beijing in May.
This will be Xi’s first visit to the U.S. capital in a decade, after he met then-U.S. President Barack Obama in 2016. Back then, the agenda centered on the much-touted issues of cyberespionage and commercial hacking. Today, there are new concerns.
Both domestically and internationally, this visit is taking place amid considerable friction. On the domestic front, the United States will be holding midterm elections roughly 40 days after the visit. This makes the timing an unusual choice, as noted by Pew Research: many Americans still view the Chinese leader unfavorably, despite a 6-percentage-point rise since last year. Presidents generally avoid such risks to optics as midterms near.
At the international level, the world is still living under the shadow of the Iran-U.S. war. Consequently, Brent crude is trading around $100 per barrel. At the same time, the China-Russia alignment has deepened; a few months ago – just after the last Trump-Xi summit, in fact – Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin reaffirmed their close partnership and signed a joint statement to deepen their strategic partnership. Beijing is underwriting Moscow’s war machine in Ukraine as Washington prepares to welcome Xi.
Meanwhile, Pew Research noted in another survey that Beijing is viewed favorably in more countries than Washington, adding another nuance to the global attention focused on the summit.
However, one must note that Beijing has yet to officially confirm the meeting, even though the United States has given the date of September 24. Some reports even suggested that the meeting will be canceled by Beijing if Washington gives approval for a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan.
Therefore, the coming week will tell us much about the relationship between China and the United States.
Real Stakes Amid Low Expectations
Even assuming the meeting does go ahead as planned, there are low expectations for what will be achieved. The consensus holds that the tangible outcomes will be modest, possibly just an extension of what was achieved at the last summit held in China. There are four topics of particular interest at the Trump-Xi summit.
First is the tariff question. At the Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Busan, South Korea, on October 30, 2025, Washington and Beijing agreed to a one-year truce in their trade war. The United States reduced its fentanyl-related tariff on Chinese goods to 10 percent. The U.S. also suspended a 10 percent reciprocal tariff and secured a commitment from Beijing to buy 25 million tons of U.S. soybeans every year through 2028. China also deferred export controls on rare earths. But this truce will expire in November this year.
The upcoming Trump-Xi meeting will build on these arrangements rather than introduce something entirely novel. Already, the rare earth element in the deal is quite fragile. Some reports have suggested that exports of yttrium – a rare earth element used in the aerospace and defense industries – to the United States have declined sharply after April 2025, despite China’s commitment to waive export controls. Some U.S. officials and analysts have discussed imposing new tariffs and charges on certain Chinese goods. This could be used as leverage in negotiations before the meeting.
The second focal point is Iran. The ceasefire in the Middle East has collapsed multiple times, a recurring feature of Trump’s foreign policy. Just over a week ago, Iran retaliated against the U.S. strikes on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and hit Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq.
China is currently Iran’s largest trading partner and the top buyer of its oil, and Washington has declared economic war on Iran. In practice, as Iran is already heavily sanctioned, the new U.S. Treasury Department campaign – dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast” – involves pressuring those who “enabled” Iran’s actions.
Trump mentioned speaking directly to Xi over this and asking him not to get involved. In May, both China and the United States agreed that Iran should not have a nuclear weapon, but this small point of agreement is being overshadowed by the heightening tension over other issues.
Third is Taiwan. Taiwan has long remained a thorn in China-U.S. relations. After the summit held in May 2026, Trump called U.S. arms sales to Taiwan a “very good negotiating chip” that he kept in abeyance. This transactional framing alarmed many of the U.S. allies. Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te immediately pushed back against it by declaring that the sovereignty of the island will not be “sacrificed or traded away.”
More recently, reports emerged that China had threatened to cancel the summit if Trump approved the sale. Getting Washington to agree, even temporarily, to halt arms sales to Taiwan has been a major priority for Beijing since the 1980s. Now that Trump has signaled a willingness to view arms sales as a bargaining chip, rather than a routine aspect of the Taiwan-U.S. relationship, Xi will be looking to lock in that mindset.
Even if the sale eventually gets approved, the fact that it is seen as a point of leverage by Trump shows the limits of his interest in Taiwan for its own sake. This problem extends well beyond Taiwan itself. Manila’s ongoing standoff with Beijing over maritime features in the South China Sea, notably Scarborough Shoal, is seen by allies as a test of whether Washington will prioritize optics with Beijing over its interests. If Trump signals that he will, not only Taiwan but Tokyo, Manila, and others can interpret their security guarantees as “negotiable,” especially when they clash with China. This will test the whole alliance architecture in Asia.
The fourth area to watch is AI, which is at the heart of the U.S. strategy on China. Under the Biden administration, export controls effectively banned advanced AI chips from reaching China. Trump also tightened these restrictions in April 2025. However, he sharply reversed that policy between December 2025 and January 2026. The administration changed its approach to Nvidia’s H200 chips from a “presumption of denial” of exports to China to case-by-case approval. Chinese firms placed orders for millions of H200 chips. Trump touted it as a business deal, not as a national security issue. This caused some alarm and pushback within the United States.
On the other hand, even strict export control rules are easy to circumvent. Big Chinese firms like ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have been using Nvidia chips sourced from third countries such as Japan, Thailand, and Malaysia rather than shipping them directly into China.
Amid all these controls, China is still progressing well in AI, though it remains behind the United States. However, their models now account for a much larger share of global AI usage than before, thanks to China’s open-weight strategies and more efficient models. Such contradictions in the U.S. policy will be very visible in the upcoming meetings.
Anyone hoping for a serious discussion on AI safety regulations, meanwhile, is likely to be disappointed. While there have been rumors of upcoming AI talks around the time of the Trump-Xi summit, both states see themselves locked in competition for dominance of AI, and are unlikely to pump the brakes.
Implications for India
India will be closely watching all developments in Washington next week. Last year, Trump left no stone unturned in pressuring India, adding a 50 percent tariff on Indian goods in response to New Delhi’s continued purchases of Russian oil. Trump himself, after seeing Xi, Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi together in a summit last year, posted that the U.S. had “lost India and Russia to deepest, darkest, China.” In February 2026, a framework India-U.S. deal eased the effective tariff rate from 50 percent to 18 percent, but the damage to the trust was already done.
Just days before the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting, Xi was in Delhi for the BRICS summit; both governments said they were committed to working toward the border dispute, resuming direct flights and relaxing investment restrictions. The New Delhi Declaration also voiced opposition to unilateral imposition of tariffs and trade restrictions and called for reform in the multipolar global order. However, genuine issues still prevail between New Delhi and Beijing.
Seen from New Delhi, therefore, the meeting next week will signal to India where it stands in Washington’s priorities and whether Trump’s transactional policy continues to impact India-U.S. ties. Many countries will be watching the summit for similar signs, meaning the ripples will spread far beyond bilateral China-U.S. relations.

Alibaba open-sources medical AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
Tested on nearly 40,000 real-world exams, the model outperformed most radiologists, according to a new study published in Science
Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has open-sourced an artificial intelligence model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions – including cancers – by reading computed tomography (CT) scans, marking the latest step in the firm’s growing medical AI efforts.
The vision-language model, called Damo Radar, was designed to analyse contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs and identify a broad range of diseases and other abnormalities, such as malignant tumours, the institute said on Friday.
The model was trained using CT scans paired with clinical reports. In nearly 40,000 real-world examinations, it achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings. An AUC of 1.0 represents perfect diagnostic accuracy.
The research team said the training method could eventually be extended to other types of medical imaging, calling the model “the world’s first expert-level generalist medical imaging model”.

Researchers used Claude to breach OpenAI’s internal systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Researchers used Claude to breach OpenAI’s internal systems
- Researchers from Hacktron used Anthropic's Claude AI to breach OpenAI's internal systems via a flaw in its public help forum.
- OpenAI fixed the vulnerability within 14 hours and rewarded the researchers US$6,500 for reporting it.
- The flaw affects many companies, raising concerns about AI enabling faster, cheaper cyberattacks on various platforms.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A security research company said on Sept 18 it managed to break into OpenAI’s internal systems using the latest software from Anthropic, exposing how quickly the technology can carry out sophisticated cyberattacks.
The researchers from security firm Hacktron said they found a security flaw in OpenAI’s public help forum, run by the Discourse platform, that allowed them to take control of the site.
“We immediately reported the initial vulnerability to OpenAI and Discourse and worked with them to coordinate the patch,” Hacktron said in a blog post.
“We appreciate their attention to detail and fast resolution of this issue,” the post added.
OpenAI confirmed the flaw was fixed within about 14 hours of being notified and paid the researchers a US$6,500 (S$8,300) reward.
“We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings. We narrowed the permissions on Community sign-in tokens and revoked affected tokens and sessions,” said Drew Pusateri, an OpenAI spokesperson.
The Hacktron researchers said they initially used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 to identify and exploit the software flaw, but struggled to make it work consistently.
After Anthropic released Claude Opus 5, the researchers said the newer model produced a working hack within about three hours.
The hackers did not use Claude Mythos, a more capable Anthropic model that is restricted to a small group of vetted cyber-defence organisations.
Anthropic has described Mythos as having the strongest cybersecurity capabilities of any model it has built.
Hacktron said the underlying software flaw is not unique to OpenAI and is used across many companies’ products, including those made by Slack and Meta.
The firm said it is continuing similar tests at other companies.
The case adds to growing concern among security experts that AI tools are making it faster and cheaper to carry out sophisticated cyberattacks that once required specialised teams and months of work. AFP

New Bolivian cat claws its way into species list: What we meow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:25:53 UTC
23:25:53 KST

New Bolivian cat claws its way into species list: What we meow
Purrfectly new to science: the first new wild cat found in more than a century proves that cats do have nine (secret) lives.
A new species of wildcat, discovered in Bolivia, has been formally identified after the accidental discovery of a lost kitten and nearly 10 years of painstaking research.
The Leopardus tilcayo, which local people in the Bolivian Yungas, a band of cloud forest which runs along the eastern slope of the Andes, were aware of, was previously thought to be related to other wildcats in the region.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3New tiger cat species identified in Bolivia, first in over a century
- list 2 of 3How Virunga Park protects people and gorillas from Ebola in eastern DRC
- list 3 of 3Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
It wasn’t.
Here’s what we know.
What has been announced?
A study published in Current Biology this week has announced the first new cat species to be discovered in more than 100 years. The last was the pampas cat, reported in 1923.
Scientists have named the new cat Leopardus tilcayo, after the local Bolivian name for the animal.
The Leopardus tilcayo has been found living in the Bolivian Yungas, a band of cloud forest which runs along the eastern slope of the Andes, forming a transitional zone between the high mountains and the Amazon basin. This is a rugged, humid and largely under-studied ecoregion, which spreads into Peru and northern Argentina, although so far the tilcayo has only been genetically confirmed in Bolivia.
Researchers don’t yet know whether the species is confined to a single pocket of this forest or spread more widely across it.
Jonas Lescroart, a researcher at the University of Antwerp and coauthor of the study, said such a discovery is rare for the cat family. New species are sometimes “declared” when older scientific names are reinstated after genetic research shows a population was wrongly grouped with another species. That happened with the clouded tiger cat two years ago and the southern tiger cat, Leopardus guttulus, in 2013.
But this cat is different.
“It had never been given a scientific name, and it had never been formally described in a scientific way that was published,” Lescroart told Al Jazeera. “So we had the honour of coming up with a name for this animal and doing the formal scientific description.”
How was the cat found?
A local man found a kitten alone near the forest and, mistaking it for a stray domestic cat, brought it home to care for it. It lived with his family for about a year until 2016 when its wild instincts became impossible to ignore, and it started chasing the neighbours’ chickens.
Once the family could no longer manage the cat themselves, they surrendered it to Senda Verde, a refuge for animals. The refuge called in biologist and lead scientist of the Bolivian Felids Research Program, Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, telling her they had found a “weird cat”.
“Unfortunately, that’s the problem with the illegal wildlife trade,” Nogales Ascarrunz, told Al Jazeera. “When you want to pet a wild animal, then you think the power of love is going to change the behaviour of this animal. But a wild animal, it doesn’t matter if you give him the best food, it’s not going to behave.”
She added that this kind of case is common in Bolivia, particularly in the aftermath of wildfires, when orphaned young animals are captured and sold into the illegal pet trade before eventually being surrendered once new owners realise they can’t be kept.
When she went to see the for herself, she says she found an animal with a small, scrunched face, short round ears, long whiskers, and covered in leopard-like spots – but clearly too large and too wild to be a domestic cat.
Initially, she believed it was a Leopardus tigrinus, or tigrina, a small spotted cat found across much of Central and South America.
But, she says, something about the size and shape of the cat’s spots bothered her. It would take nearly a decade, a genetics collaboration spanning three countries, and DNA pulled from century-old museum skulls to prove she was right to be suspicious.
Perhaps leopards can’t change their spots but apparently, you can discover a new Leopardus with new spots altogether.
How was it found to be a new species?
While Nogales Ascarrunz was puzzling over her “weird cat” in Bolivia, an entirely separate effort was under way to study tiger cats across the continent.
Lescroart and co-researchers in Belgium, Brazil, Bolivia, the United States, Colombia, the United Kingdom and Peru were busy collecting tiger cat DNA from across South America to resolve a long-standing taxonomic puzzle.
“The group of tiger cats has always been a contentious group with an uncertain taxonomy, and no one could really tell with certainty how many different species of tiger cats there were walking around,” Lescroart said.
By combining existing genomic data from northeast Brazil, Colombia and southern Brazil with new samples from the Guianas, Peru and Bolivia, the team built a far more complete picture of the group than had existed before, ultimately identifying five distinct species rather than the two to four previously expected.
Lescroart said the results were surprising. “When I started working on tiger cats, I was already aware from the start that, regardless of the results, something would have to be rearranged … but we would never have expected to find a completely undescribed species.”
Because tiger cats are what scientists call a “cryptic species” group, nearly identical in appearance but genetically distinct, the differences were essentially invisible without DNA analysis. “Physically, they are very similar and hard to tell apart at first instance,” Lescroart said, “and you need genetic research to dig down and find that there are important differences.”
“When we managed to put our data together, that is when the pieces clicked,” Lescroart said, “and we realised that the one in Bolivia is really a separate thing from the other tiger cats that we already had on our radar as suspected species or subspecies.”
How was the cat’s name chosen?
The name, tilcayo, came from the people who live alongside it and who used the name for the animal to distinguish it from other small spotted cats in the region, such as Geoffroy’s cats and margays.
“It doesn’t have any meaning in Spanish, even Quechua,” Nogales Ascarrunz said. When the team asked local people where the name came from, “they would say things like ‘my grandpa told me’ or ‘my mother told me that’s the name of the cat’ – knowledge passed down with no accompanying origin story.”
What else do we know about this cat?
Very little.
Researchers do not know how many of them may exist. “We hope, thousands of them, but we have no idea,” Lescroart said.
They also do not know the cat’s full range within the Yungas, or whether the species extends into neighbouring Peru or Argentina.
Nogales Ascarrunz added that basic biology, including diet, predators and reproduction, is still undocumented.
What happens next?
Lescroart said the new species classification could change how tiger cats are protected.
Tiger cats are assessed collectively as “vulnerable” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. But splitting one species into five means each newly recognised group covers a smaller population, which conservationists say could mean more of them need urgent, individual protection.
Genomic data adds to that concern: most tiger cat lineages show long-term declines, with some populations reduced by as much as 80 percent from historical highs, a trend that lines up with what Bolivian elders have told Nogales Ascarrunz: That they are seeing fewer and fewer tilcayos in the forest.

Anthropic quietly sets up biology lab as it ramps AI drug programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-18
14:21:00 UTC
23:21:00 KST

Anthropic quietly sets up biology lab as it ramps AI drug programme
- Anthropic has established a wet biology lab to advance AI-driven drug research, focusing on rare diseases and physical experiments beyond computer simulations.
- The company integrates AI automation with human oversight to accelerate lab work safely, balancing innovation with concerns over AI risks and ethical deployment.
- Anthropic targets drug development for neglected conditions, expanding its resources and partnerships while avoiding direct clinical trials to complement the pharmaceutical industry.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic has quietly set up a laboratory to do physical biology work as it pushes its artificial-intelligence ambitions into the world of drug science.
At a time when fears of AI are gripping the public, the start-up has built a wet lab, or place for physical experiments, in the San Francisco Bay Area, two people familiar with the matter said. Anthropic has said it wants to unlock treatments for rare diseases, and its biology work has gone beyond “in silico” or computer evaluations.
In a Reuters interview on Sept 15, Anthropic’s head of life sciences, Eric Kauderer-Abrams, confirmed the start-up’s wet lab.
“We believe that to do biology, the final test is still and will be for a while in real lab work,” he said. “We absolutely are doing that today, and I would describe our approach as being typical of what you would see in most biotech companies, where there’s some amount of that that we’re doing in our own facilities and some amount of that that we’re working with external partners on.”
A spokesperson later clarified that Anthropic’s lab is not for drug discovery specifically, declining to elaborate.
The move represents a small step toward Anthropic’s enormous ambition to tackle diseases that it thinks the pharmaceutical industry is neglecting – and to do so before staff and the public lose faith that AI justifies erasing jobs and possibly human life, one of the people said. The success of any drug programme it runs is not certain; most drugs fail to pass trials for clinical safety and efficacy.
For Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, the effort is personal. A disease killed his father only a few years before a cure came about, he said in a recent essay. Kauderer-Abrams echoed the sentiment.
“The mission of the company is to develop powerful AI in such a way that benefits the world,” Kauderer-Abrams said. “By far, we see the biggest opportunity for that in the life sciences, and that is motivating everything that we’re doing.”
Balancing ambition with fears of catastrophe
Like other biotech companies, Anthropic is embracing physical automation, said the two people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The start-up wants to push how its Claude AI can direct robotic units to carry out science experiments with limited human intervention, one of the people said. Still, Anthropic believes that human oversight and involvement are essential for safety, its spokesperson said.
“We’re in the very early innings of using AI to automate the execution of lab work,” said Kauderer-Abrams, “an area that has the potential to bring about meaningful acceleration in so many different processes.”
Anthropic’s race to apply rapidly evolving technology to a biology lab comes at an extraordinary time for the company.
In the past two weeks, some of its researchers warned that AI could lead to human extinction, and Anthropic said it found examples where its systems could have been used towards biological weapons development, which met some scepticism.
Amodei also called for a development slowdown, saying that a future AI more capable than the OpenAI agents that hacked Hugging Face could cause catastrophic damage. At the same time, Anthropic is preparing to go public in a potentially US$2 trillion (S$2.56 trillion) IPO to raise more money for such AI development.
“In our life-science work, we’re always balancing these things,” Kauderer-Abrams said, “making models better in ways that we think will uplift and accelerate developing medicines, and being thoughtful and careful about how we deploy it to limit the risk.”
Procurement ramp-up
Anthropic staked out its intention to start running drug programmes, at a San Francisco event in June. On stage there, Kauderer-Abrams said Anthropic would do pre-clinical work in areas that traditional companies did not find attractive financially.
The company also launched software called Claude Science, and it earlier added Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan to its board and bought the start-up Coefficient Bio for about US$400 million in stock, according to media reports. Anthropic confirmed the acquisition, which will help it build tools for drug development, but it had no comment on the deal price.
Now, Anthropic is bulking up its in-house lab efforts for speed and for first-hand experience in biology, though it outsources work when efficient, Kauderer-Abrams told Reuters.
“There’s some things that we can do much faster in our own hands,” he said, with the goal “to operate at the largest possible scale”.
Anthropic has looked to hire a leader who could ramp up procurement and other operations, it said in a recent LinkedIn job post. Another Anthropic role solicited via Jobera sought an expert on “protein and nucleic acid characterisation,” among other biochemical work. A third Anthropic job listing read: “Our goal is to speed up progress in the life sciences by an order of magnitude.”
Life sciences already represents one of Anthropic’s biggest investment areas by headcount and resources, Kauderer-Abrams said.
Targeting ‘undruggable’ conditions
His view is that AI could fast-track development for conditions previously thought to be “undruggable” – too difficult to treat. The technology could speed up discovery, for instance, of bispecific and trispecific antibodies, complex molecules that can be directed at multiple points on a targeted protein or cell, or hit multiple targets.
The precise diseases Anthropic is addressing and its progress remain unclear. Once a molecule is identified, it can take years to bring a drug to market as it is tested in human trials, a challenge that Anthropic has not taken on. Isomorphic Labs, the drug discovery arm of rival Alphabet, has worked for years to get to the clinic and earlier delayed that goal to the end of 2026.
In its efforts at lab and other industry automation, Anthropic launched the Model Hardware Standard in August, which helps AI operate equipment. A release out of academia called PyLabRobot, unrelated to Anthropic, earlier addressed related though different automation needs.
Anthropic is providing work like the Model Hardware Standard and broader AI services and tools to all manner of top pharmaceutical companies, such as Roche’s Genentech, Bristol Myers Squibb and Novo Nordisk.
At the same time, Anthropic is navigating a trust problem, the two people familiar with its efforts said. Its customers may worry that Anthropic will learn from their competing drug programmes, even as the AI start-up walls off their data from view.
Kauderer-Abrams said that Anthropic, due partly to competition concerns, has set a boundary that it is not running clinical trials for now and is focusing on needs that industry would not address.
“We’re not competing with pharma and biotech companies that make their business in bringing drugs to market,” he said. REUTERS

Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, a GOP House hardliner and proponent of limited government, said during a Friday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that he feels Congress has an oversight role to play when it comes to artificial intelligence.
But that doesn't necessarily means he thinks the legislature should demand regulation of the technology.
"I don't want to regulate anything," Roy said. "I'm a free market conservative. I'm a limited government conservative."
Instead, Roy said, he'd be in favor of AI CEOs testifying at congressional hearings and explaining what they're doing to address safety concerns.
"There's a perfect role in our federal form of government, our republican form of government, for Congress to have these guys come tell us what they're doing for something that's so pervasive," Roy said.
Roy, who will leave the House at the end of this year after falling short in his bid for Texas attorney general, is part of a growing group of lawmakers that has spoken out on AI in recent weeks, after a former Anthropic employee posted an alarming message about the existential threat of the rapidly evolving technology. In an essay published last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for additional AI regulation as part of a broader slowdown. Other leaders of major AI companies, including OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk, endorsed Amodei's sentiment.
At an event this week hosted by the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit that advocates against large-scale technological risks, Roy joined an unlikely group of his colleagues on stage, including progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, and former White House strategist Steve Bannon.
While there is bipartisan concern at the pace with which AI is developing, there's little consensus on how the federal government should respond. The House left Washington on Wednesday without having taken any major action to address AI safety. The Senate will remain in session for another two weeks, before its members head back to their districts for a pre-election recess.
President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., have both argued the U.S. could lose the AI race to China if it slows its development. Trump went further, calling potential AI threats a "hoax" and opposing regulation. Meanwhile, progressives like Sanders have argued for stricter guardrails and a ban on AI "superintelligence."
Roy, at the Future of Life Institute conference, pushed back on an assertion from Trump that the president should be the lone person making decisions on AI. But he also diverged with his Democratic colleagues and, in his Friday appearance on CNBC, said he wasn't an AI "doomer."
"We have a responsibility to protect our communities and our lives. I want competition and free enterprise to rule the day. I don't want crony capitalism, crony government interference," Roy said.

The world's 20 best airlines for 2026 have been announced – with only six in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

There were wins for Air France, Turkish Airlines and Vueling in individual categories, but Europe struggled to match the haul of awards picked up by carriers from Asia and the Middle East
European airlines have been largely pushed down the pecking order in this year’s World Airline Awards, with Asian and Middle Eastern carriers dominating the top 10.
Singapore Airlines took the overall title, followed by Qatar Airways and Cathay Pacific, while Turkish Airlines was the highest-ranked European carrier in fifth place.
Just six European airlines made the top 20, with Air France, Lufthansa, Iberia, Virgin Atlantic and Swiss International Air Lines joining Turkish Airlines.
The 2026 World Airline Awards were announced at a gala ceremony in London hosted by air transport rating organisation Skytrax.
Known as “the Oscars of the aviation industry”, the awards have been running since 1999 and, according to Skytrax’s CEO Edward Plaisted, “highlights the level of product and service excellence they are providing to customers”.
More than 300 airlines were assessed in the ranking and, although Europe’s operators didn’t blow the competition away in the main category, they did have a decent showing in others.
European airlines triumph in some categories – and fall down in others
Air France did particularly well, scooping awards for the world’s best first class, the world’s best first class lounge dining, and the world’s best first class comfort amenities, as well as being given the nod as the best airline in Western Europe.
Spanish-headquartered Vueling won the award for the best low-cost airline in Europe, a category which also saw the inclusion of Germany’s Eurowings, Spain’s Iberia Express and Volotea and Dutch Transavia.
Meanwhile, Turkish Airlines took a trio of awards, scooping gongs for the best airline in Europe, the world’s best business class catering and the best airline in Southern Europe.
“Being recognised as ‘Europe’s best airline’ for the 11th time and ranking first in two other categories is a great source of pride for us as the Turkish Airlines family,” Murat Şeker, Turkish Airlines chairman of the board, said.
In other categories, Iberia won the award for the best airline staff service in Europe, while LOT Polish Airlines received the award as the best airline in Central Europe.
All European airlines were absent from the world’s best cabin crew category, which was topped by Cathay Pacific Airways, and only Greece’s Aegean Airlines made the top 10 of the world’s best regional airlines category, coming in fourth place.
Qatar Airways loses its top spot
In the overall ranking, Qatar Airways, a nine-time winner of the world’s best airline title, dropped to second spot behind Singapore Airlines.
Nevertheless, the Doha-based operator did manage to scoop four top awards, including the world’s best business class airline – the 13th time the airline has received this accolade – and the best airline in the Middle East.
It also received the first-ever award for the World’s Best Onboard Wi-Fi. That category was introduced this year to recognise the importance of fast and free onboard connectivity for many modern travellers.
